Other variants include the Korn shell (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ksh</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pdksh</samp>) and the C shell (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">csh</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tcsh</samp>). To try one of these shells after installation, you need to start a terminal window and run the respective shell name in it; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exit</samp> returns to the last active shell:

```
user$ zsh
hostname% ls     # run commands in zsh
...
hostname% exit   # back to the previous shell
user$ 
```

A separate default shell is provided for each Linux user. This shell is executed when you open a terminal window or when you log into a text console. The default shell is stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> file. To set a different default shell, you must run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chsh</samp> command (change shell):

```
user$ chsh -s $(which zsh) 
```

A list of the shells that are installed in your distribution and thus usable is located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shells</samp>.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is considered relatively slow and takes up a lot of memory—not least because of its many functions—some distributions use a more efficient shell to run scripts instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. On Debian and Ubuntu, for example, the Debian Almquist shell (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dash</samp>) is used when a script is to be executed quite generally by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/sh</samp> and not explicitly by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/bash</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dash</samp> is almost but not entirely compatible with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. If you use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>-specific functions when programming, you must explicitly specify <samp class="listingcharacter">#!/bin/bash</samp> in the first line.

## 7.2    Configuration

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> works right out of the box in all Linux distributions. Changes to the configuration are only necessary if you want to implement additional functions, set environment variables different from the default, and so on. You can usually make such changes in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> file. This section explains which other configuration files exist and what file is taken into account when.

[Table 7.1](#07_002.html_t7.1) provides an overview of the most important global configuration files (first column) as well as user-specific configuration files in the respective home directory, together with information about which type of shell considers which configuration file. Note that this table is somewhat simplified and doesn’t include all distribution-specific features. For example, on Debian and Ubuntu, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> reads <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bash.bashrc</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bashrc</samp>. In the local directory, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.profile</samp> is also analyzed if neither <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bash_profile</samp> nor <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bash_login</samp> exist.

| Global | Local | Login Shell | Interactive Shell | Script |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/profile</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bash_profile</samp> | • | • |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bashrc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> | ⸰ | ⸰ |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/inputrc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.inputrc</samp> | ⸰ | ⸰ |  |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bash_login</samp> | • |  |  |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bash_logout</samp> | • |  |  |

**Table 7.1**     Different bash Configuration Files Considered Depending on Type of Shell and on Linux Distribution

Consider a brief overview of the meaning of the files:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">profile</samp> files are used to set environment variables. They contain information that is analyzed by the shell and by various programs (see [Section 7.7.1](#07_007.html_h7.7.1)). Environment variables can also be set in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/environment</samp>. However, this file applies system-wide to all processes and not only to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> or other shells.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bashrc</samp> files are used to configure <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> functions intended for interactive use (not scripts). Custom changes to the configuration are almost always stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp>. So if you want to define your own shortcuts (aliases), extend the path (<samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp>) to all executable programs, or modify properties of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> is the right place.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">inputrc</samp> files only concern the configuration of the keyboard and apply to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">readline</samp> library, which is used internally in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> to process keyboard input. There is rarely a reason to touch the configuration predetermined by the distribution. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bashrc</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">inputrc</samp> files are not read by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> by default. However, most Linux distributions are configured to take these files into account after all.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">login</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">logout</samp> files are only considered by login shells (discussed ahead) and are executed when you log in or out.

[Table 7.1](#07_002.html_t7.1) takes into account three types of use: login shells, interactive shells, and scripts. The easiest to understand is a script: Here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is used as an interpreter to execute program code. No configuration files are loaded in the process. However, when the script is started interactively in a terminal window, the already existing settings still apply.

The difference between a login shell and an interactive shell is a bit more difficult—not least because both types of shells are interactive and therefore the names are not very conclusive:

*   A login shell exists when you log in to a text console or when you work via SSH on an external computer. This means that the shell is started immediately after authentication and then (interactively) accepts and processes your commands.

*   On the other hand, we speak of an interactive shell if the login has already happened earlier and the shell is started later—if required. This is always true if you first log into a desktop system and then open a terminal window. There again a shell is started, which waits for your commands.

In the shell, the name of the computer, the user, and/or the current directory is displayed at the beginning of each input line, depending on the distribution. This string is referred to as a prompt. At its minimum, the prompt consists of only one character: <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> for ordinary users. Depending on the configuration, the prompt can also display the name of the computer, the name of the logged-in user, the current directory, and so on—and all this possibly in different colors.

The content of the prompt is defined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp> environment variable—on a system-wide basis often in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bash.bashrc</samp> file, or on Red Hat/Fedora in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bashrc</samp>. To set the <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp> variable individually, you need to modify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> file. Background information on handling environment variables is covered in [Section 7.7.1](#07_007.html_h7.7.1). The following line causes only the current directory to be displayed as the prompt:

```
# Change in ~/.bashrc
PS1="\w \$ " 
```

Within <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">\u</samp> is a placeholder for the user name, <samp class="listingcharacter">\h</samp> for the host name, <samp class="listingcharacter">\w</samp> for the entire current directory, <samp class="listingcharacter">\W</samp> for the last part of the current directory, and <samp class="listingcharacter">\$</samp> for the prompt ending (<samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>).

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">\[\e[0;nnm\]</samp> to embed the formatting code <samp class="listingcharacter">nn</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp>. A comprehensive prompt configuration guide including a listing of all ANSI color codes can be found in the how-to document located at [https://tldp.org/HOWTO/Bash-Prompt-HOWTO](https://tldp.org/HOWTO/Bash-Prompt-HOWTO).

On my computers, I use the following setting:

```
PS1='\[\e[0;34m\]\u@\h:\W\$\[\e[0;39m\] ' 
```

This will display a blue prompt in the following format: <samp class="listingcharacter">username@computername:directory</samp>. However, the prompt does not show the entire path, but only the last part—such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nautilus</samp>, for example, if the current directory is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib/nautilus</samp>. This saves space if you are in a multipart directory. In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp>, you can also set the <samp class="listingcharacter">PROMPT_COMMAND</samp> variable. This variable contains a command that is executed each time before <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp> gets displayed.

### More Color in Life

Colors don't play too big a role in the terminal. Relatively few commands use colors to highlight important information. A whole collection of tips on how to coax some important commands to be more colorful can be found on the following website: [https://www.baeldung.com/linux/terminal-shell-colors](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/terminal-shell-colors).

## 7.3    Command Input

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> supports you with a lot of keyboard shortcuts for entering commands. In particular, you can use the (↑) and (↓) cursor keys to reedit the most recent commands you entered, which saves a lot of typing work. When you log out of a shell, the most recently entered commands are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">~/.bash_history</samp> file and are thus available again after the next login.

Command lines can be modified as in a text editor; that is, you can navigate within the entered line using the cursor keys and make corrections. By default, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> keyboard mapping adopts the most important keyboard shortcuts of the Emacs editor: (Ctrl)+(A) moves the cursor to the beginning of the line, (Ctrl)+(E) to the end, and so on. Vi fans can alternatively activate a Vi mode using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set -o vi</samp> statement in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp>.

Note that as a text-only command, the shell does not provide any mouse support. In particular, you cannot change the cursor position by mouse click. However, you can select text using the mouse and paste it at the current cursor position using the middle mouse button. For a Linux fan whose mouse or trackpad doesn’t have a middle button, many terminals also provide corresponding keyboard shortcuts—usually (Shift)+(Ctrl)+(C) and (Shift)+(Ctrl)+(V).

### 7.3.1    Expanding Command and File Names

By automatically expanding command and file names, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> helps you to minimize the amount of typing work required. For this purpose, you must first enter the first letters of the command or file name and then press (Tab). If the name is already clearly identifiable, it will be completed in full. If there are multiple names that start with the same letters, the name will be expanded only as far as the names match. In addition, in this case you will hear a beep indicating that the file name may not be complete yet.

The easiest way to understand the file name expansion is to use an example. On my computer, the input

<samp class="listingcharacter">user$</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">ema</samp> (Tab) <samp class="listingcharacter">ba</samp> (Tab)

in the directory with the files for this book is automatically expanded to

<samp class="listingcharacter">user$</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">emacs bash.tex</samp>.

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">emacs</samp> is the name of my favorite editor and <samp class="listingcharacter">bash.tex</samp> is the name of the LaTeX file of this chapter. To complete <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ema</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> searches all directories specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> variable for executable programs. To complete the file name, on the other hand, only the current directory is taken into account.

The expansion also works for file names that are prefixed with multiple directories. When you enter

<samp class="listingcharacter">user$</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">ls /usr/sh</samp> (Tab),

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> expands this input to

<samp class="listingcharacter">user$</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">ls /usr/share/</samp>.

If a unique expansion isn’t possible (signaled by a beep), you can simply press (Tab) again. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> will then display all possible additions in the lines below the current input line. On my computer, the input

<samp class="listingcharacter">user$</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp> (Tab) (Tab)

results in the output of an almost endless list of all commands and programs that start with the letter <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp>. The input can then be continued.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> provides similar expansion functions also for the names of home directories and for variable names: <samp class="listingcharacter">~ko</samp> (Tab) returns <samp class="listingcharacter">~kofler/</samp> on my machine, for example, and when I enter <samp class="listingcharacter">$PAT</samp> (Tab), I get <samp class="listingcharacter">$PATH</samp>.

The automatic command expansion conceals where a program is actually located. There are several ways to find that out:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">whereis</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> searches all default directories.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> searches all directories contained in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> and determines the program that would be executed if the command were entered without a path. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> is interesting if there are several versions of a program located in different directories.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">type name</samp> works similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp>, but also takes into account commands that are built into <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> or defined as aliases.

When you run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">latex</samp> command, only files ending with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> can be considered as possible parameters. With <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">latex</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">na</samp> (Tab), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> should therefore only consider the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in the current directory. If you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man na</samp> (Tab), on the other hand, only expansions for which <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> help texts exist are relevant. Similarly, there are numerous other commands and programs where the selection of possible files or parameters is limited from the outset.

When you search for suitable completions, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">complete</samp> command can help you. Many distributions are equipped with an extensive <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">complete</samp> configuration, which sometimes has to be installed separately (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash-completion</samp> package). The configuration is usually done by one of the following files:

```
/etc/bash_completion
/etc/bash_completion.d/*
/etc/profile.d/complete.bash
/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash-complete</samp> usually works on the first try. If you also want to define your own expansion rules, you will have to familiarize yourself with the rather confusing syntax of <samp class="listingcharacter">complete</samp>. A concise description is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">help complete</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man bash</samp> (search for “Programmable Completion”).

### 7.3.2    Important Keyboard Shortcuts

[Table 7.2](#07_003.html_t7.2) summarizes the most important keyboard shortcuts of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. The table assumes that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is configured for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">emacs</samp> mode, as is the case with almost all distributions. The <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> keyboard shortcuts are predefined by the aforementioned <samp class="listingcharacter">readline</samp> library, which <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> uses to process input. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">readline</samp> provides even more abbreviations.

| Shortcut | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| (↑), (↓) | Scrolls through the most recently entered commands |
| (í), (î) | Moves the cursor backward or forward |
| (Ctrl)+(A), (Ctrl)+(E) | Moves the cursor to the beginning or to the end of the line |
| (Alt)+(B), (Alt)+(F) | Moves the cursor backward or forward by one word |
| (Alt)+(D) | Deletes a word |
| (Ctrl)+(K) | Deletes everything to the end of the line |
| (Ctrl)+(Y) | Reinserts the most recently deleted text again |
| (Ctrl)+(T) | Swaps the two preceding characters |
| (Alt)+(T) | Swaps the two preceding words |
| (Tab) | Expands the command or file name |
| (Ctrl)+(L) | Clears the screen |
| (Ctrl)+(R) | Searches for previously entered commands |
| (Alt)+(.) | Inserts the most recently used parameter |
| (Ctrl)+(_) | Undoes the last change |

**Table 7.2**     Most Important bash Shortcuts

The function of the (Alt)+(.) shortcut can be understood only by means of an example. Let’s suppose you have just copied a file (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp name1 name2</samp>). Now you want to delete the copy in the next command. Instead of “rm name2”, type “rm” and then press (Alt)+(.). <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> then automatically inserts the last command parameter used. By pressing (Alt)+(.) multiple times, you can also access all other parameters; for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name1</samp> can be accessed by pressing the shortcut twice.

The (Ctrl)+(R) shortcut also requires a more detailed explanation. This shortcut enables you to search for commands that have already been entered: press (Ctrl)+(R) at the start of a line and then type the first characters of the command line you are looking for. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> then automatically displays the most recently used command with these initial letters.

By pressing (Ctrl)+(R) several times, you can toggle between different suitable options. (Ctrl)+(S) works like (Ctrl)+(R), but it runs through the list of matching commands in the opposite direction. (Enter), (Tab), and the cursor keys cancel the search and execute the command that has been found or allow you to edit the command line found.

Many consoles consider (Ctrl)+(S) a statement to temporarily stop the output. (This keyboard shortcut often causes confusion. It looks like the execution of the command has ended.) The output does not resume until you press (Ctrl)+(Q).

If your console responds to (Ctrl)+(S) in this way, you must first suppress the so-called flow control by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">stty -ixon</samp> command before you can use (Ctrl)+(S) as a search function.

### 7.3.3    Alias Abbreviations

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> command can save you some typing when you enter commands in the shell. This command is used to define abbreviations. When processing the command line, it checks if the first word contains an abbreviation. If so, the abbreviation is replaced with the full text.

Abbreviations for a certain combination of options or for file names are not possible because <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> does not search the other parameters of a command for abbreviations. However, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> recognizes special cases where multiple programs are named on a command line (pipes, command substitution, sequential execution of commands with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">;</samp>) and searches all occurring command names for abbreviations.

The following command defines the abbreviation <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cdb</samp>, which allows me to quickly change to the directory I often need, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/kofler/linuxbook</samp>:

```
user$ alias cdb='cd ~kofler/linuxbook' 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> calls can also be nested. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> abbreviations take precedence over commands with the same name. This fact can be used to avoid the unwanted invocation of a command:

```
user$ alias more=less 
```

From now on, any attempt to call the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">more</samp> command will result in the start of the more powerful <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> program. If for some reason you still need <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">more</samp>, you must specify the entire pathname (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/more</samp>) or prefix it with a backslash (<samp class="listingcharacter">\more</samp>). The backslash prevents the alias analysis in this case.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> abbreviations can be deleted again using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unalias</samp>. Otherwise, they will remain valid until you leave the shell (i.e., until you log out at the latest). If you need certain shortcuts repeatedly, you should include the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> statements in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bashrc</samp> file (applies to all users) or the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> file in your home directory (applies only to that user).

Many distributions have various predefined <samp class="listingcharacter">alias</samp> abbreviations. For example, if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> keeps asking if you really want to delete the file, this is usually caused by a predefined alias, <samp class="listingcharacter">rm=rm -i</samp>.

A list of all currently valid abbreviations is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> command. The following lines indicate where Debian, Fedora, SUSE, and Ubuntu consider <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> definitions:

```
/etc/bashrc
/etc/profile.d/*.sh
.bashrc
.alias  (SUSE only) 
```

Custom shell scripts that are stored in a directory contained in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> can have a similar effect to abbreviations. A script has the advantage over an alias in that it can process parameters.

## 7.4    Input and Output Redirection

When you run commands in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, there are three standard files. The term file can cause a little confusion here. These are not actually real files, but file descriptors that are treated like files at the operating system level:

*   Standard input
    The currently executing program, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> or any command started from there, reads all input from standard input. If you work interactively in a terminal window, then the keyboard is considered the default input source.

*   Standard output
    The entire output of the program is directed here—for example, the listing of all files via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>. Usually, the terminal window is the standard output.

*   Standard errors Error messages are also usually displayed in the current terminal.

In itself, all this is self-evident: Where else but from the keyboard should the inputs come? Where else but on the screen should results or errors be displayed? However, the ability to redirect the standard input or output is noteworthy. For example, the case may arise that the table of contents of the current directory is not to be displayed on the screen, but saved in a file. This means the standard output is supposed to be redirected to a real file. This can be done in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> by using the <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> character:

```
user$ ls *.tex > content 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">content</samp> text file now contains a list of all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in the current directory. This type of output redirection is certainly the most common method. However, there are many other variants (see also [Table 7.3](#07_004.html_t7.3)):

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">2> file</samp> redirects all error messages to the specified file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">>& file</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">&> file</samp> directs both the standard output and all error messages to the specified file.

*   If instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> the duplicate <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> is used, then the respective outputs will be appended to the end of an already existing file.

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command > file</samp> | Directs standard outputs to the specified file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command < file</samp> | Reads input from the specified file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command 2> file</samp> | Redirects error messages to the specified file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command >& file</samp> | Redirects outputs and errors |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command &> file</samp> | Also redirects outputs and errors |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command >> file</samp> | Appends standard output to the existing file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command &>> file</samp> | Appends output and errors to the file (as of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> 4.0) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command1 &#124; command2</samp> | Forwards output from command 1 to command 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command &#124; tee file</samp> | Displays the outputs and saves a copy at the same time |

**Table 7.3**     Input and Output Redirection

You can perform an input redirection by using <samp class="listingcharacter">< file</samp>. Commands that expect input from the keyboard then read it from the specified file.

### Warning

It is not possible to edit a file and write the result back to this file at the same time! <samp class="listingcharacter">sort file</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">> file</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">sort < file > file</samp> causes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">file</samp> to be deleted!

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sponge</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">moreutils</samp> tool collection, which can be installed as a package in many distributions, provides a solution here. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">moreutils</samp> contains various commands that are useful both for the interactive use of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> and for script programming. An amazing number of commands have to do with input and output redirection in various shapes, just like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sponge</samp>.

Pipes are formed using the <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character. The output of the first command is used as input for the second command. In practice, you will often form pipes together with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> command when you want to view longer outputs page by page.

The following command determines the table of contents of the current directory and writes it to a pipe. From there, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> command executed in parallel reads its input and displays it on the screen:

```
user$ ls -l | less 
```

Pipes are also excellent for combining different commands. Thus, the following command returns a sorted list of all installed RPM packages:

```
user$ rpm -qa | sort 
```

Instead of pipes, so-called FIFO files can also be used for input and output redirection. FIFO stands for first in, first out and implements the idea of a pipe as a file. The input of FIFO files is much more complicated than that of pipes, but they make it clear what the <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character actually does. In practice, they are used so that two independent programs can communicate with each other.

The following three commands first set up a FIFO file, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> is started as a background process, which writes its outputs to the file. From there, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> reads the data again and displays it on the screen:

```
user$ mkfifo fifo
user$ ls -l > fifo &
user$ less < fifo 
```

Only commands that read the commands to be processed from the default input channel are suitable for formulating a pipe. If this is not the case, you can achieve similar effects by a command substitution or by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> command. These and other substitution mechanisms are described in [Section 7.6](#07_006.html_h7.6).

### 7.4.1    Output Multiplication Using tee

It sometimes happens that the output of a program should be saved in a file, but you still want to follow the progress of the program on the screen. In this case, a duplication of the output is required, whereby one copy is displayed on the screen and the second copy is saved in a file. This task is performed by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tee</samp> command:

```
user$ ls | tee filelist 
```

The table of contents of the current directory is thus displayed on the screen and simultaneously stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filelist</samp> file. The standard output is first forwarded to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tee</samp> command. By default, this command displays the standard output in the terminal and saves the copy of it in the specified file. You will notice that this is really a multiplication of the output when you also forward the standard output of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tee</samp> to a file:

```
user$ ls | tee filelist1 > filelist2 
```

The result consists of two identical files, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filelist1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filelist2</samp>. The preceding command is purely exemplary. Somewhat more difficult to understand, but more meaningful, is the following example:

```
user$ ls -l | tee filelist1 | sort -k 5 -n > filelist2 
```

In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filelist1</samp>, there is again the “normal” table of contents, which was automatically sorted by file names by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>. The copy of this output was passed to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sort</samp>, sorted there by file size (fifth column), and stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filelist2</samp>.

## 7.5    Executing Commands

Usually you start commands simply by entering the command name. In addition to that, there are some options to execute multiple commands in a row (see [Table 7.4](#07_005.html_t7.4)).

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd1; cmd2</samp> | Executes the commands one after the other |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd1 && cmd2</samp> | Executes command 2 if command 1 was successful |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd1 &#124;&#124; cmd2</samp> | Executes command 2 if command 1 returns an error |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd &</samp> | Starts the command in the background |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd1 & cmd2</samp> | Starts command 1 in the background, command 2 in the foreground |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(cmd1 ; cmd2)</samp> | Executes both commands in the same shell |

**Table 7.4**     Executing Commands

### Scripts in the Home Directory

Scripts or programs stored in the currently active directory cannot be executed easily for security reasons. Rather, you must prefix the script name with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">./</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">./myscript</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.</samp> is an abbreviation for the current directory.

The most important and most frequently used special character is <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>. When entered at the end of the command line, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> starts this program in the background. This is especially useful for time-consuming programs, because work can be continued immediately:

```
user$ find / -name '*sh' > result &
[1] 3345 
```

The preceding command searches the entire file system for files ending with the letters sh. The list of files will be written to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">result</samp> file. Because the command is executed in the background, you can continue working immediately. The output <samp class="listingcharacter">[1] 3345</samp> means that the background process has the process identification (PID) number 3345\. The PID number is of interest if the process is to be terminated prematurely via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp>. The number in square brackets indicates the number of the background process started in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> and is usually not of interest.

If you forget the <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> character when starting a command, you do not need to wait, nor do you need to forcibly stop the program via (Ctrl)+(C). Rather, you should interrupt the program using (Ctrl)+(Z) and continue it as a background process via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bg</samp>.

After the <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> character, you can also enter another command. In this case, the first command will be executed in the background, while the second one gets executed in the foreground. In the following example, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> command is started again in the background. At the same time, however, the current table of contents is output via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>:

```
user$ find / -name '*sh' > result & ls 
```

If you specify a semicolon instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> character, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> executes the commands one after the other and in the foreground:

```
user$ ls; date 
```

The preceding command first displays the current table of contents and then outputs the current date. If all this information is to be redirected to a file via <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, you need to put both commands in parentheses. This means that both commands are executed by a single shell:

```
user$ (ls; date) > content 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">content</samp> file now contains the file list created by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> and the current date determined via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">date</samp>. The parentheses cause the two commands to be executed within a new shell (a subshell) and therefore also provide a common result.

You can use the character combinations <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> to execute commands conditionally—that is, in dependence on the result of another command:

```
user$ command1 && command2 
```

The preceding command executes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">command 1</samp>. Only if this command was successful (no error; return value 0) will <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">command 2</samp> be executed afterward. A typical example (that applies to Debian and Ubuntu) is first updating the package sources and then performing an update without prompting:

```
root# apt update && apt full-upgrade -y 
```

In practice, the OR combination of two commands is less common:

```
user$ command1 || command2 
```

This executes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">command 1</samp>. Only if an error occurs during the execution of this command (return value unequal 0) will <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">command 2</samp> be executed afterward as well.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">if</samp> command provides further options for creating conditions and branches, although this is only of interest for shell programming.

## 7.6    Globbing and Substitution/Expansion

This section deals with various mechanisms used by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> to process an expression composed of special characters into a new result. Consider the following examples:

*   Globbing If you type “cmd *.txt”, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> searches all files corresponding to this pattern, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">readme.txt</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">copyright.txt</samp>, for example. What actually is executed then is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cmd readme.txt copyright.txt</samp>. This means that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> replaced the search pattern with actual matching file names. This process is referred to as globbing.

*   Substitution/expansion Say that there is a variable named <samp class="listingcharacter">$name</samp> that contains the string “Peter”. If you now execute <samp class="listingcharacter">echo "Hello, $name!"</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> replaces the variable with its contents and prints “Hello, Peter!”. In addition to this simple parameter substitution, various other mechanisms exist. Depending on which documentation you consult, this mechanism is referred to as substitution or expansion. In this book, I stick with substitution.

In the following sections, I present the most important globbing and substitution mechanisms. This involves the use of various special characters (see [Table 7.5](#07_006.html_t7.5)). I discuss the parameter substitution mentioned earlier in more detail in [Section 7.10](#07_010.html_h7.10).

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp> | Exactly one character |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> | Any number (also zero) of arbitrary characters (but no .* files!) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">**</samp> | All files and directories, also from all subdirectories (from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> 4.0 with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shopt -s globstar</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[abc]</samp> | One of the specified characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a-f]</samp> | A character from the specified range |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[!abc]</samp> | None of the specified characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[^abc]</samp> | As above |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> | Abbreviation for the home directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> | Current directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">..</samp> | Parent directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ab{1,2,3}</samp> | Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">ab1 ab2 ab3</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a{1..4}</samp> | Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">a1 a2 a3 a4</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$varname</samp> | Returns the content of the variable |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$((3*4))</samp> | Arithmetic calculations; returns 12 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">`command`</samp> | Replaces the command with its result |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$(command)</samp> | As above; alternative style |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command "character"</samp> | Prevents the analysis of all special characters except <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command 'character'</samp> | As above, but even more restrictive (no variable substitution) |

**Table 7.5**     Special Characters for Globbing and Substitution in bash

If you type “rm *.bak” and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> command actually deletes all files ending with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bak</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is responsible for that. The shell searches the current directory for matching files and replaces <samp class="listingcharacter">*.bak</samp> with the corresponding file names.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp> (exactly one arbitrary character) and <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> (any number, including zero, of arbitrary characters) wildcard characters are permitted. The <samp class="listingcharacter">[abe-h]*</samp> string represents file names that start with one of the <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">g</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">h</samp> characters. If <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> is specified as the first character inside the square brackets, then all characters except the specified characters are allowed. <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> can be used as an abbreviation for the home directory.

You can easily test the function of special characters using the following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp> command. The first command returns all files and directories in the root directory. The second command restricts the output to files and directories starting with the letters <samp class="listingcharacter">a-f</samp>:

```
user$ echo /*
/bin /boot /dev /etc /home /lib /lib64 /lost+found /mnt /opt /proc
/root /run /sbin /srv /sys /tmp /usr /var

user$ echo /[a-f]*
/bin /boot /dev /etc 
```

Because the formation of the file names is not done by the respective program but by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, the results sometimes look different than you would probably expect. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls *</samp> can result in an almost endless list of files, even if there are only a few files in the current directory. After expansion with <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, a list of all files and directories is passed to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>, in turn, displays not simply the names of directories, but the entire contents of these directories. If you just want to have a simple list of all files and directories, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp> option, which prevents displaying the contents of the directories that are in the parameter line.

If you want feedback on how <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> works internally, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">-x</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> then displays the way the command line is parsed (with any preset options and with the file names expanded) before executing any further command.

By default, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*</samp> does not take files or directories into account that start with a dot (i.e., those that are “hidden”). If you want to capture those as well, you need to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shopt</samp> to set the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dotglob</samp> option in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>:

```
user$ shopt -s dotglob
user$ echo *
...
user$ shopt -u dotglob   # deactivate dotglob again 
```

If you want to enable <samp class="listingcharacter">dotglob</samp> permanently, you must add the <samp class="listingcharacter">shopt</samp> line to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">**</samp> character combination recursively covers all (sub)directories. To maintain compatibility with older <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> versions and to protect against erroneous use of this character combination (there are often tens of thousands of subdirectories and files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/</samp> ), this new feature, already introduced in version 4, is not active by default. If you want to use it (e.g., in a script), you have to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shopt -s</samp> to set the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">globstar</samp> option in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>:

```
user$ shopt -s globstar
user$ echo **
... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">**</samp> provides a very simple way to recursively find or process (copy, delete, etc.) all files of a certain type. The following command determines the number of PDF files in the current directory and all subdirectories:

```
user$ ls **/*.pdf 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> assembles all conceivable character string combinations from character strings that are specified in curly brackets. The official name for this substitution mechanism is brace expansion. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">part{1,2a,2b}</samp> becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">part1 part2a part2b</samp>. Brace expansions can reduce the typing effort when accessing multiple similar file names or directories. Compared to wildcard characters like <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp>, they have the advantage that file names that do not yet exist can also be formed (e.g., for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkdir</samp>):

```
user$ echo {a,b}{1,2,3}
a1 a2 a3 b1 b2 b3

user$ echo {ab,cd}{123,456,789}-{I,II}
ab123-I ab123-II ab456-I ab456-II ab789-I ab789-II 
cd123-I cd123-II cd456-I cd456-II cd789-I cd789-II 
```

You can formulate enumerations elegantly in the notation <samp class="listingcharacter">{a..b}</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> may optionally be numbers or letters. The following examples explain how this works better than any description:

```
user$ echo {1..5}
1 2 3 4 5

user$ echo {z..t}
z y x w v u t 
```

Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is not able to perform calculations. If you enter <samp class="listingcharacter">2+3</samp>, the shell does not know what to do with this expression. If you want to perform a calculation within the shell, you need to enclose the expression in double parentheses and prefix it with a <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character:

```
user$ echo $((2+3))
5 
```

Inside the parentheses, most operators known from the C programming language are allowed: <samp class="listingcharacter">+ - * /</samp> for the four basic arithmetic operations, <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> for modulo calculations, <samp class="listingcharacter">== != < <= ></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> for comparisons, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> for bit shifts, <samp class="listingcharacter">!&&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> for logical NOT, AND, and OR, and so on. All calculations are performed for 32-bit integers (number range between +/-2147483648). If individual values are to be taken from variables, they must be preceded by a <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character.

An obsolete but still acceptable notation for arithmetic expressions is <samp class="listingcharacter">$[expression]</samp>. An alternative way to perform calculations is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">expr</samp> command. This is a unique Linux command that works independently of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>.

### 7.6.1    Command Substitution

Command substitution allows you to replace a command within the command line with its result. To do this, this command must be enclosed between two <samp class="listingcharacter">`</samp> characters. An alternative notation is <samp class="listingcharacter">$(command)</samp>. This latter notation is preferable, first because it reduces the confusion of using three different marks (<samp class="listingcharacter">"</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">'</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">`</samp>), and second because it can be nested.

Thus, the command marked in this way is replaced by its result. This substitution allows for the nested call of multiple commands, where one command passes its result to the other command. The following two equivalent commands illustrate this very powerful mechanism:

```
user$ ls -l `find /usr/share -name '*README*'`
user$ ls -l $(find /usr/share -name '*README*') 
```

This command first executes <samp class="listingcharacter">find /usr/share -name '*README*'</samp>. The result of this command is a list of all files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share</samp> directory that contain the string “README”. This list is then inserted into the command line instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> command. The command line then reads, for example:

```
user$ ls -l ...  \
    > usr/share/doc/secureboot-db/README.Debian \
    > /usr/share/doc/sed/README ... 
```

This command leads to the following result:

```
...
-rw-r--r-- 1    995 Dez  4  /usr/share/doc/secureboot-db/README.Debian
-rw-r--r-- 1    731 Jan 17  /usr/share/doc/sed/README
... 
```

This result would not be possible by using a simple pipe with the <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> does not expect any input via standard input and therefore also ignores the information that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> provides via the pipe. The following command therefore simply displays the contents of the current directory; the results of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> are not displayed:

```
user$ find /usr/share -name '*README*' | ls -l  # does not work! 
```

However, there is another solution that does not require command substitution. By using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> command, data from standard input will be passed to the command you specify after <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp>:

```
user$ find /usr/share -name '*README*' | xargs ls -l 
```

A major advantage of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> is that there is no size limit for the data to be processed. If necessary, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> calls the command multiple times and passes the data coming from the standard input in several steps. Command substitution, on the other hand, is limited by the maximum size of a command line—usually several thousand characters. Sharing file names causes problems if the file names contain spaces. You can work around these problems by passing the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-print0</samp> option to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--null</samp> option to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp>. The following command sets the execute bit for all directories:

```
user$ find -type d -print0 | xargs --null chmod a+x 
```

I have used <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> in the preceding examples as a starting point to show variations on how to process the result. In fact, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> can do this itself. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find ... ‐ls</samp> lists the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> results in detailed notation, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find ... -exec ...</samp> applies another command to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> results, etc. More information about <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> follows in [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.3.3](#09_003.html_h9.3.3).

What is true for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp>, however, is not true for the majority of the other commands you usually deal with. And then you have to rely on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> or the substitution mechanisms of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>.

### 7.6.2    Single versus Double Quotation Marks

Because virtually every character in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> except letters and numbers has some special meaning, it seems almost impossible to use these characters in strings or file names. This problem can be solved in two ways: either the special character is preceded by a backslash <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp>, or the entire string is enclosed in apostrophes or quotation marks. Thus, by specifying apostrophes, you can, for example, delete a file with the file name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ab* $cd</samp>:

```
user$ rm 'ab* $cd' 
```

Note the difference between straight apostrophes (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">'</samp>) to indicate strings and the accented character falling to the right (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">`</samp>, for command substitution!).

Quotation marks have a similar effect to apostrophes. However, they are less restrictive and allow the interpretation of some special characters like <samp class="listingcharacter">$ \</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">`</samp>. For this reason, in character strings that are enclosed in quotation marks, variables with a preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character are parsed:

```
user$ echo "This is the access path: $PATH".
This is the access path: /home/kofler/.local/bin:/home/kofler/bin:... 
```

If single apostrophes are used instead of quotation marks, the entire string is output unchanged by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp>.

## 7.7    Variables

The functionality of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> and that of many other Linux programs is controlled by the state of variables. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> variables can only store strings. The assignment of variables is done by the assignment operator <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>. The easiest way to display the contents of a variable is to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp>, prefixing the variable name with a <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character:

```
user$ var='abc'
user$ echo $var
abc 
```

Strange rules apply to the handling of variables in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. For reading variables, the name must be preceded by a dollar character. However, this does not apply to assignments. The preceding listing is therefore correct!

Also note that you do not specify a space between the variable name and the <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> operator when making assignments. <samp class="listingcharacter">var = abc</samp> is syntactically incorrect and will not work!

Simple strings without special characters and spaces may also be formulated without apostrophes. The statements <samp class="listingcharacter">a=3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">a="3"</samp> are therefore equivalent.

If you want to read the content of a variable in a string, you normally use the already mentioned substitution, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">b="a is $a"</samp>. Only if the variable names cannot be separated from the rest of the text do you have to use the somewhat more complicated <samp class="listingcharacter">${varname}</samp> notation:

```
user$ a=3
user$ b="\${a}xxx\${a}"
user$ echo $b
3xxx3 
```

In the next example, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bin</samp> directory in the home directory is added to the predefined <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> environment variable. This allows for all scripts in this directory to be executed without an explicit path specification:

```
user$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
user$ PATH="$PATH:/home/kofler/bin"
user$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/home/kofler/bin 
```

Calculations with variables can be performed in the already presented notation with parentheses. The character strings contained in variables are evaluated as numbers. In addition, the dollar character may be omitted:

```
user$ a=3
user$ b=$((a*4))
user$ echo $b
12 
```

If the result of a command is to be stored in a variable, the command substitution with <samp class="listingcharacter">$(command)</samp>, which has already been described as well, must be performed. In the following example, the current directory is stored in <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>:

```
user$ a=$(pwd)
user$ echo $a
/home/kofler 
```

The contents of variables are stored within a shell session and are lost when the shell is exited. If certain variables are constantly needed again, the assignments should be made in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/profile</samp> file or in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.profile</samp> in the home directory. These two files (if present) are automatically executed when <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is started.

### 7.7.1    Environment Variables

Usually, variables are not passed on to newly started processes. So if you assign <samp class="listingcharacter">a=3</samp> and then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> or start a script, neither the command nor the script can read the variable. <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> is only usable within the local shell session.

There is one exception to this rule: Variables can be explicitly declared as environment variables. To do this, you need to call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">export varname</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">declare -x varname</samp>. Environment variables can then be analyzed by all commands or scripts started thereafter.

There are numerous commands for variable management within the shell, whereby there are functional overlaps. The following examples attempt to alleviate some of the confusion by using similar commands:

```
let a=3           # normal variable
declare a=3       # equivalent
a=3               # usual short notation, also equivalent
export a          # makes a the environment variable
export a=3        # combines the two previous statements
declare -x a=3    # equivalent to export a=3
set               # lists all variables
printenv          # lists only environment variables
export            # also lists environment variables
unset a           # deletes the variable 
```

### 7.7.2    Predefined Environment Variables

In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, some environment variables are predefined that have a special meaning. These variables are capitalized throughout. Be careful not to accidentally overwrite or incorrectly change any of these variables! The following list describes the most important variables in alphabetical order:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BASH</samp>
    Contains the path to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HOME</samp>
    Contains the path of the home directory—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/kofler</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">LOGNAME</samp> Contains the login name (user name).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HOSTNAME</samp> Contains the host name (computer name).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">OLDPWD</samp>
    Contains the path of the last active directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> Contains a list of directories separated by colons. When <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is supposed to execute a command, it searches all directories listed in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> for the desired command.

    <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> is set distribution-specifically at various points during the startup process. The best place to make changes that apply to all users of the computer is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/profile</samp>. If the changes only affect your own account, you should simply manipulate <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp>:

    <samp class="listingcharacter"># addition in /etc/profile or in .bashrc</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH=$PATH:/myown/bin</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">PROMPT_COMMAND</samp> Can contain a command that is executed each time before <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> displays the command prompt.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">PS1</samp> Contains a string whose content is displayed at the beginning of each input line (prompt). Within the string, the following character combinations are provided, among others: <samp class="listingcharacter">\t</samp> for the current time, <samp class="listingcharacter">\d</samp> for the date, <samp class="listingcharacter">\w</samp> for the current directory, <samp class="listingcharacter">\W</samp> for the last part of the current directory (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssl</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cups/ssl</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">\u</samp> for the user name, <samp class="listingcharacter">\h</samp> for the host name (computer name), and <samp class="listingcharacter">\$</samp> for the prompt character (<samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> for regular users, <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">PS2</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PS1</samp>, but the string is only displayed for multiline entries—that is, if the first line has been terminated using <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp>. A typical setting is <samp class="listingcharacter">">"</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">PWD</samp>
    Contains the path of the current directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">RANDOM</samp> Returns a new random number between 0 and 32767 at each readout.

In addition to the variables described here, numerous other environment variables are normally defined that control functions of the shell as well as various other programs. You can get a list of all defined variables via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">printenv | sort</samp>.

## 7.8    Bash Scripts

Scripts are text files that contain Linux and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> commands.

Scripts can contain branches, loops and functions. This means that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is a simple programming language. A typical application for scripts is the automation of frequently needed command sequences for installing programs, administrating the system, performing backups, configuring and running individual programs, and so on.

The following pages only provide an introduction to programming using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. A large amount of further information and examples can be found on the website [https://linuxconfig.org/bash-scripting-tutorial](https://linuxconfig.org/bash-scripting-tutorial) or in Scripting: Automation with Bash, PowerShell, and Python (2024), also published by Rheinwerk Publishing.

Many commands and functions in Linux are based on scripts. The following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find/grep</samp> command searches the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/</samp> directory for shell scripts. All files that are marked as executable and that contain the <samp class="listingcharacter">\#! ... sh</samp> string will be recognized:

```
user$ find /etc -type f -executable -exec \
  grep -q '#!.*sh' {} \; ‐print 
```

### 7.8.1    Example 1: grepall

Let’s suppose you frequently use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> commands to search the current directory and all subdirectories for files that contain a certain string and have changed in the last seven days. The correct command looks as follows:

```
user$ find . -type f -mtime -7 -exec grep -q 'suchtext' {}  \; ‐print 
```

If, like me, you puzzle over which combination of options is required each time, it makes sense to define the new <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall</samp> command, which takes over this task. To do this, start your favorite editor to write the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall</samp> text file. The file consists of only two lines, the first of which specifies the program name of the interpreter that will execute the script file:

```
#!/bin/bash
find . -type f -mtime 7 -exec grep -q $1 {}  \; -print 
```

The first line of the bash script is called shebang or hashbang and starts with the <samp class="listingcharacter">#!</samp> character combination. This is followed by the path to the interpreter that will execute the following code. For this and the following examples, this results in the line <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">#!/bin/bash</samp>.

Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/bash</samp>, you can also specify <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/sh</samp>. On many distributions, the script is then also executed by <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> because <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/sh</samp> is simply a link to <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp>. On Debian and Ubuntu, however, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/sh</samp> references the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dash</samp> shell interpreter. This program is optimized for higher speed, but is not fully compatible with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>.

The attempt to execute the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall</samp> file just created ends with an error message, permission denied. The reason for this message is that new files generally have the access bits (x) disabled to execute the file. But you can quickly change that using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall abc</samp> then returns the desired list of all files that contain the string “abc”:

```
user$ ./grepall abc
bash: ./grepall: Permission denied
user$ chmod a+x grepall
user$ ./grepall abc
./bashprg.tex 
```

To run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall</samp> command without specifying the directory where the code is stored each time, you must move the file to a directory contained in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">$PATH</samp>. In many distributions, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bin</samp> directory within the home directory is provided for this purpose:

```
user$ mv grepall ~/bin 
```

If the command is to be made available to all users of the computer, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/local/bin</samp> directory is a good choice:

```
user$ sudo mv grepall /usr/local/bin 
```

#### Creating Small Text Files without an Editor

If you want to avoid calling the editor, you can also create the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall</samp> file using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp>. First, enter the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat > grepall</samp> command. The command expects data from the standard input (keyboard) and writes it to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grepall</samp> file. Then enter the command with all its options. Finally, exit <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp> using (Ctrl)+(D) (this corresponds to end of file [EOF]). You can view the resulting file via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat grepall</samp>.

### 7.8.2    Example 2: stripcomments

The second example is also a one-liner. You pass a text file to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">stripcomments</samp> command. The three nested <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> commands now eliminate all lines that start with the <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> characters or are completely empty. Comments are also removed if there are space or tab characters before the <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> characters. The command is excellent for removing all comment lines from configuration files and displaying only the settings that are actually valid:

```
#!/bin/bash
grep -Ev '^[[:space:]]*#|^[[:space:]]*;|^$' $1 
```

Here’s why: The <samp class="listingcharacter">^[[:space:]]*#</samp> pattern finds lines starting with <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>, where there may be any number of spaces and tab characters between the start of the line (<samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp>) and <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>. Similarly, the <samp class="listingcharacter">^[[:space:]]*;</samp> expression captures all lines starting with <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>. The third pattern applies to empty lines consisting only of the beginning and end of line (<samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp>).

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-v</samp> option inverts the usual function of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp>: instead of extracting the lines found, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> returns all lines to which the pattern does not apply. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐E</samp> option enables the extended <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> syntax, which allows for combining multiple search expressions with the <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character.

### 7.8.3    Example 3: applysedfile

The previous two examples show how you can save yourself some typing and thinking, but they do not even indicate the far-reaching possibilities of script programming. The next example offers more in this respect.

Let’s suppose you are faced with the task of performing a series of similar find-and-replace runs in a whole bunch of files. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">applysedfile</samp> script program can help you with such tasks. The call of this script looks as follows:

```
user$ applysedfile *.tex 
```

This creates a backup copy <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.bak</samp> of all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files. Then the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> command is used to execute a whole list of commands for each <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> file. These commands must be located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">./sedfile</samp> file, which is automatically used by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">applysedfile</samp>. The code of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">applysedfile</samp> looks as follows:

```
#!/bin/bash
IFS=$'\n'
for fn in $*; do
  echo "process $fn"
  # first create backup file
  cp "$fn" "${fn%.*}.bak" 
  # then apply sed
  sed -f ./sedfile < "${fn%.*}.bak" > "$fn"
done 
```

The script starts with a strange assignment to the <samp class="listingcharacter">IFS</samp> variable. This internal field separator determines at which characters the bash separates words—by default, at tabs, spaces, and line breaks. However, if there is now a <samp class="listingcharacter">file with blank.tex</samp> file, the file name variable <samp class="listingcharacter">fn</samp> passes through <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">with</samp>, and finally <samp class="listingcharacter">blank.tex</samp> in order. The subsequent commands <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> then trigger errors because these files do not exist.

<samp class="listingcharacter">IFS=/samp>\n'</samp> causes word separation to occur only on a newline character. This is true for the file list passed with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp>. The preceding dollar character ensures that <samp class="listingcharacter">\n</samp> is parsed correctly and the script thus also processes files with spaces correctly. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">for</samp> initiates a loop. For each loop pass, a file name is inserted into the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fn</samp> variable. The list of file names comes from <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp>. This character combination is a placeholder for all parameters and file names passed to the program.

The loop body outputs the name of each file. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> creates a backup copy of the file. First, all characters starting from the first dot in the file name are deleted. Then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bak</samp> is appended.

Finally, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> command is executed for the file, using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sedfile</samp> control file from the local directory.

To correct typos that happen to me regularly, I have a file that starts as follows:

```
s,athome,at home,g
s,tohelp,to help,g
s,everytime,every time,g
s,without furtherado,without further ado,g
... 
```

This is a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> command for each line, which replaces the first string with the second one (command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">s</samp>). The trailing letter <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">g</samp> means that the command should also be executed multiple times within one line, if the error in question should occur several times within one line.

### 7.8.4    Example 4: Backup Script

The following script is automatically executed on my root server every week:

```
#!/bin/bash
m=$(date "+%m")
cd /var
tar czf - www | curl -T - --netrc-file pw.txt \
  ftp://1.2.3.4/www-$m.tgz
mysqldump -u cms -pxxxx cms | curl -T - --netrc-file pw.txt \
  ftp://1.2.3.4/cms-$m.sql 
```

First, the <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> variable is initialized, which contains the current month as a number. The date command returns the current date and time. The format string <samp class="listingcharacter">+%m</samp> extracts the month from it.
