Now <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> creates a backup of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www</samp> directory. The archive is not saved directly to a file, but redirected to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> command using <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> transfers the data to an FTP server (IP address 1.2.3.4), reading the login name and password from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pw.txt</samp> file. On the FTP server, the backup is stored under the name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">www-MM.tgz</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">MM</samp> indicates the month (<samp class="listingcharacter">01</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp>).

In this way, monthly backup versions are created over the course of a year, so that I can reconstruct an older state of my website if needed. At the same time, the space required for the backup files is small. At any given time, there is a maximum of 12 versions: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">www-01.tgz</samp> through <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">www-12.tgz</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">mysqldump</samp> command creates a backup of the MySQL database <samp class="listingcharacter">cms</samp>, where the content management system (CMS) of my website stores all pages and countless other data. Again, the backup is passed to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> and stored on my FTP server.

I saved the entire script as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/myscripts/backup</samp>. The daily call is taken care of by Cron (see [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10), [Section 10.6](#10_006.html_h10.6)). The matching configuration file <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d/backup</samp> looks like this:

```
# every Sunday at 3:15 am
15 3 * * 0 root /etc/myscripts/backup 
```

### 7.8.5    Example 5: Creating Thumbnails

Thumbnails are reduced versions of image files.

The following script is called via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">makethumbs *.jpg</samp>. It creates the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">400x400</samp> subdirectory where it stores reduced copies of the original images. The maximum size of the new images is 400 × 400 pixels, preserving the proportions of the original image. Images that are smaller remain unchanged, so they are not enlarged.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop analyzes <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp>. This character combination allows the evaluation of all parameters passed to the program. The script applies the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">magick</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">imagemagick</samp> package. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-resize</samp> option is responsible for the reduction. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-size</samp> only causes faster processing:

```
#!/bin/bash
IFS=$'\n'
if [ ! -d 400x400 ]; then     # create subdirectory
  mkdir 400x400
fi
for filename in $*;  do    # process all JPEG files
  echo "processing $filename"
  magick -size 400x400 -resize 400x400 "$filename" \
  "400x400/$filename"
done 
```

### 7.8.6    Example 6: Setting Up Student Accounts

I needed the following script when I wanted to set up an account for all students at the beginning of a Linux course. The starting point was the <samp class="listingcharacter">students.txt</samp> file, which contained the last names line by line:

```
huber
mueller
schmidt
... 
```

Now, I could have set up each student individually, either with a graphical user interface or by manually running <samp class="listingcharacter">useradd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">passwd</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">chage</samp>. Instead, I wrote the following miniscript:

```
#!/bin/bash
while read username; do 
  pw="$username-1234" 
  echo "Account: $username  Password: $pw" 
  useradd $username
  echo "$username:$pw" | chpasswd 
  chage -d 0 -E 2024-12-31 $username
done < students.txt 
```

The script runs through the names of all students in the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. The current name is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter">username</samp> variable. The <samp class="listingcharacter">pw</samp> variable contains the initial password, which consists of the name plus <samp class="listingcharacter">-1234</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">huber-1234</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">useradd</samp> sets up the account. <samp class="listingcharacter">echo</samp> prints the account name and password. Of course, this output is not displayed, but is redirected to the <samp class="listingcharacter">chpasswd</samp> command via <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">chage -d 0</samp> makes sure that every student has to change his or her password immediately after the first login. The <samp class="listingcharacter">-E 2024-12-31</samp> option has the effect that the accounts expire at the end of December 2024 and can then no longer be used. To delete the accounts together with the assigned <samp class="listingcharacter">/home</samp> directories later, there is another script:

```
#!/bin/bash
while read username; do
  userdel -r $username
done < students.txt 
```

### 7.8.7    Example 7: Changing Multiple MySQL/MariaDB Databases

In my role as a database administrator, I occasionally have to make changes to a lot of databases of the same type, such as adding a column to a table in 50 customer databases of the same structure. If I wanted to do this manually, I would have to create a connection to each database using <samp class="listingcharacter">mysql dbname</samp> and then run <samp class="listingcharacter">ALTER TABLE tblname ADD ...</samp>.

But just three lines of <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> code are much more efficient:

```
#!/bin/bash
for db in $(cat /etc/mydbs.txt); do
  mysql $db < updates.sql
done 
```

The script runs through all databases listed line by line in the <samp class="listingcharacter">/etc/mydbs.txt</samp> file. For each database, <samp class="listingcharacter">mysql</samp> executes the SQL commands stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">updates.sql</samp> file.

The only requirement is that the user running the script can connect to all databases without explicitly entering a password. For this to work, the MySQL-specific <samp class="listingcharacter">.my.cnf</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">.mylogin.cnf</samp> file must contain the required authentication data.

## 7.9    Basic Rules for Bash Scripts

As I mentioned when describing the examples from the previous section, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> scripts must start with the line <samp class="listingcharacter">#!/bin/bash</samp>. This line, the so-called shebang or hashbang, specifies by which interpreter the following code is executed—in the examples in this chapter, by <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp>.

Shell scripts can only be executed if the access bits for read access (<samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp>) and execution (<samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>) are set. The <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> bit is set by default for new files anyway, but you have to take care of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> bit (for execute) yourself once:

```
user$ chmod +x myscript 
```

If you write a collection of your own shell script programs for daily use, it makes sense to store them in a central location.

The best directory to use is <samp class="listingcharacter">~/bin</samp>. If you then make the following change in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.profile</samp>, these script programs can be run without a full path specification (in some distributions this is not necessary at all, because there <samp class="listingcharacter">~/bin</samp> is always part of <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp>):

```
# addition in ~/.profile resp. in ~/.bashrc
PATH=$PATH':~/bin' 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">exit</samp> terminates the running script, and thus the script returns the return value of the last executed command. If you don’t want this, you can explicitly pass a value to <samp class="listingcharacter">exit</samp>. The value 0 signals an error-free end to the program, 1 indicates a general error, and 2 indicates an error in the passed parameters. All other error codes are application-specific.

In most programming languages, the following holds true: as soon as an unhandled error occurs, the program terminates. Things are much more relaxed in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> scripts: the fact that errors occur during command execution—that is, that a command ends with an error code not equal to 0—is accepted as an everyday occurrence. The execution of the script simply continues with the next statement.

Obvious syntax errors represent an exception—for example, for a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">for</samp> loop without <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">done</samp> or for a character string that begins with <samp class="listingcharacter">"</samp> but where the second <samp class="listingcharacter">"</samp> character is missing. In such cases, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> can no longer decode the remaining program structure: it displays an error message and aborts the code execution.

Even though the high error tolerance of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> is often convenient, sometimes you do want a script to abort at the first error and not produce possible subsequent errors. You can achieve this by including <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set -e</samp> in the code. From this position on, errors lead to the immediate end. If you want this strict error control to apply to the entire script, you need to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-e</samp> option right in the first line:

```
#!/bin/bash -e
# this script will abort at the first error
... 
```

For linked commands, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set -e</samp> or the bash option <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-e</samp> apply only to the overall result. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cmd1</samp> fails in the following example—even if it is because the command does not exist—then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cmd2</samp> will be executed. Only if this command also leads to an error will the script abort:

```
#!/bin/bash -e 
cmd1 || cmd2 
```

## 7.10    Variables in Bash Scripts

I have already provided some initial information on dealing with variables in [Section 7.7](#07_007.html_h7.7). This section covers other aspects of variable management that are particularly relevant to shell programming. In detail, it is about the scope of variables, about some variables predefined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">$?</samp>), about the mechanism of parameter substitution for analyzing and processing strings in variables, and finally about the input of variables in shell programs.

### 7.10.1    The Scope of Variables

To run a command or a script, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> creates a new process with its own PID number. This is an internal Linux number to identify and manage the process. Of the variables, only those declared as environment variables (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">export</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">declare -x</samp>) are passed to the new process. When a command is started in the foreground, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> enters the background during its execution and waits for the command to finish.

The processing of a script takes place not in the running shell, but in a subshell started especially for this purpose. So now there are two instances of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> running: one as its command interpreter and the second one to execute the script. This is useful in that the original shell and the script can run in the background without interfering with each other, if necessary.

The concept of subshells affects variable management in that each (sub) shell has its own variables. As is the case when any other program is started, only environment variables are passed to the subshell. After that, the variables in the two shells are independent of each other. Changing variables in one shell has no effect on variables in the other shell.

Sometimes you want to declare new variables or permanently change existing variables using a shell program. To make this possible, you can also run a script within the current <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>—that is, without automatically starting a subshell. To do this, you need to put a period and a space before the script's file name. This corresponds to the short notation of the shell command, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">source</samp>.

Let's look at an example. Say that you want to write a shell program that extends the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> variable with the path of the current directory. The required <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addpwd</samp> program is quite simple:

```
#!/bin/bash
# shell program addpwd adds the current directory to the path
PATH="$PATH:$(pwd)" 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> variable thus stores the previous content of this variable, a colon, and finally the result of the <samp class="listingcharacter">pwd</samp> command via command substitution. The following test run proves that the content of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> variable in the current shell does not change until <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addpwd</samp> is started with a preceding dot. Within the subshell that was started when <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addpwd</samp> was first called, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> is of course also changed—but this change only applies as long as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addpwd</samp> is running:

```
user$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin

user$ ./addpwd      # Caution: no change of PATH
user$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin

user$ . addpwd      # this is how it works!
user$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/home/user
```

### 7.10.2    Variables Predefined by the Shell

Within shell programs, some variables predefined by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> can be accessed. These variables cannot be changed by assignments, but only read. The name of the variable is formed by various special characters. In [Table 7.6](#07_010.html_t7.6), the variables are specified with the preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character.

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$?</samp> | Return value of the last command |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$!</samp> | PID of the last started background process |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> | PID of the current shell |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$0</samp> | Filename of the currently executed shell script (or of the symbolic link referencing the file) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$#</samp> | Number of parameters passed to the shell program |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">$9</samp> | Parameters 1 to 9 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">$@</samp> | Totality of all passed parameters |

**Table 7.6**     $ Variables

On the use of these variables, note that <samp class="listingcharacter">$0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">$9</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">$#</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp> are used to analyze the parameters passed to the batch program. Almost every script example in this chapter shows possible applications for this.

In connection with the analysis of parameters, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shift</samp> is quite interesting. This command virtually pushes the passed parameters through the ten variables <samp class="listingcharacter">$0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">$9</samp>. If you execute <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shift 9</samp>, the first nine parameters passed to the program are lost, but then the next nine parameters can be conveniently addressed. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shift</samp> without further specification shifts the parameter list by one parameter.

<samp class="listingcharacter">$?</samp> can be used to create conditions to make the further course of the program dependent on the result of the last command.

Basically, it’s also possible to specify a command directly as a condition in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">if</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">$?</samp> variable has the advantage of avoiding overly long and confusing statements.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> variable contains the PID. This numerical value is used internally in Linux to manage the processes. The PID is unique; that is, there is never any second process with the same number in the entire system. That is why this value is excellent for creating a temporary file. For example, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">ls > tmp.$</samp> to store a list of all files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tmp.nnn</samp> file. Even if the same batch file is running in another terminal at the same time, there is certain to be no name conflict because of the different PIDs of the two shells.

### 7.10.3    Arrays

Besides simple variables, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> also uses arrays. Up to and including version 3, the index must be a number. Note the <samp class="listingcharacter">${field[n]}</samp> syntax for accessing the nth element, which differs from C:

```
x=()                     # definition of an empty array
x[0]='a'                 # assign array elements
x[1]='b'
x[2]='c'
x=('a' 'b' 'c')          # short notation for the previous four lines
echo ${x[1]}             # read an array element
echo ${x[@]}             # read all array elements 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> also supports associative arrays, where the array elements can be accessed by freely chosen strings instead of by passing index numbers. To do this, you must explicitly declare the field variable as associative by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">declare -A</samp>! Otherwise, the variable is considered a normal field. The character strings used in the index are evaluated to 0, and you get an ordinary array consisting of only one element (index 0):

```
declare -A y                # definition of an empty associative array
y[abc]=123                  # assign an element of associative array
y[efg]="xxx"
y=( [abc]=123 [efg]="xxx" ) # Short notation for the above two lines
echo ${y[abc]}              # Read an array element 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mapfile</samp> to read an entire text file line by line into the elements of an array:

```
mapfile z < textfile 
```

### 7.10.4    Parameter Substitution

Under the term parameter substitution, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> provides a number of commands that can be used to edit character strings stored in variables. Note that the variable name is specified without a preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character. If, on the other hand, the comparison pattern is to be read from a variable, a <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> character must be used there:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var:-default}</samp>
    If the variable is empty, the construct returns the default setting as a result; otherwise, it returns the content of the variable. The variable is not changed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var:=default}</samp>
    The content of the variable is changed at the same time if it was previously empty.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var:+new}</samp>
    If the variable is empty, it remains empty. If, on the other hand, the variable is already being used, the previous content is replaced by a new setting. The construct provides the new content of the variables.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var:?errormessage}</samp>
    If the variable is empty, the variable name and the error message are output, and the shell program then gets terminated. Otherwise, the construct returns the content of the variable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${#var}</samp>
    Returns the number of characters stored in the variable as the result (0 if the variable is empty). The variable is not changed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var:n}</samp>
    Returns the character string stored in <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> from the nth character, with the count starting at 0.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var:offset:len}</samp>
    Skips <samp class="listingcharacter">offset</samp> characters and then returns <samp class="listingcharacter">len</samp> characters.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var#pattern}</samp>
    Compares the beginning of the variable with the specified pattern. If the pattern is recognized, the construct returns the contents of the variable minus the shortest possible text that matches the search pattern. If, on the other hand, the pattern is not found, the entire contents of the variable are returned. In the search pattern, the wildcard characters known for creating file names can be used (<samp class="listingcharacter">* ? [abc]</samp>). The variable is not changed in any case:

    ```
    user$ dat=/home/mk/book/book.tar.gz
    user$ echo ${dat#*/}
    home/mk/book/book.tar.gz
    user$ echo ${dat#*.}
    tar.gz 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var##pattern}</samp>
    As the previous item, but now the largest possible string that matches the pattern is eliminated:

    ```
    user$ dat=/home/mk/book/book.tar.gz
    user$ echo ${dat##*/}
    book.tar.gz
    user$ echo ${dat##*.}
    gz 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var%pattern}</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">${var#pattern}</samp>, but now the pattern matching is done at the end of the variable content. The shortest possible string from the end of the variable is eliminated. The variable itself remains unchanged:

    ```
    user$ dat=/home/mk/book/book.tar.gz
    user$ echo ${dat&#x25;/*}
    /home/mk/book
    user$ echo ${dat&#x25;.*}
    /home/mk/book/book.tar 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var%%pattern}</samp>
    As the previous item, but the largest possible character string is eliminated:

    ```
    user$ dat=/home/mk/book/book.tar.gz
    user$ echo ${dat%%/*}
          - no output - 
    user$ echo ${dat%%.*}
    /home/mk/book/book 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var/find/replace}</samp>
    Replaces the first occurrence of the <samp class="listingcharacter">find</samp> pattern with <samp class="listingcharacter">replace</samp>:

    ```
    user$ x='abcdeab12ab'
    user$ echo echo ${x/ab/xy}
    xycdeab12ab 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${var//find/replace}</samp>
    Replaces every occurrence of the <samp class="listingcharacter">find</samp> pattern with <samp class="listingcharacter">replace</samp>:

    ```
    user$ x='abcdeab12ab'
    user$ echo echo ${x//ab/xy}
    xycdexy12xy 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">${!var}</samp>
    Returns the content of the variable whose name is contained in <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> as a character string:

    ```
    user$ abc="123"
    user$ efg=abc
    user$ echo ${!efg}
    123 
    ```

### 7.10.5    Read Variables Using "read"

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">read</samp> to process user input. As a rule, you first use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp> to output a short text informing the user what input you expect—for example, y/n, a numerical value, and so on. In this context, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-n</samp> option is useful so that the entry is made immediately after the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp> text and not in the subsequent line:

```
echo -n "Your name please: "
read name
echo "Hello, $name!" 
```

## 7.11    Branches, Loops, and Functions

This section describes which <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> keywords you can use to structure your code. You can create branches using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">if</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">case</samp>; loops using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">for</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">while</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">until</samp>; functions using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">function</samp>; and so on.

### 7.11.1    If Branches

As in almost any programming language, you can formulate branches using <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>. The syntax is as follows:

```
if condition1; then 
    command1a
    command1b
[ elif condition2; then
    commands2 ]
[ else
    commands3 ]
fi 
```

A concrete example looks as follows:

```
if [ $# -ne 2 ]; then
    echo "Two parameters must be passed to the command!"
    exit 2  # error code for wrong parameters
else
    echo "Parameter 1: $1, Parameter 2: $2"
fi 
```

The criterion for branching is the return value of the last command before <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">then</samp>. The condition is met if this command returns 0\. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">then</samp> is specified in the same line (and not in the next line), then the command must be terminated by using a semicolon.

#### Reversed Logic

Note that in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, the truth values for true (0) and false (not equal to 0) are defined in reverse compared to most other programming languages! Commands that are terminated properly return 0\. Any value other than 0 indicates an error. Some commands return different error values depending on the error type.

### 7.11.2    Formulating Conditions

In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, you are not allowed to formulate conditions using ordinary operators as in other programming languages, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">if $a < 3; then</samp>, for example. Instead, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test</samp> in order to formulate conditions in loops and branches. The correct wording of the introductory example is <samp class="listingcharacter">if test $a -lt 3; then</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">-lt</samp> stands for less than.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test</samp> is used for multiple tasks: to compare two numbers, to compare character strings, and to test whether a file exists and has certain properties. The following examples show some syntax variants:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">test "$x"</samp>
    Checks whether <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is in use. The result is false if the string has 0 characters, otherwise it is true.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">test $x -gt 5</samp>
    Checks whether the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> variable contains a numerical value greater than 5\. If <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> does not contain a number, an error message occurs. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-gt</samp> (greater than), the following relational operators can also be used: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-eq</samp> (equal), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-ne</samp> (not equal), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-lt</samp> (less than), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-le</samp> (less equal), and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-ge</samp> (greater equal).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">test -f $x</samp>
    Checks whether a file with the name specified in <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> exists.

    If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test</samp> is to be executed interactively in the shell, after the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test command</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">$?</samp> variable (return value of the last command) can be read using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp>:

    ```
    user$ a=20
    user$ test $a -eq 20; echo $?
    0
    user$ test $a -gt 20; echo $?
    1 
    ```

In the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">if</samp> example, I used the short notation <samp class="listingcharacter">[ expression ]</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test expression</samp>. Note the syntactically prescribed spaces within the square brackets:

```
user$ if [ $a -eq 20 ]; then echo "a=20"; fi
a=20 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> also uses a variant with two square brackets with some additional test options (see [Table 7.7](#07_011.html_t7.7)). Note, however, that these tests are not available in simpler shells (e.g., in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/sh</samp>)!

| Test Expression | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[[ zk = pattern* ]]</samp> | True if the string starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">pattern</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[[ zk == pattern* ]]</samp> | As above |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[[ zk ~= regex ]]</samp> | True if the regular pattern is true |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[[ bed1 && bed2 ]]</samp> | True if both conditions are true (and) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[[ bed1 &#124;&#124; bed2 ]]</samp> | True if one of the conditions is true (or) |

**Table 7.7**     Bash-Specific Test Variants

### 7.11.3    Case Branches

Case distinctions are introduced by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">case</samp> keyword, followed by the parameter to be analyzed. After the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">in</samp> keyword, you need to specify sample strings with which the parameter will be compared. In this context, the same wildcard characters as for file names are allowed. The pattern is terminated with a parenthesis, <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>—that is, for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">--*)</samp> to recognize strings starting with two minus signs. You can separate alternative patterns using <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>.

The commands that follow the parenthesis must be terminated by two semicolons. If an <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">else</samp> branch is needed, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*</samp> must be specified as the last pattern; all strings match this pattern. When processing a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">case</samp> construct, only the first branch where the parameter matches the specified pattern is considered:

```
echo -n "yes/no? "
read answer
case $answer in
    y | yes ) echo "yes";;
    n | no  ) echo "no";;
    *)        echo "invalid input";;
esac 
```

### 7.11.4    For Loops

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> uses three commands for creating loops: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">for</samp> executes a loop for all elements of a specified list. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">while</samp> executes a loop until the specified condition is no longer fulfilled, whereas <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">until</samp> executes it until the condition is fulfilled for the first time. All three loops can be exited prematurely by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">break</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">continue</samp> skips the remaining loop body and continues the loop with the next loop pass.

In the first example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> variable is assigned the strings <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> in sequence. In the loop body, the content of the variable is output between <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">do</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">done</samp>. Note that a semicolon is required at the end of the list as well as at the end of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp> command. These semicolons can only be omitted if the input is distributed across multiple lines (which often happens in script files):

```
user$ for i in a b c; do echo $i; done
a
b
c 
```

The equivalent multiline formulation of the preceding command in a script file would look as follows:

```
#!/bin/bash
for i in a b c; do 
  echo $i
done 
```

The list for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">for</samp> can also be created using wildcards for file names or using <samp class="listingcharacter">{..}</samp> constructs to create strings. In the following example, all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files are copied to <samp class="listingcharacter">*.tex.bak</samp> files. In the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> command, <samp class="listingcharacter">$file</samp> is always enclosed in quotation marks so that file names with spaces are also handled correctly:

```
user$ for file in *.tex; do cp "$file" "$file.bak"; done 
```

If you want to analyze the file names passed to a script (<samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp> variable), you need to initialize the previously mentioned <samp class="listingcharacter">IFS</samp> variable with a newline character. Otherwise the analysis of <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp> will not work correctly for file names with spaces:

```
IFS=$'\n'
for file in $*; do
    cp "$file" "$file.bak"
done 
```

You often need loops to process a text file line by line. That’s no problem: simply pass the result of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat file</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">in</samp> keyword! The following miniprogram creates a compressed backup in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">db.sql.gz</samp> file for all databases named line by line in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dbs.txt</samp> file:

```
#!/bin/bash
# Loop through 
for db in $(cat dbs.txt); do
  mysqldump $db | gzip -c > $db.sql.gz
done 
```

The simplest way to formulate loops through a range of numbers is as follows:

```
for i in {1..12}; do
  echo "$i"
done
# Output 1, 2, 3, ..., 12 
```

If you need leading zeros, you must specify them in the first parameter in <samp class="listingcharacter">{n1..n2}</samp>:

```
for i in {01..12}; do
  echo "$i"
done
# Output 01, 02, 03, ..., 12 
```

For loops with a given increment, you need to use the notation <samp class="listingcharacter">{n1..n2..step}</samp>—so, for example:

```
for i in {1..12..3}; do
  echo "$i"
done
# Output 1, 4, 7, 10 
```

Finally, you can also resort to the classic C syntax:

```
for ((i=1;i<=12;i++)); do
  echo "$i"
done
# Output 1, 2, 3, ..., 12 
```

Note that <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> does not provide any floating-point arithmetic. So all constructs presented here work only for integers.

### 7.11.5    While Loops

In the following example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> variable is assigned the value 1\. Then the variable in the loop body between <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">do</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">done</samp> is incremented by 1 until the value 5 is exceeded. Note that conditions must be specified using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test</samp> command or its short form in square brackets, as with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">if</samp> branches:

```
user$ i=1; while [ $i -le 5 ]; do echo $i; i=$(($i+1)); done
1
2
3
4
5 
```

The following loop processes all file names resulting from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls *.jpg</samp> command:

```
ls *.jpg | while read file
do
  echo "$file"
done 
```

### 7.11.6    Until Loops

The only difference between <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">until</samp> loops and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">while</samp> loops is that the condition is formulated in a logically negated way. The following command is therefore equivalent to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">while</samp> loop presented previously. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-gt</samp> is used to formulate the condition <samp class="listingcharacter">i>5</samp> (greater than):

```
user$ i=1; until [ $i -gt 5 ]; do echo $i; i=$(($i+1)); done 
```

### 7.11.7    Functions

The <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> keyword defines a function that can be called in the script like a command. The code of the function must be enclosed in curly brackets. Within the function, local variables can be defined by using <samp class="listingcharacter">local</samp>. Functions can be called recursively. Functions must be declared before their first call!

Parameters can be passed to functions. Unlike many programming languages, the parameters are not enclosed in parentheses. Within the function, the parameters can be taken from the <samp class="listingcharacter">$1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">$2</samp> variables, which means that a function processes parameters in the same way as a <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> script. The following miniscript outputs Hello World, Linux!:

```
#!/bin/bash
function myfunc {
  echo "Hello World, $1!"
}
myfunc "Linux" 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> keyword is optional. If you omit <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp>, however, the function name must be followed by parentheses. Thus, the following program is equivalent to the preceding example:

```
#!/bin/bash    
myfunc() {       
  echo "Hello World, $1!"
}
myfunc "Linux" 
```

### 7.11.8    Heredoc Syntax

The Heredoc syntax allows you to formulate multiline constructs ending with a freely chosen string. This syntax is used particularly often to create multiline files or to define multiline variables:

```
# writes a multiline text to the myfile file
cat <<EOF > myfile
Line 1
Line 2
EOF

# stores a multiline text in the $myvar variable
read -r -d '' myvar <<EOF
Line 1
Line 2
EOF
echo "$myvar" 
```

Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">EOF</samp>, you can use any other string. It is customary to specify this string in uppercase characters. In the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">read</samp> command, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> option causes the character string to be accepted unchanged (raw). <samp class="listingcharacter">-d ''</samp> (delimiter) means that the end of the line does not count as the end of the input. For the output of multiline character strings via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo</samp>, it’s important to enclose the variable in quotation marks; otherwise, the line breaks will be lost.

## 7.12    Important Special Characters in Bash: Quick Reference

[Table 7.8](#07_012.html_t7.8) summarizes all the special characters I introduced in this chapter.

| Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> | Separates multiple commands |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> | Shell command that does nothing |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> | Insert shell code here (<samp class="listingcharacter">. file</samp> corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">source file</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> | Introduces a comment |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#!/bin/bash</samp> | Identifies the desired shell for the shell program |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> | Executes the command in the background (<samp class="listingcharacter">com &)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> | Conditional execution of the command (<samp class="listingcharacter">com1 && com2</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&></samp> | Redirection of standard output and errors (corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">>&</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;</samp> | Creates pipes (<samp class="listingcharacter">com1 &#124; com2</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;&#124;</samp> | Conditional execution of the command (<samp class="listingcharacter">com1 &#124;&#124; com2</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> | Wildcard character for file names (any number of characters) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp> | Wildcard character for file names (any character) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[abc]</samp> | Wildcard character for file names (one character from <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[ expression ]</samp> | Short notation for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test expression</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[[ expression ]]</samp> | As above, but additional, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>-specific syntax variants |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(...)</samp> | Execute commands in the same shell (<samp class="listingcharacter">(com1; com2)</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp> | Group commands |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">{ , , }</samp> | Assemble strings (<samp class="listingcharacter">a{1,2,3}</samp> → <samp class="listingcharacter">a1 a2 a3</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">{a..b}</samp> | Assemble strings (<samp class="listingcharacter">b{4..6}</samp> → <samp class="listingcharacter">b4 b5 b6</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> | Abbreviation for the home directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> | Output redirection to a file (<samp class="listingcharacter">com > file</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> | Output redirection; append to existing file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">>&</samp> | Redirection of standard output and errors (corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">&></samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&>></samp> | Append standard output and errors to file (as of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> 4.0) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">2></samp> | Redirection of standard error output |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> | Input redirection from a file (<samp class="listingcharacter">com < file</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><< end</samp> | Input redirection from active file to <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> | Marking of variables (<samp class="listingcharacter">echo $var</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$!</samp> | PID of the last started background process |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> | PID of the current shell |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$0</samp> | File name of the currently executed shell script |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">$9</samp> | The first nine parameters passed to the command |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$#</samp> | Number of parameters passed to the shell program |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">$@</samp> | Totality of all passed parameters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$?</samp> | Return value of the last command (0 = OK or error number) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$(...)</samp> | Command substitution (<samp class="listingcharacter">echo $(ls)</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">${...}</samp> | Various special functions for editing strings |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$((...))</samp> | Arithmetic analysis (<samp class="listingcharacter">echo $((2+3))</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">"..."</samp> | Prevent analysis of most special characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">'...'</samp> | Prevent analysis of all special characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">`...`</samp> | Command substitution (<samp class="listingcharacter">echo `ls`</samp>) |

# 8    Zsh (Shell)

For decades, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> was the default shell of almost all Linux distributions. In recent years, however, there has been some movement in the selection of shells. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> (pronounced as z-shell) is not only gaining popularity among professionals but is now enabled by default by some distributions (such as Manjaro and Kali Linux). Fans of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> cite the following benefits, among others:

*   Better (“smarter”) completion of commands and parameters

*   Command history shared across multiple shells

*   Extendable through modules

*   More visual design options for the input prompt

In this short chapter, I want to show how you can switch from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, explain the benefits of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, and introduce you to the popular Oh My Zsh extension. Throughout the chapter, I assume that you know what a shell is and that you know the basic functions of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. If necessary, you should take another look at [Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8).

Interestingly, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> is also gaining popularity outside of Linux: current versions of macOS also rely on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, but Apple's motivation has less to do with functionality and more with licensing issues. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> uses a BSD-style license, while more recent <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> versions are based on GPL 3\. Apple, on the other hand, avoids integrating open-source code with a GPL-3 license into its products.

## Personal Assessment

I only switched from <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>—admittedly a bit by accident—in 2020\. I primarily wanted to take advantage of the cool Git features that the Oh My Zsh extension brings. The changeover was trouble-free, with few changes in the operation of the shell. However, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> behaves better, is more refined, and is more mature than <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> in many details. There is not one decisive argument, but it is the total of many little things that make <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> so attractive. In a nutshell: I don't want to go back to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>!

Countless options and expansion modules lead to the temptation of playing around with configuration for days in search of the perfect setup, but has one big disadvantage: Usually you work on many systems, at least as an administrator. The more elaborate your setup is, the more dependent you become on it and want to set it up on each of your systems. The time you might gain with your super setup is lost on the other hand by migrating the setup from one computer to the next.

Like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> can be used to program scripts. However, this is rather uncommon, apart from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>-specific extensions. As a scripting language, <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp> will probably remain the standard, even though the syntax of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> is the same as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> except for a few subtle differences. In any case, this chapter focuses on the interactive use of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> and does not address programming.

## 8.1    Installation and Configuration

If you are unsure about which shell is used in your Linux distribution, you can simply output the contents of the <samp class="listingcharacter">SHELL</samp> environment variable. It contains the path to the active shell, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/bash</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin/zsh</samp>:

```
user$ echo $SHELL
/usr/bin/zsh 
```

All common distributions provide a package for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>. To switch to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, you first need to install this package, then use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> to determine the path, and then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chsh</samp>. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chsh</samp> always applies only to the user executing the command. If there are multiple users on a computer, each of them can set and use their favorite shell:

```
user$ sudo apt/dnf/zypper install zsh
user$ which zsh
/usr/bin/zsh
user$ chsh -s $(which zsh)
Password: ********** 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chsh</samp> enters the shell you want in the last column of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> file. The change will not take effect until the next login, so you have to log out and log in again.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chsh</samp> command may not be available. In this case, you must install the appropriate package beforehand, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">util-linux-user</samp> on Fedora or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> on Debian/Ubuntu.

After switching to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, the command prompt will probably look different from what you are used to from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>. In addition, various functions of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, such as self-defined aliases, may no longer work. The reason for this can be found in the configuration. While <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> parses <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> and some other configuration files by default, the corresponding files of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> have different names (see [Table 8.1](#08_001.html_t8.1)) and are probably still partly empty in your case—unless you use a distribution like Manjaro with a great default configuration (see [Figure 8.1](#08_001.html_f8.1)).

[![Zsh in Default Configuration on Manjaro: Displaying Current Directory and Status of Git Repository](bilderklein/klein08_001.png)](img-f8.1.html)

**Figure 8.1**     Zsh in Default Configuration on Manjaro: Displaying Current Directory and Status of Git Repository

| Global | Local | Login Shell | Interactive Shell | Script |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zshenv</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshenv</samp> | • | • | • |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zshrc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp> | • | • |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zprofile</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zprofile</samp> | • |  |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zlogin</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zlogin</samp> | • |  |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zlogout</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zlogin</samp> | • |  |  |

**Table 8.1**     Different Zsh Configuration Files Considered Depending on Type of Shell

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> parses the global configuration files first (first column), then the local files. Note that depending on the distribution, the global configuration files are not located directly in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> directory, but in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zsh</samp> directory. This is true for Debian and Ubuntu, for example.

A login shell exists if the shell is started directly during the login process, such as in a text console or via SSH. The shell is considered interactive if it accepts and responds to commands via a console, while the start did not occur as part of the login. Provided you work in a graphical user interface, this is the normal case.

First, you log in, then you start a terminal and run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> in it. [Table 8.1](#08_001.html_t8.1) shows that the two most important configuration files are <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshenv</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshenv</samp> is primarily intended for defining environment variables that should also be available in scripts. In real life, the file often remains empty. On the other hand, .zshrc is the right place to set options for interactive use of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, to define custom aliases, and so on.

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> detects that there are no configuration files in your home directory yet, it starts the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-newuser-install</samp> configuration help:

```
This is the Z Shell configuration function for new users, zsh-newuser-install.

You are seeing this message because you have no zsh startup files (the files .zshenv, .zprofile, .zshrc, .zlogin in the directory ~).  This function can help you with a few settings that should make your use of the shell easier.

You can

(q)  Quit and do nothing.  The function will be run again next time.
(0)  Exit, creating the file ~/.zshrc containing just a comment.
     That will prevent this function being run again.
(1)  Continue to the main menu.
(2)  Populate your ~/.zshrc with the configuration recommended
     by the system administrator and exit (you will need to edit
     the file by hand, if so desired). 
```

If you choose option 2, the setup program copies the /etc/zsh/newuser. zshrc.recommended file to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp>. The content of this default configuration varies depending on the distribution. Some distributions do not provide the file at all, in which case this option is missing.

If you want to use all the design options yourself, you have to choose variant 1 anyway. This will take you to another menu where you can configure various <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> functions step by step. I will focus on the most important items here:

*   History This item is about whether <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> should remember the most recently executed commands, what the maximum number of these commands is, and where they should be stored. The default is to store a maximum of 1,000 commands in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.histfile</samp> file.

*   Completion <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> acts extremely intelligently when you complete commands, options, files, and so on using the (Tab) key. Behind the scenes, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> component <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">compsys</samp> is responsible for this. In the setup program, you can simply activate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">compsys</samp> with the default settings or perform a more detailed configuration. If necessary, you can also start this later using the following two commands:

    ```
    user$ autoload -Uz compinstall
    user$ compinstall 
    ```

*   Keys To change the input in the command line, the Emacs keyboard shortcuts usually apply: (Ctrl)+(A) jumps to the beginning of the line, (Ctrl)+(E) to the end, and so on. Alternatively, you can also activate the usual keyboard shortcuts in the Vi editor here.

*   Options In this menu item, you can switch some additional options on or off:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">autocd</samp>
        If you enter the name of a directory and press (Enter), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> goes directly to that directory. It is not necessary to precede the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">autocd</samp> works only for directories whose name does not match that of a command.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">extendedglob</samp>
        This option provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> (imprecise search), <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> (negation), and <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> (exception rule) characters with a special meaning for globbing (i.e., for describing file names by patterns). Application examples follow in the next section. The option has the disadvantage that dealing with file names in which these three characters actually occur becomes more difficult. You must then enclose the corresponding expression in quotation marks.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nomatch</samp>
        This option causes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> to throw an error if you specify a search pattern that does not match any file.

    More information about these and a lot more options is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man zshoptions</samp>.

If you decide to save at the end of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-newuser-install</samp>, your settings will be added to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp> file. This file then looks similar to the following listing:

```
# .zshrc file
# History
HISTFILE=~/.histfile
HISTSIZE=1000
SAVEHIST=1000
# Completions
zstyle :compinstall filename '/home/kofler/.zshrc'
autoload -Uz compinit
compinit
# Emacs Keybindings
bindkey -e
# Options
setopt autocd extendedglob nomatch 
```

Internally, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-newuser-install</samp> is not a script, but a function. If you want to run it again, you need to execute the following two commands:

```
user$ autoload -U zsh-newuser-install
user$ zsh-newuser-install -f 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-newuser-install</samp> cannot be executed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-newuser-install</samp> gets you off to a good start, but it leaves out some useful features of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>. The following listing contains some ideas that you can incorporate into your own <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp> file if you want:

```
# Configuration ideas for .zshrc
setopt correct           # tries to correct typing errors

setopt sharehistory      # share and always update history file 
                         # between multiple zsh processes immediately

setopt histignorealldups # do not store duplicates in history file 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setopt <name></samp> command enables you to activate an option on a test basis, while <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unsetopt <name></samp> allows you to deactivate it again. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setopt</samp> without further parameters lists all currently active options. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man zshoptions</samp> provides a reference of well over a hundred <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> options. The options are highlighted there with capital letters and underscores. Because <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setopt</samp> is not case-sensitive and ignores underscores, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setopt AUTO_CD</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setopt autocd</samp> are equivalent. If you want to be inspired further, you should take a look at the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> configuration of various distributions as well as the sample files provided:

*   Debian/Ubuntu
    File /etc/zsh/newuser.zshrc.recommended or file /usr/share/doc/zsh/examples/zshrc

*   Kali Linux
    File .zshrc or /etc/zsh/newuser.zshrc.recommended

*   Manjaro
    The /usr/share/zsh directory

Before you waste too much time with a manual configuration, you should try the Oh My Zsh extension. Many configuration requests, especially those relating to the design of the input prompt, then virtually solve themselves.

## 8.2    Usage

Basically, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> works like any shell: you can execute commands, redirect the inputs and outputs using <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, link commands using the pipe operator <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>, and so on. I have already presented these basic functions to you in detail in [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7). For this reason, I describe only some features at this point, ones that are missing in this form in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>.

If the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">correct</samp> option is set, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> compares the command you enter with existing commands. If your incorrect entry differs only by a minor detail (e.g., a transposed letter as in the following example), the shell automatically suggests a suitable correction. The four options of <samp class="listingcharacter">nyae</samp> stand for no (execute command despite error), yes (correct the command), abort (abort the command), and edit (edit the command again). With yes, the command will be not only executed correctly, but also included correctly into the history:

```
user$ mdkir mydocuments
zsh: correct 'mdkir' to 'mkdir' [nyae]? y 
```

As in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, you can press (Tab) at any time in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> to complete the current input. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> is even more sophisticated than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, especially when it comes to completing file names.

In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, the completion function requires you to know the initial letters of the file or command. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> doesn’t find a matching command or file, it will search for the specified letters further down the line. So if there is a file named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">linux-content.ods</samp> in your directory and you type <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls content</samp> (Tab), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> will make it <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls linux-content.ods</samp>. But this only works if there is no other file that starts with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">content</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> is also very clever when it comes to changing directories: In most cases, it’s sufficient to enter the initial letters. To change to the directory with the text files for this book on my computer, I type <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd n/l/t</samp> (Tab) (Enter). (Tab) immediately turns the sparse directory specification into <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">no-sync/linux/text</samp>. This assumes that there is no other directory that matches this combination of initial letters.

If the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">autocd</samp> option is active, the directory change works without the explicit <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> command. (Tab), however, must not be left out, as otherwise <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> will complain that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">n/l/t</samp> directory does not exist.

The term globbing refers to applying search patterns to file names. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls *.pdf</samp> lists all PDF documents in the current directory. While <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> does not perform globbing until the command is executed, you can initiate the process in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> prior to that. To do this, you want to press (Tab) after <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls *.pdf</samp>. In the command line, <samp class="listingcharacter">*.pdf</samp> will then be replaced by the files that have been found. With <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> this is rarely useful, but before <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm *.pdf</samp> it is certainly a good idea to have a quick look at the names of the files to be deleted.

The trailing expression <samp class="listingcharacter">(qualifier)</samp> allows <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> to consider only the files that have a certain property for globbing (see [Table 8.2](#08_002.html_t8.2)).

| Qualifier | For |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(/)</samp> | Directories (no files) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(.)</samp> | Files (not directories) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(@)</samp> | Symbolic links |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(*)</samp> | Executable files (oktal 100/010/001) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(r)</samp> | Files readable by the owner (400) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(w)</samp> | Files modifiable by the owner (200) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(x)</samp> | Files executable by owner (100) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(s)</samp> | setuid files (4000) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(S)</samp> | setgid files (2000) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(md-2)</samp> | Files that have been modified in the last two days |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(md+2)</samp> | Files that have been modified more than two days ago |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(mh-6)</samp> | Files that have been modified in the last six hours |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(md+6)</samp> | Files that have been modified more than six hours ago |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(Lm+1000)</samp> | Files larger than 1,000 MiB |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(Lk-250)</samp> | Files smaller than 250 KiB |

**Table 8.2**     Examples of Recursive Search for Specific Files

The following examples illustrate the qualifier syntax:

```
user$ ls *             
(lists all files and directories)
user$ ls *(.)          
(lists only files, no directories)
user$ ls *(/)          
(lists only directories)
user$ ls *.tex(md-7)   
(lists files that have been modified in the last week) 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> manual contains a list of countless other globbing qualifiers; see [http://zsh.sourceforge.net/Doc/Release/Expansion.html#Glob-Qualifiers](http://zsh.sourceforge.net/Doc/Release/Expansion.html#Glob-Qualifiers).

If you prefix a search pattern with <samp class="listingcharacter">**</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> recursively searches all subdirectories according to the pattern. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls **/*.pdf</samp> takes into account files in the current directory as well as in all subdirectories. Of course, with large directory trees, this can take some time.

You can also specify a qualifier for the recursive search. <samp class="listingcharacter">**/*(qualifier)</samp> only considers files that have a certain attribute (see [Table 8.2](#08_002.html_t8.2)). The simple syntax avoids cumbersome <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> commands. This is especially useful for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> commands where you often want to treat files and directories differently:

```
root# chmod 750 **/*(/)
root# chmod 640 **/*(.) 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">(variant1|variant2|variant3)</samp> to formulate alternative globbing expressions. <samp class="listingcharacter">ls *.(c|h)</samp> thus lists all files ending with <samp class="listingcharacter">.c</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">.h</samp>.

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">extendedglob</samp> is active, <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> negates the search expression. <samp class="listingcharacter">ls -d ^*.pdf</samp> thus lists all files or directories that do not end with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.pdf</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">^*.*</samp> applies to all file names that do not consist of two parts (such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Makefile</samp>, but not <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.c</samp>).

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">extendedglob</samp> is active, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> to exclude individual files from the globbing pattern. <samp class="listingcharacter">ls *.md~key.md</samp> lists all markdown files except <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">key.md</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">ls *.md~sql?.md</samp> refers to all markdown files except <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sql1.md</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sql2.md</samp>, and so on.

Once again with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">extendedglob</samp>, the character combination <samp class="listingcharacter">(#a<n>)</samp> has a special meaning. It enables you to specify by how many errors the file name may deviate from the search expression. Missing characters, transposed characters, deviating characters and additional characters are considered as errors. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter">(#a<n>)</samp> is not a qualifier and must precede (not follow) the file name or search expression:

```
user$ ls concept.md        
(exact match)
concept.md 
user$ ls (#a2)concept.md   
(fuzzy search with two errors)
concept.md  concept.pdf
user$ ls (#a3)concept.md   
(fuzzy search with three errors)
concept.html  concept.md  concept.pdf  concept-v1.md 
```

(Tab) replaces not only globbing patterns with their corresponding file names, but also variable names with their contents. Thus, if you type “echo $PWD” and then press (Tab), it becomes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo /home/kofler/linux-book</samp> or whatever your current directory is.

## 8.3    Oh My Zsh

There are countless extensions available for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>. These can be divided into two groups: plugins that provide additional functionality and themes that change the look of command prompts.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> script with the funny name Oh My Zsh helps you to add such extensions to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> configuration in an uncomplicated way. A wide range of plugins and themes is already included in the standard delivery, while others can be installed and integrated later. Besides Oh My Zsh, there are other plugin management systems for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp>, but I won't cover them here.

To install it, you need to download and run a small script from the project page at [https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh](https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh). The script assumes that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">git</samp> command from the package of the same name has already been installed. Instead of typing the following command, it’s better to copy the code from the GitHub page:

```
user$ sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/\
        ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)" 
```

During the installation, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp> will be overwritten. The previous content ends up in the backup file named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc.pre-oh-my-zsh</samp>. From now on, Oh My Zsh will check for updates at startup. Accordingly, when you open a new terminal window, you are often prompted to update Oh My Zsh.

By default, Oh My Zsh is characterized by a relatively moderate basic configuration. The prompt is predefined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">robbyrussell</samp> theme. As the only active plugin, <samp class="listingcharacter">git</samp> contributes countless aliases that help with the operation of git. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias</samp> lists all the abbreviations. The plugin also influences the prompt: when you use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> to change to a directory under the control of this version control system, it displays the information about the Git status as well as the name of the currently active branch.

To regard Oh My Zsh purely as a tool for Git enthusiasts falls far short of the mark. The real power of Oh My Zsh is that by changing a few lines in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp>, you can enable more plugins as well as a theme of your choice. For this purpose, all you have to do is change the settings of the <samp class="listingcharacter">ZSH_THEME</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">plugins</samp> variables. The following listing shows the syntax that you must adhere to. In particular, you must not separate the plugins with commas. Spaces are sufficient:

```
# .zshrc file
...
ZSH_THEME="robbyrussell"
...
plugins=(git dirhistory) 
```

For the changed configuration to take effect, you must start a new shell, and the easiest way to do this is to open a new terminal window. By the way, the <samp class="listingcharacter">dirhistory</samp> plugin mentioned in the previous listing provides the (Alt)+(í) and (Alt)+(î) keyboard shortcuts, which allow you to quickly jump through the last 20 directories used.

Themes control the color scheme of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> and especially the design of the prompt. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> provides an almost infinite number of design options in this regard. Instead of dealing with this yourself, it's much easier to try out one of the many predefined themes. On the following page, you will find screenshots of the many included themes: [https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/wiki/Themes](https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/wiki/Themes).

There are also other themes that are not directly integrated into Oh My Zsh, such as Powerlevel10k (see [Figure 8.2](#08_003.html_f8.2)). You must first install these themes manually before you can activate them in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp>. Note that with some themes you also need custom fonts to display various special and status characters in the prompt. Copy the font files to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.fonts</samp> directory, then open the configuration dialog of your terminal program and set the appropriate font.

[![Zsh Terminal with Oh My Zsh Plugin and Powerlevel10k Theme](bilderklein/klein08_002.png)](img-f8.2.html)

**Figure 8.2**     Zsh Terminal with Oh My Zsh Plugin and Powerlevel10k Theme

A detailed description of Powerlevel10k can be found on the project's GitHub page at [https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k](https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k). Do I still need to mention that Powerlevel10k itself again offers countless configuration options? I have already warned you that in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> the real work is left behind because of all the tuning.

An almost endless number of plugins for all conceivable tasks, tools and programming languages can be found at [https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/tree/master/plugins](https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/tree/master/plugins). A better guide is the following top 20 list, though it was compiled in 2018: [https://safjan.com/top-popular-zsh-plugins-on-github](https://safjan.com/top-popular-zsh-plugins-on-github).

Each editor can highlight different parts of a program code. This must also work in the shell, right? I will briefly introduce three corresponding extensions here.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">colored-man-pages</samp> plugin provided by Oh My Zsh formats <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> pages using more colors.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">colorize</samp> plugin, also included in Oh My Zsh, provides the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ccat</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cless</samp> commands. When you use it to view text files, the commands try to recognize the syntax and highlight text in a meaningful way.
