Before adding <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">colorize</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">plugin</samp> line of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp>, you must install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pygments</samp> package or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">python-pygments</samp>, depending on your distribution.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ccat</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cless</samp> commands are aliases that refer to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> functions <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">colorize_cat</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">colorize_less</samp>. They are noticeably slower than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp>, which is why the obvious <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alias less=cless</samp> statement is not recommended.

A completely different approach is taken by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-syntax-highlighting</samp> plugin, which is not included in Oh My Zsh. This plugin changes the colors of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> command you just entered. What may seem superfluous at first glance is actually a great tool for recognizing before you press (Enter) for the command whether it contains a typo (the command is then displayed in red instead of green) or whether a quotation mark is not closed.

For the installation, you need to run the following command, which you can also find on the GitHub project page (see [https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting/blob/master/INSTALL.md](https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting/blob/master/INSTALL.md)):

```
user$ git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting.git \
   ${ZSH_CUSTOM:-~/.oh-my-zsh/custom}/plugins/zsh-syntax-highlighting 
```

After that, you just need to add <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh-syntax-highlighting</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">plugin</samp> line of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp>.

# 9    Files and Directories

This chapter describes the handling of files. In detail, we’ll cover the following topics:

*   Files, directories, and links

*   Copying, moving, deleting, and finding files

*   Access rights for files (including access control lists [ACLs])

*   Linux directory structure

*   Device files

In a way, the continuation to this chapter follows in [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18). That chapter deals with questions that are primarily of interest to system administrators: What file systems are available? How do I access external data media and USB flash drives? How are file systems integrated into the directory tree (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount options</samp>)? How do I change the partitioning of a hard disk or SSD? How can a software RAID system be used? What is LVM? How can an entire file system be encrypted?

The topic of backups is covered in [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28). There, I will introduce you not only to user interfaces for performing backups, but also to a wide range of commands for compressing files, bundling them into archives, synchronizing them, encrypting them, and so on.

## 9.1    Handling Files and Directories

Let me start with a brief summary of the most important facts about file names:

*   On Linux, file names with lengths of up to 255 characters are permitted.

*   A distinction is made between uppercase and lowercase letters.

*   Spaces in file names are permitted but often cause problems when they are processed by scripts. File names with spaces or special characters must be placed in quotation marks, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">"a b"</samp>. Avoid using spaces!

*   International characters in the file name are allowed, but can cause problems if different character sets are used, such as on a network. All common Linux distributions use Unicode UTF-8 as their default character set. From the point of view of the Linux kernel, the file name is simply a byte sequence in which only the / character and the code 0 must not occur. The question how this byte sequence is interpreted depends on the currently valid character set.

*   File names may contain any number of dots. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">README.bootutils.gz</samp> is a normal file name indicating that it is a compressed readme file about boot utilities.

*   Files that start with a dot are considered hidden files. Hidden files are usually not displayed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> or by various file managers.

The size of files is almost unlimited with current Linux distributions and is in the terabyte range depending on the file system.

### 9.1.1    Directories

The directory tree of Linux starts in the root directory, /. Drive specifications like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">C:</samp> are not possible on Linux. Within this book, all other directories are considered subordinate; figuratively speaking, the root directory is therefore right at the top. In some books, the naming system is reversed, which corresponds better to the tree image (root at the bottom, branching at the top), but does not correspond to common usage.

Linux beginners often find it difficult to find files in the widely ramified directory system. For a solution to this problem, read [Section 9.3](#09_003.html_h9.3) and [Section 9.8](#09_008.html_h9.8)! There you will learn about various search tools and how the Linux directory tree is structured.

In text consoles or terminal windows, the so-called home directory is initially automatically active. All files and subdirectories contained therein are yours. Other users with the exception of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> are not allowed to modify or delete these files and, depending on the access rights settings, are not even allowed to read them.

The home directory is usually located at <samp class="listingcharacter">/home/<loginname>/</samp> in the Linux directory tree. Only for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> is the home directory <samp class="listingcharacter">/root</samp>. As it would be cumbersome to always write out <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/<loginname></samp>, your own home directory can be abbreviated by using the tilde character, <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> (see Table 1.1). For accessing the home directories of other users, the notation <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">~<loginname></samp> is also possible.

In each directory, there are two special subdirectories, which are used for the formal management of the directory hierarchy. The directory named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.</samp> is a reference to the current directory, while the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">..</samp> directory is a reference to the parent directory. The following two copy commands show how you can use these directories. The first command copies the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp> file to the current directory, and if the current directory is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/name</samp>, then the new file is named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/name/fstab</samp>:

```
user$ cp /etc/fstab . 
```

The second example first activates the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">linuxbook</samp> directory in the home directory by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp>. The copy command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> then creates a backup copy of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fileuse.tex</samp> file, which contains the text of this chapter. The name of the backup copy is <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp><samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/fileuse.tex.bak</samp>:

```
user$ cd ~/linuxbook
user$ cp fileuse.tex ../fileuse.tex.bak 
```

So if the home directory is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/name</samp>, then you’ve just created a copy of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/name/linuxbook/fileuse.tex</samp>. The full name of the backup copy is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/name/fileuse.tex.bak.</samp> More <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> examples follow in the next section.

| Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> | Home directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> | Current directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">..</samp> | Parent directory of the current directory |

**Table 9.1**     Short Notations for Important Directories

### 9.1.2    Elementary Commands for Editing Files and Directories

As an alternative to the desktop system's file manager, experienced Linux users like to use text-based commands to manage files and directories. [Table 9.2](#09_001.html_t9.2) summarizes the most important commands.

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> | Changes the current directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> | Copies files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> | Changes to a directory that was last used |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> | Displays text files page by page |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> | Displays all files in a directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkdir</samp> | Creates a new directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv</samp> | Moves files or changes their names |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> | Deletes files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rmdir</samp> | Deletes directories |

**Table 9.2**     Elementary Commands for Handling Files and Directories

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> command changes to another directory. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd -</samp> changes back to the last active directory, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd ...</samp> changes to the parent directory, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> without further parameters changes to the home directory:

```
user$ cd /etc/samba 
```

In some distributions, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">autojump</samp> package to change directories. As a rule, you must install this package first. Autojump remembers which directories you work in most often. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">jumpstats</samp> provides you with the corresponding statistical data if needed.

If you want to change to a previously used directory, you need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j abc</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> represents the first letters of the directory name. Entering the often long path to the directory is not necessary!

If there are multiple matching directories, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> will change to the directory you used most recently. In addition, you can use the (Tab) key to choose between the directories available for selection.

The autojump website describes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> as a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> command that learns along, which is quite an apt description. It only takes a short time to get used to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp>; after that, you don't want to miss the command (see [https://github.com/joelthelion/autojump/wiki](https://github.com/joelthelion/autojump/wiki)). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> cannot replace <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp>, however, but only supplement it: Completing the pathname by using the (Tab) key works only for directories that are already in the autojump database. Thus, if you type <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd /e</samp> (Tab), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/e</samp> is usually added to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/</samp>. The analogous completion of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j /e</samp> (Tab), on the other hand, doesn’t work until <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> is already in the autojump database. In other words, to change to a directory autojump doesn’t know, it’s still better to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp>. (You can also get to the relevant directory by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp>, but you have to type the entire directory name). Too bad: it would be even more elegant if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> could be used as a full <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> replacement!

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> returns a list of all files in the current directory. If you want to see hidden files also, you must specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp> option as well. If you are interested not only in the file name but also in the file size, owner, and other details, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐l</samp> option will help you. By default, the output of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> is in alphabetical order. To sort the file list by the time of the last modification, file size, or file identifier, you want to use the <samp class="listingcharacter">-t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-S</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">-X</samp> options. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> reverses the sort order. The following command shows all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in the <samp class="listingcharacter">linuxbook</samp> directory, ordered by size (the largest file first):

```
user$ ls -l -S linuxbook/*.tex
...
-rw-r--r-- 1 kofler kofler  30113 2023-05-11 09:09 linuxbook/intro.tex
-rw-r--r-- 1 kofler kofler  63173 2023-01-29 08:05 linuxbook/kde.tex
-rw-r--r-- 1 kofler kofler  76498 2023-06-08 15:43 linuxbook/kernel.tex
... 
```

Briefly, some comments on the interpretation of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> results: the 10 characters at the beginning of the line indicate the file type and the access bits. The following file types are possible: the hyphen <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> for a normal file, <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> for a directory, <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> for a device file (block or char), or <samp class="listingcharacter">l</samp> for a symbolic link. The next three characters (<samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp>) indicate whether the owner is allowed to read, write, and/or execute the file. Analogous information follows for the members of the group as well as for all other system users.

The number following the 10 type and access characters indicates how many hard links reference the file. [Section 9.2](#09_002.html_h9.2) describes what links are. Details on managing access to Linux files follow in [Section 9.5](#09_005.html_h9.5). The other columns indicate the owner and group of the file (here <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler</samp> in each case), the size of the file, the date and time of the last modification, and finally the file name.

In most distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> is configured to display files and directories in different colors depending on their type. If that isn’t the case in your distribution, you can achieve this effect via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--color</samp> option. Conversely, to prevent the colored display, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">l --color=none</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> takes into account only the files of the current directory. To include the files from subdirectories as well, you want to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-R</samp> option. By the way, this option is also available for many other commands. The following command lists all files in all subdirectories. This list usually becomes quite long. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter">| less</samp> passes the result of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> on to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> so that you can scroll through the result:

```
user$ ls -lR | less 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp name1 name2</samp> copies the <samp class="listingcharacter">name1</samp> file. The copy gets the name <samp class="listingcharacter">name2</samp>. To copy multiple files, you need to call the command in the following way: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp name1 name2 ... target directory</samp>. The following commands make <samp class="listingcharacter">linuxbook</samp> the active directory, create <samp class="listingcharacter">bak</samp> as a subdirectory, and copy all <samp class="listingcharacter">*.tex</samp> files there:

```
user$ cd linuxbook
user$ mkdir bak
user$ cp *.tex bak/ 
```

To copy entire directories along with their contents, you must use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp -r</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">-r</samp> option causes the entire contents of the source directory to be processed recursively (including hidden files). If you want access rights and times to be preserved when copying, you need to use the <samp class="listingcharacter">-a</samp> option instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">-r</samp>.

The question whether the source directory itself or only its content is copied is somewhat difficult. If the target directory already exists, the new subdirectory named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sourcedirectory</samp> will be created in it and the entire contents of the source directory will be copied there. If, on the other hand, the target directory does not yet exist, it will be created. In this case, only the contents of the source directory will be copied to the newly created target directory, but not the source directory itself. The following examples illustrate the difference:

```
user$ mkdir test
user$ touch test/a
user$ mkdir test/b
user$ touch test/b/c
user$ mkdir target1
user$ cp -r test target1         
(the target1/ directory already exists)
user$ ls target1
test
user$ cp -r test target2         
(the target2/ directory does not exist yet)
user$ ls target2
a  b 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm file</samp> deletes the specified file irrevocably. Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> can only be used for files, but not for directories. For directories, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rmdir directory</samp> command is provided, but it works only if the directory is empty. In practice, you will often use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-rf</samp> option to delete directories. This means that recursively all subdirectories and files are deleted without confirmation:

```
user$ rm -rf linuxbuch-bak/    
(delete backup directory) 
```

It should therefore be clear to you that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm -rf</samp> is a very dangerous command!

### 9.1.3    Determining Space Requirements of Files and Directories

Although <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> tells you how big a file is, you’ll often want to know how much space the files take up in the entire directory, how much free space is still available on the hard disk, and so on. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp> commands help you in this regard.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> shows for all partitions or disks mounted in the file system how much storage space is available in total and how much of it is still free.

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> returns results for four partitions or volumes. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-h</samp> option causes all capacity information to be specified in readable numbers in KiB, MiB, or GiB. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> normally also displays various temporary file systems that are only used for internal administration and are not intended for storing regular files. You can avoid including those file systems in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> result by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-x tmpfs</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-x squashfs</samp> options (the latter option eliminates the Ubuntu-specific snap file systems):

```
user$ df -h -x tmpfs -x squashfs
File system          Size    Used Avail. Used% Mounted on
udev                  16G       0    16G    0% /dev
/dev/nvme0n1p4       119G     17G    96G   16% /
/dev/nvme0n1p1      1021M    238M   784M   24% /boot/efi
/dev/mapper/vg-root  1,5T    223G   1,2T   16% /crypt 
```

You can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> to determine which partition a directory is physically located in. In the following example, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/crypt/home/kofler</samp> directory is located in a logical volume that is responsible for the entire <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/crypt</samp> directory. On my notebook computer, there is an encrypted file system in this location:

```
user$ df -h /crypt/home/kofler/
/dev/mapper/vg-root  1.5T    223G  1.2T   16% /crypt 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp> determines the space requirements for the current directory as well as for all subdirectories contained therein. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-h</samp> option again makes sure that the result gets displayed in readable form (not in KiB blocks):

```
user$ du -h photos/2023
74M     photos/2023/04-easter
66M     photos/2023/06-miscellaneous
162M    photos/2023/08-corsica
...
2.0G    photos/2023 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">du</samp> does not provide the option to sort the result. This is exactly what the interactive <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ncdu</samp> command can do, which you have to install separately. It also provides the option to navigate through subdirectories using the cursor keys. I highly recommend it!

### 9.1.4    Wildcard Characters

In your daily work with files, you will often edit whole groups of files—for example, all files with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.pdf</samp> extension. To make this possible, wildcard characters are provided for entering Linux commands (see Table 1.3). Behind the scenes, the globbing shell mechanism is responsible for parsing these characters (see [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7), [Section 7.6](#07_006.html_h7.6)).

| Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp> | Exactly one character of your choice |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> | Any number (also zero) of any characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[abc]</samp> | Exactly one of the specified characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a-f]</samp> | A character from the specified range |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[!abc]</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">[^abc]</samp> | None of the specified characters |

**Table 9.3**     Wildcard Characters for Filenames

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">?</samp> is used to specify any character, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*</samp> is used to specify any number of characters (including zero). Those who are still familiar with DOS will not recognize any difference at first glance. But this impression is not quite true:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*</samp> captures almost all characters, including dots, so long as they are not at the beginning of the file name. If you want to edit all files, then you must use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*</samp> on Linux, not <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.*</samp>! Notes on hidden files follow later in this chapter.

*   Even multiple wildcard characters do not throw Linux off balance. For example, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*graph*</samp> to search for all files that contain <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">graph</samp> in their name, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">graphic.doc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">applegraph</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">README.graph</samp>.

If the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">?</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*</samp> wildcard characters are too general for you, you can achieve a higher degree of restriction by specifying square brackets. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">[abc]</samp> is a placeholder for one of the three letters <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">b</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">c</samp>. If a hyphen is specified between two letters or digits within the square brackets, then it represents a character between them:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">[a-f]*</samp> thus covers all files that begin with a letter between <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">f</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*[_.-]*</samp> represents all files that contain at least one dot, underscore, or hyphen somewhere in their file names.

*   The expression can be negated by an exclamation mark. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">[!a-z]*</samp> refers to all files that start with an uppercase letter or with a special character.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.[hc]</samp> captures all files ending with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.c</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.h</samp>.

The wildcard characters can also be used for directories. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*/*.jpg</samp> captures all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.jpg</samp> files located in subdirectories of the current directory (only one level below, so not also files in sub-sub-directories). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/*bin/*</samp> captures all files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/sbin</samp> directories.

The shell from which the command is called is responsible for analyzing the wildcard characters, not the command called in each case. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp>, the most commonly used shell on Linux, uses a lot of other special characters besides the wildcard characters just described, which have a special effect when a command is executed (see [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7), [Section 7.6](#07_006.html_h7.6)).

The following command copies all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.c</samp> files from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">project</samp> directory to the current directory:

```
user$ cp project/*.c . 
```

### 9.1.5    Complications with Using Wildcard Characters

Dealing with wildcard characters looks easier at first glance than it actually is. If you have difficulties with wildcard characters, you should just do some experiments with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">echo <wildcard_character></samp>. This command simply displays all file names captured by a wildcard character combination on the screen without changing the file names.

One problem is that <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> captures not only files, but also directories. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter">ls *</samp> displays not only all files in the current directory, but also the contents of all subdirectories captured via <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>. With the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> command, this problem can be circumvented by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp> option; however, this option is not available with other commands.

If you only want to edit directories, but no files, the character combination <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*/.</samp> will help you: it is only true if the searched object (<samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>) contains a back reference to itself (<samp class="listingcharacter">/.</samp>). This condition applies only to directories:

```
user$  echo */. 
```

The fact that not the respective program but the shell is responsible for the processing of the wildcard characters also has some drawbacks. For example, it’s impossible to search for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files even in subdirectories by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -R *.tex</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-R</samp> option for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> command actually causes a recursive search of subdirectories.

The reason that the command still doesn’t work is simple: the shell expands the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> pattern for the current directory and passes the list of found files to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>. This command then displays information about these files. If you don't have any directories with the extension <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.tex</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> is finished with that; even the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-R</samp> option can't change that anymore. Only directories that are passed as parameters are searched recursively.

To search for files, Linux therefore provides the much more flexible <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> command. The following example shows a list of all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in the current directory and in all subordinate directories (basic information on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> and additional examples follow in [Section 9.3.3](#09_003.html_h9.3.3)):

```
user$  find . -name '*.tex' 
```

Unfortunately, in Linux you cannot rename all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.x</samp> files to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.y</samp> files using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv *.x *.y</samp> command. The reason for this restriction is again the same as described earlier: the shell replaces <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.x</samp> with the list of all files matching this pattern; for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.y</samp>, there may be no matching files at all. For this reason, a list of several files and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.y</samp> expression are passed to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv</samp> command—and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv</samp> doesn’t know what to do with these arguments.

Here’s a concrete example. Let’s suppose that the current directory contains only the following files: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">marcus.x</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">peter.x</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">janet.x</samp>. When you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv *.x *.y</samp>, the shell replaces the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.x</samp> pattern with the three named files. The shell doesn’t find any matching files for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.y</samp> and passes the pattern as is. Only now will the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv</samp> command be started. It gets the following parameters, with which it can do nothing, as expected:

```
user$ mv marcus.x peter.x janet.x *.y 
```

Even if <samp class="listingcharacter">marcus.x peter.x janet.x marcus.y peter.y janet.y</samp> were passed to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv</samp> as a parameter list, the effect would not be the desired one. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv</samp> is generally not able to rename multiple files. So either multiple files are moved to another directory or only one file is renamed.

Of course, Unix experts have found a solution to this problem as well: You must use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> stream editor. Because of the rather complicated operation of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp>, examples like the following are really only suitable for shell programming.

Here’s briefly how it works: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> returns the list of files to be renamed and passes it to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">s</samp> command (regular search and replace) to create a list of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp> commands from it and in turn passes it to a new <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sh</samp> shell, which finally executes the commands. The following line copies all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.x</samp> files into <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.y</samp> files:

```
user$ ls *.x | sed 's/\(.*\)\.x$/cp & \1.y/' | sh 
```

Another solution is to formulate a small loop. The following command creates backup copies of all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files with the <samp class="listingcharacter">tex~</samp> extension. The <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> suffix is often used to indicate backup copies:

```
user$ for i in *.tex; do cp $i $i~; done 
```

### 9.1.6    Hidden Files and Directories

On macOS and Linux, files and directories whose names begin with a dot are considered hidden. The <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> wildcard character doesn’t even consider all files in a directory. Files starting with a dot (often configuration files that should be invisible) are ignored.

Now, if you think you can capture invisible files using <samp class="listingcharacter">.*</samp>, things will get worse: this refers not only to invisible files that start with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.</samp>, but also to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">..</samp> directories (i.e., the current and the parent directory). If the respective command is able to process entire directories, the consequences can be fatal.

The problem can be avoided by using the search pattern <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.[!.]*</samp>, which covers all file names for which the first character is a dot, that have at least one other character that is not a dot, and that have any number (including zero) of other characters:

```
user$ echo .[!.]* 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp> option can be used along with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> command. It causes all files to be displayed, even invisible ones. However, masks (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">*rc*</samp>) must not be specified when using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> in this way. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp> only works if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> is allowed to search for the files itself and the shell doesn’t take over this task.

In this case too, only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> really works universally. The following command finds all hidden files in the current directory:

```
user$ find -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '.*' 
```

### 9.1.7    Special Types of Files (Links, Devices, and the Like)

In addition to ordinary files, Linux knows a number of special types, like directories, links, and device files for accessing hardware components. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls ‐l</samp> identifies such special types by the first character of the output (see [Table 9.4](#09_001.html_t9.4)):

```
user$ ls -l /dev/s*
brw-rw----. 1 root disk ... /dev/sda                  
(block device)
brw-rw----. 1 root disk ... /dev/sda1                 
(block device)
crw-rw----. 1 root disk ... /dev/sg0                  
(character device)
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root ... /dev/stderr -> /proc/self/fd/2  
(link)
... 
```

| Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> | Ordinary file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> | Directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">l</samp> | Symbolic link |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> | Character-based device (character device) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | Block-based device (block device) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> | Socket (interprocess communication) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp> | Pipe, first in first out (FIFO) |

**Table 9.4**     Identification of Special Files in First Column of ls Results

You’ll learn more about links in the next section, and about device files in [Section 9.9](#09_009.html_h9.9). FIFO files allow one process to write to the file and a second process to read the data from it. Socket files are also used for communication between processes, but they are implemented much more efficiently internally.

## 9.2    Links

Links are references to files or directories. They allow you to access the same file from different locations in the directory structure without having to physically store that file multiple times. Links are thus an important tool for avoiding redundancies. In the Linux file system, links are particularly common in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib</samp> directories. For example, take a look at the result of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l /usr/bin</samp> command.

The easiest way to understand links is to use an example. Let’s suppose there is a file named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test</samp> directory; the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ln abc xyz</samp> command apparently creates a new file named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xyz</samp>. But in reality, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xyz</samp> are just two references to one and the same file. The only way to check this is to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> command using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-l</samp> option. In the second column, it indicates how many links reference a specific file; in this example, that’s two files. If the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-i</samp> option is also used, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> also specifies the inode of the file, which is identical for links. Inodes are internal identification numbers of the file system.

```
user$ ls -li
 59293 -rw-r--r--   1 root     root    1004 Oct  4 16:40 abc
user$ ln abc xyz                
user$ ls -li                    
 59293 -rw-r--r--   2 root     root    1004 Oct  4 16:40 abc
 59293 -rw-r--r--   2 root     root    1004 Oct  4 16:40 xyz 
```

If you now change one of the two files (no matter which one), the other file will automatically change as well—because in reality there is only one file! If you delete one of the two files, you will only reduce the number of links.

### Backup Files from Linked Files Are an Issue

If you edit hard-linked files using a text editor, strange results sometimes occur: the link references the backup file after the first save and nothing on the second save.

Here’s why: Some editors create a backup file when saving by renaming the existing file, like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc~</samp>. The changed file is created completely new, gets a new inode, and is thus free of any links. A solution to this problem can be to use symbolic links discussed ahead.

Linux uses two types of links. The previous example presented hard links as created by default by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ln</samp> command. Aside from that, if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ln</samp> is used with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-s</samp> option, the command creates symbolic links. Symbolic links are sometimes also referred to as soft links. They have the advantages that they can point from one disk to another and that they can be applied not only to files but also to directories. Neither is usually possible with hard links. A special case is hard links to directories, which are possible but can only be created by <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>.

With symbolic links, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> indicates where the original file is located. However, no counter is maintained to indicate from how many places the source file is referenced.

Internally, the difference between hard links and symbolic links is that in the one case the inode is saved, and in the other case the file name or (for links beyond a directory) the path specification is saved:

```
user$ ln -s abc efg
user$ ls -li
 59293 -rw-r--r--   2 root     root    1004 Oct  4 16:40 abc
 59310 lrwxrwxrwx   1 root     root       3 Oct  4 16:52 efg -> abc
 59293 -rw-r--r--   2 root     root    1004 Oct  4 16:40 xyz 
```

### Tip

Before setting up a symbolic link, you should always change to the directory that will contain the link. Otherwise, the link may not point where you expect it to.

Symbolic links behave a little differently than fixed links. Deleting the source file (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc</samp> from the previous example) does not change the link to this file, but <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efg</samp> then references a file that does not exist at all. If, on the other hand, the symbolic link is deleted, this will have no effect on the source file.

Symbolic links can be created not only for files, but also for directories. This can cause some confusion because a symbolic link apparently duplicates entire directory trees. But in reality the directory link is just an additional path to the same files and subdirectories.

In general, you should try to use only relative paths in links if possible. This will help you to avoid problems that can arise when you mount directories via NFS or when you move directories.

### Hard Links versus Symbolic Links

Both hard links and symbolic links have advantages. Symbolic links are easier to use, but hard links consume less memory and are faster.

## 9.3    Finding Files (find, grep, and locate Commands)

Linux provides various options to search for files (see [Table 9.5](#09_003.html_t9.5)). The most suitable command depends on the type of file (text file, program, etc.) and what information is known—such as the parts of the file name or search terms for the content.

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> | Searches for text in a text file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> | Searches for files by name, date, size, and so on |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> | Searches for files by their name |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">whereis</samp> | Searches for files in predefined directories |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> | Searches for programs in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> directories |

**Table 9.5**     Commands for Finding Files

### 9.3.1    which and whereis

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> searches for the specified command. It returns the full name of the command that would be executed if the command name were called without path information. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> searches only the directories specified in <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> and therefore works exceptionally fast. <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> contains a list of directories where programs are located. Note, however, that <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> contains more directories for <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> than for ordinary users. So if you are looking for system commands, you have to log in as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>:

```
user$ which emacs
/usr/bin/emacs 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">whereis</samp> searches all common paths for binary files, configuration files, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> pages and source code for the specified file name. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">whereis</samp> thus covers more directories than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">which</samp> and is not limited to programs. However, it fails for files that are not in the directories predefined for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">whereis</samp> (see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man whereis</samp>):

```
user$ whereis fstab
fstab: /etc/fstab /usr/include/fstab.h /usr/share/man/man5/fstab.5.gz 
```

### 9.3.2    locate

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate <pattern></samp> finds files where the specified search pattern occurs in the full file name—that is, in the path plus the file name.

The search is very fast: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> does not search the file system, but accesses a database that contains a list of all file names in the file system. Depending on the distribution, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> displays only those files to which the user actually has access. If necessary, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> when searching for system files. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> can only be used if the appropriate package is installed, which is not the case by default for all distributions.

The following command searches the X configuration file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xorg.conf</samp>:

```
user$ locate xorg.conf
/usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d
/usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/10-evdev.conf
/usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/10-quirks.conf
/usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/11-evdev-quirks.conf
... 
```

The search for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dvips</samp> returns a lot of hits (if this package and LaTeX is installed) because the search term occurs in multiple directory names. Instead of displaying all search results, they are counted using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wc</samp>:

```
user$ locate dvips | wc -l
    421 
```

The number of results will be much smaller if you search only for files ending with <samp class="listingcharacter">dvips</samp>:

```
user$ locate '*dvips'
/usr/bin/dvips
/usr/bin/odvips
/usr/bin/opdvips
/usr/bin/pdvips
/usr/local/texmf/dvips
/usr/local/texmf/fonts/map/dvips
... 
```

The quality of the search results is highly dependent on the up-to-dateness of the database for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp>. In most distributions, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> database is updated once a day by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">updatedb</samp> command. Of course, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">updatedb</samp> can also be run manually at any time, but this requires <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges.

For performance reasons, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">updatedb</samp> are being installed less and less by default. This can be solved in most distributions by installing the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">plocate</samp> package. The file database is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/plocate/ #plocate.db</samp> file and is regularly updated by a cron or timer job. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/updatedb.conf</samp> configuration file determines which directories and file systems are not included (e.g., network file systems).

On openSUSE, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp> is implemented by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mlocate</samp> package, which must be installed if required. The configuration is also done in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/updatedb.conf</samp> file. The resulting database ends up in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/mlocate</samp> directory.

### 9.3.3    find and grep

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> is a powerful and complex command for searching files. It takes into account various search criteria: a pattern for the file name, the file size, the date of creation or last access, and so on. A complete reference of all options is contained in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man find</samp>.

However, the following examples are probably the best introduction to using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp>. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> is a comparatively slow command because it searches the file system directory by directory.

Without any additional parameters, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> returns a list of all files in the current directory and in all subdirectories:

```
user$ find
... 
```

The following command searches for all files in the current directory and in all subdirectories that begin with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.e</samp>:

```
user$ find -name '.e*'
./.evolution
./.emacs
./.emacs~
./.esd_auth
... 
```

Starting from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/texmf</samp> directory, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> searches for all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in a directory ending with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">latex</samp>:

```
user$ find /usr/share/texmf -path '*latex/*.tex'
/usr/share/texmf/ptex/platex/base/plnews03.tex
/usr/share/texmf/ptex/platex/base/kinsoku.tex
... 
```

In the next example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> searches for all directories inside <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/</samp>. Ordinary files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp>, on the other hand, will not be displayed. The results list is sorted alphabetically by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sort</samp>, which is not the case by default:

```
root# find /etc -type d | sort
/etc
/etc/acpi
/etc/acpi/actions
... 
```

Next, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> searches for all files in the (sub)directories of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp> that belong to users of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">users</samp> group and whose contents have been modified in some way in the last five days:

```
root# find /home -group users -mtime -5
... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find -mtime +5</samp> finds files that were modified more than five days ago, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐mtime 5</samp> returns such files that were modified exactly five days ago. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> calculates in multiples of 24 hours from the current time. If you use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-ctime</samp> option instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-mtime</samp>, the inode change time will be taken as the time of change. This point in time also changes, for example, if the access rights are changed rather than the content.

The following command deletes all backup files in the current directory and in all subdirectories. The list of all relevant files is created using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> and passed on to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> by means of command substitution <samp class="listingcharacter">$(command)</samp>:

```
user$ rm $(find . -name '*~') 
```

If there are many files, an error will occur when you run the above command: The command line with all <samp class="listingcharacter">*~</samp> files will become so long that it exceeds the maximum command line length. In such cases, you must use either the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-exec</samp> option of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> command or the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> command.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> command searches a text file for a search pattern. Depending on the options settings, the command then displays the text passages it has found or simply indicates in how many lines the search pattern was found. The search pattern is a so-called regular expression. The following command searches all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in the current directory for the string “emacs”. The list of all lines found, each preceded by the file name, is displayed in the terminal.

```
user$ grep emacs *.tex
... 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> determines how often the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">arctan</samp> function is used in the specified <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.c</samp> files:

```
user$ grep -c 'arctan\(.*\)' *.c 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep -v</samp> returns all lines that do not contain the search pattern. In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> removes all lines from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">configfile</samp> that begin with the # character—that is, all comments. In addition, the trailing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp> command eliminates all empty lines. The final result will be stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nocomments</samp> file. The instruction is useful when a few configuration lines are drowned out by hundreds or thousands of comment lines:

```
user$ grep -v '^#' configfile | cat -s > nocomments 
```

You can also combine <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> to perform particularly effective searches. In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> scans all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files to see if they contain the “emacs” string. If they do, the respective file name will be displayed on the screen. Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-print</samp> option must not be specified before <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-exec</samp>. Unlike the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep emacs *.tex</samp> example, this example also takes into account <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files in subdirectories nested to any depth:

```
user$ find -name '*.tex' -type f -exec grep -q emacs {}  \; -print
... 
```

The following command searches all files in the current directory that are smaller than 10 KiB for the regular expression, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">case.*in</samp>. The list of found files is saved in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">result</samp> file. By limiting the file size to 10 KiB, an attempt is made to exclude binary files, which are usually considerably larger, from the search:

```
user$ find -name '*' -maxdepth 1 -size -10k -exec grep -q \
        case.*in {} \; -print > result 
```

## 9.4    Greater Convenience with Modern Commands

Most of the Linux commands I present in this book are decades old. That's not necessarily a bad thing: the commands are established, mature, and available on virtually any Linux machine or cloud instance.

Nevertheless, more and more “new” commands have been introduced in recent years that perform similar functions to existing commands but are more convenient to use and present their results more clearly and in colors (see [Table 9.6](#09_004.html_t9.6)). Most of these commands are explicitly intended for interactive use, not for use in scripts!

I would like to briefly introduce you to four selected tools here. The command you probably run most often in the terminal is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exa</samp> command or its fork <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">eza</samp> ([https://github.com/eza-community/eza](https://github.com/eza-community/eza)) performs the same task, but formats the result in a more readable way and has various additional functions. You can try, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exa -l --tree</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exa -l --git</samp>! <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exa</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">eza</samp> can be installed as a package in many distributions. (For RHEL, you must enable the EPEL package source.)

In the list of the most important commands, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> commands follow immediately after <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> to view the contents of a text file. How many times have you been annoyed by the monotonous presentation of the text? This can be remedied by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bat</samp> command, which is available as a package in most distributions. It tries to recognize the content of the text and then uses appropriate syntax highlighting and displays line numbers (see [Figure 9.1](#09_004.html_f9.1)).

[![Representation of Python Script in Terminal Using bat](bilderklein/klein09_001.png)](img-f9.1.html)

**Figure 9.1**     Representation of Python Script in Terminal Using bat

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bat</samp> relies on your terminal to use a dark background by default. To make the screenshots in this book easier to read, I use a light background. In this case, you must pass an appropriate theme option to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bat</samp> (such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--theme</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gruvbox-light</samp>) or set it permanently in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.config/bat/config</samp> configuration file.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> stands for fuzzy finder. If the command is started without any other options, it searches the current directory like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find . -type f</samp> for files and displays the result list. By entering a search pattern, you can filter the result interactively and then select a file using the cursor keys and (Enter) or multiple files by pressing the (Tab) key. The file names will then be displayed.

This basic function sounds rather unspectacular. As a matter of fact, however, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> provides countless usage options. For example, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> to pass the selected file to another program:

```
user$ fzf | xargs -r $EDITOR 
```

Provided that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> is installed correctly, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> can also be triggered by typing <samp class="listingcharacter">**</samp> and pressing (Tab), allowing the interactive completion of commands: Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">emacs **</samp> (Tab), you can open the previously selected file. When you enter <samp class="listingcharacter">kill -9 **</samp> and press (Tab), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> provides processes you can select, and when you enter <samp class="listingcharacter">ssh **</samp> and press <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement"></samp> (Tab), it provides host names for selection. (Ctrl)+(T) lists all files, (Ctrl)+(R) lists recently executed commands, and (Alt)+(C) helps <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> to change to a subdirectory.

### Tip

On YouTube, you can find various videos that illustrate the application of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> pretty well. Even though I'm not usually a video fan, in this case, it’s worth it!

If you want to know how much space is required by various directories and subdirectories, you usually use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp>. However, the result is not ordered by size. A much more convenient option is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ncdu</samp>, which is available in the package of the same name in many distributions. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ncdu</samp> first runs through the entire directory tree, which can take a while. Then it shows only the first directory level, with the largest directory first. Subsequently, you can comfortably explore the subdirectories using the cursor keys.

| Command | Replaces.../Similar Function To... |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bat</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> with syntax highlighting and line numbers |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">duf</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">erd</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">erdtree</samp>) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tree</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fd</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fx</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> for JSON files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fzf</samp> | Fuzzy finder (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">glow</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> for markdown files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">j</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lfs</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsd</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ncdu</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp>, but interactively |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tldr</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> (example-based short version) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">z</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> |

**Table 9.6**     New Commands for Standard Tasks

### Disadvantages of the New Commands

The main problem with the commands presented here is their installation. If you work primarily on one Linux computer, the required installation commands aren’t important, especially since many of the tools presented here are already so well established that there are packages in the usual package sources. But in my day-to-day work, I'm constantly switching back and forth between countless Linux installations, most of which are in virtual machines, in the cloud, or in Docker containers. Before I go to the trouble of installing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">duf</samp>, I use the conventional <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp>.

## 9.5    Access Rights, Users, and Group Membership

Linux is a multiuser system and therefore needs mechanisms to control who can access which files, who can modify them, and so on. The basis of the access system is the management of users and groups, which is described in [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14), [Section 14.5](#14_005.html_h14.5). For now, let's just assume that every user on Linux is assigned to a user account and one or several groups. This minimum requirement is sufficient to understand the concept of file access rights.

### 9.5.1    Access Rights for Files

The following information is stored with each file or directory:

*   The owner of the file

*   A group to which the file is to be assigned

*   Nine access bits (<samp class="listingcharacter">rwxrwxrwx</samp> for read/write/execute for the owner, for all group members and for the rest of the world)

*   A few more additional bits for special functions

The owner of a file is usually the person who created the file. The primary group of the owner is typically used as the group—as the owner's default group.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> access information controls who may read, write, and execute the file. This information is stored separately for the owner, for the group, and for all other users. This makes it possible to give the owner more rights than other users. The information is usually referred to as access bits because it is stored internally as a number with bitwise coding.

#### Who Is Allowed to Delete a File?

The access rights to a file have no influence on who is allowed to delete a file. This is decided solely by the person who has access to the directory in which the file is located! A file may be deleted by anyone who has the <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> rights for the directory. More information about directory access rights follows in the next section.

The access bits, the owner, and the group membership of a file can be viewed via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp>. For a typical text file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> returns the following result:

```
michael$ ls -l file.txt
-rw-r-----   1 michael  users        3529 Oct  4 15:43 file.txt 
```

Brief interpretation: The first character indicates the file type. The <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> sign means that it is a normal file. Other possibilities are <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> for a directory, <samp class="listingcharacter">l</samp> for a symbolic link, and so on.

The three characters <samp class="listingcharacter">rw-</samp> indicate that the file can be read and modified by the owner <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">michael</samp>. For a text file, the first <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> bit is disabled, so the file cannot be executed.

The following three characters, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">r--</samp>, indicate that all members of the <samp class="listingcharacter">users</samp> group may read the file but not modify it.

The final three characters, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">---</samp>, indicate that other users—who are neither <samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp> nor members of the <samp class="listingcharacter">users</samp> group—are not allowed to read or modify the file.

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">michael</samp> wants this file to be readable by all users, then he must enable the final <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> bit. To do this, he uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod o+r</samp> command:

```
michael$ chmod o+r file.txt
michael$ ls file.txt -l
-rw-r--r--   1 michael  users        3529 Oct  4 15:43 file.txt 
```

Sometimes two or more users should be allowed to modify the file. A new group to which these users belong can be created for this purpose. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">michael</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">catherine</samp> form the documentation team of a company, the group name would be something like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">docuteam</samp>. Then the group membership can be changed using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chgrp</samp>:

```
michael$ chgrp docuteam file.txt
michael$ chmod g+rw file.txt
michael$ ls file.txt -l
-rw-rw-r--   1 michael  docuteam     3529 Oct  4 15:43 file.txt 
```

As a matter of fact, file sharing is even a little more tricky: it is also necessary to ensure that all users have access to the directory in which the files are located. More details on this topic will follow shortly.

Instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">rwxrwxrwx</samp> notation, the nine access bits as well as three additional special bits are often also represented in octal. This is probably the most popular application of this number system based on the number eight to date. The access bits for the user, the group, and all others are each assigned a digit (see [Table 9.7](#09_005.html_t9.7)).

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">4000 = s = setuid</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">2000 = s = setgid</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">1000 = t = sticky</samp> | Special bits |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">400 = r = read</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">200 = w = write</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">100 = x = execute</samp> | Access bits for the owner (u = user in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">40 = r</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">20 = w</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">10 = x</samp> | Access bits for group members (g = group) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">4 = r</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">2 = w</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">1 = x</samp> | Access bits for all others (o = others) |

**Table 9.7**     Octal Codes for Access Bits

Each digit is composed of the values <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">4</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">2</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">1</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">r</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">w</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">x</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">660</samp> thus means <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rw-rw----</samp>, while <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">777</samp> stands for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rwxrwxrwx</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">setuid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">setgid</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">sticky</samp> bits presented in [Section 9.6](#09_006.html_h9.6) have octal values of 4000, 2000, and 1000, respectively.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> command enables you to also set the access bits in octal, which many experienced users prefer because of the reduced typing effort:

```
user$ chmod 640 file.txt 
```

Surprisingly, however, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> is not able to represent the access bits in octal form. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">stat</samp> command can help you in this respect:

```
user$ stat -c "%a %n" *
755 php53 samples
550 Private
755 samples
... 
```

Access to hardware components such as hard disks, DVD drives, interfaces, and so on is provided on Linux via devices (see [Section 9.9](#09_009.html_h9.9)). To be able to specifically control which user may access which devices, different user groups are assigned to the devices. For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ttyS*</samp> devices for the serial ports are assigned to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dialout</samp> group on Debian and Ubuntu:

```
root# ls -l /dev/ttyS1
crw-rw----   1 root     dialout       5,  65 Jul 18  /dev/ttyS1 
```

If the system administrator wants the user <samp class="listingcharacter">herbert</samp> to be allowed to use the serial port, he adds <samp class="listingcharacter">herbert</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">dialout</samp> group:

```
root# usermod -a -G dialout herbert 
```

### 9.5.2    Access Rights for Directories

Basically, the nine access bits are also valid for directories, but they have a slightly different meaning there:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> bit allows you to get the list of file names (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> command).

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> bit gives you the right to change the contents of a directory—for example, to create a new file or rename or delete an existing file.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> bit allows you to change to a directory (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> command). However, you can only access files whose names you know. Only the <samp class="listingcharacter">rx</samp> combination makes it possible to process a directory correctly—for example, using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> to determine a list of all file names, including detailed information on each file. If both <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> are set, new files can be created in the directory.

The somewhat strange interpretation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> access rights is due to the fact that directories are regarded by the file system as a special case of a file; the contents of the “file” directory is a listing of the names of the files that are in the directory and their inode numbers.

[Table 9.8](#09_005.html_t9.8) summarizes which access rights are required for a directory and the file it contains in order to perform certain actions. The - sign in the File column indicates that the file access rights are not relevant. As usual, these rules apply only to ordinary users. <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> is allowed to do everything regardless of the access rights set!

| Action | Command | File | Directory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Change to directory | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd directory</samp> | - | x |
| Determine list of files | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls directory/*</samp> | - | r |
| Read file information | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l directory/*</samp> | - | rx |
| Create new file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">touch directory/newfile</samp> | - | wx |
| Read file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less directory/file</samp> | r | x |
| Change existing file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat >> directory/file</samp> | w | x |
| Delete file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm directory/file</samp> | - | wx |
| Run program | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">directory/program</samp> | x | x |
| Run script file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">directory/script</samp> | rx | x |

**Table 9.8**     Required Access Rights for Standard Actions

For nested directories, the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> bit is particularly decisive for the base directories. If it isn’t set, the subdirectories cannot be used. In practice, it’s usually convenient to set the <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> bit for base directories as well. If the read permission is missing, the user must know the name of the subdirectory. The operations permitted in the subdirectory depend exclusively on the <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> bits of this directory. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> rights are set for the subdirectory, files can be read, created, modified, and deleted—even if the <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> rights are missing in the base directories!
