For a better understanding, you can take a look at the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/</samp> directory, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp> directory, and a user directory contained in it:

```
root# ls -ld /
drwxr-xr-x ... root root ... /home/
root# ls -ld /home/
drwxr-xr-x ... root root ... /home/
root# ls -ld /home/kofler/    
(on Debian, Ubuntu)
drwxr-xr-x ... kofler kofler ... /home/kofler/ 
```

For <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp>, the following applies: Anyone is allowed to determine the names of the files and subdirectories contained in this directory, as well as query detailed information about them; that is, anyone can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l /home</samp>. However, only <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> is allowed to set up new home directories using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkdir /home/newuser</samp>.

For <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/kofler</samp>, the following applies: Only the user <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler</samp> is allowed to create new files in this directory. All other users may look into the directory (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp>), but they cannot change anything. It is up to the owner of the home directory to set the access rights for his or her own files and subdirectories, if necessary, so that read access is also impossible.

Note that <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler</samp> is of course allowed to create, modify, and delete files in the home directory, although this user has no write permissions in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp>!

Some Linux distributions, such as Fedora or Red Hat, set the access rights for the home directories more restrictively and really only allow the owner to look into the directory:

```
root# ls -ld /home/kofler/    
(on Fedora, RHEL)
drwx------ ... kofler kofler ... /home/kofler/ 
```

The home directories just mentioned are an example of directories that are intended for a specific user only. But how do you set up directories that multiple users can share—for example, a project directory for users <samp class="listingcharacter">sebastian</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">matthew</samp> so that both can read and modify files in the directory?

The solution to such problems is the use of groups. You can create a new <samp class="listingcharacter">projectxy</samp> group and assign <samp class="listingcharacter">sebastian</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">matthew</samp> to this group. Then you still need a project directory that is assigned to this group:

```
root# addgroup projectxy
root# usermod -a -G projectxy sebastian
root# usermod -a -G projectxy matthew
root# mkdir -p /projects/xy
root# chgrp projectxy /projects/xy
root# chmod 755 /projects
root# chmod 2770 /projects/xy
root# ls -ld /projects/xy
drwxrws--- ... root projectxy ... /projects/xy 
```

The setting of access rights for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/projects</samp> is the same as for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp> directory: Only <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> is allowed to create new files and directories in it. All others may use the directories.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/projects/xy</samp> directory, all members of the <samp class="listingcharacter">projectxy</samp> group have read and write permissions, so in this example that’s <samp class="listingcharacter">sebastian</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">matthew</samp>.

The only special feature is the setgid bit for this directory (octal code 2000). It causes files and directories created in this directory to be automatically assigned to the <samp class="listingcharacter">projectxy</samp> group, not to the group of the user who creates the file. This avoids the case where <samp class="listingcharacter">sebastian</samp> creates a new file, and <samp class="listingcharacter">matthew</samp> sees and reads it but cannot modify it. Background information on the setgid bit follows in the next section.

## 9.6    Special Bits and the umask Setting

You are now familiar with the principle of access rights, but two finishing touches are still missing: First, there are three more access bits with the strange names of setuid, setgid, and sticky, the meaning of which will be explained ahead. Second, there is still the question of who owns newly created files. Here the so-called umask setting plays a major role.

### 9.6.1    Setuid, Setgid, and Sticky Bit

The meaning of the three times three access bits, <samp class="listingcharacter">rwxrwxrwx</samp>, is easy to understand. In addition, three other pieces of information can be stored with the access information of files and directories: the setuid bit, the setgid bit, and the sticky bit. As a rule, only system administrators need to know these special bits.

The setuid bit is often called the suid bit for short. It causes programs to always run as if the owner himself had started the program. Often the owner of programs is <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>; then anyone can run the program as if they were <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. Internally, the user identification number of the owner of the file and not the UID of the current user is used for the execution of the program.

The bit is used to give additional rights to ordinary owners, which are valid only when this program is executed. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin/passwd</samp> command is an example of using the setuid bit. It allows each user to change their own password. However, the passwords are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp> file, to which only <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> has read and write access. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> must be run with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> displays the letter <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">S</samp> instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> for such programs at the user access bits—that is, in the first <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> group: a lowercase <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> if the execute bit is also set (the normal case), and an uppercase <samp class="listingcharacter">S</samp> if only the setuid bit but not the execute bit is set. The octal value of this bit for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> is 4000:

```
user$ ls -l /bin/mount
-rwsr-xr-x    1 root   root    68508 Feb 25  01:11 /bin/mount

user$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
-rwsr-xr-x ... root root ... /usr/bin/passwd 
```

If you want to find all programs that have the setuid bit set, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-perm -4000</samp> option. In a default Ubuntu installation, the command finds around 15 setuid programs:

```
user find /usr/bin /usr/sbin/ /bin /sbin -perm -4000
/usr/bin/chsh
/usr/bin/chfn
/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/gpasswd
/usr/bin/newgrp
/usr/bin/sudo
... 
```

#### Attention: Security Risk!

The setuid bit can easily become a security risk—especially if other programs are started while the program is running. For this reason, you should avoid using the setuid bit whenever possible.

For script files (<samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp>, Python, Tcl, and so on) the setuid bit is generally ignored on Linux! So it is impossible to give root privileges to a script by using a setuid bit.

The setgid bit has a similar effect on programs as setuid. However, the group identification number of the file is used during the execution of the program, not the group ID (GID) of the current user. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> displays the letter <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">S</samp> instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> for the group access bits—that is, in the second <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> group—for such programs. The octal value of this bit is 2000.

For directories, the setgid bit has a completely different meaning: if it is set, newly created files within this directory will be assigned the group of the directory—instead of the group of the person who creates the file, as is usually the case.

In reality, the setgid bit is used when multiple users are supposed to share a directory. In this case, it’s useful to have new files be assigned to the common group and not to the currently active group of the user who creates the file. For this reason, the setgid bit in the previous section was used for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/projects/xy</samp> directory.

For directories in which everyone is allowed to change the files, the sticky bit makes sure that everyone is only allowed to delete their own files and not those of other users. For example, the bit is set for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/tmp</samp> directory. Every user is allowed to create temporary files in this directory. However, you should avoid allowing all users to rename or delete foreign files at will. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> displays the letter <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> for all valid access bits in such programs. The octal value of this bit is 1000\. The meaning of the sticky bit is specific to Linux! In other Unix variants, the bit may have a different meaning or no meaning at all:

```
user$ ls -ld /tmp/
drwxrwxrwt  ... root root ... /tmp/ 
```

The easiest way to set the special bits is to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> if you use octal code—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod 2770 directory</samp>. But of course, it’s also possible to change the <samp class="listingcharacter">owner+ bit</samp> in the usual <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> syntax:

```
root# chmod u+s file  
(sets the setuid bit)
root# chmod u-s file  
(deletes the setuid bit)
root# chmod g+s file  
(sets the setgid bit)
root# chmod g-s file  
(deletes the setgid bit)
root# chmod +t  file  
(sets the sticky bit)
root# chmod -t  file  
(deletes the sticky bit) 
```

In the past, you could use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> only to set special bits in octal notation, but not to remove them again. Meanwhile this possibility exists, but under certain circumstances; for example, to delete the setgid bit from directories, you have to specify the octal code with five digits: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod 2770 dir</samp> sets the setgid bit. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod 0770 dir</samp> leaves the setgid bit unchanged! Only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod 00770 dir</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod g-s dir</samp> disables it again.

Interpreting the results of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> is no straightforward task:

*   The setuid bit is indicated by the letters <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">S</samp> instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> in the first <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> group.

*   The setgid bit is indicated by the letters <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">S</samp> instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> in the second <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> group.

*   The sticky bit is indicated by the letters <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> in the third <samp class="listingcharacter">rwx</samp> group.

The uppercase letters <samp class="listingcharacter">S</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> are only applied if the corresponding execute bit is not set. This is usually an indication that the special bits are being used incorrectly.

Within Linux, information about the function of a file is stored together with the access bits and the special bits. For example, it can be a normal file, a directory, a link, a block device, and so on.

Most file management programs hide this additional information.

However, there are a few programs that display this information as a numerical value. For an ordinary file, the complete specification is then <samp class="listingcharacter">100000</samp> (identifier for an ordinary file) plus <samp class="listingcharacter">N000</samp> (special bits) plus <samp class="listingcharacter">xxx</samp> (access bits)—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">100760</samp>. The numeric codes for the file types are described in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man 2 stat</samp>.

### 9.6.2    Owner and Group of New Files

This section deals with the question of what factors determine the access information of new files. To try this out easily, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">touch</samp> command. This command creates a new, empty file if the specified file doesn’t yet exist.

Say that the user <samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp> creates a new file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">myFile1</samp>. It should come as no surprise that this file again belongs to <samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp>; after all, he just created it himself. The group membership was automatically set to <samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp> is the primary group of the user <samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp>. Some distributions do not assign a separate group to each user but instead assign the <samp class="listingcharacter">users</samp> group to all users:

```
michael$ touch myFile1
michael$ ls -l myFile1
-rw-r--r--    1 michael   michael           0 Jun 14 16:45 myFile1 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">michael</samp> belongs to a number of other groups (<samp class="listingcharacter">groups</samp> command). To create a file that does not belong to the primary group, the active group must be changed first (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newgrp</samp> command):

```
michael$ groups
michael adm admin cdrom docuteam dialout lpadmin plugdev sambashare
michael$ newgrp docuteam
michael$ touch myFile2
michael$ ls -l myFile2
-rw-r--r--    1 michael   docuteam           0 Jun 14 17:02 myFile2 
```

Of course, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">myFile2</samp> could also have been created without a preceding <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newgrp</samp>. Then the group membership would have had to be changed afterward using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chgrp</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newgrp</samp> is useful when multiple new files are created that should automatically belong to a certain group.

The previous two examples show that new files are automatically owned by the user who creates them. Typically, the user's primary group is used as the group membership. However, there are two exceptions to this:

*   If the user has made another of his groups the current group via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newgrp</samp>, the new file belongs to that group.

*   If the setgid bit is set in a directory (see the previous section), then files created in it are automatically assigned to the same group as the directory. The user's active group is not taken into account.

### 9.6.3    Access Bits of New Files (umask)

Regarding the access bits, things are a bit more complicated. Linux actually provides that new files get the access bits <samp class="listingcharacter">rw-rw-rw</samp> (octal 666), so they may be read and modified by everyone. New directories and program files created by a compiler automatically get the access bits <samp class="listingcharacter">rwxrwxrwx</samp> (777), so they can be executed by anyone.

However, this basic setting would be too permissive for practical work with multiple users. That is why all Linux shells provide for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umask</samp> setting. This is a numerical value that specifies the bits that are subtracted from the standard access bits. You can determine the current setting of the <samp class="listingcharacter">umask</samp> value by using the command of the same name and, if necessary, change it for the course of the active session. Depending on the distribution, different default settings apply:

```
michael$  umask  
(Arch Linux, Debian, Fedora, RHEL, SUSE)
0022
michael$  umask  
(Ubuntu)
0002 
```

Thus, many Linux distributions use the <samp class="listingcharacter">umask</samp> value 022 (<samp class="listingcharacter">----w--w-</samp>). For this reason, new files get the access bits 666 - 022 = 644 (<samp class="listingcharacter">rw-r--r--</samp>), while new directories and programs get the access bits 777 - 022 = 755 (<samp class="listingcharacter">rwxr-xr-x</samp>). The <samp class="listingcharacter">umask</samp> value 002, which is common in Ubuntu, is more liberal: new files get the access bits 666 - 002 = 664 (<samp class="listingcharacter">rw-rw-r--</samp>), new directories 777 - 002 = 775 (<samp class="listingcharacter">rwxrwxr-x</samp>).

As each user typically uses their own group on Linux, the difference is negligible in practice. In both cases, custom files are readable by other users, but not modifiable.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>, the setting 0022 is valid for all distributions I tested:

```
root# umask
0022 
```

How must <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umask</samp> be set so that new files get the access rights <samp class="listingcharacter">rw-r----- = 640</samp> and new directories <samp class="listingcharacter">rwxr-x--- = 750</samp>? The answer results from the subtraction of 777 minus the octal target value for directories—that is, 777 – 750 = 027:

```
michael$ umask 27
michael$ touch new-file
michael$ mkdir new-directory
michael$ ls -ld new*
-rw-r----- ... michael michael ... new-file
drwxr-x--- ... michael michael ... new-directory 
```

The setting of the <samp class="listingcharacter">umask</samp> value is done in the configuration files of the shells. For <samp class="listingcharacter">bash</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">umask</samp> is usually set in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/profile</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bashrc</samp>.

In some distributions, PAM (see [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14), [Section 14.6](#14_006.html_h14.6)) takes care of setting <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umask</samp>. Among other things, the PAM module <samp class="listingcharacter">pam_umask</samp> analyzes the optional <samp class="listingcharacter">umask=xxx</samp> entry in the fifth column (General Electric Comprehensive Operating System; GECOS) of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp>. In addition, the settings from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/login</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/login.defs</samp> are taken into account. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/login.defs</samp> file contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">umask</samp> setting on Ubuntu, for example (see the documentation on the <samp class="listingcharacter">UMASK</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">USERGROUPS_ENAB</samp> options contained in the file).

Individual users can make different settings in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bashrc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.zshrc</samp> file. For example, if you want files you create to be read/executed only by group members and not by other users, you should use the following setting:

```
# in ~/.bashrc or in ~/.zshrc
umask 027 
```

#### Who Is Allowed to Change Access Information?

Once a file is created, neither the owner nor the access bits change when it’s edited by another user. Only the owner may change the group membership and access bits. And only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> is allowed to change the owner of a file. This means that it isn’t possible for the owner of a file to give it to someone else, as it were.

## 9.7    Access Control Lists and Extended Attributes

The Unix-typical administration of users and groups as well as the access rights for directories and files based on them have proven themselves for decades. The concept is so simple that it can be understood after only a few hours. However, there are cases where this simple system is insufficient.

For this reason, a more finely meshed system for managing access rights was developed, based on so-called access control lists (ACLs). ACLs make it possible to set up any number of rules for each file or directory as to which users and groups are allowed to read or modify the file or directory and who is not allowed to do so—in deviation from the Unix access rights. ACLs thus act in addition to the standard access rights and can grant additional rights or revoke existing rights.

ACLs are active by default on popular Linux file systems. (In the past, ACLs had to be explicitly activated for some file system types by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> option, <samp class="listingcharacter">acl</samp>.)

The Samba file server is by far the most important program that really benefits from ACLs. It is able to mimic Windows access rights on Linux thanks to ACLs.

Just because ACLs offer more options does not mean that they replace traditional rights management by any means! For experienced administrators of large networks, ACLs may provide additional security or at least simplify administration, but for most Linux users, ordinary rights management is absolutely sufficient. If you don't use the complex ACL system correctly, you may open security gaps. For this reason, there are currently hardly any distributions that use ACLs by default.

A key problem is that many Linux commands and programs do not process ACLs correctly. It can happen that a copied file suddenly lacks the ACL information of the original. Also, most file managers cannot properly display or modify ACLs. The Dolphin file manager in KDE is a positive exception.

Closely related to ACLs are extended attributes (EAs), which allow you to store additional attribute-value pairs for each file. Thus, for example, you can assign the <samp class="listingcharacter">charset</samp> attribute with the <samp class="listingcharacter">utf8</samp> setting to a text file in order to store the character set used. Of course, this only brings advantages if there are also programs that analyze this information. Depending on which file system you use, EAs must also be enabled by a corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">mount</samp> option—for example, via <samp class="listingcharacter">user_xattr</samp> for the <samp class="listingcharacter">ext</samp> file system.

For more background and details on using ACLs and EAs, see the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> pages on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acl</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfacl</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfacl</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">attr(5)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfattr</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfattr</samp>.

In the following examples, I assume that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">attr</samp> package with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">attr</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfattr</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfattr</samp> commands is installed and that you are working with a file system that has ACLs and EAs enabled. This is the case by default for the <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file systems. If ACL is not available, you will receive errors like <samp class="listingcharacter">Operation is not supported</samp> when you execute <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfacl</samp>. The solution to this is usually the <samp class="listingcharacter">acl</samp> option in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command or in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp> file.

### 9.7.1    Access Control Lists

Even on a file system with ACLs, the default access rights, often referred to as the minimum ACL, usually apply. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfacl</samp> displays these rights in ACL terms:

```
user$ touch file1
user$ getfacl file1
# file: file1
# owner: kofler
# group: kofler
user::rw-
group::r--
other::r--
user$ ls -l file1
-rw-r--r-- 1 kofler kofler ...  file2 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfacl</samp>, you can now define additional access rules. The following commands grant the user <samp class="listingcharacter">gladys</samp> and all members of the <samp class="listingcharacter">docuteam</samp> group read and write access to the file, but deny the user <samp class="listingcharacter">catherine</samp> any access:

```
user$ setfacl -m gladys:rw file1
user$ setfacl -m g:docuteam:rw file1
user$ setfacl -m catherine:- file1 
```

The rights list of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfacl</samp> is now a bit longer. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> shows the ACL mask for group member access rights. The access letters are followed by the <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> character to indicate that there are ACL rules:

```
user$ getfacl file1
# file: file1
# owner: kofler
# group: kofler
user::rw-
user:gladys:rw-
user:catherine:---
group::r--
group:docuteam:rw-
mask::rw-
other::r--
user$ ls -l file1
-rw-rw-r--+ 1 kofler kofler ... file1 
```

A typical use of ACLs is that you want to give a certain user access to your files, but without making the files immediately available to all other users (of a certain group).

Typically, you would now have to ask the administrator to create a new group that includes you and the other users with whom you want to share the files. With ACL, you simply execute <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfacl -m user:rw file</samp>.

The ACL mask limits the rights provided by ACL rules. For example, if you set the ACL mask to <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp>, no ACL rule can give a user write or execute permissions. Thus, the ACL mask takes precedence over the ACL rules. However, it has no effect on the rights that result from the traditional access rights for the owner of the file or for group members of the file. Whenever an ACL rule is changed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfacl</samp>, the mask is automatically recalculated so that all other ACL rules can be complied with. This mask is displayed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfacl</samp> and is also taken into account by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp>.

You can explicitly set the mask by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfacl -m m:RWX file</samp> to limit ACL permissions. Note that you need to replace <samp class="listingcharacter">RWX</samp> with the desired access bits. However, your own mask is only valid until you define a new ACL rule. This will automatically recalculate the ACL mask (unless you prevent this by using the <samp class="listingcharacter">-n</samp> option).

For directories, you can specify a second set of rules for the default ACL. The default ACL does not control access to the directory but is considered a pattern for new files. Each file that is newly created within the directory inherits the directory's default ACL, so to speak. For many ACL applications, a new directory with a cleverly chosen default ACL serves as a starting point.

The biggest obstacle to the wider adoption of ACLs is that many standard commands and almost all application programs simply ignore ACLs. If you simply copy a file with ACL rules using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp>, the copy will lose all ACL rules. The same applies if you open the file in an editor, such as LibreOffice or GIMP, and save it under a different name. For <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-p</samp> option solves this problem, but most other commands and programs lack comparable options or ACL-compliant behavior.

Backups are another issue as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> eliminate ACL rules. The file systems of CDs and DVDs does not provide for ACLs, so this information is lost there as well. There are two ways out: you can either use the ACL-compatible <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">star</samp> variant instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> or create an additional text file containing the ACL rules of all files before the backup. After the backup, you can then restore the ACL rules using that file:

```
user$ getfacl -R --skip-base . > acl-backup   
(backup ACL rules)
user$ setfacl --restore=acl-backup            
(restore ACL rules) 
```

### 9.7.2    Extended Attributes

The following examples show how you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfattr</samp> to store attributes and how to read them using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfattr</samp>:

```
user$ touch file2
user$ setfattr -n user.language -v en file2
user$ setfattr --name=user.charset --value=utf8 file2
user$ getfattr -d file2
# file: file2
user.charset="utf8"
user.language="en" 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfattr</samp> usually returns only attributes whose names start with user. If you want to see other attributes, you must specify their names using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-n</samp> or their patterns by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-m</samp>:

```
user$ getfattr -n security.selinux -d tst
# file: tst
security.selinux="user_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0^000" 
```

Unfortunately, there are hardly any programs at the moment that preserve extended attributes during copy, archiving, or similar processes. Even <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp -p</samp> ignores the attributes. For backups, the best approach is similar to ACLs in that you create a file with all EAs prior to the backup. Then you can use this file to restore the EAs later:

```
user$ getfattr -R . > ea-backup        
(backup attributes)
user$ setfattr --restore=ea-backup     
(restore attributes) 
```

### 9.7.3    Capabilities

One of the most interesting uses of extended attributes is the ability to specify, for executable files, which operations are allowed for the program—that is, which capabilities the program has. This would allow fewer programs to be marked with the setuid bit and in this way increase the security of Linux distributions.

For capabilities to work, two conditions must be met:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libcap</samp> library must be installed (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/libcap*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib64/libcap*</samp>).

*   The file system must support EAs because the capability data is stored as EAs. This is the case by default for the most common Linux file systems.

To administrate capabilities, you need the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getcap</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setcap</samp> commands. They are mostly included in the <samp class="listingcharacter">libcap-ng-utils</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">libcap-progs</samp> package. You need to install this package separately for many distributions.

More and more distributions are using capabilities to grant commands the right to send network packets or generate new UIDs/GIDs without <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> rights:

```
root# getcap /usr/bin/*   
(results for Fedora 38)
/usr/bin/arping    cap_net_raw=p
/usr/bin/clockdiff cap_net_raw=p
/usr/bin/newgidmap cap_setgid=ep
/usr/bin/newuidmap cap_setuid=ep 
```

In the past, the insecure SetUID bit was set for such commands—or the application was restricted to <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>.

## 9.8    The Linux Directory Structure

A typical Unix system consists of thousands of files. During the development of Unix, certain rules have emerged about in which directories what files are usually stored. These rules were adapted to the specifics of Linux and summarized in a separate document: the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS; see [https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/fhs.shtml](https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/fhs.shtml)). Most Linux distributions adhere to this standard.

The information summarized in this section will give you some initial guidance. I have taken not only the FHS into account, but also the common habits of popular Linux distributions.

The file system starts with the root directory. There are usually no files there, only directories:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/bin</samp>
    Contains elementary Linux commands for system administration that can be executed by all users. Other programs are located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin</samp>. In modern distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin</samp> is simply a link to <samp class="listingcharacter">/usr/bin</samp>; the separation between <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin</samp> has thus been removed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/boot</samp>
    Contains files that are used to boot the system (usually via GRUB). In most distributions, the kernel is also located here.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/dev</samp>
    Contains all device files. Almost all hardware components—such as the serial interface or a hard disk partition—are accessed via so-called device files. These are set up dynamically by the <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> system (see [Section 9.9](#09_009.html_h9.9)). In most distributions, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev</samp> directory is located in a RAM disk; that is, the contents of the directory are not preserved when the computer is rebooted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/etc</samp>
    Contains configuration files for the entire system. Within <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp>, there are numerous subdirectories that organize the configuration files into groups—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apt</samp> for files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> package management system. A large number of files from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> are described in the configuration chapters of this book. You can also take a look at the index (letter E)!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/home</samp>
    Contains the home directories of all regular Linux users. The home directory is the directory in which the user is automatically located after logging in and to whose files he or she has unrestricted access rights. As so often, <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> is a special case: its home directory is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/lib[64]</samp>
    Contains some shared libraries or symbolic links to them. The files are needed to run programs. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/modules</samp> contains kernel modules that are dynamically enabled or disabled during operation. Other libraries are located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib[64]</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/firmware</samp> directory contains the firmware of various hardware components (e.g., a Wi-Fi controller).
    In current distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib</samp> is a link to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib</samp>. This link places all libraries centrally in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr directory</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/lost+found</samp>
    Exists only in <samp class="listingcharacter">ext</samp> file systems. The directory is usually empty. If it does contain files, then these are file fragments that could no longer be allocated when <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fsck</samp> attempted to repair the file system. In other words, sectors were found, but it is unclear to which file each sector once belonged. Instead of simply deleting such file fragments, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fsck</samp> copies them to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lost+found</samp> directory.
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fsck</samp> is automatically executed during system startup if Linux was not shut down properly (power failure, crash, etc.) or if the file system has not been checked for a long time. The goal of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fsck</samp> is to restore the file system to a clearly defined state.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/media</samp>
    Contains subdirectories like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cdrom</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement"><usb-drive-name></samp> where external file systems are mounted. Traditionally, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/mnt</samp> was used for this, but in recent years <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/media</samp> and finally the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run/media/<username>/<data_medium name></samp> directory have become established instead.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/opt</samp>
    Is intended for add-on packages, but is rarely used by the common distributions—probably because it is unclear how add-on packages differ from normal packages.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/proc</samp>
    Contains subdirectories for all running processes. These are not real files! The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc</samp> directory merely reflects the administration of the processes within Linux.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/root</samp>
    Contains the files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> user—that is, the system administrator.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/run</samp>
    Contains files with the process IDs and other information of some system services for many current distributions. In the past, these files were stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run</samp> directory.

    The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run/lock/</samp> subdirectory contains locking files. In older distributions, you will find the locking files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lock</samp> instead.

    Many distributions store either the entire <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run</samp> directory or at least individual <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run</samp> subdirectories in a RAM disk. The predominantly very small files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run</samp> are therefore never physically stored on a hard disk or SSD and are lost when the computer is rebooted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/sbin</samp>
    Contains commands for system management. A common feature of all programs stored in it is that they may only be executed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. In modern distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sbin</samp> is a link to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/sbin</samp>; all system administration commands are now stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/sbin</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/share</samp>
    Sometimes contains architecture-independent files—that is, files that are independent of the processor. The correct location is actually <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/srv</samp>
    Contains data for server processes in some distributions (Fedora, RHEL)—for example, in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/srv/www</samp> files of the web server or in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/srv/ftp</samp> files of the FTP server.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/sys</samp>
    Contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">sysfs</samp> file system. Like the <samp class="listingcharacter">proc</samp> file system, it provides information about the state of the computer.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/tmp</samp>
    Contains temporary files. However, temporary files are often stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/tmp</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/usr</samp>
    Contains all application programs, the complete X system, the source code for Linux, and so on. The contents of this directory usually change only during package installations and updates. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var</samp> directory is intended for mutable files, but [Table 9.9](#09_008.html_t9.9) gives a brief description of the most important subdirectories of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">/var</samp>
    Contains mutable files. Important subdirectories include <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">docker</samp> (docker files), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lock</samp> (locking files to protect access to devices), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">log</samp> (logging files), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mail</samp> (email files, often also in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/mail</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mysql</samp> (MySQL database files), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run</samp> (files with process IDs of some system services), and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">spool</samp> (cached print files).

So the basic structure of the root-level directories is quite easy to understand. The problems only start with the subdivision of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var</samp> into countless subdirectories. Basically, many directories are named in the same way as in the root level—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bin</samp> for executable programs.

The problem here is that there are several groups of executable programs: text-based commands, X programs, and so on. In the past, there were individual directories for these groups of programs, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin/X11</samp> for programs with graphical user interfaces. By now, most distributions try to install all programs into one directory—namely, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin</samp>. Symbolic links establish compatibility with past standards.

| Directory | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin</samp> | Executable programs |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/games</samp> | Games; possibly links to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/games</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/include</samp> | C include files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib[64]</samp> | Various libraries, also countless subdirectories for C compilers, various other programming languages, large program packages such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">emacs</samp> or LaTeX, and so on |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/local</samp> | Applications and files that do not directly belong to the Linux distribution or were installed later |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/sbin</samp> | Programs that can only be executed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share</samp> | Architecture-independent data (e.g., Emacs Lisp files, Ghostscript character sets, etc.), documentation (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/doc</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/src</samp> | Source code for Linux and possibly other programs |

**Table 9.9**     /usr Directories

## 9.9    Device Files

Not only files and directories are managed in the Linux file system, but also so-called devices. These are specially marked files that do not store data, but rather connect to the Linux kernel (see [Table 9.10](#09_009.html_t9.10)).

Devices enable access to many hardware components of the computer, such as hard disks/SSDs, serial and parallel interfaces, the main memory (RAM), and so on. Devices are characterized by three pieces of information: the major device number, the minor device number, and the type of access (block-based or character-based).

The major device number specifies which Linux kernel driver is responsible for management. Most drivers are listed with their major device number on the following page: [https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/admin-guide/devices.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/admin-guide/devices.txt).

In many drivers, the minor device number is used to differentiate between different (related) individual devices—for example, in the driver for hard disks between different partitions.

The access type indicates whether the devices are buffered (this is the case for all block-based devices such as hard disks and the like) or not (this applies to character-based devices such as the serial interface).

If you use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp> to view the table of contents of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev</samp>, the device numbers (major and minor) are output instead of the file size. The first character of the access bits is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">b</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">c</samp> (block-based or character-based):

```
user$ ls -l /dev/sda?
brw-rw---- 1 root root 8, 1 ... /dev/sda1
brw-rw---- 1 root root 8, 2 ... /dev/sda2
... 
```

Inside Linux, there are only so-called inodes in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev</samp> directory: these are the smallest administrative units of a file system, but not real files with content. New device files can be set up using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mknod</samp> command. In practice, however, this is rarely necessary because the <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> system takes care of it automatically. The major and minor device numbers are combined to form a 64-bit number.

For security reasons, only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> or members of a specific group are allowed to access many devices. To allow other users to access these devices, you need to add the user to this group.

Some device files have a special function: thus, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/null</samp> serves as a “black hole” into which data can be sent that will disappear there forever—for example, to redirect command output that should not be displayed. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/zero</samp> is an inexhaustible source of 0-bytes, sometimes used to fill files up to a given size with zeros. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/random</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/urandom</samp> supply random numbers.

In the past, distributions generated thousands of device files during installation. At most, a few hundred files are actually used; however, there are different device files on each computer—depending on the hardware equipment. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">udev</samp> system provides a workaround. The background program <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">udevd</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-udevd</samp> in current distributions, detects all hardware components connected to the computer and creates the necessary device files as required. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">udevd</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-udev</samp> is started by the init process. The configuration is done by the files in the /etc/selinux directory.

As part of the effort to get Linux up and running faster, the <samp class="listingcharacter">devtmpfs</samp> file system has been added to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">udev</samp>. This temporary file system maps the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev</samp> directory. During the boot process, <samp class="listingcharacter">devtmpfs</samp> can be used without the overhead of the full <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> system.

| Device | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/console</samp> | The currently active virtual terminal |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/disk/*</samp> | Additional links to hard disk and partition devices |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/dri/*</samp> | Direct rendering infrastructure (3D graphics with X) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/dsp*</samp> | Access to the sound card (digital sampling device) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/fb*</samp> | Frame buffer (graphics card) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/input/*</samp> | Keyboard and mouse |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/kmem</samp> | Memory (RAM) in core format (for debuggers) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/mapper</samp> | Mapping files for LVM, crypto containers, and so on |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/md*</samp> | Meta devices (RAID, etc.) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/mem</samp> | Memory (RAM) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/mixer*</samp> | Access to the sound card |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/nvme*</samp> | SSDs that support the NVME protocol |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/port</samp> | IO ports |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/pts/*</samp> | Virtual terminals according to Unix 98 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ptyp*</samp> | Virtual terminals under X (master) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ram</samp> | RAM disk |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/raw1394</samp> | Direct access to Firewire devices |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/scd*</samp> | CD/DVD drives |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sd*</samp> | SATA/SCSI/USB/Firewire media |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/shm</samp> | POSIX shared memory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/snd</samp> | ALSA sound (link to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/asound/dev</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sr*</samp> | SCSI/SATA/USB/Firewire CD/DVD drives |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/tty*</samp> | Virtual terminals in text mode |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ttyp*</samp> | Virtual terminals under X (slave) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ttyS*</samp> | Serial interfaces (modem, mouse, etc.) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/usb/*</samp> | USB devices (see also <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/bus/usb</samp>) |

**Table 9.10**     Important Device Files

# 10    Process Management

This chapter describes the way Linux handles processes. In the course of this chapter, you will learn

*   Which options you have to start programs and to terminate them again (if necessary, also by force)

*   How to run a program with root privileges

*   What demons are

*   How to start programs automatically at specific times using cron or systemd timers

## 10.1    Starting, Managing, and Stopping Processes

This chapter mainly deals with processes. At the operating system level, a process is responsible for the execution of a program or command. This sounds like a rather trivial task; however, as many programs and background services run in parallel, it isn’t at all easy to distribute the computing time between all programs fairly or in such a way that it makes sense.

### Programs and Commands

As a matter of fact, a program or command is just an executable file. Thus, a program file differs from other files in that the execute bit <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is set. Within Linux, there is no distinction between a program like Firefox or a command like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>. In everyday language, however, text-based programs such as ls are often referred to as commands.

The program file doesn't become an active process managed by the Linux kernel until it is started. Seen in this light, the heading of this section should actually read “Starting Programs and Commands, and Managing and Stopping Processes”.

Every now and then, the question arises where the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.exe</samp> files are located on Linux. The usual answer is: there are no <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.exe</samp> files. Executable programs are identified by the access bit <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>; the file identifier <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.exe</samp> known from Windows is thus superfluous.

This answer is not quite correct insofar as there can actually be isolated <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.exe</samp> files on Linux. These are programs that were developed in the C# programming language and use the Mono library for execution. The Mono library is in turn an open-source implementation of Microsoft's .NET framework.

### 10.1.1    Launching Programs

In a desktop system, you usually launch programs from a menu or by clicking an icon. The (Alt)+(F2) or (Windows) keyboard shortcuts are an additional way to quickly launch programs.

Alternatively, you can start programs in a terminal window or in a text console. To do this, you simply need to type the name of the program and press (Enter). Especially Linux professionals often choose this method because it is faster to type a few letters than to search for the program in branched menus. <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> causes the program to run in the background and not block the terminal.

Usually it’s enough to simply specify the name of the program. The shell interpreter then searches for the program in all directories specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">PATH</samp> environment variable. The following lines show a typical setting of this variable:

```
user$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin 
```

If you want to start a program that isn’t located in any of these directories, you must specify the full path. This also applies to programs in the current directory! Here the path is simply specified by a dot, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">./myprogram</samp>.

Provided a desktop system such as GNOME or KDE is installed, you can also open images and documents via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xdg-open filename</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xdg-open</samp> automatically starts the desktop program associated with the file type. In some distributions, you can simply use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">open</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xdg-open</samp> (as on macOS).

### 10.1.2    Foreground and Background Processes

When you launch programs in the start menu of your desktop, they run as background processes—that is, without interfering with each other. You can launch more programs without waiting for the previously started programs to finish.

The behavior is completely different when you run a program in a text console or terminal because then the program is launched as a foreground process. Before you can enter the next command in the terminal, you must wait for the program that was launched last to finish.

But you can also start programs in the background in text consoles or terminal windows. To do this, you simply want to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> character at the end of the command:

```
user$ firefox & 
```

If you forget to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> character, you can also convert the program to a background process afterward. What you need to do is interrupt the program execution using (Ctrl)+(Z) and continue the program by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bg</samp>:

```
user$ firefox
<Ctrl>+<Z>
+  Stopped  firefox
user$ bg
+ firefox & 
```

If you use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fg</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bg</samp>, the program will continue running as a foreground process.

For some commands, various text outputs interfere with the background execution. However, you can easily suppress them by redirecting them to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/null</samp>. For example, the following command sets up a file system in the background:

```
root# mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdc1 > /dev/null & 
```

### 10.1.3    List of All Running Processes (ps and top)

You can generate a list of currently running processes very easily via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp>. If you enclose the process name in square brackets, then it’s a process of the kernel. Without any additional options, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp> shows only your own processes that you have started in the terminal. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp> can be controlled by countless options, many of which are specified without the otherwise usual preceding minus sign. In the following example, the list of processes has been greatly shortened for reasons of space. A typical Linux system with a graphical user interface usually has well over 100 processes running at the same time:

```
user$ ps ax
  PID TTY      STAT   TIME COMMAND
    1 ?        Ss     0:00 init [2]  
    2 ?        S      0:00 [kthreadd]
    3 ?        S      0:00 [ksoftirqd/0]
 ...
 3064 pts/2    S      0:39 emacs command.tex
 3151 pts/2    S+     1:23 /bin/sh ./lvauto
 3735 pts/4    S      0:00 su -l
 3740 pts/4    S+     0:00 -bash 
```

Often <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> is more useful than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp>. This command orders the processes according to how much load they put on the CPU and displays the currently active processes first. The program also provides an overview of the current memory requirements, and so on. The process list is updated every few seconds until the program is terminated using (Q). The following lines show a web server that is almost idle:

```
top - 20:50:38 up 11 days, 12:18, 1 user, load average: 0.10, 0.09, 0.08
Tasks: 114 total,   1 running, 113 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
Cpu(s):  2.6%us,  0.2%sy,  0.0%ni, 96.8%id,  0.4%wa,  0.0%hi,  0.0%si,  0.0%st
Mem:   4049808k total,  1580060k used,  2469748k free,   203396k buffers
Swap:   521212k total,        0k used,   521212k free,   804400k cached

  PID USER      PR  NI  VIRT  RES  SHR S %CPU %MEM    TIME+  COMMAND
32601 www-data  20   0  346m  32m 4296 S    5  0.8   0:00.15 apache2
32592 www-data  20   0  344m  31m 4324 S    3  0.8   0:00.47 apache2
  851 mysql     20   0 1403m  53m 7948 S    0  1.4   6:40.10 mysqld
    1 root      20   0 24336 2184 1272 S    0  0.1   0:01.07 init 
  ... 
```

The value in the PID column indicates the process number. If you know this number, you can forcibly stop out-of-control programs or background processes using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp> command.

Processes can assume different states. The two most common states are R (running) and S (sleeping; i.e., the program has nothing to do at the moment and is waiting for input). Programs can also be temporarily interrupted and then have the state T (stopped). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> also accepts commands interactively. This means you can stop processes ((K); <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp>) or change their priority ((R); <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">renice</samp>).

A convenient alternative to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">htop</samp> command, which must be installed separately in most distributions. Among other things, it allows horizontal and vertical scrolling in the process list.

If you want to track not the CPU and memory usage but the accesses to hard disks and other volumes, you should start the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iotop</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">-o</samp> option enables you to restrict the output to processes that actually cause IO activity. <samp class="listingcharacter">-u</samp> restricts the output to your own processes. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iotop</samp> is part of the package of the same name, which usually has to be installed separately.

If you want to know the program name and determine the associated process number (PID), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pidof</samp> can help you. If there are several processes with the same name, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pidof</samp> returns a whole list of numbers:

```
root# pidof sshd
4429 4393 4172 
```

Sometimes it is also useful to determine which programs access a particular file or directory. You can determine the corresponding process numbers by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fuser</samp>. A directory is considered used even if a program has been started in it. The following command shows that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zsh</samp> shell and the Docker program use the current directory:

```
user$ fuser -v .
                     USER        PID ACCESS COMMAND
                     kofler     4211 ..c.. zsh
                     kofler     7515 ..c.. docker 
```

Note that a file access can be detected only if the program has actively opened the file. This is usually not the case with a text editor: the editor opens the file for loading, but then closes it again. It only opens the file again for a short time before saving.

Some background processes store a PID file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run</samp> directory—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run/httpd.pid</samp>. This file contains the process number in the first line; further lines may contain additional information, such as the network interface. PID files enable the targeted termination of a specific process by the init system, even if multiple processes with the same name exist.

There are also graphical alternatives to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">htop</samp> commands, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ksysguard</samp> (KDE) or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gnome-system-monitor</samp> (GNOME). Conky provides incomparably more display and configuration options. On the internet, you can find Conky configurations that are true works of art and turn a bland desktop background into an original and useful information center. Unfortunately, setting up a Conky configuration involves a lot of work. The configuration files offered on the internet are mostly outdated or fit only for a special distribution.

If you don’t want to monitor your own computer but several external servers, the best option is to use tools such as Nagios or Munin. However, their configuration is complex and requires experience in server administration. A simpler alternative for a single server is the Linux Dash project. After an uncomplicated installation, a page that can be opened in the web browser summarizes the most important status information.

### 10.1.4    Process Hierarchy

Internally, the PID number of the parent process is also stored with each process. This information enables the representation of a process tree, at the top of which there is always the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd</samp> program. This program is started immediately after the kernel has been loaded (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20)). The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pstree</samp> command, which sometimes has to be installed separately, shows the hierarchy of the process tree. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-h</samp> option can be used to highlight the parent processes of the currently running process in bold.

[![Process Overview with pstree](bilderklein/klein10_001.png)](img-f10.1.html)

**Figure 10.1**     Process Overview with pstree

### 10.1.5    Terminating Processes by Force (kill and xkill)

Usually, a process runs until the regular end of the program. But unfortunately, it also happens on Linux that programs contain errors, can no longer be stopped, and may possibly consume more and more memory and CPU capacity. In such cases, the process must be terminated by force. For text-based commands, (Ctrl)+(C) helps in most cases. This will terminate the program immediately.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp> command sends signals to a running process specified by the PID number. You can determine this number via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp>. To end a program “politely,” you need to use signal 15\. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp> uses this signal by default. If this doesn’t help, signal 9 must be used (here for process 2725):

```
user$ kill -9 2725 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp> only for your own processes. Only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> may also terminate foreign processes.

You can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> to terminate processes: simply enter (K) and then the process number and the desired signal!

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">killall</samp> is more convenient in that not a process number but the program name can be specified. However, all processes of this name will then be terminated:

```
root# killall -9 firefox 
```

Provided your graphics system uses the X Window System and not the modern Wayland library, there is an even more convenient way to terminate a program: for this purpose, you need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xkill</samp> in a terminal and then click the window of the program you want to stop. Again, signal 9 is then sent to the process. On KDE, you can also start <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xkill</samp> using (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(Esc). If this happens by mistake, you can cancel <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xkill</samp> with (Esc).

Sometimes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xkill</samp> closes the window, but the process or parts of it continue to run. Use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp> to make sure that the program is really finished. If necessary, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill -9 <pid></samp>.

It becomes really unpleasant when a desktop program not only hangs, but also takes over the keyboard and mouse focus or blocks the graphics system in some other way. The computer then no longer responds to any input. In such cases, the magic key combination (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(F#) sometimes can help, which switches to the # text console. There you can log in, search for, and quit the relevant program by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp>.

If the keyboard is completely blocked, it’s still possible to log in through a network via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> and run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill</samp> that way. Of course, this variant is only possible if you work in a local network and an SSH server is running on your computer.

For programs started from a shell (such as all commands executed in a terminal), you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ulimit</samp> command to limit the maximum memory consumption, the maximum size of created files, and so on. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ulimit</samp> is usually set in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/profile</samp>.

### 10.1.6    Distribution of Compute Time (nice, renice, and ionice)

In everyday Linux operation, the compute capacity is usually sufficient to execute all running processes without delays. However, when Linux is busy with computing-intensive processes—for example, while compiling a large program—it tries to distribute the available computing time evenly to all processes.

In some cases, it makes sense to deliberately allocate more or less compute time to a process. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nice</samp> command, which can be used to launch programs with reduced or increased priority, is used for this purpose. Here, the desired priority is passed to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nice</samp>, ranging from 19 (very low) to -20 (very high). By default, processes are started with priority 0\. In the following example, a backup program is launched with lower priority so that it doesn’t interfere with other processes. It doesn't matter if the backup takes a few seconds longer:

```
user$ nice -n 10 ./my-backup-script 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">renice</samp> can also be used to change the priority of processes that are already running. The process ID that was previously determined using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp> must be specified as a parameter. Details about <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">renice</samp> can be found on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> page. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp> is also able to interactively change the priority of a process; to do this, just press (R).

However, only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> can start programs with a higher priority than 0 or increase the priority of an already running process.

Often it isn’t the CPU but the data medium that is the limiting factor in the execution of programs. For example, if you want to prevent a backup script from taking up the entire I/O capacity of the computer and thus slowing down other, perhaps more time-critical processes, you can run it with reduced I/O priority using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ionice</samp>. The following command reads a logical volume, compresses its contents, and saves it to an image file:

```
root# ionice -c 3 cat /dev/vg1/snap | lzop -c > /backup/image.lzo 
```

### 10.1.7    Input and Output Redirection and Pipes

Almost all text-based commands expect input via the standard input channel (the keyboard by default) and send output to the standard output channel; the resulting text is then simply displayed in a terminal. Both input and output can be redirected, providing many options. For example, the following command saves the list of all files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xy</samp> directory in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">z</samp> file:

```
user$ ls xy > z 
```

Pipes allow the output of a command to be used as input for the next command. In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">egrep</samp> filters out from the list of all installed packages those that contain the “mysql” or “mariadb” strings in uppercase or lowercase. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sort</samp> finally sorts this list:

```
user$ dpkg -l | egrep -i 'mysql|mariadb' | sort
ii  libmysqlclient21:amd64  8.0.23   amd64 MySQL database client library
ii  mysql-client            8.0.23     all MySQL database client ...
...
rc  mariadb-common          1:10.3.25  all MariaDB common metapackage
```

In other words, the output of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> command is passed to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> thanks to the first <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character, and its output is passed to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sort</samp> via the third <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character. (The second <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> character is interpreted by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">egrep</samp> in the sense of or). For more details and examples on input and output redirection, see [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7), [Section 7.4](#07_004.html_h7.4).

## 10.2    Running Processes under a Different Identity (su)

There are two restrictions on the execution of programs by ordinary users:

*   Ordinary users are allowed to run only those processes where the access rights (owner, group, r, and x access bits) allow it. For ordinary programs, this is not a limitation. However, there are some system administration commands in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/sbin</samp> directory, for example, that can only be started by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>.

*   Processes belong to the user who started them, as it were. This means that a process is allowed to access the same files as the user. Put another way, files that you as a user are not allowed to modify must also not be modified by programs that you start. Files newly created by the process also belong to the user who started the program (see also [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.7.2](#09_007.html_h9.7.2)).

For these reasons, you cannot perform many administrative tasks as an ordinary user. The easiest way out is to log in as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. However, I have already pointed out several times in this book that it is not a good idea to work as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> all the time. The risk is simply too great that you could cause damage by mistake. For this reason, some distributions block the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login completely. Thus, a direct <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login is impossible on Ubuntu.

This section describes how you can still perform administrative activities using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp> without logging out as an ordinary user. [Section 10.3](#10_003.html_h10.3) describes an alternative approach using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>, which has many advantages over <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp>. Finally, [Section 10.4](#10_004.html_h10.4) presents another way using the PolicyKit program, which has established itself primarily on desktop systems.

### 10.2.1    The su Command

In many cases, you just need to quickly execute a command as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. It would be inconvenient to leave the currently active desktop system or terminal window and log in again as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>.

The easiest way to change the user within a terminal window is to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su name</samp> command. If you don’t execute the command as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>, you’ll be asked for the password of the respective user. Inside the terminal, you can then execute commands under the changed name until you return to normal mode via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exit</samp> or (Ctrl)+(D).

The following lines show how an ordinary user logs in briefly as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>, mounts a disk partition in the directory tree as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>, and then logs out again as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> and continues working normally:

```
user$ su -l root
Password: *********
root# mount -t ext2 /test /dev/sda7
root# <Ctrl>+<D>
logout
user$ ls /test 
```

For <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp> to be a full replacement for a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> login, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-l</samp> option! This ensures that all login start files are imported, which is necessary for the correct definition of <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp>, among other things.

Depending on the configuration and graphics system (like Wayland), desktop programs cannot be run in a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp> session.
