Rather, most distributions use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pkexec</samp> command to launch programs with admin privileges in the desktop environment. Behind the scenes, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pkexec</samp> again uses PolicyKit (see [Section 10.4](#10_004.html_h10.4)).

The setuid and setgid access bits provide another way to mark certain programs so that anyone can run them as if he or she were <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> or another user or member of another group. However, this removes an important protective mechanism: the setuid bit applies to all users, regardless of whether they know the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password (for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp>) or belong to a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> group. For more information about the setuid and setgid access bits, see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.6.1](#09_006.html_h9.6.1).

## 10.3    Running Processes under a Different Identity (sudo)

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> takes a different approach than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp>. The program, after appropriate configuration, allows certain users to run programs with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. For security reasons, the user's own password must be entered again—that is, not the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password. This is especially useful on servers because it eliminates the tedious and insecure management of a common <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password for multiple administrators.

<samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> then runs these programs as if they were started by a different user (default: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>). This allows individual users to perform admin tasks or run system-critical commands without having to know the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> password. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> logs all executed commands and failed authentication attempts in the syslog.

Depending on the configuration, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> authentication remains valid for a few minutes. If you execute another command using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> within this period, you will not be asked for the password again. The timeout can be changed in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sudoers</samp> using the <samp class="listingcharacter">timestamp_timeout</samp> keyword.

The configuration of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> is done through the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sudoers</samp> file. In simple terms, the file describes in three columns which users are allowed to run which programs from which computer. The following line means that user <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">catherine</samp> is allowed to execute the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/sbin/parted</samp> command. Because of the first <samp class="listingcharacter">ALL</samp>, this rule applies regardless of the hostname. <samp class="listingcharacter">=(ALL)</samp> means that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">catherine</samp> may execute the command under any account—as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>, but also as, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">peter</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ann</samp>:

```
# in /etc/sudoers
catherine ALL=(ALL) /usr/sbin/parted 
```

If the first column of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudoers</samp> is prefixed with the <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> character, the entry applies to all members of the specified group. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">(ALL)</samp>, the setting <samp class="listingcharacter">(All:ALL)</samp> is often used as well. This means that commands can be executed in any account and in any group. Other syntax variants are described in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man sudoers</samp>.

### Modify /etc/sudoers Using visudo!

For security reasons, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sudoers</samp> should only be edited using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">visudo</samp> command (see also its <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> page)! <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">visudo</samp> performs a syntax test before saving and thus ensures that you do not exclude yourself from further admin work due to a faulty <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudoers</samp> file. This is especially important for distributions like Ubuntu, which do not provide a <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">visudo</samp>, as the name suggests, typically uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vi</samp> editor; if you prefer a different editor, you must specify its exact path in the <samp class="listingcharacter">EDITOR</samp> environment variable before running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">visudo</samp>—<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">export EDITOR=/usr/bin/jmacs</samp>, for example.

The configuration of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sudoers</samp> provides a lot more syntactic options than have been mentioned here. You should therefore read the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> pages on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> and on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudoers</samp>! You can find even more details on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> homepage at [https://sudo.ws](https://sudo.ws).

Catherine can now run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">parted</samp> as follows, authenticating herself with her own password:

```
catherine$ sudo /usr/sbin/parted /dev/sda
Password: xxxxxx 
```

For <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">parted</samp>, the full path must be specified if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">parted</samp> is not in one of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">catherine</samp>'s <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> directories. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">parted</samp> is automatically run in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> account. You can select a different account by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo -u <account></samp>.

It’s possible to allow a specific user to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> without specifying a password. To do this, you need to add a line in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudoers</samp> according to the following pattern:

```
maria ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL 
```

This is a security risk, of course, but if you often need to perform admin tasks, you will appreciate the convenience gained. Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">NOPASSWD</samp> tag is only valid if there are no other <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudoers</samp> lines that require a password from the same user. This also applies to group entries, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">%admin</samp>.

In real life, it’s often useful to exempt only the invocation of individual commands from authentication. The following setting allows <samp class="listingcharacter">peter</samp> to execute the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo docker</samp> command without specifying a password:

```
peter  ALL=(ALL:ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/docker 
```

If you use input and output redirection in a command executed using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>, it’s executed directly by the shell, not by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>—and thus only with your local privileges, not with the root privileges. This causes errors:

```
user$ sudo ls /etc > /etc/ls-out.txt
-bash: /etc/ls-out.txt: No authorization 
```

You can work around this problem by passing a shell to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> and executing the desired command in it:

```
user$ sudo sh -c 'ls /etc > /etc/ls-out.txt' 
```

Sometimes it happens that you want to execute multiple commands automatically with a script via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>. The correct syntax then looks as follows:

```
user$ sudo bash script.sh
user$ sudo ./script.sh     
(if the script starts with shebang) 
```

For more extensive admin tasks, it becomes increasingly annoying to prefix <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> to every command. It’s more elegant to switch to the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> mode by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo -s</samp>. All other commands are executed as if by <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. You can <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exit</samp> this mode using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exit</samp> or (Ctrl)+(D).

```
user$ sudo -s   
(switch to root mode)
root# cmd1
root# cmd2
root# cmd3
user$ exit      
(leave root mode) 
```

In the Xorg graphics system, you can easily run graphical programs using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>. When Wayland is active, different rules apply depending on the version. In current distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> works like under X without restrictions. In older distributions, on the other hand, you must also specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-E</samp> option (preserve environment) to start Wayland-compatible programs. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nautilus</samp> is the program name of the GNOME file manager:

```
user$ sudo nautilus           
(on X and in current Wayland versions)
user$ sudo -E nautilus        
(gedit on old Wayland version) 
```

### 10.3.1    sudo with Ubuntu

In Ubuntu and some other distributions, the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> user is set up by default without a valid password. A <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login is therefore impossible! In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh -l root</samp> do not work. The only way to execute admin commands is thus provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sudoers</samp> file contains only a few lines:

```
# Default configuration in /etc/sudoers on Ubuntu
Defaults   env_reset
Defaults   mail_badpass
Defaults   secure_path=
  "/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"
Defaults   use_pty
root       ALL=(ALL) ALL
%admin     ALL=(ALL) ALL
%sudo      ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Defaults env_reset</samp> causes all environment variables to be reset when the user changes. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Defaults mail_badpass</samp> causes a warning email to be sent to the administrator after an incorrect login attempt. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Defaults secure_path</samp> sets the contents of the <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> environment variable for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> commands.

The fourth line grants <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> unrestricted access to all programs. This line is actually useless on Ubuntu because the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login is locked.

The last two lines are the most important: They allow all members of the <samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">admin</samp> groups to call all programs. Usually, on Ubuntu, only the first user, the one set up during the installation, is a member of the <samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> group. Other users can also be assigned to this administrators group. In older Ubuntu versions, the <samp class="listingcharacter">admin</samp> group was used instead of the <samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> group.

#### Special Treatment of Home

In the past, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo -s</samp> did not use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root</samp> as the home directory, but <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/<name></samp>. This had the advantage that configuration files like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/<name>/.emacs</samp> applied equally to the user in question and to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. However, this configuration also caused conflicts with access rights (new configuration files created under <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> could not be modified in normal operation without <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>) and security problems. To avoid this, Ubuntu now also uses <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root</samp> as the home directory for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> commands.

### 10.3.2    sudo with Raspberry Pi OS

Even with the Raspberry Pi OS distribution optimized for the Raspberry Pi, there is no <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login by default. The first user set up during setup has an unusually liberal <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> entry:

```
# /etc/sudoers
...
username ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">username</samp> may thus execute any command using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> without a password. It is safer to prefix this line with the comment character <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">username</samp> can then continue to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> because it belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> group. However, the user must authenticate himself with his password.

### 10.3.3    sudo with Debian

On Debian, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> is installed by default. Whether it is also active depends on how you carried out the installation:

*   If you used the live image installer, or if you skipped entering the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password in the traditional installing program, then, as with Ubuntu, there is no <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password. However, the user created during the installation is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> group.

*   On the other hand, if you have specified a <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password in a traditional installation, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> is not active (i.e., there is no user in the <samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> group by default). To gain <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> privileges, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su -l</samp> and specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password.

### 10.3.4    sudo for RHEL and Fedora

In Fedora, as well as RHEL, you can set up a user during the installation process and make that user the administrator. The user is thus assigned to the <samp class="listingcharacter">wheel</samp> group. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sudoers</samp> contains the following line for this group:

```
# in /etc/sudoers in Fedora
...
%wheel     ALL=(ALL) ALL 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wheel</samp> group members must provide their own password to execute <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> commands. Separate from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>, there is still the root user with its own password.

### 10.3.5    sudo with SUSE

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> is also set up by default in SUSE distributions. However, the configuration differs significantly from that of Ubuntu, Fedora, and the like:

```
# Default configuration in /etc/sudoers with openSUSE
Defaults always_set_home  
Defaults env_reset        
Defaults env_keep = "LANG LC_ADDRESS LC_CTYPE ..."
Defaults targetpw    # sudo asks for the password of the target user
..
ALL  ALL=(ALL) ALL        # with the right password everyone 
                          # is allowed to do everything
root ALL=(ALL) ALL 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">Defaults targetpw</samp> means that basically the password for the account in which the command is to be executed must be specified, usually the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password. The advantage of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>—namely, that not all users with administrator tasks need to know the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password—is lost. Finally, the <samp class="listingcharacter">ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL</samp> line allows all users to execute any command, provided the correct password for the target account is known.

To run desktop programs using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter">-E</samp> option—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo -E console</samp>.

## 10.4    Running Processes under a Different Identity (PolicyKit)

The basic idea of PolicyKit is to split programs into two components: One part contains the user interface and runs with ordinary user rights. The second part of the program, referred to as the mechanism in PolicyKit terminology, is responsible for system interventions and runs with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges.

This separation has the fundamental advantage that it is no longer necessary to run a huge program with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges, but only small parts of it. This reduces potential security risks. In addition, it is theoretically possible for different user interfaces (such as a GNOME program and a KDE program) to use a unified set of mechanisms.

The communication between the two components takes place via a so-called bus system, usually via D-Bus. Whether a certain mechanism may be executed or not is decided by functions of the PolicyKit library, which use a central rights database. Three criteria are considered for the decision:

*   Subject Who or which user wants to make system changes?

*   Object Which object should be changed (e.g., a file, a partition, or a network connection)?

*   Action What should be done (e.g., mount a partition to the file system)?

In many cases, the user doesn’t notice anything about PolicyKit. For example, the default configuration in most current distributions allows the file manager to mount external disks in the file system. No further authentication is required for this; the process takes place automatically as soon as the data medium is connected.

You will come across another variant in various GNOME administration tools: here, a button marked with a padlock takes you to the authentication dialog. Only after specifying the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> or user password can system changes be made.

PolicyKit is configured in three places:

```
/etc/polkit-1/*                      
(global configuration, default settings)
/usr/share/polkit-1/actions/*.policy 
(actions)
/var/lib/polkit-1/*                  
(rights) 
```

There are distribution-specific peculiarities in the basic configuration. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/polkit-1/localauthority.conf.d/51-ubuntu-admin.conf</samp> on Ubuntu systems gives admin privileges to all users of the <samp class="listingcharacter">admin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> groups.

One component of the PolicyKit package is the aforementioned <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pkexec</samp> command, which is responsible for the actual execution of commands and analyzes the policy configuration in the process. For commands to be executed in the terminal, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pkexec</samp> works without further configuration. Of course, it would be even easier to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> in this case:

```
user$ pkexec nano 
```

However, for graphical programs not configured for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pkexec</samp>, the call fails with the error message <samp class="listingcharacter">cannot open display</samp>:

```
user$ pkexec gnome-text-editor
Unable to init server ..., cannot open display 
```

Fortunately, it isn’t difficult to set up your own <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.policy</samp> file. The PolicyKit file of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gparted</samp> partition editor can serve as a sample. Once you have installed this program, you should take a look at the following file, which I reproduce here in a highly abbreviated form:

```
user$ cat /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/org.gnome.gparted.policy

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE policyconfig PUBLIC ...>
<policyconfig>
    <vendor>The GParted Project</vendor>
    <vendor_url>https://gparted.org</vendor_url>
    <icon_name>gparted</icon_name>
    <action id="org.gnome.gparted">
        <description>Run GParted as root</description>
        <message>Authentication is required for GParted ...</message>
        ...
        <defaults>
            <allow_any>auth_admin</allow_any>
            <allow_inactive>auth_admin</allow_inactive>
            <allow_active>auth_admin</allow_active>
        </defaults>
        <annotate key="org.freedesktop.policykit.exec.path">
           /usr/bin/gparted
        </annotate>
        <annotate key="org.freedesktop.policykit.exec.allow_gui">true</annotate>
    </action>
</policyconfig> 
```

You can create the equivalent <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">myown.editor.policy</samp> file from a copy of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">org.gnome.gparted.policy</samp>. To do this, you only need to change a few lines and simply delete the translation texts in all conceivable languages:

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE policyconfig ... (as above) >
<policyconfig>
    <action id="myown.editor">
        <description>Run GNOME Text Editor as root</description>
        <message>Authentication is required for GNOME Text</message>
        <defaults>
            <allow_any>auth_admin</allow_any>
            <allow_inactive>auth_admin</allow_inactive>
            <allow_active>auth_admin</allow_active>
        </defaults>
        <annotate key="org.freedesktop.policykit.exec.path">
           /usr/bin/gnome-text-editor
        </annotate>
        <annotate key="org.freedesktop.policykit.exec.allow_gui">true</annotate>
    </action>
</policyconfig> 
```

The existence of this file subsequently allows you to start the editor in a terminal window by using <samp class="listingcharacter">pkexec gedit</samp>. Of course, a dialog for entering the <samp class="listingcharacter">sudo</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password still appears first.

## 10.5    System Processes (Daemons)

Background processes for system management are referred to as daemons. These processes are typically started as part of the init process when the computer boots up. If you’re more familiar with Windows lingo, Linux daemons simply correspond to services. [Table 10.1](#10_005.html_t10.1) very briefly describes the tasks of the most important daemons.

Where programs are described in this book, the relevant sections are indicated.

### 10.5.1    Kernel Threads

Besides ordinary server services like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd</samp> (Apache), there are background processes, which are not real programs but subprocesses (threads) of the kernel. You can recognize these processes by the fact that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps axu</samp> puts their names in square brackets.

Some of these subprocesses are suffixed with a number that indicates the CPU. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kblockd/0</samp> thus manages the block device buffer for the first CPU, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kblockd/1</samp> the buffer for the second CPU, and so on.

Most kernel threads are related to low-level tasks of the operating system (memory management, process management, CPU control, etc.). They are usually started during system initialization. No special configuration is required for standard requirements.

The functions of the most important kernel threads are summarized in [Table 10.2](#10_005.html_t10.2). If you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ps</samp> to display only kernel threads, you should run the command with the following options:

```
user$ ps -f -p 2 --ppid 2 
```

| Kernel Thread | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kacpid</samp> | ACPI functions |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kblockd</samp> | Manages the block device buffer |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kdevtmpfs</samp> | Manages the temporary <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev</samp> file system |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">khelperd</samp> | Loads or removes kernel modules for user programs |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kthread</samp> | Manages threads |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ksoftirqd</samp> | Hardware interrupt management |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kswapd</samp> | Swapping |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kworker</samp> | Execute kernel functions ("work") |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">md</samp> | RAID functions |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">migration</samp> | Determines which processes run on which CPU |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scsi_eh</samp> | Manages SCSI errors and timeouts |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">watchdog</samp> | Monitors whether the system is still responding |

**Table 10.2**     Selected Kernel Threads

### 10.5.2    Starting and Stopping System Services

The daemons listed in [Table 10.1](#10_005.html_t10.1) are started via the init system, which I describe in detail in [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20). Almost all common distributions use systemd as the init system.

For now, I offer only a brief summary of how to start or stop a system service manually, what you need to do to make the daemon start automatically at system startup, or how to avoid an automatic startup.

You’ll need this information frequently, especially when setting up and configuring network services. Note that not only the command but also the service name may vary depending on the distribution. For example, the service for the Apache web server is called <samp class="listingcharacter">apache2</samp> in Debian, Ubuntu, and SUSE, but <samp class="listingcharacter">httpd</samp> in Fedora and Red Hat:

```
root# systemctl start   name       
(start once)
root# systemctl stop    name       
(stop)
root# systemctl status  name       
(get status)
root# systemctl restart name       
(restart)
root# systemctl reload  name       
(reload configuration)
root# systemctl enable  name       
(start automatically in future)
root# systemctl disable name       
(do not start in future) 
```

On Debian and Ubuntu, newly installed server services will run immediately and automatically on every reboot in the future. For other distributions, once you have completed the configuration, you must run these two commands once:

```
root# systemctl start   name       
(start now once)
root# systemctl enable  name       
(also start in future)
root# systemctl enable --now name  
(corresponds to start + enable) 
```

## 10.6    Starting Processes Automatically (Cron)

If your computer suddenly—seemingly unexpectedly—starts to search the hard disk or SSD, sends you emails, and so on, then the cause is almost always the automatic launch of processes through the Cron daemon.

This program is started automatically by the init process when the computer boots. It becomes active once per minute, analyzes all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">crontab</samp> files, and launches the programs specified there. Cron is primarily used for maintenance tasks: to compress and archive logging files, to delete temporary files, to update directories, to perform backups, and so on.

The global configuration of Cron is done by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/crontab</samp> file. In addition, users are allowed to define their own cron jobs in the user-specific files at <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/cron/[crontabs/]username</samp>.

The permission for user-specific cron control can be set using two files: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/cron/allow</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/deny</samp>.

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">allow</samp> exists, only the users entered here may execute <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cron</samp> commands. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deny</samp> exists, the users entered here are excluded. If none of these files exist, it depends on the compilation of Cron whether any users other than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> are allowed to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cron</samp>.

### Cron, Where Are You?

Many Linux installations have Cron installed automatically—but this is not a matter of course (any more); modern distributions such as Fedora have completely switched to an alternative system for starting jobs periodically (see [Section 10.7](#10_007.html_h10.7)).

Cron is also sometimes missing in minimal installations, which are common in the server and virtualization area. To solve this problem, run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf install cronie</samp> (Fedora/RHEL/SUSE) or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt install cron</samp> (Debian/Ubuntu)!

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/crontab</samp> file or the files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d</samp> contain line-by-line entries for the programs to run. The syntax looks as follows (see also [Table 10.3](#10_006.html_t10.3)):

```
# in /etc/crontab
min hour day month weekday user command 
```

If an asterisk is entered in the first five fields instead of a number, this field is ignored. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">15 * * * *</samp> means that the command should always be executed 15 minutes after the full hour, in every hour, on every day, in every month, regardless of the day of the week. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">29 0 * * 6</samp> means that the command is executed every Saturday at 0:29.

For the time fields, the notation */n is also allowed. This means that the command will be executed every nth minute/hour/and so on. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*/15 * * * *</samp> would therefore mean that the command is executed every quarter of an hour (n:00, n:15, n:30, and n:45). To change the global Cron configuration, you can edit <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/crontab</samp> or the files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d/*</samp> directly in an editor.

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">min</samp> | Specifies in which minute (0–59) the program is supposed to be executed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hour</samp> | Indicates the hour (0–23) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">day</samp> | Indicates the day in the month (1–31) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">month</samp> | Indicates the month (1–12) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">weekday</samp> | Indicates the day of the week (0–7; 0 and 7 both represent Sunday) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">user</samp> | Specifies for which user the command is executed (often <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">command</samp> | Finally contains the command to be executed |

**Table 10.3**     crontab Columns

Instead of the five time columns summarized in [Table 10.3](#10_006.html_t10.3), the <samp class="listingcharacter">@</samp> abbreviations listed in [Table 10.4](#10_006.html_t10.4) can also be used. Another additional rule states that a minus sign at the beginning of the first column prevents syslog from logging the command execution. However, this is only allowed if the sixth column contains <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>.

| Abbreviation | Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@reboot</samp> | - | Run after each reboot |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@yearly</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0 0 1 1 *</samp> | Run once a year |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@annualy</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0 0 1 1 *</samp> | Like <samp class="listingcharacter">@yearly</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@monthly</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0 0 1 * *</samp> | Run once a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@weekly</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0 0 * * 0</samp> | Run once a week |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@daily</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0 0 * * *</samp> | Run once a day |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">@hourly</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0 * * * *</samp> | Run once per hour |

**Table 10.4**     crontab Interval Abbreviations to Replace First Five Columns

### The crontab Syntax Requires a Line Break after the Last Line

Make sure that all Cron configuration files end with a line break: otherwise the last line will be ignored!

The following lines provide a few examples of entries in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/crontab</samp>:

```
# Run backup every night at 1:45
45 1 * * * root /myscripts/backup-site
# Cleanup on 1st day of each month at 6:00
0  6 1 * * root /myscripts/cleanup
# Log network connection every 10 minutes
*/10 * * * * root /myscripts/log-ping-result 
```

When a Cron job returns output or error messages, they are automatically sent to <samp class="listingcharacter">root@localhost</samp>. By setting the <samp class="listingcharacter">MAILTO</samp> variable in <samp class="listingcharacter">crontab</samp>, you can also set a different email address. Note, however, that sending nonlocal emails requires a configured email server.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/cron/[crontabs/]user</samp> files have the same format as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">crontab</samp>. The only difference is that the <samp class="listingcharacter">user</samp> column is missing because this information already comes from the name of the crontab file. To change user-specific Cron entries, you should use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">crontab -e</samp> command. Run <samp class="listingcharacter">export EDITOR=emacs</samp> beforehand if you do not want to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vi</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man cron</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man crontab</samp> contain more detailed information.

### 10.6.1    /etc/cron.hourly, .daily, .weekly, and .monthly

All common distributions have the following four directories set up:

```
/etc/cron.hourly/    
(run contained scripts hourly)
/etc/cron.daily/     
(run contained scripts daily)
/etc/cron.weekly/    
(run contained scripts weekly)
/etc/cron.monthly/   
(run contained scripts monthly) 
```

Thus, you can store your own scripts in these directories, but don't forget to set the execute bit (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod a+x file</samp>)! The scripts are then executed once per hour, day, week, or month with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. Using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.xxx-ly</samp> directories prevents you from thinking about the correct crontab syntax. In addition, compared to conventional crontab entries, these directories have the advantage that scripts defined in this way are executed reliably even if the computer isn’t running all the time.

The distributions differ significantly in the way the scripts contained in the four directories are executed. Most distributions require the Anacron program described in the next section to be installed, and Anacron then takes care of the execution.

However, on Ubuntu, running the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.xxx-ly</samp> scripts works without Anacron. This is accomplished by the following crontab configuration:

```
# /etc/crontab on Ubuntu
SHELL=/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin
17 *    * * *   root    cd / && run-parts --report /etc/cron.hourly
25 6    * * *   root    test -x /usr/sbin/anacron || \
  ( cd / && run-parts --report /etc/cron.daily )
47 6    * * 7   root    test -x /usr/sbin/anacron || \
  ( cd / && run-parts --report /etc/cron.weekly )
52 6    1 * *   root    test -x /usr/sbin/anacron || \
  ( cd / && run-parts --report /etc/cron.monthly ) 
```

In plain language, this means that Cron does the following:

*   Runs all script files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.hourly</samp> directory 17 minutes after every full hour

*   Runs all script files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.daily</samp> directory at 6:25 a.m. every day

*   Runs all script files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.weekly</samp> directory every Sunday at 6:47 a.m.

*   Runs all script files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.monthly</samp> directory on every first day of the month at 6:52 a.m.

If Anacron is installed, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">test -x</samp> returns a positive result and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-parts</samp> is not called. This isn’t even necessary because now Anacron takes control of the scripts in the four <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.xxx-ly</samp> directories.

#### Rules for File Names in /etc/cron.daily, -.weekly, and -.monthly

On Debian and Ubuntu, the file names of custom scripts in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cron.daily</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cron.weekly</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cron.monthly</samp> may only consist of numbers, letters, hyphens, and underscores! As soon as the filename contains even one dot, the script will be ignored by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-parts</samp>! These rules are intended to prevent backup files that are created when a script file is modified from being executed as well.

If you want to check which scripts from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run.daily</samp> are executed daily, you need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-parts --test /etc/cron.daily</samp>.

SUSE distributions are also independent of Anacron. Here, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-crons</samp> script takes care of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.xxx-ly</samp> directories. This script is executed every quarter of an hour:

```
# /etc/crontab on SUSE
-*/15 * * * *   root  test -x /usr/lib/cron/run-crons && \
                    /usr/lib/cron/run-crons >/dev/null 2>&1 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-crons</samp> isn’t quite as pedantic as Ubuntu's <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-part</samp> when it comes to checking file names. Only those scripts whose names look like backup files will not be executed.

### 10.6.2    Anacron

Cron assumes that the computer is running all the time, as is the case with servers. The situation is quite different for notebook computers or desktop PCs, which are frequently switched on and off again: Anacron was developed to ensure that tasks to be performed daily, weekly, or monthly are completed even in that case.

Anacron stores the execution time in files of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/anacron</samp> directory. This prevents a script intended for daily execution from being executed twice on the same day.

Anacron is controlled by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/anacrontab</samp>. In most distributions, the default configuration is as follows:

```
# File /etc/anacrontab (Debian, Ubuntu)
1        5   cron.daily       nice run-parts /etc/cron.daily
7        10  cron.weekly      nice run-parts /etc/cron.weekly
@monthly 15  cron.monthly     nice run-parts /etc/cron.monthly 
```

Here, the first column indicates how often the task should be done (1 = daily; 7 = once a week). The second column gives a delay time in minutes that Anacron allows to elapse before executing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">run-parts</samp>. This time period is to prevent daily, weekly, and monthly tasks from being completed at the same time.

On RHEL, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.hourly/0anacron</samp> script, which is executed once an hour by Cron, is responsible for Anacron.

If many Cron jobs start at the same time, this may cause heavy CPU or I/O load for the system. One option is to just consistently set up the jobs so that this doesn’t occur. Another option is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">RANDOM_DELAY</samp> variable, which can be defined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">anacrontab</samp>. This variable specifies a random delay time in minutes. <samp class="listingcharacter">RANDOM_DELAY=20</samp> causes each job executed by Anacron to be delayed by a random period of 0 to 20 minutes.

## 10.7    Starting Processes Automatically (systemd Timer)

Almost all distributions use systemd as an init system—that is, to automatically start and stop processes when the computer boots or is shut down. A detailed introduction of systemd in this function follows in [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20), [Section 20.1](#20_001.html_h20.1). However, systemd can also take care of the regular execution of processes, similar to Cron. This aspect of systemd is the focus here.

Most distributions make very sparing use of the systemd timer functions. In this respect, systemd should not yet be seen as a replacement for Cron, but rather as a supplement. The systemd timer does, however, have the potential to replace Cron in the longer term. A pioneer in this respect is, as usual, Fedora, which has already been completely converted to systemd timers. Cron is no longer installed by default (but is of course still available as a package).

The time-controlled execution of programs is controlled in systemd by timer unit files—that is, files with the extension <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.timer</samp>. An overview of active timers is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp>, although the following output is abbreviated to save space:

```
user$ systemctl list-timers
NEXT              LEFT      LAST              UNIT              
2024-04-13 11:01  3min 14s  2024-04-13 09:41  dnf-makecache.timer
2024-04-14 00:00  13h       2024-04-13 07:21  logrotate.timer
2024-04-14 00:00  13h       2024-04-13 07:21  plocate-updatedb.timer
2024-04-14 00:00  13h       2024-04-13 07:21  unbound-anchor.timer
2024-04-14 09:36  22h       2024-04-13 09:36  systemd-tmpfiles-clean.timer
2024-04-18 01:00  4 days    2024-04-13 07:21  raid-check.timer 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.timer</samp> files are in an easy-to-understand text format. The following lines show the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf-makecache.timer</samp> file, which is responsible for the daily start of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf makecache</samp> command. It updates the package database:

```
# file /usr/lib/systemd/system/dnf-makecache.timer
[Unit]
Description=dnf makecache --timer
ConditionKernelCommandLine=!rd.live.image
ConditionPathExists=!/run/ostree-booted
Wants=network-online.target

[Timer]
OnBootSec=10min
OnUnitInactiveSec=1h
RandomizedDelaySec=60m
Unit=dnf-makecache.service

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">OnBootSec=10min</samp> causes the process to be executed for the first time ten minutes after a reboot of the computer. <samp class="listingcharacter">OnUnitInactiveSec=1h</samp> means that the service should be restarted one hour after the end of the last run. If the time is given without a unit, seconds are meant. The syntax of the time specifications is documented in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.time</samp>. For example, two hours, 15 minutes or two weeks or four months is permitted.

<samp class="listingcharacter">RandomizedDelaySec=60min</samp> increases the time between two starts by a random time between 0 and 60 minutes. On average, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf makecache</samp> thus runs every 90 minutes.

Instead of these rather free defaults, you can also enter the time specifications in absolute terms in the <samp class="listingcharacter">[Timer]</samp> section. The following settings will cause the task to be completed every day at 8:15 a.m. <samp class="listingcharacter">Persistent=true</samp> causes missed jobs to be caught up on immediately the next time the computer boots:

```
# in a .timer file
[Timer]
OnCalendar=8:15
Persistent=true 
```

For absolute time specifications, systemd provides a complex syntax, which is documented in detail in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.time</samp> in the Calendar Events section. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">OnCalendar=Sun 2023-*-* 17:15</samp> causes a job to run every Sunday at 5:15 p.m. in the year 2023\. Systemd attempts to run set up timer jobs in a one-minute window after the scheduled time by default. If you want systemd to adhere more precisely to your specifications, you can enter a shorter time interval in the <samp class="listingcharacter">[Timer]</samp> section using <samp class="listingcharacter">AccuracySec</samp>—for example, from <samp class="listingcharacter">1s</samp> (one second) to <samp class="listingcharacter">1us</samp> (theoretically one millionth of a second, but in reality the start will not always be quite as precise).

Each <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.timer</samp> file must be matched by a corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.service</samp> file that contains details of the process to be executed. For the <samp class="listingcharacter">dnf-makecache</samp> example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">.service</samp> file looks as follows:

```
# file /usr/lib/systemd/system/dnf-makecache.service
[Unit]
Description=dnf makecache
ConditionPathExists=!/run/ostree-booted
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
Nice=19
IOSchedulingClass=2
IOSchedulingPriority=7
Environment="ABRT_IGNORE_PYTHON=1"
ExecStart=/usr/bin/dnf makecache --timer 
```

Newly set up timers must be started for the first time via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start</samp> and activated permanently (i.e., until after the next reboot) by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable</samp>. Similarly, you can end the call using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl stop</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl disable</samp>. For changes to take effect in already active timers, the easiest way is to run the following command:

```
root# systemctl reenable --now name.timer 
```

After setting up new timer jobs, you should always use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl list-timers</samp> to make sure that systemd has correctly interpreted your <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.timer</samp> specifications.

The following example shows how you can use systemd to run a simple script that checks the network connection every 10 minutes. By <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pinging</samp> three times, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping-kofler</samp> script tests whether and how fast the <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler.info</samp> server responds to network requests. The current time and the <samp class="listingcharacter">ping</samp> output are logged in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/ping-kofler.log</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">&>></samp> causes both the standard output and any errors that occur to be added to an existing file. This operator requires <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> version 4\. Do not forget to make the script executable by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod a+x</samp>.

```
#!/bin/bash
# file /usr/local/bin/ping-kofler
date &>> /var/log/ping-kofler.log
ping -c 3 kofler.info &>> /var/log/ping-kofler.log 
```

The following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.service</samp> file is responsible for calling the script:

```
# file /etc/system/system/ping-kofler.service
[Unit]
Description=simple ping test

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/ping-kofler 
```

The settings for an automatic startup are located in the following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.timer</samp> file. The script is supposed to be run for the first time 30 seconds after <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start</samp> and then every 10 minutes. The <samp class="listingcharacter">[Install]</samp> section is required to enable the timer permanently via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable</samp>:

```
# file /etc/systemd/system/ping-kofler.timer
[Unit]
Description=ping-kofler timer

[Timer]
OnActiveSec=30s
OnUnitActiveSec=10m

[Install]
WantedBy=basic.target 
```

To start the script execution and set it up permanently, another <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp> command is needed:

```
root# systemctl enable --now ping-kofler.timer 
```

### Cron/Anacron versus Systemd

The example immediately makes it clear that setting up a systemd timer involves much more effort than the one <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">crontab</samp> line that would be required for a periodic Cron execution.

The advantages of systemd are that systemd jobs can be controlled more precisely (own environment, see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.exec</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cgroups</samp> rules, etc.) and that their calls are logged in the systemd journal.

But there are also disadvantages: for example, an email is not automatically sent in case of an error.

For more information about the systemd timer configuration, see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.timer</samp> and the following pages:

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Systemd/Timers](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Systemd/Timers)

*   [https://blog.thalheim.io/2013/06/09/use-systemd-as-a-cron-replacement](https://blog.thalheim.io/2013/06/09/use-systemd-as-a-cron-replacement)

# 11    Network Tools

This chapter introduces commands for using, controlling, and analyzing essential network services. You will learn how to log into another computer on the network using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> and how to transfer files by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wget</samp>. The Lynx and Mutt programs even enable you to visit websites and read and compose mails in text mode.

Note that this chapter is only an initial starting point. Descriptions of other network commands follow in the context of other topics:

*   Commands for network configuration in [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15)

*   SSH variants and alternatives in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23)

*   Access to Windows and Samba network directories in [Chapter 27](#27_001.html_h27), [Section 27.7](#27_007.html_h27.7)

*   Network security and firewalls in [Chapter 29](#29_001.html_h29)

## 11.1    Determining the Network Status

This section provides an overview of commands for testing the basic functions of the network. More information about the commands presented here follows in [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15), [Section 15.3.1](#15_003.html_h15.3.1).

Without any additional options, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname</samp> command displays the host name as expected. What is less well known is that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname -I</samp> (this is an uppercase i—not a one, not even an L) shows the IP addresses under which the computer is visible to the outside world or within the local network. In the following example, the computer is assigned one IPv4 and two IPv6 addresses:

```
user$ hostname -I 192.168.178.50 2001:871:264:5779:82fd:84b3:6e09:60db
2001:871:264:5779:fcd1:5235:d5d6:20dd 
```

The result of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname -I</samp> is a simplification in that every Linux computer has multiple IP addresses even with simple setups. If you use the computer for program development and use virtual machines, Docker, or the like, then a dozen or more IP addresses are quickly in play. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> command (discussed ahead) lists all IP addresses—but the really relevant information is often difficult to find in the resulting jumble of numbers. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname -I</samp> attempts to filter out the really relevant addresses.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip link</samp> command returns a list of all network interfaces. The following result is from a different <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">host</samp> than that of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname -I</samp>:

```
user$ ip link
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue ...
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00
2: enp0s31f6: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ...
    link/ether 48:2a:e3:16:aa:24 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
3: wlp0s20f3: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500 ...
    link/ether 34:e1:2d:e7:c1:c4 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
4: virbr0: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500 ...
    link/ether 52:54:00:90:3c:0b brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
5: docker0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ...
...
25: vnet8: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ... 
```

In this result, <samp class="listingcharacter">lo</samp> denotes the loopback interface, which is a virtual internal network interface that is always assigned the localhost addresses 127.0.0.1 (IPv4) and ::1 (IPv6). Local programs on the computer can communicate with each other via these addresses.

Typical interfaces are <samp class="listingcharacter">eth<n></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">enp<n>s<m></samp> (Ethernet) and <samp class="listingcharacter">wlan<n></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">wlp <xxx></samp> (Wi-Fi). Most common distributions include the internal bus number in the name of the Ethernet interface, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s1</samp>. On PCs and notebook computers with only one Ethernet interface, the name seems cumbersome. But the bus-specific numbering ensures that on servers with many network interfaces, the numbering doesn’t change even when more network adapters are added. So in this example, <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s31f6</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">wlp0s20f3</samp> are names for two real interfaces.

The first twelve-digit number combination after <samp class="listingcharacter">link</samp> indicates the so-called MAC address, which uniquely designates each interface (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">48:2a:e3:16:aa:24</samp> for the Ethernet interface).

All other interfaces from the preceding example exist only virtually; that is, they are generated by software. They enable network traffic between Docker containers and virtual machines.

Details of the IP addresses assigned to an interface are provided via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr show <name></samp>. In its short form, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr</samp>, the command shows details of all interfaces, but this often overshoots the mark. The following listing shows that the <samp class="listingcharacter">enp1s0</samp> interface from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname</samp> example has one IPv4 address and three IPv6 addresses assigned to it. The address beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">fe80</samp> is only intended for internal communication on the local network (for details on this and on IPv6 configuration, see [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15)):

```
root# ip addr show enp1s0
2: enp1s0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc ...
    link/ether 52:54:00:6e:38:8e brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.178.50/24 brd 192.168.178.255 scope global ...
       valid_lft 861765sec preferred_lft 861765sec
    inet6 2001:871:264:5779:82fd:84b3:6e09:60db/64 scope ...
       valid_lft 7097sec preferred_lft 2863sec
    inet6 2001:871:264:5779:fcd1:5235:d5d6:20dd/64 scope ...
       valid_lft 7097sec preferred_lft 2863sec
    inet6 fe80::f126:174:824e:22cc/64 scope link noprefixroute 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> sends a small network packet to the specified address once per second. If there is a computer there, it sends a response, unless a firewall prevents this. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> keeps running until it is terminated via (Ctrl)+(C). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping localhost</samp> checks whether the loopback interface and thus the elementary network functions of its own computer are working:

```
user$ ping localhost
PING localhost (127.0.0.1): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 127.0.0.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=255 time=0.152 ms
64 bytes from 127.0.0.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=255 time=0.114 ms
... 
```

By passing the IP number of another computer in the local network to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localhost</samp>, you can test whether the local network is working. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c 2</samp> means that ping does not run endlessly, but that it will terminate after two packets:

```
user$ ping -c 2 192.168.178.1
PING 192.168.178.1 (192.168.178.1) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.178.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.33 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.178.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.817 ms
... 
```

If there is a name server on the local network that assigns IP addresses to host names, or if the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> file takes care of this task, you can specify the host name instead of the IP number when <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pinging</samp>:

```
user$ ping -c 2 raspberrypi
PING raspberrypi(raspberrypi.fritz.box (2001:...:6973)) 56 data bytes
64 bytes from raspberrypi.fritz.box (2001:...:6973): icmp_seq=1 ... time=0.525 ms
64 bytes from raspberrypi.fritz.box (2001:...:6973): icmp_seq=2 ... time=0.606 ms
... 
```

If both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are available, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> usually opts for IPv6\. If you want to explicitly test one protocol or the other, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping -4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping -6</samp>. On Debian and Ubuntu, there are even separate commands available for this (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping4</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping6</samp>).

Next, you can test if the connection to the internet succeeds. The following command tests two aspects of the network configuration simultaneously—the reachability of the name server and the function of the gateway:

```
user$ ping -c 2 google.com
PING google.com(fra24s04-in-x0e.1e100.net (2a00:...::200e)) 56 data bytes
64 bytes from fra24s04-in-x0e.1e100.net (2a00:...::200e): ... time=19.4 ms
64 bytes from fra24s04-in-x0e.1e100.net (2a00:...::200e): ... time=20.1 ms
... 
```

If this doesn’t work, several causes are conceivable:

*   Google's server may be unreachable right now (this is very unlikely), or the server may have disabled the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> response for security reasons. Try another well-known internet address.

*   The name server is responsible for determining the IP address for <samp class="listingcharacter">google.com</samp>. If you receive the error message <samp class="listingcharacter">unknown host google.com</samp>, there are problems with the name server. Verify that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> contains the address of a name server.

*   The gateway is responsible for forwarding IP packets from the local network to the internet. If this doesn’t work, you’ll receive the error message <samp class="listingcharacter">connect: Network is unreachable</samp>. You can check the gateway configuration using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip route</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip -6 route</samp>. The command usually returns multiple lines. The gateway address is located in the line that starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp>:

    ```
    user$ ip route
    default via 10.0.0.138 dev eth0 
    10.0.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.0.42 
    ```

*   If you’ve set up your own computer as a gateway in a local network, it’s possible that you’ve forgotten the masquerading function. In that case, internet access for the entire local network wouldn’t work.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">traceroute</samp> to determine which route a network packet takes from your computer to another computer and how many milliseconds the runtime is to the respective intermediate station. By default, the command makes three attempts and therefore returns three separate times accordingly. The command won’t work if there is a firewall on one of the intermediate stations that blocks UDP port 33434 used by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">traceroute</samp>. In this case, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">traceroute</samp> returns only three stars for this and all other stations.

The following lines show the route from my work computer to <samp class="listingcharacter">google.com</samp>. Line 1 specifies the IP address of my router, line 2 the gateway of the internet provider:

```
user$ traceroute google.com
traceroute -I google.com
traceroute to google.com (142.250.186.46), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  fritz.box (192.168.178.1)  0.829 ms  1.050 ms  1.423 ms
 2  62-46-79-254.adsl.highway.telekom.at (62.46.79.254)  6.399 ms  ...
 3  195.3.74.153 (195.3.74.153)  10.155 ms  10.279 ms  11.405 ms
 ...
 8  fra24s04-in-f14.1e100.net (142.250.186.46)  19.852 ms  18.986 ms  19.081 ms 
```

### Bypassing Firewalls

Sometimes security settings and firewalls hinder the work of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">traceroute</samp>. Instead of IP addresses, the command then displays only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">* * *</samp>. In such cases, you can try using other methods to trace the route of packets using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-T</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-I</samp> options. Both options require <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> privileges.

In GNOME, you can find most of the information listed so far (and much more) quite comfortably using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gnome-nettool</samp> program (see [Figure 11.1](#11_001.html_f11.1)). Some distributions require you to install the package of the same name first.

[![Network Diagnostics in GNOME](bilderklein/klein11_001.png)](img-f11.1.html)

**Figure 11.1**     Network Diagnostics in GNOME

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mtr</samp> command periodically sends network packets to the specified host and analyzes the responses. The result list combines data from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">traceroute</samp>:

```
user$ mtr -c 10 -r google.com
Start: 2024-04-16T14:17:47+0200
  HOST: u2104         Loss%  Snt  Last   Avg  Best  Wrst StDev
  1.|-- fritz.box      0.0%   10   1.4   1.3   1.0   1.9   0.3
  2.|-- dynamic-2ky... 0.0%   10   5.9   5.7   5.1   6.3   0.4
  3.|-- 2001:850:1:... 0.0%   10   8.8   8.5   7.6   9.0   0.4
 ...
 11.|-- 2001:4860:0   10.0%   10  19.7  19.9  19.6  20.1   0.2
 12.|-- fra24s07-in... 0.0%   10  19.8  20.0  19.6  20.3   0.2
```

## 11.2    Working on Other Computers (SSH)

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> command allows you to work on another computer in text mode as if it were in front of you. This would also be possible by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rlogin</samp>—but these two commands are considered obsolete for security reasons as they require you to transmit login information, including the password, unencrypted.

The basic requirement for using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> is that an SSH server is running on the second computer—that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sshd</samp> program. In some Linux distributions this is the case by default; in others, the program (mostly as the <samp class="listingcharacter">openssh-server</samp> package) has to be installed and/or enabled first (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start sshd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable sshd</samp>). If firewalls are running on the computers, they must not block port 22.

### Setting Up Your Own SSH Server

Information on installing, configuring, and securing an SSH server follows in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23). There you will also learn how to secure the SSH server.

If you use the <samp class="listingcharacter">uranus</samp> machine and want to start a shell session on the <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> machine on the local network, you need to run the following command to establish the connection:

```
user@uranus$ ssh mars
user@mars's password: ******** 
```

When you connect to a new computer for the first time, a warning appears according to the following pattern:

```
The authenticity of host 'mars (192.168.0.10)' can't be established.
RSA1 key fingerprint is 1e:0e:15:ad:6f:64:88:60:ec:21:f1:4b:b7:68:f4:32.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)? yes
Warning: Permanently added 'mars,192.168.0.10' (RSA1) to the list 
  of known hosts. 
```

This means that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> isn’t sure whether it can trust the computer <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> with the IP address 192.168.0.10. It could be that a foreign computer is pretending to be <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mars</samp>. If you answer “yes” to the prompt, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> stores the name, address, and RSA fingerprint (a code to uniquely identify the partner host) in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">~/.ssh/known_hosts</samp>.

If you want to work on <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> under a different login name than on <samp class="listingcharacter">uranus</samp> (e.g., as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>), you can use the notation <samp class="listingcharacter">username@hostname</samp>:

```
user@uranus$ ssh root@mars
root@mars's password: ********* 
```

### SSH Authentication with Keys

Authentication using a key is much more secure than logging in with a password. The procedure is described in detail in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.4](#23_004.html_h23.4). The use of keys also allows SSH-based commands and scripts to be executed automatically via script.

If you perform a Linux reinstall on a machine while keeping the previously used hostname, a dramatic security warning appears the next time you log in:

```
user$ ssh pi@raspberrypi
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@       WARNING: POSSIBLE DNS SPOOFING DETECTED!          @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
The ECDSA host key for raspberrypi has changed,
and the key for the corresponding IP address 2001:...:60db
is unknown. This could either mean that
DNS SPOOFING is happening or the IP address for the host
and its host key have changed at the same time.
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@    WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!     @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!

Someone could be eavesdropping on you right now (man-in-the-middle attack)!

It is also possible that a host key has just been changed.

The fingerprint for the ECDSA key sent by the remote host is
SHA256:HX5LOrT526ZqWrKKbWEvTAyIVGq+6XNf+Oc+76efqGY.

Please contact your system administrator.

Add correct host key in /home/kofler/.ssh/known_hosts to get rid of this message.

Offending ECDSA key in /home/kofler/.ssh/known_hosts:235
  remove with:
  ssh-keygen -f "/home/kofler/.ssh/known_hosts" -R "raspberrypi"
ECDSA host key for raspberrypi has changed and you have requested strict checking.

Host key verification failed. 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> command is suspicious that the SSH key used by the <samp class="listingcharacter">raspberrypi</samp> computer has changed since the last connection was established and it fears that you could be the victim of a hacking attack. If it is a foreign server, you will now have to go to the trouble of finding out why the SSH key change occurred. In most cases, you or someone else has performed a fresh installation on the computer. At the first start, the SSH server has generated a new key. In this case, the solution is simple. You delete the previous key from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.ssh/known_hosts</samp> (either using the following command or in a text editor) and then repeat the connection setup:

```
user$ ssh-keygen -f "/home/kofler/.ssh/known_hosts" -R "raspberrypi"
user$ ssh pi@raspberrypi
The authenticity of host 'raspberrypi (2001:871:264:5779:82fd:84b3:6e09:60db)' 
can't be established.

ECDSA key fingerprint is SHA256:HX5LOrT526ZqWrKKbWEvTAyIVGq+6XNf+Oc+76efqGY.

Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)? yes 
```

Instead of using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> interactively, you can run a command directly on the remote computer. The command and its parameters are simply passed as additional parameters to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> ends after this command:

```
user@uranus$ ssh mars command options
user@mars's password: ********* 
```

There are far-reaching possibilities that arise from this seemingly trivial function. For example, you can now run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> on the remote machine, redirect the archive it creates to standard output (enter a dash <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> after the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-f</samp> option, i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">-f -</samp>), and use the standard output with <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> as input for a second <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> command that runs locally. This allows you to copy an entire directory tree securely via SSH.

The following command shows how I copy the entire /var/www directory tree of my <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler.info</samp> web server to the local ~/bak directory. The command assumes that all files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www</samp> can be read by the user <samp class="listingcharacter">username</samp>:

```
user$ ssh username@kofler.info tar -cf - /var/www | tar -xC ~/bak/ -f -
username@kofler.info's password: ****** 
```

If you want to execute multiple commands in one script via SSH, it’s best to use the Heredoc syntax described in [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7), [Section 7.11.8](#07_011.html_h7.11.8):

```
#!/bin/bash
pw=newPasswordForUsername
...
ssh -T root@host <<ENDSSH
echo username:$pw | chpasswd  
rm -f /etc/file1
cp /root/file2 /userxy/file3
ENDSSH
... 
```

This causes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> to execute all commands until the line marked <samp class="listingcharacter">ENDSSH</samp> is reached in the script. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-T</samp> option prevents SSH from trying to open a pseudoterminal. This is not desirable here because the command execution isn’t supposed to be interactive.

The first time you establish an SSH connection to a new host, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> asks if you trust the host. Basically, this query is useful. However, if you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> to perform automated work on multiple hosts or virtual machines, the query interferes. The solution in such cases is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-o Strict\-HostKeyChecking=no</samp> option. You can also set this and other options globally in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/ssh/ssh_config</samp> or individually for a user in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.ssh/config</samp>. But do not confuse <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/ssh/ssh_config</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/ssh/sshd_config</samp>! The first file contains SSH client options; the second file contains options for the SSH server.

In an SSH connection that you have initiated using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh -X</samp>, you can also run graphics programs. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-X</samp> option is required for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> to take care of setting the <samp class="listingcharacter">DISPLAY</samp> variables correctly. Thanks to XWayland, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh -X</samp> for X programs also works in combination with Wayland.

```
user@localhost$ ssh -X otheruser@otherhost
otheruser@otherhost$ firefox  
(Firefox runs externally, but is displayed locally)
```

### 11.2.1    Copying Files Securely Using scp

To copy a file via SSH over the network, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scp</samp> command. The syntax looks as follows:

```
user$ scp [[user1@]host1:]filename1 [[user2@]host2:][filename2]
user2@host2's password: ****** 
```

This transfers the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filename1</samp> file from <samp class="listingcharacter">host1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">host2</samp>, where it’s stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">filename2</samp> file. Some notes on the many optional components of the copy statement:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">host1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">host2</samp> do not need to be specified if the local <samp class="listingcharacter">host</samp> is meant.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">user1</samp> need not be specified if the active user is meant.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">user2</samp> doesn’t need to be specified if the current user name of <samp class="listingcharacter">host1</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">user1</samp> is to be used on <samp class="listingcharacter">host2</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">filename1</samp> can also be a directory. You must then specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> option so that the entire directory with all subdirectories gets transferred.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">filename2</samp> need not be specified if the filename is to remain unchanged. The file is then copied to the home directory of <samp class="listingcharacter">user2</samp>.

    Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">filename2</samp>, the target directory can also be specified, using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">~</samp> for the home directory of <samp class="listingcharacter">user2</samp> as usual.

Let’s assume that user <samp class="listingcharacter">gladys</samp> works on computer <samp class="listingcharacter">uranus</samp>. She wants to transfer the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc.txt</samp> file to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">~/efg</samp> directory on computer <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scp</samp> command looks as follows:

```
gladys@uranus$ scp abc.txt mars:~/efg/
gladys@mars's password: ****** 
```

If you want to specify an IPv6 address in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scp</samp> command, you must enclose it in square brackets. Otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scp</samp> will be confused by the many colons:

```
user$ scp kofler@[2001:1234:5678::1]:file.txt . 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scp</samp> can also recursively transfer entire directory trees:

```
user$ scp -rp srcdir user@desthost:/destdir 
```

Instead of copying files using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scp</samp>, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> (see [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Section 28.6](#28_006.html_h28.6)).
