The SSH-based SFTP protocol is used for this purpose.

### 11.2.2    SSH Tunnel

One possible SSH application for advanced Linux users is tunneling. While the resulting tunnels aren’t suitable for transporting cars or trains, they do enable the transmission of all IP packets directed to a specific port. SSH tunnels thus provide a secure way to transfer IP packets between two computers—even if there is a firewall between the two computers that actually blocks the port. For an introduction to the world of IP packets and an explanation of the term port, see [Chapter 29](#29_001.html_h29).

If tunneling is done from the client computer, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-L localport:localhost: remoteport</samp> option is used. For example, the following command causes port 3306 of host <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> to be accessible through port 3307 of the local host. The command will start an SSH session at the same time, but you can prevent this by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-N</samp> (if you only need the tunnel, but not a shell). If the login to <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> is supposed to be under a different name, you must specify the login name as usual by <samp class="listingcharacter">-l name</samp> or by <samp class="listingcharacter">name@remotehost</samp>:

```
user@uranus$ ssh -L 3307:localhost:3306 username@mars
user@mars's password: ****** 
```

The tunnel remains open until the SSH session is terminated via (Ctrl)+(D). If you started <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-N</samp> option, the program must be stopped using (Ctrl)+(C). The usual MySQL port is 3306\. You can now access the MySQL server running on <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">uranus</samp> computer via its port 3307.

For the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mysql</samp> command, you must specify port 3307 and the host name 127.0.0.1 so that the SSH tunnel is actually used. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mysql</samp> makes local connections through a socket file:

```
user@uranus$ mysql -u mysqllogin -P 3307 -h 127.0.0.1 -p
Enter password: ******* 
```

For the MySQL login to work, two requirements must be met:

*   First, the MySQL server on computer <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> must accept IP connections in general. The MySQL server can also be configured to allow connections only through a socket file for security reasons. Then a tunnel does not help, because a tunnel can only connect ports.

*   Second, the MySQL server must accept the login name and host name combination. The host name used is the name of the computer to which <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> has established the tunnel: in this case, <samp class="listingcharacter">mars</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">mars.sol</samp> if the domain is <samp class="listingcharacter">sol</samp>.

### 11.2.3    SSH File System

You can integrate the file system of an external computer into the local directory tree using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sshfs</samp> command, which is included in the package of the same name in many distributions. This can make it easier to perform backups, for example:

```
root# mkdir /media/ext-host
root# sshfs user@hostname /media/ext-host
root# ...
root# umount /media/ext-host 
```

Note, however, that you will mostly get lower throughput in the SSH file system than with Samba or NFS because of the encryption of all data. For this reason, the SSH file system is only suitable for use in local networks to a limited extent. I have also found that <samp class="listingcharacter">sshfs</samp> reacts allergically to brief network outages and then freezes. I have therefore abandoned the use of this otherwise useful file system.

### 11.2.4    telnet

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> was a predecessor of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp>. Because <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> doesn’t encrypt any data, the command should never be used to work on external computers. Current Linux distributions don’t allow this by default anyway, but you can always find routers that allow this kind of communication.

The reason I present <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> to you here at all is that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> is good for checking whether a network service is running on an external computer on a certain port and waiting for a connection to be established. For example, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> to make sure that the mail server you set up earlier is actually running. To do this, you need to pass <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">telnet</samp> the name or IP address of the server and the port number:

```
user$ telnet kofler.info 25
Trying 5.9.22.29...

Connected to kofler.info.

Escape character is '^]'.
220 kofler.info ESMTP Postfix (Ubuntu)
helo kofler.info
250 kofler.info
^]    
(terminate connection using (Ctrl) 
+ (¡)
) 
```

## 11.3    Transferring Files (FTP and Others)

FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol and refers to a rather old method of transferring files through a network. FTP owes its great popularity to anonymous FTP: many large internet servers offer all users access to FTP archives. This access is not blocked by a password (unlike the other FTP).

A major drawback of FTP is that during the login process the username and password are transmitted unencrypted. A secure alternative is SFTP (Secure FTP) based on SSH (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23)). HTTP, the protocol used to transfer web pages, is also often used as an alternative to FTP.

This chapter is only about using FTP—that is, from the client point of view. For FTP to work, an FTP server must be running on the remote site.

The ancestor of all FTP clients is the interactive text command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp>. Because it typically transfers files from or to the current directory, you should use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp> to change to the relevant working directory before starting <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp>. The FTP session can then be initiated using the command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp user@ftpservername</samp> or simply <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp ftpservername</samp>. If you want to use anonymous FTP, you need to enter <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">anonymous</samp> as the user name.

Once the connection has been established and the password entered, you’re ready to go: You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pwd</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> commands, which have the same meaning as in Linux, to move through the directories of the FTP archive. To transfer a file from the FTP archive to the current directory of your computer, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">get file</samp>. The file name remains unchanged. Conversely, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">put</samp> to transfer a file from your current directory to a directory of the FTP archive. Of course, this is only possible if you have write permission for the directory. With anonymous FTP, this is usually only the case for a directory with a name like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/pub/incoming</samp>. The FTP session can be terminated using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">quit</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bye</samp> command. For a reference of the main FTP commands, see [Table 11.1](#11_003.html_t11.1).

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">?</samp> | Displays a list of all FTP commands |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd dir</samp> | Changes to the specified FTP directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">close</samp> | Terminates the connection to the FTP server |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">get file</samp> | Transfers the file from the FTP archive to the current directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lcd dir</samp> | Changes the current directory on the local computer |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> | Displays the list of files on the FTP server |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lls</samp> | Displays the list of files on the local computer |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mget *.pattern</samp> | Transfers all matching files from the FTP archive to the current directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">open</samp> | Establishes the connection to the foreign computer (if it did not work at the first attempt) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">put file</samp> | Transfers the file to the FTP archive (upload) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">quit</samp> | Terminates FTP |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reget file</samp> | Resumes the transfer of a file that has already been partially transferred |

**Table 11.1**     Important FTP Commands

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp> command isn’t very easy to use. Fortunately, there are countless alternatives. Most web browsers and file managers available on Linux can also be used for FTP downloads. If you want to work in text mode, you can use the interactive <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ncftp</samp> command. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wget</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lftp</samp> commands help with the automated transfer of files or entire directory trees via FTP.

### 11.3.1    SFTP (Secure FTP)

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sftp</samp> command is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssh</samp> package. Internally, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sftp</samp> uses a completely different protocol than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp> and, like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp>, can only be used if an SSH server is running on the remote site. Anonymous FTP is not possible with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sftp</samp>. Apart from that, the operation of the program is the same as that of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sftp -b batchfile</samp> allows you to automate SFTP downloads.

You can also use the Dolphin (KDE) or Nautilus (GNOME) file managers to initiate an SFTP connection by entering the address “sftp://user@servername”. After the password request, the programs display the FTP directory as a local directory. Both file managers also directly support the SSH protocol, which works even if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sftp</samp> is not available. For this purpose, you need to specify the address in the following format: <samp class="listingcharacter">fish://user@servername</samp>.

### 11.3.2    wget

The interactive approach of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp> command is unsuitable for automating downloads—such as in a script. But <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp> is also very inflexible in other respects. For example, it’s impossible to resume an interrupted download on your own. This can be avoided by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wget</samp> command, which is specifically designed to carry out large downloads or transfer entire directories. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wget</samp> supports the FTP, HTTP, and HTTPS protocols in equal measure.

In its basic form, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wget</samp> simply downloads the specified file:

```
user$ wget ftp://myftpserver.com/name.abc 
```

If the download is interrupted for any reason, it can be resumed without any trouble by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp>:

```
user$ wget -c ftp://myftpserver.com/name.abc 
```

Downloads of large files, like ISO images of Linux distributions, can take several hours if the internet connection isn’t very good. That's why it's a good idea to perform the download overnight. The following command almost ensures that the file is actually on the computer the next morning:

```
user$ wget -t 20 --retry-connrefused \
  http://mydownloadserver.com/name.iso 
```

Due to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-t 20</samp>, the download is retried up to 20 times after a connection failure. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--retry-connrefused</samp> causes a new attempt to be started even after the connection refused error. This is useful if the download server is known to be unreliable and is repeatedly unavailable for short periods of time.

The following command downloads all the files necessary to later read the specified web page offline in an unchanged state:

```
user$ wget -p -k -E -H http://mywebsite.com/page.html 
```

Let me briefly explain the meaning of the options: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-p</samp> also downloads CSS files and images. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-k</samp> changes the links in the downloaded files so that they refer to local files. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-E</samp> adds the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.html</samp> identifier to downloaded script files (ASP, PHP, etc.). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-H</samp> also tracks links to external websites.

If you want to read an entire website offline, the following recursive download command (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> option) will help. The recursion depth is limited to four levels by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">–l 4</samp>:

```
user$ wget -r -l 4 -p -E -k http://mywebsite.com 
```

### 11.3.3    curl

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> command helps to transfer files from or to FTP, HTTP, or other servers. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> page lists an impressive range of protocols that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> can handle. In this section, however, I will restrict myself to FTP uploads. For script programming, it’s particularly useful that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> can also process data from standard input or write to standard output. So you don't need to create a *.tar.gz file first and then transfer it to the FTP server, but can perform both operations simultaneously using a pipe.

The following command transfers the specified file to the FTP server <samp class="listingcharacter">backupserver</samp> and saves it in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dir</samp> directory:

```
user$ curl -T file -u username:password ftp://backupserver/dir 
```

To process data from the standard input channel, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-T</samp> to specify a hyphen as the file name. The following command saves the result of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> command directly in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.tgz</samp> file on the FTP server:

```
user$ tar czf - dir/ | curl -T - -u usern:pw ftp://bserver/name.tgz 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">curl</samp> is also well suited for testing REST APIs. In the following example, a service on the [https://ipinfo.io](https://ipinfo.io) website tries to determine your location based on the IP address of your call:

```
user$ curl https://ipinfo.io
  {
    "ip": "91.115.157.28",
    "hostname": "91-115-157-28.adsl.highway.telekom.at",
    "city": "Graz",
    "region": "Styria",
    "country": "AT",
    "loc": "47.0667,15.4500",
    "postal": "8041",
    "timezone": "Europe/Vienna", ...
  } 
```

### 11.3.4    lftp

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lftp</samp> is a convenient interactive FTP client. However, the command is also well-suited to execute FTP uploads or other commands in a script. For this purpose, you can either use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp> to pass several FTP commands separated by semicolons to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lftp</samp> or use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-f</samp> to specify a file that contains these commands line by line. The first command will always be <samp class="listingcharacter">user username,password servername</samp> to connect to the FTP server. The following command demonstrates a file upload:

```
root# lftp -c "open -u username,password backupserver; put www.tgz" 
```

If you want to give the file a different name on the FTP server, you need to additionally specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">-o <newName></samp> option. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lftp</samp> displays the current progress during the upload.

To transfer an entire directory to the backup server instead of a file, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mirror -R</samp> command. This command usually copies directories from the FTP server to the local computer. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-R</samp> reverses the transfer direction. Here is another example:

```
root# lftp -c "open -u usern,passw bserver; mirror -R directory" 
```

Unlike other FTP clients, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lftp</samp> supports the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp> command, which you can use to determine how much disk space your backup files already consume. This is important if your storage space on the backup server is strictly limited. The following command shows how you can determine the amount of memory already used without interactive intervention. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-s</samp> option indicates that you are only interested in the final sum. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-m</samp> ensures that MiB is used as the unit of measurement:

```
user$ lftp -c "open -u username,password bserver; du -s -m"
2378   . 
```

If you want to use the result for a calculation, the second column (i.e., the dot indicating that the numerical value refers to the current directory) will interfere. Simply add <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cut -f 1</samp> after the command to extract the first column:

```
user$ lftp -c "open -u usern,passw bserver; du -s -m" | cut -f 1
2378 
```

### 11.3.5    rsync, mirror, and sitecopy

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> helps you to copy or synchronize entire directory trees. For a detailed description of this command, see [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Section 28.6](#28_006.html_h28.6). If neither an SSH nor an <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server is running on the partner computer, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mirror</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sitecopy</samp> commands instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>. The Perl script <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mirror</samp> from the package of the same name copies entire directory trees from an FTP server to the local computer. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sitecopy</samp> command, on the other hand, is optimized to upload a directory tree to a web server, with the data transfer taking place either via FTP or WebDAV.

## 11.4    Lynx

Web browsers such as Firefox or Chrome are unusable in a text console or terminal window. Nevertheless, to quickly visit a web page or read an HTML document even in text mode, programs such as ELinks, Lynx, or w3m can help you. You also can use these programs to convert simple HTML documents into plain text. All three programs are similar in operation. Numerous options as well as keyboard shortcuts are documented in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> pages or in the integrated help system.

The operation of Lynx is simple: You usually start the program by specifying a WWW address or the name of an HTML file as a parameter. Lynx loads the document and displays the first page, with headings and links indicated by different colors. If you start Lynx with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-use_mouse</samp> option, you can also operate the program by mouse: you can follow a link with the left button, the middle button displays a context menu, and the right button takes you back to the previous page. Lynx uses the Latin-1 character set for output by default. To ensure that special characters are displayed correctly in Unicode consoles, you must specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">-display_charset=utf-8</samp> option. The following command shows how you can use Lynx as a converter from HTML to plain text:

```
user$ lynx -dump source.html > target.txt 
```

## 11.5    Mutt

The text-based email program Mutt can be used to read local emails (see [Figure 11.2](#11_005.html_f11.2)). The package, usually of the same name, must be installed prior to its first use. In a console window, you first need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">su -l</samp> to log in as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>, and then start the program using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mutt</samp> command.

The program displays the subject lines of all emails on the start page. If the active user hasn’t received a single email yet, Mutt complains that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/mail/user</samp> file does not exist yet. You can ignore this warning; it will stop appearing as soon as the first email arrives.

[![Reading Local Emails in Mutt](bilderklein/klein11_002.png)](img-f11.2.html)

**Figure 11.2**     Reading Local Emails in Mutt

You can use the cursor keys to move through the inbox. (Enter) displays the text of the selected email. The space bar allows you to scroll through the message. (J) takes you to the next message, (I) back to the inbox, and (?) displays a help text with all important keyboard shortcuts.

To compose a new email, you want to press (M) and specify the recipient and the subject line. Mutt then starts the editor that you selected using the <samp class="listingcharacter">$EDITOR</samp> environment variable or via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/alternatives/editor</samp> link. There you write the message text, save it, and exit the editor. Then send the email in Mutt by using (Y). (Q) terminates the program. Upon terminating, Mutt asks two questions: Should emails that have been marked as deleted with (D) be permanently deleted? And should messages that have been read be moved to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/username/mbox</samp>? If you plan to edit the emails later in a different program, you should answer (N) to both questions. The second question in particular is critical: in the local <samp class="listingcharacter">mbox</samp> file, only Mutt finds the emails, not an external program such as the Dovecot POP server.

Mutt works right out of the box if your email is in an mbox file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/mail/name</samp> directory. On the other hand, if your emails are stored in Maildir format in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Maildir</samp> directory, you need to set up the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/Muttrc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.muttrc</samp> configuration file with the following content:

```
# File /etc/Muttrc (global) or .muttrc (user-specific)
set mbox_type=Maildir
set folder="~/Maildir"
set mask="!^\\.[^.]"
set mbox="~/Maildir"
set record="+.Sent"
set postponed="+.Drafts"
set spoolfile="~/Maildir" 
```

More Maildir configuration tips for various special cases can be found at the following websites:

*   [https://gitlab.com/muttmua/mutt/wikis/MuttFaq/Maildir](https://gitlab.com/muttmua/mutt/wikis/MuttFaq/Maildir)

*   [https://eising.wordpress.com/mutt-maildir-mini-howto](https://eising.wordpress.com/mutt-maildir-mini-howto)

If you write an email as <samp class="listingcharacter">peter</samp> in Mutt, the program typically uses <samp class="listingcharacter">peter@ hostname</samp> as the sender address. On Debian and Ubuntu, the contents of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/mailname</samp> file are taken into account instead of the hostname, if it exists. If a computer is configured as a mail server, then this file contains the domain for which the mail server is responsible.

Sometimes you won’t want Mutt to use the full host name. Maybe the host name of your mail server is <samp class="listingcharacter">host1.a-company.com</samp>, for example, but emails that you compose in Mutt as <samp class="listingcharacter">peter</samp> should use only <samp class="listingcharacter">one-company.com</samp> as the host name. On Debian and Ubuntu, this works automatically thanks to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/mailname</samp> (see [Chapter 26](#26_001.html_h26), [Section 26.2](#26_002.html_h26.2)). On other distributions, you get equivalent behavior if you include <samp class="listingcharacter">set hidden_host=yes</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/Muttrc</samp> or in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.muttrc</samp>. This way, Mutt uses the domain name instead of the full host name.

If you’re unsure which setting applies to a particular Mutt option, you should press (:) and then run the command <samp class="listingcharacter">set ?optionsname</samp>. A good overview of the most important Mutt settings can be found on the Arch wiki at [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/mutt](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/mutt).

# Part IV

Text and Code Editors

# 12    Vim

The focus of this chapter is the Vi editor and its open-source implementation, Vim (Vi Improved). These editors are relatively difficult to learn, as is the Emacs editor presented in the next chapter. But this effort is worth it if you frequently edit text, program code, configuration files, and the like—that is, if a text editor is a constant and indispensable tool for you.

Vi and Emacs have the advantage that the programs can be executed in text mode in a console if required—that is, also in an SSH session. That is why administrators in particular prefer Vi or Emacs to modern editors that necessarily require a graphical user interface.

That still leaves us with the question of all questions: Vi or Emacs? The programs are primeval rocks of the Unix/Linux history. Both tools provide countless special functions, such as automatic syntax highlighting for numerous programming languages and document types or search and replace with regular expressions. There have been endless discussions on the web about which program is better. I can't really answer the question objectively: because written all other chapters of this book of this book with Emacs variants (except this chapter, of course), I am more familiar with Emacs than any Vi variants.

Personally, I find the Emacs editor more intuitive to use and easier to learn. With Vi, the distinction between standard and insert mode can drive you crazy at first. On the other hand, the fact that the program is a true standard on Unix/Linux speaks for Vi and its variants. It uses significantly fewer resources and is available even on minimal rescue systems. Real Unix/Linux freaks should know both editors in their basic functions anyway—and I don't teach much more than that in this book.

The original Vi editor is a commercial program and therefore not available on Linux. Vim, on the other hand, is an open-source program that is compatible with Vi and also provides countless improvements and extensions. The program can be started with the command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vi</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vim</samp>.

Basically, Vim is executed in a text console or console window. If you prefer a proper menu and neat scroll bars, you should take a look at <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gvim</samp> (see [Figure 12.1](#12_001.html_f12.1)). This graphical variant to Vim may need to be installed separately, and the package name is often <samp class="listingcharacter">vim-gnome</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">vim-gtk3</samp>.

[![Graphical Variant of Vim Editor](bilderklein/klein12_001.png)](img-f12.1.html)

**Figure 12.1**     Graphical Variant of Vim Editor

Due to space limitations, this chapter can only provide an introduction to Vim. The tutorial, which you can start using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vimtutor</samp> command, is very helpful for beginners. (This starts Vim and loads a help text containing an introduction and examples to try out). The following links reference pages with further information:

*   [https://www.vim.org](https://www.vim.org) (homepage)

*   [https://vimhelp.org/vim_faq.txt.html](https://vimhelp.org/vim_faq.txt.html) (FAQ)

*   [https://fprintf.net/vimCheatSheet.html](https://fprintf.net/vimCheatSheet.html) (keyboard shortcuts)

*   [https://truth.sk/vim/vimbook-OPL.pdf](https://truth.sk/vim/vimbook-OPL.pdf) (500-page Vim book)

Lead developer Bram Moolenaar refers to Vim as charityware. Vim is available free of charge under a GPL-compatible license. However, those who use Vim regularly are asked to show their gratitude in the form of a donation, which will go to a children's charity in Uganda. Further information is provided by the Vim command (Esc :) <samp class="listingcharacter">help iccf</samp> (Enter).

## 12.1    Quick Start

You usually start Vim by entering “vim [file name]” within a text console or in a console window. The file to be modified is displayed directly in the console.

Before you can start writing, however, you need to deal with a peculiarity: the program distinguishes between different editing modes (see [Table 12.1](#12_001.html_t12.1)). The default mode is not for entering text, but for executing commands. For example, if you type (L) in standard mode, this will move the cursor one character to the right. (D), (W) deletes a word; (P) reinserts it at the current cursor position; and so on.

To enter text, you need to switch to the insert mode via (I) (insert) or (A) (append). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vim</samp> displays the text <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-- INSERT --</samp> in the left-hand corner of the bottom line. In insert mode, you can enter text, move the cursor, and delete individual characters ((Del) and (Backspace)). The difference between (I) and (A) is that with (I) the input starts at the current cursor position, and with (A) at the character behind it.

Before you can enter a command again, you must press (Esc) to return to standard mode. This mode is not marked separately, so the left-hand part of the bottom line is then left blank.

### Changing Modes without Changing the Cursor Position

When switching from insert mode to standard mode, the cursor moves one character to the left—unless it is already at the beginning of a line. According to the Vim FAQs, this strange behavior is intentional and cannot be prevented. To execute a single command without leaving the insert mode—and thus without changing the current cursor position—you need to initiate the command input using (Ctrl)+(O).

In insert mode, you can use (Del) and (Backspace) to delete individual characters as usual. If you want to delete words, lines, or entire areas, you must first switch to standard mode by pressing (Esc). Then (D), (W) deletes a word and (D), (D) deletes an entire line. If you prefix a number, the delete command is repeated a corresponding number of times. (5), (D), (D) thus deletes five lines. (.) repeats the command that was executed most recently. (P) (put) inserts the most recently deleted text after the current cursor position, (Shift)+(P) before it. (U) (undo) undoes the last changes, (Ctrl)+(R) (redo) restores the changes.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (I) | Activates the insert mode. |
| (A) | Activates the insert mode. The text input starts at the next character. |
| (Esc) | Activates the standard mode or cancels the command input. |
| Commands in Standard Mode |
| (D), (W) | Deletes a word. |
| (D), (D) | Deletes the current line. |
| n (D), (D) | Deletes n lines. |
| (P) | Inserts the last deleted text after the cursor position. |
| (Shift)+(P) | Inserts the most recently deleted text before the cursor position. |
| (.) | Repeats the last command. |
| (U) | Undoes the last change. |
| (Shift)+(U) | Undoes all changes in the current line. |
| (Ctrl)+(R) | Undoes the undo (redo, as of Vim 7). |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> | Saves the file. |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q</samp> | Exits Vim. |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q!</samp> | Exits Vim even if there are unsaved files. |
| Commands in Insert Mode |
| (Ctrl)+(O) <samp class="listingcharacter">command</samp> | Executes the command without leaving the insert mode. |

**Table 12.1**     Basic Commands

To save the changed file, you need to switch to standard mode by pressing (Esc) and then enter the following command: (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> (Enter) (write). (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q</samp> (Enter) (quit) exits the editor if all open files are saved. Using (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q!</samp> (Enter), you can force an end even if there are unsaved changes. (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">wq</samp> (Enter) combines saving and exiting the program.

### 12.1.1    Help

Vim provides comprehensive online help. You can get to the start page of the help system from any mode by pressing (F1). Alternatively, in standard mode, use (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help</samp> or (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">topic</samp> to open the help. If you want to know what help topics there are that contain the keyword abc, for example, you need to type (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> (Ctrl)+(D).

The help text is displayed in a separate section of Vim (a so-called window, even though it isn’t a separate window in the sense of the Linux graphics system). You can close this window again using (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q</samp>. However, you can also leave the help window open and continue working in the original text. To do this, switch the currently active window using (Ctrl)+(W), (W). More information on handling Vim windows and buffers and editing multiple files follows in [Section 12.5](#12_005.html_h12.5).

In the help text, references to other help topics are highlighted (light blue in the version I tested). To jump to this topic, you must move the cursor to the keyword and run (Ctrl)+(¡). It is even easier if the mouse is activated (see [Section 12.7](#12_007.html_h12.7)): in that case, double-clicking the help topic is enough to go there. (Ctrl)+(T) returns you to the original page.

## 12.2    Cursor Movement

The cursor keys work in standard mode as well as in insert mode. You can also change the cursor position using various key combinations in standard mode (see [Table 12.2](#12_002.html_t12.2)). Vi freaks move through the text more efficiently in this way than by using the cursor keys.

A peculiarity of Vim is that (í) at the beginning of a line doesn’t place the cursor at the end of the previous line. Similarly, (î) at the end of a line doesn’t work as usual. To achieve the usual behavior of other editors, you need to execute in default mode, with (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set whichwrap=b,s,<,>,[,]</samp>, or add this <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set</samp> command to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.vimrc</samp>.

(M) <letter> stores the current cursor position in a position marker. Press (') <letter> to move the cursor back to the position thus saved.

Vim remembers the cursor position where a new cursor movement starts. ('), (') leads back to this position. Once again ('), (') moves the cursor back to the last position. ('), (¿) or ('), (¡) move the cursor to the beginning or end of the last changed text section.

In insert mode, Vim displays the current row and column numbers in the status bar on the right, as well as a percentage indicating which section of the text you are in (e.g., 92%). Via (Ctrl)+(G), Vim also shows in the status line the name of the file, its state (such as modified), the total length in lines, and the relative position in the text in percent.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Cursor keys | The cursor keys have the commonly known meaning. |
| (H)/(L)/(J)/(K) | Moves the cursor left/right/down/up. |
| (Shift)+(H)/(Shift)+(L) | Moves the cursor to the beginning or end of the current page. |
| (Shift)+(M) | Moves the cursor to the center of the current page. |
| (B)/(W) | Moves the cursor one word to the left/right. |
| (E) | Moves the cursor to the end of the word. |
| (G), (E) | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the word. |
| (¿), (¡) | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the current/next block. |
| ({), (}) | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the current/next paragraph. |
| (^), ($) | Moves the cursor to the beginning or end of the line. |
| (Shift)+(G) | Moves the cursor to the end of the line. |
| (G), (G) | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line. |
| n (Shift)+(G) | Moves the cursor to line n. |
| n (&#124;) | Moves the cursor to column n. |
| (%) | Moves the cursor to the corresponding bracket: ()[]{}. |

**Table 12.2**     Keyboard Shortcuts for Cursor Movements in Standard Mode

## 12.3    Editing Text

To insert a text character more than once, you must enter the number in standard mode, the command (A) (append), the relevant character, and finally press (Esc). So to enter the = character 50 times, you need to enter (5), (0), (A), (=), (Esc). Once you have entered the command, you will be back in standard mode.

Vim also helps you to correct typical typos: (~) changes the case of the current letter, and (X), (P) swaps the following two letters.

[Table 12.3](#12_003.html_t12.3) provides an overview of the most important commands for deleting text. If you enter a number before the delete command, the delete command will be repeated a corresponding number of times. As for all other Vim commands, (.) repeats the last command, and n (.) repeats it n times.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function in Insert Mode |
| --- | --- |
| (Del), (Backspace) | These keys have the usual meaning. |
| Function in Standard Mode |
| (X) | Deletes the character at the cursor position or the selected text. |
| (Shift)+(X) | Deletes the character before the cursor. |
| (D), (D) | Deletes the current line. |
| (D) <samp class="listingcharacter">cursorcommand</samp> | Deletes the text according to the cursor movement command (see [Table 12.2](#12_002.html_t12.2)). Examples: (D), ($) deletes everything to the end of the line. (D), (B) deletes the previous word. (D), (W) deletes the next word. |

**Table 12.3**     Deleting Text

Text is always deleted into a copy register. From there, the most recently deleted text can be reinserted into the text by using (Shift)+(P) at the current cursor position or using (P) behind the cursor position.

A peculiar way to delete text and then replace it with new text is provided by the (C) commands (change): For example, (C), (W) deletes the current word and activates the insert mode. You then enter the new word and finish the entry by pressing (Esc). (C) works similarly for other cursor commands.

You can also insert text into the copy register without deleting it. [Table 12.4](#12_003.html_t12.4) summarizes the corresponding commands. All commands apply to the standard mode.

Some (delete) commands require you to first select a text section. Vim provides three different selection modes, which you can activate or deactivate using (V), (Shift)+(V) or (Ctrl)+(V) at the starting point of the selection. While one of these modes is active, the bottom Vim line contains the text <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐- VISUAL --</samp>.

You then move the cursor to the endpoint of the selection or expand the selection using some specific selection commands (see [Table 12.5](#12_003.html_t12.5)).

As long as the selection mode is active, various commands are available for editing the selected text (see [Table 12.6](#12_003.html_t12.6)).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Y) | Copies the selected text to the copy register. |
| (Y), (Y) | Copies the current line to the copy register. |
| (Y) <samp class="listingcharacter">cursorcommand</samp> | Copies the text captured by the cursor movement. Example: (Y), (}) copies the text to the end of the paragraph. |

**Table 12.4**     Copying Text to the Copy Register

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (V) | (De)activates the character selection mode. |
| (Shift)+(V) | (De)activates the line selection mode. |
| (Ctrl)+(V) | (De)activates the block selection mode. |
| (A), (W) | Extends the selection by one word. |
| (A), (S) | Extends the selection by one block. |
| (A), (P) | Extends the selection by one paragraph. |
| (A), (B) | Extends the selection by one () level. |
| (A), (Shift)+(B) | Extends the selection by one {} level. |
| (G), (V) | Selects the most recently selected text again. |
| (O) | Toggles the cursor position between the start and end of the selection. |

**Table 12.5**     Selecting Text

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (X) | Deletes the selected text. |
| (Y) | Copies the selected text to the copy register. |
| (~) | Changes uppercase/lowercase. |
| (Y) | Merges the selected lines into one long line. |
| (G), (Q) | Performs a line break (for continuous text). |
| (>), (<) | Indents or outdents the text by one tab position. |
| (=) | Indents the text according to the current <samp class="listingcharacter">indent</samp> mode. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">!sort</samp> | Sorts the lines using the external <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sort</samp> command. |

**Table 12.6**     Editing Selected Text

Especially when editing code, the correct indentation of lines is important.

Vim helps you with this in many ways. The most basic commands are (>), (>) or (<), (<). You move the current line in or out by one tab position. If you select several lines of text beforehand, you can apply the commands to an entire block. The simple input of (>) or (<) is sufficient.(:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set shiftwidth=N</samp> changes the indentation depth (typically eight characters).

Vim can also attempt to automatically indent new lines as they are typed. To do this, you need to activate an indent mode—for example, by (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set cindent</samp>. The following is a brief summary of the basic functions of the main Vim indent modes:

*   autoindent Indents the subsequent line as far as the previous one.

*   smartindent Works like <samp class="listingcharacter">autoindent</samp>, but additionally considers {} bracket levels. For Vim to recognize the closing brackets correctly, they should be specified at the beginning of a new line. You can control the extent of indentation depending on the bracket level using the <samp class="listingcharacter">shiftwidth</samp> option. Previously selected text can be reindented by (=).

*   cindent Works like <samp class="listingcharacter">smartindent</samp>, but also takes into account various code structures of C or C++. The indenting mechanism can be adjusted to personal preferences via various options (see (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help C-indenting</samp>).

Vim is preconfigured so that writing code or changing configuration files works as well as possible. For this reason, Vim doesn’t perform an automatic line break (i.e., you must start new lines yourself by pressing (Enter). However, you can of course use Vim to compose ordinary text (such as for emails). [Table 12.7](#12_003.html_t12.7) summarizes some special commands and options that can help with this.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Shift)+(J) | Connects the current line with the subsequent one |
| n (Shift)+(J) | Connects n lines to one long line |
| (G), (Q), (A), (P) | Breaks the current paragraph again and places the cursor at the beginning of the next paragraph |
| (G), (W), (A), (P) | As above, but leaves the cursor at the current position |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set textwidth=nn</samp> | Automatic line break after a maximum of nn characters (normally: 0 = disabled) |

**Table 12.7**     Editing Continuous Text

The (G) commands take into account the <samp class="listingcharacter">autoindent</samp> mode as well as the <samp class="listingcharacter">textwidth</samp> setting. If <samp class="listingcharacter">textwidth</samp> contains 0, the maximum line length is 79 characters. Configuration options for particularly convenient continuous text input are provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">formatoptions</samp> option (see the associated help text).

Typing long words and function and variable names is tedious and prone to errors. Vim helps you do this in an ingenious way: you just need to type the first letters and then press (Ctrl)+(P).

If the word is already clearly identified, it will be completed immediately. Otherwise you can select the required word using (Ctrl)+(P) or the cursor keys. Vim takes all words of all loaded files into account for the word completion function, preferring words from the current file and especially words near the cursor position.

## 12.4    Search and Replace

In the default mode, (/) <samp class="listingcharacter">searchtext</samp> (Enter) moves the cursor to the text being searched for. (N) repeats the search, while (Shift)+(N) repeats the search backwards. To search backwards from the beginning, you want to start the search using (?) <samp class="listingcharacter">searchterm</samp>. [Table 12.8](#12_004.html_t12.8) explains the most important special characters you can use to search for patterns.

| Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> | Any character. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">^ $</samp> | Start of line/end of line. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\< \></samp> | Start of word/end of word. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a-e]</samp> | A character between a and e. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\s</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">\t</samp> | A space or a tab character. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\( \)</samp> | Summarizes a search pattern as a group. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\=</samp> | The search term must occur 0 times or once. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> | The search term may occur any number of times (even 0 times). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\+</samp> | The search term must occur at least once. |

**Table 12.8**     Special Characters in Search Term

Vim is case-sensitive by default when searching. If you don't want this, you must initiate the search pattern with <samp class="listingcharacter">/c</samp> (applies only to this search) or run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set ignorecase</samp> (applies to all subsequent searches).

You can use (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set incsearch</samp> to activate the incremental search: Vim moves the cursor to the first matching location as soon as you enter the search text using (/) <samp class="listingcharacter">searchterm</samp>. (Enter) ends the search; (Esc) cancels it. After the search, all matches in the text remain highlighted until you perform a new search or run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">nohlsearch</samp>.

To replace all occurrences of the text <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">efg</samp> without prompting, you need to run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">%s/abc/efg/g</samp> in standard mode. ('), (') then returns to the beginning of the search. [Table 12.9](#12_004.html_t12.9) presents some variants of the search-and-replace command. When searching and replacing with a query, you can use (Y) or (N) for each search term found to specify whether it should be replaced by the new text or not. (Q) cancels the operation; (A) replaces all further occurrences. In the replace term, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp>n to refer to the nth group in the search pattern. You can find a lot more tips on searching and replacing along with numerous examples in the online help ( (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help substitute</samp>).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">%s/abc/efg/g</samp> | Replaces all occurrences of abc by efg without a query |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">%s/abc/efg/gc</samp> | Replaces all occurrences of abc with efg with a query |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">%s/abc/efg/gci</samp> | Replaces without considering uppercase or lowercase |

**Table 12.9**     Search and Replace

## 12.5    Editing Multiple Files Simultaneously

In default mode, (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">e filename</samp> loads a new file. The new file replaces the currently edited file, which you must save prior to that, as otherwise Vim will abort the operation. You can force loading the new file using (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">e! filename</samp>, but then you will lose all changes made to the last current file.

Of course, you can also edit multiple files at the same time in Vim. Before that, however, you should understand the not particularly intuitive concept of how Vim internally manages and displays text. Each text displayed in the editor is internally located in a buffer.

This applies to both files and help texts. So long as there is only one buffer, it will be displayed in the entire Vim workspace. To display multiple buffers at the same time, the workspace is divided into several windows, as is the case when you display help texts. Such a window is not an independent window in the sense of the Linux graphics system, but only a subarea of the workspace.

The buffers of modified files are always visible in a window. On the other hand, buffers of files that haven’t been changed since the last save can be hidden. The buffers remain in the memory but are no longer considered active. (Use caution! If you close a window with a file that hasn’t yet been saved, all changes will be lost! The file's inactive buffer remains available but contains the file as it was at the time of the last save.) Vim is also able to display a file in multiple windows at the same time—for example, to edit different parts of a very long text.

Vim facilitates the editing of multiple files by using dialog sheets in text mode (see [Figure 12.2](#12_005.html_f12.2)). This works really conveniently if you’ve activated the mouse (see [Section 12.7](#12_007.html_h12.7)). Then you can easily select the currently active file using the mouse or close it via the X button in the top-right-hand corner. For more information about these tabbed pages, use (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help tabpage</samp>.

[![Three Files in Three Tabbed Windows](bilderklein/klein12_002.png)](img-f12.2.html)

**Figure 12.2**     Three Files in Three Tabbed Windows

Depending on whether you want to work with windows or tabbed windows, you can load new files using (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">new filename</samp> or (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabnew filename</samp>. If you pass multiple files at program startup—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vim file1 file2 file3</samp>—only the first file will be displayed; the other files will be loaded into invisible buffers.

To open each file in a window or tabbed window, you must also pass the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-o</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-p</samp> option. [Table 12.10](#12_005.html_t12.10) summarizes the most important commands for loading and saving files, switching between (tabbed) windows, and so on.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">e filename</samp> | Loads a file into the current buffer |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> | Saves the current file |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">wall</samp> | Saves all open files |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">wq</samp> | Saves and closes the buffer |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q</samp> | Closes the current buffer and exits Vim when no more buffers are open |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">q!</samp> | Closes the buffer even with unsaved changes |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">qall</samp> | Closes all buffers and exits Vim |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">split</samp> | Splits the window and displays the same text in both parts |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> | Creates an empty buffer and displays it in a window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">new file</samp> | Loads a file into a new buffer |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">only</samp> | Maximizes the current window and closes the other buffers |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">all</samp> | Shows all buffers in correspondingly reduced windows |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">buffers</samp> | Returns the list of all buffers |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">buffer n</samp> | Displays buffer n and deletes the current buffer |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">buffer file</samp> | Displays the buffer with the file in the current window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabnew</samp> | Creates a buffer and displays it in a tabbed window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabnew file</samp> | Loads a file and displays it in a tabbed window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabnext</samp> | Switches to the next tabbed window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabprevious</samp> | Switches to the previous tabbed window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabclose</samp> | Closes the current tabbed window |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabonly</samp> | Closes all other tabbed windows |

**Table 12.10**     Files, Buffers, and Windows

## 12.6    Internal Details

In the previous sections, special functions of Vim were repeatedly activated or modified by options, and this section introduces a number of additional options.

Note that some options apply only locally to the current file or buffer. In this case, (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> only changes the local setting. To change the option globally, you need to use (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">setglobal</samp>. [Table 12.11](#12_006.html_t12.11) summarizes the most important commands for editing options.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help options</samp> | Provides general information as well as an option reference |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">help 'option'</samp> | Provides information about the specified option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> | Returns all options that are not in the default state |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"><booleanoption></samp> | Enables the Boolean option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set no</samp><samp class="listingcharacter"><booleanoption></samp> | Disables the Boolean option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set inv</samp><samp class="listingcharacter"><booleanoption></samp> | Inverts the current state of the option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set option?</samp> | Shows the setting of the option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set option=value</samp> | Resets the option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set option+=value</samp> | Changes the option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set option-=value</samp> | Changes the option |
| (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set option&</samp> | Resets the option to the default state |

**Table 12.11**     Working with Options

All option settings are lost when you exit Vim. To set options permanently, you need to modify the Vim configuration file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.vimrc</samp>. Note that comments must be introduced by the <samp class="listingcharacter">"</samp> character! The following lines contain a simple example of what <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.vimrc</samp> can look like. All options used there have been or will be presented in this chapter. If you search the internet for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vimrc</samp>, you will find countless other examples:

```
" Example for ~/.vimrc
" Set cursor position with the mouse
set mouse=a

" <cursor left> at the beginning of the line moves the cursor to the end of the previous line,
" <cursor right> at the end of the line moves the cursor to the beginning of the next line

set whichwrap=b,s,<,>,[,]
" Create backups (name~) on save
set backup
" activate incremental search
set incsearch
" generally insert spaces instead of tabs
set expandtab 
```

The configurability of Vim goes much further still. You can set Vim options differently for different file types, program new functions yourself, and so on. But don't try to reinvent the wheel! At [https://www.vim.org/scripts](https://www.vim.org/scripts), you’ll find countless ready-made solutions that you can use with little effort. It’s usually sufficient to include the relevant file in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.vimrc</samp> by using <samp class="listingcharacter">source filename</samp>.

Regardless of the backup setting, Vim periodically updates a swap file while you are writing. The name of this file is a combination of a preceding dot, the current file name, and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.swp</samp> extension (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.mycode.c.swp</samp> if you are currently editing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mycode.c</samp>). This file contains all the changes you have made since the last save in a binary format. It’s automatically updated when you’ve entered more than 200 characters of new text or haven’t made any entries for four seconds. The swap file is deleted when Vim is exited in a regular way.

If the power fails, Linux or Vim crashes, or some other problem strikes, you can restore your unsaved work the next time you start Vim. Vim notices that a swap file exists when the file is opened and provides various options to choose from. Typically, you will choose (W) (restore) and then save the file thus restored. After that, you should exit Vim and explicitly delete the swap file. (This doesn’t happen automatically!)

Vim handles most major character sets by default, including various Latin variants, Unicode (<samp class="listingcharacter">utf-8</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">utf-16</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ucs-2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ucs-2l</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ucs-4</samp>, etc.), and some Asian two-byte character sets (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">euc-kr</samp>—that is, Korean).

Vim determines the default character set of the operating system during the startup process (<samp class="listingcharacter">encoding</samp> option). When reading a new file, Vim tries to detect its character set as well (<samp class="listingcharacter">fileencoding</samp> option). All character sets listed in the <samp class="listingcharacter">fileencodings</samp> option are tried in turn until a character set is found for an error-free display of the entire text. (The default setting for <samp class="listingcharacter">fileencodings</samp> is often <samp class="listingcharacter">utf-8,latin1</samp>.) To determine what character set the file you are currently editing uses, you want to run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set fileencoding?</samp>. You can use (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set fileencoding=<newcharacterset></samp> to change the character set. If you then save the file, it will be saved in the new character set!

## 12.7    Tips and Tricks

When entering commands that start with (:), there are some entry helpers: You can use the cursor keys to scroll through the most recently used commands. (Vim stores the commands in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.viminfo</samp> and thus remembers the commands even after the program ends.) Furthermore, you can complete keywords using (Tab) (e.g., when entering options). And finally, you can abbreviate many (:) commands (such as (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabn</samp> instead of (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabnext</samp>).

(:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set number</samp> displays the line number next to each line, while (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set nonumber</samp> deactivates this mode again.

By default, Vim doesn’t create a backup (i.e., a copy of the original file) upon saving. If you wish to do so, you need to run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set backup</samp> in standard mode. The backup file is given the name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">altername~</samp>. To enable backups in general, you can insert <samp class="listingcharacter">set backup</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.vimrc</samp>.

If you use Vim in a text console or in a console window, then the function of the mouse is limited to its basic functions on X: you can use it to copy and paste text at the current cursor position, but you cannot change the current cursor position, and so on.

To provide the mouse with more functions in Vim, you can either use the graphical <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gvim</samp> variant or run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set mouse=a</samp> in standard mode. Then you can reposition the cursor via a mouse click, select the active Vim window, scroll through the text using the mouse wheel, and so on.

However, this mouse mode has a disadvantage: the middle mouse button then inserts the most recently deleted text in Vim. The mouse can no longer be used to copy text between Vim and other programs. But you can easily solve this: the conventional mouse functions are still available if you also press the (Shift) key. But make sure that Vim is actually in insert mode when you insert text! Otherwise, the text inserted using the mouse will be interpreted as a command, and that can go wrong.

To make Vim always insert spaces instead of tab characters in your text, you should run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set expandtab</samp> or add the statement to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.vimrc</samp>. To replace all tab characters in the existing file with the appropriate number of spaces, you then need to run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">retab</samp>. Conversely, to replace spaces with tabs, you must run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set unexpandtab</samp> and then (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">retab!</samp>.

(.) repeats the last command; you already know that. But if you want to execute a whole sequence of commands multiple times, you should define a macro. To do this, start the macro mode in standard mode via (Q).

The next character specifies the name of the macro (to be precise, the name of the register where the macro is stored). All other commands are stored in the macro until you end the input by pressing (Q) again. After that, you can run the macro recorded in this way by using (@) <samp class="listingcharacter">macroname</samp>. (Once you exit Vim, all saved macros will be lost.) For example, the following key sequence records the macro a, which inserts the quotation mark <samp class="listingcharacter">"</samp> at the beginning and end of a word: (Q), (A), (I), ("), (Esc), (E), (A), ("), (Esc), (Q). If the cursor is now inside a word and you execute (@), (A), then this word will be put in quotes. (@), (@) repeats the last register command without you having to remember the macro or register name.

If you want to execute a Linux command in Vim without leaving Vim, you must run (:)<samp class="listingcharacter">!commandname</samp> in standard mode (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">!ls</samp> to get the list of files in the current directory). Vim then displays the result of the command. You can press (Enter) to return to the editor. To execute multiple commands, you must open a new shell using (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">sh</samp>. From there, (Ctrl)+(D) will take you back to the editor.

If you can't get used to the different Vim modes, but don't want to do without Vim anymore, it's best to start the program via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vim -y</samp> or run (:) <samp class="listingcharacter">set insertmode</samp>. This way the editor always will remain in insert mode. This means that you must initiate each command with (Ctrl)+(O). To execute multiple commands at once, you can also switch to standard mode for a longer period of time by pressing (Ctrl)+(L) and exit it by pressing (Esc).

Vim behaves even more like other editors when you launch <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">evim</samp>: this will start the editor in the graphical user interface, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gvim</samp>. Text selections can be made using (Shift) and the cursor keys. Texts can be copied using (Ctrl)+(C), deleted using (Ctrl)+(X), and pasted using (Ctrl)+(V). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man evim</samp> refers to the easy mode as “Vim for gumbies” (whatever a gumby is). You’ll have to make do without so many of the basic features of Vim that it makes more sense to use a different editor right away.

# 13    Emacs

To call Emacs simply an editor is not enough: the program is suitable not only for editing texts, but also as a complete development environment and, die hard Linux fans, even as an email client. Those who have grown up with Unix use Emacs as a substitute operating system, as it were, for all the functions of everyday work. In my case, it isn’t quite so dramatic, but the fact is that I have written this book (and many others) in Emacs since the first edition!

Where there is a lot of light, there are also shadows. The operation of Emacs looks daunting at first glance: it’s teeming with (Ctrl) and (Alt) sequences that are used to call the countless commands. It’s not without reason that mockers claim the name Emacs stands for Escape Meta Alt Control Shift. (As a matter of fact, Emacs stands for Editor MACroS.) At the same time, the user interface (menu, toolbar) looks antiquated. The configuration is cumbersome. Long story short: Emacs is an editor for professionals who are willing to invest time in learning it and who are not bothered by appearances.

## 13.1    Quick Start

This chapter focuses on GNU Emacs (see [Figure 13.1](#13_001.html_f13.1)).

[![GNU Emacs](bilderklein/klein13_001.png)](img-f13.1.html)

**Figure 13.1**     GNU Emacs

The Emacs fork XEmacs, which had a wider distribution for a while, no longer plays a role in everyday Linux. Much more interesting are the “small” Emacs variants like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">jed</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">jmacs</samp> (from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">joe</samp> package), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">jove</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zile</samp>: their main advantage is that their resource requirements are much lower. This makes these programs ideal for emergency systems or on servers where a configuration file only needs to be changed now and then.

For more information on Emacs, please visit the following websites:

*   [https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/emacs.html](https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/emacs.html)

*   [https://www.emacswiki.org](https://www.emacswiki.org)

### 13.1.1    Loading and Saving Texts and Exiting the Program

In Emacs, you can load a file using (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(F) <samp class="listingcharacter">filename</samp> (Enter). (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(S) saves a modified file. To save a file under a different name, you need to type (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(W) <samp class="listingcharacter">filename</samp> (Enter).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(F) <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> (Enter) | Loads a file (find) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (I) | Inserts a file into existing text (insert) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(S) | Saves a file (save) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (S) | Saves all files (with query) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (S), (!) | Saves all open files (without query) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(W) <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> (Enter) | Saves under a new name (write) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(C) | Exits the editor |

**Table 13.1**     Loading and Saving Files; Exiting Emacs

You can use (Ctrl)+(X), (U) (undo) or (Ctrl)+(^) to undo the most recent changes. This undo function works for any complex commands and is practically unlimited!

If you make a mistake while entering a command, you can cancel the command entry by using (Ctrl)+(G). This is especially useful if you press (Esc) by mistake.

(Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(C) terminates Emacs. If there are any unsaved files, a confirmation prompt will appear asking if you really want to exit Emacs without saving. Respond to this prompt by typing “yes” and pressing (Enter) if you actually want to discard the changes. If you use Emacs in a text console, you can temporarily exit the program by pressing (Ctrl)+(Z). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fg</samp> then lets you resume the work. In graphics mode, (Ctrl)+(Z) only causes the image to be reduced to an icon.

Emacs automatically creates a backup name~ containing the original text when saving. Also, Emacs periodically saves the current state of the text in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">#name#</samp> file. You can use this file if a power failure occurs while you’re working or if you can’t exit Emacs properly for some other reason.

### 13.1.2    Online Help

Emacs provides numerous commands for calling the online help. The most important command for getting started is (F1), (T) (tutorial). (Ctrl)+(X), (B), (Enter) will return you to the original text.

If after executing a help command, multiple text sections (windows) remain, you can use (Ctrl)+(X), (O) (the letter O) to place the text cursor in the next window in each case. (Ctrl)+(X), (0) (zero) removes the current window; (Ctrl)+(X), (1) deletes all windows except the current window. So with these three commands, you can jump back and forth between the help window and the text window and finally remove the help window again. If, on the other hand, the help text fills the entire page, you can use (Ctrl)+(X), (B), (Enter) to return to your actual text. Internally, the management of multiple texts—for example, your text and the help text—is handled by buffers ([Section 13.5](#13_005.html_h13.5)).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (F1), (F1) | Overview of existing help commands |
| (F1), (B) | Overview of all keyboard shortcuts (bindings) |
| (F1), (C) <samp class="listingcharacter">keyboard_shortcut</samp> | Short description of the assigned command (command) |
| (F1), (F) <samp class="listingcharacter">command</samp> (Enter) | Short description of the command (function) |
| (F1), (Shift)+(F) | Emacs FAQs |
| (F1), (I) | Starts the <samp class="listingcharacter">info</samp> system for displaying hierarchical help texts (for operation, see [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), [Section 6.3](#06_003.html_h6.3)) |
| (F1), (T) | Introduction to using Emacs (tutorial) |
| (F1), (Ctrl)+(F) <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> | Starts the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">info</samp> system and displays information about the specified command |

**Table 13.2**     Using Online Documentation

### 13.1.3    Editing Modes

Emacs provides different editing modes in which additional commands are available for editing special files. A distinction is made between the main and secondary modes: only one main mode can be active at a time. However, it can be supplemented by several submodes.

The most important main modes include those for almost all common programming languages (C, C++, Java, etc.) and the LaTeX mode for editing LaTeX files. When loading a file, Emacs automatically activates the mode that seems appropriate to it (e.g., C mode if the file name ends in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.c</samp>). If Emacs can’t detect a suitable mode, it selects the fundamental mode as the default.

The most important secondary modes include the fill mode for editing continuous text with paragraphs across multiple lines and the abbrev mode for the automatic resolution of abbreviations.

If you want to disable peculiarities of Emacs due to a certain mode (such as the automatic indentation of program lines in C mode), you can simply switch to the fundamental mode by using (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">fundamental-mode</samp> (Enter). For more detailed information on editing modes, see [Section 13.6](#13_006.html_h13.6).

### 13.1.4    Keyboard

In general, there are three ways to enter Emacs commands: the menu, using keyboard shortcuts (mostly a combination with (Ctrl) or (Alt)), or typing the entire command name. The third variant is introduced with (Alt)+(X), such as (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">delete-char</samp> (Enter).

The input of commands and other parameters is facilitated by two mechanisms:

*   During input, you can add the command name with (Tab) as you would when entering commands in the shell terminal. Emacs distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters.

*   You can return to commands previously entered using (Alt)+(X) (after introducing the new command with (Alt)+(X)) using (Alt)+(P) (previous) and (Alt)+(N) (next).

In this book, the key sequences are provided as they would be entered on a keyboard. A plus sign means that several keys must be pressed simultaneously, while a comma indicates that the keys are pressed one after the other. Note that Emacs distinguishes between (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(B) and the similar looking combination (Ctrl)+(X), (B)! So it does matter how long you hold down the (Ctrl) key.

In the Emacs documentation, keyboard shortcuts are presented somewhat differently: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">DEL</samp> refers to (Backspace)! <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">C</samp> represents control (meaning (Ctrl)) and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">M</samp> stands for meta (meaning (Alt)).

There is no direct equivalent of the meta key on a standard PC keyboard. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">M‐x</samp> can be emulated on a PC keyboard in two ways: by (Esc) and (X) (in succession) or by (Alt)+(X). In this chapter, I use the (Alt) key combination in each case. With some Emacs-compatible programs or when you use Emacs in a text console, there are sometimes problems with the (Alt) key. Instead of (Alt)+(X), you have to use (Esc), (X) there.

Unicode characters that are not available on the keyboard can be entered by their hexadecimal code. To do this, you need to execute (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">ucs-insert n</samp> or, shorter, (Alt)+(X), (8), (Enter) <samp class="listingcharacter">hexcode</samp>. For example, you can enter the euro sign (€) using (Alt)+(X), (8), (Enter) <samp class="listingcharacter">20ac</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">ucs-insert</samp> command also accepts the names of Unicode characters. Thus, (Alt)+(X), (8), (Enter) <samp class="listingcharacter">euro sign</samp> also inserts the euro sign.

## 13.2    Cursor Movement

Besides the cursor keys, Emacs uses numerous keyboard shortcuts for the cursor movement.

The most important shortcuts are listed in [Table 13.3](#13_002.html_t13.3).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Alt)+(F)/(Alt)+(B) | Moves the cursor one word forward or backward (forward/backward) |
| (Ctrl)+(A)/(Ctrl)+(E) | Places the cursor at the beginning or the end of the line |
| (Alt)+(A)/(Alt)+(E) | Places the cursor at the beginning or the end of the paragraph |
| (Ctrl)+(V)/(Alt)+(V) | Moves the text one page down or up |
| (Alt)+(<)/(Alt)+(Shift)+(>) | Moves the cursor to the beginning or end of the text |
| (Ctrl)+(L) | Scrolls the text so that the cursor is in the center of the screen |
| (Alt)+(G) n (Enter) | Places the cursor in line n |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (R), space <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> (Enter) | Saves the current cursor position in register <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (R), (J) <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> (Enter) | Jumps to the position stored in register <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> |

**Table 13.3**     Cursor Movement

Emacs is able to execute any command several times in a row. To do this, you must first type (Alt)+n, where n represents any number. The digits must come from the alphanumeric keyboard section (not from the number pad). You must hold down (Alt) during the entire number input. Then specify the command you want to use. For example, (Alt)+n, (Page ↓) scrolls the text down by n pages.

This method can also be used to enter text characters. For example, (Alt)+60, (-) draws a line.

In a longer text, you may often wish to be able to quickly jump back and forth between different places in the text. For this purpose, the current cursor position can be stored with a command in a so-called register (see the penultimate line in [Table 13.3](#13_002.html_t13.3)). A register is a memory location that is identified by a text character (letter or number). At a later time, you can then jump back to the originally saved location by specifying this register. Note that registers are not saved when you exit Emacs.

## 13.3    Editing Text

You have already become familiar with the (Del) or (Ctrl)+(D) keys and (Backspace) to delete individual characters. To delete larger chunks of text, you can use the commands listed in [Table 13.4](#13_003.html_t13.4). If you execute the delete commands listed there multiple times in immediate succession, (Ctrl)+(Y) will reinsert the entire deleted text.
