(Ctrl)+(Y) can be executed multiple times and at any position in the text. The command thus allows you to move or copy the deleted text to another place.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Alt)+(D) | Deletes the next word |
| (Alt)+(Backspace) | Deletes the previous word or the beginning of the word up to the cursor |
| (Ctrl)+(K) | Deletes the end of the line from the cursor position |
| (Alt)+(0), (Ctrl)+(K) | Deletes the beginning of the line before the cursor position |
| (Alt)+(M) | Deletes the next paragraph |
| (Alt)+(Z), <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> | Deletes all characters up to the next occurrence of x (the x character gets deleted as well) |
| (Ctrl)+(Y) | Reinserts the most recently deleted text |

**Table 13.4**     Deleting and Reinserting Text

The commands in [Table 13.4](#13_003.html_t13.4) are relatively inflexible because the amount of text to be deleted is rigidly specified. If you want to delete any text excerpt, you must first select it. To do this, you can either use the cursor keys together with (Shift), or first set an invisible marker point at the beginning or end of the range by using (Ctrl)+(Space) (see [Table 13.5](#13_003.html_t13.5)). From now on, the selected range is the text between the selected point and the current position of the text cursor.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(Space) | Sets an (invisible) marker point |
| (Ctrl)+(W) | Deletes the text between the marker point and the current cursor position |
| (Ctrl)+(Y) | Reinserts the most recently deleted text |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(X) | Swaps cursor position and marker point |

**Table 13.5**     Selecting Text

Using (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">cua-mode</samp>, you can activate the common-user-access mode. If you have selected text using (Shift), you can copy it to the clipboard by using (Ctrl)+(C) or cut it using (Ctrl)+(X) as in almost any other program. (Ctrl)+(V) inserts the current clipboard content at the cursor position. If no text is selected, (Ctrl)+(X) initiates various Emacs commands as before.

Emacs is usually in insert mode. That is, newly entered text is inserted into the existing text at the current cursor position. If you want to overwrite the existing text instead, you need to switch to overwrite mode via (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">overwrite-mode</samp> (Enter) or by using (Ins). Executing the command again switches the mode off again.

A common typo occurs when two letters are swapped. You can use (Ctrl)+(T) to easily correct such swaps. The cursor must be positioned on the second of the two letters in question; for example, on w in the word sawp.

Similarly, you can use (Alt)+(T) to swap two words. If the cursor is positioned at the beginning of a word, this word will be swapped with the previous one. If, on the other hand, the cursor is somewhere in the word, then the word is swapped with the following word. Running (Alt)+(T) multiple times causes the first of the two words to move further and further forward. Finally, (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(T) enables you to swap the current line with the previous line. A repeated execution of the command causes the line above the cursor to slide further and further down.

### 13.3.1    Tabs

By default and when you edit a normal text, (Tab) inserts a tab character. Tabs are not visible. You will not notice whether there is a tab character or multiple spaces at a position until you move the cursor over it. With tabs, the cursor moves in jumps.

If you edit program code, (Tab) causes the beginning of the line to be indented according to the program structure. In LaTeX mode, the (Tab) key has no effect at all. So if (Tab) doesn't work as you expect, it's mostly the edit mode that is to blame. To enter a tab character anyway, you must run (Ctrl)+(Q), (Tab).

Typically, the tab width is eight characters. But you can use (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">set-variable tab-width</samp> to set a different tab width. If you generally want to work with four instead of eight characters per tab, you can also make this setting in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">~/.emacs</samp> configuration file.

In some editing modes, Emacs automatically replaces long sequences of spaces with tabs. The (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">tabify</samp> commands allow you to replace all blank character series with tab characters in the previously selected area. (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">untabify</samp> works the other way round and replaces tabs with a sufficient number of spaces.

If you include the following line in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp> configuration file, Emacs generally inserts spaces instead of tab characters:

```
(setq-default indent-tabs-mode nil) 
```

### 13.3.2    Indenting and Outdenting Text Manually

Text indenting and outdenting is required especially in program listings to structure the code. The most important command can be called via (Ctrl)+(X), (Tab) (see [Table 13.6](#13_003.html_t13.6)). This command indents the text between the marker point ((Ctrl)+(Space)) and the current cursor position by one space. If you execute (Alt)+<samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> before this command, the selected text area will be indented by n characters. A preceding (Esc), (-) moves the text out instead of in.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(Space) | Sets a marker point |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Tab) | Indents text between the marker point and cursor position by one character |
| (Esc), (-), (Ctrl)+(X), (Tab) | Outdents text by one character |
| (Alt)+<samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>, (Ctrl)+(X), (Tab) | Indents text by n characters |
| (Esc), (-), (Alt)+n, (Ctrl)+(X), (Tab) | Indents text by n characters |

**Table 13.6**     Indenting and Outdenting Text

If you want to insert or delete rectangular text blocks within lines (e.g., when editing tables or to indent or outdent comments at the end of program lines), you must use the rectangle commands (see [Table 13.7](#13_003.html_t13.7)). All characters in the area between the marker point and the cursor position are considered to be rectangles. Rectangular text blocks can be edited even more comfortably in CUA mode. When this mode is active, you can start rectangle marking by using (Ctrl)+(Enter). Then you can delete characters in all lines using (Del) or insert new text with all other keys.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(Space) | Sets a marker point |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (R), (O) | Opens a rectangular area (rectangle open)—that is, inserts spaces into the rectangular area |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (R), (K) | Deletes a rectangular area (rectangle kill) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (R), (Y) | Inserts a deleted rectangular area at the cursor position (rectangle yank) |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">string-rectangle</samp> | Inserts a text before each line of the range |
| (Ctrl)+(Enter) | Rectangle marker in CUA mode |

**Table 13.7**     Rectangle Commands

### 13.3.3    Continuous Text

To this point, I have assumed that you use Emacs to edit program code, configuration files, and so on. But dealing with Emacs is a little different when you want to edit continuous text. Emacs does not normally perform automatic wrapping. If lines are longer than the screen or window width, then a <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> character is displayed at the left end and the text continues on the next line.

If you want to break a single longer line, you need to execute the (Alt)+(Q) command: this replaces spaces with line breaks in appropriate places. Thus, one long line becomes multiple short lines.

Emacs considers all lines that are not explicitly separated from other lines by a completely blank line as one paragraph. For a program listing, the consequences of this command are of course fatal! Perform an undo operation using (Ctrl)+(X), (U).

#### Line Breaks in LaTeX Documents

If you edit TeX or LaTeX files, a special feature applies to (Alt)+(Q): Lines beginning with a <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> character are considered paragraph boundaries and do not break. To perform a wrap anyway, you have to manually join this line with the previous line and execute (Alt)+(Q) again. It is even more convenient to install and activate the AUC-TEX package: then Emacs understands LaTeX better and performs the line break more intelligently.

When you enter new text, it is of course annoying to constantly press (Alt)+(Q). For this reason, a separate continuous text mode exists, which can be activated using (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">auto-fill-mode</samp> (Enter) (see [Table 13.8](#13_003.html_t13.8)).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Alt)+(Q) | Performs a manual line break |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">auto-fill-mode</samp> (Enter) | Activates the continuous text mode (automatic line break) |

**Table 13.8**     Wrapping Continuous Text

When Emacs is in this mode, all new input is automatically wrapped. Existing text isn’t changed by this mode. Even deleting text doesn’t lead to an automatic wrap, which is why a manual wrap via (Alt)+(Q) often has to be forced after changes in an already existing continuous text. The wrap typically occurs after 70 characters at the latest. You can change the wrap column using the following command: (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">set-variable</samp> (Enter) <samp class="listingcharacter">fill-column</samp> (Enter) n (Enter).

A special feature of Emacs is that you can use keyboard shortcuts without any preliminary work. To do this, you just enter the first letters of a word and press (Alt)+(/). Emacs then searches first in the preceding text, then in the following text, and finally in all open files for words that begin with these characters. If you type <samp class="listingcharacter">env</samp> (Alt)+(/) at this point in the text, Emacs replaces env with environment. If you press (Alt)+(/) more often, Emacs offers other possible additions, such as envelope and envy.

Dynamic extensions work only if a word is already in the text of a loaded file (it doesn’t have to be the current file) and if the initial letters match.

## 13.4    Search and Replace

The fastest way to find text is to use (Ctrl)+(S) <samp class="listingcharacter">searchtext</samp>. The command starts the search immediately after the first character has been entered. So if you want to search for secondary mode and type (Ctrl)+(S) “sec”, the cursor will already jump to the first word that starts with sec. Instead of typing the other letters, you can then jump to the next word that also starts with sec by pressing (Ctrl)+(S) again. (If you enter only lowercase letters, there is no distinction between uppercase and lowercase.) If you now suddenly decide that you actually want to search for severity, you can delete the c by using the (Backspace) key. Emacs then jumps back to the first word (starting from the position at the beginning of the search) that begins with se. If you then type “v”, Emacs jumps further to the first word that starts with sev.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(S) | Incremental search forward |
| (Ctrl)+(R) | Incremental search backward |
| (Alt)+(P) | Selects a previously used search text (previous) |
| (Alt)+(N) | Selects a search text to be used later (next) |
| (Ctrl)+(G) | Cancels the search |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(X) | Swaps the marker point (start of the search) and the current cursor position |
| (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(S) | Incremental pattern search forward |
| (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(R) | Incremental pattern search backward |
| (Alt)+(%) | Search and replace without pattern |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">query-replace-r</samp> (Enter) | Search and replace with pattern |

**Table 13.9**     Search and Replace Commands

As soon as you press (Enter) or a cursor key, the program assumes that the search is complete and places the cursor at the position it has found. The start of the search is saved by a marker point. For this reason, you can use (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(X) to easily move the cursor back to where it was at the start of the search. Repeating this (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(X) pattern will take you back to the place of the search text.

By pressing (Ctrl)+(S) twice, you can resume the search and jump to the next occurrence of the search text. If you want to search backward, just press (Ctrl)+(R) instead of (Ctrl)+(S).

If at a later time you want to search for a text that you have already searched for previously, you can select a text from the saved list of search texts using (Alt)+(P) (previous) and (Alt)+(N) (next) after pressing (Ctrl)+(S).

### 13.4.1    Searching for Patterns (with Regular Expressions)

The incremental search finds texts that exactly match the search text. But in many cases, it’s preferable to search for texts that correspond to a certain pattern. You can start such a search via (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(S) or +(R).

| Search Pattern | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\<</samp> | Beginning of a word |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> | End of a word |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> | Beginning of the line |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> | End of the line |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> | Any character (except the line break) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.*</samp> | Any number (including 0) of arbitrary characters (like * in filenames) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.+</samp> | Any number of arbitrary characters (but at least one) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.?</samp> | None or any character |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[abc..]</samp> | One of the listed characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[^abc..]</samp> | None of the listed characters |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\(</samp> | Start of a group (see [Section 13.4.2](#13_004.html_h13.4.2)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\)</samp> | End of a group |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\x</samp> | Special character x (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">\\</samp> to search for a <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> character or <samp class="listingcharacter">\.</samp> to search for a dot). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\&</samp> | Placeholder in the replace pattern for the entire text that has been found |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\1</samp> | Placeholder in the replace pattern for the first <samp class="listingcharacter">\(...\)</samp> group in the search text |

**Table 13.10**     Structure of Regular Search Pattern

The search text is case-sensitive. Here are some examples to show the syntax of the pattern string (see [Table 13.10](#13_004.html_t13.10)):

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">\<[Tt]he\></samp> searches for the article the, whether it is lowercase or uppercase. Compound words that contain the (such as thesis) are ignored.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">[Tt]he[a-z]+</samp> searches for compound words beginning with The or the followed by at least one other letter. The cursor stops at the end of each word (at the first character that is not a letter between a and z).

The character pairs <samp class="listingcharacter">\(</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">\)</samp> have no influence on the actual search. However, the characters in the searched text that correspond to the characters contained in the group can then be reused to form the replace text (see the next section).

### 13.4.2    Search and Replace

Emacs also distinguishes between the normal command and the extended version with pattern search when searching and replacing. The normal variant with (Alt)+(%) ignores uppercase and lowercase during the search. When replacing (see [Table 13.11](#13_004.html_t13.11)), the initial letters of words remain as they were before if the replace text is completely lowercase. The find and replace command cannot be used for multiline texts because the wildcard characters * and + are not effective beyond one line.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Space) or (Y) | Replace, continue search. |
| (,) | Replace, but leave the cursor so that the result can be checked. If everything is OK, the command can be continued by pressing the spacebar. |
| (Backspace) or (N) | Do not replace, continue search. |
| (Esc) | Do not replace, cancel command. |
| (!) | Perform all further replacements without confirmation. |
| (Ctrl)+(R) | Temporarily interrupt the command to make a manual correction at the cursor position (recursive edit). |
| (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(R) | Resume replace command. |

**Table 13.11**     Keyboard Shortcuts for Editing Found Text

You can start the search and replace process with patterns using (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">query-replace-r</samp> (Enter). In the replace string, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">\&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp>n to specify placeholders that correspond to the entire search pattern or part of it (see [Table 13.10](#13_004.html_t13.10)). This allows very complex operations to be carried out efficiently.

The following example illustrates this: You replace <samp class="listingcharacter">function(\([^,]*\),\([^,]*\))</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">funktion(\2,\1)</samp>. Each time <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> is called, the two parameters are swapped. Therefore, <samp class="listingcharacter">function(a+b,2*e)</samp> becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">function(2*e,a+b)</samp>. The only condition is that there must be no commas in the parameters of the function. If the parameters in <samp class="listingcharacter">function(f(a,b), g(x,y))</samp> are swapped, the command fails.

You should use the search and replace command with patterns with caution and save your text first. Especially during the first attempts, it often happens that the search pattern captures completely different (often much larger) texts than you planned. (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(U) undoes incorrect replace commands if necessary.

## 13.5    Buffers and Windows

When editing multiple texts, Emacs manages each text in a buffer. Even if you work with only one text, there are multiple buffers: one for the text (the name of the buffer matches its file name), one for an info or help window that was opened at some point (buffer name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*info*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*help*</samp>), one for the last displayed list of possible commands that were completed by (Tab) (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*completions*</samp>), and so on.

Besides the term buffer, Emacs also uses the term window; a window is an area within Emacs where a buffer is displayed.

Typically, only one window is used, which uses the entire available space. When multiple commands are executed (e.g., to display help or other internal Emacs information), the screen will be split horizontally into two windows. It can also be divided into multiple horizontal or vertical strips. Each area (window) can then display a different buffer.

It’s also possible to display the same buffer in two windows. This is especially useful for very long texts as you can edit two different sections of the text without having to constantly move the cursor.

The commands in [Table 13.12](#13_005.html_t13.12) refer to the currently active window (i.e., the window in which the cursor is located). The commands change the buffer displayed in this window.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (B), (Enter) | Activates the previously used buffer. |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (B), <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> (Enter) | Activates the specified buffer. |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(B) | Displays the list of all possible buffers in a window. This window can be deleted again using (Ctrl)+(X), (1). |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (K) <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> (Enter) | Deletes the specified buffer. If the buffer contains a file that hasn’t yet been saved, a confirmation prompt appears. |

**Table 13.12**     Buffer Commands

The commands in [Table 13.13](#13_005.html_t13.13) only affect the display of buffers in different screen areas (windows). The dividing line between the windows can be moved with the mouse. The buffers are not affected by deleting a window. They become invisible but remain in the memory and can be displayed again at any time.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (O) | Jumps to the next window (letter O) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (0) | Deletes the current window (zero) |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (1) | Deletes all windows except the one where the cursor is |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (2) | Divides the current window into two horizontal areas |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (3) | Divides the current window into two vertical areas |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (<) | Moves the window content to the left |
| (Ctrl)+(X), (>) | Moves the window content to the right |

**Table 13.13**     Window Commands

### Different Types of Windows

The term window in Emacs has nothing to do with a conventional window on GNOME or KDE, but refers only to a subarea within the Emacs window. If you actually need a second Emacs window—for example, to conveniently edit two program listings side by side—you should run File • New Frame.

## 13.6    Special Editing Modes

Numerous editing modes change the functionality of the editor and provide additional special commands. This way, Emacs is adapted perfectly to a text type. Depending on the mode, keywords and comments are also highlighted in color. Emacs distinguishes between major modes and minor modes (see [Table 13.14](#13_006.html_t13.14) and [Table 13.15](#13_006.html_t13.15)).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">fundamental-mode</samp> (Enter) | Standard mode (default setting) |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">text-mode</samp> (Enter) | Mode for convenient text indentation |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">c-mode</samp> (Enter) | C mode |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">c++-mode</samp> (Enter) | C++ mode |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">emacs-lisp-mode</samp> (Enter) | Edit Emacs Lisp files (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">~/.emacs</samp>) |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">html-mode</samp> (Enter) | HTML mode |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">java-mode</samp> (Enter) | Java mode |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">latex-mode</samp> (Enter) | LaTeX mode |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">sh-mode</samp> (Enter) | Mode for editing shell scripts |

**Table 13.14**     Major Emacs Modes

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">auto-fill-mode</samp> (Enter) | Continuous text mode (automatic word wrap) |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">cua-mode</samp> (Enter) | CUA mode ((Ctrl)+(C), (Ctrl)+(X), and (Ctrl)+(V)) |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">font-lock-mode</samp> (Enter) | Colored syntax marking |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">iso-accents-mode</samp> (Enter) | Input of special characters for foreign languages |
| (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">abbrev-mode</samp> (Enter) | Abbreviation mode (automatic resolution of abbreviations) |

**Table 13.15**     Minor Emacs Modes

Only one main mode can be active at a time. This mode is automatically selected according to the filename identifier and keywords in the text. The major mode can be supplemented by minor modes. Each file that is edited in Emacs (for each buffer) has its own mode setting. The manual change of the mode always affects only the current buffer. Changing to another main mode deactivates the previous mode. Turning a minor mode on or off does not change the major mode.

(F1), (A) <samp class="listingcharacter">mode</samp> (Enter) provides an overview of all available modes. Information about the currently active main mode can be obtained by pressing (F1), (M).

Perhaps the most attractive feature of the editing modes is the syntax highlighting. You can use this feature to highlight commands, comments, and so on by colors or font attributes. This makes program code, LaTeX documents, and the like much clearer.

Inexplicably, Emacs does not feature a PHP mode by default. A mode for editing markdown documents is also missing. At the end of [Section 13.7.4](#13_007.html_h13.7.4), you’ll discover how you can easily install these and other Emacs extensions.

### Automatic and Explicit Mode Setting

When loading a file, Emacs tries to detect its file type and then activates the adequate mode. If that does not work, you can activate the mode manually as described previously. Alternatively, you can add a comment to the first line of the file containing the characters <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*-*</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">modusname</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*-*</samp>—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*-* html *-*</samp>.

## 13.7    Configuration

This section provides an overview of the Emacs configuration files and describes some elementary configuration steps.

The user-specific configuration can be performed either by using menu commands (Options menu) or by a direct modification of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp> configuration files. Note that some distributions automatically copy Emacs configuration files from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/skel</samp> to the user directory when creating new Linux users!

If your version of Emacs behaves differently than described in this book, the configuration of your Linux distribution is often responsible. The settings can be located in both personal and global configuration files (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">site-start.el</samp>):

```
/usr/share/emacs/site-lisp/site-start.el
/usr/share/emacs/site-lisp/debian-startup.el       
(Debian, Ubuntu)
/usr/share/emacs/site-lisp/site-start.d/*          
(Red Hat, Fedora)
/usr/share/emacs/site-lisp/site-start.el           
(SUSE) 
```

### 13.7.1    Setting the Font

Let's start with two important keyboard shortcuts: (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(+) enlarges the default font, while (Ctrl)+(X), (Ctrl)+(-) reduces it. So if you want to increase your reading comfort or to get more space to display particularly long lines, these key combinations will get you there quickly.

To permanently reset the default font, you need to run Options • Set Default Font. You can then set the relevant font in a dialog. Note that this setting is not saved to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp> until you run Options • Save Options.

### 13.7.2    Configuration at the Click of a Mouse

All advanced customization options, of which there are thousands, are accessible via Options • Customize Emacs • Top-Level Customization Group (see [Figure 13.2](#13_007.html_f13.2)).

The buttons on this page lead to more dialogs for different groups of options. On each page, you can use buttons to save all changes made either only until the program terminates or permanently in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp> (Set for Current Session or Save for Future Sessions). Unfortunately, the dialogs are deeply nested. It isn’t always easy to find the right dialog for a particular option.

[![Emacs Configuration](bilderklein/klein13_002.png)](img-f13.2.html)

**Figure 13.2**     Emacs Configuration

### 13.7.3    Manual Configuration Directly in .emacs

Instead of clicking through nested dialogs, you can also perform the configuration directly in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp>. There isn’t enough space here for a detailed description, but the following commented listing provides some examples of commonly used options and settings. Depending on the Linux distribution, some of these settings apply by default:

```
; file .emacs
; no welcome screen
(setq inhibit-startup-message t)

; show row and column number in the status bar
(line-number-mode 1) 
(column-number-mode 1)

; make selected text area visible
(setq-default transient-mark-mode t)

; use <Tab> to insert spaces instead of tabs
(setq-default indent-tabs-mode nil)    

; end last line automatically with newline code
(setq require-final-newline t)

; save cursor position
(require 'saveplace)
(setq-default save-place t)

; activate AUC TEX (this is an extended LaTeX mode; 
; the auctex package must be installed separately; the package
; name is emacs-auctex for many distributions
(require 'tex-site)                   

; highlight associated bracket 
; https://www.emacswiki.org/emacs/ShowParenMode
(show-paren-mode 1)

; store all backup files (name~) in *one* directory
; https://www.emacswiki.org/emacs/AutoSave
(setq backup-directory-alist
  `(("." . ,(concat user-emacs-directory "backups"))))
; custom function; swaps the letter 
(defun swap-char()       ;two letters at the cursor position
  (interactive)          ;swap: 
  (save-excursion
  (forward-char)
  (transpose-chars 1)))

; a few custom keyboard shortcuts
(global-set-key [f2]  'switch-to-buffer)     ;switch buffers
(global-set-key [f3]  'goto-line)            ;go to line n
(global-set-key [f4]  'advertised-undo)      ;undo function
(global-set-key [f5]  'swap-char)            ;swap letters 
```

You have even more configuration options if you engage in Emacs Lisp programming. Doing so allows you to program your own commands in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp> configuration file and then associate them with keyboard shortcuts.

### 13.7.4    MELPA

MELPA ([https://melpa.org](https://melpa.org)) stands for Milkypostman's Emacs Lisp Package Archive and is probably the best maintained archive of Emacs extensions. MELPA is preconfigured in current Emacs versions. You can access the central package management dialog using Options • Manage Emacs Packages or (Alt)+(X) <samp class="listingcharacter">list-packages</samp>.

As usual, you can quickly search the text with (Ctrl)+(S). Clicking a package displays detailed information and an Install button. Some of my favorites are the <samp class="listingcharacter">php-mode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">markdown-mode</samp> extensions. They make editing PHP and markdown files much easier.

# Part V

System Configuration and Administration

# 14    Basic Configuration

This chapter is the first of a whole series of chapters on Linux system configuration. The focus is on rather elementary functions:

*   Text console configuration

*   Setting the date and time

*   User administration

*   Internationalization, character set, Unicode

*   Overview of the hardware configuration

*   CPU tuning

*   Notebook optimization (energy saving measures, battery charging behavior, etc.)

*   CUPS printing system

*   Logging with syslog and journal

*   Cockpit (web console for system administration)

The other chapters then cover topics like network configuration, package management, system library management, configuring the graphics system (X and Wayland), file system administration, system startup (GRUB, systemd), and dealing with the kernel and its modules.

## 14.1    Introduction

This and the following chapters provide a behind-the-scenes look at Linux configuration programs. You will learn what is controlled and preconfigured where and how. For this reason, you will find a lot of background information about how the overall system works.

Unfortunately, the various distributions differ in many small details when it comes to configuration. In this book I try to describe the common denominator of as many Linux systems as possible. Nevertheless, it can happen that your distribution may approach some individual details a little differently.

In those cases, you’ll need to consult the documentation or search the internet. Even if this may be inconvenient for you from time to time, I’m still convinced that the general approach is a better one than a book on Red Hat administration, another one on Ubuntu administration, and so on—not least because the individual distributions also change from version to version. So, sooner or later, you will have to learn to read and understand the various manuals, help pages, and the like. This book is intended not to replace original manuals or step-by-step instructions, but to provide basic knowledge!

Some distributions offer convenient configuration programs that can be used both during and after the installation. SUSE with YaST particularly stands out here. Desktop systems such as KDE and GNOME also contain configuration tools whose effects extend beyond the desktop.

These tools should always be the first choice in case of basic configuration issues!

In addition to the configuration programs supplied, there are also external tools or Linux distributions of their own with additional admin tools. Many of them can be operated via a web interface. [Table 14.1](#14_001.html_t14.1) provides an overview of some popular tools.

| URL | Function | Is It Free? |

**Table 14.1**     Selected Administration Tools

The purpose and functionality of these tools varies greatly. Some of the tools listed are specifically intended for maintaining a large number of similar Linux installations; others are for server configuration only. In this book, I will only introduce the Cockpit program in more detail (see [Section 14.14](#14_014.html_h14.14)).

A bullet in the Is It Free? column means that it’s open-source software that can also be used free of charge by companies. Most commercial products also have free variants with reduced functionality.

### Avoid Dependencies!

Using commercial administration tools, you can easily drift into new dependencies. Also, I’ve seen a lot of administration tools come and go in the past. Do not lightly opt for external administration tools!

Sophisticated configuration tools with nice user interfaces take the hassle out of modifying Linux configuration files directly. Especially for Linux beginners, this is undoubtedly very useful. However, there are a number of reasons to take a closer look at the configuration files and thus the internal workings of Linux:

*   The configuration files can be modified with any text editor, even in a text console or via an SSH connection.

*   Once you understand how to configure a particular Linux feature, you can apply that knowledge to almost any other Linux distribution.

*   You can only control all aspects of a system function if you change the configuration files directly. Configuration tools, on the other hand, are often limited to a few particularly important details.

*   It’s easy to copy configuration files from one computer to another. This can save a lot of time when you change distributions, reinstall Linux on another computer, and so on.

*   The better you understand the structure of the configuration files and the control options they provide, the better you will understand Linux, and the less your computer will be the proverbial black box that nobody can see into.

*   Simple configuration files can be managed pretty well in a version control system like Git. You can use it to track changes and clone configurations to different systems.

### The End of the Line Can Be Crucial!

When editing configuration files, be sure to end the last line using (Enter). Some Linux programs do not process files correctly if the end of line is missing in the last line.

Almost all Linux configuration files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> directory. For this reason, a reference of all configuration files discussed in this book can be found in the index under the letter E.

Related configuration files of larger programs are often organized in their own subdirectories (see [Table 14.2](#14_001.html_t14.2)).

| Directory | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron*</samp> | Cron files (see [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10), [Section 10.6](#10_006.html_h10.6)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default</samp> | Distribution-specific files (Debian, Ubuntu) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/init.d</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/rc*.d</samp> | Init-V system (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20), [Section 20.4](#20_004.html_h20.4)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd</samp> | Systemd (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20), [Section 20.1](#20_001.html_h20.1)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig</samp> | Distribution-specific files (Fedora, Red Hat, SUSE) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/X11</samp> | Graphics system |

**Table 14.2**     Important /etc Directories

It’s a good idea to back up the entire <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> directory every now and then. This allows you to quickly determine what the original state of a particular configuration file was at any time after changes have been made:

```
root# mkdir /etc-backup
root# cp -a /etc/* /etc-backup 
```

### Wonder Weapon: etckeeper

If you are familiar with the Git version control program, then you can use a fantastic tool called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">etckeeper</samp>. This tool backs up the state of all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> files in a Git repository at each package installation or once per day. If necessary, you can restore individual configuration files from it at any time. The installation instructions can be found here: [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Etckeeper](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Etckeeper).

If you can’t find a configuration file in your distribution, this can have several causes: the underlying program packages may not even be installed, or the configuration files may be in a different location in your distribution. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locate</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">find</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> commands for searching. The following command shows how you can search <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> and all subdirectories for files whose contents (not the filename) contain the word <samp class="listingcharacter">abcde</samp> in any case:

```
root# cd /etc
root# grep -r -i abcde 
```

For some programs, changes to the configuration files don’t take effect until you restart the program or explicitly ask it to reread the configuration files. For this purpose, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl reload</samp> is provided. A few services do not support <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reload</samp>, in which case you must use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">restart</samp> instead:

```
root# systemctl reload  servicename   
root# systemctl restart servicename 
```

In contrast to Windows, it’s almost never necessary to restart the computer. The only exceptions are changes to the kernel and some hardware-specific settings that can only be made immediately at system startup.

## 14.2    Configuration of the Text Consoles

In modern distributions, Linux starts the graphics system directly, and Linux beginners often don't even know that text consoles exist at all. From time to time, however, it happens that the configuration for the graphics system is faulty or that no graphics system is available for other reasons. In server installations or in virtual machines, the graphics system is often deliberately omitted. In those cases, you’ll have to get used to the text consoles. For elementary settings like keyboard layout and font, either the <samp class="listingcharacter">kbd</samp> system or the newer <samp class="listingcharacter">console</samp> system is responsible, depending on the distribution. In detail, the configuration looks a little different for each distribution.

### 14.2.1    Keyboard Layout

On Debian and Ubuntu, the programs of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">console-setup</samp> package are responsible for the keyboard layout. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/keyboard</samp> configuration file controls the keyboard layout:

```
# /etc/default/keyboard
# keyboard
XKBMODEL="pc105"
XKBLAYOUT="en"
XKBVARIANT=
XKBOPTIONS="lv3:ralt_switch" 
```

Whether you’re using Debian or Ubuntu, if possible, you should make changes to the keyboard layout not by directly modifying the configuration files, but by using the following command instead:

```
root# dpkg-reconfigure keyboard-configuration 
```

The analysis of the files is taken care of by systemd (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">keyboard-setup</samp> service), which executes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/console-setup/keyboard-setup.sh</samp> script.

In Arch Linux, Fedora, and RHEL, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kbd</samp> package and systemd are responsible for setting the keyboard layout. The configuration is stored in two files—in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/vconsole.conf</samp> for text mode and in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/00-keyboard.conf</samp> for the X graphics system:

```
# file /etc/vconsole.conf
KEYMAP="en"
FONT="eurlatgr" 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">list-keymaps</samp> returns a list of all possible keyboard layouts. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl set-keymap</samp> for configuration purposes. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp> tries to apply the setting to the graphics mode as well, but this isn’t always successful. In the following example, all German keyboard layouts are determined first, and then the variant for Apple's Mac keyboard is set:

```
root# localectl list-keymaps | grep '^de'
de-deadacute
de-mac
...
root# localectl set-keymap de-mac 
```

On Fedora and RHEL, the systemd service <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-localed</samp> is responsible for the configuration. On Arch, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-vconsole-setup</samp> takes care of it.

SUSE also uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kbd</samp> package. The configuration is located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/keyboard</samp> and is analyzed by systemd (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-vconsole-setup</samp> service). As with Red Hat systems, the keyboard settings for X are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/00-keyboard.conf</samp> file created by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-consoled</samp>.

### 14.2.2    Font

Consoles are basically Unicode-compatible. However, the maximum number of possible characters in console fonts is very small (256 or 512). For this reason, console fonts can only ever represent a tiny fraction of all Unicode characters.

The configuration settings are located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/console-setup</samp>. The file is analyzed by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">console-setup</samp> systemd service:

```
# /etc/default/console-setup (Debian default settings)
...
# Font
CHARMAP="UTF-8"
CODESET="Lat15"
FONTFACE="fixed"
FONTSIZE="8x16" 
```

Arch, Fedora and RHEL store the desired console font in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/vconsole. conf</samp> file (<samp class="listingcharacter">FONT</samp> variable). This file is analyzed by systemd (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-vconsole-setup</samp> service).

On current SUSE versions, the console font is set in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/console</samp>. Systemd parses this file (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-vconsole-setup</samp> service).

## 14.3    Date and Time

Due to the international networking of computers, the use of a worldwide standardized time is required. On Linux computers, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the measure of all things or time. This is the successor of the better-known Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

When you save a file, it saves not the current local time, but a time converted to this international standard. If you then view the file using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -l</samp>, the time is converted back to the local time at the computer's location. This procedure makes it possible to determine, for example, which file is more current: a file saved at 6:00 p.m. local time in Munich or a file saved at 12:30 p.m. local time in New York.

The time setting during the computer startup is mostly done in two phases. First, the mainboard clock is read. Its main drawback is its relatively low accuracy. Once connected to the internet, Linux can synchronize its time with other servers on the internet (see [Section 14.4](#14_004.html_h14.4)).

To read the hardware clock, often called the CMOS clock or real-time clock (RTC), you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hwclock</samp> command. In some distributions, this is executed by systemd (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-timedated</samp> service).

For commands like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp> or the file managers of KDE and GNOME to convert GMT time to local time and display it accordingly, each program must know in which time zone it is running. Almost all Linux programs make use of functions of the glibc library for this purpose. This library analyzes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/localtime</samp> file. This file is the link to a time zone file from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/zoneinfo</samp> directory or a copy of this file. The time zone file also contains information on whether a particular daylight saving time scheme applies in a particular time zone (such as Central European Summer Time [CEST]).

The most convenient way to determine the current setting is to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">timedatectl</samp>:

```
user$ timedatectl
               Local time: Wed 2023-04-26 17:42:08 CEST
           Universal time: Wed 2023-04-26 15:42:08 UTC
                 RTC time: Wed 2023-04-26 15:42:08
                Time zone: Europe/Vienna (CEST, +0200)
System clock synchronized: yes
              NTP service: active
          RTC in local TZ: no 
```

To change the time zone, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">timedatectl list-timezones</samp> to determine all time zones available for selection and then set the relevant time zone using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">timedatectl set-timezone</samp>:

```
user$ timedatectl list-timezones | grep Europe
Europe/Amsterdam
Europe/Andorra
Europe/Astrakhan
Europe/Athens
...
root# timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Vienna 
```

Behind the scenes, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">timedatectl set-timezone</samp> simply changes the link from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/localtime</samp>:

```
root# ln -s -f /usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/Vienna /etc/localtime 
```

In Debian and Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/timezone</samp> text file also specifies the time zone. However, this file is analyzed not directly by the glibc library, but only by the tools for resetting the <samp class="listingcharacter">localtime</samp> file.

Depending on the distribution, desktop or init system, you can use a configuration program to change the time zone and date and time of the computer clock:

*   GNOME
    System settings, Date and Time module

*   KDE
    System settings, Regional Settings module • Date & Time

*   Systemd
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Timedatectl</samp>

*   Debian, Ubuntu
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg-reconfigure tzdata</samp>

*   SUSE
    YaST module, System • Date and Time

## 14.4    Synchronizing Date and Time via NTP

As soon as a computer has an internet connection, the time is regularly synchronized with time servers on the internet. The Network Time Protocol (NTP) is provided for this purpose. NTP makes it possible that the local time on the computer deviates only minimally (in the microsecond range) from the time given by atomic clocks. Another advantage is that the then (almost) perfectly accurate time can also be used to readjust the CMOS clock from time to time.

There are various ways to use NTP:

*   In distributions with systemd (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20), [Section 20.1](#20_001.html_h20.1)), the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">time-sync</samp> target can be active. This invokes the start of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-timesyncd</samp> daemon, which takes care of the time setting via NTP.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntpdate</samp> command obtains the exact time from the internet once and sets the clock of the computer. For computers that are switched on and off frequently, this is sufficiently accurate.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntpd</samp> background service synchronizes the time permanently with external NTP servers.

*   This task can also be performed by the modern Chrony program.

### Abrupt Time Changes Are Dangerous

There are quite a lot of programs that do not tolerate sudden time changes well. These include, for example, the Kerberos authentication system, the Dovecot POP3 and IMAP servers, and database servers. It is recommended to shut down and then restart such programs before running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntpdate</samp> or manually changing the time. Dovecot automatically stops when it detects that the time has been reset.

More information about date and time management can also be found on the following pages:

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/System_time](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/System_time)

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Network_Time_Protocol_daemon](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Network_Time_Protocol_daemon)

### 14.4.1    The systemd-timesyncd Process (Debian, Raspberry Pi OS, and Ubuntu)

In current Debian and Ubuntu distributions, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-timesyncd</samp> background process is usually running. It’s executed as part of the systemd target, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">time-sync</samp> (see also <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.special</samp>).

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-timesyncd</samp> background service accesses NTP servers that have already been fixed at compile time. You can determine this as follows:

```
root# strings /lib/systemd/systemd-timesyncd | grep ntp
sd_network_get_ntp
ntp.ubuntu.com
property_get_ntp_message 
```

Deviating from this, other NTP servers can be named in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf</samp>.

### 14.4.2    Chrony (Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE)

On Fedora, the classic NTP tools were replaced years ago by the Chrony program. On RHEL, this step took place with version 8.

Chrony is particularly well-suited for notebooks and virtual machines that are not constantly connected to the internet and whose time often needs to be significantly corrected after longer offline periods. You can find more information on Chrony at [https://chrony.tuxfamily.org](https://chrony.tuxfamily.org).

SUSE Enterprise and openSUSE have also switched to Chrony with version 15\. The configuration is done in the YaST System • Date and Time module; when the configuration is changed, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntpdate</samp> is run once. To set up an NTP server yourself, start the YaST Network Services • NTP Configuration module and enable the Start NTP Service Now and at System Startup option. openSUSE-specific information can be found at [https://doc.opensuse.org/documentation/leap/reference/html/book-reference/cha-ntp.html](https://doc.opensuse.org/documentation/leap/reference/html/book-reference/cha-ntp.html).

The configuration is done via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/chrony.conf</samp>. By default, the <samp class="listingcharacter">pool</samp> parameter there causes Chrony to obtain the time from several public NTP servers of the [http://pool.ntp.org](http://pool.ntp.org) project. Alternatively, you can explicitly specify your own NTP servers via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">server</samp> (see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man chrony.conf</samp>):

```
# file /etc/chrony.conf
pool 2.fedora.pool.ntp.org iburst
... 
```

If the automatic resetting of the time doesn’t work correctly after a long offline period, you should restart Chrony using the following command:

```
root# systemctl restart chronyd 
```

Chrony consists of two programs: the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chronyd</samp> background service (daemon) and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chronyc</samp> command. The latter allows you to set various parameters monito the chrony status. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chronyc help</samp> provides an overview of the available commands. Similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntpq -p</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chrony sources</samp> summarizes which NTP servers Chrony uses as time source and how big the time deviations are at a given moment:

```
root# chronyc sources

210 Number of sources = 4
MS Name/IP address         Stratum Poll Reach LastRx Last sample
=====================================================================
^* ntp.cnh.at          2   8   377   458   -129us[ -163us] +/-   49ms
^+ mail.hoco.at        2   9   377   270   +107us[ +107us] +/-   86ms
^+ 193.170.62.252      2  10   377   134   -421us[ -421us] +/-   62ms
^+ ns5.nosuchhost.net  2   9   377   337  +1123us[+1123us] +/-   42ms
```

## 14.5    Users, Groups, and Passwords

On Linux, access rights control who can access which files, who can run which programs, and who can access which hardware components or device files (see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.6](#09_006.html_h9.6)). These access rights are based on user administration: By default, various users are set up during the installation of Linux. Each user is assigned to at least one, but possibly several groups. Groups are used to allow multiple users to access common files or programs.

By its very nature, user management provides the option to set up multiple users on one computer, who can then log in and work in isolation from each other. However, user management is also important if you work alone on your Linux computer: For security reasons, many system services are not executed with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges, but also in special system accounts with restricted rights. These accounts are blocked for ordinary login and are intended only for the execution of programs.

This section describes which tools help you set up users and groups, and which configuration files are responsible behind the scenes for assigning users, groups, and passwords.

Basically, you can manage users manually as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> by directly changing the files described in this section. It’s more convenient and secure to use the user and group management tools provided with most distributions:

*   GNOME
    User system settings module

*   KDE
    User system settings module

*   SUSE
    Security • User and Group Management YaST module (see [Figure 14.1](#14_005.html_f14.1))

[![User Management in OpenSUSE](bilderklein/klein14_001.png)](img-f14.1.html)

**Figure 14.1**     User Management in OpenSUSE

If you have to do without comfortable user interfaces or if you want to automate the user administration in scripts, you can use the commands summarized in [Table 14.3](#14_005.html_t14.3).

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp> | Sets up a new user (Debian) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addgroup</samp> | Sets up a new group (Debian) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chage</samp> | Controls how long a password remains valid |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chgrp</samp> | Changes the group membership of a file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod</samp> | Changes the access bits of a file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chown</samp> | Changes the owner of a file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chsh</samp> | Changes the default shell of a user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">delgroup</samp> | Deletes a group (Debian) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deluser</samp> | Deletes a user (Debian) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupadd</samp> | Sets up a new group |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupdel</samp> | Deletes a group |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupmod</samp> | Changes group properties |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groups</samp> | Displays the groups of the current user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">id</samp> | Displays the current user and group ID number |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newgrp</samp> | Changes the active group of a user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newusers</samp> | Sets up multiple new users |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> | Changes the password of a user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">useradd</samp> | Sets up a new user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">userdel</samp> | Deletes a user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">usermod</samp> | Changes user properties |

**Table 14.3**     Commands for User and Group Management

The following example shows how you can create the new <samp class="listingcharacter">testuser</samp> user and assign a password to it:

```
root# useradd -m testuser
root# passwd testuser
New passwd: xxxxxxxx 
Re-enter new passwd: xxxxxxxx 
```

You’ll notice that there are two commands for some tasks, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">useradd</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Adduser</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addgroup</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deluser</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">delgroup</samp> are Debian-specific extensions to the traditional commands, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">useradd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupadd</samp>, and so on. On Debian and Ubuntu, these commands take into account the rules defined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/adduser.conf</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/deluser.conf</samp> .

Red Hat and Fedora cause some confusion in this regard: There, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">addgroup</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deluser</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">delgroup</samp> commands are also available. However, these are not the commands familiar from Debian, but links to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">useradd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupadd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">userdel</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupdel</samp>. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp> on Fedora has a different syntax than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp> on Debian!

### 14.5.1    User Management

There are three types of users in Linux:

*   Super user (also known as system administrator or root) This user usually has the name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. Anyone who knows the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password and logs in as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> has unrestricted rights: He or she may view, modify, or delete all files, run all programs, and so on. Such a long list of rights is only required for system administration purposes. For security reasons, you should not perform all other tasks as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>!

*   Ordinary users These users perform their day-to-day work in Linux. They have full access to their own files, but limited access to the rest of the system. The first or last name of the user is often used as the login name, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">catherine</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smith</samp>.

*   System users for daemons and server services Finally, there are a number of users that are not intended for interactive work on the computer but are used to run specific programs. For example, the Apache web server is not run by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> user but by a separate user called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apache</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wwwrun</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd</samp>, or something similar, depending on the distribution. This approach is chosen to achieve the highest possible system security.

The list of all users is stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> file. This is where the login name, full name, UID and GID numbers, home directory, and shell are stored for each user. The following format applies:

Login:Password:UID:GID:Name:Home Directory:Shell

The following lines show some user definitions in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> on Ubuntu Linux:

```
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/bin/sh
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/bin/sh
sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/bin/sh
...
kofler:x:1000:1000:Michael Kofler,,,:/home/kofler:/bin/bash
hoover:x:1001:1001:Herbert Hoover,,,:/home/hoover:/bin/bash 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> name suggests that the passwords are also stored in the file. That was indeed the case in the past. Today, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> contains only the x character instead of the password information. The encrypted password hash is stored in the separate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp> file, which I will introduce in [Section 14.5.3](#14_005.html_h14.5.3).

The login name should consist of lowercase letters only (US-ASCII letters and numbers) and should not be longer than eight characters. Although both non-ASCII characters and more than eight characters are basically allowed, problems may occur in combination with some programs. These restrictions do not apply to the separately stored full name.

The UID number is used for the internal identification of the user. In particular, the number is saved as additional information for each file so that it’s clear who the file belongs to. There are rules for assigning UID numbers. First, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> always has UID=0\. UID numbers between 1 and 999 then are reserved for server services and daemons in most distributions. Accordingly, numbers starting from 1000 are provided for ordinary users. The GID number indicates to which group the user belongs. (Details on groups follow in [Section 14.5.2](#14_005.html_h14.5.2).)

The home directory is the place where users can store their private data. For ordinary users, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/<loginname></samp> path is usually used for this purpose. The home directory also stores a user's personal configuration settings for various programs. For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.emacs</samp> file contains the configuration settings for the Emacs editor. Because the names of such configuration files usually start with a dot, they are invisible. They can be displayed using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls -la</samp> command.

To ensure that new users immediately have sensible default settings for the most important programs, all files should be copied from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/skel</samp> to the newly created home directory when creating a new user. Many programs for creating new users perform this step automatically. The contents of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/skel</samp> thus represent the initial setting for each new user.

The shell is an interpreter that allows a user to execute commands after login. As there are several shells to choose from on Linux, the shell to be used must be specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> file. On Linux, this is mostly the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bash</samp> shell. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> file must contain the full filename of the shell—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/bash</samp>.

### 14.5.2    Group Management

The purpose of groups is to allow multiple users to share access to files. For this purpose, each user is assigned to a primary group (initial group). In addition, a user can be assigned to any number of additional groups (supplementary groups); that is, the user can be a member of multiple groups.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp> file contains the list of all groups. The following lines show some group definitions in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp>. The following format applies:

Group name:Password:GID:Users list

The following lines are from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">group</samp> file of an Ubuntu system:

```
root:x:0:
daemon:x:1:
bin:x:2:
sys:x:3:
adm:x:4:syslog,kofler
cdrom:x:24:kofler 
...
kofler:x:1000:
huber:x:1001:
... 
```

The assignment between user and group is done in two ways:

*   The primary group of a user is stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp>. For user <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kofler</samp>, the primary group is also <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kofler</samp>; this is evident from the value 1000 in the GID column in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> file.

*   Membership in additional groups is stored by specifying the user's name in the last column of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp> file. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kofler</samp> also belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adm</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">cdrom</samp> groups. This allows user <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler</samp> to perform admin tasks on Ubuntu systems and access CDs/DVDs.

For GID numbers, 0 is for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> and 1 to 99 are for system services. GID=100 is usually reserved for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">users</samp> group. GIDs greater than 1000 are then used for user-specific groups or may be defined for custom purposes.

There are two common strategies for mapping between users and their primary groups:

*   In the traditional method, which has been used on Unix/Linux for many years, all ordinary users are assigned to the primary <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">users</samp> group. SUSE is still a follower of this very simple strategy today.

*   Debian-based distributions as well as Red Hat and Fedora use a different method: each user gets their own primary group. In this case, there is a group of the same name for each of the users <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">users</samp> group no longer plays a role.

    This method has advantages in certain circumstances—such as when several members of a secondary group create common files. However, these advantages only come into play with appropriate system administration. The differences are explained in detail on the Debian Wiki page at [https://wiki.debian.org/UserPrivateGroups](https://wiki.debian.org/UserPrivateGroups).

It’s often necessary to assign an additional secondary group to a user. This allows you to give the user additional permissions, such as access to general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins on the Raspberry Pi or permission to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>. Depending on the distribution, two commands are available to assign another group (here <samp class="listingcharacter">admin</samp>) to a user (here <samp class="listingcharacter">bob</samp>):

```
root# usermod -a -G admin bob 
(all distributions, -a -G stands for append group)
root# adduser bob admin       
(equivalent, Debian/Ubuntu only) 
```

### 14.5.3    Passwords

Linux passwords usually consist of ASCII characters only. International special characters are basically allowed, but can easily cause problems, such as when typing on a keyboard that is not yet configured correctly. For security reasons, passwords should contain both uppercase and lowercase letters and at least one digit.

In Linux, passwords are stored as hash codes, which allow passwords to be checked but not reconstructed. The passwords can have any length. Current distributions use the hash algorithm SHA512, which is considered secure, in combination with a random initialization code for the password, the salt. This salt causes a different hash code to be stored for the same password each time. This makes it impossible to see in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp> whether multiple users have the same password. The algorithm is specified by the <samp class="listingcharacter">ENCRYPT_METHOD</samp> variable in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/login.defs</samp>.

To make life more difficult for potential attackers, the encrypted password codes are not stored directly in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp>, but in the separate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp> file. The advantage is that this file can be read only by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. In contrast, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp> are readable by all users of the system because they contain basic admin information. With <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp>, on the other hand, it’s sufficient if only the programs for password verification and change are allowed to access it. Potential attackers must therefore first gain <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> access before they can even read the encrypted password codes.

The following format applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shadow</samp> file:

Login:Password code:d1:d2:d3:d4:d5:d6:reserved

The following lines show an excerpt from a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shadow</samp> file:

```
root:$y$Ecrkix...:14391:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:14391:0:99999:7:::
bin:*:14391:0:99999:7:::
...
kofler:$y$TZR7...:14391:0:99999:7::: 
```

For most system users, like <samp class="listingcharacter">daemon</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">bin</samp>, only an asterisk or exclamation mark is stored instead of a password. This means that there is no valid password, so logging in is impossible. The system accounts can still be used; programs that are first started with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> privileges can later change ownership and then continue as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bin</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">daemon</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lp</samp>, and so on. This is exactly the case with most system processes: they are started by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> during system startup and then change hands immediately for security reasons.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">d1</samp> through <samp class="listingcharacter">d6</samp> fields can contain optional time information:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">d1</samp> indicates when the password was last changed (calculated as the number of days elapsed since January 1, 1970).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">d2</samp> specifies in how many days the password can be changed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">d3</samp> specifies the maximum number of days until the password must be changed before it becomes invalid. (Details about the field can be found in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man 5 shadow</samp>.)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">d4</samp> specifies how many days the user is warned before the password expires.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">d5</samp> specifies after how many days an expired account without a valid password will be completely deactivated.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">d6</samp> indicates how long it has been since an account has been deactivated.

Typically, default values are used for <samp class="listingcharacter">d1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">d3</samp> so that the password can be changed at any time and remains valid indefinitely. <samp class="listingcharacter">d1</samp> through <samp class="listingcharacter">d6</samp>, however, can also be used to limit the validity of passwords, to automatically deactivate login accounts for a certain time, and so on—for example, to manage student accounts at a university or school.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">d1</samp> through <samp class="listingcharacter">d6</samp> fields are set by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chage</samp> command (change age). In the following example, the user is forced to change their password immediately after the first login. Also, in the future, this user will have to change the password every 100 days. Finally, the account is only available until December 31, 2024. After that, any login will be blocked:

```
root# chage -d 0 -M 100 -E 2024-12-31 loginname 
```

A lot of parameters for the internal administration of passwords and logins are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/login.defs</samp> file. The settings apply to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">useradd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">groupmod</samp>, and so on. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">logins.def</samp> specifies how many days passwords are valid by default, what range of values is used for new UIDs and GIDs, and so on.

The PAM configuration (see [Section 14.6](#14_006.html_h14.6)) also defines rules for password verification. The PAM rules are taken into account, among other things, by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> command and at every login.

To change your own password, you need to run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> command. You will then first be asked for your old password and then prompted twice in a row to type in a new password. Only if both entries match will the new password be accepted. From then on you will have to use the new password every time you log in.

While ordinary users can only change their own password, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> may also change the passwords of other users:

```
root# passwd hoover
New password: ******
Re-enter new password: ******
Password changed. 
```

In most distributions, PAM extensions ensure a minimum password quality. Often, passwords must be at least eight or nine characters long, differ from dictionary entries, contain numbers, and so on. The way in which this quality control is carried out depends on the distribution:

*   In Fedora and RHEL, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pam_pwquality</samp> ensures password quality. The configuration is done through <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/security/pwquality.conf</samp>. A good introduction to how it works can be found at [https://deer-run.com/users/hal/linux_passwords_pam.html](https://deer-run.com/users/hal/linux_passwords_pam.html).

*   Arch Linux and SUSE use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pam_cracklib</samp> library instead. How to define rules that differ from the default settings is documented in detail at [https://deer-run.com/users/hal/linux_passwords_pam.html](https://deer-run.com/users/hal/linux_passwords_pam.html).

*   Debian and Ubuntu make use of the password tests integrated in the <samp class="listingcharacter">pam_unix</samp> PAM module. Details on how this works can be found via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man pam_unix</samp>, where the description of the <samp class="listingcharacter">obscure</samp> parameter is particularly relevant. This parameter is active in Debian as well as in Ubuntu (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pam.d/common-passwd</samp> file). If necessary, you can influence the minimum password length by the additional <samp class="listingcharacter">minlen</samp> parameter.

The password rules apply only to ordinary users. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> may use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> command to choose arbitrarily bad passwords for itself as well as for any other user, although this is of course not recommended.

#### Generating Secure Passwords

If you frequently set up user accounts, it’s convenient to use automatically generated passwords. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkpasswd</samp> program from the Fedora or RHEL package <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">expect</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">makepasswd</samp> from the Debian or Ubuntu package of the same name, can provide help for this:

<samp class="listingcharacter">root#</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">makepasswd</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">aGjoQK1Ezo</samp>
