To assign automatically generated passwords to new users in a script, it’s best to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chpasswd</samp> command.

What do you do if you forget your <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> password? In most distributions, you need a live or rescue system that you boot from a USB flash drive. Then, you must mount the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/xxx</samp> system partition of your Linux system in a directory of your choice. Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chroot</samp>, you can make this directory the new root directory. Then you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> to reset the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> password:

```
root# mkdir /rescue
root# mount -t auto /dev/xxx /rescue
root# chroot /rescue
root# passwd
root# <Ctrl>+<D>
root# reboot 
```

If you want to prevent other users from changing the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> password in the way just described, you must disable all boot media except the first hard disk in your computer's BIOS/EFI and password-protect the BIOS/EFI itself. But then you really must not forget this password! Even this method does not provide perfect protection as an attacker could easily remove your computer's hard disk/SSD and install it in their own computer. In that case, the procedure described previously works.

A much more effective way to secure a Linux system is to encrypt the entire system partition. The corresponding password must then be entered for each boot process, which is why this procedure is particularly useful for desktop installations. For server operation, encryption only makes sense if the server is easily accessible for you as an administrator! This is because even in this case you have to enter the password locally every time you restart. This is impossible for servers located in an external data center.

On Debian and Ubuntu, incorrect login attempts are logged in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/faillog</samp>. Unlike many other logging files, this one uses a binary format. The configuration of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog</samp> file is done in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/login.defs</samp>.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog -u name</samp> to determine how many incorrect login attempts have occurred for a particular user since the last valid login.

With <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog -u name -m max</samp>, a maximum number of failed login attempts for a given user can be fixed. If this number is exceeded, the login is blocked until <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> allows the login again by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog -u name -r</samp> command. (This will reset the login counter.) You can also set the maximum login count in general via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog -m max</samp>. However, you should then always also run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog -u root -m 0</samp> so that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> is excluded from this protection measure. Otherwise, you might not be able to log in even as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> after another user has made several unsuccessful <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login attempts.

On Fedora and RHEL, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillog</samp> is not available. A comparable function is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pam_faillock</samp> PAM extension and the associated <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">faillock</samp> command. These components are installed by default but are not active. You can find an example of a corresponding configuration at [https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/182091](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/182091).

As with individual users, passwords can also be defined for groups (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gpasswd</samp> command). But while passwords are strongly recommended for users, group passwords are uncommon. Their main disadvantage is that all group members must know the password, which complicates administration and makes the application inherently insecure. If group passwords are actually used, they are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/gshadow</samp> file. A group password must be entered when a user changes their currently active group using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newgrp</samp> command.

### 14.5.4    Interaction of the Configuration Files

The following lines summarize again how the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">group</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shadow</samp> files interact. For each user, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp> contains a line according to the following pattern:

```
# one line in /etc/passwd
kofler:x:1000:1000:Michael Kofler:/home/kofler:/bin/bash 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler</samp> is the login name; 1000 is both UID and GID; <samp class="listingcharacter">Michael Kofler</samp> is the full name; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/kofler</samp> is his user directory; and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/bash</samp> is his shell. The UID must be a unique number because it is important for managing file access rights.

The corresponding line in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp> with the password information looks as follows:

```
# one line in /etc/shadow
kofler:$y$9dkO$...:13479:0:99999:7::: 
```

The string after <samp class="listingcharacter">kofler:</samp> is the encrypted password. If the string is omitted, the login can be used without a password. If a <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> is entered instead of the string, the login is blocked.

The GID number in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> must match a group from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp>. In many distributions, each ordinary user is assigned a group of the same name:

```
# one line from /etc/group
kofler:x:1000: 
```

### 14.5.5    Network User Management

If you want to network several Linux computers and use NFS to enable mutual access to files, then you must make sure that the UID and GID numbers are consistent on all computers. This alone becomes quite time-consuming with several computers. If you now also want every user to be able to log in on every computer, and of course always under the same login name and with the same password, then you must constantly synchronize all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> files. The administration effort then becomes huge.

To avoid this effort, a central server is usually used for user administration in such cases. There are many alternative methods and protocols available for authenticating clients, but describing them is beyond the scope of this book:

*   Samba or Windows user management (Active Directory)

*   Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

*   Kerberos

*   Network Information Service (NIS; obsolete)

## 14.6    PAM, NSS, and Nscd

After presenting the principles of user and group management in the previous section, here are a few more technical details. The following procedures are represented by the three abbreviations in the heading:

*   PAM Pluggable authentication modules (PAMs) are central libraries that provide authentication functions to various commands.

*   NSS The name service switch (NSS) decides which sources are used to resolve user, group, and host names.

*   Nscd The Name Service Caching Daemon (nscd) is a cache for name queries. It can make the most recently required user, group, and host names available again particularly quickly.

### 14.6.1    PAM

A PAM is a library whose functions provide help with authentication tasks. When you perform a login or otherwise authenticate yourself or change your password on a Linux machine, the respective programs access the PAM library. Cron and PolicyKit also use PAM. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ldd</samp> to determine whether a particular command uses PAM libraries:

```
root# ldd /usr/bin/passwd | grep libpam
  libpam.so.0 => /usr/lib/libpam.so.0 (0x00007f7f98420000)
  libpam_misc.so.0 => /usr/lib/libpam_misc.so.0 (0x00007f7f9841b000) 
```

The PAM documentation can be found on the project page at [https://github.com/linux-pam/linux-pam](https://github.com/linux-pam/linux-pam).

PAM is configured by default to analyze the local password files, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/shadow</samp>. If another authentication method is also to be used (e.g., LDAP), the PAM configuration must be changed accordingly. Depending on the distribution, different tools can help you with this:

*   Fedora, RHEL
    <samp class="listingcharacter">authselect</samp>

*   SUSE
    YaST: Security • User and Group Management

*   Debian, Ubuntu
    <samp class="listingcharacter">pam-auth-update</samp>

The configuration files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pam.d/</samp> directory. In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pam.conf</samp> file is analyzed as well. The configuration files contain rules line by line. Each rule consists of at least three parts or columns:

<samp class="listingcharacter">Type Response PAM module [module_arguments]</samp>

Entries in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pam.conf</samp> must also be prefixed with the name of the service, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">login</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> for standard entries. For the files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pam.d</samp>, the service name is derived from the filename.

PAM distinguishes between four rule types. In Debian, SUSE, and Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">common-account</samp>, common-auth, common-password, and common-session files contain default rules for these four types:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">account</samp>
    Allows limiting the services depending on the time of day, load, login location (e.g., console), and so on

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">auth</samp>
    Concerns authorization (i.e., password query and verification) and the subsequent assignment of privileges, such as group memberships

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">password</samp>
    Concerns the method for changing the password

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">session</samp>
    Allows you to perform actions before or after the actual service: logging, mounting/unmounting file systems, showing the mailbox status, and so on

If the rule type is preceded by a minus sign, there will be no error message if a module specified in the rule is not available. This syntax variant allows the definition of rules that become active only when the corresponding PAM module is actually installed.

The second column in the configuration files specifies how PAM should react when a rule is complied with or not. There are two ways to describe the response: either by a simple keyword (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">required</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">requisite</samp>) or by a value/result pair enclosed in square brackets (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">[success=1 new_authtok_reqd=done default=ignore]</samp>). The meaning of the four most important keywords of the simple syntax variant is explained in [Table 14.4](#14_006.html_t14.4).

In the second syntax variant, you can specify multiple value/result pairs in the following format: <samp class="listingcharacter">[value1=result1 value2=result2 ...]</samp>. For <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp>, there is a whole set of predefined keywords available that express the result of a rule. <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> can either be a number that specifies how many more rules should be skipped, or a keyword that specifies the desired PAM result (<samp class="listingcharacter">ignore</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">bad</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">die</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ok</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">done</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">reset</samp>). The following listing indicates how the keywords of the first syntax variant are expressed in the second notation:

```
requisite  = [success=ok new_authtok_reqd=ok ignore=ignore default=die]
required   = [success=ok new_authtok_reqd=ok ignore=ignore default=bad]
sufficient = [success=done new_authtok_reqd=done default=ignore] 
optional   = [success=ok new_authtok_reqd=ok default=ignore] 
```

| Keyword | Response |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">requisite</samp> | In the event of a rule violation, the PAM function immediately returns a negative result and the other rules are no longer processed. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">required</samp> | In case of a rule violation, the PAM function returns a negative result; further rules are processed, but their result is not taken into account. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">sufficient</samp> | If the rule is followed, PAM immediately returns a positive result (unless there is already a violation of a previous <samp class="listingcharacter">requisite</samp> rule); no other rules are considered. In case of a rule violation, PAM continues with the next rule. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">optional</samp> | The rule result is relevant only if it is the only rule for a particular rule type and service (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">su</samp>). |

**Table 14.4**     Response to PAM Rule Violations

The third column specifies the name of the PAM module that analyzes the rule. The behavior of the module can be influenced by options. Unfortunately, there is no central documentation of the permissible options and their meaning.

The following listing, somewhat abbreviated for space reasons, summarizes Fedora's settings. Note that the default settings vary greatly depending on the distribution and are often spread across several files—for example, in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">common-xxx</samp> in Debian, SUSE, and Ubuntu:

```
# file /etc/pam.d/password-auth (Fedora)
# Generated by authselect. Do not modify this file manually.
auth       required                        pam_env.so
auth       required                        pam_faildelay.so delay=2000000
auth       [default=1 ignore=ignore ...]   pam_usertype.so isregular
auth       [default=1 ignore=ignore ...]   pam_localuser.so
auth       sufficient                      pam_unix.so nullok try_first_pass
auth       [default=1 ignore=ignore ...]   pam_usertype.so isregular
auth       sufficient                      pam_sss.so forward_pass
auth       required                        pam_deny.so

account    required                        pam_unix.so
account    sufficient                      pam_localuser.so
account    sufficient                      pam_usertype.so issystem
account    [default=bad success=ok ...]    pam_sss.so
account    required                        pam_permit.so

password   requisite                       pam_pwquality.so try_first_pass  local_users_only
password   sufficient                      pam_unix.so yescrypt shadow nullok  use_authtok
password   sufficient                      pam_sss.so use_authtok
password   required                        pam_deny.so

session    optional                        pam_keyinit.so revoke
session    required                        pam_limits.so
-session   optional                        pam_systemd.so
session    [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_succeed_if.so service in crond  quiet use_uid
session    required                        pam_unix.so
session    optional                        pam_sss.so 
```

#### PAM Configuration on Fedora and RHEL

On Fedora and RHEL, you should avoid modifying files directly in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pam.d</samp>. The PAM configuration is generated by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">authselect</samp> command, which has replaced the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">authconfig</samp> command commonly used in older distributions. Details about <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">authselect</samp> can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> documentation and at [https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/Authselect](https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/Authselect).

### 14.6.2    Name Service Switch

When logging in, managing access rights to files, network access, and so on, all possible information about user and group names, UIDs and GIDs, host names, ports of network services, and so on is required. By default, this data is located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/services</samp>, and other files.

In Unix or Linux terminology, access to this data is summarized under the term name services. The NSS, a collection of functions from the <samp class="listingcharacter">libc</samp> library, is responsible for this task. Similar to authentication, the data source for NSS can be set, for example, if an LDAP server provides the data. The crucial configuration file is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/nsswitch.conf</samp>. The following lines show the default configuration on Debian or Ubuntu:

```
# file /etc/nsswitch.conf (Ubuntu)
passwd:         files systemd sss
group:          files systemd sss
shadow:         files systemd sss
gshadow:        files systemd
hosts:          files mdns4_minimal [NOTFOUND=return] dns
networks:       files
protocols:      db files
... 
```

The first column in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nsswitch.conf</samp> designates the database or file. After the colon, keywords describe the method of accessing the data and optionally, in square brackets, the response to lookup results. The following list explains the most important keywords for the access methods. If a line names multiple access methods, they will be applied in sequence until one method succeeds. Further syntax details can be found in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man nsswitch.conf</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">files</samp>
    Accesses the traditional configuration files<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">(/etc/passwd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/group</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">compat</samp>
    Same as <samp class="listingcharacter">files</samp>, but the user and group specifications can be preceded by the <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> signs. This increases the compatibility with NIS. <samp class="listingcharacter">compat</samp> cannot be combined with other keywords.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">db</samp>
    Reads the data from a BDB database file (BDB = Berkeley Database).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">dns</samp>
    Contacts a name server.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">mdns</samp>
    Uses multicast DNS (aka Zeroconf or Apple Bonjour/Rendezvous).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">sss</samp>
    Contacts the System Security Services Daemon (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sssd</samp>). This is a local service that acts as a cache for external authentication services such as Kerberos or LDAP.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">systemd</samp>
    Determines users and groups temporarily created by systemd to run a service (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">DynamicUser</samp> option; see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.exec</samp>).

The access methods require the corresponding library to be installed, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">libnss_db</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">db</samp>. If the library is missing, the corresponding keyword is simply ignored without reporting an error.

### 14.6.3    Name Service Caching Daemon

In SUSE, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp> program is installed by default and activated during the boot of the computer. In most other distributions an optional installation is possible. If configured accordingly, the program remembers login, group, and host names as well as their IP numbers and makes them available to the local computer. It makes sense to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp> especially if the user management is done by a network service (such as LDAP). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp> then serves as a cache for information and avoids unnecessary LDAP queries, which are often answered comparatively slowly.

The configuration of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp> is done via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/nscd.conf</samp>. The file contains entries for several groups: <samp class="listingcharacter">passwd</samp> for login names, <samp class="listingcharacter">group</samp> for groups, <samp class="listingcharacter">host</samp> for host names, and so on. The settings for each group determine the duration for which the data is stored, the maximum number of entries to be managed, and so on.

### 14.6.4    System Security Services Daemon

Fedora and RHEL prefer <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sssd</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/nsswitch</samp> looks as follows:

```
# file /etc/nsswitch (Fedora, RHEL)
passwd:     files sss systemd
shadow:     files
group:      files sss systemd
... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sssd</samp> is not a complete replacement for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp>, but it provides other additional functions. In any case, using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nscd</samp> and/or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sssd</samp> is only appropriate if your Linux clients access a central authentication system.

## 14.7    Language Setting, Internationalization, and Unicode

This section is about two things:

*   Localization or language setting This setting determines in which language error messages, menus, dialogs, help texts, and so on will be displayed. Also the formatting of the date, time, currency amounts, and the like changes accordingly.

*   Character set The character set determines which codes are used to store letters. A character set describes the assignment between numeric codes and letters. Known character sets are ASCII (seven bits), ISO-Latin-n (eight bits), and Unicode (16 or 32 bits). Within Unicode, there are again different encodings. The most common one is UTF-8\. ASCII characters are represented with only one byte. However, up to four bytes are needed to map rarer characters.

### What Do l10n and i18n Mean?

In connection with the localization of programs, you will repeatedly come across the strange abbreviations i18n and l10n: these are the short forms for internationalization (i plus 18 letters plus n) or localization, respectively. These abbreviations are also good search terms if you want to search the internet for more information.

The font must not be confused with a character set. It’s responsible for how a particular character is displayed on the screen. There are various fonts for this purpose (such as Arial, Courier, Helvetica, and Palatino, to name but a few well-known ones). Most fonts contain only a subset of all Unicode characters due to space limitations. If a character (such as an emoji) is not displayed correctly, this is usually because the character is missing from the font.

### 14.7.1    Setting the Localization and Character Set

Depending on the distribution or desktop system, you can use different tools to configure the language. For all distributions, you must log in again for changed language settings to take effect. UTF-8 is almost always used as the character set.

*   Debian
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg-reconfigure locales</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp>

*   Fedora, RHEL
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp>

*   SUSE
    YaST module System • Language

*   Ubuntu Languages (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gnome-language-selector</samp>)

*   GNOME
    System settings Region and Language module

*   KDE
    System settings Regional Settings module

*   Systemd
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp>

In addition, some display managers provide the option to select the desired language for the next session in the login dialog for the desktop system.

The configuration settings are stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/locale</samp> in almost all distributions. To set a new default language, you need to run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl set-locale xxx</samp> command:

```
root# localectl set-locale C.UTF-8         
(neutral/English)
root# localectl set-locale en_US.UTF-8     
(US English)
root# localectl set-locale fr_FR.UTF-8     
(French)
root# localectl set-locale de_DE.UTF-8     
(German) 
```

A list of all possible settings is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl list-locales</samp>. If this list contains only very few entries for Debian-based distributions, you must first install or set up the corresponding languages. To do this, you need to call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg-reconfigure locales</samp>.

SUSE (still) moves away from the common Linux standards. The language setting is preferably done using YaST and is stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/language</samp>.

Internally, both the localization and character set are controlled by environment variables such as <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_CTYPE</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">LANG</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">glibc</samp> library, which is used in almost all Linux programs, is responsible for analyzing these variables. Localization can be performed category by category. This makes it possible, for example, to use the format common in Germany for dates and times, but still display error messages in English. [Table 14.5](#14_007.html_t14.5) lists the most important variables.

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> | Determines the default value for all LC variables that have not been set |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LANGUAGE</samp> | Allows the settings of multiple languages (see below) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_CTYPE</samp> | Determines the character set |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_COLLATE</samp> | Determines the sorting order |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_MESSAGES</samp> | Determines the display of messages, error messages, and so on |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_NUMERIC</samp> | Determines the representation of numbers |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_TIME</samp> | Determines the display of date and time |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_MONETARY</samp> | Determines the representation of monetary amounts |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_PAPER</samp> | Determines the paper size |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_ALL</samp> | Overwrites all individual LC settings |

**Table 14.5**     Important Localization Variables

Note that you can set all of these variables in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/locale</samp>, with one exception: <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_ALL</samp>! This variable can only be changed interactively or for testing purposes in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/profile</samp> (see [https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/567826](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/567826)).

Of course, not every program takes all categories into account; some programs even ignore the <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_</samp> variables in their entirety. If individual categories are not set, programs use C or POSIX as the default value. This means that error messages appear in English, dates and times are displayed in American format, and so on.

Instead of setting all variables individually, you can simply set the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">LANG</samp> variable, which uses the default <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> value for all undefined variables. The POSIX default setting remains only for <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_COLLATE</samp>. In most distributions, the entire language setting is done via the <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> variable.

<samp class="listingcharacter">LC_ALL</samp> has an even stronger effect than <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp>. If this variable is set, all categories will have this setting, no matter how <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> or other <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_</samp> variables are set.

A special case is <samp class="listingcharacter">LANGUAGE</samp>: this variable is not part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">glic</samp> variables. Rather, it is specific to the GNU <samp class="listingcharacter">gettext</samp> function. The function is used in many programs to output messages or error texts in the desired language. If <samp class="listingcharacter">LANGUAGE</samp> is defined, the variable for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gettext</samp> has priority over all other variables (including <samp class="listingcharacter">LC_ALL</samp>). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">LANGUAGE</samp> allows you to set multiple languages. <samp class="listingcharacter">LANGUAGE=de:fr</samp>, for example, causes output to be preferentially performed in German. If no German translation is available, French will be used.

For most programs, error messages and other texts for each language are located separately in their own directories, such as in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/locale/language/LC_MESSAGES</samp>. You can find more details about this at [https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual).

The easiest way to determine the current state of the localization setting is to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locale</samp> command. This command also analyzes <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">LC_ALL</samp> to determine the resulting settings. The following example shows the setting on my computer:

```
user$ locale
LANG=de_DE.UTF-8
LC_CTYPE="de_AT.UTF-8"
LC_TIME="de_AT.UTF-8"
...

LC_ALL= 
```

To test the localization, you can execute any command with errors. The error message appears in the set language. If <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> is set to <samp class="listingcharacter">de_DE</samp>, the error message of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command looks as follows:

```
user$ mount /xy
mount: Konnte /xy nicht in /etc/fstab finden 
```

If you work on a non-English system and want to research the background of an error on the internet, error messages in the local language are not very helpful. Whether you work in Germany, France, or Mexico, you want to see error messages in English!

To execute a single command with a different language setting without changing the entire configuration, you can simply prefix the command with <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG=</samp>. This means that the <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> variable will be reset, but only for the execution of the command! Alternatively, <samp class="listingcharacter">LANGUAGE=en</samp> works with a little more typing:

```
user$ LANG= mount /xy
mount: can't find /xy in /etc/fstab
user$ LANGUAGE=en mount /xy
mount: can't find /xy in /etc/fstab 
```

To change the language for the entire course of a shell session, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">export</samp>:

```
user$ export LANGUAGE=en 
```

You can determine a list of all possible settings by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locale -a</samp>. Usually the <samp class="listingcharacter">x_y</samp> notation is used, where <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is replaced by two letters indicates the language and <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> by two letters indicates the country. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">en_US</samp> (US English), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">en_GB</samp> (British English), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fr_FR</samp> (French in France), or <samp class="listingcharacter">de_DE</samp> (German), for example. For the English default setting, the short notation <samp class="listingcharacter">C</samp> is allowed. Newer glibc versions also understand settings like <samp class="listingcharacter">german</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">deutsch</samp>.

The file <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/locale/locale.alias</samp> contains a table that maps the allowed short notations to the full locale name.

Whether menus, dialogs, error messages, help texts, and so on are displayed in the correct language also depends on whether the necessary localization files are installed. For space reasons, this is often the case for only one or two languages used during the installation, such as for English and German. If you now want to use your distribution also in French, you need to install appropriate additional packages for GNOME, KDE, LibreOffice, Firefox, and so on. On SUSE and Ubuntu, the configuration tools listed in the introduction to this chapter will help you with this, but in other distributions, manual work is required in this case.

Not every Linux program has been localized for every language. There are particularly large gaps in online documentation—<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> pages, manuals, and help texts. If suitable localization files are missing, Linux displays English texts.

### 14.7.2    “Cannot Set/Change Locale” Error Message

Recently, I have been encountering the following error messages over and over again, especially during minimal installations in the cloud or in virtual machines:

<samp class="listingcharacter">Cannot set xxx to default locale: No such file or directory ...</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">setlocale: LC_ALL: cannot change locale</samp>

This is apparently due to the efforts of many distributions to avoid installing more localization files than absolutely necessary. But if a <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">LC</samp> variable then uses a localization that isn’t installed, errors will occur.

The correct solution varies depending on the distribution. On Fedora and RHEL systems, the following command often helps, where you replace <samp class="listingcharacter">XX</samp> with the language you need (so, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">langpacks-de</samp> for German):

```
root# dnf install -y langpacks-en langpacks-XX glibc-all-langpacks 
```

On Debian and Ubuntu, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg-reconfigure locales</samp> is the fastest way to achieve this. Alternatively, you can search for the supposedly missing localization (such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">en_US.UTF-8</samp>) in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/locale.gen</samp> file) and remove the # character located at the beginning of the line. Then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">locale-gen</samp>. This procedure recently helped me with an apparently faulty Manjaro installation in which <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg-reconfigure</samp> was not available.

## 14.8    Hardware Reference

This book does not contain a separate chapter on hardware. Instead, the correct configuration of hardware components is covered in the corresponding chapters. Thus, if you have network problems, for example, [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15) is the place to start.

This section has two tasks: On the one hand, it is intended to facilitate the search for further information on specific hardware components. On the other hand, you will find brief information on hardware topics that are neglected in the rest of the book. Of course, there are a lot of hardware components that are not described here or in other chapters of the book. That's because I don't have the testing capabilities that, say, a computer magazine has.

### Research First, Then Buy!

Find out if your new hardware is Linux compatible before you buy it! Perform a search on the internet using the term linux and the hardware model name.

Most hardware components are addressed via so-called devices—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/nvme0n1</samp> for a modern SSD. The device files are dynamically created on demand by the <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> system. For a list of the most important Linux device files, see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.9](#09_009.html_h9.9).

The drivers for countless hardware components are located in kernel modules. Some of these modules are loaded during system startup; the remaining modules are loaded only when needed. If the automatic loading of modules doesn’t work, you should take a look at the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/modprobe.conf</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/modprobe[.conf].d/*</samp> file. The handling of modules and the function of these files are described in [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.1](#21_001.html_h21.1).

The kernel messages show what happens when modules are loaded and whether the hardware can be initialized successfully. You can read these messages by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dmesg</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lspci -k</samp> indicates which PCI device (i.e., the graphics card, the audio adapter, etc.) is served by which driver.

For many components, virtual file systems in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sys</samp> directories provide detailed information. For an overview of such hardware files, see [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.7](#21_007.html_h21.7).

To get an overview of the running hardware, you can execute the following commands: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsblk</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lscpu</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lshw</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lspci</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsscsi</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsusb</samp>. Once again, a look at the kernel messages with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dmesg</samp> also provides useful information.

A great tool to determine a visually appealing summary of all hardware components and their associated drivers is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">inxi</samp> command. The Perl script can be installed on most distributions without any problems. Without further options, it only outputs the key data of the computer. In the terminal, keywords of the output are highlighted in color, which makes the text more readable than in the following listings:

```
user$ inxi
CPU: 6-core Intel Core i7-8750H (-MT MCP-) speed/min/max: 1733/800/4100 MHz
Kernel: 6.3.1-arch1-1 x86_64 Up: 1h 6m Mem: 11689.0/31556.3 MiB (37.0%)
Storage: 2.29 TiB (32.5% used) Procs: 398 Shell: Zsh inxi: 3.3.27 
```

With appropriate options, it displays detailed information about certain functions—for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-A</samp> for the audio system, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-G</samp> for the graphics system, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-E</samp> for all Bluetooth components. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">inxi -F</samp> (think of f for full) provides all the data that the command can determine:

```
user$ inxi -A
Audio:
  Device-1: Intel Cannon Lake PCH cAVS driver: snd_hda_intel
  Device-2: NVIDIA GP107GL High Definition Audio driver: snd_hda_intel
  Device-3: C-Media USB Audio Device
    driver: hid-generic,snd-usb-audio,usbhid type: USB
  API: ALSA v: k6.3.1-arch1-1 status: kernel-api
  Server-1: PipeWire v: 0.3.70 status: active 
```

### 14.8.1    CPU and Memory

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/cpuinfo</samp> file shows which CPUs are running in your computer. The following heavily abbreviated output was created on a computer with an AMD Ryzen processor. Linux treats the cores like independent processors. The <samp class="listingcharacter">cpu MHz</samp> line contains the maximum base frequency, which can be exceeded for a short time in many models (depending on the manufacturer, this process is referred to as turbo boost, turbo core, etc.):

```
user$ cat /proc/cpuinfo
processor       : 0
model name      : AMD Ryzen 5 3600 6-Core Processor
cpu MHz         : 2195.694
...
processor       : 1
model name      : AMD Ryzen 5 3600 6-Core Processor
... 
```

[Section 14.9](#14_009.html_h14.9) contains some tips on how you can influence the behavior of the CPU.

Information about the available memory can be obtained using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">free</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsmem</samp> shows the internal organization of the memory.

If you suspect your computer to have defective memory modules, the MemTest86 program is a good way to test the RAM. In some distributions (such as Fedora), the program can be started conveniently in the GRUB menu after switching on the computer. If that doesn’t work for you, you can find an ISO image at [https://memtest86.com](https://memtest86.com). Transfer this image to a USB flash drive and use it to restart the computer.

### 14.8.2    Power Management

Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) controls the power-management functions of all commercially available PCs and notebook computers. ACPI is supported by Linux, which you can check by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dmesg | grep -i acpi</samp>.

ACPI supports various sleep modes in which the computer consumes little (standby, suspend mode) or no (hibernate mode) power at all. In most distributions or desktop systems, you put the computer into sleep mode via the system menu.

In standby mode, the CPU is put into a sleep mode in which it requires little power. The RAM continues to be supplied with power, but displays and data storage media are switched off.

In hibernation mode, on the other hand, the current RAM content is saved in the swap partition of the hard drive or SSD and the computer is then completely switched off. In this state, it no longer needs any power at all. This requires the swap partition or file to be sufficiently large! When waking up, the memory is read from the hard drive or SSD again.

In addition, all hardware components must be reinitialized. This process is very complex and requires an optimal interaction of the Linux kernel, its modules, and the ACPI system.

#### Waking Up from the Calm…

Unfortunately, my personal experiences with hibernation mode are mostly negative. Unless an error had already occurred when trying to activate it, it was often not possible to wake up the computer from sleep mode again. For this reason, many distributions have moved away from offering the activation of hibernation mode in the system menu at all.

Things look much better with standby mode, which often works without any problem in simple cases. Simple here means that no external devices are connected to the computer via USB-C hubs and no brand-new hardware components are in use. Otherwise, it can happen that the computer wakes up again, but the screen remains black or the speakers remain mute.

#### Saving Energy, Protecting the Battery

A collection of tips on how to minimize your notebook's power consumption and possibly optimize your battery life follows in [Section 14.10](#14_010.html_h14.10). There, I will introduce the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tlp</samp> programs, among others.

### 14.8.3    Interfaces and Bus Systems

On Linux, serial or parallel interfaces are accessible via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ttyS<n></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/lp<n></samp> device files. You are most likely to encounter these interfaces, which are no longer common in the PC sector, in min-computers or embedded devices.

Hard disks, DVD drives, and other data storage media are usually connected to the computer via the SATA or SCSI bus systems (see [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), [Section 18.3](#18_003.html_h18.3)). Particularly fast SSDs use the PCI Express (PCIe) standard instead. Information about the state of such devices is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsscsi</samp> command from the package of the same name and the following files:

```
/sys/bus/scsi/*
/proc/scsi/* 
```

Universal Serial Bus (USB) is used to connect the computer to various external devices—from a mouse to an external hard drive. The required USB kernel modules are loaded automatically.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/bus/usb</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sys/bus/usb</samp> directories contain information about all connected USB devices. A detailed listing of all USB interfaces and devices is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsusb -v</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">usbutils</samp> package). In case of USB problems, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">usbreset</samp> to perform a reset during operation. (Disconnect all external data media beforehand!)

The best way to find information about PCI components in your computer is to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lspci</samp> command. The files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/bus/pci/</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sys/bus/pci/</samp> contain the same information but are much more difficult to interpret. The following output is heavily abridged for reasons of space:

```
root# lspci
00:00.0 Host bridge: Intel Corporation 8th Gen Core Processor Host Bridge/DRAM Registers (rev 07)
00:02.0 VGA compatible controller: Intel Corporation CoffeeLake-H GT2 [UHD Graphics 630]
00:1f.6 Ethernet controller: Intel Corporation Ethernet Connection (7) I219-V 
02:00.0 Non-Volatile memory controller: Samsung Electronics Co Ltd NVMe SSD Controller SM981/PM981
... 
```

Information on configuring LAN and Wi-Fi interfaces follows in [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15). The use of graphics cards or GPUs requires separate drivers. Their configuration is the subject of [Chapter 17](#17_001.html_h17).

### 14.8.4    Bluetooth

Bluetooth is a method for hardware devices to communicate via radio. Bluetooth is mainly used in small electronic devices (keyboards, mice, speakers, smartphones, and so on). In desktop systems such as GNOME or KDE, convenient interfaces help you set up Bluetooth devices. However, patience is sometimes required as it often takes some time before the devices are recognized.

Behind the scenes, the implementation of the Bluetooth stack is the responsibility of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bluetoothd</samp> daemon in interaction with <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> for the management of Bluetooth devices. The corresponding configuration files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/bluetooth</samp> directory. More information about Bluetooth on Linux can be found at [http://www.bluez.org](http://www.bluez.org).

Only in rare cases is it necessary to configure Bluetooth at the command line level. One possible scenario is to use the Raspberry Pi without a monitor if control and communication is to be done exclusively via SSH. In such cases, it’s best to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bluetoothctl</samp> command, which is intended for interactive use. After it starts, you enter a command mode where you can execute various commands: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">list</samp> lists all Bluetooth controllers (such as a USB adapter), and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">devices</samp> lists all devices in radio range. Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exit</samp> or (Ctrl)+(D), you can return to the input mode of the terminal.

To connect a new Bluetooth device to your computer, you should do the following within a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bluetoothctl</samp> session:

*   Activate the coupling mode using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pairable on</samp>.

*   Activate the scan mode using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scan on</samp>. The program then lists all detected devices within radio range. This process can take quite some time as individual devices are listed again and again. When you have found the device you want, you can simply switch the mode off again using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">scan off</samp>.

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">agent on</samp> lets you activate a so-called Bluetooth agent. It takes care of the authorization of new devices (for keyboards: password entry).

*   Then use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pair xx:xx:xx</samp> to initiate the connection setup to a device. If you use a keyboard, you will then be prompted to type in a six-digit code. Do not forget to finish the input by pressing (Enter)! You can recognize a successful pairing by the pairing successful message. For devices without input options (keyboard, speakers, etc.), pairing is fortunately possible without entering a code.

*   And by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">trust xx:xx:xx</samp>, you make clear to the Bluetooth system that you trust the device.

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">connect xx:xx:xx</samp>, you indicate that you actually want to use the device. (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bluetoothctl</samp> could have realized that by now!) If everything works out, the response is connection successful. The device can now be used!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">info xx:xx:xx</samp> displays the connection status and various other information about the device.

It’s important to keep pressing the Bluetooth button (pairing button) on Bluetooth devices that you want to reconfigure so that the device signals to the environment that it’s ready to connect. On many devices, a blue LED then flashes. If there is no such button, you can also try turning the device off and on again.

The following lines show in slightly abbreviated form the inputs and outputs for configuring a Bluetooth keyboard. All inputs and outputs take place in a terminal window:

```
user$ bluetoothctl
[bluetooth]# agent on
[bluetooth]# pairable on
[bluetooth]# scan on
Discovery started
[CHG] Controller 00:1A:7D:DA:71:13 Discovering: yes
[NEW] Device 70:10:00:1A:92:20 70-10-00-1A-92-20
[CHG] Device 70:10:00:1A:92:20 Name: Bluetooth 3.0 Keyboard
...
[bluetooth]# scan off
[bluetooth]# pair 70:10:00:1A:92:20
Attempting to pair with 70:10:00:1A:92:20
[CHG] Device 70:10:00:1A:92:20 Connected: yes
[agent] PIN code: 963064
[CHG] Device 70:10:00:1A:92:20 Paired: yes
Pairing successful
[bluetooth]# trust 70:10:00:1A:92:20
[bluetooth]# connect 70:10:00:1A:92:20
[bluetooth]# info 70:10:00:1A:92:20
Device 70:10:00:1A:92:20
        Name: Bluetooth 3.0 Keyboard
        Paired: yes
        Trusted: yes
        Connected: yes
    ...
[bluetooth]# exit 
```

The Bluetooth configuration for a particular device is stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/bluetooth/id1/id2/info</samp>. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">id1</samp> is the ID code of the Bluetooth controller and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">id2</samp> is the ID code of the Bluetooth device.

The Bluetooth device should now also be detected correctly at the next startup. In my tests on a Raspberry Pi, however, I failed at this point with some Bluetooth devices. The solution was to execute the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">connect</samp> statement at the end of the boot process:

```
# file /etc/rc.local
...
echo -e "connect FC:58:FA:A0:4D:E7\nquit" | bluetoothctl
exit 0 
```

### 14.8.5    Hotplug System

USB flash drives and hard disks, monitors, loudspeaker boxes, and so on can be connected or removed during operation. Linux must respond to the changed hardware situation quickly and as automatically as possible. This task is performed by the hotplug system:

*   Kernel The kernel detects changes to the hardware—for example, that the user has plugged in a USB flash drive.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp>  The kernel creates new device files via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">udev</samp> (see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.9](#09_009.html_h9.9)) and starts appropriate programs to manage the new devices or to send notifications to the desktop system. Rule files from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/udev/rules.d</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/udev/rules.d</samp> directories are analyzed in this process.

*   DeviceKit DeviceKit helps manage some devices or components. It consists of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libudisk2</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libgudev</samp> libraries, which are usually packaged in packages of the same name. For hard disks (partitions) and external disks, the programs and scripts of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">udisks2</samp> package are responsible. Power management is taken care of by the rules and programs of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">upower</samp> package. You can find information on this topic at the following web pages:

    *   [https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/DeviceKit](https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/DeviceKit)

    *   [https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/udisks](https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/udisks)

    *   [https://upower.freedesktop.org](https://upower.freedesktop.org)

*   Desktop In KDE, the Solid framework is responsible for processing D-Bus messages. On GNOME, Nautilus takes care of the external disks in interaction with PolicyKit (see [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10), [Section 10.4](#10_004.html_h10.4)). The configuration is done in the Removable Media module in the system settings.

*   D-Bus The D-Bus communication system is used for the communication between the different levels of the hotplug system. Based on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libdbus</samp> library, communication can be done directly between two programs. If messages are to be exchanged between multiple programs, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dbus-daemon</samp> background program is used as the central exchange.
    D-Bus is implemented outside the kernel. Plans to integrate the communication system into the kernel as part of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kdbus</samp> project have failed.

The Thunderbolt protocol makes it possible to route the PCIe bus to the outside and connect various external devices to a computer—from high-resolution monitors to network adapters. The first Thunderbolt implementations were still based on DisplayPort; USB-C is now more common. Thunderbolt has been part of the USB standard since version 4.

Basically, Thunderbolt works without problems on Linux. However, Thunderbolt can be a security risk, among other things because the PCIe bus gives direct access to the RAM. For this reason, a notebook computer's Thunderbolt outputs can (and should) be protected in the BIOS/EFI. They are then not available until the user explicitly releases them during operation. This, in turn, is associated with disadvantages; for example, a keyboard connected to the USB-C hub cannot be used to enter the hard drive encryption password during the boot process.

On GNOME, security-critical devices connected via Thunderbolt can be enabled with RAM access in the Privacy • Thunderbolt module of the system settings. (Ordinary USB devices and monitors work without explicit permission, which is why the Thunderbolt module in [Figure 14.2](#14_008.html_f14.2) somewhat misleadingly claims that no devices are connected at all.)

[![Thunderbolt Configuration in GNOME](bilderklein/klein14_002.png)](img-f14.2.html)

**Figure 14.2**     Thunderbolt Configuration in GNOME

At the command level, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">boltctl</samp> to list detected Thunderbolt devices (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">boltctl list -a</samp>) and authorize them if necessary (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">boltctl authorize</samp>). You can read more details about the safe use of Thunderbolt devices in Christian Kellner's excellent blog, as well as a couple of other websites:

*   [https://christian.kellner.me](https://christian.kellner.me)

*   [https://juho.tykkala.fi/Lenovo-Thunderbolt-3-dock-Linux](https://juho.tykkala.fi/Lenovo-Thunderbolt-3-dock-Linux)

*   [https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/ThunderboltEnablement](https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/ThunderboltEnablement)

### 14.8.6    Audio System

Advanced Linux Sound Architecture (ALSA) is responsible for the control of sound cards at the lowest level in the kernel. For audio controllers supported by the kernel, the required ALSA module is loaded automatically. The names of all ALSA modules start with <samp class="listingcharacter">snd</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsmod | grep snd</samp> command therefore provides a quick overview of all active ALSA modules. Access to various sound functions is provided by files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/asound</samp> directory.

You can configure the ALSA system by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/alsa/*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/asound.conf</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.asoundrc</samp> files. When the computer is shut down or rebooted, the init system saves or restores the volume settings.

For ordinary use of the audio system, there is no need to change the ALSA configuration. The hardware detection should succeed automatically. If you have special audio requirements (musicians), want to differentiate between several audio cards, or have other special requests, you’ll find comprehensive background information about ALSA and its configuration at the following website and the associated wiki: [https://alsa-project.org](https://alsa-project.org).

For the direct use of ALSA, various commands are available (<samp class="listingcharacter">alsa-utils</samp> package), the most important of which are briefly introduced here: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alsactl</samp> saves or loads all ALSA settings, such as the last set volume; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alsamixer</samp> changes the volume or the input level of various ALSA audio channels (see [Figure 14.3](#14_008.html_f14.3)); <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aplay</samp> plays an audio file; and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">arecord</samp> records an audio file.

[![ALSA Configuration in Terminal with alsamixer](bilderklein/klein14_003.png)](img-f14.3.html)

**Figure 14.3**     ALSA Configuration in Terminal with alsamixer

#### Troubleshooting the Audio System

If the speakers remain silent, the cause is often just a volume control set to 0\. Modern distributions sometimes lack graphical user interfaces to set all audio inputs and outputs individually. A solution to this problem is as follows: Start <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">alsamixer</samp> in a text console. Now you can use the cursor keys to select the channels and adjust their levels. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">M</samp> switches a channel completely on or off again (mute).

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">speaker-test</samp> ALSA command is helpful for initial tests of the audio system. When executed with the following parameters, the words front left and front right should be heard alternately in the left and right speakers:

<samp class="listingcharacter">speaker-test -t wav -c2</samp>

The topic of audio often seems more trivial than it actually is. In the past, it was enough to address the (only) speaker output with an MP3 player. Today, multiple signal sources are the norm, from YouTube videoes in the web browser to an audio player to the notebook's internal microphone and an external one for video conferencing. Things are similarly complex on the output side: the built-in speaker is joined by a headset, the monitor connected via HDMI with speakers, and a Bluetooth box. The user wants to be able to easily change the input and output source at any time. Ideally, Linux should restore all settings at the next reboot.

For this reason, most audio programs do not use ALSA directly, but rely on audio frameworks. This intermediate layer between the low-level system ALSA and the actual audio applications simplifies programming, makes audio applications network-compatible, and ensures conflict-free cooperation of simultaneously running audio programs.

The problem now is that there is currently no unified audio architecture above ALSA: KDE and GNOME each go their own way. Sophisticated audio applications, for which the existing audio libraries are insufficient, reimplement elementary audio functions themselves. It is therefore difficult to develop audio programs that simply work regardless of the desktop system.

The following points briefly introduce some common audio systems:

*   GStreamer The GStreamer library is a comprehensive multimedia framework used by many GNOME programs. Thanks to its plugin architecture, it can be extended well. (Most codecs are implemented as plugins.) The GStreamer library doesn’t contain its own sound daemon; merging multiple audio signals is handled directly by ALSA. You can find information on this topic at [https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org](https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org).

*   Phonon The multimedia foundation of KDE is called Phonon. The library provides a uniform programming interface for the use of audio and video functions, which uses existing multimedia libraries (often GStreamer or VLC; occasionally also Xine). Phonon is also used by the Qt library as a multimedia interface.

*   PulseAudio PulseAudio is a network-enabled sound server that has been used in almost all Linux distributions for several years. Today, however, PulseAudio is more and more often replaced by PipeWire (see the following point).
    PulseAudio enables you to control audio streams and assign them to different audio cards or output devices by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pavucontrol</samp> program. PulseAudio automatically detects external audio hardware (such as USB speakers).

*   PipeWire The latest star in the Linux audio firmament is PipeWire. This is a new audio and video server. Thanks to a compatibility layer for PulseAudio, the changeover, which has already been completed by many distributions, has gone unnoticed by most users.

    One advantage of PipeWire is its lower latencies. At the same time, PipeWire enables secure screen sharing and remote desktop applications on Wayland. For this reason alone, there will probably be no way around PipeWire in the future. A good description of the concepts of PipeWire can be found at [https://venam.nixers.net/blog/unix/2021/06/23/pipewire-under-the-hood.html](https://venam.nixers.net/blog/unix/2021/06/23/pipewire-under-the-hood.html).

    Various <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pw</samp> commands (in Fedora in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pipewire-utils</samp> package) help you to control and analyze the audio system. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pw-top</samp> lists all active audio components, including latency times.

For musicians or professional audio users, there are separate distributions that are specially optimized for the trouble-free use of audio programs and often use a Linux kernel optimized for real-time operation. Popular distributions include, for example, Ubuntu Studio ([https://ubuntustudio.org](https://ubuntustudio.org)) and AV Linux ([http://www.bandshed.net/avlinux](http://www.bandshed.net/avlinux)).

## 14.9    CPU Tuning

Modern CPUs provide many options to analyze and influence their behavior. In this section, I'll explain how you can determine the current clock frequency and temperature and how to disable the turbo boost function. The examples refer to Intel CPUs. AMD CPUs provide quite similar control options but require different tools and use different <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sys</samp> paths.

You can get information about the CPU in your computer using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lscpu</samp> command or via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat /proc/cpuinfo</samp>. The easiest way to determine the number of CPU cores is to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nproc</samp> command. If the CPU supports hyperthreading, then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nproc</samp> displays twice as many cores as there actually are. To find out how many “real” cores are available, you can use the second of the following commands, which extracts this information from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/cpuinfo</samp>:

```
user$ nproc
12
user$ grep ^cpu\\scores /proc/cpuinfo | uniq | awk '{print $4}' 
6 
```

### 14.9.1    Controlling the CPU Frequency

The CPU typically controls at which clock frequency it runs by itself. If there is little to do at the moment, the clock frequency is reduced. Conversely, the clock frequency can be increased for some time in the so-called turbo boost mode to complete complex tasks faster. However, this increases the CPU temperature considerably, which is why the amount of time for which the CPU can run at maximum clock frequency is strongly limited by the cooling. This is especially true for notebook computers.

The following command provides the current clock frequency of all real and virtual cores:

```
user$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq
1000033
1658625
1519742
1198860
... 
```

You can get even more detailed information using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cpupower</samp> command, which can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">linux-tools-common</samp> package on Debian and Ubuntu:

```
root# apt install linux-tools-common linux-tools-generic

user$ cpupower frequency-info
analyzing CPU 0:
  ...
  hardware limits: 800 MHz - 4.10 GHz
  available cpufreq governors: performance powersave
  current policy: frequency should be within 800 MHz and 2.20 GHz.
                  The governor "powersave" may decide which speed to
                  use within this range.
  current CPU frequency: 1.00 GHz (asserted by call to kernel)
  boost state support: Supported: yes, Active: yes 
```

If you want your notebook computer to run as long and quietly as possible, it’s recommended to deactivate the turbo boost mode:

```
user$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo       
(current state)
0
root# echo 1 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo  
(turbo boost off)
root# echo 0 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo  
(turbo boost on)
```

The so-called governor of the CPU is responsible for regulating the clock frequency. Current Intel CPUs only support the <samp class="listingcharacter">powersave</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">performance</samp> modes. In <samp class="listingcharacter">powersave</samp> mode, the clock frequency of all cores is controlled dynamically and as energy-efficiently as possible (default state). In <samp class="listingcharacter">performance</samp> mode, all cores usually run at the same clock frequency, although higher frequencies are also permitted at low loads. The following commands show how you can determine or change the current governor mode:

```
user$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor
root# for cpu in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/ \
                  cpufreq/scaling_governor; do 
        echo powersave > $cpu
      done
root# for cpu in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/ \
                  cpufreq/scaling_governor; do 
        echo performance > $cpu
      done 
```

With a little effort, you can influence further parameters of the CPU and, for example, set the minimum or the maximum allowed clock frequency, how many cores can run at maximum at the same time, under which circumstances the clock frequency should be changed, and so on. Some of these tricks are documented on the following pages:

*   [https://vstinner.github.io/intel-cpus.html](https://vstinner.github.io/intel-cpus.html)

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/CPU_frequency_scaling](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/CPU_frequency_scaling)

*   [https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/cpu-freq/governors.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/cpu-freq/governors.txt)

Depending on the distribution or desktop system, you can set the CPU power directly in the graphical user interface. In current GNOME versions, you switch between three power modes in the Power module of the system settings or in the Quick Settings menu at the top right of the panel. On Pop!_OS, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">system76-power</samp> command or the corresponding GNOME extension.

Behind the scenes, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">power-profiles-daemon</samp> is mostly used as the backend. This background service cannot be used simultaneously with other programs that also control the CPU (such as TLP).

### 14.9.2    Monitoring the CPU Temperature

If you want to know the current temperature of your computer's CPU, you need to install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lm-sensors</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lm_sensors</samp> package. After installation, you can run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sensors-detect</samp> command as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. This command determines which hardware components provide information about their state. Besides the CPU, this can also include the hard drive, the graphics card, or various fans that report their speed. Finally, the required kernel modules are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/modules</samp> configuration file (Debian/Ubuntu) or in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/lm_sensors</samp> after a query.

After this preparatory work, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sensors</samp> command provides an up-to-date temperature list:

```
root# sensors
...
coretemp-isa-0000
Package id 0:  +53.0°C  (high = +100.0°C, crit = +100.0°C)
Core 0:        +50.0°C  (high = +100.0°C, crit = +100.0°C)
Core 1:        +51.0°C  (high = +100.0°C, crit = +100.0°C)
...
pch_cannonlake-virtual-0
Adapter: Virtual device
temp1:        +44.0°C 
```

There are various programs that display this data more elegantly. For first experiments, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xsensors</samp>, which shows the data of all sensors in one window. On Ubuntu, you can install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">psensor</samp> package (see [Figure 14.4](#14_009.html_f14.4)).

The [https://extensions.gnome.org](https://extensions.gnome.org) website also provides various GNOME extensions that display the temperature and other performance data in the panel. Unfortunately, these extensions are rarely maintained in the long term and often stop working with the next GNOME update.

[![Temperature Display Using psensor](bilderklein/klein14_004.png)](img-f14.4.html)

**Figure 14.4**     Temperature Display Using psensor

## 14.10    Notebook Optimization

Annoyingly, many notebook computers run longer in battery mode on Windows than on Linux. This is mainly due to better optimized drivers. This section provides some tips on how you can optimize both the runtime and the life of your notebook battery on Linux. The section also briefly covers the topic of fan control: you can influence the fan behavior on Linux for selected models.

### CPU and Graphics Tuning

To make your notebook computer run as long as possible, you should deactivate the turbo boost mode of your CPU and activate the <samp class="listingcharacter">powersave</samp> governor. If you have a notebook with NVIDIA hybrid graphics, you should only use the Intel GPU if possible. For tips on this, see [Chapter 17](#17_001.html_h17), [Section 17.3](#17_003.html_h17.3).

### 14.10.1    powertop

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> command from the package of the same name helps you to search for programs that cause high power consumption or torpedo the power-saving functions of the CPU. The program provides tips on how you can minimize energy consumption. In the following command, <samp class="listingcharacter">LANG=</samp> causes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> to display menus and status texts. This is especially useful if you want to search the internet for details about individual parameters:

```
root# LANG= powertop 
```

[![The Tunables View of powertop](bilderklein/klein14_005.png)](img-f14.5.html)

**Figure 14.5**     The Tunables View of powertop

After it starts, you can switch between several status pages by pressing the (Tab) key. These pages show which processes wake the CPU from an idle state and how often, how often the CPU is in what idle state, how often the CPU runs at what clock frequency level, which devices are used and how much, and so on.

The most interesting page from the point of view of energy-saving functions is called Tunables (see [Figure 14.5](#14_010.html_f14.5)). There, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> shows a list of settings whose current state can be Bad or Good. You can then select individual points with the cursor keys and change them by pressing (Enter). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> shows which command it is executing.

Then you can try changing individual settings step by step and test what effect this has. Does the energy consumption of the previously charged notebook, recorded with a power meter, actually drop noticeably? Do the disabled functions cause problems? Can USB devices still be used? Does switching the Wi-Fi adapter on and off still work? Does the audio system work without noise? And so on.

The changes made using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> are only valid until the next computer restart. To activate the power-saving measures permanently, you must enter the commands displayed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">echo '1' > /sys/xxx</samp>) into a file that is executed at every system start. In some distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/rc.d/rc.local</samp> is suitable for this purpose. If necessary, you must create this file and mark it as executable by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod a+x</samp>.

A radical solution would be to enter <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop --auto-tune</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rc.local</samp> instead of individual tuning commands. Then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> simply performs all known optimization measures. Unfortunately, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> often overshoots the mark with this: What good is it if the notebook runs for an hour longer than before, but the network connection only works unreliably, or the connection to the Bluetooth mouse is constantly interrupted?

Note that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop --auto-tune</samp> will not work until <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> has run on battery power for about half an hour beforehand and has gotten a picture of the activity on your notebook.

#### Creating a list of all tuning commands

You can get a list of all possible tuning commands by running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--html</samp> option. After a measurement time of about 20 seconds, the command then generates the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop.html</samp> file, which contains various statistical data as well as a summary of all tuning parameters. For more tips on using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">powertop</samp>, see the Arch Linux wiki at [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/powertop](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/powertop).

### 14.10.2    TLP

TLP is a background service that implements various power-saving measures for Linux. TLP can be configured with countless options, but thanks to its sensible default values, much is already gained by simply installing TLP. The service is basically suitable for all notebook computers.
