You can set up a new VPN connection by clicking the plus button (+) in the Network dialog of the GNOME system settings and then selecting one of the supported methods (Cisco AnyConnect, OpenVPN, PPTP, etc.). This takes you to a dialog specific to the procedure in question. Don't be confused by the wealth of options; it’s often sufficient to fill in just a few fields. Fields for the login name and password are sometimes not included in the dialog. NetworkManager only asks for this information when the connection is actually established.

### 15.1.3    Proxy Configuration

In some companies or organizations, HTTP traffic has to flow through proxy servers, even though this is not up to date in view of ubiquitous HTTPS connections. On GNOME, a gear icon in the Network dialog of the system settings takes you to the proxy configuration. You have the choice between an automatic or a manual configuration.

The proxy settings are stored in the GNOME-specific <samp class="listingcharacter">dconf</samp> database. You can also access the GNOME proxy settings using the following command:

```
user$ gsettings list-recursively org.gnome.system.proxy
...
org.gnome.system.proxy.http enabled true
org.gnome.system.proxy.http host '10.0.0.1'
org.gnome.system.proxy.http port 8080 
```

After logging in to a GNOME session, you can set the respective environment variables such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">http_proxy</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">https_proxy</samp>.

For the changed proxy configuration to take effect, you must log out and log in again.

The configuration options provided by KDE and some other desktop systems are comparable to those of GNOME. To configure the proxy settings separately from a desktop environment, the easiest way is to add the following lines to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/environment</samp> file:

```
# file /etc/environment
http_proxy=http://10.0.0.1:8080
https_proxy=http://10.0.0.1:8443 
```

More details about the manual proxy configuration can be found on the following web pages:

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Proxy_settings](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Proxy_settings)

*   [https://wiki.gnome.org/Projects/NetworkManager/Proxies](https://wiki.gnome.org/Projects/NetworkManager/Proxies)

All common web browsers should automatically adopt the proxy configuration. If necessary, you can change the proxy configuration directly in the settings dialogs of Firefox or Chrome.

To make sure that the package management tools also take the proxy into account, their configuration files may need to be modified. On Debian and Ubuntu, you must set the <samp class="listingcharacter">Acquire::http::Proxy</samp> parameter in an <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> configuration file:

```
# for example in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/01-proxy.conf
Acquire::http::Proxy "http://hostname-or-ipaddress:8080"; 
```

On RHEL or Fedora, you must add the following lines to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/dnf/dnf.conf</samp>:

```
# in /etc/dnf/dnf.conf 
proxy=http://hostname-or-ipaddress:8080
# only if necessary
proxy_username=name
proxy_password=pw 
```

### 15.1.4    Configuring NetworkManager in Text Mode

Up to this point, I have assumed that you work on GNOME or another desktop system with NetworkManager-compatible configuration tools. When you configure a server or a virtual machine, these requirements are rarely met.

Instead of manually editing the configuration files, which are very distribution-specific, you can call the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmtui</samp> command. (The command name stands for NetworkManager Text User Interface). Even though the design of the dialogs is minimalistic (see [Figure 15.5](#15_001.html_f15.5)), the program offers extensive configuration options. Among other things, you can use these options to set up VPN connections, network bridges, and so on.

[![Static Configuration of Network Connection Using nmtui](bilderklein/klein15_005.png)](img-f15.5.html)

**Figure 15.5**     Static Configuration of Network Connection Using nmtui

### 15.1.5    Internal Details

You can also manage all NetworkManager settings using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmcli</samp> command. This allows you to control NetworkManager via scripts or, in the case of server installations, without a graphical user interface. The following commands first list all interfaces known to NetworkManager and then disable the Wi-Fi interface, <samp class="listingcharacter">wlp0s20f3</samp>:

```
root# nmcli dev
nmcli dev
DEVICE             TYPE      STATE                   CONNECTION     
lo                 loopback  connected (externally)  lo             
enp0s31f6          Ethernet  unavailable             –              
wlp0s20f3          wifi      connected               wlan-sol3      
br-72ad8975ca21    bridge    connected (externally)  br-72ad8975ca21
docker0            bridge    connected (externally)  docker0        
virbr0             bridge    connected (externally)  virbr0         
...
root# nmcli dev disconnect wlp0s20f3 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmcli dev show</samp> command provides pages of information on all connection parameters for all interfaces.

In most distributions, you can determine the address of the active nameserver by looking at <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> or extracting the information from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmcli dev show</samp>:

```
user$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by NetworkManager
search fritz.box
nameserver 192.168.178.1
nameserver fd00::3e37:12ff:feb7:a1cb
nameserver 2001:871:264:daef:3e37:12ff:feb7:a1cb

user$ nmcli dev show | grep -i dns
  IP4.DNS[1]: 192.168.122.1 
```

Some distributions (e.g., Fedora and Ubuntu) delegate the administration of the DNS record to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-resolvd</samp> service, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> then points to a local address. The actual DNS address can again be determined using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmcli dev show</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">resolvectl</samp>:

```
user$ cat /etc/resolv.conf     
(Fedora, Ubuntu)
  # This file is managed by man:systemd-resolved(8). Do not edit.
  nameserver 127.0.0.53
user$ nmcli dev show | grep -i dns
  IP4.DNS[1]:   192.168.178.1
  IP6.DNS[1]:   fd00::9a9b:cbff:fe06:8399
user$ resolvectl status | grep -i 'dns server'
  Current DNS Server: 192.168.178.1
  DNS Servers:        192.168.178.1 fd00::9a9b:cbff:fe06:8399 
```

Background information about the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> file follows in [Section 15.3](#15_003.html_h15.3), while <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-resolved</samp> is described in [Section 15.4](#15_004.html_h15.4).

The basic configuration for the network manager can be found in the following files:

```
/var/run/NetworkManager/conf.d/*.conf       
(lowest priority)
/usr/lib/NetworkManager/conf.d/*.conf
/etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/*.conf
/etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf     
(highest priority) 
```

An elementary problem for NetworkManager is that many Linux distributions in the past developed their own systems to manage and store the network configuration (see also [Section 15.4](#15_004.html_h15.4)). The challenge for the cross-distribution NetworkManager was to maintain compatibility with all these distributions, a challenge that could be solved by using plugins. You decide where and in which syntax network settings are stored, such as static IP addresses, Wi-Fi passwords, and so on. The active plugins are specified in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf</samp>. The choices include the following:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">keyfile</samp>
    NetworkManager's own syntax (applies by default); configuration files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ifcfg-rh</samp>
    Deprecated Fedora/RHEL syntax; configuration files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ifupdown</samp>
    Debian syntax (ENI format); configuration file in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp>

In many distributions, the tendency goes in the direction of <samp class="listingcharacter">keyfile</samp>. For example, on Debian and Ubuntu, NetworkManager stores its own connection data in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> file is analyzed only to determine which interfaces NetworkManager is supposed to ignore.

The big exception used to be Red Hat–like distributions, which relied on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifcfg-rh</samp> plugin for a long time. However, RHEL 8 has put an end to that. The Red Hat syntax, which is around 20 years old, is now considered obsolete (but is still accepted for compatibility reasons). The new standard for RHEL and its clones is also the <samp class="listingcharacter">keyfile</samp> syntax of NetworkManager.

It’s possible to automatically execute scripts when establishing or terminating a connection. These scripts must be set up in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/NetworkManager/dispatcher.d/</samp> directory. Details and examples of this method can be found on the following web page: [https://www.linux-magazine.com/Issues/2020/239/Dispatcher-Scripts](https://www.linux-magazine.com/Issues/2020/239/Dispatcher-Scripts).

## 15.2    Manual LAN and Wi-Fi Configuration

Typically, your LAN or Wi-Fi controller is automatically detected and initialized when your computer boots. This section describes how this process works behind the scenes or which steps are required to perform the initialization manually. This helps you to better understand network fundamentals and more confidently use the user interfaces of common configuration tools.

### 15.2.1    Activating the LAN Controller Manually

The network or LAN controller is usually a chip on the mainboard of your computer that provides Ethernet network functions. However, the controller can also be integrated into the CPU.

The first step is to make sure that the correct kernel module is loaded for your network controller. Often the kernel manages this automatically. In this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip link set enp4s0 up</samp> command is executed without an error message. If problems occur at this point, you must determine which network controller is in your computer and which kernel module is responsible for it. First pieces of information are provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lspci</samp> in such cases:

```
root# lspci -k | grep -i -3 net
...
00:1f.6 Ethernet controller: Intel Corporation Ethernet 
                             Connection (7) I219-V (rev 10)
    Subsystem: Lenovo Ethernet Connection (7) I219-V
    Kernel driver in use: e1000e
    Kernel modules: e1000e 
```

So the notebook uses an Ethernet controller from Intel and a driver that is included in the kernel module <samp class="listingcharacter">e1000e</samp>:

```
root# modinfo e1000e
filename:     /lib/modules/.../kernel/drivers/net/Ethernet/intel/e1000e/e1000e.ko
description:  Intel(R) PRO/1000 Network Driver
... 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lsmod</samp> you can now check if the module has already been loaded. This will typically be the case; that is, Linux has already recognized the controller correctly during system startup. Only if this is not the case do you have to load the appropriate module via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">modprobe</samp>:

```
root# modprobe e1000e 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dmesg</samp> shows whether errors occur when loading the module (which is not the case here). The link is not ready warning only says that the interface is currently not active due to the lack of configuration:

```
root# dmesg
...
e1000e: Intel(R) PRO/1000 Network Driver - 3.2.6-k
e1000e: Copyright(c) Intel Corporation.
..
e1000e 0000:00:1f.6 enp0s31f6: renamed from eth0
ADDRCONF(NETDEV_UP): enp0s31f6: link is not ready
... 
```

Usually the module is loaded automatically during the initialization of the computer. If that doesn’t work, you need to enter the mapping between the interface and the kernel module in the module configuration file:

```
# module configuration file /etc/modprobe.d/config.conf
alias enp0s31f6 e1000e 
```

Network interfaces have different names depending on the distribution. Some distributions still use the interface names <samp class="listingcharacter">eth0</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">eth1</samp>, and so on, but more and more distributions use device names like <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s5</samp>. A list of all network interfaces available on your computer is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip link show</samp> command:

```
root# ip link show
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue ...
2: enp0s31f6: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc ...
3: wlp0s20f3: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state ... 
```

Then you want to activate the relevant network interface using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip link set <adapter> up</samp>:

```
root# ip link set enp0s31f6 up 
```

To configure the network interface, you need to run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr add</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr show enp0s31f6</samp> then displays all known network interface information:

```
root# ip addr add 192.168.0.2/24 dev enp0s31f6
root# ip addr show enp0s31f6
2: enp0s31f6: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc ...
    link/ether 00:1c:42:85:09:a1 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.0.2/24 scope global enp0s31f6
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever 
```

Now you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> to check whether you can contact other computers on the local network. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c 2</samp> option causes exactly two <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> packets to be sent:

```
root# ping -c 2 192.168.0.1
PING 192.168.0.1 (192.168.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.0.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.95 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.0.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.169 ms

--- 192.168.0.1 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1002ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.169/1.560/2.952/1.392 ms 
```

#### Commands: ip versus ifconfig and route

In many books and on websites about Linux network configuration, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifconfig</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">route</samp> commands are still described. But these commands are obsolete!

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> provides various additional functions that are missing in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifconfig</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">route</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> is specially optimized for the network functions of the Linux kernel. Experienced administrators should now get rid of old habits and switch to the new <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> command, while Linux beginners should steer clear of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifconfig</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">route</samp> right from the start.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp> currently only works if you enter the correct IP address. To allow you to specify a host name instead, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> must contain the IP address of a name server. The following example assumes that the local network has its own nameserver with IP address 192.168.0.1\. However, the nameserver can also be external and provided by the internet provider. Details about this configuration file follow in [Section 15.3.2](#15_003.html_h15.3.2):

```
# /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 192.168.0.1 
```

At this point, packets can only be sent within the local network.

To enable contact to the internet, the computer must know where to route such packets. For this purpose, you must specify the address of the internet gateway of your network by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip route</samp>. The following example assumes that the IP address of the gateway is 192.168.0.1:

```
root# ip route add default via 192.168.0.1 
```

Without any additional parameters, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip route</samp> returns the routing table. The gateway address is contained in the line that starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp>:

```
root# ip route
default via 10.211.55.1 dev enp0s31f6
192.168.0.0/24 dev enp0s31f6  proto kernel  scope link  src 192.168.0.2 
```

Now it should be possible to send packets to any address on the internet:

```
root# ping -c 2 google.com
PING google.com (172.217.22.78) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from ....1e100.net (172.217.22.78): icmp_seq=1 ttl=56 time=25.5 ms
64 bytes from ....1e100.net (172.217.22.78): icmp_seq=2 ttl=56 time=25.0 ms
--- google.com ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 2ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 25.013/25.271/25.529/0.258 ms 
```

A manual configuration of the loopback interface is rarely required. If it is, however, you need to execute the following two commands:

```
root# ip link set lo up
root# ip addr add 127.0.0.1 dev lo 
```

Basically, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr del</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip route del</samp> to undo previously performed address assignments or route definitions. You must specify exactly the same parameters as for the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr add</samp> command:

```
root# ip addr add 192.168.0.2/24 dev enp0s31f6
root# ip addr del 192.168.0.2/24 dev enp0s31f6 
```

To entirely disable a network interface—that is, to delete all address and route data—you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr flush</samp>:

```
root# ip addr flush dev enp0s31f6 
```

### 15.2.2    Retrieving DHCP Information

If there is a DHCP server on the network, you can use it for configuration purposes. After enabling the interface using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip link set enp4s0 up</samp>, you need to run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dhclient</samp> command in most distributions:

```
root# dhclient -v enp0s31f6
...

Listening on LPF/enp4s0/00:11:25:32:4f:5d
Sending on   LPF/enp4s0/00:11:25:32:4f:5d
Sending on   Socket/fallback
DHCPDISCOVER on enp4s0 to 255.255.255.255 port 67 interval 3
DHCPOFFER from 192.168.0.1
DHCPREQUEST on enp4s0 to 255.255.255.255 port 67
DHCPACK from 192.168.0.1
bound to 192.168.0.15 – renewal in 36624 seconds. 
```

#### Ad Hoc Network Configuration

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dhclient</samp> command often provides the fastest way to establish ad hoc network access on a computer that has not yet been configured. This means you do not need the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> commands and the manual setting of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp>. The only requirement is a DHCP server on the local network.

### 15.2.3    IPv6 Configuration

All the examples so far have referred to IPv4\. However, you can of course also use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> command to perform an IPv6 configuration. The following commands assume that you have the IPv6 subnet 2a01:4f8:161:107::/64 and can use the gateway address fe80::1\. The <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s31f6</samp> interface is assigned the address 2a01:4f8:161:107::2\. To try this out, use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping6</samp> to send commands to a server that you know is configured for IPv6:

```
root# ip -6 addr add 2a01:4f8:161:107::2/64 dev enp0s31f6
root# ip -6 route add default via fe80::1 dev enp0s31f6
root# ping6 -n google.com
PING google.com(2a00:1450:4009:805::1002) 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 2a00:1450:4009:805::1002: icmp_seq=1 ttl=54 time=19.7 ms
64 bytes from 2a00:1450:4009:805::1002: icmp_seq=2 ttl=54 time=19.1 ms
<Ctrl>+<C> 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping6</samp> command just mentioned is best suited for initial IPv6 testing. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping6</samp> returns the error message connect: The network is not reachable, then you can take a closer look at the IPv6 configuration using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr show <interface></samp> provides detailed data on the network interface <samp class="listingcharacter"><interface></samp> in the following listing:

```
root# ip addr show enp0s31f6
2: enp0s31f6: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ...
  link/ether 00:1c:42:d0:29:34 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
  inet  10.0.0.13/24 brd 10.0.0.255 scope global enp0s31f6
  inet6 fe80::21c:42ff:fed0:2934/64 scope link 
    valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
root# ip -6 route | grep default 
– no result -- 
```

The line beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">link/ether</samp> specifies the MAC address of the interface. The line beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">inet</samp> contains the IPv4 address including a mask in the short notation (<samp class="listingcharacter">/n</samp>) as well as the broadcast address. The lines beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">inet6</samp> specify the IPv6 addresses. Note that there can be several addresses. A “correct” IPv6 configuration requires the interface to be connected to a global unicast address, which usually starts with the number 2.

An IPv6 address alone is not enough. Linux also needs to know where to route IPv6 packets. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip -6 route | grep default</samp> to determine the default gateway for IPv6.

In the previous example, there is only an IPv4 configuration. The address specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter">inet6</samp> line is just a link local address that is set up automatically and allows for the communication within a local network (comparable to Zeroconf for IPv4; see [Section 15.5](#15_005.html_h15.5)). No IPv6 gateway has been set up.

The next example shows the results on a root server with IPv4 and IPv6 configuration. The <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s31f6</samp> interface is assigned the unicast address 2a01:xxx::2 (<samp class="listingcharacter">scope global</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> result), and fe80::1 is set up as the IPv6 gateway:

```
root# ip  addr show enp0s31f6
3: enp0s31f6: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP 
    link/ether 54:04:a6:f1:74:1f brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 5.9.22.18 peer 5.9.22.1/32 brd 5.9.22.31 scope global enp0s31f6
    inet6 2a01:4f8:161:107::2/64 scope global 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 fe80::5604:a6ff:fef1:741f/64 scope link 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
root# ip -6 route | grep default
default via fe80::1 dev enp0s31f6  metric 1024 
```

### 15.2.4    Manual Control of the Wi-Fi Controller

The kernel module for the Wi-Fi controller is usually loaded automatically. In most distributions, the interface for the wireless network is named <samp class="listingcharacter">wlan0</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">wlpxxx</samp>. If you’re unsure, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip</samp> link to determine a list of all interfaces. <samp class="listingcharacter">dmesg | egrep -i "wlan|wifi"</samp> returns all relevant kernel messages.

Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw dev NAME info</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw dev NAME link</samp>, you can determine the status of the interface. In the following example, an active connection exists:

```
root# iw dev wlp2s0 info
Interface wlp2s0
        ifindex 3
        type managed
        wiphy 2
root# iw dev wlp2s0 link
Connected to 00:16:b6:9d:ff:4b (on wlp2s0)
        SSID: wlan-sol2
        freq: 2462
        RX: 102262 bytes (1784 packets)
        TX: 12815 bytes (86 packets)
        signal: -59 dBm
        tx bitrate: 54.0 MBit/s
        ... 
```

The pseudo file <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/net/wireless</samp> also summarizes information about the current quality of the Wi-Fi connection:

```
root# cat /proc/net/wireless
Inter-| sta-|   Quality        |   Discarded packets               | Missed | WE
 face | tus | link level noise |  nwid  crypt   frag  retry   misc | beacon | 22
wlp2s0: 0020   91\.  189\.    0\.       0      0      0      0      4        0 
```

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw</samp> doesn’t recognize the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wlp2s0</samp> interface (error message no such device), you must set up the interface first. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">interface add</samp> is used for this purpose:

```
root# iw phy phy0 interface add wlp2s0 type managed 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">phy0</samp> addresses the first (and for most computers also the only) Wi-Fi controller. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">managed</samp>, you can also specify the following interface types: <samp class="listingcharacter">monitor</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">wds</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mesh</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">mp</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">ibss</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">adhoc</samp>. The new interface must then be activated:

```
root# ip link set wlp2s0 up 
```

If you no longer need the interface, you can delete it again using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw del</samp>:

```
root# iw dev wlp2s0 del 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw scan</samp> provides detailed information about all wireless networks within range. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> turns this into a simple list of all network names (SSIDs):

```
root# iw dev wlp2s0 scan | grep SSID
    SSID: myhome
    SSID: wlan-sol2
    ... 
```

You can establish a manual connection to unsecured wireless networks using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw ... connect</samp>. You must specify the name of the network (i.e., the SSID). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw</samp> only takes care of the Wi-Fi connection. You then perform the Ethernet configuration using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dhclient</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dhcpcd</samp> on SUSE):

```
root# iw dev wlp2s0 connect hotel-wlan-1
root# dhclient wlp2s0 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iw disconnect</samp> terminates the connection:

```
root# iw dev wlp2s0 disconnect 
```

### 15.2.5    Encrypting the Wireless Network

If the wireless network is secured by the now completely insecure WEP method, you can pass the key with an additional parameter in the format <samp class="listingcharacter">n:xxx</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> indicates the key number (0 to 3). The actual key is specified optionally in the form of 5 or 13 ASCII characters or by 10 or 26 hexadecimal digits:

```
root# iw dev wlp2s0 connect hotel-wlan-1 keys 0:1a790bcc31
root# dhclient wlp2s0 
```

The procedure is somewhat more complicated if WPA or WPA2 are involved. In this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa_supplicant</samp> background program from the package of the same name is responsible for initializing the connection and for the further exchange of ever-changing keys. After its installation, you need to set up a configuration file, choosing a filename such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/wpa_supplicant.conf</samp>.

The file may contain some global settings. This is followed by specific parameters for different wireless networks. The following example shows a minimum variant that is sufficient for establishing a connection to a Wi-Fi router or Wi-Fi access point using WPA or WPA2 personal encryption. The two crucial parameters are <samp class="listingcharacter">ssid</samp> to identify the network and <samp class="listingcharacter">psk</samp> with the key encrypted again for security reasons (it is also permissible to specify the WPA key in quotes as plain text):

```
# /etc/wpa_supplicant.conf
network={
     ssid="sol"
     psk=00a38f42e6681596e1a5a4c5ede9a15250fb2a01c21028c6d490bb3458b8ea00
}
network={
     ssid="wlan-sol2"
     psk=053633deb59038da9e9168e015fef97d3d54ae3794d4a12d31ee75a830cccec2
} 
```

When encrypting your WPA password, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa_passphrase</samp> can help you. If you do not pass the password as a parameter, the command expects the password at the standard input. You can copy the result of this command directly into <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa_supplicant.conf</samp>, removing the line containing the password in plain text if possible:

```
root# wpa_passphrase wlan-sol2 'My very secret password!'
network={
        ssid="wlan-sol2"
        #psk="My very secret password!"
        psk=020d93e2ddb2cdee51e800b977ff7d58fde47d0913 \
        cd394f2133648a147f513f
} 
```

Now you can start <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa_supplicant</samp>. The command runs until you end it by pressing (Ctrl)+(C). It takes care of initializing the Wi-Fi connection and the subsequently regular renewal of the keys for the connection. In other words, the program must run as long as you use the Wi-Fi connection, so you should continue working in another console.

Let me make some brief remarks about the options of the command: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-i</samp> specifies the network interface and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp> the configuration file whose name you are free to choose. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-D</samp> specifies the Wi-Fi driver(s) you are using. Just try <samp class="listingcharacter">nl80211,wext</samp>: this supports both the old Linux Wi-Fi drivers and the new implementations. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man wpa_supplicant</samp> provides a list of all supported drivers:

```
root# wpa_supplicant -iwlp2s0 -Dnl80211,wext -c /etc/wpa_supplicant.conf
Trying to associate with 00:13:46:b5:25:6e (SSID='sol' freq=0 MHz)
Associated with 00:13:46:b5:25:6e
WPA: Key negotiation completed with 00:13:46:b5:25:6e [PTK=TKIP GTK=TKIP]
CTRL-EVENT-CONNECTED - Connection to 00:13:46:b5:25:6e completed (auth)
  [id=0 id_str=]
... 
```

For more tips on how to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpasupplicant</samp>, visit the following page: [https://w1.fi/wpa_supplicant](https://w1.fi/wpa_supplicant).

There are considerations to replace <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpasupplicant</samp> with a more modern system in the longer term. Whether and when the iNet Wireless Daemon (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">iwd</samp>) will succeed in doing so remains to be seen. For more information, visit the following pages:

*   [https://iwd.wiki.kernel.org](https://iwd.wiki.kernel.org)

*   [https://lwn.net/Articles/770991](https://lwn.net/Articles/770991)

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Iwd](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Iwd)

## 15.3    LAN Configuration Files

This section introduces the most important configuration files for connecting the computer to a local network. Unfortunately, only some of these files have rules that are consistent across all major distributions. For the rest, the information compiled in this section refers to Debian, Fedora, openSUSE, RHEL, and Ubuntu (as of spring 2024). Typically, you will avoid directly modifying the configuration files and use your distribution's configuration tools instead.

For the following examples, the computer to be configured is called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">uranus</samp>. It is located on a local network with the domain named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sol</samp>. Other computers on the local network are called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">jupiter</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">saturn</samp>, and so on. The local network uses 192.168.0.* addresses. The IP address of the local computer is 192.168.0.2\. The IP address of the gateway computer on the local network is 192.168.0.1\. The gateway computer runs its own nameserver. Names and numbers are of course only examples.

### 15.3.1    Basic Configuration

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> file contains a list of known IP addresses and their associated names. The file must contain the loopback interface data in any case. The minimal variant looks like this:

```
# /etc/hosts (minimal variant)
127.0.0.1   localhost 
```

In most Linux distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localhost</samp> is also defined for IPv6\. The following lines show the default settings on Fedora and RHEL:

```
# /etc/hosts (default configuration on Red Hat and Fedora)
127.0.0.1   localhost localhost.localdomain localhost4 localhost4.localdomain4
::1         localhost localhost.localdomain localhost6 localhost6.localdomain6 
```

In the case of a static network configuration, such as on a root server, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hosts</samp> can also contain an entry with the IP address and the host name of the computer:

```
# /etc/hosts (continued, static configuration of the local host)
...
192.168.0.2  uranus.sol uranus 
```

If you want to address the other hosts on the local network by name and there is no local nameserver, you must also specify their names in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp>. So instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping 192.168.0.3</samp>, you can then simply run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping saturn</samp> to test the connection to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">saturn</samp> computer:

```
# /etc/hosts (continued, static configuration of other hosts)
...
192.168.0.1   mars.sol    mars    
192.168.0.2   uranus.sol  uranus  
192.168.0.3   saturn.sol  saturn 
```

Analogous entries are required in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> files of all computers on the local network. The more computers there are on the local network, the more tedious the administration of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> file becomes. For this reason, it is recommended to set up a nameserver on every network with more than two devices. Usually, this task is performed by the router on the local network. The device or the nameserver running in it then knows what all other computers on the network are called. The hosts on the local network can contact the nameserver to determine this information. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> then only needs the <samp class="listingcharacter">localhost</samp> lines.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/host.conf</samp> file specifies how TCP/IP should determine unknown IP addresses. The following sample file specifies that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> file should be analyzed first (<samp class="listingcharacter">hosts</samp> keyword), followed by querying the name server specified in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp>). The second line allows multiple IP addresses to be assigned to a host name specified in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp>. This file is present in almost all distributions in the form specified here and does not need to be changed (the <samp class="listingcharacter">order</samp> line applies only to old versions of the C library and can be omitted):

```
# /etc/host.conf
order hosts, bind
multi on 
```

On local networks, the address of the gateway is usually transmitted via DHCP.

For a static configuration, different files are responsible depending on the distribution. Many distributions use NetworkManager and store the configuration files in the default format (<samp class="listingcharacter">keyfile</samp>). In this case, the gateway address directly follows the IP address at the <samp class="listingcharacter">address1</samp> keyword:

```
# file /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/<ifname>.conf
...
[ipv4]
# address 192.168.0.2 and gateway 192.168.0.1
address1=192.168.0.2/24,192.168.0.1 
```

On Debian, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> describes all network interfaces. For statically configured interfaces, the gateway is set by the <samp class="listingcharacter">gateway</samp> keyword:

```
# in /etc/network/interfaces (Debian)
...
iface enp0s31f6 inet static
  address 192.168.0.2
  netmask 255.255.255.0
  gateway 192.168.0.1 
```

### 15.3.2    DNS Configuration (resolv.conf)

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> file controls how IP addresses are determined for unknown network names (host names). Unknown here means that the names are not defined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">domain</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">search</samp> keywords are used to expand incomplete names with the domain name—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">jupiter</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">jupiter.sol</samp>. This primarily increases convenience because local hostnames can be specified in a shortened form. You can specify multiple domain names with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">search</samp>, but only one with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">domain</samp>. But note that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">domain</samp> name has priority over the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">search</samp> names, which means it’s tested first. If, as here, only a single domain name is specified, then the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">domain</samp> line can be omitted.

The most important entries in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> file are prefixed with the <samp class="listingcharacter">nameserver</samp> keyword: this allows for up to three IP addresses of nameservers to be specified. These servers are always addressed when the IP address of an unknown computer name is to be determined. The specification of a nameserver is absolutely necessary so that internet addresses can be resolved to IP addresses. Most routers run a local DNS, which in turn uses the DNS of the provider. Larger local networks usually have their own nameservers:

```
# /etc/resolv.conf
domain sol                # host names apply to .sol
search sol                # host names apply to .sol
nameserver 182.92.138.35  # first DNS
nameserver 195.3.96.67    # second DNS (if the first one fails) 
```

If you use IPv6, you must also specify the address of an IPv6 nameserver. The following example provides the address of Google's public IPv6 nameserver:

```
# /etc/resolv.conf
...
nameserver 2001:4860:4860::8888 
```

Note that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">resolv.conf</samp> is mostly created dynamically:

*   If the network connection (whether via LAN or Wi-Fi) is configured with DHCP, the script for establishing the connection or NetworkManager enters the nameserver addresses transmitted by the DHCP server.

*   On Fedora and Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-resolved</samp> service takes care of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">resolv.conf</samp>, whereby a local nameserver is interposed. Details of the procedure, which may be implemented in other distributions in the future, follow in [Section 15.4](#15_004.html_h15.4). The actual (external) DNS server can be determined using the following command:

    ```
    user$ resolvectl status | grep -i 'dns server' 
    ```

    You can get more background information on the concept of the local DNS resolver at the following website, for example: [https://blueprints. launchpad.net/ubuntu/+spec/foundations-y-local-resolver](https://blueprints.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+spec/foundations-y-local-resolver).

### 15.3.3    Host Name

The current host name can be determined using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname</samp> command. Unless the host name is set by DHCP, the configuration is done in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hostname</samp> file for almost all current distributions. To change the host name, it’s best to use the following command:

```
root# hostnamectl set-hostname my-new-hostname 
```

Note that host names must not contain spaces or special characters. The <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> character is allowed, but not as the first or last character.

Umlauts and other special characters are actually not provided for in the host name. For internationalized domain names (IDNs), the host name is converted to ASCII characters according to the Punycode method. On Linux, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">idn</samp> command helps. It’s located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">idn</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libidn</samp> package, depending on the distribution. The host name is the resulting string that starts with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xn--</samp>. Only in the web browser of the clients does it turn into the “correct” representation:

```
user$ idn hellö-world.com
xn--hell-world-hcb.com
root# hostnamectl set-hostname xn--hell-world-hcb.com 
```

### 15.3.4    Mappings between Controllers and Network Interfaces

With multiple network interfaces, it’s often difficult to determine the mapping between the <samp class="listingcharacter">ethN</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">enpNsM</samp> devices and the physical hardware. Depending on the hardware, it’s possible to make an LED integrated in the socket blink for 10 seconds using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ethtool -p enp0s31f6 10</samp>. If the network driver doesn’t support this operation, you will receive the operation not supported error message.

Current Linux distributions name network interfaces so that the device names of existing interfaces do not change even when additional network hardware is added.

The naming of devices is mostly done by systemd in combination with <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> rules. Onboard devices are named <samp class="listingcharacter">enoN</samp>, PCIe adapters <samp class="listingcharacter">ensN</samp>, external devices <samp class="listingcharacter">enpNsM</samp>, and Wi-Fi adapters are assigned the name <samp class="listingcharacter">wlpNsM</samp>. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">N</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">M</samp> each refer to hardware properties, such as the PCI slot. For more information, visit [https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/PredictableNetworkInterfaceNames](https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/PredictableNetworkInterfaceNames).

## 15.4    Distribution-Specific Configuration Files

The simplest case—the integration of a notebook computer into the local network (DHCP) or into the wireless network—is now left to NetworkManager by almost all distributions. (An exception is Raspberry Pi OS.) However, when it comes to special configuration variants for server use, various manufacturer-specific special paths have emerged over the last two decades.

Having introduced you to the most important configuration files in the previous section, which are the same in almost all distributions, I’ll present here some details by which the distributions differ from one another. In doing so, I go into detail about the following distributions:

*   RHEL and Fedora
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts</samp> (deprecated)

*   Debian
    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> (ENI)

*   SUSE
    YaST and Wicked

*   Ubuntu
    Netplan and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">networkd</samp>

The information compiled in this section is especially relevant if you want to perform a server configuration or use a Raspberry Pi as a Wi-Fi router or for similar functions. For the most part, no graphical user interface is available for configuration work. Also, you often have to do without the support of a DHCP server.

### When Two Quarrel…

In many distributions, NetworkManager and the distribution's own configuration procedure run in parallel. Although NetworkManager tries not to touch interfaces that are explicitly managed by a distribution-specific procedure, sometimes this automatism fails and conflicts occur.

In the past, I would recommend simply disabling NetworkManager on servers (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl disable NetworkManager</samp>) or uninstalling it altogether. At least with Fedora and with RHEL from version 8 on, this is definitely not a good idea anymore! That’s because NetworkManager has replaced all of its own network scripts there.

### 15.4.1    RHEL and Fedora (NetworkManager)

On Fedora and on RHEL from version 8 on, NetworkManager alone controls all network connections. Up to RHEL 7, various scripts and configuration files (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifcfg-<interfacename></samp>) in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts</samp> directory were used instead.

There is still the compatibility plugin <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifcfg-rh</samp> for NetworkManager, which can process files stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">network-scripts</samp> directory. But in the meantime, it’s high time to say goodbye to these files. For this reason, I’ve decided for the first time in this edition not to describe the old configuration system. If you really want or need to continue doing network configuration in this outdated form, I refer you to the RHEL 7 documentation at [https://access.redhat.com/documentation/de-de/red_hat_enterprise_linux/7/html/networking_guide/sec-configuring_ip_networking_with_ifcg_files](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/de-de/red_hat_enterprise_linux/7/html/networking_guide/sec-configuring_ip_networking_with_ifcg_files).

Fedora and RHEL now rely entirely on NetworkManager—even for server configuration. The configuration files for the interfaces use the default format of NetworkManager (the <samp class="listingcharacter">keyfile</samp> syntax) and are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections</samp> directory. The syntax of these files is documented at the following pages:

*   [https://www.linux.org/docs/man5/nm-settings-keyfile.html](https://www.linux.org/docs/man5/nm-settings-keyfile.html)

*   [https://developer-old.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/nm-settings-keyfile.html](https://developer-old.gnome.org/NetworkManager/stable/nm-settings-keyfile.html)

In the following sections, I will show you some examples of typical configuration variants. However, I recommend that you perform the configuration in the NetworkManager dialogs. On a server without a graphical user interface, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmtui</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">NetworkManager-tui</samp> package instead (see also [Figure 15.5](#15_001.html_f15.5)). A direct modification of the configuration files in an editor should only be necessary in an absolute emergency.

#### Important Prerequisites

For NetworkManager to take your configuration files into account, they must be owned by <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> and must be readable only by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>. Make sure to execute <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod 600 filename</samp>, and if necessary, also <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chown root:root filename</samp>!

During initial experiments with one's own configuration files, dynamically generated files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run/NetworkManager</samp> directory often interfere. Perform a reboot! NetworkManager creates dynamic configuration files only for those interfaces for which there is no explicit configuration in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/NetworkManager</samp>.

An Ethernet interface that receives its network configuration via DHCP does not actually need a configuration file. NetworkManager automatically takes care of the configuration. However, you can still write the configuration in a file like the following sample:

```
# file /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
[connection]
id=myInterfaceName
uuid=27afa607-ee36-43f0-b8c3-9d245cdc4bb3
type=802-3-Ethernet
autoconnect=true
interface-name=enp1s0

[ipv4]
method=auto

[802-3-Ethernet]
mac-address=52:54:00:64:9b:85 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">method=auto</samp> is responsible for DHCP being used. You can create the mapping to the interface either via <samp class="listingcharacter">interface-name</samp> or via <samp class="listingcharacter">mac-address</samp>. The required hexadecimal address can be determined using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ip addr</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">autoconnect=true</samp> causes the network interface to be activated automatically when the computer boots.

<samp class="listingcharacter">id</samp> is a freely selectable name for the connection. This name must be used with some <samp class="listingcharacter">nmcli</samp> commands to select the interface. It’s often convenient to simply use the interface name (here <samp class="listingcharacter">enp1s0</samp>) as the ID.

Basically, you’re also free to decide on the file name for the configuration file. However, it makes sense to follow the <interface name>.nmconnection syntax that applies on Fedora and RHEL. NetworkManager takes into account all files that are not clearly identifiable as backup files.

It takes a little persuasion to make changes to the configuration effective. You must first prompt NetworkManager to reread existing configuration files. Then you explicitly tell it your wish to actually apply the changes for a specific interface—here, <samp class="listingcharacter">enp1s0</samp>:

```
root# nmcli connection reload     
(reload configuration)
root# nmcli dev reapply enp1s0    
(apply new configuration)
root# nmcli connection show       
(interface overview) 
```

For a static IPv4 configuration, you need to change a few lines in the <samp class="listingcharacter">[ipv4]</samp> section:

```
# file /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
...
[ipv4]
address1=192.168.122.244/24,192.168.122.1
dns=192.168.122.1
method=manual 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">method=manual</samp> activates the static configuration. <samp class="listingcharacter">address1=...</samp> assigns an IP address, the mask, and (if required) the corresponding gateway address to the interface. <samp class="listingcharacter">dns</samp> sets the nameserver you want. If required, you can also specify multiple nameserver addresses separated by commas.

The relevant lines for a static IPv6 configuration look as follows:

```
# file /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
...
[ipv6]
addr-gen-mode=default
address1=2abc:1234:1234::10/64,2abc:1234:1234::1
dns=2001:4860:4860::8888,2001:4860:4860::8844
method=manual 
```

In the <samp class="listingcharacter">[ipv6]</samp> section, <samp class="listingcharacter">address1</samp> again assigns the IP address including mask as well as the corresponding gateway address. The public Google nameservers are used as nameservers in this example.

You can include the desired zone for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">firewalld</samp> program in the <samp class="listingcharacter">[connection]</samp> section of the configuration files:

```
# file /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
[connection]
...
zone=trusted 
```

Without this specification, the firewall system automatically uses the default <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> zone. The currently valid zones for all interfaces can be determined by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">firewall-cmd --get-active-zones</samp> command. Background information on firewall configuration follows in [Chapter 29](#29_001.html_h29).

For an example of a network bridge configuration, please see [Chapter 32](#32_001.html_h32), [Section 32.4](#32_004.html_h32.4).

### 15.4.2    Debian

On Debian, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> file is responsible for configuring all interfaces. The configuration procedure is sometimes called ENI, derived from the first letters of the directories or files.

The syntax is clearer than for all other variants described in this book: each interface that is to be activated at computer startup must be named by <samp class="listingcharacter">auto name</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">iface name options</samp> describes the basic configuration of the interface. In case of a static configuration, the <samp class="listingcharacter">address</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">netmask</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">gateway</samp> parameters follow in the other lines.

For the interaction with NetworkManager, it reads the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">interfaces</samp> file by default and only takes care of interfaces that are not named in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">interfaces</samp>.

If the computer is supposed to obtain the network parameters via DHCP, the entire configuration comprises only four lines! The first two lines activate the loopback interface, which is always required as it is used for computer-internal network communication. The two other lines activate the <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s31f6</samp> interface:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback
# dynamic connection to a DHCP server, 
# which transmits the key data of the internet access
auto enp0s31f6
iface enp0s31f6 inet dhcp 
```

If the connection to the internet is configured as static, the <samp class="listingcharacter">iface</samp> line contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> keyword. The network parameters are subsequently specified by several keywords, the meanings of which are self-explanatory:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback

# static network configuration
auto enp0s31f6
iface enp0s31f6 inet static
  address         211.212.213.37
  netmask         255.255.255.224
  gateway         211.212.213.1 
```

For a static configuration, you must specify the nameserver addresses directly in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp>:

```
# /etc/resolv.conf (Debian)
nameserver 211.222.233.244    # first DNS
nameserver 212.223.234.245    # second DNS 
```

If you also want to use IPv6, you can simply define the interface in question a second time in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">inet6</samp> keyword. The <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> keyword specifies that the IPv6 configuration takes into account the so-called router advertisement of the gateway or IPv6 router. This procedure enables a kind of self-configuration of IPv6 networks:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (automatic IPv6 configuration)
...
auto enp0s31f6
iface enp0s31f6 inet dhcp
iface enp0s31f6 inet6 auto 
```

If the IPv6 gateway uses a DHCPv6 server, the correct method is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dhcp</samp>. If, in addition, the router address is to be configured via router advertisement, then the additional <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">accept_ra 1</samp> option is required. This is the case, for example, if you use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnsmasq</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">enable-ra</samp> option as the DHCP server:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (DHCPv6 configuration)
...
auto enp0s31f6
iface enp0s31f6 inet dhcp
iface enp0s31f6 inet6 dhcp
  accept_ra 1 
```

For a static configuration, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">interfaces</samp> must look as follows:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (static IPv6 configuration)
...
auto enp0s31f6
iface enp0s31f6 inet static
  ... (IPv4 configuration as before)

iface enp0s31f6 inet6 static
  address 2a01:4f8:161:107::2
  netmask 64
  gateway fe80::1 
```

Wi-Fi interfaces are basically configured in the same way as Ethernet interfaces. You can control the interaction with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa_supplicant</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa</samp> parameters. In the simplest case, the configuration may look as follows:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (manual Wi-Fi configuration with WPA)
auto wlan0
iface wlan0 inet dhcp
  wpa-ssid "wlan-name"
  wpa-psk  "top-secret" 
```

If you want to set more WPA parameters, it is usually better to do this in a separate file, the location of which you can specify using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa-conf</samp>:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (manual Wi-Fi configuration with WPA)
auto wlan0
iface wlan0 inet dhcp
  wpa-conf /etc/wpa.conf 
```

The following example shows the syntax of <samp class="listingcharacter">wpa_supplicant</samp>. Instead of the password in plain text, an equivalent but not so easily readable hexadecimal code was specified using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wpa_passphrase</samp> (see [Section 15.3](#15_003.html_h15.3)):

```
# file /etc/wpa.conf
network={
  ssid="wlan-name"
  psk=113df295cd91605ce30c00d16b82bf5eb334b0e47adcf9aafc153459a731fa42
  proto=RSN
  key_mgmt=WPA-PSK
  pairwise=CCMP
  auth_alg=OPEN
} 
```

A lot of other <samp class="listingcharacter">wpa</samp> parameters for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">interfaces</samp> file are documented in the following file:

/usr/share/doc/wpasupplicant/README.modes.gz

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">up</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">down</samp> keywords to include commands in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">interfaces</samp> file that are automatically executed when an interface is enabled or disabled.

To activate a new configuration for an interface, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifdown</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifup</samp> for that interface:

```
root# ifdown enp0s31f6
root# ifup enp0s31f6 
```

These commands are part of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifupdown</samp> package. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifup -a</samp> command analyzes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> and activates all <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> interfaces. If interfaces are configured via DHCP, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifup</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dhclient</samp> command to transfer and analyze the DHCP data. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/dhcp/dhclient.conf</samp> file is responsible for the configuration.

### 15.4.3    SUSE

On SUSE, YaST decides on the default network configuration procedure during the installation. On notebook computers, NetworkManager is used, while on servers, SUSE's own development named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">wicked</samp> runs by default (see [https://github.com/openSUSE/wicked](https://github.com/openSUSE/wicked)). This daemon is particularly optimized for servers where network connections change frequently.

Of course, you can change the procedure later in the System • Network Settings YaST module, which you can find in the Global Options dialog sheet (see [Figure 15.6](#15_004.html_f15.6)). If you set Wicked Service there, YaST lists in the Overview dialog all network interfaces it has found. Then you can edit the individual interfaces. By default, YaST configures all Ethernet interfaces to obtain their IP address and all other configuration settings via DHCP from the router of the local network. Note that YaST can also be started in text mode in minimal installations.

[![Setting Network Configuration Procedure Using YaST](bilderklein/klein15_006.png)](img-f15.6.html)

**Figure 15.6**     Setting Network Configuration Procedure Using YaST

Regardless of the configuration method you choose, you can set the hostname in YaST via System • Network Settings • Hostname/DNS. This is often necessary because the hostname specification is not provided during the SUSE installation. Instead, SUSE uses a randomly generated name that is correspondingly difficult to remember.

### 15.4.4    Ubuntu

On Ubuntu, the Debian-typical <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> configuration file used to play a major role. That changed in 2017. Since then, the network configuration has been based on three pillars:

*   The Netplan configuration system, a proprietary development by Ubuntu and Canonical, is the linchpin.

*   For desktop installations, Netplan transfers the configuration to NetworkManager via all interfaces.

*   On servers, on the other hand, Netplan interacts with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">networkd</samp>. This is a network configuration system that is part of systemd and hasn’t been widely used yet.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">netplan</samp> is a network backend that communicates with NetworkManager on desktop systems and with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">networkd</samp> on server systems. The configuration is done by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.yaml</samp> files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/netplan</samp>. On the following page, <samp class="listingcharacter">netplan</samp> is wonderfully documented with many real-life examples: [https://netplan. readthedocs.io/en/stable/examples](https://netplan.readthedocs.io/en/stable/examples).

On notebook computers and desktop PCs, the following configuration file is sufficient for all network interfaces to be controlled by NetworkManager:

```
# file /etc/netplan/01-network-manager-all.yaml
# NetworkManager should take care of all network
# interfaces
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: NetworkManager 
```

On Ubuntu Server, NetworkManager is not installed by default. This is why you have to deal with the <samp class="listingcharacter">netplan</samp> syntax. In virtual machines or cloud installations, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/netplan</samp> contains the following automatically generated configuration file. It causes the Ethernet interface (here <samp class="listingcharacter">enp1s0</samp>) to obtain its IP configuration via DHCP:

```
# file /etc/netplan/50-cloud-init.yaml
# This file is generated from information provided by the datasource.  Changes 
# to it will not persist across an instance. To disable cloud-init's network 
# configuration capabilities, write a file 
# /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.d/99-disable-network-config.cfg with the following:
# network: {config: disabled}
network:
    Ethernets:
        enp1s0:
            dhcp4: true
    version: 2 
```

To perform a static configuration, you want to delete this file and then use the following listing as a guide:

```
# file /etc/netplan/10-static.yaml
network:
  Ethernets:
    enp1s0:
      addresses:
        - 192.168.122.201/24
      gateway4: 192.168.122.1
      nameservers:
        addresses:
          - 192.168.122.1 
```

Changes to the configuration files take effect via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">netplan apply</samp>:

```
user$ sudo netplan apply 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">netplan</samp> uses this to create temporary configuration files for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">networkd</samp> (see the following section) in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run/systemd/network</samp> directory. A look at the files located there can help with any troubleshooting that may be required.

For an example of a network bridge configuration, please see [Chapter 32](#32_001.html_h32), [Section 32.4](#32_004.html_h32.4).

### 15.4.5    networkd (systemd)

The systemd developers have not only set themselves the task of modernizing the init process (they have succeeded!), but they also want to bring the configuration of different Linux systems down to a common denominator. Accordingly, systemd contains various modules for network configuration.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd/network</samp> directory is intended as the location for the configuration files, while the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-networkd</samp> background process takes care of the analysis. The syntax of the configuration files seems well-thought-out and documented; you can look them it using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.network</samp>. The wiki documentation of Arch Linux is also very useful (see [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/systemd-networkd](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/systemd-networkd)).

The following lines show an example of the setup of an Ethernet interface with a static IP address:

```
# file /etc/systemd/network/static.network
[Match]
Name=enp2s0
[Network]
Address=10.0.0.15/24
Gateway=10.0.0.138
DNS=10.0.0.138 
```

Although the infrastructure for systemd network configuration is already available as standard in many distributions, only a few distributions make use of these options. Currently, the most important exception is Ubuntu (see [Section 15.4.4](#15_004.html_h15.4.4)). Its <samp class="listingcharacter">netplan</samp> system creates temporary <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">netword</samp> configuration files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run/systemd/network</samp> directory.

## 15.5    Zeroconf and Avahi

In this book, I generally assume that you either configure the computers in your network yourself or obtain the IP configuration from a central router or DHCP server. But there is a third way: automatic configuration by Zeroconf.

In this procedure, all computers connected to the network exchange their configuration data. New computers or devices connected to the network use this information to configure themselves so that they can communicate with the other devices without conflicts. The automatically configured hosts use addresses from IP range 169.254.*.* and host names ending in <samp class="listingcharacter">.local</samp>. Zeroconf communication takes place via UDP port 5454\. For Zeroconf to work, this port must not be blocked by a firewall within the LAN!

Zeroconf was first implemented by Apple as Rendezvous. This project was later renamed Bonjour and is also available for Windows. This implementation is available as open-source code, but the license is not GPL-compatible. For this reason, a separate Zeroconf project was created for Linux under the name Avahi, the code of which is independent of Bonjour. The license used is LGPL.

Thanks to Zeroconf, computers, printers, Wi-Fi-enabled lamps, and other home automation devices can see each other without complicated configuration. If you want your Linux machine to be visible to Apple devices, the machine must be running the Avahi daemon. You can find more technical details at the following page: [https://avahi.org](https://avahi.org).

### Zeroconf Is Only Required for IPv4

Zeroconf is an IPv4-specific method. In IPv6, there is no need for Zeroconf because each network interface is automatically assigned a link-local IPv6 address. This address is needed for IPv6-internal configuration tasks, but it can also be used for Zeroconf-type applications.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-daemon</samp> service is responsible for the communication between Avahi computers. The configuration is carried out via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/avahi/avahi-daemon.conf</samp>, where you can usually retain the basic settings. The only exception is often the <samp class="listingcharacter">enable-dbus</samp> variable: it controls whether Avahi allows the communication method. Some Avahi-compatible programs require D-Bus. To enable D-Bus, you need to modify <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-daemon.conf</samp> as follows:

```
# /etc/avahi/avahi-daemon.conf
[server]
...
enable-dbus=yes 
```

Then restart the service:

```
root# systemctl restart avahi-daemon 
```

If you want to address external hosts with ordinary, non-Avahi network programs via their <samp class="listingcharacter">.local</samp> names (e.g., via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping merkur.local</samp>), you need to install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-dnsconfd</samp> package and start the eponymous network daemon:

```
root# apt/dnf install avahi-dnsconfd
root# systemctl start avahi-dnsconfd
root# systemctl enable avahi-dnsconfd 
```

This is a kind of nameserver for Avahi host names. You do not need this daemon if you have a nameserver running on your network anyway.

To ensure that all programs use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-dnsconfd</samp> for name resolution, you must make sure that the <samp class="listingcharacter">libnss-mdns</samp> library is installed and that the <samp class="listingcharacter">hosts:</samp> line in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/nsswitch.conf</samp> contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">mdns4</samp> keyword. In some distributions, this is the case by default:

```
# in /etc/nsswitch.conf
...
hosts: files dns mdns4 
```

After this preparatory work, you can find out which computers or services are recognized by Avahi on your network. The console command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-browse -a -t</samp> or its graphical equivalent Avahi Discovery (program name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-discover</samp>) can help you in this regard. The commands must be installed separately in many distributions and can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-tools</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">avahi-ui-tools</samp> packages on Fedora, for example.

The GNOME file manager shows all Avahi machines in the network view by default. The KDE file manager provides a similar function under the <samp class="listingcharacter">zeroconf:/</samp> address, provided that the corresponding extension is installed (depending on the distribution, this could be included in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kde-zeroconf</samp> package). Various messaging and multimedia applications also support Zeroconf.

# 16    Software and Package Management

This chapter describes how you can install and update software or packages on Linux and which techniques are used. Central topics of this chapter are the RPM and DEB package formats; the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">yay</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp> package management commands; and the new AppImage, AppStream, Snap, and Flatpak package systems.

## 16.1    Introduction

On Windows, it’s common to install new programs from a Microsoft software installer (MSI) file or by running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setup.exe</samp>. The setup package contains all files required for the program.

Linux takes a completely different approach: a package management system maintains a database with information about all software packages already installed, and new programs are installed by the commands and downloaded from central package sources on the internet. This concept has a lot of advantages:

*   Larger programs can be divided into independent packages with libraries and language files (localization). This reduces redundancy and makes it possible to install only those components that are really needed.

*   Package management takes into account dependencies and conflicts between software packages. For example, if a program A requires library B, the package management system will not allow A to be installed until B has been installed.

*   The package database can be used at any time to trace to which package a particular file belongs and whether this file is still in its original state.

*   All packages installed on a computer can be updated together. This central update system is probably the biggest advantage compared to Microsoft Windows, where almost every major program maintains its own update program.

Two package management systems dominate the Linux market:

*   RPM Fedora, RHEL, SUSE and countless other distributions use the RPM package format developed by Red Hat.

*   DEB Debian, Ubuntu, and all their derived distributions, on the other hand, use the DEB package format.

However, the commands for installing, uninstalling, and updating these packages (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp>, and so on) are relatively primitive. You cannot download packages from package sources or resolve package dependencies.

Based on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp>, there are package-management commands with many additional functions. This includes automatically installing dependent packages, performing updates for the entire system, and taking into account package sources from the internet. Examples of such package management systems include DNF, Yum, and ZYpp for RPM packages and APT for DEB packages.

Besides the tools related to the RPM and DEB package formats, some distributions have developed their own package formats and tools, such as Arch Linux with Pacman and ClearLinux with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">swupd</samp>.

To enable distribution-independent tools and interfaces despite the diverse formats, the PackageKit library was developed. It provides a standardized interface to various package management backends (see [Figure 16.1](#16_001.html_f16.1)). As I will explain in [Section 16.8](#16_008.html_h16.8), PackageKit doesn’t seem to have a future despite its universal concept.

[![Low-Level and High-Level Package Management Systems](bilderklein/klein16_001.png)](img-f16.1.html)

**Figure 16.1**     Low-Level and High-Level Package Management Systems

In addition to these standard programs, some distributions or desktop systems have their own programs for package management and for performing updates:

*   GNOME
    Software (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gnome-software</samp>)

*   KDE
    Discover, as well as various other programs

*   Manjaro
    Pacman Manager (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pamac</samp>)

*   Ubuntu
    Ubuntu Software, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-manager</samp>

*   SUSE
    YaST modules of the Software group

Not only do the package management tools differ from distribution to distribution, there are also many other distribution-specific peculiarities despite common standards. These are summarized in [Section 16.12](#16_012.html_h16.12).

### Avoid Mixing Packages from Different Distributions

The packages of a Linux distribution are coordinated with each other. This means that they use unified libraries, were compiled by the same compiler, and so on. As a Linux beginner, you are therefore well advised to install only packages that are intended for your distribution. It is not recommended to install a Red Hat package on SUSE (or vice versa). The problems that arise, such as missing libraries or unfulfilled package dependencies, can only be fixed by Linux professionals, if at all.

If you are responsible for 50, 100, or 1,000 Linux machines, the administration and package management becomes a pain despite the tools presented in this chapter. You need a tool to perform an update centrally on all or on previously selected computers, to install a new program, or to change the configuration. Depending on the distribution, Red Hat Satellite, m23 (various distributions), or Landscape (Ubuntu) can be used. Visit the following pages:

*   [https://m23.sourceforge.io](https://m23.sourceforge.io)

*   [https://landscape.canonical.com](https://landscape.canonical.com)

*   [https://www.redhat.com/en/technologies/management/satellite](https://www.redhat.com/en/technologies/management/satellite)

### 16.1.1    Disadvantages of Linux Package Management

The package management of common distributions works well, but it also has its disadvantages:

*   The almost daily updates of many distributions unsettle users who are used to longer update periods from Windows or macOS.

*   The download requirement for the updates is large.
