*   Many Linux users want to use a distribution for a longer period of time while updating a few programs—often desktop applications like LibreOffice or GIMP. This is exactly what current distributions make virtually impossible. There are security updates available, but not fundamentally new versions.

If you want to use the latest version of LibreOffice in an older distribution, you must perform a manual installation or resort to nonofficial package sources. Both are recommended for advanced users only. On Windows or macOS, it’s much easier to install the current LibreOffice version.

There are technical reasons why this is so: Most Linux programs use countless libraries. Therefore, a version update of LibreOffice implies that some libraries have to be updated as well. This in turn can trigger incompatibilities with other programs that also rely on this library.

A possible way out is to integrate the associated libraries for important programs. Google Chrome has taken this approach right from the start, and the Firefox and Thunderbird packages are now also maintained in this way. But this approach is also associated with disadvantages due to the redundancies that are now unavoidable, the space required on the hard disk, the download volume for each update, and the RAM requirement increase when you run multiple programs simultaneously. If a security problem occurs in a library, it can no longer be fixed centrally. Rather, all programs that use this library must be updated.

### 16.1.2    New Concepts

RPM and DEB packages will probably remain with us for a while as the basis for package management. At the same time, however, alternative concepts are increasingly becoming established. On the one hand, they are intended to supplement RPM/DEB and compensate for their weaknesses; on the other hand, they can completely replace conventional package management in special cases.

AppStream is a method developed by Red Hat (originally referred to as Modularity) to offer different versions of a program in parallel in traditional DNF package sources. As a user, you then have the choice, for example, of installing PHP version 8.1 or 8.2.

AppStream is particularly well suited for long-lived server distributions with a stable, largely unchanging foundation to offer selected tools (server applications or programming languages) in current versions.

Flatpak, favored by Red Hat and Fedora, and Snap, developed by Canonical/Ubuntu, make it easier to offer current programs in current versions, independent of the distribution. Both package systems operate in parallel with conventional package management. From a user perspective, they facilitate the installation of (desktop) programs outside of the official package offerings. At the same time, a sandbox system mitigates potential security issues. A detailed description of these two package systems follows in [Section 16.11](#16_011.html_h16.11).

In the long term, there is probably no way around these package systems. On Fedora and RHEL, LibreOffice will only be available via Flatpak in the future. On Ubuntu, Firefox can only be installed as a Snap package. As of version 23.10, this should also apply to the CUPS printing system.

The Zero Install and AppImage projects pursue similar goals to Flatpak and Snap. AppImage in particular seems mature and has even received the blessing of the usually critical kernel developer Linus Torvalds: “This is just very cool.” Without the support of major distributions, however, it is unlikely that these systems will catch on. See the following pages for more info:

*   [https://0install.net](https://0install.net)

*   [https://appimage.org](https://appimage.org)

Finally, there are considerations to use the root file system in read-only mode most of the time. Updates create an updated file system in a second partition or in a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> snapshot. The active partition or branch is then changed during the subsequent boot process. (This is similar to how updates work on modern smartphones.) These ideas require a complete rebuild of both the package and boot systems. Some experimental distributions implement such concepts. For more information, visit the following pages:

*   [https://vanillaos.org](https://vanillaos.org)

*   [https://microos.opensuse.org](https://microos.opensuse.org)

*   [https://silverblue.fedoraproject.org](https://silverblue.fedoraproject.org)

*   [https://ubuntu.com/blog/ubuntu-core-an-immutable-linux-desktop](https://ubuntu.com/blog/ubuntu-core-an-immutable-linux-desktop)

## 16.2    RPM Package Management

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> command installs and manages RPM packages. It helps to do the following:

*   Run scripts as part of an installation

*   Ensure that all prerequisites are met before installing a program—that is, that all required libraries are available in the correct version

*   Check if a file has been modified since the package was installed

*   Determine to which package a particular file belongs

*   Restore all files of a program during an uninstallation

The required management information is in each RPM package.

During the installation, this information is entered into a database whose files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/rpm</samp> directory.

### 16.2.1    Basic Principles

Most RPM packages are provided in two variants: as a binary package and as a source package. The binary package contains the files necessary to run the program. However, the source code package is only interesting for developers. It contains the source code that was required to assemble the binary package.

The package name contains quite a lot of information: for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc-2.0.7-1.x86_64.rpm</samp> denotes package <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc</samp> with version number 2.0.7 and release number 1\. If an error has occurred during the compilation of a package, additional online documentation has been added, or other changes have been made, release numbers greater than 1 are generated for a specific version number. So the version number refers to the actual program and the release number to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> compilation.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">x86_64</samp> identifier indicates that the package contains binaries for Intel/AMD-compatible 64-bit processors. If package <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">abc</samp> contains script or text files that are independent of the CPU architecture, the <samp class="listingcharacter">noarch</samp> abbreviation is used instead of the CPU identifier. If the package contains the source code, the <samp class="listingcharacter">src</samp> abbreviation is commonly used instead.

In addition to the files to be installed, the package file contains a lot of administrative information: a brief package description, information about version numbers, placement in the group hierarchy, dependencies on other packages, and so on. Dependencies exist when a package requires a particular programming language, such as Perl, or a particular library. In this case, these packages must be installed first. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> maintains a database with information about all installed binary packages. This database is stored in various files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/rpm</samp> directory. The database contains only information about binary packages. Any installed packages with source code are not included in the database.

To make the RPM database match the actual installation, packages must be removed not by simply deleting the files, but by uninstalling them (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -e</samp>)!

#### Repairing the RPM Database

In rare cases, it happens that the RPM database contains inconsistent data. This manifests itself in the fact that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> command can no longer be used or returns error messages such as cannot open packages database. The following commands usually provide a solution:

<samp class="listingcharacter">root# </samp><samp class="listingcharacter">rm -f /var/lib/rpm/__db*</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">root# </samp><samp class="listingcharacter">db_verify /var/lib/rpm/Packages</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">root# </samp><samp class="listingcharacter">rpm --rebuilddb</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">root# </samp><samp class="listingcharacter">dnf clean all</samp>

This will recreate the RPM database. However, it takes a while.

To update an RPM package, you usually download the entire new package. This is particularly inefficient for security updates, which often require only tiny changes to a few files. For this reason, there are delta RPM packages that contain only the changes from a particular version of the package.

When applying delta RPMs, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">applydeltarpm</samp> command creates the new, updated RPM package from the delta RPM and the original package or its installed files. This is then installed as normal. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">applydeltarpm</samp> is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deltarpm</samp> package. The download volume is less valuable today than when this technology was introduced over 15 years ago because the use of delta packages is more complex than the simple installation of a complete package and because the parallel storage of ordinary packages and delta packages is redundant, so distributors are increasingly questioning this concept. Fedora in particular has concrete plans to do away with delta packages altogether in the near future, possibly starting with version 39 (see [https://lwn.net/Articles/925348](https://lwn.net/Articles/925348)).

### 16.2.2    The rpm Command

It may seem surprising, but you will rarely use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> to directly install a package or remove it again. For this purpose, you usually use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zipper</samp>, or a graphical user interface.

The practical use of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> command today is primarily to read the package database and extract information from it that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp> won't give you at all, or only in a much more cumbersome way. [Table 16.1](#16_002.html_t16.1) summarizes the most important <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> commands. The following examples show the practical application.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Installing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -i file.rpm</samp> |
| Updating a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -U file.rpm</samp> |
| Verifying a package installation | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -V file.rpm</samp> |
| Removing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -e package name</samp> |
| Determining all installed packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qa</samp> |
| Determining the package that provides this file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qf file</samp> |
| Displaying a package description | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qi package name</samp> |
| Determining a list of all files of the package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -ql package name</samp> |
| Determining a list of all configuration files of the package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qc package name</samp> |
| Obtaining information about a package that is not yet installed | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qpli file.rpm</samp> |

**Table 16.1**     Important rpm Commands

Let’s suppose you discover a file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> directory that you have never noticed before and want to know what its purpose is. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qf</samp> will tell you which package it belongs to, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qi</samp> provides a brief description of the package, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -ql</samp> shows all the other files that come from that package:

```
user$ rpm -qf /etc/login.defs
shadow-utils-4.13-6.fc38.x86_64
user$ rpm -qi shadow-utils
Name        : shadow
Summary     : Utilities for managing accounts and shadow password files
...
user$ rpm -ql shadow-utils
/etc/default/useradd
/etc/login.defs
/usr/bin/chage
... 
```

You may want to know which <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">perl</samp> packages are installed. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -qa</samp> provides a list of all installed packages. Use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> to filter out the relevant packages and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sort</samp> to sort the list:

```
user$ rpm -qa | grep perl | sort
perl-AutoLoader-5.74-495.fc38.noarch
perl-B-1.83-495.fc38.x86_64
perl-base-2.27-495.fc38.noarch
... 
```

Say that your Python installation is causing problems and you aren’t sure whether the package has been installed correctly. Are all installed files of this package still in their original state? To find out, run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -V</samp>. This command lists all the files that have changed. Usually, the result should be empty, as in the following example, or contain only configuration files:

```
user$ rpm -V python3 
```

On Fedora or RHEL, you can then repair the package with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf reinstall</samp> if necessary:

```
root# dnf reinstall python3 
```

## 16.3    DNF

DNF (command name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp>) helps you to manage RPM packages on Fedora and RHEL. The original name of the command was Yum; it was only later reimplemented as DNF. For compatibility reasons, you can continue to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">yum</samp> as the command name, but you will actually be running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp>. And so it happens that countless books and manuals refer to the no longer existing command <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">yum</samp> to this day.

The Babylonian language confusion also includes the configuration files. DNF uses Yum repositories defined by files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/yum.repos.d</samp>. On the other hand, there is also the configuration file <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/dnf/dnf.conf</samp> with some global settings.

### 16.3.1    Concept

DNF simplifies the management of RPM packages. It provides numerous additional functions compared to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp>:

*   Yum archives on the internet serve as the data sources (repositories). A repository is a collection of RPM packages for which additional <samp class="listingcharacter">metadata</samp> is stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">repodata</samp> directory. They provide information about the contents and dependencies of all packages.

*   DNF can manage several mirrors for a package source and tries to use the fastest mirror at the time.

*   DNF resolves package dependencies, loads all required packages, and installs them. For example, if you install a package from package source A, DNF may download dependent packages from sources B and C and install them as well, after prompting you.

*   DNF can update all already installed packages via a single command. For this purpose, each package is tested to see whether there is a newer version of the package in one of the registered package sources. If that is the case, the appropriate packages are downloaded and installed. Of course, all package dependencies are resolved in the process as well.

You cannot run multiple DNF instances in parallel. If a DNF command or program is already running, starting it again will result in an error message: another copy is running.

### 16.3.2    Configuration

The basic configuration of DNF is carried out by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/dnf/dnf.conf</samp> file. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/yum.conf</samp> link also references <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf.conf</samp>. The following lines show the configuration of RHEL 9:

```
# file /etc/dnf/dnf.conf (RHEL 9)
[main]
gpgcheck=1
installonly_limit=3
clean_requirements_on_remove=True
best=True 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gpgcheck=1</samp> causes DNF to use a key to ensure the authenticity of packages. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gpgcheck</samp> can also be set individually for each package source, different from the setting in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf.conf</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">plugins</samp> decides whether DNF takes plugins into account.

There are packages that DNF is supposed to install but not update. These include kernel packages in particular. During a kernel update, the new kernel package is installed in parallel without affecting the old kernel package. The <samp class="listingcharacter">installonlypkgs</samp> variable is used to set the names of such packages. By default, this variable has the following setting: <samp class="listingcharacter">kernel</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">kernel-smp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">kernel-bigmem</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">kernel-enterprise</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">kernel-debug</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">kernel-unsupported</samp>. Finally, the <samp class="listingcharacter">installonly_limit</samp> variable included in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf.conf</samp> controls how many versions of such packages are installed in parallel. The default setting <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> causes only the latest three kernel versions to remain installed at all times. Older kernel packages are removed. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">best=True</samp> means that updates should install the latest available version, even if dependencies cannot be met then. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man dnf.conf</samp> actually recommends the safer <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> setting here.

Each package source is defined in its own <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.repo</samp> file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/yum.repos.d</samp> directory. The following lines show the package source for Fedora's base packages:

```
# file /etc/yum.repos.d/fedora.repo (shortened)
[fedora]
name=Fedora $releasever - $basearch
metalink=https://mirrors.fedoraproject.org/ metalink?repo=fedora-$releasever&arch=$basearch
enabled=1
metadata_expire=7d
repo_gpgcheck=0
type=rpm
gpgcheck=1
gpgkey=file:///etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-fedora-$releasever-$basearch
skip_if_unavailable=False

[fedora-debuginfo]
[fedora-source]
... analogous for debug and source code packages 
```

The address of the package source can be specified either absolutely using <samp class="listingcharacter">baseurl=...</samp> or via <samp class="listingcharacter">mirrorlist=...</samp> in the form of a mirror file. This file contains a list of mirror servers. DNF chooses one of the mirrors independently. DNF replaces the variables <samp class="listingcharacter">$releasever</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">$arch</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">$basearch</samp>, and so on in the configuration file with the version number of the Linux distribution, its architecture, and other details. Let me briefly explain the origin of the three most important variables:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">$arch</samp> provides the architecture of the computer, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">x86_64</samp> for a 64-bit installation on Intel-compatible systems.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">$basearch</samp> is the basic architecture underlying $<samp class="listingcharacter">arch</samp> (also x86_64).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">$releasever</samp> results from the version number of the package whose name was specified in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf.conf</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">distroverpkg</samp> keyword. If this setting is missing, DNF uses the version number of the <samp class="listingcharacter">fedora-release-common</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">redhat-release</samp> package. For Fedora 38, <samp class="listingcharacter">$releasever</samp> simply contains the number 38.

If you want certain packages to be untouched by DNF and not updated when a new version is available, you need to add a line in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf.conf</samp> or in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.repo</samp> file of the package source; the line should contain <samp class="listingcharacter">exclude name1 name2 name3</samp>. You can use wildcards in the package names.

DNF can be extended with plugins and then can provide even more functions. The plugins are configured by files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/dnf/plugins</samp> directory.

### 16.3.3    Searching, Installing, and Updating Packages

[Table 16.2](#16_003.html_t16.2) summarizes the most important actions you can perform with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp>. When you run the command for the first time, meta information about all the package sources set up is downloaded, which may take a while. All further commands are then executed immediately until the next update of the meta information is due.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Installing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf install name</samp> |
| Installing a local package file | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf localinstall file.rpm</samp> |
| Determining the list of available updates | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf check-update</samp> |
| Updating a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf update name</samp> |
| Updating all packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf update</samp> |
| Removing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf remove name</samp> |
| Obtaining a list of all repositories | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf repolist</samp> |
| Obtaining a list of all installed packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf list installed</samp> |
| Obtaining a list of all available packages whose name starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf list available 'abc*'</samp> |
| Searching for packages that contain the term <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> in the package description | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf search 'abc'</samp> |
| Editing package groups | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf grouplist/groupinstall/...</samp> |
| Managing modules (AppStream) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module ...</samp> |
| Displaying a list of last actions | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf history</samp> |
| Determining details of action n | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf history info n</samp> |

**Table 16.2**     Important DNF Commands

The following commands demonstrate the use of DNF on Fedora 38; the output has been shortened to save space:

```
root# dnf check-update
NetworkManager-config-connectivity-fedora.noarch   1:1.42.6-1.fc38    updates
amd-gpu-firmware.noarch                            20230404-149.fc38  updates
audit.x86_64                                       3.1.1-1.fc38       updates
...
root# dnf install mariadb-server
Installing:
 mariadb-server             x86_64   3:10.5.18-1.fc38  ...

Installing dependencies:              
 mariadb                    x86_64   3:10.5.18-1.fc38  
 mariadb-common             x86_64   3:10.5.18-1.fc38  
 ...

Install  16 Packages, installed size: 117 M. Is this ok [y/N]: y 
```

If you search for a package whose name you do not know exactly, it’s best to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf list available</samp>. This command returns a list of all packages that can be installed. Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp>, you can filter the results:

```
root# dnf list available | grep mysql 
```

Alternatively, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf search</samp> can also be used. This command returns more hits because not only the package name but also the package description is taken into account:

```
root# dnf search mysql 
```

#### Autocompletion

On Fedora, if you type <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf install java</samp> and then press (Tab) twice, a list of all package names beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">java</samp> appears. This completion used to be lightning-fast, but unfortunately the process now takes several seconds.

DNF has package groups that help you to install all the packages required for a specific task with little effort:

*   A list of available package groups, including the group IDs (in parentheses), is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf grouplist -v</samp>.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf groupinfo <grpid></samp> command tells you which packages belong to a group.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf groupinstall <grpid></samp> installs all mandatory and default packages of the group (but not the optional packages).

To update or remove a package group, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf groupupdate</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf groupremove</samp>:

```
root# dnf grouplist -v   
(on RHEL 9, the group IDs in parentheses, shortened)
Installed Environment Groups:
   Server with GUI (graphical-server-environment)
Installed Groups:
   Container Management (container-management)
   Headless Management (headless-management)
Available Groups:
   RPM Development Tools (rpm-development-tools)
   .NET Development (dotnet)
   Console Internet Tools (console-internet)
   Graphical Administration Tools (graphical-admin-tools)
   Legacy UNIX Compatibility (legacy-unix)
   Scientific Support (scientific)
   ... 
```

### 16.3.4    AppStream

An elementary problem of DNF used to be that only one version of a program could be provided in the package sources at a time. Developers in particular often need a different version, a more recent one with new features or an older one because their own code is only compatible with that specific version.

After several years of experimentation, Fedora has implemented the so-called modularity concept in version 28, which addresses precisely this weakness. In RHEL 8, this feature got a new name: AppStream.

AppStream and the associated DNF commands (see [Table 16.3](#16_003.html_t16.3)) are implemented around modules. Modules form groups of related packages.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Listing modules including versions | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module list --all</samp> |
| Listing installed modules | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module list --installed</samp> |
| Displaying module details | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module info mname:n/profile</samp> |
| Installing a module | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module install mname:n/profile</samp> |
| Installing a module (short notation) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf install @mname:n/profile</samp> |
| Uninstalling a module | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module remove mname:n/profile</samp> |
| Selecting a module version (without installation) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module enable mname:n</samp> |
| Canceling the version selection | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module disable&#124;reset mname</samp> |
| Determining a module for a specified package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module provides pname</samp> |

**Table 16.3**     DNF Commands for Module Management

The difference compared to the package groups mentioned earlier is that modules can be available for selection in different version numbers as well as in multiple profiles. The module name is then followed by the version number and the profile in the following notation: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">module-name:nn/profile-name</samp>.

I tested the following examples on AlmaLinux 8 in spring 2023\. You may ask: Why not on AlmaLinux 9 or another RHEL clone in the current version? Of course, RHEL 9 also supports streams, but at the time of testing, version 9 was still relatively new and there was not a single module that was available in two versions. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module list --all</samp> lists all modules available for selection. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module list <name></samp> is clearer: This command returns only the modules with the same name. <samp class="listingcharacter">[d]</samp> marks the currently selected default variant:

```
root# dnf module list --all
Name                  Stream          Profiles                                 
389-ds                1.4                                                      
ant                   1.10 [d]        common [d]                               
container-tools       rhel8 [d]       common [d]                               
container-tools       1.0             common [d]                               
container-tools       2.0             common [d]                               
container-tools       3.0             common [d]                               
container-tools       4.0             common [d]                               
...
root# dnf module list php
php                   7.2 [d]        common [d], devel, minimal                         
php                   7.3             common [d], devel, minimal                         
php                   7.4             common [d], devel, minimal                         
php                   8.0             common [d], devel, minimal                         
... 
```

To install PHP version 8.0 in the development profile, you want to run one of the following two commands. (The shorthand notation, in which the <samp class="listingcharacter">@</samp> character identifies the name that follows as a module, is only permitted for the installation.) The selected module is enabled with the installation. If you later use <samp class="listingcharacter">dnf install</samp> to install additional packages from the module, the module that is now valid is automatically used without you having to explicitly specify it:

```
root# dnf module install php:8.0/devel
root# dnf install @php:12/server        
(short notation) 
```

If you later don't know which module a package came from, you can obtain this information using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">module provides</samp> subcommand, where <samp class="listingcharacter">[e]</samp> stands for enabled and <samp class="listingcharacter">[i]</samp> for installed:

```
root# dnf module list --enabled php
php                  8.0 [e]         common [d], devel [i], minimal 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module remove</samp> removes all packages of a module. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf module reset</samp> or (equivalently) <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf disable</samp> also resets the enabled state:

```
root# dnf module remove php:8.0/server
root# dnf module reset php 
```

### 16.3.5    Additional Functions

Copr ([https://developer.fedoraproject.org/deployment/copr/copr-cli.html](https://developer.fedoraproject.org/deployment/copr/copr-cli.html)) is an automated build system. Developers can use it to generate RPM packages from their own source code and then easily provide them to other Fedora or RHEL users as a package source. Copr thus has similarities with the better known PPA concept of Ubuntu.

At this point, I will only discuss the use of such Copr package sources. This is very simple. You set up the package source using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf copr enable</samp> and then install the relevant package—here, for example, the Remarkable markdown editor:

```
root# dnf copr enable neteler/remarkable
root# dnf install remarkable 
```

If you are interested in the source code of a package, you can download it using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf download --source</samp>. This automatically activates the usually inactive <samp class="listingcharacter">source</samp> sources in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.repo</samp> files. You can then install the resulting package <samp class="listingcharacter">name.src.rpm</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm -i</samp>. Finally, you can find the source code in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpmbuild</samp> directory in your home directory:

```
user$ dnf download --source nano
user$ rpm -i nano-n.n.src.rpm 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf-automatic</samp> add-on package takes care of automatic package updates. The associated configuration file is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/dnf/automatic.conf</samp>. In it, you want to set <samp class="listingcharacter">apply_updates</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">yes</samp>. If you want, you can also set various email parameters to control who will automatically receive an email after each update:

```
# file /etc/dnf/automatic.conf
...
apply_updates = yes 
```

A systemd timer takes care of the automatic updates:

```
root# systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic.timer 
```

If you want to know when the next update is due, you should run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl list-timers</samp>:

```
root# systemctl list-timers '*dnf*' 
```

Some updates only take effect when the computer is rebooted. Automatic reboots are not provided for in the Red Hat world. If you feel a desire for this behavior in your youthful recklessness, you can analyze the result of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">needs-restarting</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf-utils</samp> package in a Cron job. The command lists processes that should be restarted. Unfortunately, the kernel, whose update would usually be the most important reason for a reboot, is not covered:

```
root# needs-restarting | sort -n
1 : /usr/lib/systemd/systemd --system --deserialize 25 
660 : /usr/sbin/postgrey --unix=/var/spool/postfix/postgrey/socket ..
965 : /usr/sbin/sshd -D 
... 
```

## 16.4    ZYpp

Like Fedora and Red Hat, SUSE uses RPM packages. However, the ZYpp package management, which is based on RPM, is a proprietary SUSE development. ZYpp stands for ZENworks, YaST, Packages and Patches, where the use of ZENworks is optional and only provided in SUSE Enterprise distributions.

Behind the scenes, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libzypp</samp> library provides the basic ZYpp functions. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libzypp</samp> can handle both YaST and Yum package sources. All configuration, database and cache files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/zypp</samp> directory. Both YaST and PackageKit rely on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libzypp</samp> on openSUSE.

### Updates versus Patches

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp> distinguishes between updates and patches! Updates are ordinary RPM packages that are available in a newer version than the installed one. Patches, on the other hand, are supplementary or update packages (delta RPMs).

SUSE uses patches as delta RPMs to update its own packages. External package sources, such as Packman, on the other hand, provide new package versions as updates.

Package sources are stored in text files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/zypp/repos.d</samp> directory. If you modify these files in an editor, you must be sure to delete all backup copies afterward. Otherwise, you will get duplicates in the list of package sources. The following lines show the definition of the open-source package source for openSUSE:

```
# file /etc/zypp/repos.d/repo-oss.repo (openSUSE 15.5)
[repo-oss]
name=Main Repository
enabled=1
autorefresh=1
baseurl=http://download.opensuse.org/distribution/leap/$releasever/repo/oss/
type=rpm-md
keeppackages=0 
```

### 16.4.1    The zypper Command

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp> is a command interface to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libzypp</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp> is thus the SUSE counterpart to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>. You can use it to search for, install, update, and remove packages, as well as manage package sources (see [Table 16.4](#16_004.html_t16.4)). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp> must be run by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp>.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Reimporting metadata of the package source | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper refresh</samp> |
| Installing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper install name</samp> |
| Removing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper remove name</samp> |
| Obtaining a list of all updates | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper -t package list-updates</samp> |
| Updating all packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper -t package update</samp> |
| Performing a distribution update | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper dup</samp> |
| Obtaining information on a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper info name</samp> |
| Searching for packages whose package name contains <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper search abc</samp> |
| Searching for packages whose description contains <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper search -d abc</samp> |
| Deleting cached packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper clean</samp> |
| Obtaining a list of all package sources | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper repos</samp> |
| Setting up a new package source | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper addrepo uri name</samp> |

**Table 16.4**     Important zypper Commands

The following examples show how you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper</samp>. The first command lists the package sources, the second one updates the sources, and the third one installs the <samp class="listingcharacter">emacs</samp> editor:

```
root# zypper repos --show-enabled-only
 #  Alias                  Name                       Enabled  GPG Check  Refresh
 3  repo-backports-update  Update repository of ...   Yes      Yes        Yes
 8  repo-non-oss           Non-OSS Repository         Yes      Yes        Yes
 9  repo-openh264          Open H.264 Codec           Yes      Yes        Yes
10  repo-oss               Main repository            Yes      Yes        Yes
12  repo-sle-update        Update repository ...      Yes      Yes        Yes
14  repo-update            Main Update Repository     Yes      Yes        Yes
15  repo-update-non-oss    Update Repository (Non ... Yes      Yes        Yes
...
root# zypper refresh
All repositories have been refreshed.

root# zypper install emacs
The following 10 NEW packages are going to be installed:
  emacs emacs-info emacs-x11 etags libXaw3d8 libm17n0 libotf0 m17n-db
  m17n-db-lang system-user-games
10 new packages to install. Overall download size: 26.9 MiB.

Continue? [y/n] (y): y 
```

To install all required packages for a certain task, such as to use the computer as a file server, ZYpp uses patterns. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper search -t pattern</samp> retrieves a list of all such package groups. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper info -t pattern name</samp> shows which packages belong to a package group. Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper install -t pattern name</samp>, you can install all packages of a package group.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/zypp/history</samp> file contains a very useful reference about when which package was installed or removed from which package source and what configuration work was done.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper dup</samp> to perform a distribution update on the fly. However, you will need to take care of the necessary changes to the package sources yourself:

```
root# zypper update   
(update for the previous version)
root# ...             
(change package sources to the new version)
root# zypper dup      
(replace old packages with new ones)
root# reboot          
(reboot) 
```

## 16.5    Debian Package Management (dpkg)

Debian packages are managed on two levels. This section describes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> command, which is responsible for installing and managing packages at the lower level. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> is similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp>. The command can install, update, and remove individual packages, testing if all package dependencies are fulfilled.

Similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> fails to resolve unfulfilled package dependencies itself or load packages from package sources on its own. APT (Advanced Package Tool; see [Section 16.6](#16_006.html_h16.6)) fulfills precisely these tasks. It is based on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> and provides similar features as the DNF and ZYpp systems just presented. For the actual package management, there are three commands to choose from: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp>. When it comes to interactive work, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> is the most convenient option. However, the differences among the three commands are small.

Although this and the following section refer to Debian packages, the information applies to all Linux distributions that use this package format. Besides Debian, these include, for example, the Ubuntu family, Raspberry Pi OS, and Linux Mint. If you switch from an RPM-based distribution to a distribution with Debian packages, you will find an excellent overview of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rpm</samp> commands and equivalent <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> commands on this page: [https://help.ubuntu.com/community/SwitchingToUbuntu/FromLinux/RedHatEnterpriseLinuxAndFedora](https://help.ubuntu.com/community/SwitchingToUbuntu/FromLinux/RedHatEnterpriseLinuxAndFedora).

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> manages comprehensive meta information for all packages (a package description, a list of all files in the package, dependency data, etc.). This data is in Debian control (dctrl) format. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dctrl-tools</samp> package contains various commands to perform queries in the dctrl data. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man grep-dctrl</samp> provides a detailed description of these commands and concrete usage examples.

### 16.5.1    The dpkg Command

[Table 16.5](#16_005.html_t16.5) provides an overview of the most important <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> options. In practice, you will mostly use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> to determine information about installed or available packages.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Installing or updating a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --install file.deb</samp> |
| Configuring a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --configure file.deb</samp> |
| Removing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --remove package name</samp> |
| Removing a package entirely (also changed files) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --purge package name</samp> |
| Determining all installed packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --list</samp> |
| Searching for packages whose package description contains <samp class="listingcharacter">abc</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --list abc</samp> |
| Determining a list of all files of the package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --listfiles package name</samp> |
| Determining a list of all configuration files of the package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat /var/lib/dpkg/info/ name.conffiles</samp> |

**Table 16.5**     Important dpkg Commands

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --list</samp> displays a status code consisting of two or three letters (see [Table 16.6](#16_005.html_t16.6)). The two most common status codes are <samp class="listingcharacter">ii</samp> for a correctly installed package and <samp class="listingcharacter">rc</samp> for a removed package where the configuration files are still available. To remove <samp class="listingcharacter">rc</samp> packages entirely, you need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --purge name</samp>. More details about package status and troubleshooting are provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man dpkg</samp>.

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| First Letter | Desired State |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> | Unknown |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> | Install |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> | Remove |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp> | Purge |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">h</samp> | Hold |
| Second Letter | Actual State |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> | Not installed (not) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">h</samp> | Partially installed (half-installed) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> | Unpacked, but not configured (unpacked) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> | Installed but not configured (failed config file) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> | Fully installed (installed) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> | Only the configuration files are installed (config file) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> | Waits for the trigger of another package (trigger) |
| Third Letter (Optional) | Error Code |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">h</samp> | Package should not be changed (hold) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> | New installation required (reinstall required) |

**Table 16.6**     Letter Codes of dpkg-list Results

The following examples illustrate how to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> in standard situations:

```
root# dpkg --install test.deb
root# dpkg --search /etc/sensors3.conf
libsensors-config: /etc/sensors3.conf
root# dpkg --listfiles joe
/.
/etc
/etc/joe
/etc/joe/ftyperc
/etc/joe/jicerc.ru
/etc/joe/jmacsrc
/etc/joe/joerc
... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --list</samp> returns a list of all installed packages. I have shortened the output of the following example somewhat for better readability:

```
root# dpkg --list 'cups*'
    Name              Version   Architecture  Description
ii  cups              2.4.2-3   amd64         Common UNIX Printing ...
ii  cups-browsed      1.28.17-2 amd64         OpenPrinting CUPS Filters
un  cups-bsd          <none>    <none>        (no description available)
ii  cups-client       2.4.2-3   amd64         Common UNIX Printing ...
ii  cups-common       2.4.2-3   all           Common UNIX Printing ...
ii  cups-core-drivers 2.4.2-3   amd64         Common UNIX Printing ...
... 
```

#### Reconfiguring a Package

During the installation of Debian packages, installation and configuration scripts are automatically executed. For a few programs, there are also interactive setup programs that help with the individual configuration of the package—for example, with the basic configuration of the Postfix email server. If you want to repeat the configuration later, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg-reconfigure package-name</samp>.

To quickly retrieve a sorted list of all installed packages, you want to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --get-selections</samp>. The package list contains less detailed information than that of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --list</samp> and is therefore easier to read. If you redirect the list to a text file and save it, you can install all packages later on another machine by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg --set-selections</samp>:

```
root# dpkg --get-selections
accountsservice                                 install
acl                                             install
... 
```

The hold status (i.e., the third letter in [Table 16.6](#16_005.html_t16.6)) means that a package is not to be updated during an update. The following two commands show how you can put a package into hold and how to remove it from hold:

```
root# echo "<package-name> hold"    | dpkg --set-selections
root# echo "<package-name> install" | dpkg --set-selections 
```

## 16.6    APT

APT is for Debian packages what DNF or ZYpp is for RPM packages: a high-level package management system that downloads packages automatically from package sources and resolves package dependencies automatically. The combination of Debian packages and APT currently results in probably the most mature package management system for Linux. Ubuntu and Debian, among others, use it as the standard system for package management.

Like DNF and ZYpp, APT requires special package sources that provide meta information about the contents of the packages and their dependencies in addition to the DEB packages.

For the actual package management, there are three commands to choose from: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp>. The commands are very similar and even share the same syntax for many operations. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp> are optimized for interactive use, while <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp> is better suited for script programming and the automated execution of package management commands, respectively.

Current Debian and Ubuntu systems have <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp> installed by default; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp> must be installed later if required. Ubuntu recommends the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> command for interactive package management. Regardless, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp> is still more popular, if only because a large number of tutorials on the internet use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp>. But you won't go wrong with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp> either. It’s also no problem to use one command and then the other.

The following three commands are equivalent. They download and install the <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> package and any packages that depend on it:

```
root# apt      install name
root# apt-get  install name
root# aptitude install name 
```

### 16.6.1    Configuration

The configuration of APT is carried out by the two <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt.conf.d/*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sources.list</samp> files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apt</samp> directory. Additional package source definitions can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sources.list.d</samp> directory.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt.conf.d/*</samp> file usually contains only a few basic settings, which you mostly leave as they are specified by your distribution. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sources.list</samp> file is more interesting as it contains the APT package sources line by line. The syntax of each line looks as follows:

<samp class="listingcharacter">package type uri distribution [component1] [component2] [component3] ...</samp>

The package type is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deb</samp> for ordinary Debian packages or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deb-src</samp> for source packages. The second column specifies the root directory of the package source. Besides HTTP and FTP directories, APT also supports ordinary directories, RSH or SSH servers, and CDs or DVDs. The third column indicates the distribution. In the following listing, this is Ubuntu 23.04 (codename Lunar Lobster). All other columns indicate the components of the distribution that can be taken into account. The component names depend on the distribution and the package source! For example, Ubuntu distinguishes among main, restricted, universe, and multiverse packages, while Debian differentiates among main, contrib, nonfree, and similar components.

The package sources mentioned first are preferred. Thus, if a particular package is available for download from multiple sources, APT downloads it from the first source. The following listing illustrates this; for space reasons, each entry was spread across two lines:

```
# file /etc/apt/sources.list (Ubuntu)
deb http://de.archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ lunar           main restricted universe multiverse
deb http://de.archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ lunar-updates   main restricted universe multiverse
deb http://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu    lunar-security  main restricted universe multiverse 
```

The easiest way to make changes to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sources.list</samp> is to use a text editor. Alternatively, you can also use a graphical user interface, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">software-properties-gtx</samp>.

For most APT sources on the internet, the metafiles describing the package sources are signed by a key. Furthermore, the APT content directories contain checksums for all packages. This control mechanism can be used to ensure that no package has been subsequently modified. However, this check only works if APT knows the public part of the key and can thus determine the authenticity of the packet archive.

All package keys are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d</samp> directory. If you want to use an additional package source, download the key file from the project page and copy it to this directory—for example, as follows:

```
user$ curl https://myrepo.com/myrepo.asc | \
      sudo tee /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/myrepo.asc 
```

The associated package source must explicitly reference the filename of the key file by using <samp class="listingcharacter">signed-by</samp>:

```
# /etc/apt/sources.d/myrepo.list
deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/myrepo.asc] https://apt.myrepo.com ...
```

In the past, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-key</samp> command was used to manage APT keys, but this is now considered obsolete and should no longer be used. You can find more details on that at [https://askubuntu.com/a/1307181](https://askubuntu.com/a/1307181).

### 16.6.2    apt Command

The actual package management can be carried out using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> command or its alternatives, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp>. Ubuntu explicitly recommends <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> for interactive use. I haven’t found any information about this for Debian, but even there it’s true that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> is more user-friendly and contains commands that are missing in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp> and for which you would otherwise have to call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-cache</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp>. The most important <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> commands are listed in [Table 16.7](#16_006.html_t16.7).

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Updating metadata from package sources | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt update</samp> |
| Installing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt install name</samp> |
| Updating all packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt upgrade</samp> |
| As above, but uninstalling packages if necessary | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt full-upgrade</samp> |
| Removing a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt remove name</samp> |
| Uninstalling packages that are no longer needed | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt autoremove</samp> |
| Deleting cached packages from cache | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt autoclean</samp> |
| Listing all available packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt list</samp> |
| Displaying all installed packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt list --installed</samp> |
| Searching for a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt search keyword</samp> |
| Displaying package information | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt show package-name</samp> |

**Table 16.7**     Important apt Commands

Before installing packages, you should run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt update</samp> to download the latest information from the package sources. This neither installs nor updates packages; it only concerns the package descriptions—that is, the metadata! Most other package-management systems (DNF, ZYpp) update this metadata on their own when needed, but this is just not true for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aptitude</samp>. You can then download and install a new package using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt install</samp>:

```
root# apt update
root# apt install dovecot-imapd
...

The following additional packages will be installed:
  dovecot-core liblua5.4-0
Suggested packages:
  dovecot-gssapi dovecot-ldap dovecot-lmtpd dovecot-lucene 
  dovecot-managesieved dovecot-mysql dovecot-pgsql dovecot-pop3d 
  dovecot-sieve dovecot-solr dovecot-sqlite dovecot-submissiond 
  ntp ufw
The following NEW packages will be installed:
  dovecot-core dovecot-imapd liblua5.4-0
0 upgraded, 3 newly installed, 0 to remove and 32 not upgraded.

Need to get 6151 kB of archives.

After this operation, 14.4 MB of additional disk space will be used.

Do you want to continue? [Y/n] y 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt remove package-name</samp> removes the specified package. However, dependent packages originally installed together with the package remain unaffected. You can fix this via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt autoremove</samp>: this command removes all packages that are no longer needed.

In addition to strict dependencies, some package descriptions also contain lists of other packages that are suggested or even recommended. The default behavior of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> is to ignore suggested packages, but to install recommended packages as well:

```
user$ apt-config dump | egrep -i 'recommend|suggest'
APT::Install-Recommends "1";
APT::Install-Suggests "0"; 
```

This behavior is not always appropriate. For example, I wanted to install the Emacs editor on Ubuntu 23.04\. It turned out that the list of recommended packages includes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postfix</samp> mail server. This is absurd! If I need an editor, I don't want to add a mail server that might cause all kinds of security problems. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--no-install-recommends</samp> option provides a solution in such cases:

```
root# apt install --no-install-recommends emacs 
```

The correct command to perform updates is usually <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt full-upgrade</samp>. If required due to changed package dependencies, this will also install additional packages or remove existing packages. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt upgrade</samp> will also perform an update, but it will not involve packages if other packages need to be removed at the same time due to changed dependencies:

```
root# apt full-upgrade 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt source package-name</samp> installs the source code of the relevant package into the current directory.

To update to the next version of Debian or Ubuntu, you first need to adjust the package sources in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apt/sources.list</samp> accordingly. In particular, you must replace the code name of the respective old version with that of the new version there; for example, when updating from Debian 11 to version 12, you must replace <samp class="listingcharacter">bullseye</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">bookworm</samp>. Then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt dist-upgrade</samp>. The download and installation of the packages will take about half an hour, depending on the size of the installation. After that, reboot your computer, and you’re done!

Unfortunately, release updates are a tricky business despite the basically excellent package-management system. The fact that all programs and server services really work as before after the update is more a case of luck than the rule. That's why I prefer a new installation most of the time.

### 16.6.3    The apt-get Command

The subcommands of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get command</samp> are mostly the same as those of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">full-upgrade</samp>, it’s a bit misleadingly called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dist-upgrade</samp>, although the version of the distribution does not change. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">list</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">search</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">show</samp> subcommands are not available. Instead, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dpkg</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-cache</samp> commands provide comparable functions. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp> is recommended primarily for the use in scripts or in Dockerfiles—that is, for noninteractive applications.

### 16.6.4    Additional APT Commands

To install package groups, Debian and Ubuntu usually use meta packages: these are empty packages that just define a lot of package dependencies. For example, a whole collection of packages with basic development tools (compiler, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">make</samp>, etc.) is installed together with the <samp class="listingcharacter">build-essential</samp> meta package.

There is a second mechanism for defining package groups, which is based on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tasksel</samp> command. This mechanism is mainly intended to easily select package groups during the installation of the distribution, but <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tasksel</samp> can of course also be used later during operation. A list of all available package groups is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tasksel --list-task</samp>. To install package groups, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tasksel install groupname</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tasksel</samp> is executed without options, a dialog for selecting the desired package groups appears.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-cache</samp> retrieves various data about the available or already installed packages:

```
root# apt-cache show apache2
Package: apache2
Description: next generation, scalable, extendable web server
...
root# apt-cache  search scribus | sort
lprof - Hardware Color Profiler
scribus - Open Source Desktop Publishing
scribus-template - additional scribus templates 
```

On Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apturl</samp> package is installed by default with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apturl-gtk</samp> program. This program allows you to install packages simply by clicking special <samp class="listingcharacter">atp</samp> links in the web browser after a query. You will come across such links mainly on Ubuntu wikis and forums.

All operations performed by the APT system (whether using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-get</samp>, or any other command) are logged in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/apt/history.log</samp>. If this file does not exist or is empty, it may have been rotated (i.e., renamed and compressed). If necessary, you should then decompress <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">history.log.1.gz</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">history.log.2.gz</samp>, and so on, and take a look at these files.

### 16.6.5    Automating Updates

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unattended-upgrades</samp> package takes care of performing updates automatically, if they have been configured correctly. On Ubuntu, the package is installed by default; on Debian and Raspberry Pi OS, you need to perform the installation yourself.

While <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unattended-upgrades</samp> used to be started by a Cron job in the past, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt-daily-upgrade</samp> systemd timer now takes care of the daily execution. You can determine the planned next execution time in the following way:

```
root# systemctl list-timers '*apt*' 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unattended-upgrade</samp> upgrade script then analyzes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apt/apt. conf.d/*</samp> configuration files.

Unfortunately, the defaults in the configuration files are quite different depending on the distribution. Basic requirements are the following two parameters, which you may need to correct or add to a separate configuration file. I often use <samp class="listingcharacter">99myown</samp>. This file is processed at the end; its settings therefore take precedence over options from other files:

```
// file /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99myown
// Update package list once a day
APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1";
// Actually perform updates
APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1"; 
```

Now you need to clarify which packages should be updated automatically. On Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Allowed-Origins</samp> parameter in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">50unattended-upgrades</samp> file is preconfigured to install regular updates as well as security updates—a setting that makes a lot of sense:

```
// file /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades (Ubuntu)
Unattended-Upgrade::Allowed-Origins {
    "${distro_id}:${distro_codename}";
    "${distro_id}:${distro_codename}-security";
    // also for Extended Security Maintenance, if available
    "${distro_id}ESMApps:${distro_codename}-apps-security";
    "${distro_id}ESM:${distro_codename}";
} 
```

Debian and Raspberry Pi OS, on the other hand, control the packages to be updated through <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Origins-Patterns</samp>. The default configuration provides for the installation of security-critical updates only. If you also want to install normal updates, you must remove the <samp class="listingcharacter">label</samp> specification from the configuration file:

```
// file /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades 
// (Debian/Raspberry Pi OS)
Unattended-Upgrade::Origins-Pattern {
    "origin=Debian,\
     codename=${distro_codename},label=Debian";
    "origin=Debian,\
     codename=${distro_codename},label=Debian-Security";
    "origin=Debian,\
     codename=${distro_codename}-security,label=Debian-Security";
  };
```

To install all available updates from all package sources, you must modify the configuration as follows:

```
// file /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades (Raspberry Pi OS)
Unattended-Upgrade::Origins-Pattern {
  "origin=*";
}; 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">Package-Blacklist</samp>, you can exclude individual packages from the automatic update, if you want:

```
// do not update the following packages
Unattended-Upgrade::Package-Blacklist {
  "vim";
  ...
}; 
```

In the course of the automatic updates, new kernel versions are of course also installed if required. However, such updates only take effect when the computer is rebooted. By default, this is not the case, but brave administrators can solve this with the following settings in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">50unattended-upgrades</samp> or in their own configuration files:

```
# if necessary, automatic reboot the next night at 2.00 am
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "02:00"; 
```

If you want to manually determine if a reboot is required, simply test for the existence of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run/reboot-required</samp> file. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run/reboot-required.pkgs</samp> lists which packages require a reboot. Usually these are the kernel or system-related libraries. Alternatively, you can install the <samp class="listingcharacter">needrestart</samp> package and then call the command of the same name.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unattended-upgrades</samp> logs its efforts in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades</samp> file. The file is especially of great help if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unattended-upgrades</samp> does not work and you want to find out the reason. The timestamp files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/apt/periodic</samp> directory also show when certain operations were last carried out.

### 16.6.6    Synaptic

The most popular graphical user interface for the administration of Debian packages based on the APT commands was called Synaptic for a long time. Current versions of Debian and Ubuntu now provide the Software GNOME program for installing programs (as shown in Figure 4.14 in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4)), but I personally still prefer the more technically oriented Synaptic program for finding specific packages (see [Figure 16.2](#16_006.html_f16.2)).

To install a specific package, double-click it to select it for installation. If the package depends on other packages, a dialog will appear with all other packages that also need to be installed.

The actual installation can be started by clicking the Apply button, where you still need to confirm a summary of all planned actions.

[![Package Management Using Synaptic](bilderklein/klein16_002.png)](img-f16.2.html)

**Figure 16.2**     Package Management Using Synaptic

A package is considered “defective” if a problem occurs during installation or uninstallation and the process cannot be completed correctly. Synaptic and other package management tools refuse to work until this problem has been resolved.

To fix this, click the Custom Filters button in the page list in Synaptic and then on the Defect item. Synaptic then displays a list of all defective packages. Highlight all packages by pressing (Ctrl)+(A), right-click the list, and select the Mark for Reinstallation entry. Then run the reinstallation by applying it. However, if you encounter problems again, mark the affected packages for removal.

#### Locking Problems

Only one package management program can run at a time. When trying to run two package management programs at the same time, the unable to get exclusive lock warning appears. This means that the program cannot access the internal package management files alone. To solve this problem, exit one of the two programs.

In rare cases, the lock warning occurs even when no other package management program appears to be running. The cause is usually that a program has not properly removed the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lock</samp> file at the end of the program. If necessary, simply delete the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lock</samp> file: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm /var/lib/dpkg/lock</samp>.

## 16.7    Pacman

Pacman stands for Package Manager and refers to the package management system for Arch Linux and derived distributions such as Manjaro. (Do not confuse Pacman with the openSUSE-specific package source, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">packman</samp>!) It is controlled by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman</samp> command, whereby, in contrast to the RPM and DEB world, there is no separation between a low-level and a high-level command.

Arch Linux packages are basically simple TAR archives that contain binaries of the respective program or library. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.pkg.tar.zst</samp> identifier indicates the intended use as a pacman package and the compression via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zstd</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> option <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--zstd</samp>). The package also contains some files with meta information about the package, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.BUILDINFO</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.MTREE</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.PKGINFO</samp>.

Pacman and its package sources are configured through the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pacman.conf</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pacman-mirror.conf</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pacman.d/*</samp> files. By default, Pacman distinguishes among the following package sources:

*   Core, for absolutely necessary basic packages

*   Extra, for add-on programs, desktop environments, and so on

*   Community, for packages provided by the community

In addition, there are optional package sources such as multilib for packages with 32-bit programs and libraries; testing for new, not yet sufficiently tested program versions; and gnome-unstable or kde-unstable for the development branches of KDE and GNOME. To enable an optional repository, it’s sufficient to add two lines to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman.conf</samp> according to the following pattern:

```
# Enable testing package source in /etc/pacman.conf file
...
[testing]
Include = /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist 
```

The name of the package source must be specified in square brackets. The following line can either refer directly to an HTTP server via <samp class="listingcharacter">Server</samp>, or to another file with this information via <samp class="listingcharacter">Include</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mirrorlist</samp> contains a list of active Arch Linux mirror servers.

Package management is carried out using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman</samp> command. Unfortunately, the options of this command differ fundamentally from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp>, and the like and are not easy to memorize (see [Table 16.8](#16_007.html_t16.8)).

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Installing a package (sync) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -S --needed name</samp> |
| Updating or reinstalling a package | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -S name</samp> |
| Installing a package from a specific repository | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -S reponame/name</samp> |
| Reimporting package sources | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -Sy</samp> |
| Updating all installed packages | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -Su</samp> |
| Updating package sources and packages (system update) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -Syu</samp> |
| Searching packages (also not installed ones) | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pacman -Ss pattern</samp> |
