```
root# touch file
root# chattr +C file
root# chattr +C directory 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chattr +C</samp> deactivates COW for a file or an entire directory. In the second case, however, the attribute applies only to new files created in that directory. To disable COW on existing files with a size not equal to 0 bytes, you must copy the files:

```
root# mv dir backup
root# mkdir dir
root# chattr +C dir
root# cp -a backup/* dir
root# rm -rf backup 
```

### 18.11.3    Compressing Files

<samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> supports the automatic and transparent compression of files. For this purpose, the file system must be mounted in the directory tree with the <samp class="listingcharacter">mount</samp> option <samp class="listingcharacter">compress=zlib</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">compress=lzo</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">compress=zstd</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">compress</samp> option applies only to new or modified files. Existing files remain unchanged as long as they are read-only. The option applies to the entire file system, so it cannot be enabled only for individual directories.

The three compression methods differ in their efficiency and speed: <samp class="listingcharacter">lzo</samp> is the fastest algorithm, but <samp class="listingcharacter">zlib</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">zstd</samp> save more space.

<samp class="listingcharacter">compress</samp> can accelerate file operations on conventional hard disks. At first glance, this may seem surprising as compression or decompression causes additional effort during reading. With a fast CPU, however, this effort is small compared to the savings that result from the fact that fewer data blocks of the hard disk have to be read or modified. (Of course, compression also saves space on the much faster SSDs, but noticeable speed improvements are not to be expected.) You can certainly use the compressed file system later without the <samp class="listingcharacter">compress</samp> option. New or modified files are then no longer compressed, but already existing files remain compressed as long as the files are only read.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">compress</samp> option is especially well suited for directories that contain a large number of text files (such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/</samp>; the space saved here is almost 50 percent!). On the other hand, the option is not recommended for your user directory if it predominantly contains already compressed files, such as audio, video, PDF, and LibreOffice files. Further compression will then not succeed. The <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> driver also recognizes this and does not compress the file in question. Nevertheless, this test takes some time.

In reality, for desktop systems it’s convenient to use <samp class="listingcharacter">compress</samp> for the system partition, but often not for the home partition. Unfortunately, not every distribution allows you to set the <samp class="listingcharacter">mount</samp> options during installation. Needless to say, there are also special cases: for example, if you’re running a MySQL database server using the InnoDB table driver that automatically compresses the tables, the MySQL database directory <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/mysql</samp> should not be in a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system with <samp class="listingcharacter">compress</samp> option.

### 18.11.4    Subvolumes

From conventional file systems you know the rule that one partition or one logical volume has one file system. With <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>, it’s different. A subvolume is a separate virtual file system. Within the “real” <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system, there can be any number of subvolumes. Subvolumes can be treated like directories, but they can also be embedded in the directory tree at any location like file systems.

Subvolumes form a hierarchy according to the directory structure. At the top is the default subvolume, which is automatically created when a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system is set up.

The easiest way to understand this is to take a look at an example. I assume that the <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sdb1</samp> partition and mounted in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/mnt/btrfs</samp> directory. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume create</samp> command now creates two new subvolumes, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sub1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">data/sub2</samp>:

```
root# btrfs subvolume create /mnt/btrfs/sub1
root# mkdir /mnt/btrfs/data
root# btrfs subvolume create /mnt/btrfs/data/sub2 
```

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume list</samp> command to get an overview of all subvolumes and snapshots. The three <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-p</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-t</samp> options have the effect that the location of the subvolume within the directory hierarchy is specified exactly, that the parent subvolume is also specified for each subvolume or snapshot, and that the result is formatted as a table:

```
root# btrfs subvolume list /mnt/btrfs/ -a -p -t
ID      gen     parent  top level       path    
–      ---     ------  ---------       ----    
256     8       5       5               sub1
257     9       5       5               data/sub2 
```

When a new <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system is created, a default subvolume is automatically set up for the root directory. It always has the ID 5 and is not listed separately. However, in the previous listing, you can see that the new subvolumes were created within this default subvolume (<samp class="listingcharacter">parent = 5</samp>).

Subvolumes behave almost like ordinary directories. You can create and delete files in them. You can also mount subvolumes like your own file systems at any location in the directory tree. To do this, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">subvolid=n</samp> option:

```
root# mkdir /mnt/sub2
root# mount -o subvolid=257 /dev/sdb1 /mnt/sub2 
```

The explicit execution of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> is required to use subvolumes created in a currently inactive subvolume (i.e., outside the default subvolume with ID=5).

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume set-default</samp> to specify the subvolume that will be used by default on the next <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command unless a different subvolume is explicitly selected by using the <samp class="listingcharacter">subvolid</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> option. You must pass the volume ID that you previously determined using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume list</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">set-default</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume delete name</samp> command enables you to delete a subvolume, including all files contained in it. The subvolume must of course be detached from the directory tree prior to that:

```
root# umount /mnt/sub2
root# btrfs subvolume delete /mnt/btrfs/data/sub2 
```

Note that the memory used by subvolumes is not released immediately with the execution of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume delete</samp>, but gradually. A kernel process takes care of the necessary cleanup in the background.

Alternatively, you can simply delete subvolumes by deleting the affected directory and its contents (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm -rf /mnt/btrfs/data/sub2</samp>). However, for subvolumes with many subdirectories and files, this takes much longer.

### 18.11.5    Snapshots

A snapshot is initially a virtual copy of a subvolume. It is virtual because no data is copied when a snapshot is created. Not until the original subvolume or the snapshot is modified are two separate branches formed. Snapshots only affect the base subvolume directly, not any existing sub-sub-volumes. Snapshots are often created as a kind of backup of the subvolume in question. Subsequently, the subvolume is then further used and modified, while the snapshot is only used to archive the previous state or to make its contents available to a backup program. But this is only one possible approach. <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> allows changes in the snapshot! The original subvolume and the snapshot created from it thus become two branches of a start state. (However, <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> also knows read-only snapshots).

Internally in <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>, snapshots are treated like subvolumes. Therefore, most <samp class="listingcharacter">subvolume</samp> commands of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs</samp> apply equally to subvolumes and snapshots. The main difference between subvolumes and snapshots is that subvolumes are initially empty, while snapshots contain a virtual copy of the source directory.

The term snapshot is used completely differently in <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> and LVM (see [Section 18.16](#18_016.html_h18.16)). In LVM, a snapshot is an immutable image of a logical volume. When you create the snapshot, you must specify the maximum amount of disk space that the snapshot can consume. This memory space is used to archive data blocks of the original LV, if necessary, before they are changed. When the snapshot space is used up, the snapshot becomes invalid and can no longer be used.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>, on the other hand, the contents of the snapshot are mutable. A snapshot is therefore a new branch of a directory tree that is identical to the snapshot at the time it is created. From this point on, both branches can develop independently of each other. The two branches take up more memory the more files are changed. <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> simply uses the <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> memory pool to store the changes. This works until the capacity of the entire file system is exhausted. <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> snapshots thus provide a lot more features and flexibility than LVM snapshots!

The starting point for the following example is a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sdb1</samp> partition. The file system is integrated into the directory tree at the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/mnt/btrfs</samp> location. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume snap</samp> then creates a snapshot of the entire file system. At the same time, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/mnt/btrfs/snap1</samp> directory is created. The snapshot can be used via this directory or integrated like a separate file system in the directory tree via <samp class="listingcharacter">mount</samp>. Note that you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount option</samp> option of <samp class="listingcharacter">subvol=name</samp> that you already know from the previous section:

```
root# btrfs subvolume snapshot /mnt/btrfs/ /mnt/btrfs/snap1
root# mkdir /mnt/snap1
root# mount -o subvol=snap1 /dev/sdb1 /mnt/snap1/ 
```

You can now independently create, modify, and delete files in both the original file system and the snapshot (i.e., without affecting each other).

Typically, <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> snapshots are mutable. If you want a read-only snapshot for backups, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs subvolume snapshot</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> option.

### 18.11.6    Distributing btrfs File Systems across Multiple Devices (RAID)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> driver can distribute file systems across multiple hard disks or devices and supports RAID levels 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10 without resorting to the usual Linux RAID driver, <samp class="listingcharacter">mdadm</samp>.

The simplest case of multidevice file systems occurs mostly when a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system becomes too small. You can then easily add another device (i.e., an empty disk partition or an unused logical volume). This increases the size of the file system accordingly. You don't need to reformat a partition or explicitly resize the file system; <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> does all these tasks on its own:

```
root# btrfs device add /dev/sdb2 /mnt/btrfs 
```

Initially, all data is then located on the first device, while the second device is only used gradually. If the devices are located on different physical hard disks (and only then!), you will achieve a speed gain by distributing the existing files across all devices using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs filesystem balance</samp>:

```
root# btrfs filesystem balance /mnt/btrfs 
```

Note, however, that running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs filesystem balance</samp> takes a long time and is rarely worth the effort. New or changed files are automatically distributed across both devices anyway.

It’s also possible to remove a device again. The data stored on the device is then transferred to the other devices first, which is why the execution of the following command can take a very long time:

```
root# btrfs device delete /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs/ 
```

You can also set up a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system with multiple devices from the start by passing multiple devices to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.btrfs</samp>:

```
root# mkfs.btrfs /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 
```

By default, the file system metadata is then duplicated (equivalent to RAID-1), but the actual data is distributed across all devices. The metadata contains the management information of the file system, such as inode lists as well as trees for searching files. Unfortunately, the resulting file system is then neither optimal in terms of speed (it’s slower than a RAID-0 system because of the duplication of metadata) nor able to keep up with RAID-1 in terms of security because the actual data is not stored redundantly.

When you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp>, you specify any device of the file system. After a computer reboot, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs device scan</samp> command must be executed so that <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> knows which devices with <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file systems exist and how they are associated with each other:

```
root# mount -t /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs 
```

You can find out which RAID variant is used for which type of data by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs filesystem df</samp>:

```
root# mkfs.btrfs /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 
root# mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs
root# cp -a /etc /mnt/btrfs
root# btrfs filesystem df /mnt/btrfs
Data, single:          total=1.01GiB,   used=14.28MiB
System, DUP:           total=8.00MiB,   used=16.00KiB
Metadata, DUP:         total=511.94MiB, used=1.86MiB
GlobalReserve, single: total=16.00MiB,  used=0.00B 
```

This (somewhat abbreviated) output means that the data is distributed across both devices (RAID-0), but internal file system data (<samp class="listingcharacter">system</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">metadata</samp>) is mirrored. If a hardware failure occurs on either medium, duplicates of at least all metadata are available.

If you want to create a “real” RAID system where data and metadata are handled consistently, you need to pass the desired RAID level to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.btrfs</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">-d</samp> (for the data) and <samp class="listingcharacter">-m</samp> (for the metadata). In addition, you need to pass the desired number of devices to <samp class="listingcharacter">mkfs.btrfs</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.btrfs</samp> detects that a partition already contains a file system, you must also specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-f</samp> option (force) to overwrite that file system. The following command creates a RAID-0 system (striping):

```
root# mkfs.btrfs -f -d raid0 -m raid0 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 
```

A RAID-1 file system is set up in a similar way by using the following command:

```
root# mkfs.btrfs -d raid1 -m raid1 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 
```

It gets interesting when a device fails. To test this case, I removed the <samp class="listingcharacter">/dev/sdc</samp> disk. To be able to use the file system, the additional <samp class="listingcharacter">mount</samp> option <samp class="listingcharacter">degraded</samp> must now be used:

```
root# mount -o degraded /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs 
```

To restore the RAID array, you must add a new device of the same size as the file system. In the following example, this is again <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sdc1</samp>, but this partition is now from a new hard disk. To redistribute the file system across both devices and thus restore RAID-1 redundancy, you must also run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs filesystem balance</samp>. For large file systems, the execution of this command naturally takes a long time. The file system can be used during this process, albeit at greatly reduced speed:

```
root# btrfs device add /dev/sdc1 /mnt/btrfs
root# btrfs filesystem balance /mnt/btrfs 
```

Only now can the defective device be removed from the file system. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">missing</samp> keyword to specify the device:

```
root# btrfs device delete missing /mnt/btrfs 
```

Finally, you can now omit the <samp class="listingcharacter">degraded</samp> option from the next <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command.

### 18.11.7    Determining the Use of a btrfs File System (df)

For other file systems, you can easily use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df -h</samp> to determine how much space is available, how much of it is used, and how much is still free. However, for <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file systems, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> sometimes returns misleading results, especially in the context of RAID. The reasons for this are the separation between system data, metadata, and the actual files; the use of different RAID levels for data and metadata; possibly active compression functions; and the use of pools that <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> reserves in advance for different purposes.

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp>, you can also run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs</samp> commands <samp class="listingcharacter">filesystem show</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">filesystem usage</samp>. The following example should help you to at least correctly interpret the data that <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> provides. The starting point is a small <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> RAID-1 system consisting of two 10 GiB partitions. The entire <samp class="listingcharacter">/usr</samp> directory of the test system was copied to this file system (space requirement according to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">du</samp> is approximately 4.6 GiB):

```
root# mkfs.btrfs -d raid1 -m raid1 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
root# mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs
root# cp -a /usr /mnt/btrfs 
```

The result of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> is almost perfect here despite the use of RAID-1\. This is a big improvement over older <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> versions where <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">df</samp> was way off in the same scenario:

```
root# df -h /mnt/btrfs/
Filesystem   Size  Used  Avail.  Used%  Mounted on
/dev/sdb1     10G  4.5G   4.8G   49%    /mnt/btrfs 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs filesystem show</samp> tells you that the file system is composed of two 10 GiB devices and that both devices are filled to the same extent:

```
root# btrfs filesystem show  /dev/sdb1 
Label: none  uuid: e4f2c9d3-5b88-4019-af19-682a3417d8e6
        Total devices 2 FS bytes used 4.43GiB
        devid    1 size 10.00GiB used 6.01GiB path /dev/sdb1
        devid    2 size 10.00GiB used 6.01GiB path /dev/sdc1 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs fi usage</samp> provides detailed information about how the reserved data is used:

```
root# btrfs fi usage /mnt/btrfs/
Overall:
    Device size:                  20.00GiB
    Device allocated:             12.02GiB
    Device unallocated:            7.98GiB
    Device missing:                  0.00B
    Used:                          8.87GiB
    Free (estimated):              4.72GiB      (min: 4.72GiB)
    Data ratio:                       2.00
    Metadata ratio:                   2.00
    Global reserve:               16.00MiB      (used: 0.00B)
Data,RAID1: Size:5.00GiB, Used:4.27GiB
   /dev/sdb1       5.00GiB
   /dev/sdc1       5.00GiB
Metadata,RAID1: Size:1.00GiB, Used:169.08MiB
   /dev/sdb1       1.00GiB
   /dev/sdc1       1.00GiB
System,RAID1: Size:8.00MiB, Used:16.00KiB
   /dev/sdb1       8.00MiB
   /dev/sdc1       8.00MiB
Unallocated:
   /dev/sdb1       3.99GiB
   /dev/sdc1       3.99GiB 
```

In summary, this means that <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> has reserved 5 GiB each for storing files on both partitions, 0.73 GiB of which is still free. Another 1 GiB has been reserved for metadata, but so far only 169 MiB of this is in use. Finally, there is just under 4 GiB of free space on each of the two partitions.

#### Disk-Full Problems

You should size <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> systems as generously as possible! <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp> file systems can be written to almost to the last byte (even though this is not recommended). <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>, however, causes a much larger overhead for subvolumes, snapshots, and the like compared to <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp>. For this reason, you should allow for more space than with other file system types to ensure smooth operation.

### 18.11.8    btrfs Configuration in openSUSE

No other Linux distribution uses <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> as extensively by default as SUSE. Current versions of openSUSE or the SUSE Enterprise distributions use <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> for the system partition and <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> for the home partition. Within the system partition, YaST creates various subvolumes during the installation for directories such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/xxx</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/opt</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/srv</samp>. When you install openSUSE on a relatively small volume, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp> is also integrated into the <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system.

In addition, YaST creates two snapshots for each administrative task: a <samp class="listingcharacter">pre</samp> snapshot (before) and a corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">pre-post</samp> snapshot (after). The benefit of this configuration is that you can restore your system to an older state in the YaST Filesystem Snapshot module (formerly called Snapper; see [Figure 18.3](#18_011.html_f18.3)) without also making a leap into the past with your personal data (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home directory</samp>). Alternatively, you can reset only individual files. If there are boot problems, you can even select an older snapshot in GRUB and boot the system in this state.

[![Managing Snapshots in YaST](bilderklein/klein18_003.png)](img-f18.3.html)

**Figure 18.3**     Managing Snapshots in YaST

The price for this security against admin errors is a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> system in which you can get dizzy from all the subvolumes and snapshots:

```
root# btrfs subvol list / -p -a  -t
ID      gen     parent  top level   path    
–      ---     ------  ---------    ----    
256     32      5       5           <FS_TREE>/@
258     7705    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/var
259     7158    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/usr/local
260     7704    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/tmp
261     46      256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/srv
262     7703    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/root
263     35      256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/opt
264     7704    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/home
265     26      256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/boot/grub2/x86_64-efi
266     4376    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/boot/grub2/i386-pc
267     7169    256     256         <FS_TREE>/@/.snapshots
268     7705    267     267         <FS_TREE>/@/.snapshots/1/snapshot
... 
```

The configuration files for the Filesystem Snapshots system are located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/snapper</samp>. From <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/snapper/configs/root</samp>, it appears that snapshots for the last ten YaST actions are backed up by default. Older snapshots are automatically deleted. Optionally, you can also enable hourly snapshots in this file, which also includes the automatic deletion of older snapshots.

Instead of YaST, you can also use the command of the same name for Snapper configuration:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper list</samp> lists all available snapshots.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper create</samp> creates a new snapshot.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper delete n</samp> deletes the specified snapshot.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper delete n1-n2</samp> deletes the snapshots with numbers between <samp class="listingcharacter">n1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">n2</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper cleanup type</samp> deletes old snapshots, with several cleanup algorithms to choose from: <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">timeline</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">empty-pre-post</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper undochange n1..n2 [files]</samp> undoes the changes made between snapshot <samp class="listingcharacter">n1</samp> and snapshot <samp class="listingcharacter">n2</samp> either for all affected files or only for the files specified as parameters.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper rollback [n]</samp> makes the specified or the most recent available snapshot the new default subvolume.

We’ve already dealt with the question of how much storage space is still free in a <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system. But maybe you want to know how much disk space a single subvolume or snapshot takes up. To answer this question, you must first enable the quota features of <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>:

```
root# btrfs quota enable / 
```

After a while (usually after a few minutes), <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">btrfs qgroup show</samp> then shows which subvolume or snapshot is taking up how much space:

```
root# btrfs qgroup show -e --human-readable --sort=qgroupid  /
qgroupid         rfer         excl     max_excl 
--------         ----         ----     -------- 
0/5          16.00KiB     16.00KiB         none 
0/256        16.00KiB     16.00KiB         none 
0/258       260.24MiB    260.24MiB         none 
0/259        16.00KiB     16.00KiB         none 
...
0/356         5.46GiB     48.00KiB         none 
0/357         5.46GiB     48.00KiB         none 
0/358         5.48GiB      2.57MiB         none 
1/0           6.83GiB      1.48GiB         none 
```

Unfortunately, the result is difficult to read in this format. First, the subvolumes or snapshots are not designated by their names, but only by their ID numbers. Second, I still owe you the explanation of what the difference is between the <samp class="listingcharacter">rfer</samp> column and the <samp class="listingcharacter">excl</samp> column: <samp class="listingcharacter">rfer</samp> specifies the total memory requirement of a subvolume/snapshot, while <samp class="listingcharacter">excl</samp> specifies the extent to which this memory is exclusively used by the subvolume/snapshot in question. So this storage is not shared with other subvolumes/snapshots.

Three actions are required to disable automatic snapshots:

*   YaST snapshots during admin tasks YaST is responsible for creating these snapshots. Accordingly, there is an option for this in the YaST configuration file, which can be set to <samp class="listingcharacter">yes</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">no</samp>:

    ```
    # file /etc/sysconfig/yast2
    USE_SNAPPER="no" 
    ```

*   Snapshots during package installations (Zypper) A Zypper plugin is responsible for creating snapshots during the installations of software or updates. You will need to uninstall that plugin:

    ```
    root# zypper remove snapper-zypp-plugin 
    ```

*   Hourly snapshots Hourly snapshots are turned off by default on openSUSE. To enable or disable, you simply need to set the <samp class="listingcharacter">TIMELINE_CREATE</samp> variable to <samp class="listingcharacter">yes</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">no</samp>:

    ```
    # file /etc/snapper/configs/root
    TIMELINE_CREATE="no" 
    ```

If the root file system is already bursting at the seams, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper delete</samp> or YaST to delete snapshots that are no longer required and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zypper clean</samp> to clear the cache of the package management system.

#### Recommendations for SUSE Installations

For private users of openSUSE, I recommend using the <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp> file system for the system partition instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> during installation.

The benefits associated with <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> come with such complexity and hard-to-predict side effects that only <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> experts can help with problems.

Personally, I also avoid <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> in professional use—but admittedly, you may have a different opinion here. So if you decide to use <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp>, be sure to size the system partition twice as large as in conventional installations!

### 18.11.9    btrfs Configuration in Fedora

Since version 33, Fedora uses <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> by default for desktop installations. However, the configuration (last tested on Fedora 38) is much simpler than on SUSE: by default, only three subvolumes are created for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/machines</samp>. The only real <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> feature activated is automatic compression.

The Fedora setup is very clear, but it has the disadvantage that handling images and large database files is not as efficient as on SUSE because of the always active COW. If necessary, you must set up subvolumes without COW for the data directories themselves before installing virtualization or database systems.

In case you are wondering how much you will benefit from automatic compression, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">compsize</samp> command provides answers (although the following listing is slightly abbreviated):

```
root# compsize -x /
Type       Perc     Disk Usage   Uncompressed Referenced  
TOTAL       60%      5.4G         9.0G          10G       
none       100%      3.5G         3.5G         3.9G       
zstd        34%      1.8G         5.4G         6.7G 
```

According to this, <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> has dispensed with compression for files with a volume of 3.5 GiB (<samp class="listingcharacter">none</samp> line). Other files of 5.4 GiB were compressed and therefore consume only 1.8 GiB on the disk (<samp class="listingcharacter">zstd</samp> line). In total, the entire file system takes up only about 60% of the space it would require without compression (<samp class="listingcharacter">TOTAL</samp> line).

The difference between the <samp class="listingcharacter">Uncompressed</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Referenced</samp> columns concerns the handling of files that are empty in wide areas and contain only 0 bytes. Not only <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> but also most other Linux file systems recognize such sparse files and deal with them efficiently. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Referenced</samp> column indicates how much space the files would take up on a file system that is not optimized in this respect.

Fedora does not use snapshots by default. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">snapper</samp> tool familiar from SUSE can also be installed on Fedora—for example, to create a snapshot with every <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnf</samp> action. The installation instructions can be found at the following address: [https://sysguides.com/install-fedora-38-with-snapshot-and-rollback-support](https://sysguides.com/install-fedora-38-with-snapshot-and-rollback-support).

## 18.12    The xfs File System

The <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file system was developed by SGI for their workstations with the Unix-like operating system IRIX. Later, the file system was ported for Linux and gradually improved again and again. The file system is considered to be mature, stable, and especially efficient in handling very large files. This also applies to file systems that are larger than 16 TiB.

Since 2014, <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> has been used as the default file system by both RHEL and current SUSE distributions. (SUSE differentiates between the system partition and the data partitions; for the system partition, <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> is provided, for the data partitions <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp>). You can find more information about the <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file system at [https://xfs.wiki.kernel.org](https://xfs.wiki.kernel.org).

Entries for an <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file system in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp> usually look like the following example. Additional <samp class="listingcharacter">mount</samp> options are needed only very rarely. They are listed in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man mount</samp>:

```
# /etc/fstab
/dev/sdb13      /data          xfs  defaults 0 0 
```

To set up an <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file system in a partition, you simply need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.xfs</samp>. If the command is not available, you must first install the <samp class="listingcharacter">xfsprogs</samp> package. The parameters output by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.xfs</samp> can be read later via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_info</samp> if required:

```
root# mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
meta-data=/dev/sdb1    isize=256    agcount=4, agsize=1048512 blks
         =             sectsz=512   attr=2, projid32bit=1
         =             crc=0        finobt=0
data     =             bsize=4096   blocks=4194048, imaxpct=25
naming   =version 2    bsize=4096   ascii-ci=0 ftype=0

log      =internal log bsize=4096   blocks=2560, version=2
         =             sectsz=512   sunit=0 blks, lazy-count=1
realtime =no           extsz=4096   blocks=0, rtextents=0 
```

Now all that's missing is a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command, and you're ready to use the file system:

```
root# mount -t xfs /dev/sdb1 /test 
```

The integrity of <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file systems is automatically checked during each <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> operation. However, only the journaling log is analyzed. For a manual check, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_check</samp>. This is only possible if the file system is not mounted. If the command detects errors, you can try to fix them using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_repair</samp>.

To ensure compatibility with the other file systems, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fsck.xfs</samp> command can be used. However, this command does not perform any task and always returns OK as a result.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_growfs</samp> enlarges an <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs</samp> file system during operation. For this to work, the file system must be mounted! The command assumes that the underlying data partition was previously enlarged. The name of the command already suggests it: an <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file system can only be enlarged using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_growfs</samp>, not reduced. (Functions to shrink XFS file systems are being worked on.)

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_admin</samp> changes various parameters of the file system, such as the name (label) and the UUID number. The file system must be removed from the directory tree upfront (with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umount</samp>).

## 18.13    Windows File Systems (vfat and ntfs)

Some Linux users have a Windows version installed on their computer in parallel. But external data media also often use Windows file systems (USB flash drives, memory cards of digital cameras, etc.). In the following sections, you’ll learn how you can access Windows file systems on Linux—no matter whether they are located in a partition of the internal hard disk or on an external data medium.

There are three fundamentally different Windows file systems:

*   FAT, VFAT, and exFAT There are countless variants of the FAT file system. The oldest versions historically are FAT12 for floppy disks, FAT16 for file systems up to 2 GiB, and FAT32 for file systems up to 8 TiB and files up to 4 GiB. Windows 95 also introduced VFAT, which finally allowed file names of more than 8+3 characters. The combination of FAT32 and VFAT is most commonly used today, such as on many SD cards up to 32 GiB.
    The FAT variant exFAT was developed especially for large flash cards (e.g., for digital cameras). exFAT allows files up to 16,777,216 TiB in size and supports ACLs and transactions.

*   New Technology File System (NTFS) NTFS was introduced with Windows NT and is used by all current Windows versions. Compared to FAT, NTFS offers a higher degree of security (access rights, journaling, etc.) as well as various additional functions. The file system size is almost unlimited at 16,777,216 TiB.

*   ReFS Since Windows 8 or Windows Server 2012, ReFS can also be used as an alternative to NTFS. This new file system is more modern than NTFS, but it also has some limitations. It hasn’t yet achieved widespread use and is not used in standard desktop installations. This might change with the upcoming Windows 12 OS.

Almost all Linux distributions can read and write (V)FAT and NTFS file systems right away. In the past, exFAT support was somewhat more problematic. But because Microsoft gave its consent in 2019 to allow the driver to be integrated into the kernel, it is now available by default in many modern distributions. There is no open-source driver for ReFS yet, but there is a proprietary driver from the Paragon company ([https://www.paragon-software.com/business/refs-linux](https://www.paragon-software.com/business/refs-linux)).

It’s rarely necessary to set up Windows file systems on Linux, but it is of course possible. Before you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.exfat</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.ntfs</samp>, you may need to install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">exfat-utils</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfsprogs</samp> package:

```
root# mkfs.vfat -F 32  /dev/sdb1  
(VFAT)
root# mkfs.exfat       /dev/sdb1  
(exFAT)
root# mkfs.ntfs --fast /dev/sdb1  
(NTFS) 
```

### Be Sure to Avoid Data Loss when Accessing Windows File Systems!

On a dual-boot machine running either Linux or Windows, writes performed on Linux can result in an inconsistent Windows file system and data loss. Windows is not shut down completely by default for speed reasons. Instead, a quick start function is active, which is based on Windows being put into a special hibernation state.

Recent changes to the file system are saved in a special file that Linux does not see. You should always deactivate the quick start function if you are running a mixed Windows/Linux setup. You can find relevant instructions on this at [https://pureinfotech.com/disable-fast-startup-windows-11-10](https://pureinfotech.com/disable-fast-startup-windows-11-10).

To shut down Windows completely only once, you must first close all programs and then execute the <samp class="listingcharacter">shutdown /p</samp> command in <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd.exe</samp>.

The easiest way to avoid these problems is to synchronize shared Windows/Linux data externally, such as in a cloud directory.

VFAT does not know the concept of access rights at all. NTFS does support access rights, but not in the typical Unix/Linux way. This results in a problem: Which Linux user has what access rights for Windows files? The answer is given by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> options <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">uid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gid</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umask/fmask/dmask</samp>. These options set the owner, group membership, and access bits for the Windows file system uniformly for all files of this file system and independent of any NTFS access rights.

### 18.13.1    The VFAT File System

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vfat</samp> driver detects the FAT type (FAT12/-16/-32) independently. On Linux, Windows file names are represented in the Latin-1 (ISO 8859-1) character set. By default, the user running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> is allowed to read and write all files and directories; all other users are allowed to read everything, but not to modify anything. Of course, you can change these settings by way of options.

A typical entry in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp> for a local VFAT partition on the hard disk looks as follows:

```
# /etc/fstab
/dev/sda1      /media/win1  vfat    utf8,uid=1000,noexec  0 0 
```

This ensures that the user with the user number 1000 can change all files and that special characters in Windows file names are displayed as UTF8 characters on Linux. For security reasons, you must not run programs stored in the Windows file system (<samp class="listingcharacter">noexec</samp> option).

The following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fstab</samp> line does not automatically mount the Windows partition in the directory tree (<samp class="listingcharacter">noauto</samp>). Thanks to <samp class="listingcharacter">users</samp>, however, any user may run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gid=users</samp> causes the group membership of the Windows files to be determined by the user's default group (and not the currently active group):

```
/dev/sda1      /media/win1  vfat    noauto,users,gid=users,utf8  0 0 
```

### 18.13.2    The NTFS File System

The <samp class="listingcharacter">ntfs</samp> driver of Linux supports read and write access and can handle streams. However, the driver cannot read or write encrypted files and cannot create compressed files (although it can read them).

Unlike most other file system drivers, <samp class="listingcharacter">ntfs</samp> is not implemented as a kernel module, but as a FUSE driver. This is a kernel module that communicates with external programs. FUSE thus allows the actual file system driver to be implemented outside the kernel.

To grant the user with the UID 1000 write access to an NTFS disk, you need an <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fstab</samp> line, as shown in the following pattern:

```
# /etc/fstab
/dev/sda1    /media/win   ntfs   uid=1000,gid=1000  0 0 
```

Streams are a special feature of the NTFS file system, and an NTFS file can consist of multiple streams. Each stream has the same function as a conventional file. The default stream is automatically read or changed during a normal file access. For the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfs</samp> driver, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">streams_interface</samp> option controls access to streams. In the default <samp class="listingcharacter">xattr</samp> setting, streams are considered like file attributes. Streams are accessed using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">get-</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">setfattr</samp> commands from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">attr</samp> package (see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.7](#09_007.html_h9.7)). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getfattr -d -e text</samp> returns a list of all attributes, displaying their contents as text:

```
root# mount /dev/sda1 /media/win
root# cd /media/win
root# cat > streamtest
abc <Ctrl>+<D>

root# setfattr -n user.stream1 -v "efg" streamtest
root# setfattr -n user.stream2 -v "xyz" streamtest
root# cat streamtest
abc
root# getfattr -d -e text streamtest
# file: streamtest
user.stream1="efg"
user.stream2="xyz"

root# cd
root# umount /media/win 
```

Alternatively, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">streams_interface=windows</samp>. This setting activates the typical Windows notation in the form <samp class="listingcharacter">filename:streamname</samp>:

```
root# mount -o streams_interface=windows /dev/sda1 /media/win
root# cd /media/win
root# cat streamtest
abc
root# cat streamtest:stream1
efg 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfsprogs</samp> package contains various commands that support the administration of NTFS file systems. [Table 18.7](#18_013.html_t18.7) gives an overview.

| Command | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkfs.ntfs</samp> | Sets up an NTFS file system |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfsclone</samp> | Copies an NTFS file system |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfsinfo</samp> | Provides information about an NTFS file system |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfslabel</samp> | Assigns a name to an NTFS partition |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfsresize</samp> | Changes the size of the NTFS file system |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntfsundelete</samp> | Tries to restore deleted files |

**Table 18.7**     Commands of ntfsprogs Package

## 18.14    Swap Partitions and Files

If there isn’t enough memory to run all programs, and swap partitions or files are available, then Linux swaps parts of the memory there (paging). This way, Linux can use more memory than is available in RAM.

Setting up a swap partition is usually done as part of the installation. You can check whether and how much swap space is available or actually used by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">free</samp> command. In the example ahead, 1,519 MiB of RAM and 2,000 MiB of swap memory are available. Of the RAM, 401 MiB is currently used for programs and data, and the rest is used as a buffer or cache for files. The swap memory is currently unused:

```
root# free -m
             total     used     free     shared    buffers     cached
Mem:          1519     1479       39          0         67       1010
-/+ buffers/cache:      401     1117
Swap:         2000        0     2000 
```

If a computer is running for a longer time, it will use the swap memory even if a lot of RAM is available. Here’s why: The kernel manages a cache for read accesses to files. If a file is needed again later, it can be read from the cache. As soon as the cache is larger than the otherwise free RAM, Linux swaps out memory blocks that have not been used for a long time to the swap partition. This is by no means a sign that too little RAM is available. Linux simply tries to use the available memory as efficiently as possible.

The following lines show two entries for swap partitions in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pri</samp> option causes the two partitions to be treated equally by Linux. This provides a speed increase as with striping or RAID-0 (see [Section 18.15](#18_015.html_h18.15)), provided that the partitions are located on two separate hard disks. If there is only one swap partition, you should just specify <samp class="listingcharacter">defaults</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">pri=0</samp>:

```
# /etc/fstab: Swap partitions
/dev/sda9   swap   swap    pri=1   0 0
/dev/sdb7   swap   swap    pri=1   0 0 
```

When RAM runs out of memory, the Linux kernel uses a relatively complex algorithm to decide whether to free cache memory in favor of other memory requests or to swap out recently unused memory areas to the swap partition. Using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/sys/vm/swappiness</samp> kernel parameter, you can define yourself whether the kernel should shrink the cache or swap data if possible. To learn what kernel parameters are and how to set them, see [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.7](#21_007.html_h21.7).

The default setting for <samp class="listingcharacter">swappiness</samp> is 60; the possible value range is from 0 to 100\. The value 0 means that the kernel avoids paging if possible, while 100 means that memory that has been unused for a long time ends up in a swap partition as soon as possible. More details about the <samp class="listingcharacter">swappiness</samp> parameter can be found at [https://lwn.net/Articles/83588](https://lwn.net/Articles/83588).

In practice, you’re most likely to notice swap behavior if you leave your computer running overnight and a program accesses many files on the hard disk in your absence, such as a backup script or a program to create a search index. Because of the large number of file accesses, the cache grows a lot. Using <samp class="listingcharacter">swappiness=60</samp> or an even higher value, the kernel will then swap out memory that has not been used for hours. For example, this could affect the memory pages of Firefox or GIMP. If you want to continue using GIMP the next day, it will take a few seconds to transfer those pages from the swap partition back into the memory. By using <samp class="listingcharacter">swappiness=0</samp>, you avoid this wait time.

In the past, the recommendation was to provide memory equal to approximately twice the amount of RAM as swap memory. With increasing RAM size, however, this rule of thumb is no longer useful. If you use Linux primarily as a desktop system, a much smaller swap partition is quite sufficient (such as 2 GiB of swap space with 16 GiB of RAM). The swap memory only needs to be larger than the RAM if you want to use hibernation mode on your notebook computer. I wouldn't take that into account, though; I've had mostly bad experiences with hibernation and only use standby mode now.

Again and again, the question comes up as to whether you can or should completely do without a swap partition if you have a lot of RAM. Although opinions differ, a sensibly sized swap space will generally increase the efficiency of Linux. If you use Linux as a desktop system on a modern, well-equipped notebook computer, the efficiency improvement will be so small that you can hardly measure it. On a server or on a computer that is used intensively for software development or other memory-intensive applications, you are simply giving away computing power without swap space.

If you want to dig deeper into the pros and cons of a swap partition, I recommend a great blog article available at [https://chrisdown.name/2018/01/02/in-defence-of-swap.html](https://chrisdown.name/2018/01/02/in-defence-of-swap.html).

Swap files are not quite as efficient as swap partitions but are easier to resize. (Unfortunately, automatic resizing like you’d find on Windows or macOS is not possible.) Currently, Ubuntu is the only major distribution that sets up a swap file by default for desktop installations.

To create a new swap file yourself, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dd</samp> command to create an empty file with a specified size. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/zero</samp> is used as the data source. The size specification results from the product of the <samp class="listingcharacter">bs</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">count</samp> parameters, here 1 GiB. Then the swap file can be formatted like a swap partition using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mkswap</samp> and activated via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">swapon</samp>:

```
root# dd bs=1M if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile count=1024
root# mkswap /swapfile 1000
root# sync
root# swapon -v /swapfile
swapon on device /swapfile 
```

Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system does not support swap files!

To resize a swap file, you must first disable it using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">swapoff</samp> and then set up a new file of the size you want.

Swap files are included in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fstab</samp> like swap partitions:

```
# extension to /etc/fstab
/swapfile  none      swap          sw       0  0 
```

## 18.15    RAID

The basic idea behind Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) is to logically link partitions of multiple hard disks or SSDs. The goal here is to create a more reliable overall system through redundancy.

There are two basic ways to implement RAID: through hardware (i.e., a controller that executes the RAID logic itself) or through software executed by the computer's CPU. Hardware RAID is mainly used in expensive server systems. Its greatest advantages are that the RAID controller acts independently of the operating system.

With regard to software RAID, a distinction is made among different types, depending on where the software comes from:

*   Linux software RAID Linux can combine multiple disks into a RAID. From a Linux perspective, this RAID variant is preferable. If this book talks about RAID without further explanation, it always means Linux software RAID!

*   Windows software RAID Windows also supports different RAID variants in the form of software RAID. Windows file systems set up in this way are not readable by Linux.

*   Host RAID (fake RAID) In this variant, the BIOS or EFI implements different RAID levels in combination with an operating system driver. The derogatory term fake RAID is explained by the fact that in the past many RAID controllers were advertised as if they were real hardware RAID controllers. Today, fake RAID is hardly ever used.

There are several methods to join partitions. These variants are referred to as RAID levels:

*   RAID-0 (striping) In RAID-0, multiple physical partitions are combined into one larger partition. Here, the data is distributed in parallel in small blocks to the individual partitions so that the data is read alternately from all disks when accessed. Ideally, this results in a multiplication of the data rate—a tripling, for example, in the case of three hard disks. Such speed increases are more difficult to achieve with SSDs because the maximum speed is often limited by the bus system. Apart from that, the speed gain is often much smaller than hoped for and only comes into play with large files.
    RAID-0 has a serious disadvantage: the risk of failure increases because one defective hard disk or SSD leads to the loss of all data.

*   RAID-1 (mirroring) With RAID-1, the same data is stored on two hard disks or SSDs. If one disk fails, all data is still available on the other device. The advantage is higher safety, while the disadvantage is halved capacity. RAID-1 does not provide any speed advantages.

*   RAID-10 RAID-10 combines RAID-1 and RAID-0 and requires at least four disks: disks 1 and 2 form a RAID-1 array while disks 3 and 4 form another RAID-1 array. At the next level, the two RAID-1 arrays are combined into a RAID-0 array. RAID-10 thus combines the advantages of RAID-0 (speed) and RAID-1 (security).

*   RAID-5 (parity striping) Basically, RAID-5 works like RAID-0, but additional parity information is stored in a partition, which changes for each data block. If a disk fails, the entire data can be reconstructed. However, the failure of two or more disks will still result in a complete loss of data. RAID-5 requires at least three disks.

    RAID-5 is as secure as RAID-1 and about as fast as RAID-0 for read accesses. In addition, RAID-5 has the advantage that the data portion required for redundancy becomes smaller with the number of hard disks: with RAID-1, the capacity loss is always 50%, but with RAID-5, it is only 33% with three hard disks, 25% with four, 20% with five, and so on.

    However, RAID-5 also has disadvantages compared to RAID-1\. First, write operations are slower than in RAID-1, especially when small amounts of data change frequently. The reason is that even for small changes, the parity information for an entire block of data has to be recalculated and stored. Second, after replacing a defective disc, the reconstruction of the RAID-5 array takes a very long time, much longer than with RAID-1.

*   RAID-6 RAID-6 works like RAID-5, but it’s double redundant and requires at least four hard disks. Even if two hard disks fail, there is no data loss.

Information about more RAID levels as well as many interesting details and basics of RAID can be found at [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAID).

This section deals exclusively with the administration of Linux software RAID based on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp>. For space reasons, I will only describe RAID levels 0 and 1.

If you use the <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system and want to use RAID levels 0, 1, 5, 6, or 10, you can do without the RAID functions of the multidevice driver described here. <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> contains RAID functions itself.

In real life, RAID is used almost exclusively on servers. The primary motivation is to protect against data loss in the event of defective hardware. RAID-1 is typically used for “small” servers. Most data centers where you can rent Linux servers help with configuration tools or scripts for setting up RAID-1\. A RAID configuration on a notebook or desktop computer is theoretically possible, but nowadays completely uncommon.

LVM can be combined with RAID by using a RAID array as the basis for LVM. In this case, RAID must be configured first, followed by LVM.

### 18.15.1    Manual Configuration Using mdadm

As mentioned earlier, RAID setup usually takes place during the Linux installation. Nevertheless, in this section I’ll show you the steps necessary to set up software RAID manually. If you plan to use software RAID on a “real” server, you should definitely familiarize yourself with the basic principles and with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> command before that. The easiest way to do this is in a virtual machine. Once you have set up a Linux distribution of your choice, you can add two or more virtual disks. These will then be your playground for learning RAID.

Unless you have already set up a RAID array during the installation, you must install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> package, which contains the RAID administration command of the same name. In some distributions, the package management command suggests that you also install a mail server. When the RAID system detects a hardware defect, it can then automatically send an email to the administrator.

If you have not yet dealt with the subject of the mail server or if you only want to try out RAID in a virtual machine, you can do without the mail server. For this reason, on Debian and Ubuntu, you should use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--no-install-recommends</samp> option when using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt</samp> for the installation.

Within Linux, the so-called multidevice driver is responsible for software RAID. In some distributions, this driver is integrated directly into the kernel; otherwise the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">md_mod</samp> kernel module (formerly simply <samp class="listingcharacter">md</samp>) will be loaded automatically during system startup. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dmesg</samp> should contain appropriate messages in any case. You should also make sure that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/mdstat</samp> pseudofile exists. It provides information about the current state of the RAID system.

<samp class="listingcharacter">md_mod</samp> places a logical layer between the hard disk or SSD access driver and the file system driver (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ext4</samp>). In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">md_mod</samp> forms a new logical device from multiple hard disk partitions that can be accessed by the file system driver (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/mdN</samp>). After the RAID configuration, you no longer use a hard disk partition directly, but a RAID partition—<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/mdN</samp>—to set up your file system on.

The central configuration file is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/mdadm.conf</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf</samp>. This file should contain data about all active RAID arrays in addition to some global RAID settings. You can create a completely new configuration file using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/mdadm/mkconf</samp>. This is useful if the configuration file has been lost or if you are working on a live or rescue system.

The usual configuration procedure is unusual. First, you set up or modify the required RAID arrays by executing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> commands. Then you extend the predominantly existing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm.conf</samp> file based on the configuration now present. You can determine the key data of the active RAID arrays using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --examine --scan</samp>, and you add them to the existing configuration file by using <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>:

```
root# mdadm --examine --scan >> /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf 
```

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm.conf</samp> contained RAID definitions before, you must remove them using an editor so that no array is defined twice. The following lines show an example of the structure of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm.conf</samp>:

```
# file /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf oder /etc/mdadm.conf
DEVICE partitions
CREATE owner=root group=disk mode=0660 auto=yes
HOMEHOST <system>
MAILADDR root
ARRAY /dev/md0 level=raid1 num-devices=2 UUID=36c426b0:...
ARRAY /dev/md1 level=raid1 num-devices=2 UUID=71dfc474:...
ARRAY /dev/md2 level=raid1 num-devices=2 UUID=e0f65ea0:... 
```

Current information about the RAID status is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/mdstat</samp> file. In the following example, there are three RAID-1 arrays, each consisting of two partitions. All three arrays are active and running without errors. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">[UU]</samp> means that the first and the second partition of the array are up (i.e., working without problems):

```
root# cat /proc/mdstat 
Personalities : [raid0] [raid1] [linear] [multipath] 
                [raid6] [raid5] [raid4] [raid10]

md0 : active raid1 sda1[0] sdb1
      979840 blocks [2/2] [UU]
md1 : active raid1 sda2[0] sdb2
      1951808 blocks [2/2] [UU]
md2 : active raid1 sda3[0] sdb3
      387730624 blocks [2/2] [UU]
unused devices: <none> 
```

Now of course, it isn’t useful to constantly check this file to see if everything is okay. It’s much more convenient to have <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --monitor</samp> take over this task. Usually, this command is started by the init system when the computer boots. However, depending on the distribution, you may need to configure <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> accordingly beforehand. To do this, you want to run the following command on Ubuntu, for example:

```
root# dpkg-reconfigure mdadm 
```

Four dialogs then guide you through the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> configuration. In the first step, you can enable an automatic redundancy check that compares the data on the RAID partitions once a month. This check helps to detect hard disk defects even in areas or files that have not been read or modified for a long time. Internally, the redundancy check is performed by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">checkarray</samp> command, which is started by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d/mdadm</samp> Cron script.

In the second and third steps, you activate the monitoring of the RAID status and specify the email address to which any warnings or error reports are to be sent. Internally the monitoring is done by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --monitor</samp>. On Debian and Ubuntu, the command is started by the init system if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/mdadm</samp> contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">START_DAEMON=true</samp> setting. The email address is stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm.conf</samp>. If a problem occurs, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> sends a notification email to <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. For this to work, a mail server must be installed on the computer (see [Chapter 26](#26_001.html_h26))! You can set the email address in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm.conf</samp> using the <samp class="listingcharacter">MAILADDR</samp> variable.

Finally, in the fourth step, you specify whether your server should start on restart even if it detects a defect in a RAID partition. This is recommended for root servers.

### 18.15.2    Administration

You usually set up RAID during the installation process (see [Chapter 22](#22_001.html_h22), [Section 22.1](#22_001.html_h22.1)). Of course, as in the following examples, you can also create a RAID array at a later stage, set up a file system in it, and integrate it into the directory tree. However, it is impossible (with simple means) to convert an existing root file system to RAID. Thus, the root file system remains the weak point of the overall system.

The starting point for the following example is a virtual machine with three disks. The first disk contains the distribution, while the other two are supposed to be connected to a RAID-1 device:

```
root# lsblk
...
vdb       252:16   0   20G  0 disk 
vdc       252:32   0   20G  0 disk 
```

For this purpose, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">parted</samp> to set up a partition each on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/vdb</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/deb/vdc</samp> and mark them for RAID use. The following commands apply to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/vdb</samp>:

```
root# parted /dev/vdb
(parted) mklabel gpt
(parted) mkpart part1 1mib -1mib
(parted) set 1 raid on
(parted) unit mib
(parted) print
Number  Start    End       Size        Name     File system     Flags
 1      1.00MiB  20479MiB  20478MiB    part1                    raid
(parted) quit 
```

A single <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> command is sufficient to create a RAID-1 array from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/vdb1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/vdc1</samp> partitions:

```
root# mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=0 --raid-devices=2 \
  /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1
mdadm: Defaulting to version 1.2 metadata
mdadm: array /dev/md0 started. 
```

Next, you need to create a file system on the new virtual <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/md0</samp> partition. This partition can be mounted into the Linux file system via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp>. Here, the partition is addressed via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/mnt/safedata</samp> directory; of course, you can also use another name instead:

```
root# mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0
root# mkdir /mnt/safedata
root# mount /dev/md0 /mnt/safedata 
```

If everything works, you should add the new partition to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp>. In all current Linux distributions, the RAID system is automatically initialized by the init system at the next system start:

```
# in /etc/fstab
/dev/md0    /mnt/safedata   ext4    defaults    0 0 
```

You must also add a line to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm.conf</samp> configuration file that describes the new RAID-0 array. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --examine --scan</samp> provides the line in the required syntax:

```
root# mdadm --examine --scan >> /etc/mdadm.conf 
```

To test the functionality of a RAID-1 array—preferably before you have stored critical data there—you should flag a partition as defective:

```
root# mdadm /dev/md0 --fail /dev/vdc1 
```

Provided that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --monitor</samp> was started as part of the system startup, <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> on the local machine should now immediately receive an email notification. Otherwise, you can continue to use the array; however, all changes are now stored only on the remaining disk partition. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc/mdstat</samp> now shows the <samp class="listingcharacter">_U</samp> status. This means that one partition is running (<samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp> for up) and one is missing (<samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp>):

```
root# cat /proc/mdstat
md0 : active raid1 vdb1
      979840 blocks [2/1] [_U] 
```

To add <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/vdc1</samp> back to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/md0</samp>, you must first explicitly remove the partition that is flagged as defective:

```
root# mdadm --remove /dev/md0 /dev/vdc1
root# mdadm --add    /dev/md0 /dev/vdc1 
```

The automatic resynchronization of the two partitions then begins, which takes quite some time depending on the size of the network (approximately 20 minutes per 100 GiB for conventional hard disks; significantly less for SSDs). You can continue to work during this time, but the file system will respond more slowly than usual:

```
root# cat /proc/mdstat
md0 : active raid1 vdb1 vdc1[2]
      485454656 blocks [2/1] [U_]
      [>....................]  recovery =  3.0% (14577856/485454656) 
                               finish=72.8min speed=107724K/sec

root# mdadm --detail /dev/md0  
(while synchronization is running)
...
          State : clean, degraded, recovering
 Active Devices : 1
Working Devices : 2
 Failed Devices : 0
  Spare Devices : 1
 Rebuild Status : 75% complete
...
    Number   Major   Minor   RaidDevice State
       0       3        3        0      active sync        /dev/vdb1
       1       0        0        -      removed
       2      22        2        1      spare rebuilding   /dev/vdc1

root# mdadm --detail /dev/md0  
(after completion of synchronization)
...
          State : clean
 Active Devices : 2
Working Devices : 2
 Failed Devices : 0
  Spare Devices : 0
...
    Number   Major   Minor   RaidDevice State
       0       3        3        0      active sync   /dev/vdb1
       1      22        2        1      active sync   /dev/vdc1 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --stop</samp> disables a RAID array. The file system contained by it must first be removed from the directory tree by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umount</samp>:

```
root# umount /mount-directory/
root# mdadm --stop /dev/md0 
```

Only if you have not made any changes to the underlying partitions after <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --stop</samp> can you reassemble and activate the RAID array via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --assemble</samp> without any data loss:

```
root# mdadm --assemble /dev/md0 /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1
mdadm: /dev/md0 has been started with 2 drives. 
```

Context information (metadata) has been saved in a special block in all hard disk partitions that you have assembled into RAID partitions using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp>. You can read this information using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --query</samp>—for example, to determine the status of an unknown system:

```
root# mdadm --query /dev/sda3
/dev/vdb1: is not an md array
/dev/vdb1: device 0 in 2 device active raid1 /dev/md0\.  
Use mdadm --examine for more detail.
root# mdadm --query /dev/md0
/dev/md0: 19.98GiB raid1 2 devices, 0 spares. 
Use mdadm --detail for more detail. 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --examine</samp> provides detailed information about a partition that is part of a RAID array:

```
root# mdadm --examine /dev/sda3
/dev/vdb1:
     Raid Level : raid1
   Raid Devices : 2
 Avail Dev Size : 41904129 (19.98 GiB 21.45 GB)
     Array Size : 20952064 (19.98 GiB 21.45 GB)
            ...
    Device Role : Active device 0
    Array State : AA ('A' == active, '.' == missing, 'R' == replacing)
```

Similarly, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm --detail</samp> provides detailed information about a RAID array:

```
root# mdadm --detail /dev/md0
/dev/md0:
        Raid Level : raid1
               ...
    Active Devices : 2
   Working Devices : 2
    Failed Devices : 0
     Spare Devices : 0
               ...
    Number   Major   Minor   RaidDevice State
       0     252       17        0      active sync   /dev/vdb1
       1     252       33        1      active sync   /dev/vdc1 
```

How do you know that all redundantly stored data is really correct? Usually, the RAID system performs integrity tests only when it reads or writes files. However, many files are often not touched for months. Thus, in order to determine with certainty that the hard disks are OK, the RAID system must read all the data blocks and compare the redundant data. This process is also referred to as scrubbing:

```
root# echo check > /sys/block/mdn/md<n>/sync_action 
```

If errors occur in the process, they can be repaired:

```
root# echo repair > /sys/block/mdn/md<n>/sync_action 
```

On Debian and Ubuntu, this is taken care of by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/share/mdadm/checkarray</samp> script, which is started monthly via <samp class="listingcharacter">cron</samp>. On Fedora, the same function is performed by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d/raid-check cron</samp> script.

Storing RAID metadata in otherwise unused sectors of the RAID partition is usually a useful thing to do. However, if you want to use the hard disk differently at a later time, the RAID metadata can turn into a problem: Linux installation programs and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mdadm</samp> recognize the remnants of the RAID configuration and refuse to see that these partitions should now be used differently. To solve this problem, run the following command, which must be applied to all RAID partitions:

```
root# mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/vdb1 
```

### 18.15.3    Replacing a Defective RAID-1 Hard Disk

The starting point for this section is a Linux distribution where a RAID-1 setup has already been set up during the installation process (see [Chapter 22](#22_001.html_h22), [Section 22.1](#22_001.html_h22.1)). The device names for this example are <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sda</samp> for the first disk and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sdb</samp> for the second (defective) disk:

```
/dev/sda1:             Partition without RAID
/dev/sdb1:             Partition without RAID
/dev/sda2 + /dev/sdb2: RAID-1  ->  /dev/md0
/dev/sda3 + /dev/sdb3: RAID-1  ->  /dev/md1 
```

If the defective hard disk or SSD is still active in the RAID mounts, you must explicitly remove all partitions of this hard disk:

```
root# mdadm --remove  /dev/md0 /dev/sdb2
root# mdadm --remove  /dev/md1 /dev/sdb3 
```

After that, you need to get a replacement hard disk as soon as possible. The new hard disk must have enough space to create partitions on it that are as large as those on the existing hard disks.

Make sure that you really do remove the defective hard disk and not the still working one by mistake! This recommendation sounds trivial, but when a computer contains two or more identical hard disks, it isn’t that easy to find the right hard disk. Only the serial number is unique! You can find out which serial number is associated with which device name via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hdparm</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smartctl</samp>.
