The appearance of GRUB can vary greatly depending on the configuration. Some distributions start GRUB in graphics mode and thus take away the spartan look of the program. To be able to use various additional functions of GRUB, you must exit the graphics mode by pressing the (Esc) key.

Other distributions avoid displaying the GRUB menu at all if possible. For example, if Ubuntu is the only operating system installed on a computer, you will only get to see the GRUB menu if you press a key during the computer startup ((Shift) is enough).

[![Minimalistic GRUB Menu](bilderklein/klein19_002.png)](img-f19.2.html)

**Figure 19.2**     Minimalistic GRUB Menu

GRUB can be secured by a password. In this case, you can use GRUB's interactive functions only after pressing (P) and then specifying the password.

Unless the GRUB menu is secured by a password, you can change the GRUB menu entry just selected with the cursor keys by pressing (E) (edit). A few lines are then displayed, which describe in a rather idiosyncratic syntax how the operating system is to be started.

GRUB's editing functions are mainly used to specify additional kernel options before Linux starts—for example, to work around hardware problems. To do this, you want to look for a line that resembles the following pattern:

```
linux /pfad/vmlinuz-n.n.n root=/dev/xxx [various options] 
```

At the end of this line, you can add or change parameters. (Ctrl)+(X) or (F10) then starts Linux with the changed parameters. However, the changes are not saved!

GRUB reads the boot menu from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> file, which is stored in different locations depending on the distribution. The file contains commands that describe the GRUB menu items. So if you want to change the GRUB menu permanently, you need to start Linux and change the GRUB menu file (see the following section).

## 19.3    GRUB Configuration

The GRUB menu is defined by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/grub/grub.cfg</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/grub2/grub.cfg</samp> file. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> in the EFI directory contains a few lines of text that can be read by GRUB to indicate where the “correct” <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> file is located. Also, on Fedora and RHEL, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/grub2-efi.cfg</samp> link points to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/grub2/grub.cfg</samp>.

Manual changes to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> are not provided! The access rights of this file are therefore set to read-only. If you want to modify the GRUB menu, you must modify the underlying configuration files:

```
/etc/grub.d/*          
(general GRUB configuration files)
/etc/default/grub      
(additions: Debian, RHEL, SUSE, Ubuntu)
/etc/sysconfig/grub    
(additions: Fedora) 
```

To regenerate the GRUB menu file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp>, after changes to these files or after a kernel update, you must run one of the following commands:

```
root# update-grub                               
(Debian and Ubuntu)
root# grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg    
(Fedora, RHEL, SUSE) 
```

The resulting <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> file looks something like the following example. The following listing of an automatically generated version of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> on Ubuntu is heavily shortened for space reasons. By the way, don't be confused by the <samp class="listingcharacter">insmod ext2</samp> line: this GRUB module is responsible for all <samp class="listingcharacter">ext</samp> file systems, including <samp class="listingcharacter">ext3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp>. Further explanations of the syntax in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> follow later in this section:

```
# Example for /boot/grub/grub.cfg
# from /etc/grub.d/00_header
# Variable management code ...
# Definition of various functions: savedefault, recordfail, load_video
# Find font files ...

# from /etc/grub.d/05_debian_theme
# Set colors for text mode ...

# from /etc/grub.d/10_linux
# Definition of the gfxmode function ...

# Start Ubuntu
menuentry 'Ubuntu' ... {
  recordfail
  load_video
  gfxmode $linux_gfx_mode
  insmod gzio
  insmod part_gpt
  insmod ext2
  set root='hd0,gpt2
  search ... --set=root 508de33b-b057-4e5f-b936-db8eb1f5ae51
  linux   /boot/vmlinuz-6.2.0-20-generic root=UUID=4d68... ro quiet splash  $vt_handoff
  initrd  /boot/initrd.img-6.2.0-20-generic
}

# Menu with old Ubuntu versions and the rescue system
submenu 'Advanced options for Ubuntu' ... {
  menuentry 'Ubuntu, with Linux 5.11.0-13-generic' ... { ... }
  menuentry 'Ubuntu, with Linux 5.11.0-13-generic (recovery mode)' ... {
    ...
    linux   /boot/vmlinuz-5.11.0-13-generic root=UUID=4d68... ro recovery  nomodeset
    ...
  }
} 
```

On Debian and Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-grub</samp> command creates a new version of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp>. On Fedora and openSUSE, you need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub2-mkconfig -o /path/to/grub.cfg</samp> instead. The Debian- or Ubuntu-specific <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-grub</samp> script also contains only this command.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub2-mkconfig</samp> analyzes the configuration files or scripts described ahead. Among other things, GRUB menu entries are created for all kernel files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot</samp>. In addition, all accessible partitions are scanned. If they contain other operating systems, GRUB menu entries will also be created for them. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-grub</samp> takes a while to run on machines with many partitions. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub2-mkconfig</samp> is run automatically with each kernel update and ensures that the latest Linux kernel is included in the GRUB menu.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/grub</samp> file contains some global GRUB settings. Remember that changes made here will not take effect until you regenerate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp>! On Ubuntu, the configuration file contains the following settings:

```
# file /etc/default/grub (Ubuntu)
GRUB_DEFAULT=0
GRUB_TIMEOUT=10
GRUB_DISTRIBUTOR=`lsb_release -i -s 2> /dev/null || echo Debian`
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash"
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX= 
```

The default Fedora configuration looks as follows:

```
# file /etc/sysconfig/grub (Fedora)
GRUB_TIMEOUT=5
GRUB_DISTRIBUTOR="$(sed 's, release .*$,,g' /etc/system-release)"
GRUB_DEFAULT="saved"
GRUB_DISABLE_SUBMENU="true"
GRUB_TERMINAL_OUTPUT="console"
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="rhgb quiet"
GRUB_DISABLE_RECOVERY="true"
GRUB_ENABLE_BLSCFG="true" 
```

In the following sections, I explain the meaning of some parameters, even those that are not active by default:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_DEFAULT</samp> specifies which GRUB menu item should be selected by default. The <samp class="listingcharacter">saved</samp> setting means that the last selected menu item will be activated. However, this only works if the GRUB files are located in an ordinary partition! If instead LVM or RAID is involved, GRUB cannot save any environment variables after the menu selection.

    Another option is to assign the <samp class="listingcharacter">menuentry</samp> string of the desired menu item to <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_DEFAULT</samp>. However, you must be careful to keep the spelling exact.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_TIMEOUT</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">=n</samp> specifies how many seconds GRUB waits for a menu item to be selected. If this time elapses without user input, then GRUB starts the selected operating system. The time set here only comes into effect when the GRUB menu appears at all.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_DISTRIBUTOR</samp> variable is analyzed by the <samp class="listingcharacter">10_linux</samp> script, which I describe ahead. It specifies the name of the current distribution, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">Ubuntu</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Fedora</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT</samp> are also considered by <samp class="listingcharacter">10_linux</samp> and specify which options must be passed to the kernel. The <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX</samp> options apply to every boot; the <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT</samp> options are added additionally for standard boot, but not for recovery mode.

*   By default, the GRUB menu is displayed in graphics mode at a resolution of 640 × 480 pixels. If you want a higher resolution, you can set it using <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_GFXMODE</samp>. If you want to dispense with the graphics mode altogether, you can activate the <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_TERMINAL="console"</samp> (Debian/Ubuntu) or <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_TERMINAL_OUTPUT="console"</samp> (Fedora/RHEL) setting provided for this purpose. Both variables are analyzed by the <samp class="listingcharacter">00_header</samp> script. In the default setting, there is no clearly visible difference between text and graphics mode, but Unicode characters can only be displayed in graphics mode.

*   GRUB normally passes the root directory as a UUID number to the Linux kernel to be started. If you prefer to specify the device name instead (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sda1</samp>), you need to enable the <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_DISABLE_LINUX_UUID="true"</samp> line. This setting applies only to the start of the active distribution (<samp class="listingcharacter">10_linux</samp> script), not to other distributions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-grub</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub2-mkconfig</samp> usually also creates menu entries for starting Linux in recovery mode. This starts Linux in single-user mode and without displaying a splash screen. With <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_DISABLE_RECOVERY</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">="true"</samp>, no recovery entries are created.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">GRUB_ENABLE_BLSCFG="true"</samp> causes GRUB to analyze the configuration files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/loader/entries</samp> when creating the boot menu. Currently, this concept is only implemented in Fedora and RHEL. It causes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">boot.cfg</samp> to be much shorter because the actual boot entries are missing there. Their contents are loaded from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/loader/entries</samp> only when GRUB is executed. The details are documented at [https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/BootLoaderSpecByDefault](https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/BootLoaderSpecByDefault).

What is usually not included in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/grub</samp> is the setting of the <samp class="listingcharacter">GRUB_RECORDFAIL_TIMEOUT</samp> variable. This variable controls how long GRUB displays the menu if the computer froze during the last boot process (or if GRUB thinks it did, which is not always the same thing). By default, the time span is half a minute. Especially on a server where you cannot watch the boot process, this can create the impression that the computer is no longer responding at all. A solution to that problem would be to set a shorter timeout! For example:

```
# /etc/default/grub or /etc/sysconfig/grub
GRUB_RECORDFAIL_TIMEOUT=5 
```

On Fedora, RHEL, and its clones, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grubby</samp> command to make basic changes to the GRUB configuration without modifying the GRUB configuration files in an editor. The following command adds the <samp class="listingcharacter">selinux=0</samp> kernel option to all GRUB menu entries, thus disabling SELinux from the next boot:

```
root# grubby --update-kernel ALL --args selinux=0 
```

The second command undoes this change and removes <samp class="listingcharacter">selinux</samp> (with whatever setting) from the list of kernel parameters:

```
root# grubby --update-kernel ALL --remove-args selinux 
```

### 19.3.1    Automatic Generation of grub.cfg

The basic idea of the GRUB configuration is that you yourself only specify the basic data of the GRUB configuration. The final configuration file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp>, is generated automatically by a script, taking these specifications into account. The key point here is that the GRUB scripts take into account all installed kernel versions (important after a kernel update). Many distributions also include boot entries for other operating systems (like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp>; discussed ahead).

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/grub.d</samp> directory contains several executable script files for this purpose. When a new version of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> is to be created, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-grub</samp> executes all scripts contained in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.d</samp> in order. The result, the standard output of the scripts, ends up in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp>. The script-based approach unfortunately makes the configuration files quite confusing. Statements like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat << EOF</samp> are repeatedly embedded in the actual code, which direct all subsequent lines up to the abbreviation EOF to the standard output. These lines themselves often contain script code that is only analyzed by GRUB at system startup.

The two most interesting scripts are <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">10_linux</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">30_os-prober</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">10_linux</samp> provides two GRUB menu entries for each kernel version in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/ directory</samp>: one for an ordinary boot and a second one for a recovery boot in single-user mode and without a splash screen. The menu items are sorted by version numbers, with the latest version at the top of the list.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">30_os-prober</samp> calls the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp> script. It provides a list of all operating systems on all accessible hard disk partitions. Menu entries are then created for each of these operating systems, whereby Linux distributions draw on the possibly existing GRUB configuration. This causes countless scripts to be called, all of which are part of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp> package. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp> is actually a relic from the BIOS past, when GRUB was still responsible for starting all operating systems on a computer. Meanwhile, the EFI can take over this task. Some distributors have therefore decided to remove <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp> (such as Ubuntu from version 22.04 and Debian from version 12). This is why <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> only contains entries to start Ubuntu or Debian, but not those to start Windows or other Linux distributions installed on the computer. The main advantage of this change is that recreating <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> is now much faster.

As I said, normally you don't need GRUB menu entries for other operating systems anyway because you can use EFI to select the operating system. But in the event that something goes wrong with the EFI configuration, the additional GRUB entries are a good plan B, which I have often resorted to in the past in the event of boot problems.

Currently, the entire <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp> infrastructure is still included. It’s therefore quite easy to reactivate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">os-prober</samp>. To do this, you need to add the following line at the end of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/grub</samp>:

```
# in /etc/default/grub
GRUB_DISABLE_OS_PROBER=false 
```

Then recreate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> by calling <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-grub</samp>.

### 19.3.2    Syntax and Internal Details

A complete syntax description of all keywords allowed in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp> is impossible to provide here due to space limitations. I therefore limit myself in the following sections to the most important keywords that appear in the examples presented here. The official GRUB manual (the PDF version comprises 150 pages) can be found at the following address: [https://www.gnu.org/software/grub/manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/grub/manual).

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set varname=value</samp> to perform variable assignments. To read variables, you should use the $<samp class="listingcharacter">varname</samp> notation. When you run GRUB commands interactively, <samp class="listingcharacter">echo $varname</samp> displays the contents of a variable, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set</samp> returns all defined variables.

GRUB has its own terminology for naming hard disks and the partitions they contain. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">hd0,1</samp> denotes the first MBR partition of the first disk or SSD, while <samp class="listingcharacter">hd1,gpt8</samp> denotes the eighth GPT partition of the second disk.

As I explained in [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), the use of numbered devices for disks is prone to errors. That is why the use of UUIDs has also become established in GRUB:

```
search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set root 724f... 
```

The preceding statement searches for a file system with the specified UUID, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">724f</samp>. If the search is successful, GRUB saves the corresponding partition name in the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> variable because of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--set</samp> option.

With <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">insmod name</samp>, GRUB loads extension modules with additional functions at runtime. GRUB looks for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.mod</samp> module files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/grub[2]</samp> directory in the partition set by the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> variable. Important modules include <samp class="listingcharacter">part_msdos</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">part_gpt</samp> (read partition tables), <samp class="listingcharacter">ext2</samp> (file systems <samp class="listingcharacter">ext2</samp> through <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">raid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">raid5rec</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">raid6rec</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">mdraid</samp> (software RAID), <samp class="listingcharacter">lvm</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">gfxterm</samp> (graphical console), <samp class="listingcharacter">vbe</samp> (graphics system), and <samp class="listingcharacter">jpeg</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">tga</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">png</samp> for reading graphics files.

### 19.3.3    GRUB Menu Items

GRUB menu entries are introduced with the <samp class="listingcharacter">menuentry</samp> keyword. The following text is in quotation marks and may contain international characters. GRUB also supports submenus. When operating GRUB, pressing (Esc) from a submenu will return you to the main menu if necessary:

```
menuentry "Linux" {
  start commands ...
}
submenu 'Submenu' {
  menuentry 'Entry 1' { ... }
  menuentry 'Entry 2' { ... }
} 
```

The minimal version of a menu entry for starting Linux looks like the following example:

```
menuentry "Linux" {
  set root=(hd0,3)
  search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set root 724f...
  linux   /boot/vmlinuz-n.n.n    root=... ro quiet splash
  initrd  /boot/initrd.img-n.n.n
} 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set root</samp> specifies the partition where the kernel and initrd files are located. Alternatively, <samp class="listingcharacter">search</samp> looks for the partition whose file system has the specified UUID. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">linux</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">initrd</samp> keywords specify filenames relative to the partition.

The parameters specified with <samp class="listingcharacter">linux</samp> are passed to the kernel. You absolutely need <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> to specify the system partition, and <samp class="listingcharacter">ro</samp> so that access to the system partition is initially read-only. All other parameters are dependent on the distribution.

Many Linux distributions (such as Fedora and RHEL) provide for a separate boot partition during the installation. In this case, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set root</samp> to specify the boot partition. In turn, this means that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">linux</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">initrd</samp> do not need to specify the boot directory:

```
menuentry "Linux - With separate boot partition" {
  set root=(hd0,2)
  search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set root 59ac...
  linux   /vmlinuz-n.n.n     root=... ro quiet splash
  initrd  /initrd.img-n.n.n
} 
```

If the partition with the kernel and initrd files is part of an LVM system and/or a software RAID, you must load the corresponding GRUB modules. For RAID-5 or RAID-6, the <samp class="listingcharacter">raid5rec</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">raid6rec</samp> module will be added. In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">set root</samp>, you can then specify the system partition in the notation <samp class="listingcharacter">(lvname)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">(mdN)</samp>:

```
menuentry "Linux - With Software RAID" {
  insmod raid mdraid
  set root=(md0)
  search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set root 735c...
  linux   /boot/vmlinuz-n.n.n    root=... ro quiet splash
  initrd  /boot/initrd.img-n.n.n
}
menuentry "Linux - With LVM" {
  insmod lvm
  set root=(vg1-root)
  search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set root 6bb3...
  linux   /boot/vmlinuz-n.n.n    root=... ro quiet splash
  initrd  /boot/initrd.img-n.n.n
}
menuentry "Linux - LVM on RAID-5" {
  insmod raid raid5rec mdraid lvm
  set root=(vg1-root)
  search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set root 8ff4...
  linux   /boot/vmlinuz-n.n.n    root=/dev/mapper/... ro quiet splash
  initrd  /boot/initrd.img-n.n.n
} 
```

## 19.4    Manual GRUB Installation and First Aid

Usually, GRUB is set up correctly during the installation of your Linux distribution. As a result, you may make changes to the GRUB configuration or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub.cfg</samp>, but you do not need to touch the GRUB installation as such.

The following section is only relevant if you want to perform a manual installation of GRUB for some reason or if you need to repair a defective GRUB installation. To do this, start your computer from a USB flash drive that contains a live system. If you want to repair a Fedora installation, it’s best to use a Fedora live system, and an Ubuntu live system accordingly for Ubuntu.

### 19.4.1    Manual Installation and First Aid for EFI PCs

To manually install GRUB on an EFI machine, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub-install</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub2-install</samp>. On Fedora and RHEL, you must install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub2-efi-modules</samp> package beforehand:

```
root# grub-install     
(Debian, Ubuntu)
root# grub2-install    
(Fedora, SUSE, RHEL) 
```

This command creates the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/efi/EFI/distribution-name</samp> directory. A new boot file with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.efi</samp> extension that contains the GRUB code is written to this directory. In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.efi</samp> file is added to the list of EFI boot entries and placed there in the first place. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub-install</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efibootmgr</samp> command for this purpose, which is described in more detail in [Section 19.4.2](#19_004.html_h19.4.2).

For <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub-install</samp> to run successfully, some prerequisites must be met:

*   The GRUB configuration in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/grub[2]/grub.cfg</samp> file must be prepared.

*   The EFI partition must be mounted in the directory tree via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/efi</samp> path.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efibootmgr</samp> command from the package of the same name must be installed.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efivarfs</samp> kernel module must be loaded or compiled into the kernel. However, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">modprobe efivarfs</samp> only succeeds if the distribution was started in EFI mode, not in BIOS mode.

The following listing summarizes the commands required for an EFI installation from a live system. For this purpose, you need to create a working directory (here, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/syspart</samp>) and mount your system partition and the active <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sys</samp> directories there. Then use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chroot</samp> to temporarily make <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/syspart</samp> the new root directory.

If necessary, you must include the boot file system there now. Now update the GRUB configuration and write it to the EFI partition by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grub-install</samp>. Don't forget to replace <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/sda<n></samp> with your own device names in the following commands:

```
root# mkdir /syspart
root# mount /dev/sda2 /syspart                    
(system partition)
root# mount -o bind /dev  /syspart/dev          
root# mount -o bind /proc /syspart/proc         
root# mount -o bind /sys  /syspart/sys          
root# chroot /syspart                           
root# mount /dev/sda1 /boot/efi                   
(EFI partition)

root# update-grub                                 
(Debian and Ubuntu)
root# grub2-mkconfig -o /etc/grub2-efi.cfg        
(Fedora)
root# grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg      
(openSUSE)

root# grub[2]-install
root# exit 
```

When LVM is involved, things get even more complicated. In that case, you should do without the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bind-mount</samp> commands, use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">arch-chroot</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chroot</samp> (available on Fedora in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">arch-install-scripts</samp> package), and also include <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/run/lvm</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chroot</samp> environment. The following commands show the basic pattern:

```
root# mkdir /syspart
root# mount /dev/mapper/<name> /syspart
root# mkdir /syspart/hostlvm
root# mount -o bind /run/lvm /syspart/hostlvm
root# arch-chroot /syspart
root# ln -s /hostlvm /run/lvm 
```

You can find more tips on this in the Arch Linux forum at [https://bbs.archlinux.org/viewtopic.php?id=242594](https://bbs.archlinux.org/viewtopic.php?id=242594).

If you have network access in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chroot</samp> environment, you can also try out the following command on Fedora or RHEL:

```
root# dnf reinstall grub2-efi shim 
```

### 19.4.2    Changing EFI Boot Entries and Settings (efibootmgr)

How does EFI actually know which operating systems are installed or which boot entries it should display? On EFI mainboards, this information is stored in nonvolatile memory (NVRAM). Each time a new operating system is installed, a corresponding entry is stored in NVRAM once the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.efi</samp> file has been set up in the EFI partition.

On Linux, you can read or modify the EFI data stored in this way using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efibootmgr</samp> command. The command assumes that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efivarfs</samp> kernel module is loaded or compiled into the kernel. If that’s not the case, you should run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">modprobe efivarfs</samp>. This only succeeds if Linux was booted in EFI mode. If necessary, you can use a Linux live system that can be started in EFI mode for repair work!

When <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">efibootmgr</samp> is run without any other options, it lists the EFI boot entries and some other parameters of the EFI bootloader. The following listing (in shortened form) was created on my work notebook, on which three Linux distributions were installed at the time:

```
root# efibootmgr

BootCurrent: 001A
Timeout: 1 seconds
BootOrder: 001A,0000,0001,001B
Boot0000* ubuntu  HD(1,GPT,717a...,0x800,0x400001)/File(\EFI\ubuntu\shimx64.efi)
Boot0001* Fedora  HD(1,GPT,717a...,0x800,0x400001)/File(\EFI\fedora\shimx64.efi)
Boot0010  Setup                     FvFile(721c...)
Boot0011  Boot Menu                 FvFile(126a...)
Boot0012  Diagnostic Splash Screen  FvFile(a7d8...)
Boot0013  Lenovo Diagnostics        FvFile(3f7e...)
Boot0014  Regulatory Information    FvFile(478c...)
Boot0015  Startup Interrupt Menu    FvFile(f46e...)
Boot0016  Rescue and Recovery       FvFile(665d...)
Boot001A* NVMe0 VenMsg(bc78..., 001c...a400)
Boot001B* NVMe1 VenMsg(bc78..., 001c...a401) 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">BootCurrent</samp> tells you that the computer was last started with boot entry 001A. The bootloader was run on the NVMe0 disk (for Arch Linux with systemd-boot; see [Section 19.5](#19_005.html_h19.5)). The <samp class="listingcharacter">BootOrder</samp> variable means that the four specified menu items are taken into account during a restart. The first available system is actually started after a short waiting period. (So if the NVMe0 disk has been removed in the meantime, Ubuntu will come into play on the other SSD.) During the short wait time before the first bootloader starts, a mainboard-specific key combination (on my test computer, (F12)) can display the EFI menu. In it all entries listed in the previous listing are displayed, but the four mentioned in <samp class="listingcharacter">BootOrder</samp> are displayed first.

If you want Fedora to start once on the next reboot, you need to specify its boot entry with <samp class="listingcharacter">-n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--bootnext</samp>:

```
root# efibootmgr --bootnext 0001 
```

If you want to change the boot order permanently, you should specify the entry or a list of entries with the <samp class="listingcharacter">-o</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--bootorder</samp> option:

```
root# efibootmgr --bootorder 0001,001A,0000,001B 
```

The following command creates a new EFI boot entry. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">‐‐disk</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--part</samp> options to specify the location of the EFI partition. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐‐loader</samp> points to the EFI code to run, usually <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shimx64.efi</samp>. The path specification is relative to the EFI partition (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/efi</samp>), and <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> must be used as the directory separator. The doubling of the <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> characters is necessary because the shell interprets a single <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> character as a special character identifier. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--label</samp> determines the name to be displayed in the EFI menu:

```
root# efibootmgr  --create --disk /dev/nvme0n1 --part 2 \
        --loader \\EFI\\ubuntu\\shimx64.efi --label ubuntu 
```

Of course, you can also remove boot entries. To do this, use <samp class="listingcharacter">--bootnum</samp> to specify the number of the entry:

```
root# efibootmgr --bootnum 0001 --delete-bootnum 
```

## 19.5    systemd-boot

In short, GRUB works as follows on modern PCs: EFI loads the GRUB files from the EFI system partition (ESP) and starts them. Then GRUB searches the Linux file system for the kernel and the initrd file and starts the kernel. And finally, the kernel takes care of the actual system startup.

The systemd-boot project, which is part of systemd (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20)), saves one step in this process: the kernel and initrd file are placed right in the ESP and started by a tiny bootloader.

The systemd-boot project evolved from the EFI boot project called gummiboot (German for “rubber dinghy”).

This section only provides a brief overview of how systemd-boot works and the available configuration options. You can find more technical information on the following web pages:

*   [https://support.system76.com/articles/bootloader](https://support.system76.com/articles/bootloader)

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/systemd-boot](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/systemd-boot)

*   [https://www.rodsbooks.com/efi-bootloaders/gummiboot.html](https://www.rodsbooks.com/efi-bootloaders/gummiboot.html)

*   [https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd-boot.html](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd-boot.html)

The obvious advantage of systemd-boot is the strong simplification and associated (rather minimal) acceleration of the boot process. Because all necessary files are located in the EFI partition, the bootloader doesn’t have to deal with various file systems and all their special cases (LVM, RAID, and encryption).

Unfortunately, there are also disadvantages, and they are why systemd-boot has not gained more acceptance so far:

*   EFI is mandatory; systemd-boot is not compatible with old PCs or virtual machines without EFI.

*   The kernel and especially the associated initrd file take up a lot of space, typically around 50 to 100 MiB per release. For security reasons, the boot system is redundant. If there are boot problems after a kernel update, the previous kernel version can be selected in GRUB or systemd-boot. Sometimes the distribution still provides for a rescue system. This means that three kernels and three initrd files are required and the space requirement is already about 250 MiB. With parallel installation of further distributions, the space requirement multiplies.

    On notebook computers with preinstalled Windows, the EFI partition is often only 250 MiB. So even with the installation of only one Linux distribution, it can happen that the EFI partition is too small.

*   sytemd-boot can only boot Linux—no other operating systems.

*   By default, systemd-boot does not support UEFI Secure Boot (or only does so if you compile and sign the kernel yourself and store the key used in the EFI).

Currently, Pop!_OS uses systemd-boot by default on computers with EFI. For Arch Linux, you need to set up the boot system yourself during the installation and have a choice between systemd-boot and GRUB. In both cases, it’s recommended that the ESP be generously sized at 1 GiB. If the EFI partition is predefined by Windows and cannot be enlarged, it usually helps to simply set up a second EFI partition.

### 19.5.1    Operation

Visually, systemd-boot looks like GRUB (see [Figure 19.3](#19_005.html_f19.3)).

[![systemd-boot Options to Change Kernel Parameters](bilderklein/klein19_003.png)](img-f19.3.html)

**Figure 19.3**     systemd-boot Options to Change Kernel Parameters

You can use the cursor keys to select the desired kernel, (Enter) starts Linux. (E) takes you to a basic editor in which you can change the options passed to the kernel. Further interventions in the boot process are not possible.

### 19.5.2    Configuration

During the installation of Linux, all boot files are copied directly to a subdirectory of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/efi</samp>. The following lines show the files of Pop!_OS:

```
root# cd /boot/efi
root# tree
EFI
   BOOT
       BOOTX64.EFI
   Pop_OS-1f37...
       cmdline
       initrd.img
       initrd.img-previous
       vmlinuz.efi
       vmlinuz-previous.efi
   Recovery-7be5...
       initrd.gz
       vmlinuz.efi
   systemd
      systemd-bootx64.efi
loader
    entries
       Pop_OS-current.conf
       Pop_OS-oldkern.conf
       Recovery-7be5....conf
    loader.conf 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.conf</samp> files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/boot/efi/loader/entries</samp> determine the systemd boot menu entries. The only file to which changes are planned is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">loader.conf</samp>. This file specifies how long you have to select the kernel and which kernel is to be started by default. By default, Pop!_OS lacks the <samp class="listingcharacter">timeout</samp> line; the boot menu is then not displayed at all:

```
# file /boot/efi/loader/loader.conf
default Pop_OS-current
timeout 5 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bootctl</samp> command provides a summary of the current configuration without any further options. To reinstall or repair systemd-boot, you must run the command as follows:

```
root# bootctl --path=/boot/efi install 
```

This copies <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd-bootx64.efi</samp> and adds it to the list of EFI boot entries. You need to take care of the kernel and initrd files as well as the configuration files yourself.

On Pop!_OS, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">update-initramfs</samp> is configured so that each time a new initrd file is created as part of a kernel update, the relevant EFI files are also updated. If necessary, you can trigger this process manually:

```
root# apt install --reinstall linux-generic linux-headers-generic
root# update-initramfs -c -k all 
```

# 20    The Init System

This chapter describes the operations that take place from kernel startup to login. The kernel starts the init system as the first process. The init system then takes care of the basic configuration of the system, the mounting of file systems, and the starting of countless network services and daemons. The same init system is also responsible for shutting down the computer properly.

In recent years, systemd has established itself as the init system. That was not always the case. Until ten years ago, the Init-V system, which originated in Unix times, was commonly used, and for some time it looked as if the Upstart system developed by Ubuntu would have a chance to prevail.

For this reason, this chapter focuses largely on systemd. Init-V is only used marginally because there are still some services whose startup scripts have not been converted to systemd. While a compatibility layer of systemd takes care of such cases, it still doesn't hurt if you have at least a rough idea of Init-V concepts.

The chapter also briefly describes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt</samp> commands and goes into some distribution-specific details in the init processes of Fedora/RHEL, Debian/Ubuntu, Raspberry Pi OS, and SUSE/openSUSE.

## 20.1    systemd

systemd is a comparatively new init system developed by Red Hat employee Lennart Poettering and was first used in Fedora in 2011\. Most current Linux distributions have followed its example.

As usual on Linux, systemd is configured using text files. systemd itself, however, is a compiled program. This is remarkable in that traditional init systems consisted of countless shell scripts. systemd uses control groups (cgroups) to execute and monitor processes. Cgroups is a kernel function that limits the resources of a process (CPU, memory, I/O). systemd starts each process in its own cgroup. When the number of processes in this group drops to 0, systemd knows that the process has terminated or crashed and can restart it if necessary.

In an increasing number of distributions, systemd is not only responsible for the administration of system services, but also takes care of the start of user-specific processes after a login—for example, when initializing a GNOME session.

### Directory Locations

This section describes systemd as it is currently implemented in most distributions. However, individual distributions use different directory locations; for example, openSUSE uses <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib/systemd</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/systemd</samp>.

The following points provide a brief overview of the system startup:

*   GRUB loads and starts the kernel.

*   The kernel starts the systemd process. The program file is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib/systemd</samp> directory or in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/bin</samp> in most distributions.

*   Any options passed to the kernel (referred to as boot options) that the kernel does not know about are passed to systemd.

*   systemd analyzes the configuration files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">[usr]/lib/systemd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd</samp>, performs the initialization tasks mentioned there, and starts network services and the display manager, including the graphics system.

*   The user will see the login prompt after a few seconds. In many distributions, another systemd instance is started at the user level after login to run various processes required for the desktop system.

systemd is therefore the first running process. All other processes are started either directly by systemd or indirectly by its subprocesses. If you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pstree</samp> in a terminal, you will immediately see the dominant role of systemd! (In some distributions, the first process seems to be <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sbin/init</samp>, not <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd</samp>, but in fact <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/sbin/init</samp> is then a link to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemd</samp>.)

When the computer is shut down, systemd is the last process still running and takes care of terminating all other processes correctly.

During system initialization, things are done that only need to be done once during computer startup:

*   Initialize various system variables (including host and domain name)

*   Enable the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/proc</samp> file system and various other temporary file systems

*   Set date and time

*   Set keyboard layout for the text console

*   Start the <samp class="listingcharacter">udev</samp> system

*   Possibly enable RAID and LVM

*   Check file systems

*   Remount root partition in read-write mode

*   Check and mount the file system of the other partitions

*   Initialize network functions

### 20.1.1    Administration

The central command to administrate systemd is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp>. This allows you to manually start and stop services described by a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.service</samp> file:

```
root# systemctl start   sshd  
(start SSH daemon)
root# systemctl stop    sshd  
(stop SSH daemon)
root# systemctl restart sshd  
(restart SSH daemon)
root# systemctl reload  sshd  
(reload configuration of SSH daemon)
root# systemctl status  sshd  
(determine status of SSH daemon) 
```

#### ssh versus sshd; httpd versus apache

Almost all distributions have now adopted systemd as their init system. However, this does not mean that all configuration files are standardized!

On Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE, the service file for the SSH server is called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sshd.service</samp>, but it is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh.service</samp> on Debian and Ubuntu! Accordingly, for Debian and Ubuntu, you would need to replace <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sshd</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> in all of the previously listed commands. Fortunately, an alias statement is included in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh.service</samp>, which is why the examples provided here work across different distributions.

However, this is not true for every service. Sometimes you need to research the correct service name. For example, the Apache web server can be started on Fedora and RHEL using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start httpd</samp>, but on Debian and Ubuntu via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start apache2</samp>!

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp> can also be used to permanently enable/disable a service (like the former <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chkconfig xxx on/off</samp>):

```
root# systemctl enable  sshd 
  Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/sshd.service
               -> /usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service.
root# systemctl disable sshd 
  Removed /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/sshd.service. 
```

So when services are activated, a new link is created, and when they are deactivated, this link is removed.

#### Start and Enable at the Same Time

It’s often necessary to start a service and enable it permanently. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable</samp>, you can simply run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable --now</samp> with current systemd versions in such cases.

Similarly, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl disable --now</samp> corresponds to the single <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl stop</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl disable</samp> commands.

When <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp> is called without any other parameters, it returns a list of all processes managed by systemd:

```
user$ systemctl
UNIT                   LOAD   ACTIVE SUB       JOB DESCRIPTION
sys-devices-xxx        loaded active plugged   /sys/devices/virtual/
                                                block/dm-0
sys-devices-yyy        loaded active plugged   /sys/devices/virtual/
                                                block/dm-1
...
-.mount                loaded active mounted   /
boot.mount             loaded active mounted   /boot
dev-hugepages.mount    loaded active mounted   Huge Pages File System
...
chronyd.service        loaded active running   NTP client/server
colord.service         loaded active running   Manage Color Profiles
crond.service          loaded active running   Command Scheduler
cups.service           loaded active running   CUPS Scheduler
...
146 loaded units listed. Pass --all to see loaded but inactive units, too.To show all installed unit files use 'systemctl list-unit-files'. 
```

### 20.1.2    Targets

Targets define operating states that a Linux system should achieve. You can determine the currently valid default target by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl get-default</samp>:

```
root# systemctl get-default
multi-user.target 
```

Common default targets include <samp class="listingcharacter">multi-user.target</samp> for servers (full functionality, but without graphics system) and <samp class="listingcharacter">graphical.target</samp> for desktop operation. Targets can depend on each other; several targets can be active at the same time. You can get a list of all targets by using the following command. The result shows the active targets of a Fedora system with an active graphical user interface:

```
user$ systemctl list-units --type=target
UNIT                   LOAD   ACTIVE SUB    DESCRIPTION                  
basic.target           loaded active active Basic System                 
cryptsetup.target      loaded active active Local Encrypted Volumes      
getty.target           loaded active active Login Prompts                
graphical.target       loaded active active Graphical Interface          
local-fs-pre.target    loaded active active Local File Systems (Pre)     
local-fs.target        loaded active active Local File Systems           
multi-user.target      loaded active active Multi-User System            
network-online.target  loaded active active Network is Online            
network-pre.target     loaded active active Network (Pre)                
network.target         loaded active active Network                      
nfs-client.target      loaded active active NFS client services          
nss-lookup.target      loaded active active Host and Network Name Lookups
nss-user-lookup.target loaded active active User and Group Name Lookups
paths.target           loaded active active Paths                        
remote-fs-pre.target   loaded active active Remote File Systems (Pre)    
remote-fs.target       loaded active active Remote File Systems          
rpc_pipefs.target      loaded active active rpc_pipefs.target            
slices.target          loaded active active Slices                       
sockets.target         loaded active active Sockets                      
sound.target           loaded active active Sound Card                   
sshd-keygen.target     loaded active active sshd-keygen.target           
swap.target            loaded active active Swap                         
sysinit.target         loaded active active System Initialization        
timers.target          loaded active active Timers                       

LOAD   = Reflects whether the unit definition was properly loaded.

ACTIVE = The high-level unit activation state, i.e. generalization of SUB.

SUB    = The low-level unit activation state, values depend on unit type.

24 loaded units listed. Pass --all to see loaded but inactive units, too. 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">isolate</samp> command allows you to change the current operating state. Thus, you can perform a reboot via the following command (of course, it’s easier to just run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp>):

```
root# systemctl isolate reboot.target   
(reboot computer) 
```

The default target is defined by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/system/system/default.target</samp> link. Changing the default target and thus resetting this link can most easily be done using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl set-default</samp>:

```
root# systemctl set-default multi-user.target
Removed symlink /etc/systemd/system/default.target.

Created symlink from /etc/systemd/system/default.target 
                  to /usr/lib/systemd/system/multi-user.target 
```

Unlike the Init-V system, systemd does not know a single-user mode. Its role is taken over by the emergency target. This target can be enabled by adding the <samp class="listingcharacter">single</samp> keyword to the <samp class="listingcharacter">linux</samp> line of the GRUB boot entry at boot time. The system initialization is then kept to a minimum; in particular, there is no network access. Login is only possible in the first text console with the root password.

The emergency target is intended for repair work. When that is successfully completed, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl isolate multi-user</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">graphical</samp> to activate the normal operating state.

If you press (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(Del) in a text console, the computer will restart. It is the special target file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/system/system/ctrl-alt-del.target</samp>, that is responsible for this behavior.

### 20.1.3    Configuration

The configuration files for systemd are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd/</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/systemd/</samp> (Debian, Fedora, RHEL, Ubuntu) or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib/system</samp> (openSUSE) directories. In total, this involves almost 1,000 files, which means that the configuration is quite complex and at least as confusing as with the Init-V system.

Units play a central role in the systemd concept. They describe objects that are to be controlled by the init system. Not only does this include services that need to be started or stopped, but also network interfaces, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> directories, swap partitions, and so on.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.target</samp> files to connect multiple units into a group. Targets are comparable to Init-V runlevels (see [Section 20.4.1](#20_004.html_h20.4.1)), but there are usually many more targets that can relate to each other. The following lines show the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">graphical.target</samp> file:

```
# file /lib/systemd/system/graphical.target (Fedora)
[Unit]
Description=Graphical Interface
Documentation=man:systemd.special(7)
Requires=multi-user.target
Wants=display-manager.service
Conflicts=rescue.service rescue.target
After=multi-user.target rescue.service rescue.target \
  display-manager.service
AllowIsolate=yes 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">graphical.target</samp> thus requires <samp class="listingcharacter">multi-user.target</samp> and also requires <samp class="listingcharacter">display-manager.service</samp>. Each target can be linked to an additional <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement"><name>.target.wants</samp> directory, in which further units are listed by means of files or by links to files; those units are supposed to be activated as well. For <samp class="listingcharacter">graphical.target</samp>, this listing contains only one entry:

```
root# cd /lib/systemd/system/graphical.target.wants
root# ls -l
 systemd-update-utmp-runlevel.service -> ../systemd-update-utmp-runlevel.service 
```

What is much more interesting is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/system/system/sysinit.target.wants</samp> directory with various links to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.service</samp> files for system initialization:

```
root# ls /lib/systemd/system/sysinit.target.wants/
cryptsetup.target
dev-hugepages.mount
dev-mqueue.mount
dracut-shutdown.service
kmod-static-nodes.service
ldconfig.service
...
systemd-udevd.service
systemd-udev-trigger.service
systemd-update-done.service
systemd-update-utmp.service
systemd-vconsole-setup.service 
```

Service (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.service</samp>) files describe which requirements must be met for starting a service and which command should be started. These files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd/system</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/systemd/system</samp> directories. As an example, the following listing shows the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd.service</samp> file, which is responsible for starting the Apache web server on Fedora:

```
# file /lib/systemd/system/httpd.service (Fedora)
[Unit]
Description=The Apache HTTP Server
Wants=httpd-init.service
After=network.target remote-fs.target nss-lookup.target \
  httpd-init.service
Documentation=man:httpd.service(8)

[Service]
Type=notify
Environment=LANG=C
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/httpd $OPTIONS -DFOREGROUND
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/httpd $OPTIONS -k graceful
# Send SIGWINCH for graceful stop
KillSignal=SIGWINCH
KillMode=mixed
PrivateTmp=true
OOMPolicy=continue
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target 
```

### 20.1.4    systemd at User Level

On an increasing number of distributions, systemd is also active at the user level, where it takes care of the execution of some processes after a login to GNOME. For this purpose, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pam_systemd</samp> PAM module starts a separate systemd process that only has the rights of an ordinary user:

```
root# ps axu | grep 'systemd '
USER      PID  ...  COMMAND
root        1       /usr/lib/systemd/systemd --switched-root --system
gdm       937       /usr/lib/systemd/systemd --user
kofler   1616       /usr/lib/systemd/systemd --user 
```

By default, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp> command always refers to the system level, even if the command is executed without <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. To determine the processes started by systemd at the user level, you must pass the additional <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--user</samp> option. The following output is, like many other listings in this chapter, heavily shortened for reasons of space (on Fedora, the command lists about 60 services!):

```
user$ systemctl --user list-units --type=service
UNIT                  LOAD   ACTIVE SUB     DESCRIPTION
at-spi-dbus-bus       loaded active running Accessibility ...
dbus...               loaded active running D-Bus User Message Bus
dconf.service         loaded active running User preferences database
evolution-...         loaded active running Evolution address ...
gnome-session-manager... loaded active running GNOME Session Manager
gnome-session-monitor... loaded active running Monitor Session leader ...
gnome-terminal-server    loaded active running GNOME Terminal Server
gvfs-...                 loaded active running Virtual filesystem ...
...
```

systemd searches the following directories for service files:

```
/lib/systemd/user
/etc/systemd/user
~/.local/share/systemd/user
~/.config/share/systemd/user 
```

Note that systemd runs at the user level, but not at the session level. The systemd process is started when the user in question logs in for the first time and is terminated with the user's last active session. This also applies if a user is logged in multiple times and therefore multiple sessions are active.

An overview of all sessions controlled by systemd is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">loginctl</samp> command:

```
user$ loginctl
SESSION     UID   USER     SEAT   TTY             
     c1      42   gdm      seat0  /dev/tty1       
      2    1000   kofler   seat0  /dev/tty2       
      4    1000   kofler 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">loginctl show-session</samp> to determine details about a session, including whether the session uses Xorg, Wayland, or just a TTY interface, as is the case with SSH logins:

```
root# loginctl show-session -p Type 2
Type=wayland 
```

### 20.1.5    Additional Functions

In the course of the changeover to systemd, Lennart Poettering has proposed also standardizing various configuration files, which in the past were stored by almost every distribution in a different location and for which different syntax rules also partly applied. By now, most systemd-based distributions use the configuration files listed in [Table 20.1](#20_001.html_t20.1). For details on some of these files and their associated configuration tools, see [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14).

| Function | Previous Location | New Location | Command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Host name | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/network</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hostname</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostnamectl</samp> |
| Server ID | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/dbus/machine-id</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/machine-id</samp> | – |
| Language | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/i18n</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/locale.conf</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp> |
| Keyboard | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/keyboard</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/vconsole.conf</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">localectl</samp> |
| Time zone | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/clock</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/localtime</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">timedatectl</samp> |
| Modules | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/modules</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/modules-load.d/*</samp> | – |
| Distribution | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/xxx-release</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/os-release</samp> | – |

**Table 20.1**     Changed Configuration Files

systemd includes a syslog-compatible logging system: the journal. The logging files are stored in a binary format and are thus protected against subsequent changes (see [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14), [Section 14.13](#14_013.html_h14.13)).

The ystem timer function can take care of the regular execution of processes, similar to Cron. This Cron variant, which is currently still rarely used, is described in more detail in [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10), [Section 10.7](#10_007.html_h10.7).

### 20.1.6    Compatibility

systemd is compatible with the conventional Init-V system. Init scripts located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/init.d/</samp> directory can thus be started or terminated as before. However, the smaller the number of conventional Init-V scripts in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/init.d</samp>, the better the respective distribution has been optimized for systemd.

In some distributions, especially Debian and all derived distributions, both Init-V and systemd configuration files are installed redundantly for important services. The systemd files have priority in this case, while the Init-V files are only considered if systemd is not used. This is the case, for example, with the Debian alternative Devuan, which does not use systemd.

Services that are started by systemd via Init-V scripts are marked by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">LSB</samp> label (for Linux Standard Base). You can therefore quickly determine the services in question by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl | grep LSB</samp>. In most modern distributions, there are no active Init-V scripts anymore; that is, the command returns an empty result.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">service</samp> command, which was widely used in the past to control init functions, also works with systemd. For example, if you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">service httpd stop</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">service</samp> detects that the web server is controlled by systemd and runs <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl stop httpd.service</samp>.

### 20.1.7    Documentation

systemd is excellently documented. All functions, strategies and advantages of systemd are completely described in various manual pages (especially <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd</samp>) and on the website of systemd developer Lennart Poettering:

*   [https://systemd.io/](https://systemd.io/)

*   [http://0pointer.de/blog/projects/systemd-docs.html](http://0pointer.de/blog/projects/systemd-docs.html)

If you prefer short and concise texts, the following two pages will be useful. They summarize the most important changes compared to Init-V and answer some FAQs:

*   [https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/SysVinit_to_Systemd_Cheatsheet](https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/SysVinit_to_Systemd_Cheatsheet)

*   [https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/FrequentlyAskedQuestions](https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/FrequentlyAskedQuestions)

## 20.2    Custom systemd Services

For network services that are available in ready-made packages, you do not need to worry about systemd configuration: the required files are supplied by all distributions. On Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE, you have to start the service using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable --now</samp> and enable it permanently. On Debian, Raspberry Pi OS, and Ubuntu, even this step is omitted.

How do you anchor a custom service in systemd? This section explains the syntax of custom systemd service files and presents two usage examples.

### 20.2.1    Custom systemd Configuration File

To set up a systemd service, you must create a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.service</samp> file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/systemd/system</samp> directory. Again, it’s convenient if you use a service file from another comparable service as a guide. The default service files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/lib/systemd/system</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib/systemd/system</samp> directories, depending on the distribution.

A minimal service file looks as follows:

```
[Unit]
Description=Foo
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/foo-daemon
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target 
```

This means that the <samp class="listingcharacter">Foo</samp> service is supposed to be started as the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">foo-daemon</samp> background process. An explicit stop command is missing; therefore systemd will first send the <samp class="listingcharacter">SIGTERM</samp> signal to terminate and, if that doesn’t help, also <samp class="listingcharacter">SIGKILL</samp> to the process.

A command name with a complete path must be passed to <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStart</samp>. In the same way, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStop</samp> to specify a second command to be executed when the background process is to be terminated.

You can distribute extensive commands across several lines with the <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> character.

Within the service file, the <samp class="listingcharacter">%n</samp> abbreviation is replaced with the name of the service.

Usually you can’t specify multiple commands using <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStart</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStop</samp>. If you want to do this, you must specify <samp class="listingcharacter">Type=oneshot</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">[Service]</samp> block. Then any number of <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStart</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStop</samp> statements is allowed, and these will be executed in sequence.

If you want to explicitly switch between two states (<samp class="listingcharacter">start</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">stop</samp>) in such a configuration, then you must also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">RemainAfterExit</samp> keyword as in [Section 20.2.3](#20_002.html_h20.2.3). The option causes systemd to remember the currently activated state. Without this option, systemd believes that the action has ended with the end of the last <samp class="listingcharacter">StartExec</samp> command after <samp class="listingcharacter">systemctl start name</samp> and immediately sets the status back to <samp class="listingcharacter">stop</samp>. An explicit execution of <samp class="listingcharacter">systemctl stop</samp> will then have no effect.

For the example in [Section 20.2.1](#20_002.html_h20.2.1), <samp class="listingcharacter">Type=simple</samp> was implicitly valid. In this case, systemd assumes that the command specified with <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStart</samp> is the service to be started. Once this program ends, systemd considers the service to have been properly terminated.

The third important type for services is <samp class="listingcharacter">Type=fork</samp>. You choose this variant if the command specified with <samp class="listingcharacter">ExecStart</samp> starts another background program (i.e., a daemon). In this case, you should use <samp class="listingcharacter">PIDFile</samp> to specify a file where the process number is stored. This allows systemd to monitor the background process or stop it if necessary.

For more information on writing your own systemd service files, see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.service</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man systemd.exec</samp>, and the following pages:

*   [https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Packaging:Systemd](https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Packaging:Systemd)

*   [https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Systemd](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Systemd)

*   [http://0pointer.de/blog/projects/systemd-for-admins-3.html](http://0pointer.de/blog/projects/systemd-for-admins-3.html)

### 20.2.2    Example 1: Setting up Docker Containers as a Service

The following example shows how you can run a MySQL server as a service in a Docker container. This is useful if the automation provided by Docker (<samp class="listingcharacter">restart always</samp>) isn’t flexible enough for the task and you want to control the container in compliance with other services as needed using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl start</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">stop</samp>, and so on.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Unit</samp> section of the service file specifies that, as a prerequisite for the service, Docker itself must first be started.

The three <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ExecStartPre</samp> statements ensure that the container named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mysql-db-book</samp> is stopped and deleted and that the latest version of the MySQL image is downloaded. The minus signs in front of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">stop</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rm</samp> commands mean that when these commands are executed, an error will simply be ignored. (If the image has already been stopped and/or deleted before, then this isn’t a cause for concern.) The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ExecStart</samp> statement that runs across several lines finally starts the container, using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/kofler/docker-mysql-volume</samp> volume directory and host port 13306\. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ExecStop</samp> specifies what needs to be done to stop the service. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">RemainAfterExit=true</samp> means that systemd memorizes the currently activated state. Without this option, systemd would assume that the service has already ended after the successful execution of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">docker run</samp>. But actually the container continues to run in the background:

```
# File /etc/systemd/system/docker-mysql.service
[Unit]
Description=starts MySQL server as Docker container
After=docker.service
Requires=docker.service
# max. 5 start attempts within 500 seconds
StartLimitIntervalSec=500
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
RemainAfterExit=true
ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/docker stop mysql-container
ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/docker rm mysql-container
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/docker pull mysql
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker run -d \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    -v /home/kofler/docker-mysql-volume:/var/lib/mysql \
    -p 13306:3306 --name mysql-container mysql
ExecStop=/usr/bin/docker stop mysql-container
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target 
```

For efficiency reasons, systemd keeps the contents of important configuration files in a cache. After configuration changes, you must therefore prompt systemd to reread the configuration files:

```
root# systemctl daemon-reload 
```

To start masquerading immediately and in the future every time the multiuser target is reached, the following command is required:

```
root# systemctl enable --now docker-mysql 
```

### 20.2.3    Example 2: Logging the Computer Startup and Shutdown

The goal of the second example is to log the time of each computer startup and shutdown in a separate logging file. This task is performed by the following service file:

```
# file /etc/systemd/system/shutdownlog.service
[Unit]
Description=Log shutdown

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=true
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo "on:  $(date)" >> /var/log/shutdownlog' 
ExecStop=/bin/sh -c  'echo "off: $(date)" >> /var/log/shutdownlog' 

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target 
```

To activate the new service, run the following commands:

```
root# systemctl daemon-reload
root# systemctl enable --now shutdownlog 
```

## 20.3    Shutdown, Reboot, and Halt

The init system is not only responsible for the initialization of a Linux system, but also for the correct shutdown. This elementary operation can be triggered by a menu command on desktop systems. For a server or in a virtual machine without a graphical user interface, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt</samp> commands instead. The three commands then forward the restart request to the active init system.

As the name suggests, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp> shuts down the computer. A time must be specified—either absolutely in the <samp class="listingcharacter">hh:mm</samp> format or relatively (<samp class="listingcharacter">+m</samp>, i.e., in <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> minutes) or immediately (<samp class="listingcharacter">now</samp>). Optionally, you can also specify a message. This message is visible to all users working in a text console or via SSH:

```
root# shutdown -r 23:00 "Reboot for maintenance". 
```

The init system then notifies all programs that they will be stopped shortly. Programs have a few seconds to save backups of open files, complete or revoke database transactions, and so on. All programs that are still running after a certain time (usually 20 or 30 seconds) are then forcibly terminated (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kill -9</samp>).

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp> can be supplemented by some options: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> causes the computer to be restarted after shutdown (reboot). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-f</samp> causes the file system to be checked on the next reboot. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp> creates the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/forcefsck</samp> file for this purpose.

With <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp> (cancel), you can revoke a shutdown that is planned for the future if it hasn’t started yet.

The additional <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-p</samp> option causes the computer to be explicitly switched off after a shutdown. On “real” computers, the option is mostly superfluous. However, virtualization systems often recognize the shutdown of a virtual machine only if the option is specified.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp> are variants of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt</samp> corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown now</samp>. In virtual machines, a complete shutdown often requires <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt -p</samp> (discussed previously).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp> corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown -r now</samp>.

In distributions with systemd, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp> are implemented as links to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/systemctl</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp> analyzes how it was started and then initiates the appropriate actions.

On my notebook computer, the hibernation mode (suspend mode) doesn’t always function properly; errors sometimes occur during its activation and during the wake-up process.

As if that weren’t annoying enough, sometimes an “exciting” follow-up problem occurs: the notebook can no longer be switched off or restarted. When the reboot is initiated in the desktop, the notebook just keeps running without any error message. A <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp> command in the terminal at least returns an error message:

```
Failed to start poweroff.target: Transaction is destructive 
```

A look at the journal then reveals the following:

```
Requested transaction contradicts existing jobs 
```
