| /etc/apache2/apache2.conf | Starting point |
| /etc/apache2/httpd.conf | User-specific configuration |
| /etc/apache2/ports.conf | Monitored ports, usually port 80 |
| /etc/apache2/conf.d/* | More configuration files |
| /etc/apache2/mods-available/ | Available extension modules |
| /etc/apache2/mods-enabled/*.conf | Links to active extension modules |
| /etc/apache2/conf-available/ | Available configuration files |
| /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/*.conf | Links to active configuration files |
| /etc/apache2/sites-available/ | Available websites (virtual hosts) |
| /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/*.conf | Links to active websites |
| /etc/apache2/envvars | Environment variables for the init script |

**Table 24.2**     Apache Configuration on Debian and Ubuntu

| Files | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf | Starting point |
| /etc/httpd/conf/magic | MIME configuration (for <samp class="listingcharacter">mod_mime</samp>) |
| /etc/httpd/conf.d/*.conf | Other configuration files |

**Table 24.3**     Apache Configuration on Fedora and RHEL

| Files | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| /etc/apache2/httpd.conf | Starting point |
| /etc/apache2/*.conf | Global configuration files |
| /etc/apache2/conf.d/*.conf | Other configuration files |
| /etc/apache2/sysconfig.d/*.conf | System configuration files |
| /etc/apache2/vhosts.d/*.conf | Websites (virtual hosts) |
| /etc/sysconfig/apache2 | Basic settings |

**Table 24.4**     Apache Configuration on SUSE

On Debian/Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mods-available</samp> directory contains a collection of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.load</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.conf</samp> files for various Apache modules. To enable additional modules, you need to set up links to these files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mods-enabled</samp>. The Debian-specific <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2enmod</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2dismod</samp> commands help you to manage the links. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2ensite</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2dissite</samp> to enable or disable virtual hosts. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sites-available</samp> contains only the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">000-default.conf</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">default-ssl.conf</samp> files: various basic settings for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www</samp> directory can be found there. The mechanism works in the same way as with the modules: The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sites-available</samp> directory contains the configuration files for all hosts, while <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sites-enabled</samp> contains the corresponding links.

The same mechanism takes care of other configuration files. The files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">conf-available</samp> directory. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2enconf</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2disconf</samp> commands are used to create and remove links to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">conf-enabled</samp> directory. On older Ubuntu versions as well as Debian, such configuration files are stored in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">conf.d</samp> and are managed manually without commands.

On SUSE, all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.conf</samp> files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sysconf.d</samp> directory are recreated by the init system at each Apache startup. It is therefore pointless to make changes to these files. Rather, you must change the variables in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/apache2</samp>. This file also defines which modules are loaded when Apache is started (<samp class="listingcharacter">APACHE_MODULES</samp> variable). If you want to add your own file to the SUSE configuration files, you must specify its filename in the <samp class="listingcharacter">APACHE_CONF_INCLUDE_FILES</samp> variable.

After making changes to the syntax, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd -t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd2 -t</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apache2 -t</samp> to test whether the configuration is free of syntax errors. On Debian and Ubuntu, you have to load some environment variables from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">envvars</samp> prior to that:

```
root# . /etc/apache2/envvars
root# apache2 -t
Syntax OK 
```

Then you want to prompt Apache to reload the configuration files:

```
root# systemctl reload apache2  
(Debian, SUSE, Ubuntu)
root# systemctl reload httpd    
(Fedora, RHEL) 
```

After making changes to the SSL configuration, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl reload</samp> is not sufficient. You need to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl restart</samp>.

The Apache web server usually works right away. However, depending on your network configuration, you may often need to change or add a line to the configuration files. <samp class="listingcharacter">ServerName</samp> should contain the name of your computer. If this setting does not take effect, you must also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">UseCanonicalName Off</samp> setting:

```
# in   /etc/apache2/apache2.conf    (Debian/Ubuntu) 
# or /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf   (Fedora/RHEL)
# enter the name of your computer here:
ServerName example.com 
```

For SUSE, you need to set the host name in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/apache2</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">APACHE_SERVERNAME</samp> variable.

### 24.1.2    Default Character Set

All common Linux distributions automatically use the Unicode UTF-8 character set. So if you use a text editor to create a text file that contains German letters like ä, ö, ü, or ß or French letters like ç or é, they will be saved in UTF-8 encoding.

Apache generally doesn’t care about the coding of the HTML files. The program simply transfers the files byte by byte to the web browser that requested the page. However, Apache also sends a so-called header, which, among other things, contains information about the character set in which the page is encoded. The web browser analyzes this information and uses the specified character set to display the page.

The crucial point is that Apache specifies the correct character set: if this goes wrong, the user will see some strange character combinations in the web browser instead of ä or ü. For this reason, Apache provides various character set configuration options:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset off</samp> This setting causes Apache to analyze the <samp class="listingcharacter"><meta></samp> tag in the HTML file to be transferred and send the character set specified there to the browser. If the HTML file starts as follows, the Unicode UTF-8 character set will be applied:

    ```
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html>
     <head>
     <meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=utf‐8" />
     ... 
    ```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset character set</samp> Apache transfers the character set specified here to the browser for all pages. The setting applies to both HTML and PHP files. The <samp class="listingcharacter"><meta></samp> tag in the HTML code will be ignored.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AddCharset character set identifier</samp> This sets a character set for files with a specific identifier. <samp class="listingcharacter">AddCharset utf-8 .utf8</samp> thus causes Unicode UTF-8 to be sent to the browser as the character set for all files whose name ends in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.utf8</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">AddCharset</samp> requires the Apache module, <samp class="listingcharacter">mod_mime</samp>.

Of course, a different default configuration will apply for different distributions. For the global default value of the character set, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/conf-enabled/charset.conf</samp> configuration file is provided on Debian and Ubuntu. Usually, this file is empty; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset off</samp> applies.

You can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">AddCharset</samp> in virtual host configuration files (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sites-available</samp> directory) and in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.htaccess</samp> files if you want a host-specific or directory-specific configuration. Note, however, that the character set settings in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.htaccess</samp> are only taken into account if <samp class="listingcharacter">AllowOverride All</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">FileInfo</samp> applies to the web directory.

For Fedora and RHEL, <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset UTF-8</samp> applies. The setting is located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf</samp>. In the same file, <samp class="listingcharacter">AllowOverride None</samp> is also set for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www/html</samp> directory.

SUSE lacks an explicit character set setting in the configuration files. This means that <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset off</samp> applies; that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><meta></samp> information in the HTML files is decisive for the correct character set recognition. A suitable place to set <samp class="listingcharacter">AddDefaultCharset</samp> is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/mod_mime-defaults. conf</samp> file. Also on SUSE, <samp class="listingcharacter">AllowOverride None</samp> applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/srv/www/htdocs</samp> directory. You can change the setting in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/default-server.conf</samp>.

### 24.1.3    Logrotate

Apache's logging files are among the fastest growing files on many servers. That's why you need to take care of renaming, compressing, and finally deleting the logging files on a regular basis. This is exactly the task performed by the <samp class="listingcharacter">logrotate</samp> program (see [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14), [Section 14.12.4](#14_012.html_h14.12.4)), which is usually installed by default on Linux servers.

The program is started once a day by Cron or by the systemd timer. In the default configuration, it processes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/httpd/*.log</samp> (Fedora/RHEL) or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/apache2/*.log</samp> (Debian/Ubuntu) Apache logging files once a week, renames them to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.nn</samp>, and compresses them. The compressed files are archived for 52 weeks and then deleted.

If you define your own logging directories when configuring virtual hosts, you must modify the first line in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/logrotate.d/apache2</samp> configuration file to specify the locations of the additional logging files.

## 24.2    Encrypted Connections (HTTPS)

In the default configuration, Apache either uses only the unencrypted HTTP protocol, or it performs the encryption required for HTTPS using a self-signed certificate. Both variants are rightly considered insecure by all major web browsers. If the web browser displays your pages at all, it will show a crossed-out lock or other security warnings in the address bar.

The solution is to use HTTPS in combination with a certificate. HTTPS combines the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocols, adding encryption capabilities to HTTP.

You can obtain a suitable certificate for Apache free of charge from organizations such as Let's Encrypt or ZeroSSL. Alternatively, you can purchase a certificate from an established certificate provider. This is inconvenient and expensive, but it gives your customers the assurance that not only the data exchange is secure, but that the website is really operated by you (by your company, by your organization) and not by someone else.

This section provides an overview of important HTTPS basics and related Apache settings. Then, in [Section 24.3](#24_003.html_h24.3), you will find specific instructions on how to set up a Let's Encrypt certificate on your server. If you're in a rush and want to deal with the basics another time, you can skip straight to the next section.

### 24.2.1    Certificates

Before you can start the configuration work, you need a server certificate. At this point, I have to elaborate a little.

The encryption of the data is based on asymmetric encryption methods. The basic idea is that there is a key pair consisting of a private (secret) key and a public key. The public key is only suitable for encrypting data. The private key is only required for decrypting data. I won't go into the details of these methods here as they have already been described and explained countless times, including on Wikipedia.

When a connection is established between the client (i.e., a web browser) and the server (Apache), a shared key is first negotiated on the basis of a random number from the client and the public key from the server (handshake method). This session key is then used to encrypt all further communication. The web browser is thus able to encrypt the data to be sent in such a way that only the web server can analyze it by means of its private key.

However, data exchange that is virtually tap-proof according to current knowledge is only one aspect of improving security. Another aspect is that a user must be certain that they are communicating with the right partner. What good is it if the data for online banking is transmitted in a tap-proof manner, but instead of going to the bank it ends up directly in the hands of a fraudster?

For this reason, certificates can also contain data about the website and some kind of signature of a certification body. Their task is to verify the identity of the certificate applicant by means of a passport copy, a trade license, or similar. Unfortunately, this control process makes such certificates relatively expensive.

It depends on the trustworthiness of the authentication authority how trustworthy a certificate is. Well-known web browsers such as Firefox or Google Chrome only accept certificates issued by established authentication organizations (such as Verisign, Thawte, or Let's Encrypt). For other certificates, obvious warnings are displayed.

A key or certificate is ultimately a simple text file that contains some metadata as well as the actual key as a Base64-encoded string. [Table 24.5](#24_002.html_t24.5) summarizes the common file identifiers for key and certificate files. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">pem</samp> stands for privacy enhanced mail. This is a method for encrypted emails that has not caught on. However, the PEM format defined there is still common today. Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.crt</samp> files contain <samp class="listingcharacter">pem</samp> files as well.

| Identifier | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.key</samp> | Private key file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.csr</samp> | Unsigned certificate (Certificate Signing Request) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.pem</samp> | Container file for a signed certificate or certificate chain |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.crt</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">*.pem</samp> file with a different identifier (Windows) |

**Table 24.5**     File Identifiers for Key and Certificate Files

### 24.2.2    Using Self-Signed Certificates

You can generate certificates yourself using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> command. This kind of certificate is not considered trustworthy, but it provides the opportunity to become familiar with certificates and to get to know the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> command. If you are not interested in this, you can skip this section. The knowledge imparted here is not absolutely necessary for the use of ready-made certificates from Let's Encrypt and the like.

In many distributions, self-signed certificates are even available by default. On Debain and Ubuntu, they are referred to as snake-oil certificates (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem</samp>). Fedora and RHEL instead have a self-signed certificate for the hostname of the machine (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/pki/tls/certs/localhost.crt</samp>).

First, you need to install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> package. It contains the command of the same name for generating, managing, and manipulating keys and certificates:

```
root# apt/dnf/zypper install openssl 
```

The following command creates a file with a private 2048-bit RSA key. You will need this key twice, once to generate a certificate signing request and then again to sign it:

```
root# openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048 \
        -out server.key 
```

Make sure that only <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> can read this file! If this file falls into foreign hands, your server certificate will be worthless and you will have to revoke it:

```
root# chmod 400 server.key 
```

#### Encrypted Keys

Keys are valuable, which is why they are usually encrypted themselves by a passphrase, a particularly long password. This passphrase is also referred to as an encrypted key. If you want to use such a key, you need to add the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐aes-256-cbc</samp> option to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> command. You must then enter this password each time you use the key for the other commands.

This is also the case for Apache: the web server needs the key to read the certificate. That's why Apache now asks for the key's password at every (re)start. This makes an automated restart, as during an update, impossible.

To avoid this problem, an unencrypted copy of the key is created for Apache (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl rsa -in server.key -out server-unencrypted.key</samp>). Apache is then configured to use the insecure key file instead of the encrypted key, which must therefore be stored in the server's file system. And now, at the latest, it becomes clear that an encrypted key in our case is just an unnecessary extra effort that does not increase security. Of course, this does not mean that encrypted keys are generally not recommended—quite the opposite!

It’s a bit more work to create the certificate. Strictly speaking, the following command does not generate the final certificate, but a certificate signing request. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">server.key</samp> key is also included in the certificate (<samp class="listingcharacter">-key</samp> option).

When running the command, you must specify in which country and place you live, what your name is, and so on. The crucial question is the common name: in this context, it is not your name that is required, but the exact name of your website as it is used for encrypted connections.

Some websites use a separate subdomain for encrypted connections (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">banking.<mybank>.com</samp>); others do not (such as <samp class="listingcharacter"><mybank>.com</samp>). However, the certificate is only valid for a certain spelling. So, for example, you cannot use a certificate for <samp class="listingcharacter">www.a-company.com</samp> also for <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> (or vice versa)! Make sure that you leave the challenge password blank; that is, answer the corresponding question by entering a dot:

```
root# openssl req -new -sha256 -key server.key -out server.csr
Enter pass phrase for server.key: ******************
You are about to be asked to enter information that will be 
incorporated into your certificate request.

What you are about to enter is what is called a Distinguished 
Name or a DN. There are quite a few fields but you can leave 
some blank. For some fields there will be a default value,
If you enter '.', the field will be left blank.
-----
Country Name (2 letter code) [US]:            EN
State or Province Name (full name) [...]:     .
Locality Name (eg, city) []:                  New York
Organization Name (eg, company) [Sample Inc.]: John Doe
Organizational Unit Name (eg, section) []:    .
Common Name (eg server FQDN or YOUR name) []: www.a-company.com
Email Address []:                             webmaster@a-company.com

Please enter the following 'extra' attributes
to be sent with your certificate request
A challenge password []:                      .
An optional company name []:                  . 
```

The next command enables you to sign your certificate yourself. With a “real” certificate, this process is carried out by the authentication authority—of course, after checking the documents you have submitted. The key of the authentication authority is then used for the signature.

By default, the ready certificate is valid only for 30 days. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-days 1900</samp> option extends the validity period to approximately five years:

```
root# openssl x509 -req -days 1900 -in server.csr  \
         -signkey server.key -sha256 -out server.pem
Signature ok
subject=/C=US/L=New York/O=John Doe/CN=www.a-company.com/
  emailAddress=webmaster@a-company.com
Getting Private key 
```

#### Unable to Write Random State

Sometimes the unable to write random state error occurs when you execute the above command. The reason for this is mostly that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> does not find the home directory—often because you have previously run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo -s</samp>. The solution to this is to run <samp class="listingcharacter">export PATH=/root</samp>.

Physically, the generated keys and certificates are relatively small text files. To display the data contained in a certificate in plain text, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl x509 -text</samp> command. The following issues are shortened due to space constraints:

```
root# ls
  server.key  
(unencrypted private key)
  server.csr  
(certificate without signature)
  server.crt  
(certificate with signature)

root# cat server.pem
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIICWTCCAcICCQCL6ExhrQiELDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQUFADBxMQswCQYDVQQGEwJB ...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

root# openssl x509 -text -in server.pem
Certificate:
    Data:
        Version: 1 (0x0)
        Serial Number: 12669601459972319941 (0xafd37766c36baac5)
    Signature Algorithm: sha256WithRSAEncryption
        Issuer: C=US, L=New York, O=John Doe, 
                CN=www.a-company.com/emailAddress=webmaster@a‐company.com
        Validity
            Not Before: Sep 28 14:48:03 2023 GMT
            Not After : Dec 10 14:48:03 2028 GMT
        Subject: C=US, L=New York, O=John Doe, 
                 CN=www.a-company.com/emailAddress=webmaster@a‐company.com
        Subject Public Key Info:
            Public Key Algorithm: rsaEncryption
                Public-Key: (2048 bit)
                Modulus:
                    00:be:37:21:23:b6:13:e4:92:74:36:9f:de:4e:9a:
    Signature Algorithm: sha256WithRSAEncryption
         43:b8:92:82:0d:f6:e2:ef:ff:07:eb:3a:1f:da:3d:d9:ba:53:
         d7:1f:4a:49:ec:5a:c1:fb:0f:95:e8:94:89:ab:7b:05:95:62: 
```

### 24.2.3    Apache Configuration for HTTPS Operation

The Apache functions required for the HTTPS protocol are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter">mod_ssl</samp> module. On Debian or Ubuntu, this module is installed by default and merely needs to be activated:

```
root# a2enmod ssl
root# a2ensite default-ssl
root# systemctl restart apache2 
```

On Fedora or RHEL, you must first install the SSL module:

```
root# dnf install mod_ssl
root# systemctl restart httpd 
```

Apache needs to read the key and certificate files, so the obvious thing to do is to copy the two files to the Apache configuration directory:

```
root# cp server.pem server.crt /etc/apache2  
(Debian, SUSE, Ubuntu)
root# cp server.pem server.crt /etc/httpd    
(Fedora, RHEL) 
```

Next, you need to change the default SSL configuration. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">SSLEngine on</samp> activates the encryption functions. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">SSLxxxFile</samp> specifies where the files with the certificate and the private key are located. The distinction between HTTP and HTTPS is made by the port number 443 set in the <samp class="listingcharacter">VirtualHost</samp> line:

```
# Change SSLCertificateFile and SSLCertificateKeyFile,
# e.g. in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf (Fedora, RHEL) 
# or in /etc/apache2/sites-available/default-ssl.conf (Debian, Ubuntu)
<VirtualHost _default_:443>
    ServerName             www.a-company.com
    DocumentRoot           /var/www/html/
    SSLEngine              on
    SSLCertificateFile     /etc/apache2/server.pem
    SSLCertificateKeyFile  /etc/apache2/server.key
</VirtualHost> 
```

To enable the HTTPS site, you must prompt Apache to reread the configuration. If you’ve done the HTTPS configuration on Debian/Ubuntu in a separate file in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/sites-available</samp>, you need to enable this file:

```
root# systemctl restart httpd       
(Fedora/RHEL)
root# a2ensite ssl-a-company        
(Debian/Ubuntu, part 1)
root# systemctl restart apache2     
(Debian/Ubuntu, part 2) 
```

If you switch from an operation without SSL to an operation with SSL for the first time, it is not sufficient to reload the configuration files. For the SSL module to be loaded, you must specify <samp class="listingcharacter">restart</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">reload</samp>!

When a web browser encounters a self-signed certificate or a snake-oil certificate, the browser displays a security warning, as in [Figure 24.2](#24_002.html_f24.2).

The warning does not refer to the encryption not being secure: it is! Rather, the web browser warns you because the identity of the entity that signed the certificate is unknown. Technically unsophisticated users will therefore consider the website insecure. However, if you only want to be able to use phpMyAdmin securely to administrate the MySQL installation on the server, for example, then this certificate is completely sufficient!

[![Warning about Self-Signed Certificate](bilderklein/klein24_002.png)](img-f24.2.html)

**Figure 24.2**     Warning about Self-Signed Certificate

### 24.2.4    Snake-Oil Certificates

For Debian and Ubuntu, a snake-oil key and a snake-oil certificate valid for 10 years are automatically generated when Apache is installed:

```
/etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem    
(certificate)
/etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key  
(key) 
```

As you know, the term snake oil is used to describe supposed miracle cures or panaceas. The certificate is generated to allow web and mail servers to be used immediately in encrypted mode without the inconvenience of generating your own certificates. Accordingly, the Apache configuration file <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">default-ssl.conf</samp> contains the following lines:

```
# Datei /etc/apache2/sites-available/default-ssl.conf
...
SSLCertificateFile    /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem
SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key 
```

The same restrictions apply to the snake-oil certificate as to certificates that you have generated and signed yourself using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp>—hence the name. The snake-oil certificate takes into account the host name (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hostname</samp>) that was valid when it was created. If you need a new certificate after changing a host name, you can call the following command:

```
root# make-ssl-cert generate-default-snakeoil --force-overwrite 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">make-ssl-cert</samp> is a relatively simple script that uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> command described earlier.

Distributions from the Red Hat family have similar, automatically created and self-signed default certificates:

```
# file /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf
...
SSLCertificateFile    /etc/pki/tls/certs/localhost.crt
SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/pki/tls/private/localhost.key 
```

The certificates are valid for one year for the host name that was set during the installation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">httpd</samp> package.

## 24.3    Let's Encrypt

Since 2016, the Let's Encrypt organization ([https://letsencrypt.org](https://letsencrypt.org)) has been offering free certificates. These certificates are very widely used. By mid-2023, there were over 300 million active certificates from Let's Encrypt in use. At the same time, there are now other providers for free certificates, such as ZeroSSL. So the obvious question is, “Why spend any more money on third-party certificates?” Let's Encrypt comes with two major limitations: For one thing, the certificates are only valid for 90 days. To get around this disadvantage, the system must be set up in such a way that the certificates are automatically updated on a regular basis. (This is not difficult.) On the other hand, the certificates from Let's Encrypt are pure domain certificates. They allow you to check that a website actually comes from the a-company.com domain, for example, and not from another server that only pretends to do so.

However, Let's Encrypt does not perform any checks to see who owns this domain (organization validation), let alone who this person or organization is (extended validation by checking a passport copy, employer ID, etc.). In other words, impostors can also use free certificates from Let's Encrypt.

Certificates from Let's Encrypt are comparable to the cheapest and at the same time most widespread certificate variant of the established certification authorities. The certificates are sufficient to encrypt your own blog or similar pages. However, companies or organizations that implement a store on their websites, offer online banking services, manage health or insurance data, and so on are still dependent on higher-quality and thus unfortunately also quite expensive certificates from other providers.

In the early months, Let's Encrypt itself offered software for certificate management, including the now obsolete <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">letsencrypt</samp> command. Now the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) takes care of the development and maintenance of the software. The official Let's Encrypt client is called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">certbot</samp> ([https://certbot.eff.org](https://certbot.eff.org)). <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">certbot</samp> was a kind of factual standard in the past due to a lack of alternatives. In recent years, however, the program has repeatedly caused massive problems, partly due to its complicated installation.

For this reason, I recommend the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> shell script. Compared to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">certbot</samp>, this script is much more straightforward to install and easier to use. However, it has fewer special functions. Besides <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">certbot</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp>, there are a number of other tools that can assist you with setting up certificates, including <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">getsll</samp>. A list of other clients, including download links, can be found at [https://letsencrypt.org/docs/client-options](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/client-options).

### 24.3.1    Installing acme.sh

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> is not available as a ready-made package. Nevertheless, the installation succeeds without any problem by using the commands ahead. You need to download a setup script from the project website and run it with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">root</samp> privileges. (Whenever you do something like this, you should take a look at the script first! Maybe some bad guy took over or manipulated the download page?) Then you pass an email address to the setup program. Let's Encrypt sends warning emails to this email address if the automatic certificate renewal should not work:

```
user$ sudo apt/dnf/zypper install curl socat tar
user$ curl https://get.acme.sh -o acme-setup
user$ less acme-setup    
(briefly check the script code)
user$ sudo sh acme-setup email=admin@a-company.com
...

Installed to /root/.acme.sh/acme.sh
Installing alias to '/root/.bashrc'
Installing cron job
OK, Close and reopen your terminal to start using acme.sh 
```

After the installation, you must log out and log in again so that the new alias for calling acme.sh works.

### 24.3.2    Applying acme.sh

You need to run the two most important <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> commands with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">‐‐issue</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--install-cert</samp> options.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh --issue</samp> requests a common certificate from Let's Encrypt for all domain names specified with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp> option. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-w</samp> option specifies the web root directory. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> temporarily stores a small file there, which the Let's Encrypt server then tries to read via a web call. This ensures that you really have access to the specified domains. (Without such checks, anyone could generate a certificate for deutsche-bank.de at Let's Encrypt, for example. Of course, this must be prevented.) <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> issues certificates from the ZeroSSL organization by default. If you prefer Let's Encrypt certificates, you must specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--server letsencrypt</samp> option.

The following command generates a certificate for the web presence of <samp class="listingcharacter">a‐company.com</samp>, also taking into account the alternative address <samp class="listingcharacter">www.a-company.com</samp>. Before calling the command, you should make sure, such as by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ping</samp>, that all the specified addresses actually reference your server—that is, that the DNS configuration is correct! As this check uses HTTP or HTTPS protocols, you must enable ports 80 and 443 before running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> if this has not already been done:

```
root# acme.sh --issue  --server letsencrypt  -d a-company.com \
         -d www.a-company.com -w /var/www/html
Using CA: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
Creating domain key
The domain key is here: /root/.acme.sh/a-company.com/a‐company.com.key
Multi domain='DNS:a-company.com,DNS:www.a-company.com'
Verifying: a-company.com
Verifying: www.a-company.com
Downloading cert.

Cert success.

Your cert is in                /root/.acme.sh/a-company.com/a‐company.com.cer 
Your cert key is in            /root/.acme.sh/a-company.com/a‐company.com.key 
The intermediate CA cert is in /root/.acme.sh/a-company.com/ca.cer 
The full chain certs is there  /root/.acme.sh/a-company.com/fullchain.cer 
```

Note that you must replace <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www/html</samp> with the path where your web server is looking for the files for the specified host. The path varies depending on which distribution you are running and how you have integrated multiple hosts into the Apache configuration, if applicable. The outputs of the command have been reproduced here in highly shortened form for reasons of space. You can see that the key files are stored by default in a subdirectory of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root/.acme.sh/a-company-com</samp>.

Let's Encrypt and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> also support wildcard certificates that are valid for all conceivable subdomains of a domain. The use of wildcard certificates is only appropriate if all subdomains are served by one server, which is rather unusual for large setups.

Issuing a wildcard certificate is more complicated and involves two steps. In the first step, you want to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp> option twice, once for the primary domain and once for all subdomains—for example, like this:

```
-d a-company.com -d ’*.a-company.com’ 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> script then prompts you to manually add two TXT records to your domain as an additional verification measure. Once the DNS changes are effective, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> again in the second step, this time with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--renew</samp> option. The required syntax of the second command can be found in the output of the first command.

Unfortunately, the manual verification will also be required for every certificate renewal in the future, which is extremely inconvenient. For many DNS providers, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> supports an API to automate the process. Details are available in the documentation at [https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh/wiki/dnsapi](https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh/wiki/dnsapi).

Setting up the certificates is not enough as they are currently located only in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root/.acme.sh</samp> directory, which the web server is not allowed to access. It is not a good idea to copy the certificates manually to another directory now; this process would have to be repeated for each certificate renewal.

Instead, you should complete this task using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh --install-cert</samp>. This has the advantage that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> remembers all the information and automatically takes care of copying renewed certificates to the specified location again in the future. The following example provides <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/acme-letsencrypt</samp> as the location for the certificates and copies the certificates from <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> there. The command specified with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--reloadcmd</samp> is executed after copying and every time after a certificate update in the future. On Fedora/RHEL, you must replace <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apache2</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd</samp>:

```
root# mkdir /etc/acme-letsencrypt
root# acme.sh --install-cert -d a-company.com \
     --cert-file      /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.cert \
     --key-file       /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.key \
     --fullchain-file /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.fullchain \
     --reloadcmd 'systemctl restart apache2'
Installing cert to:       /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.cert
Installing key to:        /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.key
Installing full chain to: /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.fullchain
Run reload cmd: systemctl restart apache2
Reload success 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> does not change the configuration files of your web server! You must therefore add the appropriate statements with the paths to the certificate files themselves. The relevant lines for the preceding example look as follows:

```
# e.g. in /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/default-ssl.conf (Debian, Ubuntu)
# or  in /etc/apache2/hosts-enabled/a-company.com.conf
# or  in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf                  (Fedora, RHEL) 
SSLCertificateFile      /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.fullchain
SSLCertificateKeyFile   /etc/acme-letsencrypt/a-company.com.key 
```

During the installation of <samp class="listingcharacter">acme.sh</samp>, one line was added to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/cron/root</samp> depending on the distribution. This makes Cron take care of calling <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh --cron</samp> on a regular basis and thus automatically renewing all certificates set up by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp>. Any certificate older than 60 days will be automatically renewed. For the web server to take the changed certificates into account, it is automatically restarted (using the <samp class="listingcharacter">reload</samp> command you specified along with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh --install-cert</samp>).

To test the renewal process, you can run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh --cron --force</samp>. Note, however, that the number of Let's Encrypt transactions per day is limited.

If you need a certificate for another subdomain, you can request either a new certificate for this subdomain only or a new joint certificate that combines all previous domains plus the new domain. In the first case, you have two independent certificates that you can use separately, which gives you more flexibility.

Using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh --remove -d</samp> name, you can deactivate the renewal for a domain, which takes place automatically every 60 days. Although the name of the option suggests otherwise, the certificates themselves will not be deleted. However, you can now delete the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root/.acme.sh/name</samp> directory yourself.

It is often preferable for all HTTP page accesses to be automatically redirected to HTTPS. If you pass the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--redirect</samp> option, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">certbot</samp> will integrate the corresponding statements right into the Apache configuration files. Of course, you can also do this yourself. The following lines provide a pattern for this:

```
<VirtualHost _default_:80>
  ...
  RewriteEngine on
  # Redirection from HTTP to HTTPS
  RewriteCond %{SERVER_NAME} =www.a-company.com [OR]
  RewriteCond %{SERVER_NAME} =a-company.com
  RewriteRule ^ https://%{SERVER_NAME}%{REQUEST_URI} [END,NE,R=permanent]
</VirtualHost> 
```

If you also want to redirect from www.a-company.com to a-company.com, you need to add the following lines:

```
# redirection from www.<hostname> to <hostname>
# source: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/21467329
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^(www\.)(.*) [NC]
RewriteRule (.*) https://%2%{REQUEST_URI} [L,R=301] 
```

### 24.3.3    SSL Settings

Setting up certificates is not the end of the story. There are countless encryption methods and versions, all of which are summarized under HTTPS. Usually, Apache and the web browser exchange information about which protocols they each support and then use the most secure method that both can handle. Some methods are unsafe from today's perspective and should therefore be blocked. For this reason, it is advisable to use <samp class="listingcharacter">SSLCipherSuite</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">SSLProtocol</samp> to explicitly specify which procedures your website supports and which ones it rejects.

The [https://ssl-config.mozilla.org](https://ssl-config.mozilla.org) website is a great help for optimal configuration. There you can specify which version of the web server you are running and how important the compatibility with old browser versions is to you. Based on these few pieces of information, the website generates a listing with settings that you only need to transfer to your server configuration (see [Figure 24.3](#24_003.html_f24.3)). Note that you must include the settings lines in the correct places:

```
# in the <VirtualHost> section:
# enable HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) and HTTP/2
Header always set Strict-Transport-Security  "max-age=63072000"
Protocols h2 http/1.1
...
# outside the <VirtualHost> section, applies to the entire web server:
# SSL intermediate configuration, see https://ssl-config.mozilla.org
SSLProtocol           all -SSLv3 -TLSv1 -TLSv1.1
SSLCipherSuite        ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES...
SSLHonorCipherOrder   off
SSLSessionTickets     off
SSLUseStapling        on
SSLStaplingCache      "shmcb:logs/ssl_stapling(32768)" 
```

[![SSL Configuration Generator](bilderklein/klein24_003.png)](img-f24.3.html)

**Figure 24.3**     SSL Configuration Generator

The configuration described here is based on the assumption that various Apache add-ons are available. These must be explicitly activated depending on the distribution. The following commands apply to Debian and Ubuntu:

```
root# a2enmod headers rewrite socache_shmcb
root# systemctl restart apache2 
```

To verify that your configuration is working, you want to enter the address of your web server at [https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest](https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest). A script then checks the security of your website and provides optimization tips (see [Figure 24.4](#24_003.html_f24.4)).

[![Online Verification of HTTPS Configuration](bilderklein/klein24_004.png)](img-f24.4.html)

**Figure 24.4**     Online Verification of HTTPS Configuration

## 24.4    Setting Up and Securing Web Directories

After the basic configuration of Apache, you will usually set up various web directories that contain those HTML and PHP files that make up your website. For example, if you want to set up WordPress as the CMS for your website, you download the installation files, set up a directory accessible to Apache, and unpack the files there. This section explains what settings you need to make in Apache for the directories where you want to set up WordPress, phpMyAdmin, NextCloud, or any other web application.

The following pages are based on the configuration as you will find it on Ubuntu or Debian. If you use a different distribution, there are small variations in the default configuration. However, the keywords and work techniques presented here apply there as well.

On Ubuntu, Apache is preconfigured to use files from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www/html</samp> directory for the default website. The required settings are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf</samp> file:

```
# file /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf (Ubuntu)
<VirtualHost *:80>
  ServerAdmin      webmaster@localhost
  DocumentRoot     /var/www/html
  ErrorLog         ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/error.log  
  CustomLog        ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/access.log combined
</VirtualHost> 
```

A Debian- or Ubuntu-specific feature of the default configuration is that all settings are bundled in a <samp class="listingcharacter"><VirtualHost></samp> group. <samp class="listingcharacter"><VirtualHost></samp> groups are used to separate settings for several independent hosts (websites; see [Section 24.5](#24_005.html_h24.5)). However, the host in the <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> file is not linked to either an IP address or a host name, and for this reason applies to all web accesses that cannot be assigned to a specific virtual host.

### 24.4.1    Host Configuration

The keywords described ahead for configuring a <samp class="listingcharacter"><VirtualHost></samp> group are used to specify the details of the host—the origin of the data, the administrator's email address, the location of the logging files, and so on:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">DocumentRoot</samp> specifies the directory in which the HTML files are located.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ServerAdmin</samp> specifies the email address of the virtual host administrator. The address is displayed in case of error messages, for example. Here you should enter an email address that is actually active. A commonly used address is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">webmaster@hostname</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ServerSignature</samp> controls whether Apache should add a signature at the end of self-generated documents (error messages, directory listings, etc.). The signature consists of the Apache version and the host name. <samp class="listingcharacter">ServerSignature=EMail</samp> also adds the administrator's email address.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">LogLevel</samp> determines to what extent web server problems should be logged. Possible values range from <samp class="listingcharacter">emerg</samp> (log only critical errors that cause Apache to terminate) to <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp> (log everything, even debugging texts). Usually, the <samp class="listingcharacter">error</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">warn</samp> settings make much sense. The latter setting applies by default.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ErrorLog</samp> specifies the filename of the log file for error messages.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">CustomLog</samp> specifies the file name of the access log. In this file, Apache logs each successful transfer of a file. To the second parameter, you must pass either the name of a predefined logging format or a string of your own format statements. The allowed format codes are described at [http://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/de/mod/mod_log_config.html](http://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/de/mod/mod_log_config.html).

    On Ubuntu, some formats are preconfigured in <samp class="listingcharacter">apache2.conf</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">combined</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">common</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ErrorDocument</samp> specifies how Apache should respond to errors. Enter the error number as the first parameter (e.g., 404 for not found) and the name of a local file or the address of an external page to be displayed in this case in the second parameter. The file name must be specified relative to <samp class="listingcharacter">DocumentRoot</samp>. The main error codes are as follows:

    *   400, bad request

    *   401, authorization required

    *   403, forbidden

    *   404, not found

    *   500, internal server error

    A list of all HTTP status codes can be found at [https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html).

    By default, <samp class="listingcharacter">ErrorDocument</samp> is not configured. To avoid unpleasant error messages, you should take the trouble to set up an error page and specify its location using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ErrorDocument</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Alias</samp> establishes a mapping between a web directory and a directory of the hard disk (even outside <samp class="listingcharacter">DocumentRoot</samp>). For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">Alias /mytool /usr/local/mytool</samp> causes the files from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/urs/local/mytool</samp> directory to be read when [http://myserver.com/mytool](http://myserver.com/mytool) is accessed.

    As a rule, you need to set the access rights for each <samp class="listingcharacter">alias</samp> directory in a <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group (see the following section). The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ScriptAlias</samp> variant of <samp class="listingcharacter">Alias</samp> is used to define directories with CGI scripts.

### 24.4.2    Directory Configuration

Following these settings, which apply to the entire virtual host, you can set the properties for individual directories of your host in one or more <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory "/directory/"></samp> groups. The following list contains only the most important keywords:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">DirectoryIndex</samp> specifies which file Apache should send if an address ends with <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> and thus affects an entire directory (<samp class="listingcharacter">index.html</samp> by default). Multiple files may also be specified. If that’s the case, Apache works through all the entries in order up to the first hit (for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">DirectoryIndex index.php index.html</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Options</samp> allows you to specify various options that apply to the directory. These include the following:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ExecCGI</samp>: Run CGI scripts

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">FollowSymLinks</samp>: Follow symbolic links

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Includes</samp>: Add include files (<samp class="listingcharacter">mod_include</samp> module)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Indexes</samp>: Show file list when <samp class="listingcharacter">index.html</samp> is missing

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">MultiViews</samp>: Automatic language selection (<samp class="listingcharacter">mod_negotiation</samp> module)

    By default, Apache uses the <samp class="listingcharacter">All</samp> setting. This activates all options with the exception of <samp class="listingcharacter">MultiViews</samp>. The Ubuntu configuration is more restrictive: <samp class="listingcharacter">Options FollowSymLinks</samp> applies to the entire file system, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Options Indexes FollowSymLinks MultiViews</samp> applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www directory</samp>.

    To deactivate individual options compared to the default settings of a parent directory, a minus sign must be placed in front of them. A preceding plus sign is also allowed but has no effect; the option is enabled exactly as if it were specified without a plus sign.

    For safety reasons, the “less is more” motto should prevail when it comes to <samp class="listingcharacter">options</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Indexes</samp> option tells curious web surfers the names of all files located in a directory if you forget <samp class="listingcharacter">index.html</samp> once. This is a potential security risk. You need <samp class="listingcharacter">MultiView</samp> only for multilingual websites with automatic language selection. If your site does not offer something like this, you can also do without this option.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AllowOverride</samp> specifies which directory-specific settings may be changed by an <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.htaccess</samp> file. The following options are available:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">AuthConfig</samp>: Set authentication method

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">FileInfo</samp>: Set file and document types

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Indexes</samp>: Modify directory index

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Limit</samp>: Change access rights (<samp class="listingcharacter">Allow</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Deny</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Order</samp>)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Options</samp>: Change directory options

    By default, all options are active in Apache; that is, each option can be changed. In most distributions, however, the default configuration is more restrictive due to security reasons. Thus, on Debian and Ubuntu, <samp class="listingcharacter">None</samp> is preset for all relevant directories (see <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/apache2.conf</samp>).

### 24.4.3    Securing Directories

There is one central aspect that I have not yet addressed: the control of access rights for directories. Apache versions 2.2 and 2.4 differ significantly in this respect. Because the version 2.2 syntax still works on many Apache 2.4 installations and is widely used, I cover both variants here. For new installations, you must make sure to use the Apache 2.4 keywords!

In Apache 2.2, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">Order</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Allow</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Deny</samp> within the <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group to set the circumstances under which Apache may read and redirect files from the respective directory. Access rules also apply to all subdirectories, unless other rules are explicitly defined in a different <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group. The access rules for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/</samp> directory therefore specify default rules for the entire file system:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Order Allow,Deny</samp> means that first all <samp class="listingcharacter">Allow</samp> and then all <samp class="listingcharacter">Deny</samp> rules will be analyzed. If no rule can be applied to a page access, the access will be blocked.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Order Deny,Allow</samp> reverses the order of the rules. However, you should note that if no rule fits for a page access, the access is allowed! This rule applies by default in Apache.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Allow from</samp> specifies from which host names or IP addresses access is allowed, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">Allow from 213.214.215.216 knownpage.com</samp>. You can specify IP address ranges in the format 213.214 or 213.214.0.0/255.255.0.0 or 213.214.0.0/16 (for 213.214.*.*). For host names, <samp class="listingcharacter">site.com</samp> also applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">www.site.com</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sub.site.com</samp>, and so on. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Allow from all</samp> rule allows every access.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Deny from</samp> works just the other way around and blocks access for the specified hosts or addresses.

By default, <samp class="listingcharacter">Order Deny,Allow</samp> applies, and in the absence of other rules, all access to all directories is thus blocked! If you place web files in other directories, you must not forget to allow access to them.

On Apache 2.4, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Order</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Allow</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Deny</samp> keywords are considered obsolete. However, the keywords are still processed by the <samp class="listingcharacter">mod_access_compat</samp> module. This module is available on most Apache 2.4 installations and ensures that an Apache 2.4 update does not overwrite the entire previous configuration.

The use of the new <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Require</samp> keyword is recommended for a new configuration. The following examples show different types of use:

```
# allows access from the computer with IP address 192.168.0.2
Require ip 192.168.0.2

# allows access from the address range 10.0.*.*
Require ip 10.0

# allows access from an IPv6 address range 
Require ip 2001:1234:789a:0471::/64

# allows access for a specific hostname
Require host intern.my-company.com

# allows access for *.my-company.com
Require host my-company.com

# allows access from localhost (IPv4 and IPv6)
Require local

# allows access for authenticated users
Require valid-user

# allows access from anywhere
Require all granted

# blocks any access
Require all denied 
```

If you formulate several conditions for a <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp>, then it is sufficient if one of these conditions is fulfilled:

```
<Directory /var/www/cms>
  Require local
  Require ip 192.168
  Require host my-company.com
</Directory> 
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter"><RequireAll></samp>, you can combine several conditions with a logical AND. Apache returns the requested page only if all conditions are true at the same time:

```
<Directory /var/www/internal-wiki>
  <RequireAll>
    Require valid-user
    Require ip 192.168.17
  </RequireAll>
</Directory> 
```

### 24.4.4    Password Protection for Web Directories

It often happens that web directories can only be released after authentication with a user name and the corresponding password. Apache provides a simple method for this, which works equally well in versions 2.2 and 2.4.

The first step toward password protection is a password file. For security reasons, the file should be created outside all web directories to prevent access via a web address. The following example assumes that the password file is stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www-private</samp> directory. If you set up a new directory, you should make sure that Apache has read permissions for it. On Fedora/RHEL, you must also keep SELinux in mind and either set up the password directory inside <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www</samp> or set the SELinux context correctly after creating the directory.

To create a new password file, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">htpasswd</samp> command with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp> option (create). The password is of course encrypted:

```
root# cd /var/www-private
root# htpasswd -c passwords.pwd username
New password: ********
Re-type new password: ********
Adding password for user username 
```

Additional username/password pairs can be added via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">htpasswd</samp> without the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp> option:

```
root# cd /var/www-private
root# htpasswd passwords.pwd name2
New password: ********
Re-type new password: ********
Adding password for user username 
```

There are now two ways to configure Apache to actually honor the password file. The first variant requires that you carry out the configuration directly in an Apache configuration file—on Debian or Ubuntu in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/sites-available/default</samp> for the server's default website, or in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.../sitename</samp> for a virtual host. In the second variant, the configuration is carried out in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.htaccess</samp> file located inside the web directory.

To ensure that the password file is taken into account by Apache, you must add various authentication options to the <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group. If the directory you want to protect does not already have its own <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group, you can create a new group. All options will automatically be taken over from the parent directory. So you just need to add the authentication options. The following lines provide a pattern for this:

```
# in /etc/apache2/sites-available/xxx (Debian/Ubuntu)
...
# password protected directory
<Directory "/var/www/admin/">
    AuthType     Basic
    AuthUserFile /var/www-private/passwords.pwd
    AuthName     "admin"
    Require      valid-user
</Directory> 
```

Let me briefly explain the keywords:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthType</samp> specifies the authentication type. I only discuss the <samp class="listingcharacter">Basic</samp> type here.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthUserFile</samp> specifies the location of the password file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthName</samp> indicates the realm for which the access is valid. The point is that you don't have to log in every time you want to access different directories that are protected by the same password file. Once you have logged in with a specific <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthName</samp> designation, this login also applies to all other directories with this <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthName</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Require valid-user</samp> means that any valid username and password combination is allowed as login. Alternatively, you can also specify here that a login is only allowed for very specific users:

    <samp class="listingcharacter">Require user name1 name2</samp>

The method outlined here is only possible if you have access to the Apache configuration files—that is, if you are the web administrator yourself. If that’s not the case, equivalent protection can also be provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.htaccess</samp> file located in the directory to be protected. This file must contain the same statements that were specified earlier within the <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group: <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthType</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthUserFile</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">AuthName</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Require</samp>.

#### .htaccess Requires AllowOverride AuthConfig

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.htaccess</samp> files are only noticed if a change of authentication information is allowed within the web directory. The (parent) <samp class="listingcharacter"><Directory></samp> group must contain <samp class="listingcharacter">AllowOverride AuthConfig</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">AllowOverride All</samp>.

## 24.5    Virtual Hosts

A separate web server for each website (for each host) would be a waste of resources given the performance of current computers! Thanks to virtual hosts, a web server can operate many websites in parallel.

From a technical perspective, there are three methods for Apache to decide which virtual host a web request is directed to. In any case, the HTTP header transmitted from the browser to the server serves as the starting point:

*   Name-based virtual hosts Apache recognizes the desired website by the host name contained in the HTTP header. This variant is the easiest to implement and the most widespread.

*   IP-based virtual hosts Apache recognizes the required website by the IP address in the header. This approach is associated with a serious disadvantage: each virtual host requires its own IP address, and IP addresses are scarce for IPv4.

*   Port-based virtual hosts Apache recognizes the required website based on the port number. This variant is unusual in practice because the port number must be specified as part of the web address. This looks confusing and is at best suitable for a technically savvy target group, such as administrators.

In this section, I again refer to the default configuration of Debian or Ubuntu. There, it is common to use a separate configuration file for each virtual host. If you set up your web server under Fedora or RHEL, the same Apache keywords will be used. However, all settings are made either in the central <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf</samp> file or in individual files for each host in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/httpd/conf.d/sitename.conf</samp>.

In the past, it was impossible to combine HTTPS with virtual hosts that differed only by host name. The problem was that the host name itself was also transmitted encrypted. It was thus impossible for the web server to “guess” the correct certificate.

Meanwhile, web browsers send the host name once unencrypted beforehand when establishing a connection. This tells Apache which certificate it must use for encryption. For this to work, <samp class="listingcharacter">SSLStrictSNIVHostCheck off</samp> must apply, which is the default for current Apache versions. You can find more details on the correct configuration of multiple hosts, each of which uses its own HTTPS certificate, at [https://wiki.apache.org/httpd/NameBasedSSLVHostsWithSNI](https://wiki.apache.org/httpd/NameBasedSSLVHostsWithSNI).

### 24.5.1    Setting Up Virtual Hosts

On Debian and Ubuntu, the default website is defined as a virtual host in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/sites-available/default</samp>.

To define a new virtual host, you need to create a new file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/sites-available/</samp> directory. This file should contain exactly one <samp class="listingcharacter"><VirtualHost></samp> group. The three listings ahead each give an example of a name-based, IP-based and port-based host. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ServerName</samp> specifies the name of the host. This host name must be included in the header information of a web request for Apache to respond to it. Optionally, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ServerAlias</samp> to name additional names. For example, for the <samp class="listingcharacter">ServerName www.myserver.com</samp> setting, it is recommended to add <samp class="listingcharacter">ServerAlias myserver.com</samp> so that a virtual host can be used with or without the preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">www.</samp> letters.

Usually, you need two files or two settings groups within one file for each host. The first group applies to HTTP and usually contains only a redirect to HTTPS. The second group of options applies to HTTPS and contains, among other things, the SSL options with the location of the certificate:

```
# /etc/apache2/sites-available/example-com.conf (Debian/Ubuntu)
# for HTTP
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName     example.com
    ServerAlias    www.example.com
    DocumentRoot   /var/www/html/example-com/
    Redirect       permanent / https://example.com/
</VirtualHost>
# for HTTPS
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName     example.com
    ServerAlias    www.example.com
    DocumentRoot   /var/www/html/example-com/
    SSLCertificateFile      \
       /etc/acme-letsencrypt/example.com/fullchain.pem
    SSLCertificateKeyFile   \
       /etc/acme-letsencrypt/example.com/privkey.pem
    # ... other settings
</VirtualHost> 
```

To enable or later disable a virtual host, you should now run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2ensite name</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2dissite name</samp> on Debian/Ubuntu and then prompt Apache to reload the configuration files:

```
root# a2ensite example-com       
(Debian/Ubuntu)
root# systemctl reload apache2 
```

Theoretically, it’s also possible to disable the server's default website using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2dissite</samp>. But you should not do that, because the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf</samp> file often contains various default settings for Apache!

Once you set up virtual hosts, the default website defined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sites-available/default</samp> displays only if web requests do not apply to any of the virtual hosts.

On Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">a2ensite/a2dissite</samp> commands are omitted because all information about the virtual hosts is located in the central <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">httpd.conf</samp> configuration file or in separate files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">conf.d</samp> directory. You can activate changes made there by using the following command:

```
root# systemctl reload httpd             
(Fedora, RHEL)
root# systemctl reload apache2           
(SUSE) 
```

By default, all web accesses are stored in central logging files. Usually it’s more convenient to provide separate logging files for each host. For this purpose, you must include the <samp class="listingcharacter">ErrorLog</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">CustomLog</samp> keywords in the two <samp class="listingcharacter">VirtualHost</samp> sections:

```
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ErrorLog    /var/log/apache2/example-com.error.log
    CustomLog   /var/log/apache2/example-com.access.log combined
</VirtualHost>
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ErrorLog    /var/log/apache2/example-com-ssl.error.log
    CustomLog   /var/log/apache2/example-com-ssl.access.log combined
</VirtualHost> 
```

You can find more information about the many variants and keywords for logging configuration at [https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/logs.html](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/logs.html).

## 24.6    Web Access Statistics

If you run your own web server or administrate it for someone else, you usually also want to know how many people visit the website per day, which web browsers are used, and so on. I'll briefly introduce a few tools here first, and then go into a bit more detail about using GoAccess.

In the past, the Webalizer or AWStats program was often used to create such statistics. These programs from the early days of the web are no longer up to date. The configuration is relatively complex because calling them must be synchronized with the rotation of the logging files.

The undisputed champion among modern web analyzer tools is Google Analytics. To be able to use it, you need to include JavaScript code on the pages of your website that redirects each page access to a central server. This approach makes it easier to distinguish between “real” visitors and search robots, and it produces more accurate results that can be observed in real time.

As Google Analytics does not analyze logging files but is based on code that is integrated directly into the website, Google Analytics copes much better with modern websites where you never leave the home page (single-page web applications).

Note, however, that the use of Google Analytics in compliance with data protection laws like GDPR is a problem! In any case, you need to include a confirmation dialog in your website that informs visitors about the use of Google Analytics. This dialog is often combined with the cookie consent form required in the European Union (albeit completely pointless; see [https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/](https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/)).

Matomo ([https://matomo.org](https://matomo.org); formerly Piwik) is an open-source alternative to Google Analytics. Its use avoids feeding Google with even more data; the data collected remains under your control. However, from a privacy perspective, Matomo acts similarly to Google Analytics; thus, even if you use Matomo, you should include a prominent notice on your website.

### 24.6.1    GoAccess

In my opinion, GoAccess ([https://goaccess.io](https://goaccess.io)) is a good compromise between the outdated Webalizer and AWStats programs on the one hand and privacy-problematic tools like Google Analytics or Matomo on the other hand. GoAccess analyzes the logging files of the web server and in this respect acts similar to Webalizer or AWStats. However, unlike these programs, the program is also suitable for real-time analysis of web traffic. Moreover, it can be used in a terminal window via SSH if required, without the otherwise usual intermediate step of generating reports as web pages.

GoAccess is available as a package in many distributions and can be installed using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">apt/dnf/zypper install goaccess</samp>. On RHEL and its clones, you must enable the EPEL package source upfront.

The easiest way is to call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">goaccess</samp> in an SSH session and pass the filename of the Apache logging file as a parameter. On Ubuntu, even a nonprivileged user can do this:

```
user$ goaccess /var/log/apache2/access.log 
```

On Fedora and RHEL, the logging files are located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/httpd</samp> and are only accessible to <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. The call of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">goaccess</samp> must then be made with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges:

```
root# goaccess /var/log/httpd/access_.log 
```

At startup, you may need to specify the format of the logging file. Usually, it is sufficient to confirm the default NCSA Combined Log Format entry. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">goaccess</samp> then displays an analysis of the logging file and updates it regularly until you exit the program using (Q) (see [Figure 24.5](#24_006.html_f24.5)).

You can use the cursor or (Tab) keys to scroll through additional sections (static accesses, 404 errors, host names and IP addresses, etc.). (Enter) adds more details to the currently active section. (S) sorts the rows according to a different criterion. A summary of other keyboard shortcuts is provided by (H).

[![Access Statistics in Terminal Window](bilderklein/klein24_005.png)](img-f24.5.html)

**Figure 24.5**     Access Statistics in Terminal Window

Most distributions set up new access log files daily or weekly and compress the older files (see also the description of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">logrotate</samp> in [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14), [Section 14.12.4](#14_012.html_h14.12.4)). The following command processes all compressed files as well as the two uncompressed <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">access.log</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">access.log.1</samp> files. Note that such a call of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">goaccess</samp> initially takes quite a long time (all logging files have to be decompressed and loaded) and that the memory requirements of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">goaccess</samp> in this case are considerable; depending on the size of the log files, this could be in the GiB range! If you replace the <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> character with <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp>, only the last ten logging files will be considered, which is often sufficient:

```
user$ cd /var/log/apache2
user$ zcat access.log access.log.*.gz | \
        goaccess --log-format=COMBINED \
        access.log access.log.1  - 
```
