You can use [Figure 26.1](#26_001.html_f26.1) to track how an email is sent from Mr. Hoover (<samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@a-company.com</samp>) to Ms. Smith (<samp class="listingcharacter">smith@target.com</samp>) or how an email is sent from <samp class="listingcharacter">anyone@sender.com</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@a-company.com</samp>.

Let's start with the first case: Mr. Hoover, an employee of <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>, is sitting in front of his notebook computer at an airport, composes an email in the Thunderbird email client to <samp class="listingcharacter">smith@target.com</samp>, and sends it off. Thunderbird now contacts the company's mail server via the SMTP protocol, via the Postfix program running on the <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> server. Postfix takes the email, determines which domain it is addressed to, and in turn contacts the mail server of target.com. The MTA of target.com verifies that the specified user smith actually has an email account on target.com and accepts the email.

[![Email Communication Flow](bilderklein/klein26_001.png)](img-f26.1.html)

**Figure 26.1**     Email Communication Flow

Meanwhile, <samp class="listingcharacter">anyone@sender.com</samp> wrote an email for Mr. Hoover and sent it. The MTA of <samp class="listingcharacter">sender.com</samp> now contacts the MTA of <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> and passes the email on. On the <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> server, Postfix detects that there is an email account for hoover. Postfix accepts the email and passes it to the local command belonging to Postfix, which stores the email in Mr. Hoover's mailbox. The mailbox is a file or directory located on the <samp class="listingcharacter">a‐company.com</samp> server.

The email remains there until Mr. Hoover's email client contacts the Dovecot program on the <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> computer via the POP or IMAP protocol. Most email programs are set to do this automatically every few minutes. Of course, if Mr. Hoover is offline at the time, it may take hours or days to get there. Now the email only needs to be transferred to the email program and can then be read there.

#### Host Names

For the sake of simplicity, only the domain names of the companies are mentioned in the previous paragraphs and in [Figure 26.1](#26_001.html_f26.1). As a matter of fact, mail servers and clients obviously use full host names. These can vary depending on the protocol and can be, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">imap.a-company.com</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mail.destination.com</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">a-hostname.sender.com</samp>.

### 26.1.4    Variants and Options

In order not to overwhelm you with details, I have shortened the previous description of an email communication a little. For example, I did not address how to deal with temporarily undeliverable emails. An email server makes delivery attempts for several hours before it gives up sending. If the delivery definitely fails, the sender receives the email back with a brief description of the cause of the error.

The topic of authentication has also been left out. Not everyone is allowed to just contact any MTA and send emails. To prevent such uncontrolled email sending, emails may only be sent locally in the basic configuration. Authentication is required so that an external email client can also send emails. Although the Postfix program presented in this chapter supports the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) protocol, it cannot perform the authentication itself. In the sample configuration in this chapter, the Dovecot program performs this task.

To prevent the content of emails from being transmitted in plain text, the connection between the client and the mail server or the connection between two mail servers (MTAs) must be encrypted. Most mail servers support the Transport Layer Security (TLS; formerly SSL) protocol for this purpose. Encryption is usually initiated with STARTTLS when the connection is established. The communication begins unencrypted; the client and server then agree on the best possible encryption method and continue the communication in encrypted form. This works great with many mail clients and servers.

The encryption outlined here only concerns the transmission of mail from one server to another. It has nothing to do with whether the content of the message itself is encrypted or at least signed. The mail client is responsible for encrypting or signing the content for the sender and displaying the message correctly for the recipient. Despite the undisputed advantages of signed or encrypted emails, you will rarely come across such emails in real life. Convenience, the relatively complex key management, and two incompatible standards (PGP and S/MIME) stand in the way of widespread use. This makes it all the more important that the email, if it is not encrypted itself, is at least transported in a tap-proof manner.

Another point is the message transfer from one MTA to the next. The path is not always as direct as in [Figure 26.1](#26_001.html_f26.1). Sometimes the transfer takes place via several stations. The intermediate MTAs only pass on the message (relaying). This is especially useful if there is one primary server and one or more backup servers for a mail domain. If the primary server is not available at a given moment, the backup servers receive the emails and forward them to the primary server later. This type of configuration mitigates the risk of the email system being unavailable during maintenance.

#### Make Sure Your Mail Server Is Secure Lest It End Up on a Blacklist!

The worst thing that can happen when you configure an email server is that the relaying process is inadequately or incorrectly secured: then anyone can send messages to your email server for forwarding without authentication.

Spammers constantly search the internet for such servers and abuse them for the omnipresent flood of advertising. This entails unpleasant consequences: within a few days, your server will end up on blacklists that list dangerous or misconfigured email servers. Many email servers do not accept emails from such servers to avoid spam. Unfortunately, it’s much more difficult to be deleted from such blacklists than to end up on them.

So be careful with the configuration! If you suspect that your server (more precisely, its IP address) has ended up on a blacklist, you can verify that very easily on the following page: [https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx](https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx).

The scenario shown in [Figure 26.1](#26_001.html_f26.1) can be further extended with server-side spam and virus protection. If you want your users to be able to read emails directly on a web page without a mail client, you also need a web interface, such as the RoundCube program or Horde.

### 26.1.5    DNS Configuration

Let me return again to [Figure 26.1](#26_001.html_f26.1): How does the MTA on the <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> computer know the IP address of the mail server for <samp class="listingcharacter">target.com</samp>?

Because of the Domain Name System (DNS) entries, of course, you will answer.

This is basically correct, but it’s not ordinary DNS entries (so-called A records) that are responsible for email traffic, but special MX entries. An MX entry specifies the host name, not the IP address, of the computer responsible for a domain's email. This makes it possible to implement the email services on a different machine than the rest of the internet services such as web, SSH, FTP, and so on. If your mail server also supports IPv6, you need an AAAA record with the IPv6 address of the mail host. The MX entry does not change.

In addition, each MX entry contains a priority number. If multiple email servers are set up with different priorities, the server with the highest priority will typically receive all emails. If this server is temporarily unavailable, the lower-priority servers come into play. These servers usually only serve as a backup system and forward the emails to the primary server (relaying) as soon as it’s online again.

[Table 26.3](#26_001.html_t26.3) summarizes a typical DNS configuration for a simple server. All Internet services, including email, run on the same computer; there is no backup email server. As the MX entry contains a domain name (not an IP address), the domain name specified there must also be defined by an A record. In the sample configuration, the full host name of the computer is <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a-company.com</samp>. The MX entry points to this host name.

| Type | Name | Value | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> | 95.217.156.167 |  |
| A | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a-company.com</samp> | 95.217.156.167 |  |
| A | <samp class="listingcharacter">www.a-company.com</samp> | 95.217.156.167 |  |
| AAAA | <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> | 2a01:4f9:c012:7e31::1 |  |
| AAAA | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a-company.com</samp> | 2a01:4f9:c012:7e31::1 |  |
| AAAA | <samp class="listingcharacter">www.a-company.com</samp> | 2a01:4f9:c012:7e31::1 |  |
| CNAME | <samp class="listingcharacter">imap</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd</samp> |  |
| CNAME | <samp class="listingcharacter">mail</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd</samp> |  |
| CNAME | <samp class="listingcharacter">pop</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd</samp> |  |
| CNAME | <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd</samp> |  |
| MX | – | <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a-company.com</samp> | 10 |
| TXT | <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">“v=spf1 ”…"</samp> |  |

**Table 26.3**     Sample DNS Configuration of Simple Web and Mail Server with IPv4 and IPv6

The <samp class="listingcharacter">CNAME</samp> entries are aliases, so to speak. They do not refer to IP addresses, but to other host names, and therefore work simultaneously for IPv4 and IPv6\. The <samp class="listingcharacter">CNAME</samp> entries for <samp class="listingcharacter">imap</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">pop</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp</samp> listed in the example are not required for mail server operation, but often facilitate the client configuration. Some email clients assume by default that there are host names beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">imap</samp>, and possibly also <samp class="listingcharacter">pop</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">pop3</samp> for the corresponding protocols.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">TXT</samp> entry contains information about the SPF spam protection system, which is described on the following pages. In addition to the entries specified in [Table 26.3](#26_001.html_t26.3), each domain usually has other DNS entries that point, for example, to additional hosts or to the underlying name servers.

Finally, there is the question of how or where you carry out the DNS configuration. Usually you use a web interface provided by the service provider with whom you have registered your domain name (see [Figure 26.2](#26_001.html_f26.2)).

[![DNS Configuration with Domain Name Registrar](bilderklein/klein26_002.png)](img-f26.2.html)

**Figure 26.2**     DNS Configuration with Domain Name Registrar

DNS entries are public. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">host</samp> command to read the entries for a specific host name. The following lines show how you can first determine the host name(s) of the mail server(s) and then query their IP address:

```
user$ host -t MX a-company.com
a-company.com mail is handled by 10 efd.a-company.com.
user$ host efd.a-company.com
efd.a-company.com has address 95.217.156.167
efd.a-company.com has IPv6 address 2a01:4f9:c012:7e31::1 
```

Do not run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">host</samp> directly on the root server, but on an external computer! Otherwise, your own name server as well as the name server of your provider may influence the result. This makes it difficult to search for any configuration errors of your own.

### 26.1.6    Reverse DNS Entry

Usually, DNS servers provides the IP address associated with a host name. If an external computer wants to contact <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>—be it with a web browser, via SSH or by email—it first contacts the next DNS server. This returns the IP number of the server of <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>. For mail traffic, the resolution is done in two stages: first the host name of the mail server is determined via the MX entry, then its IP address. Reverse DNS works the other way around: the IP number is known, but the host name is now searched for. For this to work, a reverse DNS entry must be present. If you are renting a root server, your provider must perform this reverse DNS entry. Many providers make a corresponding configuration tool available to their customers.

The reverse DNS entry has nothing to do with the other DNS entries! This is why the setting is not made on the DNS configuration page of your domain name, but as part of the configuration of your root server or your cloud instance.

The easiest way to test reverse DNS is to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">host</samp> command. Note that although several host names can lead to the same IP address (e.g., if several websites are running on one server thanks to virtual hosting), the reverse IP resolution always provides only one unique host name:

```
user$ host -t MX a-company.com
a-company.com mail is handled by 10 efd.a-company.com.
user$ host efd.a-company.com
efd.a-company.com has address 95.217.156.167
efd.a-company.com has IPv6 address 2a01:4f9:c012:7e31::1
user$ host 95.217.156.167
167.156.217.95.in-addr.arpa domain name pointer efd.a-company.com.
user$ host 2a01:4f9:c012:7e31::1
1.0.0.0.0.0...0.a.2.ip6.arpa domain name pointer efd.a-company.com. 
```

Reverse DNS entries are not actually mandatory for internet traffic. There is no internet standard that requires such entries. Nevertheless, Reverse DNS entries have become established for email servers. This is because many MTAs only accept the receipt of emails from external MTAs if a reverse DNS entry exists for the host name of the server on which the MTA is running, and this is presumably not dynamically generated. This protective measure is intended to combat computers or IoT devices infected by malware, which are misused to send spam—often without the owner's knowledge.

Even though the reverse DNS test does not provide reliable protection against spam, it is often used. This means that to prevent other MTAs from classifying mails from your server as spam, the server needs a reverse DNS entry and, if necessary, a second one for the IPv6 address.

Basically, the DNS configuration is now sufficient to set up and test a mail server. If everything works, you should also carry out Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) configurations. Both methods help you to check whether a mail has been sent from the correct server.

The practical benefits of the two methods are not undisputed. However, they are still worth implementing because they increase the chances that emails sent from your server will not be classified as spam by the recipient. Details on this topic follow in [Section 26.9](#26_009.html_h26.9).

## 26.2    Postfix (MTA)

This section describes how you can install and configure the Postfix MTA on RHEL and Ubuntu. Postfix is currently one of the most popular MTAs and is very well documented—both on [https://www.postfix.org](https://www.postfix.org) and in countless articles and some books.

Nevertheless, the choice of Postfix is by no means a foregone conclusion. While there is only one widely used program for some tasks, the open-source world offers several excellent MTAs to choose from. Whether Postfix or Exim, Qmail or Sendmail—all these programs are widely used and fulfill their purpose. If you talk to administrators, everyone will probably recommend the MTA they use themselves and know well.

Before you follow me through the various configuration details on the following pages, a few prerequisites must be met:

*   You need an email account independent of your server (e.g., at GMX, Google, or mailbox.org) to test your new email system.

*   The DNS configuration of your domain must be correct.

*   The host name of your computer must have been set correctly. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">hostname</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat /etc/hostname</samp> commands should each return the correct name of your server. In the example that runs through the entire chapter, this hostname is <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a-company.com</samp>.

*   There should be a reverse DNS entry for your root server.

*   Finally, the installation of a small text-based email client is recommended to test the MTA directly (see [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5)).

### 26.2.1    Installation on Debian and Ubuntu

On Debian and Ubuntu, a configuration program appears after the installation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">postfix</samp> package. There you need to specify what kind of basic installation you want. On a root server, Internet Site is the right choice: you want to use Postfix to send and receive emails on the server via SMTP.

In the next step, you need to specify the domain for the email server—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>. This name is used to complete email addresses without domain names. So an email to <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> becomes an email to <samp class="listingcharacter">name@a-company.com</samp>.

After this tiny configuration, Postfix starts immediately. The program performs the following functions in the basic configuration:

*   Postfix receives emails via SMTP to <samp class="listingcharacter">name@a-company.com</samp>. If there is a <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> login on the server, the email will be accepted and saved. This applies to all accounts defined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp>. For example, if Apache is installed, <samp class="listingcharacter">www-data@a-company.com</samp> is also a valid email address. If <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> is unknown, the email will be rejected (user unknown).

*   Accepted emails are stored by Postfix's own MDA in mbox format in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/mail/</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> file. The files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/mail</samp> are therefore the mailboxes of the various email users of the computer. In simple terms, the mbox format means that the emails are joined together in a file that grows larger and larger. Because emails are usually encoded in a text format, you can even view the mbox file by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> if necessary. An alternative to the mbox format is the maildir format, in which there is a separate directory for each mailbox and a separate file for each email.

*   Local users can send emails—both internally to all accounts on the server and externally to any other email addresses.

As a first test, you can send an email from an external account to <samp class="listingcharacter">name@a-company.com</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> is an active Linux account on the server. The email should show up in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/mail/name</samp> after a short time. If you log in as <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp>, you can read the email using Mutt. Next, use Mutt again to test sending an email to your external email address. If problems occur during the two tests, the most likely cause of the error is an incorrect or missing DNS configuration.

### 26.2.2    Installation on EHEL

On RHEL, Postfix is usually already installed and active. You can check this for yourself by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl status</samp>. If Postfix is not yet running with a minimal installation, you should install and activate the program as follows:

```
root# dnf install postfix
root# systemctl enable --now postfix 
```

Unlike Debian and Ubuntu, you do not have a choice of predefined configuration variants. In the default configuration, Postfix can only send email from local users to the outside world and receive email from local users as well. However, the mail server cannot accept emails from outside.

You must explicitly enable all other functions by making the appropriate settings in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/postfix/main.cf</samp>. In doing so, you can use the listing in [Section 26.2.4](#26_002.html_h26.2.4). In particular, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> must contain the <samp class="listingcharacter">inet_interfaces=all</samp> setting. You also need to specify matching names for <samp class="listingcharacter">myorigin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">myhostname</samp>. Note that the change of <samp class="listingcharacter">inet_interfaces</samp> doesn’t take effect until you restart Postfix!

In the default configuration, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> is quite confusing due to countless comments. To address this, create a backup of the file and then a cleaned up version for further editing:

```
root# cd /etc/postfix
root# cp main.cf main.cf.orig
root# grep -Ev '^#' main.cf.orig > main.cf 
```

To ensure that the mail server can be reached from the internet, ports 25 and 587 must not be blocked by a firewall. This is exactly the case with Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE. Although this does not matter for the default configuration of Postfix, if you want your mail server to be accessible from outside, you must open some ports of the firewall.

On RHEL, you first need to determine which firewall zone is assigned to the network interface to the outside (here the <samp class="listingcharacter">enp1s0</samp> interface and the <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> zone). Then open the ports using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">firewall-cmd</samp>. The command for port 465 is optional. Port 465 is for the SMTPS protocol, which is now considered obsolete:

```
root# firewall-cmd --get-active-zones  
(determine active zone)
public
  interfaces: enp1s0
root# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=smtp
root# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public \
  --add-port=465/tcp  
(optional)
root# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-port=587/tcp
root# firewall-cmd --reload 
```

[Chapter 29](#29_001.html_h29) contains background information and descriptions of other strategies for configuring a firewall. If you run your mail server in the cloud, you need to make sure that the previously mentioned ports are not blocked by the cloud firewall. In AWS EC2, you must define appropriate exception rules in the instance's security group (often in launch-wizard-nnn).

Before you run tests using Mutt, you should add the <samp class="listingcharacter">set hidden_host=yes</samp> line to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/Muttrc</samp>.

### 26.2.3    Configuration

The basic Postfix configuration files are located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/postfix</samp>. Within the configuration files, you can use preconfigured options like variables—such as <samp class="listingcharacter">option1 = value1</samp> and then <samp class="listingcharacter">option2 = $option1</samp>. Statements in the configuration file may extend across multiple lines, but the text must be indented from the second line on.

The configuration files often reference tables or lists, which are called lookup tables or mappings in the documentation. In this context, <samp class="listingcharacter">option=type:name</samp> syntax applies. The most common file type is <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp>. In this case, Postfix analyzes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.db</samp> file; that is, it adds the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.db</samp> extension to the specified filename. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.db</samp> files are tables in a binary format (Berkeley DB [BDB] format). To manipulate such files, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp> command.

Tables in text format are not provided for reasons of efficiency. The only exception is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp> text file, whose format is compatible with Sendmail. But even in this case Postfix falls back on the associated BDB file, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aliases.db</samp>. That is why <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aliases.db</samp> must be synchronized by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newaliases</samp> command after each change to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">aliases</samp>. To learn what mail aliases are and how to configure them, see [Section 26.4](#26_004.html_h26.4).

However, Postfix can also communicate with external databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, or LDAP), provided the corresponding Postfix extension packages are installed. The file named in the configuration file now doesn’t contain the actual data, but the connection information and a (SQL) query. Using external databases is especially useful if you need to manage a large number of email accounts, such as hundreds or thousands. I won’t discuss this case any further in this chapter.

```
virtual_mailbox_domains=mysql:/etc/postfix/mysql-virt-domains.cf 
```

### 26.2.4    main.cf

The main configuration file for Postfix is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/postfix/main.cf</samp>. The following listing shows the most important lines of this file in the default setting (Internet Site type) common on Ubuntu. As always in this chapter, the full host name of the mail server is <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a-company.com</samp> and the domain name is <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>:

```
# file /etc/postfix/main.cf (excerpts)
# this is how Postfix reports to other MTAs
smtpd_banner = $myhostname ESMTP $mail_name (Ubuntu)

# no notification of new mail via 'biff' (obsolete)
biff = no

# no automatic address completion with .a-company.com
append_dot_mydomain = no

# hostname
myhostname = efd.a-company.com

# domain for local e-mails without explicit domain specification
myorigin = a-company.com

# alternatively for Debian/Ubuntu:
# myorigin = /etc/mailname
# /etc/mailname contains a-company.com in the sample configuration

# location of the alias file
alias_maps = hash:/etc/aliases
alias_database = hash:/etc/aliases

# allow sending new emails only from the local computer
mydestination = a-company.com, efd.a-company.com, localhost
mynetworks = 127.0.0.0/8 [::ffff:127.0.0.0]/104 [::1]/128

# no email forwarding to other hosts (no relaying)
relayhost = 

# email reception via all network interfaces
inet_interfaces = all

# use IPv4 and IPv6
inet_protocols = all

# no limitation of email and mailbox size
mailbox_size_limit = 0 
```

In addition to the keywords included in the preceding listing, there are countless others documented in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man 5 postconf</samp>. All options have default settings. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postconf -d</samp> command shows you what these look like.

In the following list, I will briefly introduce some particularly important settings. A description of various other options can be found later in this chapter:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">myhostname</samp> contains the hostname of the server. <samp class="listingcharacter">myhostname</samp> is considered the default for many other options.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">myorigin</samp> specifies the domain to which locally sent emails are to be assigned; in the example of this chapter, that’s <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>. In the configuration file supplied with Ubuntu or Debian, <samp class="listingcharacter">myorigin</samp> is read from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/mailname</samp> file. Make sure that the correct name is included there, or change the setting in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> file!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">mydestination</samp> lists domains for which received emails are to be delivered (i.e., stored) locally in a mailbox. The default configuration on RHEL uses various variables for <samp class="listingcharacter">mydestination</samp>. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">$myorigin</samp> is missing there, which causes the Relay access denied error message to appear. If you want to stick to the default syntax, you should change the line as follows:

    ```
    mydestination = $myorigin, $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost 
    ```

    Caution: Even if Postfix is responsible for multiple domains, <samp class="listingcharacter">mydestination</samp> must only contain entries for the primary domain. You can specify virtual domains via the <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual_alias_domains</samp> option.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">mynetworks</samp> specifies the addresses from which Postfix accepts mail via SMTP without authentication. The addresses or address ranges specified here thus designate the computers that are “trusted” by Postfix.

    In the configuration presented here (i.e., for a standalone email server on a root server), <samp class="listingcharacter">mynetworks</samp> must contain only the IPv4 or IPv6 address of <samp class="listingcharacter">localhost</samp>. If you configure <samp class="listingcharacter">mynetworks</samp> incorrectly (not restrictively enough), external users can use your mail server to send emails without authentication. Beware, spammers love such computers!

    If <samp class="listingcharacter">mynetworks</samp> is not explicitly set (e.g., on RHEL), Postfix automatically uses only localhost addresses, so it is a reasonable default setting. You can verify this by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postconf -d mynetworks</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">relayhost</samp> specifies to which MTA emails should be forwarded that are not intended for local delivery. In the configuration presented here, <samp class="listingcharacter">relayhost</samp> must remain empty. Only if Postfix runs on a computer in a local network and is supposed to forward emails to be sent to an external MTA on the internet is <samp class="listingcharacter">relayhost</samp> is the decisive parameter.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">inet_interfaces</samp> controls at which network interfaces Postfix waits for incoming emails. The default <samp class="listingcharacter">all</samp> setting means that all interfaces are active. <samp class="listingcharacter">loopback_only</samp> or the specification of the <samp class="listingcharacter">127.0.0.1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">::1</samp> addresses means that only server-internal network traffic is processed. Changes to this option require a restart of Postfix (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl restart postfix</samp>)!

### 26.2.5    Changes to the Configuration

Postfix consists of a number of individual programs, many of which are restarted every time they are needed and then terminated again shortly after. These programs load the relevant configuration files anew each time.

However, there are also Postfix components that do not automatically detect configuration changes. Postfix beginners, who often do not know which changes Postfix notices on its own, should always run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl reload postfix</samp> after the configuration has been modified. This is especially true for changes to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">master.cf</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp>.

After resetting <samp class="listingcharacter">inet_interfaces</samp>, even <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl restart postfix</samp> is required. However, Postfix professionals will avoid <samp class="listingcharacter">reload</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">restart</samp> if possible because of the associated loss of speed, especially on large active systems.

Instead of changing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> in an editor and then running a <samp class="listingcharacter">reload</samp> command, you can also implement the change using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postconf -e option=value</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postconf</samp> command then also immediately notifies Postfix about the change. The command changes existing settings in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> at their previous location, while new parameters are added at the end of the file. Make sure that you do not insert a space before and after the <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> sign:

```
root# postconf disable_vrfy_command=yes 
```

If you aren’t sure which default settings apply in Postfix and which settings you have made that differ from the basic settings, the following three commands will help you:

```
root# postconf -d  
(default settings)
root# postconf     
(all currently valid settings)
root# postconf -n  
(only deviations from the basic settings) 
```

If you’re only interested in a specific parameter, you need to specify it explicitly:

```
root# postconf -d local_recipient_maps
local_recipient_maps = proxy:unix:passwd.byname $alias_maps 
```

The additional <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-f</samp> option (fold) improves the readability of the output by inserting line breaks.

Once a mail server has been put into operation, changes during operation are obviously a tricky matter. If you do something wrong, incoming emails may be rejected. These are then lost for good. That's why it's better to add <samp class="listingcharacter">soft_bounce=yes</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> before starting the modifications (and of course to keep a sharp eye on the logging files). Due to <samp class="listingcharacter">soft_bounce=yes</samp>, Postfix converts all <samp class="listingcharacter">5xx</samp> errors (permanent failures) to <samp class="listingcharacter">4xx</samp> errors (persistent transient failures). The sender will therefore make a new delivery attempt after some time and the email is not lost.

Don't forget to set <samp class="listingcharacter">soft_bounce=no</samp> again after finishing and testing the changed configuration!

Postfix uses IPv4 and IPv6 by default. The two relevant options are set accordingly by default:

```
inet_protocols = all
smtp_address_preference = any 
```

Only if you want to explicitly disable IPv6 should you use <samp class="listingcharacter">inet_protocols = ipv4</samp>.

### 26.2.6    Opening Port 587

By default, Postfix accepts messages only on port 25 for further processing. This port is intended for the communication between mail servers. While most mail clients can be configured to use port 25, port 587 is actually intended for sending such emails.

Postfix already contains the appropriate statements in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">master.cf</samp> file (not in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> as usual); they only need to be commented out. In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">master.cf</samp>, you must look for the line that starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">submission inet</samp>, and then remove the <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> comment character from that line and subsequent lines that start with <samp class="listingcharacter">-o</samp> and contain miscellaneous parameters. Only leave the three lines where <samp class="listingcharacter">$mua variables</samp> are referenced unchanged (unless you have made appropriate <samp class="listingcharacter">mua_xxx</samp> settings in <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cf</samp>):

```
# enable port 587 in /etc/postfix/master.cf
# service type  private unpriv  chroot  wakeup  maxproc command + args
#               (yes)   (yes)   (yes)   (never) (100)
...
submission inet n       -       n       -       -       smtpd
  -o syslog_name=postfix/submission
  -o smtpd_tls_security_level=encrypt
  -o smtpd_sasl_auth_enable=yes
  -o smtpd_reject_unlisted_recipient=no
# -o smtpd_client_restrictions=$mua_client_restrictions
# -o smtpd_helo_restrictions=$mua_helo_restrictions
# -o smtpd_sender_restrictions=$mua_sender_restrictions
  -o smtpd_recipient_restrictions=permit_sasl_authenticated,reject
  -o smtpd_relay_restrictions=permit_sasl_authenticated,reject
  -o milter_macro_daemon_name=ORIGINATING 
```

In short, these settings cause Postfix to accept messages at port 587, but only if the client can authenticate itself and the communication is encrypted. For the changed configuration to take effect, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl reload postfix</samp>.

### 26.2.7    Logging and Administration

Postfix logs its activities via syslog. As is so often the case, the location of the numerous messages depends on the distribution:

*   Some distributions contain several logging files in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log</samp>, which, for example, are named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mail.log</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mail.info</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mail.warn</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mail.err</samp>. This makes it easier to differentiate between more or less important messages.

*   It is more common that simply all mail-relevant messages end up in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/mail.log</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/maillog</samp>. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep</samp> to filter out the messages that concern a specific program (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep postfix mail.log</samp>), that describe an error (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">grep -i error mail.log</samp>), and so on.

    On RHEL, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/maillog</samp> file exists only if you install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsyslog</samp> package and then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl enable --now rsyslogd</samp>.

*   An increasing number of distributions use the systemd journal for logging tasks. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">journalctl -u postfix</samp> then returns all postfix messages, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">journalctl -u dovecot</samp> returns those from Dovecot, and so on. However, usually only a few warnings and error messages are logged in the journal. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mail.log</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">maillog</samp>, on the other hand, contain status messages for each mail received or sent.

If you want to know which emails are waiting to be sent, you should run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postqueue -p</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mailq</samp>. The two commands provide a list of all emails that—for whatever reason—could not be sent so far.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postqueue -f</samp> to trigger an immediate retry. (Usually Postfix itself decides when to make the next attempt).

## 26.3    Postfix Encryption (TLS/STARTTLS)

Postfix supports the TLS protocol and the STARTTLS method for establishing an encrypted connection between itself and the mail client that wants to send an email. However, this assumes that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> is configured accordingly and that you have a suitable certificate for your machine. Basic knowledge about “correct” and self-generated certificates can be found in [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.2](#24_002.html_h24.2). For more information about Postfix TLS support, visit [https://www.postfix.org/TLS_README.html](https://www.postfix.org/TLS_README.html).

Note that changes to the TLS configuration will only take effect after a restart of Postfix!

### smtpd = Incoming, smtp = Outgoing

When configuring TLS in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp>, there are two groups of parameters you must not confuse. In one of the groups, the parameter names start with <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_</samp>; these parameters control the behavior of Postfix upon receiving emails. This especially concerns the communication between the mail clients of the employees of your company/organization and the mail server.

In the other group, the parameter names start with <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp_</samp>; these parameters concern the sending of emails—that is, the communication of the local MTA with other MTAs.

Custom certificates are only required for incoming emails (<samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_*</samp>)! The mail client or an external MTA asks Postfix for the public part of the key and encrypts the message. Postfix has the private key and can use it to decrypt the incoming message.

When sending emails, it’s exactly the other way around: that's when Postfix asks the target MTA if it can provide a public key to encrypt the message. Postfix thus relies on the public part of an external key.

### 26.3.1    Sample Configuration and Keywords

The following lines reflect a sample configuration:

```
# in/etc/postfix/main.cf
...
# receive mails encrypted if possible;
# certificate, key and, if required, 
# certificate chain for the certification authority 
smtpd_tls_security_level = may
smtpd_tls_cert_file      = /etc/ssl/my-full-chain.pem
smtpd_tls_key_file       = /etc/ssl/my-key.key
# smtpd_tls_CAfile       = /etc/ssl/my-ca-bundle.pem

# send mails encrypted if possible
smtp_tls_security_level  = may

# certificate authorities for Debian/Ubuntu
smtp_tls_CApath          = /etc/ssl/certs

# certificate authorities for RHEL
smtp_tls_CApath          = /etc/pki/tls/certs
smtp_tls_CAfile          = /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt

# optional: higher efficiency through cache
smtpd_tls_session_cache_database = btree:${data_directory}/smtpd_scache
smtp_tls_session_cache_database  = btree:${data_directory}/smtp_scache 

# optional: Logging for troubleshooting
smtpd_tls_loglevel = 1
smtp_tls_loglevel  = 1 
```

The keywords used here require some further explanation:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_security_level = may</samp> causes Postfix to offer STARTTLS and accept incoming mail encrypted with TLS if possible. However, if the mail client is configured incorrectly or for old mail clients, authentication in plain text is still possible. If you want to force the encryption, you need to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">encrypt</samp> string instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">may</samp>. This guarantees an encryption, but makes it impossible to receive email from poorly configured clients or MTAs.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_cert_file</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_key_file</samp> specify which certificate Postfix should use with which key. With certificates from official certification authorities, you usually receive another file that closes the certificate chain. You need to specify this using <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_CAfile</samp>. You can do without this in the case of self-created certificates or certificates from Let's Encrypt.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp_tls_security_level = may</samp> signifies that Postfix sends emails encrypted if possible, provided that the recipient (i.e., the mail server on the other side) is capable of receiving encrypted mails. If necessary, the message can also be transmitted in plain text. A more secure solution would be <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt</samp>, but then your mail server can no longer send messages to mail servers that do not support encryption.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp_tls_CAfile</samp> references a collection of CAs (certificate authorities) Postfix should trust. The directory location for these files varies depending on the distribution.

    On Debian and Ubuntu, Postfix runs in a <samp class="listingcharacter">chroot</samp> environment and has no access to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/ssl/certs</samp> at all. For this reason, the certificates are automatically copied to the <samp class="listingcharacter">chroot</samp> directory <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/postfix/etc/ssl/certs</samp> when Postfix is started.

    Things are much easier on RHEL: there, SELinux monitors the Postfix programs, so a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chroot</samp> environment is not required.

    If <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp_tls_CAfile</samp> is not set correctly, then the Untrusted TLS connection message is logged when sending mails. This means that the message was transmitted encrypted, but Postfix could not verify the certificate of the other mail server.

    With the correct setting of <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp_tls_CAfile</samp> and assuming that the recipient server's certificate was issued by a CA that is included in the CA collection, the logging entry changes to Trusted TLS connection. The following page of the Postfix documentation provides help for interpreting Untrusted, Trusted, and and the like (see [https://www.postfix.org/FORWARD_SECRECY_README.html#status](https://www.postfix.org/FORWARD_SECRECY_README.html#status)).

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp[d]_tls_session_cache_database</samp>, Postfix manages a cache that temporarily stores TLS session information. The database is shared by multiple Postfix instances. It significantly speeds up the TLS communication. The cache files are stored in the Postfix data directory, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/postfix</samp>.

On Debian and Ubuntu, Postfix uses a so-called snake-oil certificate. This self-signed certificate is generated during the installation of Apache or Postfix (depending on which package was installed first) for the host name that was valid at that time and is valid for 10 years (see [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.2.4](#24_002.html_h24.2.4)). The <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_cert_file</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-key_file</samp> parameters in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> specify the locations of the certificate and key files:

```
# file /etc/postfix/main.cf
...
smtpd_tls_cert_file = /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem
smtpd_tls_key_file  = /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key 
```

During the configuration, the mail client will of course report that the certificate is not trusted. In most mail clients, you can still accept the certificate; this will securely encrypt the mails transferred from the mail client to Postfix, and you will have achieved your goal.

While the use of self-signed certificates is an absolute no-go for public web servers (except for test operations), the situation is completely different for mail servers. The highest priority is currently that the data flow gets encrypted at all. That's why most mail servers accept encryption when receiving mail even if the sending server uses a self-signed certificate, if it has already expired, and so on.

Current Postfix installations on Debian and Ubuntu receive email encrypted and send email encrypted. For older installations, however, only the former applies. For this reason, you need to make sure that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> contains the following two statements:

```
smtp_tls_CApath=/etc/ssl/certs
smtp_tls_security_level=may 
```

The default configuration on RHEL 8 is almost exactly the same as the listing printed earlier, with self-signed certificates in use as in Debian/Ubuntu.

### 26.3.2    Setting Up Custom Certificates

Unless your certificate is a wildcard certificate that applies to all <samp class="listingcharacter">*.a-company.com</samp> subdomains, the question arises: For which domain name should the certificate used by Postfix actually apply? For <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> or for <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.a‐company.com</samp> (i.e., for the host name according to the MX entry) or maybe for <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp.a-company.com</samp>? According to [https://serverfault.com/questions/389413](https://serverfault.com/questions/389413), only the client (e.g., Thunderbird) is responsible for verification. The client, in turn, compares the domain name of the certificate with the host name you specify during the client configuration of the mail account. The MX entry is not relevant for that.

By default, Thunderbird adds <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp</samp> as a prefix to the host name for the SMTP configuration. This results, for example, in <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp.a-company.com</samp>. Then the certificate should also have this name. If you continue this consistently, you will need a separate certificate for each mail protocol (<samp class="listingcharacter">pop.a-company.com</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">imap.a-company.com</samp>, etc.).

On Debian and Ubuntu, a snake-oil certificate including a key is set up by default during the Postfix installation—that is, a self-signed certificate that’s valid for ten years. The <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_cert_file</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-key_file</samp> parameters in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> specify the locations of the certificate and key files:

```
# file /etc/postfix/main.cf
...
smtpd_tls_cert_file = /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem
smtpd_tls_key_file  = /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key 
```

If you need a new certificate after changing the host name, you want to call the following command:

```
root# make-ssl-cert generate-default-snakeoil --force-overwrite 
```

However, the snake-oil certificate has two disadvantages: First, it’s self-signed, and second, it applies only to the host name, not to <samp class="listingcharacter">mail.hostname</samp>.

On RHEL, you can quickly generate a self-signed wildcard certificate instead of the snake-oil certificate by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp> command. It’s crucial that when you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">openssl</samp>, you prefix your host name with “<samp class="listingcharacter">*.</samp>” when entering the common name—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">*.a-company.com</samp>. Don't forget <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod 600</samp> for the key file:

```
root# mkdir /etc/ssl/private   
(RHEL only)

root# openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -nodes \
        -out    /etc/ssl/certs/postfix.pem \
        -keyout /etc/ssl/private/postfix.key
...

Common Name (eg server FQDN or YOUR name) []: *.a-company.com
...
root# chmod 600 /etc/ssl/private/postfix.key 
```

Then you must modify <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> as follows:

```
# file /etc/postfix/main.cf, use custom certificate
...
smtpd_tls_cert_file = /etc/ssl/certs/postfix.pem
smtpd_tls_key_file  = /etc/ssl/private/postfix.key 
```

Although the Let's Encrypt project was founded to advance the encryption of websites (see [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.3](#24_003.html_h24.3)), there is nothing to prevent the certificates from being used for the mail server as well. The configuration is easiest if you have a wildcard certificate. However, as issuing and updating such certificates works well only in conjunction with some large DNS servers, you will probably use ordinary certificates.

Make sure that the certificate includes the full host name (here, <samp class="listingcharacter">efd.xxx</samp>) as well as all subdomains common for mail servers, like <samp class="listingcharacter">mail.xxx</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">smtp.xxx</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">imap..xxx</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">pop..xxx</samp>. If you have not yet installed the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> command, please read the aforementioned [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.3](#24_003.html_h24.3) for instructions:

```
root# acme.sh --issue --server letsencrypt  \
        -d mail.a-company.com -d smtp.a-company.com \
        -d imap.a-company.com -d efd.a-company.com \
        -w /var/www/html 
```

This command assumes that the mail server is also running a web server and that its document root directory is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/www/html</samp>. If there is no active web server, then replace <samp class="listingcharacter">-w /var/www/html</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">--standalone</samp> option. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acme.sh</samp> script then temporarily acts as a web server itself. This is only possible if port 80 is not blocked by any other program.

Now the certificates must be copied to a directory that can be accessed by Postfix. Because the certificates are also to be used later by the Dovecot program, it’s advisable to install this program now and take it into account with the <samp class="listingcharacter">--reloadcmd</samp> option. The certificates will be renewed every 60 days in the future. For Postfix and Dovecot to then each use the current certificates, these two programs must be restarted:

```
root# mkdir /etc/acme-letsencrypt   
(if the directory does not exist yet)
root# apt install dovecot-imapd     
(Debian/Ubuntu)
root# dnf install dovecot           
(RHEL)

root# acme.sh --install-cert -d mail.a-company.com \
  --cert-file  /etc/acme-letsencrypt/mail.a-company.com.cert \
  --key-file   /etc/acme-letsencrypt/mail.a-company.com.key \
  --fullchain-file /etc/acme-letsencrypt/mail.a-company.com.fullchain \
  --reloadcmd 'systemctl restart postfix; systemctl restart dovecot' 
```

Now you must modify <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> as shown in the following sample listing:

```
smtpd_tls_cert_file = \
  /etc/acme-letsencrypt/mail.a-company.com.fullchain
smtpd_tls_key_file  = /etc/acme-letsencrypt/mail.a-company.com.key 
```

Make sure that you set the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.fullchain</samp> file as <samp class="listingcharacter">smtpd_tls_cert_file</samp>, not as <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cert</samp>.

Like Apache, Postfix also supports various encryption algorithms. If required, you can use additional options to control which methods are accepted and which are not; this way, you can increase the security of the mail server operation. The website at [https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/#server=postfix](https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/#server=postfix) provides excellent assistance in setting the options correctly.

Optimizing the options, however, resembles a tightrope walk: the more recent protocol versions your Postfix configuration requires, the greater the risk of incompatibilities with other servers or mail clients.

Changes to the TLS configuration do not take effect until Postfix has been restarted:

```
root# systemctl restart postfix 
```

## 26.4    Postfix Accounts

The following generally applies to Postfix: every regular user in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> is also a mail user. No additional configuration is required for these users. Each of these Linux users can send and receive emails.

External mail clients such as Thunderbird must authenticate with Postfix or Dovecot. The regular Linux passwords are also used for this authentication. (This is a big difference compared to Samba; this file server maintains separate passwords for each Samba user.)

### Mail Password as a Security Risk

As convenient as it is to have Linux and mail users running in parallel by default, it can also be risky.

Probably nobody would be so unwise as to use <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> as a regular email account (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">root@a-company.com</samp>) as this would require you to enter the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password when configuring the mail client. Rather, the risk of the following scenario is more likely to be overlooked: As an administrator of the <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp> server, you have an account there with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> rights—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>. For admin tasks, you log in with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh hoover@a-company.com</samp>, then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo -s</samp> and do whatever needs to be done. So far, so good.

It now makes sense to also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@a-company.com</samp> email account. As explained earlier, no further configuration work is required for this. The problem is that you now enter your <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp> password once when configuring Thunderbird on your Linux notebook, again when configuring your mail program on the smartphone, again for the tablet, and so on. If one of these devices is lost, it may be possible to find the stored password for <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>. And not only is this password sufficient to read your emails or send them in your name, but the dishonest finder can now also log in to <samp class="listingcharacter">company.abc.com</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> and has unlimited rights there thanks to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp>. In terms of security, this is the worst thing that can happen.

To solve this problem, simply never use mail accounts of users with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo</samp> privileges! Use separate accounts for email and for admin work, even if it’s inconvenient.

To set up a Linux account on the mail server for mail use only, you should set <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/bin/false</samp> as the shell. This makes it impossible to log in and work interactively.

On the other hand, the password is important, even though the user cannot log in at all. Here’s why: the password applies to the POP and SMTP authentication described in [Section 26.5](#26_005.html_h26.5).

On Debian and Ubuntu, the easiest way to set up a new account is to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--gecos ,,,</samp> suppresses the questions for the full name and other superfluous contact information:

```
root# adduser  --shell /bin/false --gecos ,,, hoover  
(Debian/Ubuntu)
Enter a new UNIX password:        ********
Enter the new UNIX password again:  ******** 
```

On RHEL, you need to call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">useradd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">passwd</samp>:

```
root# useradd -s /bin/false hoover                    
(RHEL)
root# passwd hoover
Changing password for user hoover.

New password:        ********
Retype new password: ******** 
```

### Tip

Virtual domains, which I will introduce ahead, allow you to avoid setting up a separate Linux account for each user. Postfix then supports virtual mailboxes, which are quite real but do not correspond to a valid user name. Such a configuration is useful if you do not need three or four mail accounts, but hundreds or thousands.

The parallel connection of Linux and mail accounts outlined in the introduction corresponds to the default configuration, but it will rarely remain that way. In the following sections, I will therefore explain some possibilities for a configuration that deviates from this:

*   Mail aliases make it possible to redirect emails to existing accounts.

*   By configuring an explicit list of recipients, you can control the list of email accounts and, for example, prevent system accounts such as <samp class="listingcharacter">adm</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">lp</samp> from sending or receiving emails.

*   If you use virtual domains, you can process emails from different host names using one Postfix server (not only for <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>, but also for <samp class="listingcharacter">company-xy.info</samp>).

*   Virtual mailboxes allow you to completely separate mail accounts and their passwords from Linux accounts. The data is often stored in a database.

First, however, the following section deals with the question of where emails are actually stored.

### 26.4.1    mbox or maildir Format

By default, Postfix stores incoming emails in mbox format in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/mail/name</samp> file. If emails are to be stored in a local file in the user directory instead (still in mbox format), you must specify the desired file name relative to the home directory by using <samp class="listingcharacter">home_mailbox</samp>:

```
# in /etc/postfix/main.cf
...
# save emails in mbox format in file /home/name/Mailbox
home_mailbox = Mailbox 
```

If you plan to retrieve the mails mainly via IMAP, you should prefer using the maildir format. The correct setting of <samp class="listingcharacter">home_mailbox</samp> now looks as follows:

```
# in /etc/postfix/main.cf
...
# save emails in maildir format in the /home/name/Maildir directory
home_mailbox = Maildir/ 
```

The directory name must end with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/</samp> so that Postfix uses the maildir format. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp> contains a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mailbox_command</samp> statement, you must comment it out. New incoming emails are now stored in their own files in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/<name>/Maildir</samp> directory.

Basically, the conversion to the maildir format should work without any problem. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> user on RHEL systems does cause problems. In this case, the mail delivery fails with the following error: create maildir file: permission denied. Fortunately, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/log/maillog</samp> also immediately points out the cause. For security reasons, Postfix refuses to set up the required maildir directories for <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. You must take care of this yourself in advance:

```
root# mkdir -p /root/Maildir/{cur,new,tmp} 
```

Don't forget to tell your local mail client or Dovecot the location and format of your mailbox as well ([Section 26.5](#26_005.html_h26.5))! If you use <samp class="listingcharacter">mutt</samp>, you must configure the program accordingly so that it reads the emails from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">maildir</samp> directory (see [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5)).

### 26.4.2    Mail Aliases

A mail alias is an additional mail name for receiving email. However, the email is actually forwarded to an existing account. Aliases are defined in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp> file. This file usually looks similar to the following pattern:

```
# file /etc/aliases
postmaster:      root
webmaster:       hoover
Herbert.Hoover:  hoover
... 
```

The first column specifies the alias name without a domain. The name applies to the domain defined in <samp class="listingcharacter">myhostname</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">postmaster@a-company. com</samp>. The second column contains the local recipient. In the preceding example, emails addressed to <samp class="listingcharacter">postmaster</samp> are forwarded to <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>, while emails to <samp class="listingcharacter">webmaster</samp> and to <samp class="listingcharacter">Herbert.Hoover</samp> are forwarded to <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>. It’s permissible to specify multiple recipients separated by commas for each alias in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp>.

As a recipient, you can specify an external email address instead of a local email account name, a file to which the email will be attached, or a program in the <samp class="listingcharacter">|command</samp> notation to which the email will be redirected. Redirecting to external email addresses works without any problem, but in practice often fails due to the spam protection of the target MTA. So, for example, if you redirect emails to <samp class="listingcharacter">webmaster</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">name@gmx.com</samp>, the spam filter of GMX will recognize that the email was not transmitted directly to <samp class="listingcharacter">gmx.com</samp>, but indirectly via <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>. This is enough for a suspicious spam filter to classify the email as spam.

For changed aliases to take effect, you must run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newaliases</samp> command. This command synchronizes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp> text file with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases.db</samp> BDB file.

In <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/postfix/main.cf</samp>, you usually encounter two <samp class="listingcharacter">alias</samp> options, which sometimes causes confusion:

```
# in /etc/postfix/main.cf
...
alias_maps = hash:/etc/aliases
alias_database = hash:/etc/aliases 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">alias_database</samp> specifies which database file is to be updated by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newaliases</samp> command. The file specified here (whose name is supplemented by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.db</samp>) contains the aliases specified in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp> in a binary format.

<samp class="listingcharacter">alias_maps</samp> specifies which alias databases Postfix is supposed to take into account. Typically you specify the same file here as for <samp class="listingcharacter">alias_database</samp>. However, it is permissible to specify additional sources for alias definitions. The crucial difference between the two parameters is that <samp class="listingcharacter">alias_database</samp> applies to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">newaliases</samp>, while <samp class="listingcharacter">alias_maps</samp> applies to Postfix!

#### Cleaning up Aliases on RHEL

In the default configuration, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp> on RHEL contains an almost endless list of aliases that are rarely useful in real life. Create a backup of the file, and then delete all the lines you don't currently need!

Even as a local user who does not have access to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/aliases</samp>, you can redirect your mail to another address: to do this, you should create the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.forward</samp> file and save the new destination address in it. Done!

As I mentioned previously, this simple method of email redirection usually only works as planned for local addresses. With external destination addresses, on the other hand, it can happen that the redirected emails are caught in the spam protection of the destination MTA.

### 26.4.3    Explicit Recipients List

By default, any Linux account can receive email. However, it’s rarely desirable for system accounts such as <samp class="listingcharacter">daemon</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sys</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">man</samp> to receive emails. To fix this issue, you need to tweak the <samp class="listingcharacter">local_recipient_maps</samp> parameter. The default setting is as follows:

```
local_recipient_maps = proxy:unix:passwd.byname $alias_maps 
```

This means that all users listed in the Unix <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/passwd</samp> file and all users named in the alias databases can receive email. If you want only <samp class="listingcharacter">fisher</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">smith</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> (for system notifications) to receive emails, you should proceed as follows: First, create a text file that contains the account names line by line. The file must contain an arbitrary value in a second column, because Postfix and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp> command generally expect key/value pairs even for lists where actually only the existence of a key is relevant, but the corresponding value is not considered at all:

```
# file /etc/postfix/local-recips
fisher   x
hoover   x
smith    x
root     x 
```

From this file, you then create a Postfix-readable database file named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips.db</samp> by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp>:

```
root# cd /etc/postfix
root# postmap local-recips 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap -s</samp> command enables you to check if the file was created correctly:

```
root# postmap -s hash:local-recips
hoover  x
root    x
smith   x
fisher  x 
```

Then, add a line to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/postfix/main.cf</samp> to set <samp class="listingcharacter">local_recipient_maps</samp>:

```
# in /etc/postfix/main.cf
local_recipient_maps = hash:/etc/postfix/local-recips $alias_maps 
```

From now on, Postfix will only accept emails to the recipients named in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips</samp>. However, there is still one limitation: emails are only delivered (i.e., stored locally) if the user has an account on the computer. If that is not the case, you have to create a new account using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">adduser</samp>.

#### Updating Mapping Files Safely and Securely

After each change to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips</samp>, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp> to update the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips.db</samp> database file relevant to Postfix. However, this update is a critical operation: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp> deletes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips.db</samp> and then rewrites the file. If Postfix accesses <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips.db</samp> just during this time, it will receive incorrect or incomplete data.

A safe approach therefore looks as follows: you assign a different name to the underlying text file (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips1</samp>), apply <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp> to this file and then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mv local-recips1.db local-recips.db</samp>. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">local-recips.db</samp> contains consistent data at any time—either in the old or in the new version. You can automate this process by using a script or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">make</samp> file, as described at [https://www.postfix.org/DATABASE_README.html#safe_db](https://www.postfix.org/DATABASE_README.html#safe_db).

This note applies to all mapping files that appear in this chapter.

### 26.4.4    Email Addresses Differing from the Linux Account

In many companies, email addresses of the format <samp class="listingcharacter">firstname.familyname@ company.com</samp> are common. Linux, however, doesn’t provide for such long user names—not to mention those with a dot. However, this does not prevent you from still using long email names:

*   Create a Linux account with a Linux-typical, short user name, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>.

*   Define an alias rule that forwards emails sent to <samp class="listingcharacter">Herbert.Hoover</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>.

*   When configuring the email client, use the long format as the sender address—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">Herbert.Hoover@a-company.com</samp>. Note, however, that you must specify the Linux account name for POP, IMAP, and SMTP authentication!

*   To ensure that emails sent locally (e.g., by Mutt) also contain the correct sender address in the long version, you need to set up a new table in the <samp class="listingcharacter">/etc/postfix/canonical</samp> text file and convert it to a file readable by Postfix using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp>. The table specifies how Postfix is supposed to modify email addresses:

    ```
    # /etc/postfix/canonical
    hoover Herbert.Hoover@a-company.com
    ... 
    ```

*   Then, in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp>, set the <samp class="listingcharacter">canonical_maps</samp> parameter, and then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl reload postfix</samp>:

    ```
    # in /etc/postfix/main.cf
    ...
    canonical_maps = hash:/etc/postfix/canonical 
    ```

In addition to the Canonical and alias tables, Postfix provides various other ways to manipulate email addresses at different stages of email traffic: when receiving, before sending, and so on. The page at [https://www.postfix.org/ADDRESS_REWRITING_README.html](https://www.postfix.org/ADDRESS_REWRITING_README.html) gives a good overview.

### 26.4.5    Virtual Domains with Shared Email Users

In the simplest case, Postfix is only responsible for emails sent to the host name of the computer, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">xxx@a-company.com</samp>. However, it’s often useful for one MTA to be responsible for multiple email domains, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">xxx@another-company.com</samp>, for example. All domains that do not match the host name of the computer are called virtual in Postfix terminology (they’re often called hosted domains as well).

Postfix provides several ways to implement virtual domains. The easiest way is to simply set several domains in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mydestination</samp> parameter, like this:

```
# in /etc/postfix/main.cf
...
mydestination = a-company.com, localhost, another-company.com 
```

Of course, you also need to adjust the DNS configuration of <samp class="listingcharacter">another-company.com</samp> accordingly. The MX host name must therefore be assigned the IP address of your server (see [Section 26.1.5](#26_001.html_h26.1.5)).

This ensures that mails to <samp class="listingcharacter">another-company.com</samp> are treated in the same way as mails to <samp class="listingcharacter">a-company.com</samp>. So it doesn't matter whether an email is addressed to <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@a-company.com</samp> or to <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@another-company.com</samp>: in any case, Postfix delivers the email to the local user <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>. For some cases, this is sufficient—especially if a company or organization has multiple web presences, but in reality the same people are always responsible for them.

### 26.4.6    Virtual Domains with Separate Email Users

If you want to differentiate between users with the same name depending on the domain, you must specify the domains involved using the <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual_alias_domains</samp> keyword rather than <samp class="listingcharacter">mydestination</samp>. In addition, you then need a table that establishes the mapping between the virtual domain email addresses and the real Linux accounts. Furthermore, a Linux account is required for each email address. To stick with the example of the hoover addresses: The account for <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@a-company.com</samp> is still <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover</samp>. For <samp class="listingcharacter">hoover@another-company.com</samp>, you have to create a new account—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">hooverNEF</samp>. The structure of the table for the virtual email users looks as follows:

```
# text file /etc/postfix/virtual
hoover@another-company.com      hooverNEF
miller@another-company.com    millerNEF
... 
```

Like the alias table, the table can assign the same user to multiple email addresses—for example:

```
# in /etc/postfix/virtual
webmaster@another-company.com  hooverNEF 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">postmap</samp> to turn this file into a database file that can be read by Postfix:

```
root# postmap /etc/postfix/virtual 
```

Now you need to adjust <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">main.cf</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual_alias_domains</samp> lists all virtual domains (but not the primary domain; you still have to specify that using <samp class="listingcharacter">mydestination</samp>!). <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual_alias_maps</samp> specifies the filename of the virtual alias table:

```
# in /etc/postfix/main.cf
mydestination         = a-company.com, localhost
virtual_alias_domains = another-company.com, company-xyz.com, ...
virtual_alias_maps    = hash:/etc/postfix/virtual 
```

### 26.4.7    Virtual Domains with Virtual Mailboxes

Up to this point, it has always been necessary to have a Linux account for each email address. Postfix refuses to store email in a mailbox unless there is a Linux account with the same name. However, if you have a large number of email addresses, it becomes increasingly impractical to create a new account each time. Postfix provides virtual mailboxes to solve this problem. These are ordinary mailbox files; the term virtual only refers to the fact that there are no associated Linux accounts.
