You can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smbclient</samp> to browse network directories. The command offers little comfort but is often useful for tracking down Samba issues. Once you have used <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmblookup</samp> to determine the names of the NMB servers on the local network, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smbclient -L <hostname></samp> displays all the shared resources of the specified host:

```
user$ smbclient -L win10
Enter SAMBA/user's password: ******
   Sharename       Type      Comment
   ---------       ----      -------
   ADMIN$          Disk      Remote Administration
   C$              Disk      Default Share
   IPC$            IPC       Remote IPC
   Users           Disk 
```

If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smbclient</samp> returns a login error message (session setup failed: NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED), your current Linux user name does not match the user names of the Windows computer or Samba server. The simplest solution is to pass the user name (<samp class="listingcharacter">-U</samp> option) and, if necessary, the workgroup name <samp class="listingcharacter">-W</samp>) to the command:

```
user$ smbclient -U <username> -W <workgroupname> -L <hostname>
Enter SAMBA/username's password: ****** 
```

If you’re interested in resources that are accessible without login, you should pass an invalid user name (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">-U none</samp>) and suppress the password request by using the <samp class="listingcharacter">-N</samp> option. Note that depending on the configuration of the server, network directories may also be listed in this case, access to which will later require a login after all.

Only in rare cases is it necessary to limit the highest possible protocol version with the <samp class="listingcharacter">-m</samp> option. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">-m SMB2</samp> means that you do not want to use <samp class="listingcharacter">SMB3</samp>:

```
user$ smbclient  -U none -N -m SMB2 -L libreelec 
```

You can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smbclient</samp> interactively to transfer files. To do this, first connect to the Windows computer or Samba server for the shared directory. You must specify the directory in the Windows-typical notation: <samp class="listingcharacter">\\servername\directoryname</samp>. To prevent the <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> characters from being processed by the shell, they must be duplicated. It’s easier to use the <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> characters, which are more common on Linux and which <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smbclient</samp> fortunately also accepts.

Then, as with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ftp</samp> command, you can view directories via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ls</samp>, change directories using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cd</samp>, transfer files to the local computer by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">get</samp>, and save files to the external computer via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">put</samp>. You can get an overview of the most important commands via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">help</samp>. A detailed description of the commands can be found in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man smbclient</samp>:

```
user$ smbclient -U kofler //diskstation/archive
Enter WORKGROUP/kofler's password: ******
Try "help" to get a list of possible commands.
smb:/> ls
  .            DA        0  Mon Mar 22 14:51:28 2021
  ..           DA        0  Fri Apr 16 07:01:18 2021
  audio        DA        0  Sun Mar 13 21:36:44 2016
  bak          DA        0  Sun Dec  3 18:16:27 2017
  code         DA        0  Sat Aug  1 16:43:18 2020
  ...
  1290153920 blocks of size 1024\. 396335724 blocks available
smb:/> get time-recording.ods
getting file /time-recording.ods of size 64487 ...
smb:/> exit 
```

### 27.7.4    CIFS-mount

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">smbclient</samp> is a tool to locate SMB resources in case of connection issues and to transfer individual files if necessary without establishing a permanent connection to the network directory. To be able to work persistently and comfortably, you have to integrate the network directory into the local directory tree by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp>.

The underlying technology is called Common Internet File System (CIFS). This is the successor to SMB File System (SMBFS). CIFS-compatible Samba servers pass on Unix-/Linux-compatible information about file access rights, which was not possible with SMBFS.

CIFS requires that the Samba client tools and CIFS support for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> and, in particular, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount.cifs</samp> command be available. For Debian and Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cifs-utils</samp> package must be installed for this purpose. Fedora and openSUSE have the package installed by default.

To mount an external directory, you need to specify one of the following two commands, depending on whether Windows sharing is based on user names or not:

```
root# mkdir /media/archive
root# mount -t cifs //diskstation/archive /media/archive
root# mount -t cifs -o username=<name> //diskstation/archive \
       /media/archive 
```

This mounts the directory named <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">archive</samp>, which is shared on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">diskstation</samp> NAS device into the Linux file system.

The data is now available to the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> user under the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/media/archive</samp> Linux directory. When you run the command, you must enter parameters. You can also specify the password directly, but this is insecure:

```
root# mount -t cifs -o username=name,password=xxxxxxxx \
       //diskstation/archive /media/archive 
```

In real life, many more options are often required before the network directory can be used correctly. For example, a typical <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command might look as follows:

```
root# mount -t cifs \
       -o username=name,uid=1000,gid=1000,vers=2.1 \
       //diskstation/archive /media/archive 
```

For a summary of the main <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> options, see [Table 27.4](#27_007.html_t27.4).

For a better understanding of the previous command, a few more explanations are necessary: To enable you to read and write to the network directory not only as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> but also as an ordinary user, you must specify your personal user and group identification numbers in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command using <samp class="listingcharacter">uid=n</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">gid=n</samp>; you can quickly determine these IDs via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">id</samp> command. In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter">dir_mode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">file_mode</samp> specify the access rights with which the network directories and files should be visible. Access rights are specified in an octal notation, which is explained in more detail in [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.7](#09_007.html_h9.7). The most useful settings are <samp class="listingcharacter">0700</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">0600</samp>. This allows the user who is named via <samp class="listingcharacter">uid</samp> to edit all directories and read and modify all files. Other users of the computer, however, do not have access.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">nounix</samp> option seems a little absurd: the CIFS standard has been extended by the so-called Unix extensions in order to achieve better compatibility with Unix/Linux systems. On some NAS devices, these extensions are also active. In this case, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> takes the user and group information and access rights from the NAS device and ignores the <samp class="listingcharacter">uid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">gid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">dir_mode</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">file_mode</samp> options.

However, this is only useful if this data is coordinated between the NAS device and the clients. Because this is rarely the case, the Unix compatibility mode must be disabled so that <samp class="listingcharacter">uid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">gid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">dir_mode</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">file_mode</samp> remain effective. Sometimes you can also avoid incompatibilities with <samp class="listingcharacter">nounix</samp>, which express themselves via a vague error message: operation not supported.

<samp class="listingcharacter">iocharset=utf8</samp> avoids the incorrect display of file names with international characters.

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">credentials=file</samp> | Reads the login name and password from a file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">dir_mod=n</samp> | Sets the access bits for directories |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">domain=name</samp> | Determines the workgroup or domain |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">file_mod=n</samp> | Sets the access bits for files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">gid=n</samp> | Specifies which group gets access to the files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">iocharset=utf8</samp> | Uses the UTF8 character set for file names |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nounix</samp> | Disables the Unix extensions of the CIFS protocol |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">password=xxx</samp> | Specifies the password (not secure!) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">uid=n</samp> | Specifies who gets access to the files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">username=name</samp> | Specifies the username |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">sec=ntlm</samp> | Sets the authentication mode |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">vers=n</samp> | Sets the version number of the SMB protocol |

**Table 27.4**     CIFS mount Options

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sec=ntlm</samp> option is necessary for interaction with old NAS devices or Samba servers. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntlmssp</samp> method for authentication. Older servers do not support this method, in which case you have to accept the less secure <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ntlm</samp> method.

A similar function is fulfilled by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vers=n</samp>: If you want to connect to old NAS devices, this may fail because <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> only uses the SMB protocol in a current version. If you want to explicitly use an older version, you need to specify it using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vers</samp>—for example, as <samp class="listingcharacter">vers=2.1</samp>.

You can obtain even more details on the permitted options via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man mount.cifs</samp>.

Usually, two or three attempts are required to find an ideal combination of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> options. In the future, however, you will certainly not want to type a two-line <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> command every time. If you work on a desktop computer that has permanent access to an always-on server or NAS device, you can automatically include the network directory in the directory tree. To do this, you want to add an appropriate line to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp>, like the following one, for example:

```
# in /etc/fstab
//diskstation/archive /media/archive cifs \
nofail,username=u,password=p,...  0 0 
```

All CIFS directories named in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp> are included during the init process. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nofail</samp> option prevents the start process from hanging up due to an unavailable network directory.

For security reasons, specifying the password directly in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/fstab</samp> is not recommended. A little better is to outsource this information to a separate file that can only be read by <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp>. Therefore, you should set up the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/.winshare-pw</samp> file, which contains the login name, password, and optionally the workgroup (domain) for the network directory. The structure of the file looks as follows:

```
username=name
password=xxxx
domain=workgroup 
```

The following command restricts access to the file so that only <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> can read and modify it:

```
root# chmod 600 /etc/.winshare-pw 
```

Then add the <samp class="listingcharacter">credentials</samp> option or its short variant, <samp class="listingcharacter">cred</samp>, to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fstab</samp> entry. When mounting the directory, the authentication files are read from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.winshare-pw</samp>:

```
# Addition to /etc/fstab
//diskstation/archive /media/archive cifs cred=/etc/.winshare-pw,... 0 0 
```

If your Linux machine is a notebook or if the network directory is only sometimes available (e.g., because the NAS device is not running continuously but is only turned on or woken from sleep mode when needed), you should opt for a semimanual solution. You can use the following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fstab</samp> line as a guide:

```
# /etc/fstab
//diskstation/archive /media/diskstation cifs noauto,users,cred=... 0 0 
```

Two new options are crucial for this functionality: <samp class="listingcharacter">noauto</samp> prevents the network directory from being activated immediately during the boot process, and <samp class="listingcharacter">users</samp> also allows the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> process for ordinary users without <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. You can then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">umount</samp> as needed and only need to specify the mount directory:

```
user$ mount  /media/diskstation
user$ umount /media/diskstation 
```

However, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">fstab</samp> entry is also analyzed by the GNOME file manager, which displays the Archive entry for the network directory of the same name in the sidebar. One mouse click is enough to activate the network directory; you can deactivate it again with a second mouse click. Even old GNOME versions work with this configuration, as you would expect from the beginning!

Network directories mounted using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> cause problems if the SMB device is suddenly no longer accessible—for example, because the affected computer has been switched off. Then, no matter whether you work in the file manager or in the terminal, longer delays will occur during which the program or command does not respond. Even when shutting down the computer, you have to wait several minutes for Linux to realize that any pending operations in the open network directory cannot be completed. The solution is to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo umount -f <mount directory></samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">-f</samp> stands for force. And even this command first takes a longer pause before it’s finally completed.

# Part VII

Security

# 28    Backups

Almost 20 years ago, Apple proved with its Time Machine that even a backup program can generate enthusiasm. Linux unfortunately cannot keep up in this respect: the range of backup commands and tools is large, but desktop users are still waiting for the ingenious, easy-to-use backup tool.

I'm not even going to try to convince you of the need for backups here. Instead, I want to focus on introducing you to various ready-to-use programs as well as tools and techniques for programming your own backup solutions:

*   Backup user interfaces: Déjà Dup, Back In Time, and Grsync

*   Backup command: Borg Backup

*   Developing custom backup scripts: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp>, LVM, and S3

Of course, all programs or commands are open-source software. It is up to you which tools you use in which combination; there is no universal recipe for this. The ideal backup strategy depends too much on the nature of the data, the type of computer (desktop PC/notebook/server), the backup medium (external hard disk, network directory, cloud), the type of implementation (user interface, Cron script), the internal processes (compression, encryption, deduplication), and many other factors.

## Further Reading

A good overview of backup programs for Linux, including a discussion of the techniques used, can be found in the blog article at [https://www.lullabot.com/articles/backup-strategies-for-2018](https://www.lullabot.com/articles/backup-strategies-for-2018). While the author focuses a lot on backups in the cloud, much of the information summarized in the article is still generally applicable despite the fact that it was published a long time ago.

## 28.1    Déjà Dup

Déjà Dup is probably the most popular backup tool for Linux with a graphical user interface. It is set up as the default backup program by many distributions. Déjà Dup is designed to back up the home directory as easily as possible to a local directory or a directory that can be accessed via SSH. The program is not suitable for backing up system files.

Déjà Dup performs a full backup when run for the first time and incremental backups thereafter. The backed-up files are compressed and, if desired, encrypted and then saved in a file format of your choice. They can only be extracted by Déjà Dup itself (or by using the underlying <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">duplicity</samp> command).

The greatest advantages of Déjà Dup include its extremely simple operation and good integration into the GNOME desktop. I don't know of any other backup program that is so easy to set up on Linux and that gives such easy access to the backed-up files.

The disadvantage, however, is the very complex internal backup technique based on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">duplicity</samp>. Performing regular backups as well as restoring individual files or directories takes an above-average amount of time and involves a considerable CPU load. If the backup is stored on the network or in the cloud, large amounts of data must be downloaded even to restore individual files.

You can find further information at the following pages and at the following Reddit post, which very succinctly summarizes the disadvantages of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">duplicity</samp> format:

*   [https://wiki.gnome.org/Apps/DejaDup](https://wiki.gnome.org/Apps/DejaDup)

*   [https://duplicity.gitlab.io](https://duplicity.gitlab.io)

*   [https://www.reddit.com/r/linux/comments/ahpdzk/borgbackup_frontends/eehtrfd](https://www.reddit.com/r/linux/comments/ahpdzk/borgbackup_frontends/eehtrfd)

### 28.1.1    Configuration and Use

In many distributions with GNOME as the desktop system, you start Déjà Dup by selecting the Data Backup program name. You may need to install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deja-dup</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">deja-dup-nautilus</samp> packages prior to that.

Déjà Dup is configured in two dialogs (see [Figure 28.1](#28_001.html_f28.1)). In the General dialog sheet, you specify the data medium on which you want to store the backups and how often you want the backups to be run.

Usually, you select Local Folder as the location of the backup, and then you can select any directory where you are allowed to read and write files. If you do not want to use an external hard disk or USB flash drive exclusively for backups, it’s useful to set up a separate backup directory there. A server that can be accessed via SSH or a cloud directory (such as Google Drive) can also serve as a backup destination. In the past, Déjà Dup used to support Amazon S3 as well as some other cloud services. However, these functions are now considered obsolete.

[![Backup Configuration in Déjà Dup](bilderklein/klein28_001.png)](img-f28.1.html)

**Figure 28.1**     Backup Configuration in Déjà Dup

If you activate the central Automatic Backup switch, you can set the frequency of backups (daily or weekly). In the future, Déjà Dup will always start automatically as soon as you log in and will then take care of running the backups. If the backup medium is not accessible at a given moment, Déjà Dup postpones the backup until later and starts the backup automatically as soon as the external hard disk is accessible. This is extremely convenient: you only need to make sure that a backup media is available on a regular basis, and the backup program will take care of everything else by itself.

Finally, you can specify the period over which the backup program should back up files that change. The default setting of Forever is the safest, but it inevitably means that even the largest backup medium will be full at some point. By using the At Least One Year or At Least Three/Six Months setting, all files in the backup will be saved, but in case of changed files only the versions of the last three, six, or twelve months are kept.

In the Folder dialog, you can set which directories you want to be backed up; usually, that’s only the home directory.

In Folders to Ignore, you can specify the exceptions. By default, the trash can and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Downloads</samp> directory are already provided there. It’s often useful to also exclude directories with very large files from regular backups, such as videos or the location of virtual machines if you use VirtualBox. (In general, a backup of virtual machines can only work if the virtual machines are not running during the backup.)

The Backup Now button allows you to start a backup manually at any time. For the first backup, you must also specify whether the backups should be encrypted and, if so, which password should be used. Note, however, that encrypting requires additional CPU power!

The first backup performed using Déjà Dup takes a disproportionately long time. This is because the backup is compressed. For further backups, only the changes are saved, which speeds up the process. Unfortunately, incremental backups are not really fast either, even if only a few files have changed since the last backup.

### 28.1.2    Restoring Data

You can use the Restore button to restore a full backup. For this purpose, you can select the desired backup version and specify where the backup files should be copied.

## 28.2    Back In Time

Like Déjà Dup, Back In Time is a backup program for personal data. Most current distributions provide ready-made Back In Time packages (package name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">backintime-qt</samp>). Only directories accessible locally or via SSH are supported as backup targets.

Compared to Déjà Dup, the interface of Back In Time is much more technically oriented. There is no mistaking the KDE origin of the program. During the initial configuration, there are many more options available to influence the details of the backup.

Behind the scenes, Back In Time uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> command. During the first backup, a complete backup is created. Later, only the files that have changed since then will be backed up. The connection between the different backup versions is done by hard links. However, this only works on media that support such links. (If you use an external hard disk as a backup medium, you should set up a Linux file system there.) This relatively simple backup technique has two huge advantages (compared to Déjà Dup): For one thing, the backups are created extremely quickly and with low CPU load (at least as long as you do without encryption). Second, the file and directory structure is preserved in the backups. This enables data to be restored both quickly and easily—even without Back In Time, if you want.

You can find more information about Back In Time on the following websites:

*   [https://backintime.readthedocs.io](https://backintime.readthedocs.io)

*   [https://github.com/bit-team/backintime](https://github.com/bit-team/backintime)

### 28.2.1    Configuration and Use

Back In Time allows you to set up multiple profiles for different backups. As long as you only need one profile, you can simply edit the Main Profile that already exists. The configuration of a profile is done in six dialog sheets (see [Figure 28.2](#28_002.html_f28.2)):

*   General Here you specify in which directory you want to store the backups. It can also be an external data medium if it is permanently connected to your computer. You must have write permissions for the backup directory.

    You can also set how often the backups should be performed in this dialog sheet. For computers that are not in constant use, you should select the Repeating (anacron) variant. In a second step, you can then specify after how many hours, days, or weeks a backup should be automatically performed again.

*   Include Here you select the directories you want to back up. Usually you will simply specify your home directory here. However, you can also make a differentiated selection and, for example, back up only your <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Documents</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Images</samp> directories.

*   Exclude Here you specify which directories and file patterns are excluded from the backup, such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Downloads</samp> (see [Figure 28.2](#28_002.html_f28.2)). By default, Back In Time excludes local directories such as <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.gvfs</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.cache</samp>, as well as various system files. (The rules for system files are only relevant if you create a backup of the root directory via Back In Time.) You can add rules for other directories here, such as for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">Downloads</samp> or for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.local/share/Trash</samp>.

*   Auto-remove To prevent the backup volume from growing without limits, you can specify which backup data should be deleted automatically. In most cases, it makes sense to activate the Intelligent Delete option; this way, you can make sure that backups from the current day and the day before will never be touched. Older backups are gradually deleted, but it is ensured that there is a backup for the preceding seven days, for the preceding four weeks, for the preceding 24 months, and one backup per year.

*   Options and Expert Options
    Here you will find some options for advanced users, which usually do not need to be changed.

    [![Configuration of Back In Time](bilderklein/klein28_002.png)](img-f28.2.html)

    **Figure 28.2**     Configuration of Back In Time

When the configuration is complete, the Back In Time user interface appears. Here you can start a backup manually at any time, including outside the set backup period. You can also give names to existing backups.

#### System Backups

By default, Back In Time can only back up personal files. If you want to use Back In Time to back up system files, you must start it in root mode. Both KDE and GNOME provide for corresponding startup entries.

### 28.2.2    Restoring Data

Once you set up Back In Time, Cron will take care of performing the backups automatically. It analyzes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.config/backintime/config</samp> configuration file. The Back In Time user interface does not need to be running for the automatic backups! The Cron control is enabled by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/spool/cron/crontabs/loginname</samp> file.

You do not need to restart the Back In Time user interface until you want to make changes to the backup configuration or restore files. There is a directory browser in the program for this purpose (see [Figure 28.3](#28_002.html_f28.3)). There you select the relevant backup version in the first column, the backed-up directory in the second column (usually Personal Folder), and then the file or directory to be restored in the third column. Using the context menu or the Restore menu entries, you can then reconstruct the file from the backup.

[![Back In Time Browser for Restoring Files](bilderklein/klein28_003.png)](img-f28.3.html)

**Figure 28.3**     Back In Time Browser for Restoring Files

## 28.3    Grsync

It’s an exaggeration to call Grsync a backup tool. In reality, it’s a simple user interface for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> command (see [Section 28.6](#28_006.html_h28.6)) to synchronize one directory with another.

The biggest advantages of Grsync are its ease of use and the fact that your files are copied 1:1 to a second directory. If you ever need to go back to your backup, you don't need any special tools to do so and you can restore the required files quickly and easily. The speed factor in particular should not be underestimated. Restoring data from an incremental backup system with encryption and compression can take hours!

What is annoying, however, is its all-or-nothing approach: Grsync does not provide an easy way to exclude individual subdirectories or specific file types from synchronization. (Experts can specify appropriate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> command options directly in the Advanced Options dialog sheet. But then you might as well call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> manually or in a Cron job.) In addition, Grsync lacks many features that are self-evident in “real” backup programs. In particular, only the most recent version of a file is available in the synchronized directory. If, for example, you have made changes in a text file by mistake and now need an old version of the text, you are out of luck. In this respect, Grsync is a conceivable addition to Déjà Dup; as the only backup tool, it is only useful in exceptional cases.

A possible alternative to Grsync is Syncthing. Syncthing is more complex to use, but it offers a lot more configuration options (especially for exception rules).

### 28.3.1    Configuration and Use

After installation, you connect an external hard disk to your computer, start Grsync, and copy the contents of your home directory to a directory on the external hard disk. All files must be copied the first time, then only changed or new files. You can leave the numerous options essentially as they are preset (see [Figure 28.4](#28_003.html_f28.4)).

The Delete on Destination option is important. It specifies whether Grsync should also synchronize delete operations. If you delete a file in your home directory after the first backup, this file will also be deleted in the backup directory the next time. If you want your backup to be protected against accidental deletions, you must not enable this option, which is the basic setting anyway. If, on the other hand, it is important to you that the backup has exactly the same content as the directory to be backed up, you should enable the option.

[![Synchronizing Directories Using Grsync](bilderklein/klein28_004.png)](img-f28.4.html)

**Figure 28.4**     Synchronizing Directories Using Grsync

## 28.4    Borg Backup

The backup programs presented so far are all equipped with a graphical user interface and are primarily aimed at desktop users. But servers also need backups. And advanced Linux users prefer tools to be called as commands even on the desktop.

Before I present low-level tools for programming your own backup scripts starting in the next section, I want to present Borg Backup here ([https://borgbackup.org](https://borgbackup.org)). In terms of its functions, this is a command that is in a league with Déjà Dup.

Borg Backup creates incremental, encrypted, and compressed backups, either in a local directory or on another server where Borg Backup is also installed. (This means that Borg Backup is incompatible with cloud storage such as Amazon S3\. After all, some server providers now offer Borg functions for their backup space.) Borg Backup avoids storing data multiple times by deduplicating at the block level. As with Déjà Dup, this results in backup files from which you can restore your files exclusively through Borg Backup. This black box concept is characteristic of modern backup solutions, but also gives me headaches with command-oriented tools. On the other hand, a mature backup program used by many users is usually more robust and secure than any homemade solution.

Of course, Borg Backup as a command with countless options is less accessible for beginners than a backup solution with a user interface. However, Borg Backup must be given credit for the fact that both the operation of the program and the underlying techniques are extremely well-documented. Another plus point: Borg Backup is programmed in Python, so it uses libraries that are widely used on Linux.

### 28.4.1    Installation

Borg Backup is so popular in the server scene that ready-to-use packages are available for almost all common Linux distributions. This facilitates its installation:

```
root# apt/dnf/zypper install borgbackup 
```

### 28.4.2    Usage

Borg Backup is controlled by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg</samp> command. Before you can perform your first backup, you need to create a backup repository, which is the location for the backup. In the following example, this is a local directory on an external hard disk/SSD:

```
user$ borg init --encryption=repokey \
         /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/
Enter new passphrase: **********
Enter same passphrase again: ********** 
```

When you run this command, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg</samp> generates a key that is contained in the backup directory in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">config</samp> file. The access to the key is secured by a passphrase. In the future, this passphrase must be specified each time the backup is accessed.

The following command creates a first backup of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">data/linux</samp> directory. Each backup must have a name that is appended as <samp class="listingcharacter">::name</samp> to the repo directory:

```
user$ borg create --stats \
         /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/::initialbackup \
         data/linux
Enter passphrase for key /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest:  **********
Archive name: initialbackup
Archive fingerprint: 3e5b6528...

Time (start): 2023-05-14 09:34:24
Time (end):   2023-05-14 09:34:44
Duration: 19.86 seconds
Number of files: 3329
Utilization of max. archive size: 0%
              Original size      Compressed size    Deduplicated size
This archive:       1.42 GB            848.97 MB            790.39 MB
... 
```

As expected, the second backup with few changes is much faster and requires comparatively little additional space due to deduplication:

```
user$ borg create --stats \
         /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/::secondbackup \
         data/linux
Enter passphrase for key /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest:  **********
...

Duration: 1.26 seconds
              Original size      Compressed size    Deduplicated size
This archive:       1.42 GB            848.93 MB              2.21 MB
All archives:       2.84 GB              1.70 GB            792.60 MB
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg list</samp> displays all backups available in a repository or the files contained in an explicitly specified backup:

```
user$ borg list /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/
initialbackup  2023-05-14 09:34:24 [3e5b6528...]
secondbackup   2023-05-14 09:40:04 [78f44df7...]
user$ borg list /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/::secondbackup
drwxr-xr-x  ...      0 2023-05-13 21:58:16 data/linux
-rw-r--r--  ...   3924 2023-04-27 13:40:05 data/linux/header-keys.tex
-rw-r--r--  ...  44798 2023-05-09 15:11:53 data/linux/header.tex
-rw-r--r--  ...   4559 2023-05-13 08:24:36 data/linux/book.tex
... 
```

To unpack a complete backup in the currently active directory, you want to call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg extract</samp>. Existing files and directories are overwritten without confirmation. If you want visual feedback when unpacking, you need to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--progress</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--list</samp> option:

```
user$ borg extract /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/::secondbackup 
```

It’s also possible to extract only individual files:

```
user$ borg extract /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/::secondbackup \
         data/linux2023/text/apps.tex data/linux2023/text/backup.tex 
```

To delete a backup from a repository, you must call <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg delete</samp>:

```
user$ borg delete /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/::backup123 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg prune</samp> is usually more useful. This command allows you to delete older backups in such a way that a certain number of older backups is preserved. In the following example, these are one backup each for the last seven days, for the last four weeks, and for the last 24 months:

```
user$ borg prune --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 24 --list \
        /media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/ 
```

### 28.4.3    Borg Backup in Scripts

Borg Backup is designed to automate backups. A script to perform a regular backup can be structured as shown in the following listing:

```
#!/bin/bash
export BORG_REPO='/media/kofler/p1-backup/borgtest/'
export BORG_PASSPHRASE='topsecret'
cd /crypt/home/kofler
borg create --stats ::'{now}' data/linux2023
borg prune  --list --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">BORG_REPO</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">BORG_PASSPHRASE</samp> variables are automatically analyzed by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg</samp> and specify the backup repository and the corresponding password. The script uses the current date and time as the backup name with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">::'{now}'</samp>. Other ways to pass passwords are described at [https://borgbackup.readthedocs.io/en/stable/faq.html#how-can-i-specify-the-encryption-passphrase-programmatically](https://borgbackup.readthedocs.io/en/stable/faq.html#how-can-i-specify-the-encryption-passphrase-programmatically).

### 28.4.4    Borg Backup Using SSH

Borg Backup works quite straightforwardly via an SSH connection. The only requirement is that a sufficiently up-to-date version of Borg Backup is also installed on the server:

```
user$ borg init --encryption=repokey user@remotehost:path/to/repo
Enter new passphrase: **********
Enter same passphrase again: **********
user$ borg create --stats \
  user@remotehost:path/to/repo::initial local/data
Enter passphrase for key ssh://user@remotehost/./path/to/repo: ********** 
```

### 28.4.5    Internal Details

When setting up a new repository, Borg Backup stores some information in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.config/borg</samp> in the home directory, including the location of the repository. Note that no copy of the backup key is saved. In addition, Borg Backup takes up space in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.cache/borg</samp> directory for various caches to make backups more efficient.

Borg Backup uses the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lz4</samp> compression method by default. The compression is worse than with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>, but fast and with low CPU load. Borg Backup also supports other compression methods (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--compression</samp> option; see also <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">borg help compression</samp>). You can mix different compression methods in one repository. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--compression</samp> option applies only to newly added data blocks.

### 28.4.6    Borg User Interfaces

Borg Backup is actually intended for use as a command. However, this has not stopped the open-source community from developing wrappers or user interfaces to make the program easier to use. At present, however, it isn’t yet possible to assess whether any of these programs will be able to establish themselves in the longer term:

*   [https://github.com/borgmatic-collective/borgmatic](https://github.com/borgmatic-collective/borgmatic) (simplified command)

*   [https://github.com/KenKundert/emborg](https://github.com/KenKundert/emborg) (simplified command)

*   [https://github.com/borgbase/vorta](https://github.com/borgbase/vorta) (real GUI)

In particular, the Vorta interface developed in Python looks promising. The program can be installed using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pip3</samp> Python package manager:

```
user$ pip3 install vorta
user$ vorta 
```

## 28.5    Compressing and Archiving Files

Now that I’ve introduced you to complete backup tools in the first sections of this chapter, I will now present various low-level commands that will help you archive and back up files in different ways: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zip</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp>, and more. These commands enable you to program your own backup scripts. For examples of such scripts, see [Section 28.9](#28_009.html_h28.9) and [Section 28.10](#28_010.html_h28.10).

At this point, I want to start with commands for compressing and archiving files. An initial overview is provided in [Table 28.1](#28_005.html_t28.1).

| Command | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp> | Compresses a file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gunzip</samp> | Decompresses the file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bzip2</samp> | Compresses a file (higher compression than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>, slower) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bunzip2</samp> | Decompresses the file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xz</samp> | Compresses a file (higher compression than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bzip2</samp>, slower) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unxz</samp> | Decompresses the file |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lzop</samp> | Compresses/decompresses much faster than <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> | Creates or extracts a file archive |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zip</samp> | Creates a Windows-compatible ZIP archive |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unzip</samp> | Extracts a ZIP archive |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zipinfo</samp> | Displays information about a ZIP archive |

**Table 28.1**     Tools for Compressing and Archiving Files

### 28.5.1    Compressing Files (gzip, bzip2, xz, and lzop)

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp> compresses the files specified as parameters and renames them to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">name.gz</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gunzip</samp> works in the opposite direction. The two commands use the LZ77-Lempel-Ziv algorithm, which is particularly suitable for text files, but not for audio or video files. Compression is of course lossless; that is, the original file is available again unchanged after decompression. The following commands demonstrate its use:

```
user$ ls -l filesystem.tex
... 178794  1\. Aug 17:43 filesystem.tex
user$ gzip filesystem.tex
user$ ls -l filesystem.tex.gz
...  57937  1\. Aug 17:43 filesystem.tex.gz
user$ gunzip filesystem.tex.gz 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bzip2</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bunzip2</samp> represent alternatives to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gunzip</samp>. The advantage of these commands is their slightly better compression; the disadvantage is their slightly slower execution. The file extension of files compressed in this way is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.bz2</samp>:

```
user$ bzip2 filesystem.tex
user$ ls -l filesystem.tex.bz2
...  47105  1\. Aug 17:43 filesystem.tex.bz2
user$ bunzip2 filesystem.tex.bz2 
```

Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bzip2</samp>, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xz</samp> for compression. In most cases, the result is even smaller files, but the compression requires even more time or CPU resources. If the smallest possible compression is the primary goal, you can also try the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">7zr</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">p7zip</samp> package.

The objective of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lzop</samp> is quite different: this compression command works much faster than all the commands mentioned so far, but the resulting files are comparatively large (in my tests they were about 50% larger than with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>). The use of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lzop</samp> is especially recommended if you want to compress on the fly with as little CPU load as possible—for example, to transfer a large file over a network connection.

In the following sample command, a logical volume is read using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cat</samp> and compressed using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lzop</samp>. This takes only slightly longer than copying the logical volume directly to an image file:

```
root# cat /dev/vg1/lv3 | lzop -c > lv3.img.lzo   
(55 seconds)
root# cat /dev/vg1/lv3 > lv3.img                 
(50 seconds) 
```

### 28.5.2    Creating Compressed Archives (tar and zip)

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> is the preferred command to combine multiple files into one archive on Linux, usually compressing the archive by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bzip2</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> was originally designed to write files to or read files from a streamer. Because such streamers are only used relatively rarely, I will only describe their use for file archives at this point.

The following command inserts all files from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">book</samp> directory into the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">myarchive.tgz</samp> compressed archive file. But before that, let me briefly explain the option letters: <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> stands for create; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> is supposed to create an archive. <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> stands for zip; the archive is to be compressed using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> stands for file; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> is supposed to create an archive file instead of writing the archive to a streamer cartridge. You can specify the file name you want to use after the option. The usual file identifier for such archives is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.tar.gz</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.tgz</samp> for short:

```
user$ tar -czf myarchive.tgz book/ 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar -tzf</samp> returns a table of contents of the archive. The files within the archive are ordered arbitrarily. In most distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less</samp> is configured in such a way that you can simply view the archive contents via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">less name.tgz</samp>:

```
user$ tar -tzf myarchive.tgz
linuxbook/
linuxbook/lanserver.tex
linuxbook/security.tex~

linuxbook/book.tex
linuxbook/c4.txt~
... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar -xzf</samp> unpacks the archive and extracts all contained files:

```
user$ cd other-directory/
user$ tar -xzf myarchive.tgz 
```

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> extracts only <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.tex</samp> files from the archive. Pay attention to the apostrophes for the file pattern to avoid an immediate analysis by the shell:

```
user$ tar -xzf myarchive.tgz '*.tex' 
```

If you want to compress archives using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bzip2</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp>, you should replace the <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> option with <samp class="listingcharacter">j</samp> (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar -xjf ...</samp>).

In the Unix/Linux world, TAR files are the preferred format for distributing file archives. However, if you communicate with Windows users, ZIP archives are the better choice. The following command inserts all HTML files passed as parameters into <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">myarchive.zip</samp>:

```
user$ zip myarchive.zip *.html 
```

If you want to archive the contents of entire directories, you need to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">-r</samp> option:

```
user$ zip -r myarchive.zip mywebsite/ 
```

You can view the contents of a ZIP file via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">zipinfo</samp>:

```
user$ zipinfo myarchive.zip
Archive:  test.zip   143677915 bytes   1899 files
2.3 unx    78039 tx defN 10-Jul-16 11:27 linuxbook/lanserver.tex
2.3 unx   115618 tx defN  7-Apr-15 15:58 linuxbook/security.tex
2.3 unx     3899 tx defN 28-Jul-16 16:38 linuxbook/book.tex
2.3 unx      752 tx defN 11-Feb-14 12:06 linuxbook/c4.txt
... 
```

To extract the archive, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">unzip</samp>:

```
user$ cd other-directory/
user$ unzip myarchive.zip 
```

## 28.6    Synchronizing Directories (rsync)

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> command synchronizes directory trees. You can use it to copy all files from one directory to a new directory in the first pass. In subsequent runs, only changed files will be copied and (if you want) deletions will also be replicated. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> is therefore ideal for synchronizing a complete copy of a directory on an external hard disk on a daily or weekly basis, for example. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> can also be used via network connections.

By default, the communication takes place via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp>. This means that the data transfer is also encrypted at the same time. As an alternative, you can use another external shell program or configure an <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server on the remote side.

[Table 28.2](#28_006.html_t28.2) shows the syntax for specifying the source and destination directories. [Table 28.3](#28_006.html_t28.3) summarizes the most important options for controlling <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>.

| Syntax | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">file1 file2</samp> | Local files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">directory</samp> | Local directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">host:dir</samp> | Directory on the <samp class="listingcharacter">host</samp> computer |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">user@host:dir</samp> | As above with SSH login under the name <samp class="listingcharacter">user</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync://user@host/dir</samp> | Communication with the <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync://user@host:port/dir</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server on the specified port |

**Table 28.2**     Specification of Source and Destination Directories in rsync

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-a</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--archive</samp> | Copies recursively and gets all file information |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">--delete</samp> | Deletes files or directories in the target directory that no longer exist in the source directory |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-D</samp> | Also takes into account device and special files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">--exclude=samples</samp> | Skips the specified files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-g</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--group</samp> | Receives the group membership |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-l</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--links</samp> | Duplicates symbolic links |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-o</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--owner</samp> | Receives the owner information |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-p</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--perms</samp> | Receives the access permissions |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-r</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--recursive</samp> | Recursively copies all subdirectories as well. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-t</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--times</samp> | Receives the modification time |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-u</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--update</samp> | Ignores already existing older files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-v</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--verbose</samp> | Indicates what is currently happening |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-W</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--whole-file</samp> | Copies the entire file when changes have been made |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">-z</samp> | Compresses the data transferred via SSH |

**Table 28.3**     rsync Options

To synchronize an entire directory, including all subdirectories, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp> option, which is the short notation for a whole bunch of other options (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-rlptgoD</samp>). This option causes a recursive processing of all subdirectories and ensures that as much file information as possible is retained: owner, group membership, time of last change, and so on. If <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dir2</samp> doesn’t exist yet, the directory will be created. In contrast to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp</samp>, existing files that have remained unchanged since the last copy will not be copied again:

```
user$ rsync -a dir1/ dir2/ 
```

By default, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> copies or updates all new or changed files, but does not delete anything. If you want files or directories deleted from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dir1</samp> to also be deleted in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dir2</samp>, you must also specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">--delete</samp> option. It should be clear that this option is dangerous: if you delete a directory by mistake, this very directory will also be deleted on the backup hard disk during the next backup operation!

When using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> to synchronize directories on different computers, you must specify the source and destination directories in the <samp class="listingcharacter">hostname:directory</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">username@hostname:directory</samp> notation, respectively. In the first case, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> uses the current user name.

The following command synchronizes the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dir1</samp> directory of the local user <samp class="listingcharacter">username</samp> on the <samp class="listingcharacter">saturn.sol</samp> computer with the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dir2</samp> directory on the <samp class="listingcharacter">mars.sol</samp> computer. The password entry is the responsibility of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp>. You must therefore enter the login password of the <samp class="listingcharacter">username</samp> user on the <samp class="listingcharacter">mars.sol</samp> computer:

```
username@saturn.sol$ rsync -e ssh -az dir1/ mars.sol:dir2/
username@mars.sol's password: ****** 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> can also transfer files from a remote computer to the local one. Thus, the following command synchronizes in the opposite direction:

```
username@saturn.sol$ rsync -e ssh -az mars.sol:dir2/ dir3/
username@mars.sol's password: ****** 
```

Of course, if <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> is to be called by an automatic backup script, the interactive password entry will interfere. The solution here is to set up a private key file on the local computer and the matching public key on the partner computer (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.4](#23_004.html_h23.4)). If you omit the passphrase when generating the keys, SSH login will be possible without a password. For security reasons, you should provide a separate account for the backup script.

Instead of using SSH directly, the local <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> command can communicate with an <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server on the remote computer. This assumes that an <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server has been set up on the partner computer. Its configuration is carried out by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/rsyncd.conf</samp> file.

The communication between the <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> client and the <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server takes place via port 873, which must not be blocked by a firewall.

In real life, the configuration of an <samp class="listingcharacter">rsync</samp> server is usually only recommended if the server is regularly mirrored by different clients—that is, if it serves as a mirror server:

*   [https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/26182](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/26182)

*   [https://serverfault.com/questions/100707](https://serverfault.com/questions/100707)

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> expects an SSH server on external servers. However, this requirement is not met for typical cloud services. In such cases, you may consider using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rclone</samp> or its graphical user interface Celeste (currently in alpha testing):

*   [https://rclone.org](https://rclone.org)

*   [https://github.com/hwittenborn/celeste](https://github.com/hwittenborn/celeste)

## 28.7    Incremental Backups (rdiff-backup)

An interesting alternative to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> is the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> command. The most important difference from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> is that when files are changed, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> also archives the old version in the backup directory. To save space, instead of saving a copy of the file in question, only the changes can be saved, optionally in compressed form. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> thus provides an incremental backup without much effort, from which you can also restore older versions of a file. Basically, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> provides the same functions as Apple's Time Machine on macOS—only without a spectacular user interface.

In its simplest form, you apply <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> to two local directories. If the repository directory doesn't exist yet, it will be created:

```
root# rdiff-backup /home /home-backup 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> creates the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup-data</samp> subdirectory in the backup directory. In it, it stores various statistical data and status information. In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">increments</samp> directory contains old versions of files that have since changed or that have been deleted. Only the changes are saved (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.diff</samp>) and additionally compressed. In addition, the date of the last version is integrated into the filename, which results in confusing filenames like <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">filename.2023-11-03T08:37:58+02:00.diff.gz</samp>.

If you want to access the backup, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home-backup</samp> contains the state of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp> directory at the time of the last backup, except for the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup-data</samp> directory, exactly as if you had run the backup using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cp -a</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync -a --delete</samp>. As a result, accessing the last backup is quite simple. Of course, you can also restore the backup using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp>. To do this, you need to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-r</samp> option and the time specification <samp class="listingcharacter">now</samp>. The following command restores the backup to a temporary directory on a trial basis:

```
root# rdiff-backup -r now /home-backhup /tmp/home-current 
```

If you want to access an older version of a file or a file that has since been deleted, things get more complicated: you need to apply all <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">.diff</samp> files in order (the latest one first) until you have restored the relevant time in the past. Of course, you don't have to do this manually; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> will help you. The following command restores the state of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home</samp> directory to the way it was 10 days previously:

```
root# rdiff-backup -r 10D /home-backup/ /tmp/home-historical 
```

You can specify the backup time either in absolute terms (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">2023-12-31</samp>) or relatively in hours (<samp class="listingcharacter">h</samp>), days (<samp class="listingcharacter">D</samp>), weeks (<samp class="listingcharacter">W</samp>), and so on; see also <samp class="listingcharacter">man rdiff-backup</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">TIME FORMATS</samp> section. Note that restoring old files with an increasing number of versions requires a considerable amount of CPU and is correspondingly slow!

Often you only want to restore a single file or a subdirectory in an old version. You can also specify a file that no longer exists or a directory that has been deleted in the meantime:

```
root# rdiff-backup -r 10D /home-backup/file  file-historical
root# rdiff-backup -r 10D /home-backup/dir/  dir-historical 
```

If you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> regularly, the backup directory will grow bigger and bigger over time. To delete all backup files older than four months, you should proceed as follows:

```
root# rdiff-backup --remove-older-than 4M --force /home-backup/ 
```

Instead of a specific time, you can also specify the maximum number of backup versions that should remain archived. The following command reduces the backup versions to three:

```
root# rdiff-backup --remove-older-than 3B --force /home-backup/ 
```

In all the examples so far, I have assumed that the source and destination directories are in the local file system. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp>, however, can also access external directories over the network. Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> must also be installed on the external computer! Communication with the platform occurs via web services, and no special configuration of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> is required.

When you specify external directories, almost the same syntax applies as for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>. The only difference is that two colons must be specified after the host name:

```
root# rdiff-backup user@company-abc.com::/home /home-backup 
```

You can find even more details and examples of how to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> at [https://rdiff-backup.net](https://rdiff-backup.net).

If the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> concept appeals to you, but you also want to have the backup encrypted and uploaded via SSH or FTP to an external server, it might be worth taking a look at the Python program called <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">duplicity</samp> ([https://duplicity.gitlab.io](https://duplicity.gitlab.io)). This program is similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp>, but it creates <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">tar</samp> archives. The command serves as the basis for the Déjà Dup backup user interface, which I introduced at the beginning of this chapter.

## 28.8    Incremental Backups (rsnapshot)

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> Perl script from the package of the same name also builds on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp>. Unlike the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp> command just described, it uses hard links to access previously backed up files from previous backups. This makes accessing older backup versions (snapshots) easier than when you use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rdiff-backup</samp>. A compression of the backups, on the other hand, is not provided.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> is designed to run the script automatically on a regular basis. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> backs up both local directories and, via SSH, directories from other machines on the local network when configured appropriately. All backups are stored on the local machine running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp>. This approach is exactly the opposite of many other backup tools: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> is not intended to save a backup of local files on another computer. Rather, the command backs up the data of multiple computers that are accessible via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsync</samp> to the local file system.

Instead of having to pass numerous options to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp>, you can control the command through the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/rsnapshot.conf</samp> configuration file. Two important syntax rules apply to this file: directories must end with a slash (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/directory/</samp>, not <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/directory</samp>), and the elements of the configuration file must be separated by tab characters (not spaces).

For first experiments, you can leave the configuration file provided together with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> unchanged except for a few details. The three most important parameters you need to know and set yourself if necessary are <samp class="listingcharacter">snapshot_root</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">backup</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">interval</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">snapshot_root</samp> specifies the directory in which you want to store the backups. By default, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/cache/rsnapshot</samp> directory is used, which was automatically set up during the installation of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">backup</samp> specifies which directory is to be backed up where. <samp class="listingcharacter">backup</samp> can be specified multiple times, each in a separate line, to back up multiple directories to different locations. For backups within the local file system, the <samp class="listingcharacter">backup</samp> settings look as follows:

```
# in /etc/rsnapshot.conf
...
backup  /home/   localhost/
backup  /etc/    localhost/ 
```

To back up a <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/user/mail</samp> directory of the external <samp class="listingcharacter">mars.sol</samp> host that is accessible via SSH, you need to remove the comment character (<samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>) in the already existing <samp class="listingcharacter">cmd_ssh</samp> line. In the <samp class="listingcharacter">backup</samp> line, you want to specify the login name, the host name, and the entire directory to be backed up. For this to work, you must copy an SSH key set up with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges without a passphrase to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys</samp> file of the <samp class="listingcharacter">mars.sol</samp> computer prior to the first backup (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.4](#23_004.html_h23.4)):

```
# in /etc/rsnapshot.conf
... 
cmd_ssh /usr/bin/ssh
...
backup  user@mars.sol:/home/user/Mail/  mars.sol/ 
```

Caution: The key file stored on the local computer in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/root/.ssh</samp> directory must not fall into the wrong hands!

Optionally, it’s possible to create an LVM snapshot or run scripts during the backup, exclude certain file patterns from the backup, and so on. Details can be found in the supplied configuration file as well as on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> page for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">interval</samp> defines how many backup versions should be stored for a given time interval. The default settings look as follows:

```
# in /etc/rsnapshot.conf
... 
interval        hourly  6
interval        daily   7
interval        weekly  4
#interval       monthly 3 
```

This means that six versions of backups run by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot hourly</samp> command are stored. Furthermore, seven backups of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot daily</samp> are archived as well as four backups of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot weekly</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">monthly</samp> interval is not defined by default.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">interval hourly 6</samp> setting is useful if the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot hourly</samp> command is not run every hour, but only every four hours, as provided in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d/rsnapshot</samp>. On the other hand, if you really want to run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot hourly</samp> every hour, the <samp class="listingcharacter">interval hourly 24</samp> setting would be more appropriate.

You can define any additional intervals as needed. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> stores backups for each interval in a separate directory and links unchanged backups only within the directory of an interval. This means that the memory requirement increases significantly with each additional interval.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> can be called manually, but this requires <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. You must specify a time interval as a parameter:

```
root# rsnapshot daily 
```

After the backup, you will find the backed up data in the following directory:

<samp class="listingcharacter">/var/cache/rsnapshot/<interval.n>/<hostname>/<directory></samp>

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">interval</samp> specifies the interval: <samp class="listingcharacter">hourly</samp> by default, <samp class="listingcharacter">daily</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">weekly</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">monthly</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> specifies the backup version: 0 for the most recent backup, 1 for the latest version, 2 for the version before last, and so on. <samp class="listingcharacter">hostname</samp> specifies the host from which the backed-up data originates, where <samp class="listingcharacter">localhost</samp> denotes the local host. Thus, the latest hourly backup of the local <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc</samp> directory is contained in the following directory:

<samp class="listingcharacter">/var/cache/rsnapshot/hourly.0/localhost/etc</samp>

The most recent monthly backup of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/home/user/Mail</samp> directory of the <samp class="listingcharacter">mars.sol</samp> server is located in the following directory:

<samp class="listingcharacter">/var/cache/rsnapshot/monthly.0/mars.sol/home/user/Mail</samp>

To automate the backups, a regular call of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d/rsnapshot</samp> Cron configuration file. All you have to do is remove the comment lines before the four cron lines already provided:

```
# /etc/cron.d/rsnapshot
0 */4         * * *           root    /usr/bin/rsnapshot hourly
30 3          * * *           root    /usr/bin/rsnapshot daily
0  3          * * 1           root    /usr/bin/rsnapshot weekly
30 2          1 * *           root    /usr/bin/rsnapshot monthly 
```

This will run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">rsnapshot</samp> every four hours—at 0:00, 4:00, 8:00, and so on; daily at 3:30; weekly on Mondays at 3:00; and monthly on the first day of the month at 2:30, with <samp class="listingcharacter">hourly</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">daily</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">weekly</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">monthly</samp> parameters. Of course, you can vary the times as you see fit. Note that all time intervals used in the Cron file must also be defined in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/rsnapshot.conf</samp>! This is not the case for the <samp class="listingcharacter">monthly</samp> interval by default.

## 28.9    Backup Scripts

This section focuses on real-life examples. The following script synchronizes the contents of the local <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">data</samp> directory with the directory of the same name on an external hard disk called <samp class="listingcharacter">backup</samp>. The script tests whether the external hard disk is available. If it isn’t, the backup will not be performed:

```
#!/bin/bash
if [ -d /media/backup/ ]; then
  rsync -avW --delete /home/kofler/data /media/backup/
fi 
```

As a rule, you will run backup scripts automatically on a regular basis. The easiest way to do this is to set up a Cron job. To do so, it’s easiest to save the script directly in a Cron directory—for example, under the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.daily/mybackup</samp> filename. Please note that the filename must not contain a dot and that the file must be executable (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">chmod a+x</samp>).

The other variant is to save the backup script in any directory—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/myscripts</samp>. To call the script automatically, you need to set up a new file in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/cron.d</samp>, such as according to the following pattern:

```
# file /etc/cron.d/mybackup
15 2 * * * root /etc/myscripts/mybackup 
```

Thus, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mybackup</samp> backup script will run daily at 2:15.

The following script creates a compressed TAR archive of the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">data</samp> directory. The archive is saved under two file names: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mydata-day-DD.tar.gz</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mydata-month-MM.tar.gz</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">DD</samp> indicates the day (01 to 31) and <samp class="listingcharacter">MM</samp> the month (01 to 12). If the script is run daily, you will have 43 backup versions over time, reflecting the state of the backup directory for the last 28 to 31 days and for the last 12 months:

```
#!/bin/bash
fname1=/backup/mydata-day-$(date "+%d").tar.gz
fname2=/backup/mydata-month-$(date "+%m").tar.gz
```
