```
vboxmanage list runningvms |  sed -r 's/.*{(.*)}/\1/' |
  xargs -L1 -I {} vboxmanage controlvm {} pause 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vboxmanage list runningvms</samp> returns a list of all running virtual machines. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sed</samp> extracts the ID numbers from it. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xargs</samp> passes these to a second <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vboxmanage</samp> command and executes <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pause</samp>. To resume the execution of the virtual machines, there is a second, similar script—namely, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">resume</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pause</samp>. Then I call a third script before I shut down the computer. This script sends the following ACPI shutdown signal to all virtual machines: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vboxmanage controlvm acpipowerbutton</samp>.

### 31.3.10    Enlarging Virtual Hard Disks

The VirtualBox user interface does not provide the option of subsequently enlarging a virtual hard disk. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vboxmanage</samp> command again provides a solution here. Before you get started, you need to shut down your virtual machine. In addition, a full backup is highly recommended!

Next, you need to locate the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.vdi</samp> file of the virtual hard disk and apply the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vboxmanage</samp> command to it. Then you want to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--resize</samp> option to specify the preferred new size in MiB. As a rule, the command is executed at lightning speed:

```
root# vboxmanage modifyhd debian.vdi --resize 60000 
```

But that's only half the battle. The virtual machine does not yet know that its hard disk has become bigger. For a guest installation without LVM and with the <samp class="listingcharacter">ext4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp> file system, you must now mount an ISO image of a Linux live CD in the virtual CD/DVD drive and start a live system inside the virtual machine. There you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">parted /dev/sda</samp> and can then increase the size of the last partition. After that, you also need to increase the size of the file system it contains by using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">resize2fs</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">xfs_growfs</samp>.

On the other hand, if you use LVM or the <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file system in the Linux guest, you can increase the file system size on the fly. These interventions are, of course, not without risk. That’s why you should read the relevant sections from [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18) beforehand!

Similarly, you can also enlarge a Windows file system. In this case too you must first shut down the virtual machine and enlarge the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">*.vdi</samp> file using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vboxmanage</samp> command. Then start Windows, open a command prompt window in it with admin privileges, and run the following commands:

```
> Diskpart
list disk
select disk 0
list partition
select partition 2
extend 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">list disk</samp> returns a list of all virtual disks. Usually, the first disk with index 0 must be selected. Then <samp class="listingcharacter">list partition</samp> determines the partitions. Once again, you must use <samp class="listingcharacter">select</samp> to select a partition for further processing—usually the last one. The <samp class="listingcharacter">extend</samp> command now enlarges it to the maximum size.

# 32    QEMU and Kernel-Based Virtual Machine

Kernel-Based Virtual Machine (KVM) is a Linux-specific virtualization technology for the server and enterprise segment. It extends Quick Emulator (QEMU), which has been available for a while. Red Hat and SUSE fully rely on the combination of QEMU and KVM in their enterprise distributions, and all other popular Linux distributions also include QEMU/KVM packages.

This chapter first introduces the basics of KVM and then focuses on server virtualization using KVM: this allows multiple Linux virtual servers to run on one machine. In real life, this is often done to separate server functions as much as possible to maximize security. But practical reasons also often speak in favor of server virtualization. While one user needs special Apache modules for their website, another may want to use the latest MySQL version. If many special requests of this kind are fulfilled on one system, this quickly leads to unwanted side effects and instabilities.

Essentially, KVM is also suitable for desktop virtualization, but this aspect is of secondary importance here. If you still want to use KVM on desktop systems, you can try the Boxes GNOME program in addition to the Virtual Machine Manager presented in this chapter. As is typical of GNOME, it’s very easy to use, but the program provides far too few configuration options even for simple applications.

By its nature, you can also use KVM on a root server. This enables you to set up several virtual machines on a real server, which look like your own servers to the outside world. There are two things you need to keep in mind:

*   You need a real root server. Nowadays, many hosting and cloud providers offer virtual environments. This is cheap and flexible because you can easily add RAM or CPU cores later—but it makes virtualization impossible. (From a technical perspective, nested virtualization has been possible for several years, but in reality many problems and limitations still occur.)

*   For most applications, both the KVM host and each guest require their own IP address. For numerous purposes, you need IPv4 addresses, which are rare and are therefore passed on by hosting providers at a correspondingly high price. In such cases, the routing between the KVM host and its guests is also relatively complicated.

This chapter can only give an introduction to KVM. You can find information on this topic at the following pages:

*   [https://www.linux-kvm.org](https://www.linux-kvm.org)

*   [https://libvirt.org](https://libvirt.org)

*   [https://help.ubuntu.com/community/KVM](https://help.ubuntu.com/community/KVM)

## 32.1    Basic Principles

The QEMU program emulates various CPUs and elementary hardware components of a computer: its network card, a DVD drive for installation, and so on. QEMU is also able to emulate processors incompatible with the host CPU (ARM, Sparc, PowerPC, MIPS, etc.).

KVM is a kernel module that only unfolds its effect in combination with QEMU. KVM requires a CPU with hardware virtualization capabilities and turns the QEMU emulator into a hardware virtualization system. The elegance of KVM is that it does not perform typical hypervisor tasks itself but uses memory and process management functions of the Linux kernel to do so. The KVM functions are used via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/kvm</samp> device file.

KVM works only if the host system processor supports virtualization features (Intel-VT or AMD-V). This is the case with most current processors. The exceptions include low-priced CPUs for cheap PCs or notebook computers. To determine if your CPU helps with hardware virtualization (Intel-VT or AMD-V), you should run the following <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">egrep</samp> command. If the result is empty, your CPU does not support virtualization or the feature has been disabled in BIOS/EFI:

```
user$ egrep '^flags.*(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo
flags :... vmx ... 
```

Even easier on Ubuntu systems, you can run the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kvm-ok</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cpu-checker</samp> package:

```
user$ kvm-ok
INFO: Your CPU supports KVM extensions
INFO: /dev/kvm exists
KVM acceleration can be used 
```

For the remainder of this chapter, I will assume that your CPU is KVM-compatible. If it isn’t, KVM seems to work as well. In fact, however, the virtual machines are only run through QEMU and thus without KVM support, and they then run much slower.

### Enabling Virtualization Features in the BIOS/EFI

Surprisingly, the existing virtualization features of the CPU are often disabled by the BIOS or EFI. To fix this, when you boot the computer, open the BIOS/EFI dialogs and look for the relevant setting.

To run KVM virtual machines and control them using the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt tools</samp>, you need to install the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-system-x86</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-kvm</samp> on openSUSE) and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-manager</samp> packages, and also <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt-client</samp>, depending on your distribution. In the meantime, further development of KVM is taking place as part of the QEMU project. This is why many distributions no longer have separate packages for KVM:

```
root# apt install qemu-system-x86 virt-manag           
(Debian, Ubuntu)
root# dnf install qemu-kvm virt-manager libvirt-client 
(Fedora, RHEL)
root# zypper install qemu-kvm virt-manager libvirt     
(openSUSE) 
```

Some distributions require you to explicitly start the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirtd</samp> service:

```
root# systemctl enable --now libvirtd         
(Fedora, openSUSE, RHEL) 
```

### Do Not Run an Open DNS Resolver on a root Server!

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnsmasq</samp> program is installed together with the libvirt tools. This is a simple DHCP server and nameserver. The program is used to assign virtual machines their network parameters.

However, in some Debian and Ubuntu versions, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnsmasq</samp> is not only run by the libvirt tools, but started automatically, just like any installed network service. This means that an open nameserver is running on your computer.

At home or in private networks, this is not a big issue. However, if you run KVM, libvirt, and the like on a publicly accessible root server, an open nameserver is no good for you.

Fortunately, the security issue can be easily fixed. You just need to stop the program using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl disable --now dnsmasq</samp>. (The libvirt tools still use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnsmasq</samp>. Only the unconfigured operation of the program as a top-level service is stopped.)

Fortunately, this problem no longer occurs with current versions of Debian and Ubuntu: there, the libvirt tools only install <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnsmasq-base</samp> with the program itself, but not <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">dnsmasq</samp> with the systemd files to start as a background service.

KVM provides its functions in three kernel modules: the basic functions are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter">kvm</samp> module, the Intel-VT-specific functions in <samp class="listingcharacter">kvm-intel</samp>, and the AMD-V-specific functions in <samp class="listingcharacter">kvm-amd</samp>. To use KVM, you must load the KVM module that matches your hardware. The <samp class="listingcharacter">kvm</samp> module is loaded at the same time. In most distributions, the init system takes care of this. If that does not work, you should intervene manually:

```
root# modprobe kvm-intel  (for Intel-VT processors)
root# modprobe kvm-amd    (for AMD-V processors) 
```

### Conflicts between Multiple Virtualization Systems

Note that only one program can use the virtualization functions of the CPU at a time. That is why it is impossible to use VirtualBox and KVM at the same time.

In the past, KVM virtual machines were run using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kvm</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-kvm</samp> command. Today, the command is <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-system-x86_64</samp> for almost all distributions. Only RHEL and compatible systems use <samp class="listingcharacter">/usr/libexec/qemu-kvm</samp> instead.

After starting the command, the virtual machine will be displayed in a window or must be controlled by a VNC client. In general, however, a direct use of the command is rarely recommended. You need to set the virtual machine hardware components through countless options, and this makes the application confusing and prone to errors.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools simplify the administration of virtual machines:

*   The Virtual Machine Manager (program or package name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-manager</samp>) helps with a graphical user interface to set up and run virtual machines.

*   If you prefer to work in the terminal, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> shell to create, start, and stop virtual machines and perform other admin tasks.

*   In addition, there are various commands for special tasks: <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-clone</samp> copies a virtual machine; <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-top</samp> returns a list of all virtual machines, including RAM and CPU usage; and so on, similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp>.

All major distributions provide QEMU/KVM and <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> packages. Because the development of KVM is driven to a very high degree by Red Hat, RHEL or RHEL clones are particularly well-suited for KVM deployment. If you want to test the very latest KVM features, Fedora is the ideal playground. However, this doesn’t mean that other distributions are not equally suitable. Personally, I have been running KVM hosts under various versions of Ubuntu for over a decade.

### 32.1.1    Internal Workings of libvirt

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirt</samp> is an interface for managing virtual machines and their associated virtual network and disk devices. A prerequisite for using the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools is that the host system must be running the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirtd</samp> daemon. This program is started by the init system when the host computer is booted.

The virtual machines are controlled by the <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> shell, by the Virtual Machine Manager, or by other <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> commands. Each of these programs must connect to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> daemon beforehand. The <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> daemon also allows network connections that are usually tunneled through SSH.

In addition to KVM, the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools can also control the Xen virtualization system. In this chapter, however, I refer exclusively to KVM.

KVM machines can run on two levels via <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp>:

*   User level (<samp class="listingcharacter">qemu:///session</samp>)
    This variant is primarily intended for desktop virtualization and grants the virtual machines less access to the host computer's hardware. Internally, the first time a <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tool is called at the user level, a separate <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> process is started that has only the permissions of the current user. Thus, user-level KVM machines minimize the security risks posed by virtualization.

*   System level (<samp class="listingcharacter">qemu:///system</samp>)
    System-level virtual machines are better suited for server virtualization because they can directly access hardware components of the host computer and because there are more options for integrating the virtual machines into the network. The <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> processes communicate with the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> daemon, which runs with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges.

There are strong configuration differences between distributions in the communication between the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools and the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> daemon. It’s quite simple with Fedora, RHEL, and the like: if you want to communicate with <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> at the system level, you need <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges. The Virtual Machine Manager can be started with user rights, but the program expects the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password to be specified immediately after startup.

Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools are executed with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges, but not the actual virtualization command! Rather, the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools launch the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-kvm</samp> command under the <samp class="listingcharacter">qemu</samp> user account. You have to pay attention to this subtlety, especially to ensure you’re setting the access rights for image or ISO files correctly!

Also on Ubuntu, <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools running with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges communicate with <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> at the system level. But even <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> commands executed only with user privileges are allowed to communicate with <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> at the system level, so long as the user belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> group! Strictly speaking, what matters is whether the user is allowed to access the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run/libvirt/libvirt-sock</samp> file. This file belongs to <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> group.

The association with the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> group is automatically established for the user performing the installation when the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt-bin</samp> package is installed. Additional users can be added to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> group with the following command:

```
root# usermod -a -G libvirt <username> 
```

Note that the new group assignment will not take effect until you log out and log in again!

In Debian and openSUSE, all users have read and write permissions for <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/run/libvirt/libvirt-sock</samp>. A group assignment is therefore not necessary.

The configuration files of the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> system are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/libvirt</samp> directory. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu.conf</samp> file contained in this directory is particularly interesting: it specifies various basic settings for the KVM command. Among other things, the file controls the default settings of the virtual machine's VNC or Spice server. The IP address 127.0.0.1 is used by default. Thus, only local connections are allowed, although forwarding via SSH is possible through port forwarding.

In addition, the properties of each virtual machine are recorded in an XML file in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/libvirt/qemu</samp> directory. Most settings are understandable without further explanation and correspond directly with corresponding options of QEMU/KVM. The format of <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> XML files is documented in detail on the following page: [https://libvirt.org/format.html](https://libvirt.org/format.html).

#### Always Change the Description of Virtual Machines by Using "virsh edit"!

You should not modify the XML files containing the key data of a virtual machine directly in an editor, as otherwise another <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tool may overwrite your changes. Instead, you should use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh edit</samp> command!

If you use disk images to map the virtual data carriers when setting up virtual machines, these are saved in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/libvirt/images</samp> directory by default. If you want to store disk images in another directory or use logical volumes, disk partitions, or network devices to store the disks, you need to set up a so-called storage pool beforehand. The easiest way to do this is in Virtual Machine Manager. Alternatively, you can run the appropriate <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pool</samp> commands within <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp>.

### 32.1.2    Behavior when Rebooting the Host System

What happens to virtual machines when you shut down the host system? Many distributions back up the memory contents of all virtual machines that are currently being executed by <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> at the system level. Internally, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">save virsh</samp> command is used. The next time the computer is started, the state of the virtual machine is automatically restored; that is, the virtual machine continues to run as if nothing had happened in the meantime.

When backing up or restoring multiple virtual machines, all of their RAM must be saved to or read from disk. This requires sufficient free space in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/libvirt/qemu/save</samp> directory and of course takes some time.

However, the detailed implementation varies from distribution to distribution:

*   Fedora and RHEL The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/libexec/libvirt-guests.sh</samp> script, which is called by the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirt-guests</samp> systemd service, is responsible for this mechanism. You can store configuration parameters in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysconfig/libvirt-guests</samp>. This file does not exist by default. The allowed parameters can be found in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirt-guests.sh</samp>.

*   Debian and Ubuntu Here, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib/libvirt/libvirt-guests.sh</samp> script is executed. It takes into account settings from <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/default/libvirt-guests</samp>.

*   openSUSE Current SUSE distributions also use the same mechanism as RHEL. However, the corresponding script is located in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/usr/lib64/libvirt/libvirt-guests.sh</samp>.

On some distributions, the storage service is not automatically active, but must be explicitly enabled using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl</samp>:

```
root# systemctl enable --now libvirt-guests  
(Fedora, openSUSE, RHEL) 
```

### 32.1.3    Virtual Hardware

When setting up a new virtual machine, you have a lot of choices: disk images in RAW or QCOW2 format, IDE or virtio hard disk adapters, the graphics system based on SDL, VNC, or Spice, and so on. This section summarizes the most important information in this area.

Basically, KVM performs a complete virtualization. Thus, the guest system running in the virtual machine does not require any special drivers.

The guest system can be run even more efficiently if the optional virtio drivers are used for the communication between KVM and the virtual machine. Technically speaking, this is referred to as paravirtualization; that is, the guest system helps with the virtualization.

For Linux guests, virtio drivers are available by default to accelerate disk, memory, and network access. So it's just a matter of selecting the appropriate virtio components when setting up the virtual machine.

The matter is a little more difficult if you want to run Windows in a KVM machine. In this case, you first need to set up the virtual machine with traditional hardware components—for example, with a virtual SATA interface. After installing Windows, you must install the virtio drivers, and only then can you activate the virtio components by modifying the virtual machine afterward.

For Windows 10, this approach has always worked well in my experiments, but I have reached my limits with Windows 11—or perhaps the limits of QEMU/KVM or Windows. After changing the drivers, the Windows boot process failed. My only Windows 11 installation to date uses a virtual SATA hard disk.

To offer a virtual disk to a guest, an image file is often used on the KVM host. QEMU/KVM support two image formats:

*   RAW format With the RAW format, the blocks of the virtual hard disk are simply mapped 1:1\. If the file system of the host computer supports so-called sparse files, blocks containing only zeros are not physically stored. This is how it works with the <samp class="listingcharacter">ext</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">xfs</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">btrfs</samp> file systems, among others, and this initially saves a lot of space. The RAW format is the simplest and fastest image format for virtual machines.

*   QCOW2 format QCOW2 stands for Qemu Copy-on-Write, Version 2. This format provides numerous additional features compared to RAW. The data blocks are only reserved when required, without requiring a file system that is compatible with sparse files. In addition, the virtual file system can be compressed and encrypted. Finally, QCOW2 images provide the ability to manage snapshots. QCOW2 images are slower than RAW images, but the speed disadvantage is not as great as it used to be.

QCOW2 has been the default file system of Virtual Machine Manager for several years. The development of a third format (QED) was discontinued.

Instead of image files, you can also use disk partitions, logical volumes, or iSCSI devices as virtual disks. These variants provide administrative advantages in large virtualization systems but do not offer significantly higher speed compared to RAW images.

To connect the virtual machine to the local network or the internet, you must equip it with a network adapter. For Linux guests, the virtio driver is the first choice. For Windows guests, QEMU simulates an Intel E1000 network adapter.

The second question is how to connect the adapter to your network:

*   NAT By default, the KVM command or the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools opt for the Network Address Translation (NAT) variant. This forwards the host's internet access to the guest. However, the guest is not visible on the local network or on the internet.
    There is an important difference in the NAT implementation here compared to VirtualBox: SSH connections from the host to the virtual machine are possible without any problem.

*   Network bridges For server deployment, you must connect the virtual machine to the network or internet through a network bridge or routing. This requires a special network configuration of the KVM host ([Section 32.4](#32_004.html_h32.4)).

*   MacVTap Here, a virtual network adapter is directly connected to a physical adapter.

At least during the installation, you need to see the virtual machine output. This means the guest needs a separate graphics system. This is done by emulating a VGA-compatible graphics card, whose outputs are then displayed in a window via VNC or Spice. For 2D use, this works well even with high resolution.

VNC and Spice are network-compatible. The slightly higher speed and the fact that virtual machine audio output can also be forwarded to the local Spice client via the network speak in favor of the Spice architecture.

## 32.2    Virtual Machine Manager

Virtual Machine Manager (program and package name <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-manager</samp>) is the best way to get familiar with KVM. The program has a lot to offer even for experts and is absolutely sufficient for many virtualization tasks.

To use the program, you must connect to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> daemon. In most distributions, the connection to the existing QEMU/KVM item is established automatically. On Fedora, openSUSE, RHEL, and the like, you need to enter the <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> password when starting Virtual Machine Manager.

On Ubuntu, the connection works only if the user is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> group. If that is not the case, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo adduser loginname libvirtd</samp> and log out and log in again.

### Soon to Be Obsolete?

With the introduction of RHEL 8, Red Hat has given the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-manager</samp> package the deprecated attribute. Red Hat now wants you to set up virtual machines in Cockpit using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cockpit-machines</samp> package. Although this works, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">cockpit-machines</samp> can not keep up with the functionality of Virtual Machine Manager. The deprecated note is currently understood to mean that Red Hat doesn’t want to continue developing <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-manager</samp> and sees the future in Cockpit. Let's wait and see if users will see it that way.

Another alternative to Virtual Machine Manager is Proxmox Virtual Environment (see [https://www.proxmox.com](https://www.proxmox.com)). This is a separate distribution based on Debian. It includes QEMU, KVM, and libvirt as well as a web interface for virtual machine management. According to the freemium model, the basic version is freely available. However, additional functions, updates, and support are subject to a charge. Proxmox is not very easy to test because the entire disk is erased during the installation. Parallel operation with other distributions is not intended.

The main window of Virtual Machine Manager contains a list of all <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> connections (see [Figure 32.1](#32_002.html_f32.1)). By default, this list consists of only one entry, QEMU/KVM, for the local virtualization system. However, you can specify the key data of additional KVM hosts using File • Add Connection.

Double-clicking an entry in this list establishes the connection to the KVM host and then displays all virtual machines of this host. For each virtual machine, an icon shows whether the machine is shut down, running, or paused.

To start a virtual machine, right-click its entry and execute Run. Double-clicking the entry opens a new window that displays the state of the virtual machine in two views:

*   The console view shows the graphics system of the virtual machine. There you can see the virtual machine's output and you can input data using the keyboard and mouse. For virtual machines running in text mode, clicking in the virtual machine captures the mouse cursor, as it were. (Ctrl)+(Alt) releases the cursor again.

*   The detail view shows the key data of the virtual machine. There you can change the hardware configuration of the virtual machine. However, most changes can be made only if the virtual machine has been shut down before that.

[![Virtual Machine Manager with Various Virtual Machines](bilderklein/klein32_001.png)](img-f32.1.html)

**Figure 32.1**     Virtual Machine Manager with Various Virtual Machines

To switch between the two views, you need to run View • Console or View • Details or click the corresponding buttons in the toolbar.

You can also use Virtual Machine Manager to administrate an external KVM host that can be accessed via SSH. To do this, you first need to define a connection to this server using File • Add Connection, where you select SSH as the connection method (see [Figure 32.2](#32_002.html_f32.2)). When establishing the connection, you must also enter the corresponding login password.

If the external KVM host is running RHEL or Fedora, the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> administration requires <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges and thus a <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login via SSH. For security reasons, however, SSH servers are often configured in such a way that direct <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login is impossible. A possible compromise is to configure the SSH server in such a way that a <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login is only accepted if authenticated by a key, but not by password.

For the administration of external KVM hosts, it is generally recommended to use SSH keys for authentication. To do this, you want to copy the public part of your key to the remote computer before establishing the first connection via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ssh-copy-id</samp> (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.4](#23_004.html_h23.4)).

[![Connection Setup via SSH](bilderklein/klein32_002.png)](img-f32.2.html)

**Figure 32.2**     Connection Setup via SSH

### 32.2.1    Setting Up a New Virtual Machine

Setting up a new virtual machine starts with the Create a new virtual machine button. A five-step wizard helps you to set the key data:

*   In the first step, you specify on which KVM host the virtual machine is supposed to be installed. This selection option is relevant if you use Virtual Machine Manager to administrate not only one local KVM host, but multiple virtualization machines.

    There, you also specify the installation source. A Linux installation is usually an ISO file. However, it is also possible to read the installation data from the DVD drive of the host computer. The Import Existing Disk Image option creates a copy of an existing virtual machine image file.

*   If you selected an ISO image or a CD/DVD as the installation source in the first step, you can specify the filename of an ISO file or the CD/DVD drive in the second step. The Browse button leads to a dialog that initially only displays the storage Pools known to Virtual Machine Manager. To select an ISO file directly, you must click the Browse Local button in this dialog.

    Sometimes the wizard manages to get the type of the operating system and its version from the installation media—Linux and Fedora, for example. If this does not succeed, you will have to provide this data yourself. These settings are necessary for the wizard to set up the optimal virtual hardware components for the guest system.

*   In the third step, you must specify how much memory (RAM) and how many CPU cores you want to allocate to the virtual machine.

*   In the fourth step, you will set up the virtual hard disk. Usually, you will use the already preselected Create Disk Image for the virtual machine option. By default, the new image file will be created in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/libvirt/images</samp> directory. Do not select a virtual hard disk size that is too small as subsequent enlargement is only possible with great effort.

    Alternatively, the Select and Create Custom Storage option and the associated Manage button will take you to another dialog for managing all libvirt disks. There you can set up multiple storage pools. Such a pool can be, for example, any directory in the file system or an LVM system. Within the selected pool, you can then create a new disk and select it for installation.

*   In the fifth step, you assign a name to the virtual machine and choose between different network options. By default, Virtual Machine Manager uses the NAT method. This method assigns the virtual machines to the private network 192.168.122.0/24\. Thus, the virtual machine can use the host computer's internet access but cannot connect to other computers on your local network.

    The Done button finishes the configuration and starts the new virtual machine immediately. If you do not want this, you should enable the Customize Configuration before Install option in the final dialog sheet of the wizard. This will take you to a dialog that summarizes the virtual machine hardware components after you finish the wizard (see [Figure 32.3](#32_002.html_f32.3)).

    [![Hardware Management in Virtual Machine Manager](bilderklein/klein32_003.png)](img-f32.3.html)

    **Figure 32.3**     Hardware Management in Virtual Machine Manager

The virtual machine will start as soon as you finish the configuration. You will see the virtual machine output in a new Virtual Machine Manager window. Behind the scenes, this window acts as a VNC or Spice client.

By default, virtual machines are equipped with BIOS. If you want to experiment with EFI in your virtual machines, you must first install an EFI package. On Debian and Ubuntu, the required files are in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ovmf</samp> package, on Fedora in <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">edk2-ovmf</samp>. For Virtual Machine Manager to take the new package into account, you must restart <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirtd</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">systemctl restart libvirtd</samp>.

When setting up new virtual machines, you must then make sure that you click the Customize Configuration before Install option in the final step of the wizard. After that, you can choose between the BIOS and three EFI variants (with or without Secure Boot) in the Overview dialog sheet under Firmware in the virtual machine's detailed settings.

For the exchange of text via the clipboard between the host and the virtual machines to work, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">spice-vdagent</samp> package must be installed in the virtual machines.

### 32.2.2    Stopping Virtual Machines

The virtual machines run completely independently of Virtual Machine Manager! So you can close the Virtual Machine Manager windows and open them again later, while the virtual machines will continue to run in the meantime. You can even log out and log in again without affecting the execution of virtual machines.

There are many ways to stop a virtual machine:

*   Shutdown • Reboot sends an appropriate ACPI event to the virtual machine. When the virtual machine processes ACPI events, it initiates a shutdown and then a reboot.

*   Shutdown • Shutdown initiates a shutdown via ACPI.

*   Shutdown • Force Reset or • Force Off stops the virtual machine execution immediately—just as if you would unplug the power cable from a real computer. Needless to say, you should try to avoid this type of shutdown, as it can result in data loss. The difference between the two commands is that the virtual machine is restarted after the Reset.

*   Shutdown • Save saves the contents of the machine's virtual RAM to a file and then stops execution. When the virtual machine is restarted later, it will be in exactly the same state as when it was shut down.

*   Of course, you can also shut down or restart the virtual machine itself—for example, by running the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">shutdown now</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">reboot</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">halt -p</samp> commands within the machine.

### 32.2.3    Windows Installation

Windows 11 has higher hardware requirements than previous versions. The virtualization system must support EFI including Secure Boot and TPM for the operating system to run.

Current versions of QEMU/KVM and Virtual Machine Manager support Windows 11 out of the box. In my tests with Ubuntu 23.04 as the host system, Virtual Machine Manager independently detected the Windows 11 operating system after selecting the ISO file.

If you use an older distribution, on the other hand, some manual work is required:

*   You need to install UEFI firmware files and a software implementation of TPM. The required packages are named <samp class="listingcharacter">ovmf</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">edk2-ovmf</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">swtpm</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">swtpm-tools</samp>. Depending on the distribution, you may need to activate additional package sources, such as Stefan Berger's PPA ([https://launchpad.net/stefanberger](https://launchpad.net/stefanberger)) or EPEL.

*   UEFI must be set as firmware (no BIOS). You can find the option in the Overview dialog sheet. Note that the firmware cannot be changed once the installation begins.

*   Finally, the virtual machine must contain the TPM hardware component. If the virtual machine setup assistant does not take care of it itself, you can use the Add HArdware button.

## 32.3    libvirt Commands

Now that I have presented Virtual Machine Manager as the most important representative of the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools in the previous section, here are some commands whose use does not require a graphical user interface.

### 32.3.1    virsh

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> command to start the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> shell. In it, you can execute commands to manage all virtual machines known to <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp>:

```
root# virsh
virsh# list --all
virsh # list --all
 Id   Name                    State
----------------------------------------
 1    alma9-desktop           running
 2    debian12                running
 4    win11                   running
 -    alma9-minmal            shut off
...
virsh# start fedora
Domain fedora started
virsh# exit 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp>, you can use the following commands to start, temporarily suspend and resume, shut down in an orderly fashion (ACPI shutdown), shut down immediately, save and resume, or delete virtual machines from the list of <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt definitions</samp>: <samp class="listingcharacter">start</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">suspend</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">resume</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">shutdown</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">destroy</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">save</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">restore</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">undefine</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">edit</samp> allows you to edit the XML file with the virtual machine description directly in an editor. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">EDITOR</samp> environment variable is not initialized, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh edit</samp> asks which of the installed editors you want to use the first time. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> then remembers your answer.

For all <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> commands listed thus far, you must specify the virtual machine name, its UUID number, or, for running virtual machines, the ID number. The UUID number derives from the XML definition file. Information about the ID numbers of running virtual machines is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">list virsh</samp> command.

Provided <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> detects that the machine is a KVM host, it connects to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> daemon running at the system level if possible. When <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> is run with user privileges only, a system-level connection on Ubuntu requires membership in the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> group. On Fedora and RHEL, you must run the command as <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> if you want to work at the system level.

It’s possible to change the connection within the <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> shell using the <samp class="listingcharacter">connect</samp> command. <samp class="listingcharacter">qemu:///session</samp> denotes a user-level connection and <samp class="listingcharacter">qemu:///system</samp> a system-level connection:

```
virsh# connect qemu:///system 
```

You can also connect to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> daemon on another machine via SSH. If the KVM host is a RHEL or Fedora machine, you must specify <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> as the username because only <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> is allowed to connect to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> system daemon on these systems. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter">qemu+ssh:</samp> is followed by only two slashes, not three! If a <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> login with password via SSH is not possible on the KVM host for security reasons, you must set up your public SSH key on the KVM host before the first connection is established:

```
virsh# connect qemu qemu+ssh://user@hostname/system
user@hostname's password: ******* 
```

Instead of using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> interactively, you can run a single <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> command using the format <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh command</samp>:

```
root# virsh  list --all
... 
```

If you do not want to use the connection provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> by default, you need to specify the connection string with the <samp class="listingcharacter">-c</samp> option:

```
root# virsh -c qemu:///session list --all
... 
```

Finally, I want to present some selected <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> commands. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man virsh</samp> documents at least a hundred more commands. Within the shell, you get a detailed description of the respective command via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">help name</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">connect qemu:///session</samp> establishes an ordinary user connection to <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp>. This way you can manage your own virtual machines.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">connect qemu:///system</samp> establishes a <samp class="listingcharacter">root connection</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp>. This is only necessary if global KVM options or virtual networks are to be changed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">list [--inactive</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--all]</samp> lists all running virtual machines. If you want to list only the currently inactive machines or both inactive and running machines, you need to specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">--inactive</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">--all</samp> options.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">start <vmname></samp> starts the specified virtual machine. If you want to communicate with the machine in graphics mode, you can use either the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer</samp> program or a VNC client. The connection data is determined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">vncdisplay virsh</samp> command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">suspend/resume <vmname></samp> temporarily stops or resumes the specified virtual machine. The stopped virtual machine will continue to consume RAM! So only the virtual CPU is stopped.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">shutdown/reboot <vmname></samp> shuts down or reboots the virtual machine. The virtual machine receives a shutdown signal via ACPI. However, it’s up to the virtual machine to decide whether it will respond. If this is not the case with older distributions, installing the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">acpid</samp> package in the virtual machine usually helps.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">save <vmname> <filename></samp> saves the virtual machine state to a file and then stops the machine from running.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">restore <filename></samp> reactivates the previously saved virtual machine. The state file can be deleted afterward.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">destroy <vmname></samp> terminates the virtual machine immediately. This is like unplugging the power cord on your computer—with the same consequences.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">undefine <vmname></samp> deletes the XML file that describes the virtual machine. The image file with the virtual hard disk will be preserved. If you want to delete the image file(s) as well, you need to use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--remove-all-storage</samp> option.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">autostart [--disable] <vmname></samp> specifies that the virtual machine should start automatically during the host boot process. By using the <samp class="listingcharacter">--disable</samp> option, you can deactivate the automatic start again. Automatic startup works only for machines that are set up at the system level. On the other hand, at the session level, <samp class="listingcharacter">autostart</samp> machines are not started until <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> is used to connect to <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirtd</samp> for the first time.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">console <vmname></samp> allows you to operate the specified virtual machine directly in the console. This assumes that a <samp class="listingcharacter">getty</samp> process for the serial <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/ttyS0</samp> port is running in the virtual machine. To terminate the connection, you need to press (Ctrl)+(D).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ttyconsole <vmname></samp> specifies which device of the host computer is used to access the serial port of the guest system (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/dev/pts/5</samp>). You can then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">socat - /dev/pts/5</samp> in a terminal window and communicate with the virtual machine (much like the <samp class="listingcharacter">console</samp> command described previously). Before that, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">socat</samp> package must usually be installed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vncdisplay <vmname></samp> returns the IP address (empty for <samp class="listingcharacter">localhost</samp>) and port number for the VNC display of the virtual machine. You can then launch any VNC client (such as Vinagre) to interact with the virtual machine. On the KVM host, you can also run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer vmname</samp> instead. For security reasons, VNC access works only from <samp class="listingcharacter">localhost</samp>.

    <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vncdisplay</samp> does not return a result if the virtual machine does not share its graphics system via VNC at all but uses the more modern Spice system instead. In this case, you can operate the virtual machine using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer</samp> program. You can directly pass the virtual machine name to this program.

    However, should the need arise to determine the Spice port number, it will become difficult. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh</samp> lacks a command to find the Spice port of a virtual machine, and that’s similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vncdisplay</samp>. The following command extracts the port number from the process list:

    <samp class="listingcharacter">ps aux | grep vm_name | grep -oP "(?<=-spice port=).*?(?=,)"</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">edit <vmname></samp> loads the XML file describing the virtual machine into the editor you set in the <samp class="listingcharacter">$EDITOR</samp> environment variable.

### 32.3.2    virt-clone

Setting up a new virtual machine usually takes quite some time. If you want a virtual machine that has essentially the same key data as an existing virtual machine, it’s much faster to simply copy or “clone” it. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-clone</samp> command can help with this: by default, it creates a new XML definition file, copies the virtual disk image file, and assigns a new random MAC address to the network adapter. The remaining hardware components remain unchanged. The virtual machine must be shut down before copying.

The following command copies an Ubuntu server installation. The new virtual machine is named <samp class="listingcharacter">userver6</samp>, and the new image is saved as the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/var/lib/libvirt/images/userver6.img</samp> file:

```
root# virt-clone --original userver5 --name userver6 \
                 --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/userver6.img 
```

#### SELinux

Be sure to create the new image file in a libvirt storage pool. Otherwise, the SELinux rules on RHEL/Fedora will prevent the virtual machine from running.

After copying, you need to make various adjustments in the virtual machine. For example, you need to change the network configuration so that there are no IP address conflicts. Depending on the configuration, it may be necessary to update the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hosts</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/hostname</samp> files as well. If there was an SSH server in the original virtual machine, you must make sure to create a new SSH key in the virtual machine:

```
root# systemctl stop sshd                  
(Debian/Ubuntu)
root# rm /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*
root# dpkg-reconfigure openssh-server

root# systemctl stop sshd                  
(Fedora/RHEL)
root# rm /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*
root# systemctl start sshd 
```

### 32.3.3    virt-sysprep

Instead of modifying the virtual machines manually, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-sysprep</samp> command for this purpose. The command first resets various data (SSH keys, entries in the cron spool directory, etc.) and then performs the operations specified by options. The following command first resets the virtual machine named <samp class="listingcharacter">alma</samp> and then sets a new host name:

```
root# virt-sysprep --hostname mynewhostname -d alma
Examining the guest ...

Performing "bash-history" ...

Performing "cron-spool" ...

Performing "dhcp-client-state" ...

Performing "logfiles" ...
...

Setting the hostname: testhostname 
```

You can prevent the reset operations performed by default by passing to the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--operations</samp> option a list of actions to be performed. The following command changes only the host name, but does not change the virtual machine in any other way:

```
root# virt-sysprep --hostname mynewhostname --operations customize \
        ‐d alma
Setting the hostname: testhostname 
```

By using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-sysprep</samp>, you can also add users; change passwords; install packages; add, change, or delete files; and more. The numerous options and operations are described in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">man</samp> page.

Many operations work independently of the distribution in the virtual machine. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-sysprep</samp>, however, is developed by Red Hat and is therefore particularly well-suited if the virtual machine contains RHEL or a distribution compatible with it.

### 32.3.4    virt-viewer

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer</samp> from the package of the same name is a VNC and Spice client for displaying the screen contents as well as communicating with a virtual machine. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer vmname</samp> establishes the connection to a running virtual machine. This assumes that the virtual machine uses VNC or Spice:

```
root# virt-viewer <vmname> 
```

If you run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer</samp> without <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges but want to connect to a virtual machine running at the system level, you must specify the connection string with the <samp class="listingcharacter">-c</samp> option:

```
user$ virt-viewer -c qemu:///system <vmname> 
```

Provided that the virtual machine uses VNC to share the virtual graphics system, you can use any other VNC client instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-viewer</samp>. The only difference is that you must first use the <samp class="listingcharacter">virsh</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter">vncdisplay</samp> to determine the connection data.

Spice clients for Windows and macOS can be found at [https://www.spice-space.org/download.html](https://www.spice-space.org/download.html).

### 32.3.5    virt-top

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-top</samp> command from the package of the same name provides a listing of all virtual machines, similar to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">top</samp>. For each virtual machine, its memory and CPU requirements as well as various other parameters are displayed:

```
user$ virt-top
virt-top 07:29:53 - x86_64 12/12CPU 2200MHz 31617MB
31 domains, 2 active, 2 running, 0 sleeping, 0 paused, 29 inactive D:0 O:0 X:0
CPU: 0.1%  Mem: 3072 MB (3072 MB by guests)

   ID S RDRQ WRRQ RXBY TXBY %CPU %MEM    TIME   NAME  
    1 R    0    0   52    0  0.1  6.0   8:46.14 ubuntu
    2 R    0    0    0    0  0.0  3.0   0:21.59 alma
    -                                           (fedora)
   ... 
```

## 32.4    Integrating Virtual Machines into the LAN (Network Bridge)

By default, <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> uses so-called user-mode networking. The virtual machines are assigned an IP address in the 192.168.122.* range via DHCP. On the host computer, you need to set up the IP address 192.168.122.1 as the gateway to the internet. This way, the guests have internet access and can also communicate with the host via its address, 192.168.122.1\. Apart from that, KVM guests cannot access network services on the local network, and vice versa, while computers on the LAN cannot communicate with KVM guests either.

To provide server services to the local network on KVM guests, you need a virtual network bridge that connects the virtual network adapters of the KVM machines to the physical network adapter of the host computer. What can be achieved in VirtualBox quite simply by selecting a different network type is unfortunately associated with manual work in <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> or Virtual Machine Manager.

### 32.4.1    Configuring the Network Bridge on the Host Computer

To build the bridge, you can use the tools from the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">bridge-utils</samp> package. However, as usual, the configuration details vary from distribution to distribution. I want to present the procedures for Fedora/RHEL, Ubuntu, and Debian here. For all variants, you should make sure that you replace the name of the network interface (<samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s1</samp> in the following examples) with the interface name that is relevant for you!

On Fedora and RHEL, NetworkManager is responsible for bridge building. If you use a desktop system, it’s best to start the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nm-connection-editor</samp> graphical user interface. Using this, you first need to set up a new bridge and add a connection (Bridged Connection) to the relevant Ethernet interface in the Bridge dialog sheet. Back on the main page of the program, you then want to remove the Ethernet interface. The network connection should thus take place automatically via the bridge. (In my tests, this sometimes required a reboot—quite untypical for Linux.)

If you run QEMU/KVM on a root server, there will probably be no desktop system, and the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nm-connection-editor</samp> will accordingly not be available. You can help yourself by using the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmtui</samp> text-based configuration tool (Edit • Bridge • Create), or you can create the bridge using <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">nmcli</samp> commands as in the following example:

```
root# nmcli connection add type bridge ifname br0 stp no
root# nmcli connection add type bridge-slave ifname enp0s1 master br0
root# nmcli connection show --active 
(returns UUIDs from all interfaces)
root# nmcli connection down 659b...  
(UUID of enp0s1)
root# nmcli connection up bridge-slave-enp0s1 
```

You will find helpful information on building bridges with the NetworkManager on the following two pages:

*   [https://www.xmodulo.com/configure-linux-bridge-network-manager-ubuntu.html](https://www.xmodulo.com/configure-linux-bridge-network-manager-ubuntu.html)

*   [https://linuxconfig.org/how-to-use-bridged-networking-with-libvirt-and-kvm](https://linuxconfig.org/how-to-use-bridged-networking-with-libvirt-and-kvm)

Theoretically, it’s possible to set up a network bridge to a Wi-Fi interface in a similar way. However, that’s not recommended (see [https://pve.proxmox. com/wiki/WLAN](https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/WLAN)).

For Ubuntu, the network configuration is based on <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">netplan</samp> (see [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15), [Section 15.4](#15_004.html_h15.4)). To build a bridge, use the following configuration file as a guide:

```
# file /etc/netplan/02-ethernet-bridge.yaml
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp0s1:
      dhcp4: no
  bridges:
    br0:
      dhcp4: yes
      interfaces:
        - enp0s1 
```

In this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s1</samp> interface is connected to the <samp class="listingcharacter">br0</samp> bridge. The bridge obtains its IP configuration from the DHCP server on the local network. (Alternatively, you can of course configure the bridge statically.) To test the syntax of the new configuration file, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sudo netplan apply</samp>. However, the bridge does not become active until after a reboot.

On Debian, bridge building is done in the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> file. The existing lines for manual configuration of the interface to the LAN (in this example, <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s1</samp>) must be changed so that this interface can then be controlled manually. For this purpose, the corresponding configuration settings now move to the description of the <samp class="listingcharacter">br0</samp> interface (or whatever you call the bridge).

In this example, 10.0.0.138 is the gateway and the DHCP server of the local network. The bridge itself is assigned the IP address previously held by the host computer (10.0.0.120). Don't forget that <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> must contain the address of the name server:

```
# file /etc/interfaces/network (Ubuntu)
# loopback network interface (unchanged)
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback

# interface to LAN (manual)
auto enp0s1
iface enp0s1 inet manual

# bridge to enp0s1
auto br0
iface br0 inet static
       address 10.0.0.120
       network 10.0.0.0
       netmask 255.255.255.0
       broadcast 10.0.0.255
       gateway 10.0.0.138
       bridge_ports enp0s1 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ifdown/ifup</samp> to restart the affected network interfaces. The <samp class="listingcharacter">br0</samp> bridge now has the IP address 10.0.0.120 and transmits the IP packets to the physical network adapter, <samp class="listingcharacter">enp0s1</samp>. If the bridge is supposed to obtain its IP address via DHCP, the configuration of the <samp class="listingcharacter">br0</samp> interface becomes easier:

```
# file /etc/interfaces/network
# loopback network interface (unchanged)
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback
# interface to LAN (manual)
auto enp0s1
iface enp0s1 inet manual
# bridge to enp0s1
auto br0
iface br0 inet dhcp
       bridge_ports enp0s1 
```

### 32.4.2    IP Forwarding

Regardless of the distribution, you must enable IP forwarding if you have not already done so. To do this, you need to enter two lines at the end of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">/etc/sysctl.conf</samp> and then run <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">sysctl -p</samp>:

```
# at the end of /etc/sysctl.conf
...
# forwarding for IPv4 and IPv6
net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 
```

### 32.4.3    Network Configuration on a Root Server

The configuration of the network becomes a little more complicated if you want to make several guests publicly accessible on the internet on a root server. The task then is to correctly route all traffic for multiple IP addresses through the host to the guests. The specific procedure depends strongly on the technical conditions of the hosting provider.

### 32.4.4    Configuring the Virtual Machine

When setting up the virtual machine, you must specify the name of the bridge as the network source, not the Ethernet interface on which the bridge is based. Virtual machines can use network bridges only when they run at the system level. Here’s why: The network communication between the host computer and the KVM guest is handled by so-called TUN/TAP devices. These are network interfaces simulated by the kernel that are set up each time the virtual machine gets started. Fortunately, the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools take care of all the details, but can only do their job with <samp class="listingcharacter">root</samp> privileges.

### 32.4.5    MAC Trouble

The use of a network bridge has a serious disadvantage: it leaves the MAC addresses (usually 52:54:00:nn:nn:nn:nn) of the virtual machines contained in the IP packets unchanged. Hosting providers don’t like that at all: outgoing packets must have only known MAC addresses assigned to the leased servers. If you do not adhere to this rule, the root server may be locked.

But there are several ways out. One variant is to perform a routing setup instead of a network bridge. Alternatively, you can request MAC addresses from the provider and enter them into the network configuration of your virtual machines (the easiest way is to use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virsh edit</samp>). However, this only makes sense if you run only a few virtual machines. The last time I set up a larger KVM host, I came across a third way that can be done with minimal effort. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">ebtables</samp> command to overwrite all MAC addresses in forwarded packets with the MAC address of your root server's network adapter:

```
#!/bin/bash
# file /etc/rc.local on the host system
ebtables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -j snat --to-src aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff 
exit 0 
```

You can find background information on this in Dirk Hillbrecht's blog: [https://ipv6-first-guide.hillbrecht.de/#_ensure_correct_source_mac_address](https://ipv6-first-guide.hillbrecht.de/#_ensure_correct_source_mac_address).

## 32.5    Direct Access to the Contents of an Image File

This section is about how you can read or modify the contents of a virtual disk without starting the virtual machine itself. This is useful, for example, when you want to perform repairs from the outside or modify configuration files by means of a script.

There are different procedures for accessing the virtual disk:

*   You can read or modify the contents of the virtual disks directly in the host system.

*   You can make use of various <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libguestfs</samp> tools.

*   You can use a Linux live system to help you—that is, start the virtual machine from the ISO image of a Linux distribution and access the virtual hard disks from there.

In this section, I will only discuss the first and second variants. Some of the tools presented here can only edit RAW images. You may need to convert an image file that is in a different format to this format. The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-img</samp> command helps you with this:

```
user$ qemu-img convert -f qcow2 image.qcow2 -O raw image.raw 
```

The following command creates an equivalent RAW image from a logical volume or a hard disk partition:

```
root# dd if=/dev/mapper/vg1-lv2 of=copy.raw bs=64M
312+1 records in
312+1 records out
20971520000 Bytes (21 GB) copied, 133,462 s, 157 MB/s 
```

Write access to a virtual disk is allowed only when the virtual machine is completely shut down! Otherwise you risk a corrupt file system!

### 32.5.1    Access to Partitioned RAW Images in the Host System

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">kpartx</samp> command from the package of the same name to connect all partitions contained in a RAW file to loop devices:

```
root# kpartx -av image.raw
add map loop0p1 (252:12): 0 1024000 linear /dev/loop0 2048
add map loop0p2 (252:13): 0 19945472 linear /dev/loop0 1026048 
```

In my tests, this also worked if the image file contained a GUID partition table (i.e., not a traditional partition table in the master boot record). If they are normal partitions, you can then <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">mount</samp> them directly into the file system:

```
root# mkdir /repair1
root# mount /dev/mapper/loop0p1 /repair1 
```

If you have configured LVM within the virtual machine, the resulting physical and logical volumes and volume groups are directly available. Lists of LVM elements are provided by <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">lvscan</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pvscan</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vgscan</samp>. The access to the LVs requires that the LVM tools are installed on the host system:

```
root# lvscan
ACTIVE            '/dev/VolGroup/lv_root' [7.56 GiB] inherit
ACTIVE            '/dev/VolGroup/lv_swap' [1.94 GiB] inherit
...
root# mkdir /repair2
root# mount /dev/VolGroup/lv_root /repair2 
```

Now you can access the file systems of the virtual KVM hard disk via the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">repairN</samp> directories. When you're done with that, you need to clean up:

```
root# umount /repair1
root# umount /repair2
root# kpartx -dv image.raw 
```

### 32.5.2    libguestfs Tools

Instead of analyzing the image file yourself and integrating the relevant partitions into the local file system, you can leave these tasks to various tools that are based on the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libguestfs</samp> library.

The <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libguestfs</samp> library provides direct access to the file systems located within an image file. <samp class="listingcharacter">libguestfs</samp> supports all conceivable image formats and partitions, LVM, and all common file systems. The operation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">libguestfs</samp> tools is comprehensively documented on the following website and on the <samp class="listingcharacter">man</samp> page for <samp class="listingcharacter">libguestfs</samp>: [https://libguestfs.org](https://libguestfs.org).

Current Debian, Fedora, RHEL, and Ubuntu distributions provide all the necessary packages right out of the box:

```
root# apt/dnf install libguestfs-tools libguestfs-tools-c 
```

The package contains various commands for manipulating image files. You usually specify the image file to be processed or analyzed by using <samp class="listingcharacter">-a image-file</samp>. Alternatively, you can specify the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> name of the virtual machine via <samp class="listingcharacter">-d vmname</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-df</samp> provides a quick overview of the workload of all file systems of all virtual machines that are known to the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> tools. The command can also handle logical volumes inside virtual disks:

```
root# virt-df
Filesystem                         1K-blocks       Used  Available  Use%
alma-mini:/dev/sda1                   495844      52091     418153   11%
alma-mini:/dev/sdb1                 20157836     253468   18880396    2%

alma-mini:/dev/vg_almamini/lv_root
                                     9571132    1051104    8033836   11%
alma64-vm2:/dev/sdb                  4319464    4319464          0  100%
alma64-vm2:/dev/sda1                  495844      32918     437326    7%
alma64-vm2:/dev/vg_vm2/lv_root       7539088    2369932    4786180   32%
...
```

If you are only interested in the results of a single virtual machine, you must specify the image file name with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">libvirt</samp> name of the virtual machine with <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-filesystems</samp> shows which file systems are contained in an image file. With the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--all</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--long</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">--uuid</samp> options, the command also lists LVM and swap partitions and returns the UUID numbers of the file systems:

```
root# virt-filesystems -a vm2.img --all --long --uuid
Name                Type       VFS  Label Size        Parent  UUID
/dev/sda1           filesystem ext4 -     524288000   -       7a95...
/dev/vg_vm2/lv_root filesystem ext4 -     7843348480  -       e69f...
/dev/vg_vm2/lv_swap filesystem swap -     2113929216  -       e0f4...
... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-inspector</samp> takes a look into the file systems of an image file and determines which distribution is installed in it, which partitions there are, which kernel version and which packages are installed, and so on. <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-inspector</samp> knows both the RPM and Debian package systems. The command returns an almost endless XML document as output, which is actually intended for further machine processing:

```
root# virt-inspector disk.img | less
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<operatingsystems>
  <operatingsystem>
    <root>/dev/cl/root</root>
    <name>linux</name>
    <arch>x86_64</arch>
    <distro>alma</distro>
    <product_name>Alma Linux release 7 (Core) </product_name>
    ...
    <mountpoints>
      <mountpoint dev="/dev/cl/root">/</mountpoint>
      <mountpoint dev="/dev/sda1">/boot</mountpoint>
    </mountpoints>
    <filesystems>
      <filesystem dev="/dev/cl/root">
        <type>xfs</type>
        <uuid>271158c8-8134-4082-9b74-f2413259ae4b</uuid>
      </filesystem>
   ... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-cat</samp> outputs a virtual machine file. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp> to specify the name of an image or <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp> to specify the (domain) name of the virtual machine:

```
root# virt-cat -d alma-server /etc/fstab
/dev/mapper/cl-root                       /     xfs  defaults 0 0
UUID=0112eac4-e995-4dfc-b6ca-4a5fc3b10d7b /boot xfs  defaults 0 0
/dev/mapper/cl-swap                       swap  swap defaults 0 0
... 
```

To modify the file in an editor, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-edit</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-cat</samp>. This command may only be used for virtual machines that are switched off! <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-edit</samp> takes the <samp class="listingcharacter">EDITOR</samp> environment variable into account when selecting the editor. By default, the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">vi</samp> editor is executed:

```
root# virt-edit -d alma-server /etc/fstab 
```

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-tar-out</samp> to read a directory from the file system of an image file (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-a</samp>) or a virtual machine (<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-d</samp>) and write it to a TAR archive:

```
root# virt-tar-out -d alma-server /etc etc.tar 
```

If you also want to compress the archive, you must forward the output of <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-tar-out</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">gzip</samp> using a pipe:

```
root# virt-tar-out -d alma-server /etc - | gzip > etc.tgz 
```

Conversely, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-tar-in</samp> unpacks an archive in the image. The target directory must already exist. The virtual machine must be stopped beforehand:

```
root# virt-tar-in -d alma-server data.tar /home/user01 
```

For compressed archives, you should proceed as follows:

```
root# zcat data.tgz | virt-tar-in -d alma-server - /home/user01 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-make-fs</samp> creates a new image file and stores in it the contents of a directory or TAR archive, which may optionally be compressed:

```
root# virt-make-fs mydata.tar.gz new-disk.img 
```

By default, the command creates a RAW image without a partition table with an <samp class="listingcharacter">ext2</samp> file system. Options allow you to set a different image or file system format, MBR or GPT partitioning, control the size of the image file, and so on.

### 32.5.3    Converting an Image Format

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">qemu-img</samp> can convert disk images from one format to another. The following example creates a compressed QCOW2 image from a VDI file (VirtualBox). If you want to do without the time-consuming compression, you can simply omit the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">-c</samp> option:

```
user$ qemu-img convert -f vdi vm-disk001.vdi -O qcow2 -c vm.qcow2 
```

After the conversion, you must make sure that the new image file has the correct owner or access rights so that the <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">libvirt</samp> tools can access it.

### 32.5.4    Enlarging an Image

<samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-resize</samp> copies a disk image and at the same time resizes the partitions and file systems it contains. The target image must be created beforehand. If the partition to be modified is used as a physical volume for LVM, <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-resize</samp> enlarges the PV via <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">pvresize</samp>. You must run all other LVM commands yourself later in the running system. Prior to running <samp class="listingcharacter programmingelement">virt-resize</samp>, you must shut down the underlying virtual machine!
